*Yogavāsiṣṭha* of...
Vālmīki’s Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, together with the commentary titled Tātparya-prakāśa.
The Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa, edited by Vāsudeva Śarman, son of Paṇaśīkara Upāhva Lakṣmaṇa Śarman.
Edited by Vāsudeva Laxmaṇa Śarma Paṇśīkar. First Canto. 1.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, immediately following the section on "Stability," hear this section on "Quiescence," which, when understood, brings about liberation.

I take refuge in Śiva, who is full of the nature of great majesty renowned for the creation, preservation, and pacification of the world; who is the witness to the heart of the Vedas; who is beyond all conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca); and who is a solid mass of innate bliss and consciousness. 1.
The rising with the sound of the midday conch is prescribed here;
Vasiṣṭha’s daily routine is for the day, while Viśvāmitra’s is for staying together with the night. || 1 ||

In the section on origination (*utpatti-prakaraṇa*), it was demonstrated that the construction of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is dependent solely upon the mind, in order to reveal the intended meaning of all scriptural passages concerning creation. And in the section on subsistence (*sthiti-prakaraṇa*), it is likewise [demonstrated] that [the world] is dependent solely upon the subsistence of the mind, in order to show the intended meaning of the scriptural passages that establish the subsistence of the entire universe.

Thus has been shown the state of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Now, just as the rays of the sun setting in this orb of light become unified, so too at the time of deep sleep, when everything has dissolved;
and just as rivers, flowing along, go to their end in the ocean—that which they enter upon departing.

"Having abandoned name-and-form, the fifteen constituents (kalās) return to their foundation"— in this very way, for this witness, these sixteen constituents, which have the Puruṣa as their goal, reach the Puruṣa and dissolve—
such [passages] refer to deep sleep, cosmic dissolution, meditative absorption (samādhi), direct realization, and disembodied liberation.

By demonstrating that through the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the individual soul attains its true nature as Brahman, it is shown that even those scriptural passages which characterize the non-dual reality of the one essence of the inner self and Brahman have as their purport the establishment of one's own true nature through the cessation of all conceptual proliferation, which occurs precisely through the cessation of the mind.

Commencing the Chapter on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) for the purpose of unveiling the secret, [the author], demonstrating the connection between the preceding and subsequent chapters, indicating the subject matter and the purpose, and directing the student’s attention,
makes this formal declaration with the word "Now" (*atha*). Now:

The meaning is that, immediately after describing the purport of the scriptural texts that establish [the Self's] persistence, there is a "contextual connection" (*avasara-saṃgati*) for describing the purport of the scriptural texts that indicate the conclusion. "Known [to be the Self], it brings about liberation"— thus,

since the purpose of this [chapter] is the same as that of the preceding section, one should understand that the "contextual connection" of performing a single function (*ekakāryakāritā-saṃgati*) has also been shown.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
While the autumn sky was filled with stars,
and the assembly remained tranquil as Vasiṣṭha thus spoke these delightful and purifying words.

The narrative sequence beginning with "In autumn, star-spangled... is intended to illuminate the necessity of conduct appropriate to the occasion. Just as the sky becomes star-spangled—having acquired stars—in autumn, so too, amidst all those things ending in the locative case, the sound of conchs arose at midday, as stated in the fourteenth verse.
The connection. || 2 ||
In the midst of that assembly, while the king remained silent in his desire to hear,
it was like a lotus pond where the lotuses are motionless in a windless place.
Where the kings, desiring to hear [his speech], remained silent within the assembly, in the midst of the council.
And among the wanton women, whose intoxication, delusion, and strength had been completely stilled,
they attained an inner tranquility as if they were long-ordained renunciants.
As if from hearing [the sound], the swans in the lotus-hands had dissolved away; as if on a tree, the crows had ceased their harsh cawing. || 5 ||

An *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is suggested by the observation of their motionlessness: as the fly-whisks, resembling swans upon the lotus-hands of the graceful women, were near them, they seemed to have become absorbed in meditation because they had heard the meaning [of the teaching], having ceased their movement.

[This occurs] when the sounds of the bracelets and small bells have been released—that is, when the tinkling of the *kaṅkaṇa* and *kiṅkiṇī* ornaments has been abandoned—and when there are only the birds, namely the crows.
The word "tarau" (two trees) is a simile for the assembly hall.
While those kings, who were knowers of that reality, were contemplating the subtle portion of consciousness with the tips of their index fingers resting upon the tips of their noses.
Among those who know that and who understand investigation. || 6 ||
When Rāma had blossomed forth like a lotus at dawn,
he was like the rising sun in a sky where the seat of darkness has been abandoned.

Because of its density upon the earth, darkness is figuratively imagined as a seat for the sky above; the meaning is that when the sun rises, the seat of darkness is abandoned, just as a disciple rising at the arrival of his teacher leaves behind his seat. || 7 ||
Daśaratha listened with rapture to the words of Vasiṣṭha’s daughter,
just as a peahen listens to the rumbling of clouds that have released their rain.
"From rasa" means from a state moistened by love. Its comparison is "from the shedding of rain";
that is to say, from the state of being moistened caused by the shedding of rain. || 8 ||

Having withdrawn the mind, which is as restless as a monkey, from all enjoyments, one should with effort apply it toward listening; for when the ministering faculty is established in the essence, [the goal is attained].
Having been brought with effort and turned back, it remains [there]. || 9 ||

While Lakṣmaṇa— whose own self had been fully realized through the words of Vasiṣṭha, who was as stainless as a digit of the moon, whose aim shone with clarity, and who was expert in the power of his training— [was present], || 10 ||
To him whose heart thus shines with the discernment of the power of training, in whom Brahman—the clearly manifest object—throbs; || 10 ||
When Śatrughna, the crusher of enemies, had attained fullness of heart,
he remained like the full moon of the Rākā night, having reached the height of bliss.
Enough! Full bliss has arrived; it has been attained. || 11 ||
When Sumitrā’s mind, though accustomed to sorrow, attained a state of friendliness,
her heart blossomed like a lotus at that very moment.
When Sumitra— the distinguished minister— had attained a state of friendship and submissiveness in his mind,

which was habituated to sorrow yet had become expansive in heart; and in the case of the lotus, when the beautiful friend, the sun, had attained the state of friendship by rising and bringing joy to the Mānasa lake (or the mind) at dawn, which had been accustomed to grief— that being the time.
When the heart has become blossomed. || 12 ||
At that time, while those other sages and kings present there had their jewels of minds thoroughly cleansed, they seemed to shine forth with their very hearts.
The phrase "as if they have arisen" (prollasatsu iva jāteṣu) is to be supplied everywhere throughout the passage by means of appropriate modification. || 13 ||
Then there arose the sound of midday conchs, equal to the roar of the ocean and as deep as the thundering of clouds at the end of an aeon, filling all the quarters of space.
The quarters are the directions; he is as powerful and robust as the roar of the clouds at the end of an aeon. 14.
By that great sound, the words of the sage were eclipsed,
just as the calls of the cuckoo are drowned out by the roar of a thundercloud.
Of the sage Vasiṣṭha. || 15 ||
Then, in that assembly, the sage silenced his own speech:
"By what great quality can one whose essence has been conquered be further extolled? (16)

"Antarayām cakre," "tirodadhe," and "upasaṃjahāra" mean that he concealed [it]. By what great person of supernormal knowledge (*abhijña*) is such a quality—one whose essence (*sāra*) has been conquered and overwhelmed, and which is a source of joy for people—proclaimed and manifested? || 16 ||
Having waited for a mere moment after hearing the sound of midday,
when the dense clamor had subsided, the sage spoke to Rāma.
O crusher of enemies, I have thus described to you this day’s ritual duties starting from Rāma; tomorrow morning we shall speak of the other matters that remain to be told.
That which is accomplished in a day is "daily" (āhnika). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "we shall explain. || 18 ||
This which has arrived according to destiny must be performed by the twice-born;
that which ought to be done when midday has arrived must not be neglected. (19)

The syntactical connection is as follows: "That which is appropriate at midday—whatever is fitting for the twice-born, obtained through destiny, and the duty that must be performed so that it does not fail—that very thing must be performed by me as well. (19)
You too, O fortunate one, arise and perform all the proper rites and services,
such as bathing, giving gifts, and worship, for which you are so skilled in conduct.
Having spoken thus, the sage rose up together with the lord Daśaratha,
like the sun with the moon rising from the slope of the mountain of sunrise.
Together with his sons, accompanied by the assembly and all the people, Daśaratha also rose up along with the Sage.
As the two of them rose, the entire assembly trembled to rise as well,
like a lotus pond with eyes of blue lilies brushed by a gentle breeze.
"Alilocanā" is also an epithet for the assembly hall. || 22 ||
She rose up, adorned by a circle of bees emerging from her ear-ornaments,
like a herd of female elephants with trunks moving restlessly in the rutting season.

With the intention that at this time of midday, it is the hour of sunrise on the western mountain (astācala) and thus a suitable time for the elephants to rise, he says "on the twilight-mountain" (saṃdhyādri). In the reading "on the Vindhya-mountain" (vindhyādri), there is a comparison of the location. || 23 ||
The circles of armlets on their arms were crushed by the mutual impact of their limbs,
signaling a twilight hour filled with jewels like a sea of crimson clouds.
Since it is filled with jewels, by virtue of this similarity, it indicates—meaning, serves as a reminder of—the time of twilight with its crimson clouds. 24.
The humming of bees wandering about her falling ear-ornaments filled the air,
while the sky was turned into a rainbow by the intense radiance of her crown.

She was one by whom the sky or the mass of garments was turned into a rainbow by the intense flashes of light from various jewels in her crowns, which produced a humming sound through the bees wandering about the falling ornaments. 25.
With her lovely creeper-like hands as graceful fly-whisks and flower-clusters,
she was like a forest grove agitated by a herd of noble elephants.

The meaning is that it was like a forest row wherein the creepers, characterized by beautiful locks of hair, possessed clusters of blossoms—characterized by lovely chowries—upon their leaves and sprouts, which were characterized by hands. || 26 ||
With their respective garments reddened by the weight of shimmering golden bracelets,
they were like a garland from the Mandara forest, its flowers shaken by the wind.
In which [city] the garments, drawn out and spread wide by their mutual attraction, were reddened by the shimmering luster of their bracelets. || 27 ||
With pure clouds formed from camphor-like frost,
she spread across the entire earth like a garland of autumnal horizons.
By means of camphor particles, frost, and snowflakes similar to them that were floating upward,
she formed pure and white clouds; therefore,
with the entire ground covered by frost, kāśa flowers, and the like, she stood like a garland adorning the slopes of the autumnal quarters.
With the cavities of the sky reddened at its edges by the gems on the tips of her swaying crowns,
she is like the twilight when blue lotuses have not yet blossomed— she who brings about the dissolution of all that must be done.
She brings to a conclusion all tasks and daily duties. || 29 ||

Filled with a flood of water from the rays of jewels, she was like a lotus pond with its lotuses in constant bloom; she was encircled by swarms of bees and possessed the melodious resonance of anklets.
That assembly, crowded with hundreds of kings, rose up in continuous succession,
like a new creation emerging, agitated by a multitude of beings.
By hundreds of kings, who are both rulers of the earth and mountains. || 31 ||
Then, having bowed to the king, the monarchs departed from the royal palace like waves of the ocean made into rainbows by jewels.
Then Sumantra, the ministers, and Vasiṣṭha, bowing down to the lord of the earth, departed for their bath, they who were experts in discerning flavors.
They were experts in flavors, the essence of Brahman, water, and the knowledge of sporting. || 33 ||
Vāmadeva and others, as well as Viśvāmitra and others,
stood with Vasiṣṭha at their head, looking up toward the sky.
Winning over [the assembly] means obtaining their permission; they are oriented toward that and await it. || 34 ||
King Daśaratha, the subduer of enemies, having honored the assembly of sages there and being dismissed by them, then departed for the sake of his own purpose.
Those who dwell in the forest went to the forest, those who dwell in the sky went to the sky,
and the city-dwellers likewise departed for their morning arrival at the city.
Those whose dwelling is the forest are the forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas). || 36 ||
Requested out of affection by both the lord of the earth and Vasiṣṭha,
the powerful Viśvāmitra spent the night in the residence of Vasiṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha was being attended by the foremost of brahmins, as well as by kings and sages,
and by all the sons of Daśaratha, beginning with Rāma.
The illustrious one, honored by all the worlds, went to his own hermitage,
followed by a multitude of gods, like the Lotus-born Brahmā proceeding to the world of Brahmā.
From that place, he then dismissed all the sons of Daśaratha— Rāma and the others— who were bowing at his feet, sending them back to their homes.
From that hermitage region. || 40 ||

Having dismissed those who move through the sky, those who move upon the earth, and those who move below— each according to their rank and within the scope of his well-praised virtues— the one of noble being [returned] to his own home.
He performed that daily rite of the twice-born. || 41 ||

Having dismissed, in due order, the nāgas who move below—meaning those who are the objects and supports of well-praised and extolled virtues—the remainder of the sentence is that he entered his own home; the meaning is that he performed the fivefold sacrificial rites (pañcayajña) appropriate for the day among the twice-born. || 41 ||

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Daily Routine," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki and spoken by the Divine Messenger. 1.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Daily Routine," in the *Upaśamaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Second Canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having come together and gone home, those princes, radiant as the moon, [sat down].
They performed the entire course of the day in their respective dwellings without exception.

In this [chapter], the performance of daily rites at night, Rāma’s reflection upon what he has heard, and the prayer for the stability of his intellect regarding the meaning of what was heard are described. (1)
The daily sequence of the day. || 1 ||
Vasiṣṭha, Rāghava, the kings, the sages,
and the twice-born performed their respective duties in this manner within the courtyards of their own homes.
In this manner, as will be described, they performed [the rites] in their own homes, in the streets, and likewise outside—meaning those things which were appropriate. || 2 ||
They bathed in reservoirs that captivated with lotuses, white lilies, night-blooming water-lilies, and blue lotuses, and which were lined with rows of ruddy geese, swans, and cranes.
They gave cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, beds,
seats, vessels, and fine garments as gifts to the Brahmins.
In their own palaces, variegated with gold and jewels,
they worshipped the gods beginning with Viṣṇu, Śiva, Agni, and the Sun.
In the abodes of the immortals, that is, in the temples of the gods, and in their own respective homes. || 5 ||
Together with their sons, grandsons, friends, servants, kinsmen, and circles of companions,
they then indeed partook of their appropriate meals.
At that time, it was day in this city;
however, because only one-eighth of it remained, it appeared feeble and was not beautiful.
The day became thin and subtle, because only one-eighth remained—that is, because only the eighth part was left of its eight constituent parts. || 7 ||
They spent the remainder of the day until evening with activities appropriate for that time,
along with the rays of light, until the sun went to its setting.
By means of actions appropriate to that time, such as the study of the ancient Dharmaśāstras and so forth. || 8 ||
They performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) well, recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn,
chanted meritorious hymns of praise, and sang captivating verses.
Then the dark-complexioned night arose, removing the sorrow of longing women,
like the daughter of Indra rising from the Ocean of Milk, bestowing the dew of the moon.

The word "tataḥ" (then) refers to the time following that [moment]; the points of comparison are, respectively: the Ocean of Milk for the beloved woman; the eastern quarter (Indrī-dik) for the joy of removing the sorrow caused by separation from her lover; and the dew for the alleviation of heat caused by contact with the moon. || 10 ||
The descendants of Raghu rested upon couches that were lovely with the long reflection of the moon, where flowers had been gently strewn and handfuls of camphor scattered.
Like the orb of the moon elongated among beautiful things. || 11 ||
Then, in the absence of Rāma,
that beautiful night passed slowly for those engaged in its activities there, like a single auspicious muhūrta.
Engaged in that [state], she is occupied with activities such as the enjoyment of objects appropriate to that time and sleep. || 12 ||
Rāma remained there, reflecting upon those very words of Vasiṣṭha— sweet and noble— just as a young elephant dwells upon the memory of its mother.
Just as a young elephant calf [seeks] its mother, the female elephant. || 13 ||
What indeed is this wandering in saṃsāra? Who are these people? What are these diverse beings? Why do they come and why do they go? (14)
He elaborates on the very manner of his reflection with the words beginning "What... (kimiti), etc. (verse 14).
What is the nature of the mind, and how is it pacified?
From what does this illusion arise, and how indeed is it brought to an end? (15)
What benefit or what fault could there be from this cessation?
And how has this contraction come upon the Self, which is all-pervading? (16)
If there were a cessation of all objects of enjoyment, enjoyers, and the act of enjoying, it would result in the fault of obstructing the purpose of the Puruṣa;
[this would apply] even to that which is more vast than space itself. || 16 ||
What could have been said by the Blessed One, the Sage, regarding the destruction of the mind? What was proclaimed concerning the conquest of the senses, or what was said about the self? (17)
What would be stated as the means and the fruit? The words "when the Self is known" are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 17 ||

Through these pervasive forms—such as the individual soul (jīva), the intellect (citta), the mind (manas), and illusion (māyā)—the Self alone extends this unreal cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra). 18.

When these [afflictions], which are bound like threads consisting of nothing but mind, have thus come to an end, there is the pacification of suffering; how then are they not easily curable for us? (19)
The cessation of suffering is accomplished; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. These [states] are forms of the mind such as illusion and so forth. || 19 ||
How can I separate this female crane of the intellect from the encircling cloud-mass of enjoyments, just as a swan separates a stream of water from the water itself? (20)

Objects of sense (*viṣaya*) are called "enjoyments" (*bhoga*) because they are enjoyed; these very objects, having become solidified through the nature of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), are "clouds" because they obscure the sky of the mind (*cittākāśa*) and because they rain down thousands of streams of suffering.

Following after these clouds, that which encircles and envelops like a garland is the female crane (*balākā*) characterized by the fluctuations of the intellect (*dhīvṛtti*), known as the "garland-enveloper" (*mālāvalayā*).
"How shall I separate it? means "How shall I turn it away through discernment? [The phrase] "the stream of milk" means a portion of the milk. || 20 ||
We are unable to renounce enjoyments; without their abandonment, we have no power over calamities. Alas, a great crisis has arrived! (21)

Now, one might ask: "What is the use of deliberation? Let enjoyments be abandoned. To this he replies: "Enjoyments... (the verse). The words "in the remedying of calamities" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. The meaning is that since life cannot be sustained if enjoyments are renounced in every respect, yet if even a small amount of enjoyment is accepted for that purpose, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) increase; thus, a state of crisis has arrived. || 21 ||
This object of attainment is mind-only, and that alone is the purpose;
yet, due to our ignorance, we have grasped what is as heavy as a mountain, like a child perceiving a yakṣa.
He states another difficulty as well: "manomātram" (consisting of mind alone).

This reality of the Self, which is the goal to be attained and which must necessarily be realized, has for its *mātrā*—that by which it is measured or cognized—the mind as its means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And that mind, for us, is nothing other than this external [mind].
That by which the entire range of objects is engaged— that purpose (prayojana) which serves as the cause for accomplishment and constitutes the human goal—

becomes, due to one's folly, heavier than even a mountain and difficult to extricate. Just as a yakṣa is imagined by a child out of folly, so too is the mind, whose success depends upon objects, [bound] to them.

The meaning is that it is impossible to turn back [the cognition] because it would result in the loss of its own nature; however, if it is not turned back, one cannot produce the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) for the direct realization of reality—this constitutes another dilemma. || 22 ||
Having attained supreme peace and being freed from the agitation of saṃsāra, my mind shall find no further object of attainment, like a young woman who has found her beloved. (23)

But if, even upon the cessation of all objects, the mind could be established by relying solely on the form of Brahman free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then the desired goal would be attained; reflecting thus, he says:
"The supreme... Just as a young woman who has obtained her beloved husband.
Having attained the form of Brahman, she will not obtain anything else; the meaning is that she will not remember [anything else]. || 23 ||
May my mind become purified— its agitation stilled, all curiosity vanished, free from evil, and resting in the Self (or, according to another reading, resting in the state beyond evil). 24.
He longs to reach that state, saying "When? and so forth. *Saṃrambha* is anger;
*kautuka* is desire. The mention of "evil" (*pāpa*) is an elliptical expression intended to include meritorious deeds as well as those resulting from both merit and demerit.
[May it be] cooler even than the moon, which is complete with its full array of digits.
When, having come to rest firmly established upon this state, shall I wander through the world? (25)
Having rested in such a way that it becomes firmly established up to the seventh stage—that is to say, having attained the bliss of liberation while living (jīvanmukti)—[he proceeds]. || 25 ||
When will the mind, casting off its form that is as delicate as a fiber and dissolving within itself, attain peace, like a wave in water? (26)
Being dissolved and hidden within the self. || 26 ||
When, having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra—turbulent with the waves of craving and garlanded with the sea-monsters of hope—shall I become free from the fever of suffering? (27)
In paths purified by the cessation of all faults, we who are wise and possess equanimity shall dwell without sorrow, seeking liberation for those desiring release.
In these paths and stages to be attained by those seeking liberation. || 28 ||
When will this long-lasting fever of worldly existence—by which all limbs are tormented and which strikes fear into all elements—come to an end? (29)

It is terrifying because of those things that are wasting away: the limbs, such as wife, children, cattle, and so forth; the hands, feet, and so on; the elements, such as gold, silver, and so forth; and the tissues, such as skin, blood, flesh, and so forth. (29)
O Buddha, when will the mind, like the trace of a lamp in a windless place, become free from affliction and attain peace within the dense interior of the brilliant light? (30)
When will these senses, whose bodies are scorched by evil desires, easily cross over their sufferings, as Garuḍas cross over the oceans? (31)

The meaning is: when will the senses—by which the body has been consumed by wicked efforts and evil deeds consisting of the drawing toward and attraction of sense-objects—cross over the sorrows resulting from the trivial pursuit of those objects?
Alternatively, the senses are the agents; "wicked efforts" refers to the desire for evil objects, and [the deeds] are those prompted by that desire.

The construction is as follows: "When will these burnt bodies—destined for destruction, consisting of karma—cross over from sufferings [to the state of] sufferingless-ness by means of the ease of sense objects? Regarding the phrase "from sufferings" (*duḥkhebhyaḥ*), it is derived from the verbal root *duḥkha* belonging to the *curādigaṇa*, with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) and the suffix *tumun* (the infinitive marker) expressing purpose.
The fourth case ending is used because it expresses a state or condition. 31.
"This is that same 'I,' yet I am weeping and deluded"—this is a vainly conceived delusion.
Like a dark cloud in autumn, when will this [delusion] go to its destruction? (32)

While I, a fool, weep due to the non-attainment or separation from cattle, children, wealth, food, drink, and so forth, this very body— which is the cause of my weeping— is that well-known "Self" and "I"; thus, this delusion,
produced by a succession of desires and karmas rooted in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of preceding bodies, is rendered futile upon the clarity of awakening, as in the autumn season.
The meaning is: when it has begun, like a dark cloud in the rainy season, when will it go to its destruction? || 32 ||
That mind which [once found delight] in rows of Mandāra forest groves now regards them as mere straw;
when shall we attain that state of yours which we now implore? (33)
He says that even heaven appears like a blade of grass to him due to his intense desire for liberation—this is expressed in the verse beginning with "mandāra...

"Mati" refers to the experience of pleasure. "I beg" means "I desire. The word "vayam" (we) is used in the plural according to the rule "asmado dvayośca" (the word *asmad* may take the plural when referring to two). || 33 ||
Tell me this: will the stainless insights of knowledge proclaimed by those free from passion ever find their place within you? (34)

Now, he entreats the mind and the other senses for the sake of attaining discrimination, beginning with the words "O you who are free from passion" (vītarāga): "O mind, they will establish some station or place within you. (34)
O mind, may I never again be the recipient of these cries, "Alas, father! Alas, mother! O son!", nor become the food for those who consume suffering. (35)

The syntactical connection is as follows: "May I not become the food—the prey—of the pythons characterized by suffering, who are like serpents, nor again the vessel for their cries of lamentation. (35)
O sister, fulfill my request regarding the Buddha immediately;
for the sake of liberating us both from suffering, reflect upon the words of the Sage.
The address "sister" is used because the individual soul (*jīva*) and the intellect (*buddhi*) have arisen from the same womb of ignorance; [this refers to] the sage Vasiṣṭha.
Falling at your feet with affection, O virtuous one, I entreat you, for whom a son is desired:
therefore, O auspicious lady, remain steadfast for the sake of the destruction of worldly existence.

O virtuous one! O daughter, because you were born later through the grace of the scriptures and the virtuous; O you of noble resolve! By this my request, [may there be] the attainment of perfection characterized by the cessation of worldly existence. (37)
First, the words concerning dispassion were spoken by the sage Vasiṣṭha;
then followed the conduct of one seeking liberation, and after that, the sequence of the origins [of the castes]. (38)
Having thus stabilized the mind through prayer,
he gradually directs it toward the recollection of the meaning of the four sections beginning with the Section on Detachment—
starting with the words "O Vasiṣṭha": those [teachings] spoken through my mouth, those proclaimed by myself, and those ending with the Section on Stability.
Speeches || 38 ||
Therefore, O intellect, remember properly this chapter on stability, which is beautiful with its illustrations, easily accessible through the core of higher knowledge, and exactly as it is. 39.

It is easy to access and simple because its core is consciousness; that is, it is easily accessible and easy to understand through narratives whose subjects are those whose essence is consciousness. || 39 ||
Whatever has been done with a prepared mind and investigated hundreds of times, if the intellect of the mind does not attain it,
that becomes fruitless like an autumn cloud.
Therefore, intelligence alone is the essential core of action at all times. || 40 ||

Now, one might object: since the mind was requested previously, and since the ascertainment of the meaning of the four sections can be accomplished through that very [mind] alone, for what purpose is the intellect (*mati*) requested again separately from it? To this, he says: "kṛtamati..."—that is, whatever object has been [considered] hundreds of times by the mind (*mānasa*) in such a way as to be thoroughly refined (*kṛtamati*).

The meaning is this: even if something has been investigated, if the intellect—meaning the mind characterized by determination (*adhyavasāya*)—does not attain it or accept it, then that investigation, though performed, is fruitless; like autumn clouds, it simply vanishes and does not become stable. Therefore, even when the Truth has been investigated through hearing (*śravaṇa*), the mind must constantly be applied to it through the intellect formed by reflection (*manana*).
The meaning is that since the essence (sāra) is the primary thing regarding the matter to be accomplished, it is indeed appropriate to pray for it separately for the sake of reflection. || 40 ||

Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Description of Instruction," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Chapter on Tranquility) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki;
and thus concludes the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The second canto, titled "The Description of the Instruction."
The Third Canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
As he remained there with such expansive and noble thoughts, his mind was thus occupied.
That night passed away like a lotus longing for the sun.
Herein is related the departure for the assembly hall of Vasiṣṭha by Uṣas, Snāta, Gṛhāyāta, Rāma, and others, as well as their introductory conversation.
Of this Rāma; by such a thought—that is, of the kind already described—expanded and extensive. || 1 ||
When the stars in the sky had become sparse, and the quarters of the horizon— reddened by a slight darkness yet tinged with a faint dawn— seemed as if they had been swept clean.
Upon those tawny, brownish-hued [creatures] made dark by the shadows. || 2 ||
Simultaneously with the sound of the morning trumpets,
the illustrious Rāghava, whose face is like the moon, arose like a lotus from a lotus-hand.
Having performed the ritual for the morning bath and having been joined again by his brothers,
he went to the residence of Vasiṣṭha accompanied by a small retinue sent along with him.
"Having completed," meaning having performed the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and so forth—this is understood from the context. "Sent by his brothers" means dispatched by them;
he whose retinue or attendants were few. Or, it may mean that he was sent together with his brothers, and thus he whose most trusted retinue was small. || 4 ||
From a distance, Rāma, with his neck bowed, approached that sage who was established in concentration in a solitary place, devoted solely to the Self.
Regarding the phrase "established in samādhi": it is understood that he should first bathe, perform his morning duties, and then become established in samādhi. || 5 ||
Having prostrated before him, they stood in the courtyard full of humility,
until the darkness was completely dispelled and the circle of the quarters became clearly visible.
Rāma and the others remained there until the darkness was completely cut away and severed.
Then kings, princes, sages, and brahmins arrived at the silent hermitage, like immortals reaching the world of Brahmā.
"Maunam" means silence; [it refers to] acting in such a way that there is no sound. || 7 ||
That residence of Vasiṣṭha became crowded with people,
thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, and graced by the conduct of kings.
Though its conduct was worthy of a king, it shone beautifully like the very abode of a monarch. || 8 ||
In an instant, the venerable Vasiṣṭha emerged from his meditative absorption;
with proper conduct and hospitality, he received the people who bowed before him.
By means of conduct such as discipline and by means of services such as pleasant speech. || 9 ||
Thus followed by the sages and accompanied by Viśvāmitra, the illustrious sage suddenly ascended the chariot, just as the Lotus-born Brahmā mounts his lotus.
Surrounded by a great army, he went to the home of Daśaratha, just as Brahmā, adorned by all the gods, goes to the city of Śakra. || 11 ||
There he entered the beautiful assembly hall of the son of Daśaratha, bowing low,
like a royal swan surrounded by a flock of swans entering a lotus pond.
To those who are bowed down and prostrate. || 12 ||
Then, rising from his throne, the great hero King Daśaratha quickly went forth three steps.
He went out; he approached. || 13 ||
There, all those kings headed by Daśaratha entered,
as did the sages headed by Vasiṣṭha, along with the ṛṣis and the brahmins.
And there were ministers such as Sumantra and others, wise men such as Saumya and others, princes such as Rāma and others, and the sons of ministers such as Śubha and others. || 15 ||
The subjects, beginning with the ministers; the citizens, beginning with Suhotra; likewise the servants, beginning with Mālava; and the garland-wearers, beginning with the townsmen. || 16 ||
Then, when they had each sat down upon their respective seats,
and when everyone was seated with their gaze fixed upward toward Vasiṣṭha, [the conversation began].

The meaning is: when those [persons] beginning with the sage, the king, and the minister had first sat down, and afterwards all the others had also sat down. The connection of the words beginning with "sarveṣveva" (when all were indeed... extends until the end of the canto, relating to all the locative forms up to this point in the subsequent canto where it says, "Daśaratha spoke these words."
When the clamor of the assembly had subsided, when the bards were established in silence, and when the reports on current affairs had concluded, that interior of the assembly became tranquil.

While there was a clamor and a great uproar in the assembly, and while the customary inquiries—consisting of mutual questions and answers regarding the state of one's well-being and the comfort of the night's rest—had taken place; || 18 ||
As the flickering garlands of pollen entered from the hollows of the lotuses,
it appeared as if shimmering strings of pearls were wavering amidst the swaying dust.

"Having emerged from the interior of the lotuses, [they] entered the assembly"—this is the ellipsis. For this very reason, they were moving restlessly among the lotus-pollen, which was like strings of pearls, and among those who were fickle and greedy. || 19 ||
The sweet breeze blows, carrying along a thick fragrance emitted from all sides by the large flower-swinging cradles.
While the matrons sat upon couches by the soft windows, their floors strewn with flowers, they gazed [at him]. || 21 ||
On soft couches. || 21 ||
While those flickering women— whose eyes trembled at the rays of the sun entering through the lattice and who were soft and tawny with the mass of light from their jewels—
had abandoned even a trace of their restlessness;
[She was] surrounded by women standing nearby who were holding white chowries. || 22 ||
Their eyes were tremulous because they were struck by the gaze of the sun’s rays passing through the lattice;

meanwhile, those previously mentioned women— holding white chowries, their delicate and tender hands turned tawny by the mass of light from the jewels— remained in silence, having completely abandoned even a trace of restlessness.
Upon the courtyards of his own palace, which possess the redness of sunbeams reflected in pearl ornaments, he does not perceive the heaps of flowers,
mistaking them for the reflection of the fresh morning sunlight.
When one is deluded, the swarm of bees wanders like a cloud in the sky. || 23 ||
Upon the courtyards paved with various jewels, there were reflections and images of pearls; within those [courtyards],

which were variegated with the shapes of various flowers and colored by the rays of the sun, the swarms of bees, through a deluded perception, thought, "These are indeed fresh reflections of the sunlight," having arisen [there].

Not finding—that is, failing to obtain—a mass of flowers (puṣpakaugha), a collection of scattered blossoms, he, because of that very lack of contact with the ground, wanders in the sky like a cloud. || 23 ||
That which was heard through merit, issuing from the mouth of Vasiṣṭha, has caused wonder to spread through the lineage of the noble world;
it is a discourse charming with soft words and syllables upon meeting the virtuous.
Each desired the other, who was delightful with no small measure of virtues.
In that assembly of the virtuous, in that gathering of the good, among the noble people highly esteemed by all,

he experienced a spreading wonder within his heart— an arising of astonishment— through the continuity of those words previously accumulated by merit and issued from the mouth of Vasiṣṭha, as they spread forth in full detail.

The ellipsis to be supplied is: "while they were speaking to one another words that were mutually desired, agreeable, delightful due to their many virtues, and charming with soft syllables and phrases. (24)
From the quarters, from the city, from the sky, and from the forest, the hosts of Siddhas,
Vidyādharas, noble Munis, and Brahmins entered silently around Vasiṣṭha, who was absorbed in profound silence.
In a conversation with one who possesses dignity, one should speak softly. || 25 ||

The phrase "having returned from the forest" is to be understood as the ellipsis. When [the king] had entered silently—that is, with his mouth covered—into the assembly of Vidyādharas, noble sages, and other brahmins, bowing with a silent salutation toward Vasiṣṭha; then, together with that most venerable and weighty elder, who was one with whom he must necessarily converse.

When a whisper—spoken in an extremely low voice near the ear—has occurred, [the phrase] "toward Vasiṣṭha" (*vasiṣṭhamabhitaḥ*) is used; here, by the rule "abhitaḥ, paritaḥ, samayā, nikaṣā, hā, and prati govern the accusative even when not in a reciprocal relation," the second case ending is employed in the sense of the sixth case (genitive). || 25 ||

When the wind blew, making it slightly reddish-brown with the golden pollen of the honey from the swarms of bees submerged within the soft, unblown buds of the red lotuses, and with the tinkling of dangling bells—
In the song that has brought peace, which is free from the songs of the Ṭāka-demons. || 26 ||

By the winds, [the quarters] were rendered slightly tawny— possessing a light brownish hue— by the dyes of the nectar and the golden pollen of swarms of bees that had been previously submerged within them, and which were now drawn out from the tender calyxes of the sleepless red lotuses (*kokanada*).

While such a breeze was blowing— one by which the songs of the houses were swallowed up and overwhelmed by the "ṭāṃkāra" melodies of the bells at the edges of the dwellings, which were set in motion by their own touch— the tips of the tongues of those bells [were active].
In the southern regions and in Nepal, it is well known that even a gentle breeze causes the rows of bells on the roofs of houses to ring by striking them in the shape of *pippala* leaves. || 26 ||
When the smoke of aloe and tagara, mingled with the fragrance of sandalwood,
wafts through the clouds marked by the intense scent of fresh flower garlands,
and when the breeze carries even a trace of the perfume from the lotuses of the canopy—
[He saw] a pond marked with the pollen of scattered flowers, where bees were known by their humming sounds. || 27 ||
In such a place, where the lap was marked by the drifting pollen of flowers mixed with the fragrance of sandalwood;
and likewise, where the clouds were made fragrant and marked by the intense scents of fresh flower-garlands;
and where, because their own color was obscured by the darkness of the smoke from the resin of aloe-wood and tagara, they appeared as if merely by sound alone.

The meaning is: it blows upward—that is, it flows upwards—in such a way that the bees are perceived but not directly seen, while carrying with them a mere trace of the fragrance of the lotuses whose petals are spread out like a canopy. || 27 ||
Thus ends the third canto, titled "Description of the Assembly Hall," in the section on Tranquility within the Means of Liberation of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, the work of the Sage. 3.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "Description of the Assembly Hall," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Fourth Canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
With a voice as deep as a thundercloud, beautiful with confident cadences—
Daśaratha spoke these words to the leader of the sages. || 1 ||
The praise of Vasiṣṭha’s words by the king, and the restatement by Rāma of the matters contemplated from the sage’s speech, are described. || 1 ||
It is beautiful with words that are confident and expressive of an exceeding degree of trust. || 1 ||
O Blessed One, I hope you have been freed from the exhaustion born of yesterday’s long discourse, which was even more emaciating than your ascetic penances.
By the exhaustion and fatigue born from the utterance of the sequence of words [spoken] yesterday or the day before.
We have been comforted by that very collection of words spoken yesterday, which was full of joy and solitary,
as if by a rain of nectar.
Joyful, he is by nature a delight to the ears; secluded, he is pure. || 3 ||
Like rays of the moon, these pure words of the great ones dispel darkness and, being stainless as nectar, cool the inner self.
The darknesses are ignorance and the obscurations. || 4 ||
For the well-spoken words of the great indeed bestow unprecedented joy, lead to the highest state, and utterly dispel delusion. (5)

Now he speaks of its superiority even to the rays of the moon—beginning with the word *apūrva*: "Unprecedented" (*apūrva*) means never tasted before and devoid of [ordinary] causes; "bliss" (*ānanda*) is the bliss of Brahman, which is the ultimate goal (*prayojana*).
That very bliss is the "higher station" (*uccaistaraṃ padam*), surpassing all objects of sensory pleasure from human bliss up to the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha.

They have that [Brahman] as their locus and that [Brahman] as their object. By the phrase "removing excessive delusion," another purpose of these [Upanishads], consisting in the cessation of what is harmful, has been stated. || 5 ||

He from whom arises the creeper of the discourse on the restraints (yamas) and other virtues— a single lamp illuminating the jewel of the self and possessing a delightful essence— that tree of virtuous people is worthy of veneration.
From which the creeper of light characterized by reasoning arises, and depending upon which it arises.
The well-spoken words of the virtuous wipe away every ill-deed and ill-executed act,
just as the rays of the moon dispel a mass of darkness.

“Durīhita” refers to defects of the mind; “durvihita” refers to defects of the body; and “sarvam” refers to defects of all the sense organs. “Śītāṃśoḥ” means of the moon, and “aṅghrayaḥ” means rays. || 7 ||
O Sage, our thirst, greed, and other such fetters of saṃsāra have been attenuated by your teaching, like dark clouds in autumn.
He explains those very points clearly with the word "thirst" (tṛṣṇā). "Tenuity" means the state of having only a small remainder. || 8 ||
We have set out to behold our own selves freed from all taint,
like those born blind who have been brought by Rasāñjana to see gold.

They were those who had attained vision through the collyrium prepared from the perfected elixir (siddharasa), and those who had attained the inward vision through the anointing with the essence of Brahman (brahmarasa). || 9 ||
The mist called the latent impressions of saṃsāra, which has arisen within the sky of our hearts,
is beginning to thin out for us solely through the autumn of your speech.

The ellipsis is "she resides in the sky of the heart. Since she is already included by the force of the metaphor (*rūpaka*), the repeated use of the word *iva*—though its sense is already implied—is for the purpose of indicating a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). || 10 ||
O Sage, neither the blossoms of the Mandāra tree nor the waves of the nectar-ocean gladden the inner heart as much as the words of those possessed of noble intellect.
Of the nectar-water; of the ocean of nectar. || 11 ||
O Rāghava, whichever day passes with the honor of great crowds, that day alone here possesses light;
all other days are abodes of darkness.
Whatever day passes by in the service and worship of great beings who know Brahman, that day departs filled with light; [otherwise,] people remain blind, enveloped in darkness. || 12 ||
O Rāma, lotus-petal-eyed one, awaken again the sage who is established in grace, the imperishable one here, regarding the matter at hand.
Awaken him; ask him. || 13 ||
Thus addressed by the king, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, noble-souled, stood facing Rāma and spoke these words.
"Āsthita" means seated. || 14 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, the sole moon of your lineage, O high-minded one, do you remember the meaning of what I have said, having reflected upon it from beginning to end? (15)
O crusher of enemies, do you perhaps remember the classification of all the various types of beings according to the distinctions of their qualities, such as *sattva* and the rest? (16)
Of all the aforementioned classes of living beings. || 16 ||
Someone may remember or indeed know that form which is both all and not-all, both existent and non-existent, and eternally manifest; yet it is distinct from the Supreme Self. (17)
The entire world exists as Brahman, appearing through illusion (māyā) in the guise of a drama like an actor; yet it is "not-all," being free from phenomenal proliferation (niṣprapañca).

Whether you consider the gross to be real and the subtle to be unreal, or whether you regard it as having both real and unreal forms—do you remember what I have said? By means of your own intellect, you will surely come to know that which is distinct from all visible objects.
O virtuous one, sole recipient of praise for your goodness, do you perhaps remember how this entire universe arose from the Lord of the Universe alone? (18)

From the Lord Brahmā, the Sovereign of All who is endowed with every power; the word "eva" (only) is for the purpose of refuting the theories of causation held by the Sāṃkhyas and others, such as the Pradhāna; "sādhuvādāḥ" refers to praises and excellent instructions. 18.
O one of noble mind, do you rightly remember that form, which is fragile due to the power of ignorance, though extended and infinite, yet appears as if it has an end? (19)
By force and by power; it is infinite in number, but finite in terms of space, time, and so forth.
"Man is mind alone and nothing else"—do you remember well that which was established through the investigation of characteristics and so forth? (20)
O Rāma, have you reflected upon the entire meaning of the discourse? Has what was considered yesterday been retained in your heart throughout the night? (21)

The meaning of the sentence, which was the object of yesterday’s reflection and hearing, has been refined through contemplation (*manana*) and repeatedly examined; it is now firmly established within the heart.
Its purpose bears fruit abundantly, provided it is not left in a state of neglect.

The meaning is that for such a lowest of men, by whom the established state—namely, the retention of the taught subject—is destroyed through negligence or disrespect, [the teaching] does not bear fruit. || 22 ||
O Rāghava, you are a vessel for words that are secluded and pure, for your heart is secluded like a necklace of pearls around the neck.
He has a secluded heart, a mind endowed with discernment, and a broad chest. || 23 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having been thus granted the opportunity by the sage of great luster, the son of the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā),
Rāma spoke these words.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, this is indeed the manifestation of your own power, that I, being most noble, have understood your words.
"Vijṛmbhitam" means the expansion of splendor. || 25 ||
"Everything that you command shall be exactly so and not otherwise;
having cast off sleep, I have reflected upon the meaning of your words in my heart. (26)
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it was done exactly so. He states that very point clearly: "apāsta... (verse 26).
O Lord, for the destruction of the darkness of worldly existence, the delightful mass of rays of your speech— like the sun— was made to shine forth yesterday.

By you, the agent characterized by speech, who are like the sun (vivasvat) as the instrument; or, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such that "by you" refers to one who has become the sun (*vivasvat*) in the matter of illuminating the meaning through instruction. It is gladdening, producing the happiness that removes the cold of dullness. || 27 ||
O noble-souled one, all that has passed away has been gathered within me by me—charming, meritorious, and pure, like a collection of jewels. (28)
*Antaḥkṛtam* means made within the heart; *anvitam* means endowed with the proper sequence. || 28 ||
Whose head, O Siddhas, does your instruction not bear—[an instruction] that brings beneficial consequences, is pleasing to the heart, meritorious, and a means to bliss? (29)

With the intention that "because it is followed by the abandonment of all that is undesirable, because it is exceedingly sweet, because it is a means for achieving the supreme goal of man, and because its teaching is unassailable, your word must necessarily be bowed to with the head and put into practice in the heart," he says: "followed by benefit" (*hitānubandhi*).

By whom is it not borne upon the head—by the various classes of Siddhas who have attained perfection through yoga, mantras, and so forth, or by those such as Sanaka and others who are perfected by their very nature? (29)
Dispelling the veil of the mist of saṃsāra here,
we have become clear through your grace, like days at the end of the rainy season.
Warding off the doubt that his own instruction might be fruitless, he says: "They reject," meaning they cast away. "At the end of the rains" means in autumn. || 30 ||
Your holy instruction has a commencement sweet at its onset, increases one's good fortune in the middle, and results in unsurpassed fruit in the end. (31)
He describes the beneficial nature of the instruction throughout the three periods of time with the verse beginning "āpāta": "At the outset" (āpāte) means at the time of hearing;

"in the middle" (madhye) means at the time of reflection and meditative contemplation; "of good fortune" (saubhāgyasya) refers to the happiness consisting in the perfection of tranquility and other qualities resulting from inward-turnedness; and "such a future result" (tathāvidha udarkaḥ) refers to that which has as its ultimate fruit the unsurpassed state known as liberation.
That whose time is subsequent. || 31 ||
May the flower of your speech—expansive, white, unfading, and gladdening both the auspicious and the inauspicious—constantly grant us glorious fruit. 32.

It is white, clear, and brilliant. It is that by which the auspicious and inauspicious—merit and demerit—and their fruits have been made to consist of the singular essence of bliss; it is that by which the auspicious gods and the inauspicious serpents and others have been gladdened. Your speech is characterized as a flower, a blossom of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa). || 32 ||
O you who are expert in the investigation of all scriptures,
a great singular lake for the spreading waters of merit— now, O observer of extensive vows, worship him fervently.
O destroyer of sin, [grant] a continuous lineage that has spread forth. || 33 ||
Now, characterizing the Guru as a great lake by virtue of his being a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and addressing him,
he again entreats him for a continuous stream of speech that instructs on the remaining matters, beginning with the word *sakala*:
"O you who are proficient (*viśārada*) in the investigation of place, time, and scripture" (where "place and time" constitutes the meaning of the word *sakala*).

O you who possess the great lake of the waters of merit from widespread conduct, O you of extensive vows—this is the meaning of the word *saṃtati* (lineage) as it applies to me; that is to say, "your lineage [is directed] toward me. [This is because Rāma, by virtue of being his branch of learning, belongs to Vasiṣṭha’s lineage. Now, [I shall describe] its expansion.

The meaning is: "Resort to the flow of words of instruction. In the case of the lake: "O you who shine with the movements of all birds characterized by the sciences (śāstra), such as swans and others; in whom extensive vows have been spread out by sages; and by whom the sins of those who bathe have been destroyed—O you who are thus described!"

O sole great lake of the waters of merit that have spread forth, you should now—at this present time—attain continuity, meaning a spreading stream in the form of a succession of words. In the reading "māṃ prati" at the end, the meaning is "for my purification. || 33 ||

Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Question of Rāghava," in the section on Quiescence within the *Mokṣopāya* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki in the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 4 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Question of Rāghava," in the section on Tranquility (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Fifth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O you of beautiful form, this [teaching] is beautiful with its supreme philosophical conclusion.
Listen attentively to this beneficial chapter on tranquility.
The sequential method for the complete pacification of this world, which exists as mere mind and has flourished through lack of discernment, is here correctly proclaimed. (1)
"Attentive" means one whose mind is focused. || 1 ||
O Rāma, this long-lasting illusion of saṃsāra is constantly maintained by beings of rajasic and tamasic nature, like a pavilion supported by sturdy pillars.

Having restated what was previously mentioned, he connects it with the present topic—beginning with the word "dīrgha" (long). It is sustained by the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* living beings mentioned earlier; for the meaning is that the Puruṣa is indeed the imperishable one, according to such scriptural passages as: "For this food, he produces through every act of thought by means of his ritual actions. || 2 ||
By steadfast men of noble birth like yourself, who are strengthened by virtues,
this matured illusion is cast off with ease, just as snakes shed their skin— [the reading "tucche" (trifling) is also found].
Those of noble birth established in *sattva* are those characterized by the previously mentioned qualities, namely the *rājasa-sāttvika* and the pure *sāttvika*.
O virtuous one, those classes of beings who are wise, as well as those characterized by passion and goodness, reflect upon the ancient succession of the world.

He states by what means [ignorance] is abandoned: "Those who... [referring to verse 5]. This refers to the lineage of predecessors, the lineage of the root, as shown in such scriptural passages as, "O gentle one, seek water as the root through this sprout that is food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.4). || 4 ||
For those whose debts have been cleared through association with the scriptures, the virtuous, and noble deeds, the intellect arises like a lamp, beholding the essential truth. (5)
"Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are the purifiers for the wise"—these are the words spoken by the Blessed One. (5)
By investigating the self through the self by means of inquiry itself,
as long as that which is to be known has not been realized, it is not attained.
"By oneself alone" means according to the maxim: "One should uplift oneself by oneself. "Not attained" means not known. "Attained" (adhigamyate) means reached. || 6 ||
O delight of the Raghus, you are the foremost among those who possess wisdom, who are guided by policy, who are steadfast, who are illustrious by birth, and who have the nature of kings.

But he says that you indeed possess the fitness for attaining that [state], with the words "of those possessed of wisdom. That is, of those who possess policy, meaning those skilled in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). || 7 ||
O wise one, examine for yourself the views regarding the commencement of worldly existence;
what is real and what is unreal? Be devoted to the truth.
Behold; see with discernment. || 8 ||
How can that which does not exist at the beginning and at the end possess reality?
That alone is called "real" which is eternal at the beginning and at the end, and nothing else.

"That which exists" means being existent, truly real, having a nature that is not contradicted by non-existence; how could its opposite—a nature of non-existence—possibly occur? The sense is that a reversal of intrinsic nature is impossible. It is "eternal," meaning it possesses a fixed, existent nature. (9)
For that deluded beast among living beings whose mind becomes attached to an object that is unreal from beginning to end, by what means can discernment be produced? (10)
One becomes attached through the notion that it is real, and one becomes impassioned. || 10 ||
In this world, it is the mind alone that is born; it is the mind alone that grows;
but through the vision of right insight, it is the mind alone that is liberated. 11.
With the intention that the world lacks reality not only because it is produced by the mind alone—like a palace constructed in a dream—he says: "It is born... (verse 11).
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, this has been understood by me: that in these three worlds, it is the mind alone that wanders in saṃsāra and is the vessel for old age and death.
The question is clear. 12.
Tell me with certainty that means for crossing over it;
by you, the darkness within the hearts of the Raghavas is destroyed, just as by the sun. (13)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, first let the mind be led toward merit through the scriptures, supreme dispassion, and likewise through association with the virtuous.

He states that first one must accomplish the fourfold means, such as detachment (*vairāgya*), through the study of the scriptures and association with the virtuous—beginning with the word "first": "puṇyatām" refers to purity that brings about the fitness for the arising of knowledge. (14)
When the mind, imbued with goodness, has attained dispassion,
then one should follow gurus, including those who are gurus of realized knowledge.

Kindness is the absence of pride. Those teachers who, by virtue of their realized knowledge—the knowledge of the secrets of all scriptures—are teachers and even more venerable, and who, through skill in instruction, are capable of awakening their disciples, are to be followed according to the prescribed rule. || 15 ||
Then, having performed meditation, worship, and other rites according to his instruction,
he gradually attains that state which is supremely purifying.

"Having meditated upon the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, who has Uma as his companion, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and tranquil one— the source of all beings, the witness of all, who stands beyond darkness— the sage goes [to liberation]," according to such scriptural passages; thus, first performing meditation, worship, and so forth upon the Saguna Ishvara by the path instructed by the Guru.
The meaning is: "by means of his grace, through the sequence of investigation and so forth to be described. || 16 ||
Through pure discernment, he perceives the Self by means of the self,
just as one sees the entire universe within through the cool lunar light, as if through the radiance of the sky.
The entire universe was as if filled with the sky and the moon by his splendor. || 17 ||
In the great ocean of worldly existence, a person is carried away like a blade of grass until, through the mind, they find rest upon the shore of discernment. 18.
As long as the mind, by means of the raft of intellect, does not attain rest and stability on the shore characterized by investigation (vicāra), [it remains unsteady]. || 18 ||
The intellect of this person, who has thoroughly understood reality through discernment, subdues all mental afflictions just as gentle water washes away grains of sand. (19)
*Ādhīn* refers to mental sufferings; it means he makes them low, that is to say, he casts them away. *Saumyam* means deep and serene.
Just as it is clear to a goldsmith whose very nature is the knowledge of gold that "this is gold" and "this is ash," so it is for one who possesses thorough discernment. (20)

Just as gold hidden in ashes cannot be distinguished by others, yet for one who knows gold and whose nature is always intent on purifying gold, it is clearly recognized by that goldsmith—who is skilled in discernment—as "this is gold" and "this is ash"; thus, there is no occasion for the delusion of not obtaining it. So too [is it with the Self].

This self, which is commonly known through the vision of the ignorant as the limited individual soul (*jīva*), becomes clearly manifest by itself—indestructible and devoid of limitations such as time—once it has been discerned through long investigation and realized within one's own being;
thus, how could there be any occasion for delusion? This is the connection with the subsequent verse. || 20 ||
When this imperishable and subtle Self has been realized within oneself for a long time, how could there be any occasion for delusion in a person here on earth? (21)
For if the mind is deluded within when the essence is not fully understood, yet when the essence is known, delusion certainly becomes non-existent. (22)

In a person who has not realized the essence, if he should indeed be deluded, then let him be so deluded—this is the sense of the phrase "let it be. The meaning is that [his delusion] is simply non-existent and impossible. || 22 ||
O people, the self, when not fully understood, leads to the establishment of suffering for you; but when fully understood, it leads to infinite happiness and peace. 23.

Now, out of compassion, he addresses all listeners with the words "O people. The sense is that this is based on such scriptural passages as: "For when one perceives even a slight difference in this [Brahman], then fear arises for him; indeed, fear arises for the one who knows [it] but does not contemplate [it as such]," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "but when fully known": for this is indeed the essence (*rasa*).

The meaning is that this is according to such scriptural passages as: "Having attained [this], he becomes blissful; having obtained all desires, he has become immortal; knowing Him, one transcends death; he who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere. || 23 ||
As if mixed with this body whose self is afflicted, manifest your own true nature and become established in yourselves; do not delay.
Having manifested [the Self] by means of the discrimination of the five sheaths, one perceives it. || 24 ||
O men, there is not even the slightest connection between this stainless Self and the body, just as there is no connection between gold and a speck of mud, even when the gold is situated within it.
He clarifies this very manifestation with the words beginning "by the body" (dehena) and so forth; the particle *eva* is used in the sense of "also. || 25 ||
The self is distinct from the body; they are like a water-drop and a lotus-leaf.
With arms upraised, I cry out, yet no one listens to me.

The meaning is as follows: the Self (ātman), Brahman, the embodied one (dehin), and the individual soul (jīva) are distinct from one another only due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), but not in reality—just as the great body of water that supports the lotus and the drop of water resting on the lotus leaf [are distinct only through their respective conditions].
Now, it may be objected that for the great body of water, causes such as wind are well known to bring about its rising onto the lotus leaf or its limitation [by it].

If it is asked what the cause is for the full Self to ascend into a body through limitation, it has been proclaimed more than once that it is the most wicked mind itself. Therefore, with the intention that effort must be made solely for its destruction, [the author] utters a cry of reproach out of compassion, beginning with the words "With arms upraised," and so forth. || 26 ||

As long as the mind, possessing the nature of inertia, remains like a tortoise in a well—deluded by the path of worldly enjoyment and having forgotten the inquiry into the Self—[so long does it remain bound]. (27)

As long as the mind remains— hidden like a tortoise in the muddy pit of evil latent impressions, yet firm in the attainment of enjoyments, and uninfatuated with sense-objects by means of the senses acting as gateways—
so long does the darkness of saṃsāra persist, even with the moon and the fire.

The word "api" (even) implies that it is not surpassed even by the twelve suns together with all other luminaries such as the stars and jewels; the connection with the subsequent clause is that it is not "bhidyate" (disturbed or surpassed) even in the slightest degree ("manāk" / "īṣat"). || 27 ||
Until then, the darkness of saṃsāra is not dispelled even slightly, even by the moon, nor by fire, nor even by twelve suns.
For when the mind is fully awakened, it discerns its own state; the darkness within the heart flees, just as the rising sun dispels the night.
He discerns his own ultimate state, perceiving it by distinguishing it from the unreal when [the mind] is present. || 29 ||
One should constantly awaken the mind, resting upon the bed of yoga, for the sake of supreme enlightenment;
for the purpose of breaking the cycle of existence, since existence indeed bestows extreme suffering. (30)

"Yoga" refers to the superimposition of identity with the body and so forth; having gone to a bed characterized by that [superimposition], or having gone to sleep—that is, having attained the repose of meditative absorption (samādhi)—[he remained there]. || 30 ||
Just as the sky is not defiled by dust and just as a lotus is not defiled by water, even so the self is not defiled, though it is in contact with bodies. 31.
He states how one should awaken [the disciple] with the words "yathā" (just as). || 31 ||
Just as dross and other impurities, though remaining distinct from gold,
become fused with it yet do not undergo internal transformation, so too does the inert body [remain distinct] from the Self.
In reality, it does not undergo transformation characterized by attaining identity with blood. || 32 ||
One perceives that the experience of pleasure and pain belongs to the self,
just as one might perceive the presence of water droplets or withered flowers in the sky, though they are entirely non-existent.
The fool—this is the remainder of the sentence—perceives [the self] as having the nature of being experienced, the nature of following after, and the nature of being the experiencer.

"The state of being a drop" (bindutā) refers to the form of thousands of drops, established by both scripture and experience, appearing as if small water-bubbles were falling down. "Fading away" (mlānatā) means impurity. || 33 ||
Pleasure and pain belong neither to the body nor to the Self, which transcends all; for these two pertain only to the ignorant one, and when that ignorance is destroyed, they belong to no one at all.
If pleasure and pain do not belong to the self, then do they belong to the body? He says "no"—"pleasure and pain. Then to whom do they belong?
He says "these"—belonging only to that which is characterized by ignorance (ajñānaka), namely, ignorance itself. 34.
There is no happiness for anyone, nor is there any suffering for anyone;
behold everything as consisting of the Self—tranquil and infinite, O Raghava. (35)
Consisting of the self, an emanation of the self; peaceful, eternally tranquil. || 35 ||
These expansive perceptions of creation that are seen here are like waves in water, or like a peacock's plumage in the sky, or [manifested] within the Self. 36.

He demonstrates the nature of illusory manifestation (vivartatā) by means of an illustration—namely, "these" (imāḥ). It is well known that for one lying with eyes half-closed facing the sun, a peacock feather appears in the sky due to an optical illusion. || 36 ||
Just as a gem spontaneously reflects its own images without any external cause,
even so this Self bestows creations that are composed of light.
It bestows and extends its own splendors, which consist of radiant light; that is to say, it grants and spreads them forth without cause and without being engaged in any activity. || 37 ||
O wise one, neither the self nor the world is truly one, nor is duality non-existent;
this entire manifestation now unfolds as a mere appearance. (38)

It is neither one, nor non-dual, nor dual, nor manifold, since the form of the world is unreal; for it is impossible to determine either the identity or the difference of the real with that which is unreal—this is the meaning. "Now" refers to the time of ignorance. || 38 ||
All this is indeed Brahman; everything is thus pervaded by the Self alone.
O sinless one, abandon the delusion that "I am one thing" and "this is another. 39.

But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), since even error cannot be defined as something distinct [from Brahman], he says "all" (*samastam*)—meaning that everything is indeed Brahman—in accordance with the view expressed in the Upanishadic scriptures: "All this is Brahman," and "All this is the Self. || 39 ||
O Rāma, within that eternal, dense mass of Brahman, no conceptual constructions arise; they are not composed of reality, just as the waves in the ocean of water are not truly real.
In that [Brahman], which is devoid of spatial limitation; in the mass of Brahman, which is devoid of objective limitation; in the eternal, which is void of temporal limitation. || 40 ||
In the single, all-encompassing reality of the Supreme Self, there exists no second conceptualization, just as there is no particle of frost in fire. (41)
He states that the conceptualization of duality is not real even because it contradicts actual unity: "In that which is indeed one... (verse 41).
Meditating upon the self by means of the self as consisting of consciousness alone, the self indeed unfolds within itself, being straight, radiant, and composed of pure consciousness. 42.
Now, he says that through such acquaintance with the Self, one should always practice its contemplation (*bhāvanā*) for the sake of resting therein:
"In that which consists of straightness and radiance, free from the impurity of the crookedness of *māyā*," so it is said. (42)
There is no sorrow, there is no delusion, there is no birth, and there is no one who is born.
That which exists here is indeed that alone; be free from fever, O Rāghava.
He demonstrates the repose of one who has attained that state as liberation while living (jīvanmukti) with the words beginning "no sorrow" (na śoka). || 43 ||

Free from dualities, eternally established in purity, devoid of the pursuit of acquisition and preservation, self-possessed, peerless, sorrowless in nature, and free from feverish distress— be thus, O Rāghava.

Free from dualities means being devoid of the distractions of physical dualities such as cold and heat; because he is established in eternal goodness (*sattva*), he is free from the mental distractions induced by passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*). For this very reason, he has abandoned all concern for the acquisition and preservation of the means to avoid those two. (44)
Equanimous, self-abiding, steady-minded, with a heart calmed of sorrow, a sage, silent, as pure as a precious gem, and free from fever—be thus, O Rāghava! (45)
Solitary, with thoughts stilled, wise in intellect, and having conquered your inner disposition,
follow whatever comes to you and be free from the fever of passion, O Raghava.
"Solitary" means purified of ignorance and its effects; "one who has conquered the latent tendencies" means one whose mind is self-governed. || 46 ||
Free from passion, free from exertion, stainless, and cleansed of impurity;
neither a taker nor a giver, be free from feverish distress, O Rāghava.
Having attained the state that transcends the universe, filled with all that is to be attained,
remain free from feverish anxiety, O Rāghava, as unagitated as the full ocean.
Freed from the web of conceptual constructions and devoid of the ointment of illusion, with your soul satisfied within the Self by the Self, become free from the fever of passion, O Rāghava. 49.
O Rāghava, best among the knowers of the Self, whose body is infinite, shoreless, and boundless; steadfast as the peak of the mountain that supports the earth, be free from fever.
Like Meru, the foremost among the upholders of the earth, he was likewise steadfast.
By experiencing whatever has been obtained, by not desiring anything anywhere, and by relinquishing both rejection and acceptance, become free from the fever of passion, O Rāghava.
Within yourself alone, through yourself, cultivate magnanimity like the full ocean;
within yourself alone, through yourself, cultivate joy like the orb of the full moon.
Magnificence is the absence of meanness; that is to say, the state of having one's desires fulfilled. Joy is the bliss resulting from the subsiding of all afflictions. || 52 ||
O Rāma, this world-appearance, which is unreal in nature, does not pursue that which is unreal;
you are a knower of that, you are one whose mental fluctuations are stilled, and you are free from all affliction.
Be ever-arisen, O beautiful one, with sorrow stilled. || 53 ||
Summarizing the meaning already stated, he concludes by teaching: "The universe," etc. The meaning is clear. || 53 ||
Rule for a long time, with your vision fixed upon righteousness, this kingdom under a single umbrella as instructed by your preceptor,
while the world of kings is delighted by all your virtues.
Neither detachment nor passion is appropriate here in these ritual acts. || 54 ||

Perceiving Rāma’s intention—that if one who knows the Truth does not pursue what is unreal, then what use has he for a kingdom and the like, and that the life of a wandering mendicant alone is appropriate—he said: "One umbrella," etc. [The meaning is: a kingdom under a single umbrella commanded by his father, the Guru; and kings and subjects delighted by all his virtues.
And being such as you are, protect the subjects well for a long time with impartial vision.

The meaning is that since actions have already been commenced, neither renunciation nor attachment is appropriate toward those actions and their fruits which must necessarily be experienced. Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-disciplined and without dependence—
"Even though he is fully engaged in action, he does not do anything at all"— this is the meaning, according to the words of the Blessed One.
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Instruction on Tranquility," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "Instruction on Tranquility," in the Upaśama-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa.
The Sixth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"I am performing this universal vibration"—such a latent impression (vāsanā) has been cast off.
He who engages in activities is, in my opinion, liberated. || 1 ||

Having first described here the courses of karma for those in their final birth, the general sequence for attaining the qualities [necessary] for liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is now set forth.
