In order to demonstrate the connection with the present subject— the sequence for acquiring virtues that will be described hereafter— he defines the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) as being engaged in activities that are neither enjoined nor prohibited and are free from attachment, using the words "this" (imam):
[he perceives] the entire movement of the universe.

The meaning is that, like a magnet, worldly activity—which is established by the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous—proceeds through mere proximity with the thought "I am doing it," without the latent impression (vāsanā) of being an agent, as would be the case for an ignorant person who is obsessed with agency. || 1 ||
Having assumed a human body, some who are devoted to these very activities go from heaven to hell, and again from hell to heaven. (2)
He shows that it is precisely due to attachment to the fruits of action that the ignorant incur misfortune— by means of the verse beginning with "pauruṣīm.

Although some fools have resorted to and attained a human body— a physical form born of man— they remain unattached to this activity characterized by the performance of action without attachment, being instead possessed by desire.
Having enjoyed heaven through rites performed for specific desires, they then enter hell due to the remainder of a few residual karmas—[the reading "kapūya" appears in the text]. || 2 ||
Some, though delighting in non-action and even abstaining from action,
go from hell to hell, from suffering to suffering, and from fear to fear.
They are devoted to non-action—that is, to prohibited action—and have desisted from action, meaning virtuous action. Thus says the Smṛti:
"By the non-performance of what is enjoined, by the performance of what is censured, and by the lack of restraint over the senses, a man incurs downfall. (3)
Some, bound by the threads of their own latent impressions and impelled by the fruits of their karma,
pass from the state of an animal into the body of an immobile being, and from there into the body of another animal.
Having experienced the fruits of their evil karma in succession within the hells, they have arisen and been born among the animal wombs. || 4 ||
Certain fortunate knowers of the Self, whose vision of the mind has been scrutinized and whose fetters of craving are severed, proceed to the absolute state.
Having spoken of those characterized by passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa), as well as those of pure darkness (śuddhatāmasa), he speaks of the beings who are purely sattvic: "Some" (kecit).

Those by whom the Self, which is the witness of the mind, has been investigated through the mind's vision, [attain] that state which is absolute and of the nature of supreme liberation (paramakaivalya). || 5 ||

O Raghava, having experienced only a few previous births, one who is liberated in this birth is therefore *rājasasāttvika* (of rajasic-sattvic nature). [In the phrase "therefore *rājasa*," the reading "he would be *rājasa*" is appropriate. || 6 ||
He shows those characterized by *rajas* and *sattva* with the words "In a city," etc. A few human births are progressively more excellent [than the former]. || 6 ||
Once born, he attains growth like the moon during the full-moon phase;
and as the *kuṭaja* tree does in the rainy season, good fortune follows him.

He describes his increase through qualities such as tranquility with the verse beginning "jāta" (born), etc. "Fortune" (*saubhāgya*) refers to the four means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). In the case of the *kuṭaja* tree, it refers to the beauty of its flowers. || 7 ||
O high-minded one, pure branches of knowledge enter him whose birth is his last, just as pearls enter an excellent bamboo tube.

"Vidyās" refers to the knowledge of Brahman, the means thereto, and all branches of knowledge. The phrase "like a bamboo" is used because even a specific species of bamboo is well known as a source of pearls. || 8 ||
Nobility, amiability, friendliness, gentleness, compassion, and wisdom always attend him, just as women attend upon the inner apartments.
Knowledge is cognition that is for the most part indirect.
He who performs all actions, whether they succeed or fail,
remaining equanimous toward all undertakings, neither rejoices nor grieves.

He states the introduction to the definition of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), as previously mentioned in the context of the preliminary practice, with the words "ya" (he who): when [the knowledge] is nourished and fully developed.
There, dualities come to an end like darkness at daybreak;
there, the qualities attain purity like clouds in autumn.
The pairs refer to pleasure, pain, and so forth; likewise, qualities such as fortitude, faith, and moral shame, though previously defiled. (11)
All people desire him whose conduct is sweet with gentleness, just as the forest deer in the woods long for the flute with its sweet resonance. (12)
The *veṇu* is the *kīcaka* flute, which produces a sweet sound because its holes are filled with air. || 12 ||
Such splendors of virtue pursue a man of his final birth from the very moment he is born, just as cranes follow a rain-cloud. (13)
"From the very moment of birth" means from childhood onwards. || 13 ||
Then, endowed with all virtues, he follows the teacher alone;
the teacher, for his part, enjoins him to that very same purifying solitude.

With the intention that those whose minds are distracted do not possess the qualification for hearing [the teachings] from the mouth of a guru when such a perfection of qualities is required, he says "tataḥ" (thereupon).

The meaning is that, having thus taught the means for the discrimination between the reality of the Self and the non-Self in the manner previously described by me, he now enjoins them toward the task of reflection (*manana*) even by means of their own intellect. || 14 ||
With a mind endowed with excellence and free from the passion for discursive thought,
he then beholds the Lord as his own self, uniform and free from affliction.

He shows that for one endowed with such qualities, the attainment of direct realization comes through hearing and other means preceded by [service to] the Guru—thus he says, "investigation," etc. It is of a single form, having bliss as its sole essence. || 15 ||
With a beautiful and tranquil mind, he first expands this internal contemplation of the mind for the sake of awakening through discernment. (16)
He explains the reflection (manana) indicated in the phrase "he joins" by saying, "it extends. || 16 ||
For those of great virtue first awaken the sleeping deer of the mind—devoid of qualities—who are destined for their final birth. (17)
The meaning is that they awaken [the soul] in such a way that it becomes Brahman itself—devoid of qualities and free from attributes. || 17 ||
Those men who, having diligently served teachers of renowned virtue and having investigated the jewel of the mind with a clear intellect, attain the stainless state.
Having gazed deeply within for a long time, he beheld the inner radiance.
He summarizes the aforementioned point concisely with the verse beginning "prathita": those humans who possess the aforementioned qualities and are in their final birth,
having diligently served great gurus whose qualities— the characteristics of one liberated while living— are well-known;
Having investigated the jewel within the mind— the inner self— by means of the pure intellect through the reasonings shown therein,

and having examined it with reflection as one would examine a gem, and having long gazed upon and directly experienced that supreme Brahman which shines within the mind and is non-different from the inner self, [one attains liberation] by that mere realization of it.

They attain—that is, they reach—the goal characterized by the supreme human purpose, which is defined by the acquisition of that state [of Brahman], which is stainless, and which is free from all impurities consisting of Māyā and its effects; they reach it "nearby," meaning right there in their own place, not by departing for another world like those who practice meditation (upāsakas). This is the meaning. || 18 ||

Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The First Instruction," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the seers. 6.
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The First Instruction," in the Chapter on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Seventh Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This sequence has thus been described as the common one for all embodied beings.
O lotus-eyed one, hear this further distinction.
Here, for those whose minds have attained some degree of proficiency through their own inquiry, the attainment of knowledge is described as having the fruit of illuminating [the truth]. (1)

Having restated the general sequence [of realization], he now shows— through the verse beginning with "This one" (eṣa)— the particular case of a certain fortunate person for whom, even without that [sequence], there occurs suddenly the arising of knowledge characterized by the perfection of all virtues, brought about solely by his own reflection through the power of destiny. || 1 ||
O Rāma, for those embodied beings born into this turmoil of saṃsāra,
these two supreme methods are capable of leading to liberation.
These two—the one already mentioned and the one to be described hereafter—are capable of liberation and endowed with the fruit of emancipation. || 2 ||

First of all, one [type of mantra] is declared to bestow perfection either gradually over many lifetimes or even within a single lifetime, through the performance of practices as taught by the Guru. (3)
It is declared that [this practice] bestows perfection in one birth or through many births, and leads to liberation;
this is the meaning of what was stated previously. || 3 ||
But the second [type of person], by means of his own mind which has become somewhat refined, attains knowledge as swiftly as a fruit falling from the sky. || 4 ||
The meaning is that the attainment of knowledge occurs through one's own self alone, by means of one who investigates the reality of the living world as presented by destiny. || 4 ||
In order to bring about the realization of knowledge regarding the falling of fruits from the sky, listen to this ancient account; I shall relate it to you.

In the second sequence, intending to cite the narrative of Janaka, he prepares the introductory setting: "O fortunate one, listen to the story of those of great majesty, whose flood of obstructions consisting of former merit and demerit has been removed, and who [move] like the reflection of the sky."
Like fruits that have fallen from the tree, those in their final birth attain supreme, stainless discernment.

O fortunate one, just as men of great power in their final existence and final birth attain supreme discernment like a fruit fallen from the sky, listen to the story that is about to be told; this is the meaning. || 6 ||

Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Indication of the Sequence for Attaining Knowledge, Like the Attainment of Fruits in the Sky," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sages (*Ārṣa*).
This concludes the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa* (The Illumination of the Essential Meaning of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa).
The seventh canto, titled "An Indication of the Sequence for Attaining Gnosis, Like the Attainment of the Fruit of Space. || 7 ||
The Eighth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
There is one whose noble intellect has brought all calamities to an end and in whom prosperity is ever-rising.
The powerful ruler of the Videhas was named Janaka.
It is described that while Janaka was once wandering here in this forest during the spring season, he heard auspicious verses sung by the Siddhas. (1)
The king was the protector of the earth for the people of the Videha country. || 1 ||
He is the wish-fulfilling tree for the multitudes of supplicants, the sun for the lotuses that are his friends, Mādhava for the flowers that are his kinsmen, and the god of love for women. || 2 ||
He was like springtime to the *mādhavī* flowers characterized as kinsmen for the multitudes of supplicants and crowds of beggars. || 2 ||
A cool-rayed moon to the night-lotuses of the twice-born, a sun to the darkness of his enemies,
and an ocean of the jewels of benevolence, he dwelt upon the earth like Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu, like you, has taken his stand upon the earth, having resorted to it for the sake of its protection.
Once, during the spring, when the young creepers were in full bloom, tawny with clusters of blossoms, and the cuckoos were singing in intoxication; (4)

Where the young creepers are in full bloom—the suffix *kan* being used here in the sense of compassion—and where, as if intoxicated, the spring (*madhu*) stands as though dancing to the songs of the cuckoos, expanding itself like one who is drunk. || 4 ||
He went to the lovely grove, its expanse filled with blossoming trees and its courtyards of vines full of graceful charm, just as Indra goes to the Nandana garden.
Wherein the creepers themselves are beautiful women, or else the women are like creepers. || 5 ||
In that delightful and excellent forest, where the breezes were fierce with the scent of kesara flowers,
he wandered through the mountain bowers accompanied by his followers stationed at a distance.

In those bowers—creeper-houses growing on the plateaus of pleasure-mountains—there blow breezes that are capable of carrying away the abundant particles of pollen, fragrance, and nectar from the filaments, yet not of scattering dust and the like; that is to say, breezes that are mildly fragrant and cool. || 6 ||
Then, in a certain thicket of tamāla trees, he heard words uttered by invisible siddhas during their own conversation.
"Of those who are invisible and hidden" means for the sake of their own favor, that is to say, for the purpose of bestowing grace upon them according to their own inclination. || 7 ||
O lotus-petal-eyed one, these songs, which consist of the meditation on the Self, were sung by those who dwell eternally in solitude and roam the mountain caves.

Those who cultivate the self through the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas—which are sung as the Gītā—by means of mere hearing, acting in such a way that it becomes manifest to them directly, are called "those whose meditation on the self is the Gītā. He heard the Gītās, which are the Upaniṣads based on the Smṛtis. || 8 ||

The Siddhas said: We worship that which arises from the reality of one's own self, which is motionless, and which is the certainty of the bliss of consciousness born from the union of the seer and the seen. 9.

When a cognition arises— produced by the contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) between the perceiver, who is the knower of objects through the doors of the eyes and other senses, and the visible object such as garlands, sandalwood, or women— the certainty that manifests itself as the nature of bliss within that mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) which takes the form of the object, one should realize that very nature of it by means of the purification of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*).

We worship—that is, we continuously experience—our own Self as it has manifested in the form of the unsurpassed ground, being motionless, with the vibration of both external and internal organs eliminated through non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). The intended meaning is this: within the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that takes the form of an object, [the Self] itself...

Bliss does not reside within the category of objects, because that would entail the consequence of its being insentient (*jaḍatva*). Nor does it reside within the category of the agent or the instrument, because as factors of action (*kāraka*), they are subordinate to it, which contradicts the experience of bliss itself.
Therefore, it resides only within the category of the witness (*sākṣin*); indeed, it is the witness alone.

Indeed, one whose nature is consciousness-bliss (cidānanda) has its radiance dimmed by the veil of ignorance; having imagined another self consisting of egoism (ahaṃkāra), it falls as if into a state of subservience to that.

By means of a mental modification (vṛtti) assuming the form of an object, it leads its own bliss—as manifested therein—as if into a state of subservience to that object, and thus does not realize its own Self as unsurpassed bliss. Therefore, that very [Self]...
With a concentrated mind, we worship that whose nature is unsurpassed bliss arising from the investigation of one's own true reality;

for according to the scripture, "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss," it is the bliss of Brahman itself that, through ignorance, appears delimited by mental modifications taking the form of objects.

"Because of the contemplation of the nature of the bliss of the objects. Alternatively, it is because of *yoga*— derived from the etymology of "having ascended to a union" (*melanārūḍha*)— arising from the attainment of absolute non-difference characterized by the remaining nature of pure existence alone, once the external and internal disparities between the seer, the *puruṣa*, and the seen, such as space and so forth, have been dissolved.

The meaning is: through the maturation of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), there arises from one's own direct experience itself a certainty regarding the bliss of the Infinite (*bhūmānanda*) which is trustworthy; we worship that very Self, which has arisen—that is, become manifest—in its true nature as the reality of things, as our own motionless state. Alternatively:

Because the seer (the intellect) and the objects of perception (the visible things) are joined together through their commonality in form— consisting of increase and decrease, dullness, pleasure, pain,
and so forth— and because of this connection, there arises a cognition that exists between those two and is distinct from both of them.
"Ānanda" is determined as "thus"; this is the certainty of bliss (*ānandaniścaya*).

That [certainty] is motionless, being free from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of active mental modifications; therefore, it is the arising of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), manifested in its own true form, the one essence of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda-ekarasa*), one's own innermost self (*pratyagātman*).

The meaning is "we worship together. Alternatively, that Self which is perceived and experienced even by dogs, pigs, and the like—through the conjunction characterized by the superimposition of mutual identity and association with the objects of perception such as "I am" and "this is mine"—is the very pleasure derived from sense-objects; thus, this cognition alone is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

One who possesses certainty transmigrates. Having caused the reality of the Self to arise— that is, having made it manifest in its own ultimate form— by means of one's own *mā* (measure), which is the non-dual cognitive transformation (*akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti*) produced by the Vedānta, we worship [the Self] which is motionless and unmoving.

This is the meaning. Alternatively, that cognition which is self-luminous, whose sole essence is bliss, and which is the ascertainment of one's own nature—being a union of the seer and the seen, and having become accompanied by the illusion of the forms of the seer and the seen, it "went," meaning it fell away from its true nature; [the realization] which has mounted upon the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of the final direct perception of that ascertainment of bliss...

"May she indeed become my very self through the cessation of the illusion of the seer and the seen, having arisen as the reality of the Self," and so forth, as before. Alternatively, there is a word-break: "draṣṭṛdṛśyasamā yaḥ agāt. That Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else.

Although [the Self] is capable of being determined as being of the nature of bliss—on account of the conviction that it is the object of supreme love, which is established by such scriptural texts (*śruti*) and personal experience (*anubhava*)—it nevertheless entered into states of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-dashā*) characterized by the similarity of seer and seen, and the likeness of enjoyer and enjoyed, due to the absence of the conviction arising from discrimination (*viveka*), inquiry (*vicāra*), and so forth; "taṃ" refers to that [Self]. As for the word "yat," the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of effort (*prayatna*).
That which has been directly realized through efforts such as discrimination, dispassion, hearing, and reflection—
one who measures, discerns, or destroys the entire collection of duality consisting of the seer and the seen—
is the true nature of the Self; having arisen in that state, it is once again motionless.

Having approached correctly—that is, having attained—by way of being the inner self (pratyagātman) that which is the limit of all proximity, we remain; the meaning is that we abide free from any apprehension of attachment to saṃsāra. || 9 ||
Others said:
"Having abandoned the seer, the seeing, and the seen, along with their latent impressions (vāsanā),
we worship the Self as the first manifestation of seeing."
Others, as if extracting that very Self and displaying it like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, have said:

"The seer, the seeing, and the seen. By the abandonment of this triad beginning with the seer, the two states [of waking and dreaming] are discarded. Furthermore, by the phrase "together with the latent impression" (*vāsanayā saha*), the exclusion of even the deep-sleep ignorance—which is nourished by the seeds of those two impressions—is stated.

By the phrase "appearing even before [the perception] through being the witness of its arising"—that is, prior to the activity of the eyes, the mind, and so forth, which constitute seeing—it is shown by way of analysis that the witness of the triad (tripuṭī), already established and proven by all experience, has been pointed out. The meaning is: "We worship that very Self as the Fourth (turya), because of the abandonment of the triad along with its seed. || 10 ||
Others said:
"We worship the Self, which eternally stands between the two positions of 'is' and 'is not,' and which is the illuminator of all that is to be illuminated. (11)

Regarding those who dispute whether the witness exists or does not exist at the first appearance of perception, others say "of the two," demonstrating to them a witness that is not contradicted by either of those two positions. First, for those who maintain that although there is indeed a first appearance of perception, even that is merely produced (*janya*) and not eternal (*nitya*), [the following applies]:

If those preceding appearances were self-luminous or had themselves as their own objects, they would be exhausted by the manifestation of their own selves alone and would not touch upon subsequent cognitions; thus, they could not function as witnesses to their own arising and so forth. Therefore, another witness is necessary—one that stands apart from that position.

The meaning is that even those who say "it does not exist" are included among them, because their own non-existence is likewise unestablished due to lacking any witness; thus, they fall within that very category as they attempt to prove their own position. Alternatively, the existence of the world is its effect in a manifest state, while its non-existence is its cause in a latent (tirobhāva) state. As it is said: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent."

For it is stated in the Śruti: "There was [Being], from which indeed Being was born. The meaning is that, because those two positions—existence and non-existence—are not simultaneous, it exists in the middle as the form of pure Being (sanmātra) which underlies them both. Alternatively, the meaning is that it exists in the middle as the substratum for both of the two imagined, contradictory alternatives of "it exists" and "it does not exist."
Therefore, because it touches upon the substratum of the imagined non-existence, it is the eternal illuminator of both existent and non-existent entities that are to be illuminated. || 11 ||
Others said: "We worship that Truth in which all is, from whom all is, to whom all belongs, by whom all is, and who indeed is all. (12)

"In that which all [exists]," and "for whom this [exists]"—this is the division. Starting from the locative case-ending (*saptamī-vibhakti*), all the case-endings are indicated here in reverse order to demonstrate the non-difference between the six grammatical relations (*kāraka*) and the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*). Thus, that Brahman is [the locus] because it is the substratum of all, the owner of all, and so forth.

Because it exists as the limit and the cause for all forms of appropriation (*upādāna*), because it brings about the fulfillment of all states such as being the object for another (*pārārthya*) and the recipient (*saṃpradāna*),

and because it constitutes all agents, instruments, and so forth, that which sustains all worldly transactions through *māyā* and is the self of all, is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*) and the inner self (*pratyagātman*) alone, serving as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of everything.
The meaning is: having correctly attained that through awakening, we have become one with it. || 12 ||
Others said:
"We worship that very Self, which is headless, ending with the letter *ha*, established in every form, and eternally uttering its own nature. (13)

The meaning is: that which has the letter *a* at its beginning, like the head (*śira*) [of a body]; and that which has the letter *ha* at its end—that is the word *ahaṃ* (I). It is the source of the entire web of words such as the Vedas and Śāstras that illuminate all things, consisting of all the phonemes arranged in the traditional list of syllables (*akṣarasamāmnāya*).

Because it is situated between the letters *a* and *ha*, it is not destroyed nor diminished within Brahman— which possesses all the forms of the entire world and is characterized by manifoldness (*saprapañca*)—

according to the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of "that in which nothing remains" (*na śiṣyate*). Furthermore, through the formation of the verbal root *ah* in the sense of pervasion (*vyāptau*), it is established eternally in that which is without form (*anākāra*) and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), having attained its ultimate goal and final consummation.
While engaged in one's own worldly activities, by discarding the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of egoism,

we worship— that is, we continuously meditate upon— that very referent of the word "I" described above as the Self of Brahman, which is well-known from such Vedic texts as, "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman, the Self alone. This is the meaning.

Alternatively, the world— consisting of the five great elements as expressed by the five seed-syllables ending in the letter *ha* (namely *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, *haṃ*), which abide in the form of all things without remainder—
is as if to be made "headless," meaning devoid of the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) that constitutes its head; thus, the world exists within *māyā*.
The meaning is that [the Lord] incessantly utters the word "I" (*ahaṃ*), which is formed from the stem *asmat* and ends in the letter *ha* with the vowel *a* preceding it;
this is because the word *asmad* is derived from either the roots *as* (to throw) or *as* (to eat) according to the rule *yuṣyasibhyāṃ madik*.
Alternatively, [it refers to Him] who exists in the form of the entire universe, since there is no other means of valid cognition [for such a being].

The meaning is: because it is rootless and outside the scope of the Upaniṣads (the "head" of the Vedas), we worship our own Self, which is the immediate reality, as being headless, ending with the letter *ha*, incessantly uttering "So 'ham" (That am I) due to its nature as the single essence of non-dual, supreme consciousness, moving about having cast off [all else], or having extracted and consuming [it]. However, in the *Saṃgraha*:

The reading is "with the head, beginning with the letter *ha*. And that mantra, "haṃsa," beginning with *ha* and accompanied by the head (*sa*), which resides in all forms of bodies— whether of gods, humans, animals, and so forth— is incessantly [recited] every day in the form of the *ajāpā-gāyatrī*, numbering twenty-one thousand six hundred times.

The meaning is "rising by way of the pretext of inhalation and exhalation. The substitution of *śatṛ* for the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) in the word *udaścaraḥ*—which would otherwise require the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) because it takes an object—is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively, in the word *so*, the vowel *a* is not retained where it has been removed by the rule of prior form (*pūrvarūpa*). Thus, it is a word consisting of no *a* at all (*aśeṣākāram*).

Therefore, it is established as being "headless"—meaning devoid of the first letter which constitutes the head—and ending with the letter *ha*, such that the word *ahaṃ* (I) remains as the letter *ha* alone; this refers to the mantra *so'ham*.
The phrase "uttering it incessantly" and so forth is to be understood as before. || 13 ||
Others said:
"Those who, having abandoned the Lord who dwells in the cave of the heart, go to another god,
are like those who desire a jewel while having cast away the Kaustubha gem held in their own hand."

The meaning is that this is well-known from such scriptural passages as: "The Lord of the cave of the heart, the Person the size of a thumb, the inner self, is eternally seated in the hearts of people; the Person the size of a thumb is like a smokeless light; He is the Lord of the past and the future; He alone is today, and He is tomorrow. || 14 ||
Others said:
"Indeed, by renouncing all hopes, this fruit is obtained, whereby the very root-stalks of the poisonous creepers of hope are severed. (15)

Others say that dispassion (*vairāgya*) alone is the primary means for attaining that [Brahman], stating: "All desires... This Brahman, which is the fruit of knowledge and resides within the heart, is attained—that is, reached—by which [attainment] the knot of the heart becomes loosened; that knot which is entangled by the web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) rooted in the root-ignorance. As it is said: "Even the craving for this [world] ceases upon seeing the Supreme."
The meaning is that this is because of the words of the Blessed One. || 15 ||
Others said:
"That dull-witted man who, even after perceiving the extreme lack of flavor in all worldly objects, again forms attachments to them—he is no mere donkey. (16)
Regarding objects, that is, objects of enjoyment; *bhāvanām* means the thirst for enjoyment. || 16 ||
Others said:
"One should repeatedly strike these serpents of the senses—whether they have arisen or not—with the staff of discernment, just as Indra strikes mountains with his thunderbolt. (17)

Others, with the intention that the restraint of the senses alone is the primary means of accomplishment, say: "Those who have risen," etc. *Hari* here refers to Indra. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Each single sense-organ (*indriya*) is a destroyer; yet that very same thing, when purified, becomes like nectar even though it is poison. And likewise:
Also in the *Bhārata*: "The senses alone are all that constitutes both heaven and hell;
when restrained they lead to heaven, and when unleashed, to hell. (17)
Others said:
"The pure one who possesses perfect tranquility attains the bliss of peace;
the virtuous mind reaches serenity."
For one whose mind is pacified, there arises a supreme and enduring stability in the bliss of one's own true nature. || 18 ||

Others, however, with the intention that tranquility (*upaśama*) alone is the primary means and everything else is for its sake, conclude [the discussion] with the word "tranquility" (*upaśama*). Tranquility is the cessation of the activity of the external and internal senses; by that—

One should bring about—that is, accomplish—the happiness of the Self that has become manifest, which is like the subsiding of the suffering of distraction. For that [happiness] is not a cause of defect like sensual pleasure; rather, it is pure because it is a cause of mental clarity. Through the power of tranquility (*śama*), the mind proceeds toward stillness and dissolution, like a fire without fuel. Thus, for one whose mind is pacified, there is happiness.

The meaning is that stability in one's own, innate, supreme reality— which is unsurpassed bliss— constitutes the highest seventh stage, characterized by firm establishment through the sequential ascent of the stages, lasting for a long time until the attainment of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*). || 18 ||
Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Songs of the Siddhas," in the section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki.
Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Song of the Siddhas," in the Upaśama-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Ninth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus heard these songs sung by the hosts of Siddhas, the lord of the earth—
He quickly fell into despondency, like a coward at the mere sound of battle. || 1 ||
In this world, for a learned king who has returned home out of disillusionment, a mental determination regarding the roots of wealth is set forth through deliberation. (1)
One who is timid is *bhīruḥ*, characterized by fear. When there is elision of *ḍhra*, the preceding vowel becomes long, provided it is followed by a *ṇa*. (Pāṇini 6.3.111)
He went toward his own home, drawing along his retinue,
like the flood of a river following the trees on its banks as it flows toward the ocean.
One's own family circle. || 2 ||
Having dismissed his entire retinue to their respective dwellings,
he alone ascended to the foremost palace, like the sun ascending the mountain.
Having dismissed each to their own abode, that is, their respective homes; "home" meaning a house or palace; and the immovable mountain, the Mountain of Sunrise (Udayādri). || 3 ||
There, observing the world’s course as it flickered like the wings of birds eager to fly upward, he lamented thus, overwhelmed with agitation: || 4 ||

The wings of the birds, fluttering as they soared, appeared like the quivering bases of their feathers—meaning they were agitated and frail. Thus, with agitation, he lamented in the manner about to be described regarding the courses of the world, that is, the conditions of visible objects such as the body and so forth. || 4 ||
Alas, what misery! Amidst these most painful states of worldly agitation, I am forced to wallow like one stone against others, as if I were merely a stone myself. (5)
For the living beings of the worlds, amidst the flickering conditions of birth, old age, fear, death, and so forth;
the simile of the stone is intended to illustrate their dullness and hardness of heart. || 5 ||
Only a tiny fraction of infinite time is lived by me; yet I fix my attachment upon it—shame on me, this base-minded being! (6)

Although the category of living beings (*jīvadhātu*) is intransitive, according to the statement of Kātyāyana—"time, state, and the distance to be traversed are designated as objects for intransitive verbs"—the suffix *la* is used in the sense of time as the object in the expression "it is lived" (*jīvyate*). Even in such a life, [he sought] only the state of hope. (6)
How insignificant is this so-called kingdom of mine, lasting only as long as my life!
Why do I remain in such misery without it, like one whose intellect is destroyed? (7)

"Until life lasts" means for the duration of one's life, [this] kingdom. By this alone, being satisfied with only this much, the meaning is: why do I remain like a dull-witted fool in misery, without the thought of counteracting future suffering? Or else, by this—by only this much—the one whose intellect is "struck down," whose mental adjuncts are destroyed, remains without suffering like one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
"I remain free from suffering—how so?"—this should be understood as an interrogative tone. || 7 ||
In the beginning and at the end I am infinite, yet in the middle my life is fragile;
like a child with a painted moon, why do I vainly maintain my composure? (8)
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the body itself is the self? Upon its destruction, would there not be the cessation of all suffering along with it?

To this he says, "In the beginning," etc. For, in the absence of the seeds of desire, action, and latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the birth that serves as the cause for the diversity of experiences cannot be established; furthermore, this must be accepted in accordance with the authority of the scriptures concerning injunctions, prohibitions, and liberation.

The meaning is that I am both beginningless and endless, and not merely the body. "By the body" means by that which is grasped as the self through non-selfhood—just as a child might grasp a painted moon, mistaking it for the real moon.
"Dhṛti" means consolation. || 8 ||
Alas, what a pity! I am utterly bewildered by this ensnaring net of Indra, devoid of all conceptual proliferation; by whom have I been so completely deluded? (9)
By what ensnaring magician have I been utterly deluded? || 9 ||
Whatever object there may be, whatever is beautiful, whatever is noble or unartificial—none of that exists here at all; upon what, then, is my mind fixed? (10)

That which is called a "receptacle" (vastu)—meaning that which is real, delightful, consisting solely of happiness, noble, unlimited, unartificial, and free from birth—does not exist at all here in this world. The ellipsis implies: "In what, then, could there be a finality or repose? What could be its ultimate foundation? (10)
"Even that which is far away is not far for me when it abides in my mind";
having thus resolved, I completely renounce the mental cultivation of external objects. (11)
[Objection: "But surely such an object would be well-known in a distant place? [The author] says "no": "That which is situated afar" (*dūrastham*).

Even some object that is well-known as being situated afar is, in fact, not situated afar. Why? Because it exists within my mind. For the mind does not go outside the body to a distance; if it did, it would indeed be far away.
That manifestation would not be experienced within the heart; for it is only within the heart that one experiences the cognition of all external objects.

Therefore, even the conceptualization of distance and so forth, though appearing internally, is not real and is thus merely useless; the meaning is that such contemplation should be abandoned and never adopted. || 11 ||
The constant flux and rapid movement of the world is as fragile as a whirlpool in water; though it is seen even today to lead only to suffering, why is there still this attachment to pleasure? (12)

The constant rushing to and fro of people in the world for the sake of enjoyment—consisting of activities such as the acquisition of wealth—is seen to be as fragile and perishable in its fruit as a whirlpool in water, and it is repeatedly observed to be the cause of the sufferings of birth, death, and so forth; this is with respect to the happiness of sense objects. || 12 ||
Year by year, month by month, day by day, and moment by moment,
pleasures are but lumps of suffering, while sufferings themselves recur again and again.

He elaborates on what has already been stated with the words beginning "year by year" (*pratyabdam*). The term *duḥkhapiṇḍāni* means "masses of suffering," that is, things densely packed with suffering.
The particle *tu* is used in the sense of emphasis (*evārthe*). || 13 ||
For that which is grasped is seen to be perishable and not truly cultivated;
it does not exist here for the wise, wherein their firm abiding might reside.
In this world, that which exists here— perceived for a short time and then immediately vanished,

such as the state of one's own kingdom and so forth— is not meditated upon nor even thought of because of its worthlessness; for even the distinguished state of Indra, Prajāpati, and others, renowned for being the most excellent, has been disregarded.

The meaning is that there is simply nothing here in this world where such an abiding—meaning an ultimate repose—could exist for the wise who possess discernment, even when it has been thoroughly investigated. || 14 ||
Those who today stand at the pinnacle of the great will, in a few days, fall low;
alas, what kind of confidence can there be when the greatness of the mind has been destroyed? 15.
The term *hata* (struck/ruined) is an epithet of the mind used for the purpose of censure. Regarding *mahattāyām*, it refers to the excellence of royal power and the like.
However, in the reading *hatacittamahaṃtāyām*, it should be construed as: "in such a way that the mind is ruined, [while] in the state of *ahaṃtā*—that is, in the pride of sovereignty. || 15 ||
Bound by no rope indeed, yet I am bound; free from mud, yet I am stained; fallen though standing above—alas, my state of being, O Self, is ruined! (16)
"Ātman" is a vocative address. Alternatively, it may be construed as a locative case ending (ātmani), meaning "abiding in one's own nature," with the case-ending suffix elided. || 16 ||
Why has this delusion come upon me all of a sudden, even though I am wise?
It is like a dark cloud that obscures the light and covers the sun's peak.
Asita is dark-complexioned. The "front" (agra) of the sun refers to its eastern direction. || 17 ||
"What are these great enjoyments of mine? Who are these kinsmen of mine?
I am a fool, bewildered by a convention consisting of mere phenomena. (18)
By means of convention—that is, by the conceptual construction of a relationship characterized as "mine-ness. || 18 ||
Why do I myself bind this passion for old age and death—this very attachment that causes such distress—to these [objects]? (19)
Among these enjoyments and the like, he [perceives] that steadfastness—the reliance which brings about old age and death—as one who leads away his passionate beloved friend. || 19 ||
Whether it remains or passes away, what concern do I have for this?
For its beauty is like that of a bubble, appearing only thus through agitation.
What attachment or insistence can there be toward this prosperity consisting of enjoyments, kinsmen, and so forth? || 20 ||
Those great riches and enjoyments, those virtuous and affectionate kinsmen—all have entered the path of memory; when even this present moment is thus gone, what stability can there be? (21)

They were renowned as great sovereigns (*cakravartin*) such as Pṛthu, Mura, and others, possessing immense wealth; they were virtuous and endowed with excellent qualities. "All" is used in the neuter gender for the sake of generality. What stability or reliance can there be [in them]? 21.
Where are the riches of kings, or where are the worlds of Brahmā? Those of the past have passed away; what is this confidence of mine? (22)

"Where have the worlds—the universes—gone? [this is the question] regarding the ancient Brahmā, Hiraṇyagarbha, at the times of my destruction and so forth; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 22 ||
The virtuous will laugh at me, who am intent on preserving my life, as if I were millions of Indras swallowed like bubbles in water. (23)
"Swallowed by Time"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. Or, "fallen away" (galitāni) is an alternative reading. "The virtuous" refers to those who possess discernment. || 23 ||
Tens of millions of Brahmās have passed away, and successions of creations have gone by;
kings have vanished like dust—what stability can there be in my life? (24)
The mention of "ten million" is an indication of infinity, because saṃsāra is beginningless. *Dhṛti* means steadfastness. 24.

If I continue to maintain attachment to this delusion consisting of the body— the nightmare of the night of saṃsāra, wherein the objects of thought are themselves the fear— then shame on this state of mine! (25)

Saṃsāra itself is night because it consists of darkness; therein, within the delusion of the worldly conduct of "I" and "mine"—which is like a bad dream, consisting of the body and abounding in the body—there is "abiding," meaning the lack of self-restraint and lack of discernment. || 25 ||
"This is that 'I'"—this is a futile conceptualization whose nature is unreal.
Why do I remain like an ignorant person, possessed by the demon of egoism? (26)
"This" (*ayam*) is the conceptualization of proximity in that which is near to the body; "that" (*saḥ*) is the conceptualization of remoteness in that which is distant from it;
and "I" (*aham*) is the conceptualization of selfhood within the body. All three of these are indeed of an unreal nature.
Therefore, the ellipsis is: "deluded by the demon of egoism. Why am I like an ignorant person, acting without reflection? What for?
The meaning is that he has remained for such a length of time. || 26 ||
"Slain, slain is this [life]! Why? Because of this stretched-out lifespan;
though I see it, I do not perceive the subtle line of time. (27)

Although I see this life being struck down—struck down by the subtle line of time consisting of moments, instants, and hours, severed again and again at every moment—why do I not see it? The meaning is: why do I not reflect upon it? || 27 ||
Those who once treated the footstool as their seat and played with the Śārṅga bow as a mere ball have now been devoured by the Kāla-Kāpālikas; why do you prance about, placing your hope in me?

Those by whom even the lords and masters, such as Brahmā and others, were made to bow or were treated like footstools upon worlds fashioned as footstools; those by whom the bodies of Viṣṇu and others, the wielders of the Śārṅga bow, were repeatedly tossed into the sky during activities such as battles like play-balls; such [beings].

Even those Rudras, who are Kāpālikas by virtue of holding a skull of Brahmā in their hands and whose form is the time characterized by a great kalpa, have been devoured by Mahākāla. O Hope, you who are but a remnant of my life, why do you prance and dance before me? (28)
These days continue to arrive and depart incessantly even now;
yet not a single day has been seen that is not destroyed by the one truly existent reality. (29)

They approach, meaning they come; and even at this age, they go, meaning they depart in vain. That single, indestructible, eternal, and flawless reality, whose sole essence is bliss, has been attained, yet a day such as that has not been seen even until this very moment—that is, up to the present time. || 29 ||
Just as cranes [are found] in a lake, so too within every human heart only enjoyments manifest internally, but not the vision of one's own true state. (30)
The "visions" (*dṛṣṭayaḥ*) are the direct realizations (*sākṣātkārāḥ*) of that supreme state which is one's own innermost self.
"I have fallen from misery to even greater misery, gone from suffering to even deeper suffering;
yet even now I am not dispassionate—alas, shame on me, whose disposition is so base! (31)
One whose mind (āśaya) is base because it is corrupted by passion, greed, and so forth. || 31 ||
Whatever auspicious objects one has firmly fixed their meditation upon, those very things are seen to perish; what, then, is the highest [attainment] in this world? (32)
Cultivation is joy regarding beautiful and delightful objects and sensory domains. || 32 ||
Whatever is pleasing in the middle, at the end, or upon first sight—all that is indeed impure, defiled by destruction and filth. (33)
In the middle, youth is delightful; in the end, the Dharma is delightful; at first encounter, the sense objects are delightful. || 33 ||
In whatever objects a person fixes his resolve, in those very same things, the rise of their destruction is seen by him most intensely. (34)
Firm resolve and steadfastness. Of that man. This is well known. The arising of destruction is the manifestation of suffering. || 34 ||
Day by day this dull-witted person here reaches a state that is more sinful, even more cruel, and increasingly sweat-inducing. (35)
He states that for the ignorant person, there is no hope of rest even at a later time—expressing this with the words "day after day":

[the state] becomes more sinful through the increase of passion, greed, and so forth; more cruel due to engagement in violence and other such acts; and more distressing at the time of experiencing its results. (35)
Struck solely by ignorance in childhood, struck by passion in youth, and in the remainder of life afflicted by anxiety for his wife—when and what can the fool ever do? (36)
"In the remaining stage of life," he is distressed by anxiety regarding the maintenance of his wife and family—by which the household is implied.

In the reading "distressed for wealth" (*vittārta*), it means he is distressed by the loss of his wife, wealth, and so forth. "When will he ever perform the means for his own salvation?"—the meaning is: never at all. || 36 ||
Why does that fool perceive this saṃsāra—which is subject to coming and going, tasteless, corrupted by the inequality of conditions, and whose essence is devoid of substance? (37)
It comes and goes, being non-existent at its beginning and end; even during the time of enjoyment, it is tasteless;

it is corrupted by the inequalities of states such as poverty, disease, and old age. It is indeed essence-less, yet it is grasped with the notion that it is essence. Why does one look upon it in vain? Or rather, the meaning is: for what purpose does one look at that which one sees? || 37 ||
Even by performing hundreds of sacrifices such as the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha,
one attains heaven for a duration lasting until the end of a great kalpa, but no more.

One might ask: "Could heaven not be the essential [goal], characterized as it is by the scriptural statement beginning with 'that which is unmixed with suffering'? To this he replies: "By means of the Rājasūya... Even heaven, which is enjoyed by Brahmā and others until the end of a great kalpa, one perceives through the vision of the Great Time (mahākāla) as being merely a small fragment, consisting for the most part of momentary enjoyment.
The meaning is that since it is neither more nor unlimited, it is indeed essence-less. || 38 ||
What region of heaven or of the netherworld (pātāla) exists on earth where these calamities do not overwhelm one, like ill-behaved bees? (39)

Based on the Vedic scripture, "For one who possesses a body, there is no removal of pleasure and pain," and because it is heard that even those in heaven are afflicted by asuras and others, the intention is that even for him [the soul], freedom from the intermingling of suffering is not possible; with this in mind, he asks: "Who is this? (39).
How indeed can these mental anxieties and physical ailments—which are like wild beasts in the forest of one's own mind and like sprouts upon the ground of the body—be warded off? (40)

Furthermore, with the intention that as long as there is identification with the body, mental and physical ailments (ādhi-vyādhi) are difficult to ward off and thus the ignorant person finds no rest anywhere, he says: "nijā... (verse 40).

Existence stands at the summit of non-existence; in delightful things lies the pinnacle of unloveliness; in pleasures dwell the peaks of suffering—what single thing, then, shall I take refuge in? (41)

He elaborates upon the inauspiciousness of everything due to its perishability and its being seized by suffering, beginning with the words "of that which exists" (*sataḥ*). "Of that which exists" refers to what is perceived in the present time. "Non-existence" (*asattā*) means destruction. || 41 ||
Ordinary, lowly creatures are born and die;
by them alone the earth is packed solid, yet truly virtuous men are difficult to find. (42)
Ordinary people, deluded by innate ignorance which is natural and inherent—meaning it is "nīrandhra," that is to say, dense and compact—[do not perceive this]. || 42 ||
With eyes like rows of blue lotuses and adorned with supreme love, these playful women exist merely for the sake of laughter, as they are subject to momentary destruction. (43)
The ellipsis is "they are fit only for laughter. || 43 ||
There exist such persons by whose closing and opening of the eyes the dissolution and creation of the worlds occur;
what need is there even to count those like me?
To the objection—"Surely, since you are a king, a supreme person capable of restraining all, why do you have no confidence?"—he replies with the verse beginning "yeṣām" (of whom). || 44 ||
There are things more beautiful than the beautiful and more stable than the stable; yet this splendor of material objects ends in anxiety—what do you desire? 45.
"Anxiety" refers to [the distress caused by] acquisition, preservation, separation, and so forth. "Whose ultimate result is anxiety alone"—such is this splendor of material objects;
therefore, why do you desire it? Why do you long for it? || 45 ||
And as for those various prosperities which are approved by the mind—alas, I consider even they to be great calamities, being fraught with great undertakings. (46)

The meaning is this: if those various prosperities—which are diverse, consisting of different kinds of jewels, elephants, horses, wealth, wives, and so forth—were highly esteemed and much desired by the mind, then I consider even them to be "great calamities," because they require great undertakings, are obtained with much effort, must be guarded with difficulty, and are inevitably subject to loss. || 46 ||
Even those various calamities, if they are approved by the mind, I consider them to be great undertakings—indeed, I deem them to be riches within the mind. (47)
In this way, even those calamities characterized by poverty, the loss of kinsmen, the destruction of sovereignty, and so forth—
if they are mentally accepted as being various forms of ultimate good through their leading one to the company of the virtuous, sacred fords, austerity, spiritual awakening, and the like—
then I consider them to be true riches, for they initiate the great undertakings of discernment, dispassion, and other virtues; such is the meaning.
In this world, which is a mere manifestation of mind and as fragile as a bubble on the ocean, from where has this unprecedented string of syllables "this is mine" arisen? (48)

Therefore, in this unreal world, the increase of possessiveness (*mamatā*) is indeed calamity, while its destruction through discernment (*viveka*) alone is prosperity. With this intention, he demonstrates the world’s unworthiness for possessiveness, stating: "It is a mere product of the mind" (*manomātra*). Like the moon reflected in the ocean, it is fragile—meaning its very nature is to break apart—and is false. It is merely a string of syllables.
Whence could there be a sequence of phonemes consisting of words and sentences? That is to say, it would be meaningless. || 48 ||

When the stability of the world has come about by a chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit," the distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted has been vainly imagined by a rogue. (49)

By way of a "crow-and-palm" coincidence—like the arrival of a crow and the falling of a palm fruit upon its head—through a connection established by mere lack of reflection, [it was seized] by the mind, which is cunning and greedy for enjoyment. (49)
Why am I attached to these visions—which are limited, severed, and scorched, and which bear the name of "pleasure"—any more than a moth is drawn to the flames of a fire? (50)

In the case of the lamp’s flame, it is clear that they are "cut off" by a limitation consisting of place, time, and substance; they are "delimited," and because they are seized by the three kinds of suffering, they are "tormented. || 50 ||
It would be better to wallow in the fires of Raurava, where there is constant burning,
than to remain amidst the cycles of worldly existence, which are never-ending and full of fluctuations.

With the intention that even the experience of uninterrupted suffering might become tolerable through habituation, whereas this experience of suffering—interrupted by the enjoyment of pleasure—is indeed unbearable, he says: "Better... (varam). In these [states], the alternations of pleasure and pain have been "ālūnāḥ," meaning severed. "Sthitam" means a state of being; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). || 51 ||
It is said that cyclic existence itself is the very limit of sufferings;
how, then, can happiness be found in a body fallen within its midst? (52)

He establishes through reasoning that there is no pleasure whatsoever in the pleasures of sense objects, but rather that they consist solely of specific forms of suffering—thus: "In saṃsāra... (verse 52).
Those who are established in this cycle of existence, which is characterized by unartificial and great suffering, perceive other sufferings as being quite sweet. (53)
How, then, is the experience of pleasure there justified? He states the reasoning: "akṛtrimā" (unfabricated).
The meaning is that, just as the experience of a whip-lash is considered a pleasure after the experience of a sword-stroke, they perceive and consider only sufferings to be sweet pleasures. || 53 ||
I too, remaining as indifferent toward the lowest and the highest as toward wood or a clod of earth, have attained equality with the ignorant who have grasped the supreme reality. (54)

The meaning is this: although I am skilled in the means of valid knowledge such as the Śruti and Smṛti, possessed of intelligence, and adept at inquiry, I do not at all share the same nature as those ignorant fools who have neither purified nor investigated the objects of the scriptures, the world, and the means of valid knowledge. || 54 ||
Of this tree of saṃsāra, which abounds in thousands of sprouts, branches, fruits, and shoots, the mind is the great root-sprout. (55)
Now, he brings his own proficiency in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to fruition by determining the root of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), beginning with the word "sahasra" (thousand).

The sprouts are volitions (*saṃkalpa*); the branches are the body, the worlds, and so forth; the self (*ātman*) is the whole consisting of the branches and other parts, namely the Virāj; the fruits are pleasure and pain; and the foliage consists of passion and greed—by these it is characterized as "possessing" (*śālinaḥ*).
Of the one who is shining. || 55 ||
I consider that to be nothing but volition; therefore, by the cessation of volition, I shall wither it away, so that the tree of worldly existence may reach its withered end.
He says that even the secret of the mind is known by oneself alone: "Only the volition... (verse 56).

I shall no longer take delight even today in these activities of the monkey-mind, which are charming only in their outward form and lead inevitably to destruction, once they have been fully understood.
Regarding the activities and restlessness of the monkey-mind: this very day, from this moment forward. (57)
Pierced by hundreds of snares of hope, and subject to the afflictions of repeated falls and rises, I have experienced the cycles of worldly existence; now I shall rest.
Falling is downward motion; rising is upward motion, or alternatively, decrease and increase; affliction is suffering. || 58 ||
"Alas, I am struck down! I am ruined! I am dead!"—thus have I grieved again and again;
but now that it has passed, I do not weep for it. (59)
Thus, that which I previously lamented again and again has indeed passed; the meaning is that I do not weep nor do I grieve now. || 59 ||
I am awakened; I am delighted, for this thief of the self has been seen.
This thing called "mind" I shall slay; by the mind I have long been slain.

To the question "Why do you not grieve for that?", he says: "I am awakened. He is the thief, the plunderer, of my own wealth which is the ultimate reality of the Self. He says "with the mind" to show that I shall destroy him not only because he is a thief, but also because he is an enemy. || 60 ||
For all this time, this pearl of my mind remained unpierced;
now, however, it has been pierced and is worthy of the string.

"Unpierced" means not made into a target. In the case of a pearl, it means unperforated. "Quality" (guṇa) refers to tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth; in the case of a pearl, it refers to the thread. || 61 ||
Surely this dewdrop of the mind, having long persisted, will soon dissolve through the heat of the sun of discernment. (62)

The eternal reality of Brahman exists there for the sake of engaging in [liberation] and for the sake of its firm establishment. In the case of the "particle of frost" (tuṣārakaṇikā), "long-standing activity" refers to the ever-moving wind (*sadāgati-vāyu*), for the purpose of attaining it; the meaning is that this is according to the Vedic scripture: "When the waters dry up, they merge into the wind alone. || 62 ||
I have been well enlightened by various holy Siddhas;
I follow after the Self, which is the means to supreme bliss.

[This is] through various instructions; or rather, it is a qualification of the Siddha. Merely by following [the path], there is the realization of one's own supreme bliss. Although there is non-duality, the status of being an instrument is used figuratively. 63.
Having found the jewel of the Self in solitude and beholding it with joy,
I remain here with all other worldly concerns subsided, like an autumnal cloud upon a mountain.
Therefore, he says "the Self" (ātmānam) to express that he will never abandon his steadfastness in the Supreme Self; [he will remain] on a mountain such as the Himalaya, which is immovable. || 64 ||
Having forcibly cast out from within the unreal flashings of "I am this" and "this is mine," and having struck down the exceedingly powerful enemy that is the mind, [one remains].
I attain tranquility; salutations be to you, O Viveka! 65.
Now, summarizing what has been said, he pays homage to the Guru of Discrimination with the words "This":

having cast off by the power of knowledge this pervasive, unreal form that flashes forth as "this body is I" and "this wealth, kingdom, and so on are mine," and having utterly destroyed the exceedingly powerful enemy of the mind through the practice of *samādhi*.
I attain, that is, I reach, the tranquility characterized by resting on the seventh stage. || 65 ||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Janaka’s Reflection," in the Section on Quiescence (*Upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Sages (*Ārṣa*). 9.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Reflections of Janaka," in the *Upaśamaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Tenth Canto. 10.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
As he was reflecting thus, [the Lord] entered before him.
The doorkeeper was like Aruṇa at the front of the chariot of the supreme Sun. || 1 ||
When the doorkeeper requested that the sequence of the midday rites be performed elsewhere, Janaka’s reflection was again described in silence. || 1 ||
*Pratīhāraḥ* means a doorkeeper; the lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *upasargasya ghañy amanuṣye bahulam*. || 1 ||
The doorkeeper said:
"O Lord, whose every ornament of the Vāsava dynasty rests upon the pillar of your arm,
arise and perform the royal duties appropriate for the day."
Upon whose two pillar-like arms rests the entire burden of the earth—
these women, who are worthy and fitting for his sovereignty, stand ready upon the bathing ground with jars of water scented with flowers, camphor, and saffron, like rivers incarnate.
In this regard, he states the accomplishment of the causal complex (sāmagrī) with the words beginning "these" (etāḥ), etc. (verse 3).
These bees, wandering through the groves of lotuses and water-lilies,
have fashioned pavilions of cloth from the nets of lotus fibers.

In these [regions], pavilions variegated with gold were constructed all around, beautifully fashioned from lotus-stalk ropes together with cords of lotus-fibers; it is because they are of such a nature that these banks of the lotus-filled lake Kamalavatī possess a mottled color—thus connects with what follows. || 4 ||
These grounds on the banks of the lotus pond are filled with parasols,
as well as with chowries, chariots, elephants, and horses belonging to those who attended upon him during his bathing rites.
Likewise, at the time of bathing, they were served by people of that character with chowries, and the [banks] were filled with chariots, elephants, horses, and umbrellas;
by this, it is implied that the riverbanks attained a resemblance to lakes containing swans, cranes, frogs, lotuses, and the like. || 5 ||
Likewise, the temples for the worship of the gods were prepared with caskets filled with complete garlands and overflowing with food and medicinal herbs.

With all kinds of beautiful flowers, with full vessels containing trusted servants, with cooked foods, and with medicinal herbs overflowing with barley sprouts and the like—all well-adorned; [if the reading is *ratnauṣadhī* rather than *oṣadhibhiḥ*, the meaning is clear]; with *paṭalakas*, meaning the bordering sections; "O God" is the form of address; [this refers to] the house of worship.
The houses for the worship of gods, brahmins, and guests; or alternatively, "houses for the worship of gods" may be read as a single compound. || 6 ||
Having bathed, with purifying grass in hand, and having recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn,
O God, this assembly of twice-born men worthy of sacrificial fees gazes upon you alone.

At the time of your bath, the Aghamarṣaṇa mantras must be recited all around you; for this very reason, O Supreme Lord, you are worthy of sacrificial fees and are protected by women with shimmering chowries in their hands.
Your cool dining areas have been prepared by those lovely ladies. (8)
They are cool and refreshing because they are adorned with applications of sandalwood paste, sprinkling of water, and other such refinements. || 8 ||
Arise quickly; may prosperity be yours! Perform the task that must be done. Great men do not let the proper time pass by for their own duties.
When the doorkeeper had thus spoken,
the king then reflected in that same manner upon the wondrous nature of worldly existence.
How small indeed is this so-called happiness of sovereignty!
I have no need for this, which perishes in an instant.
Having completely abandoned the entire deceptive display of Śambara,
I remain in solitude alone, like a perfectly tranquil ocean.
By the word "śambara," the illusion of Śambara (śāmbarī-māyā) is indicated; it refers to the false Śambara, which is like the water of a mirage, or something similar to that. || 12 ||
Enough with these manifestations of enjoyment of mine, which consist mostly of what is unreal;
having abandoned all activities, I shall remain in pure happiness alone. (13)
O mind, abandon this cleverness born from the delusive attachment to the practice of enjoyments, for the sake of pacifying the mire of the snare of birth, old age, and dullness. 14.
O mind, abandon cleverness and the skillfulness that relishes even a fragment of pleasure.
O mind, you shall encounter supreme suffering produced from those very same conditions toward which you perceive such agitation during their respective periods. 15.

In those states consisting of longing for sense objects, the effort toward them, the enjoyment of them, and the recollection of them, [one experiences] agitation, the delusion of tasting a mere fragment of pleasure, or enthusiasm. (15)

Whether engaged in worldly activity or withdrawn from it, the mind never attains satisfaction, even after experiencing [pleasures] again and again for a very long time across all the realms of enjoyment. (16)
Having been set in motion by the desire for enjoyments, it ceases once its power to enjoy has become blunted and due to fear of the world, the scriptures, and so forth. || 16 ||
Therefore, enough of this vain concern for enjoyments which leads only to evil;
pursue instead that by which unartificial contentment arises. (17)
Therefore, since artificial pleasures are the seeds of misfortune, seek—that is to say, obtain—that cause by which unartificial joy arises. || 17 ||
Having reflected thus, Janaka became silent indeed;
with his restless mind stilled, he was like a figure depicted in a painting. (18)
The doorkeeper, too, being well-versed in the mental dispositions of kings, spoke no further word out of both respect and fear. (19)
Regarding the fluctuations of the mind and those things that follow the lead of the mind. || 19 ||
Then, having remained silent for a moment, Janaka again reflected with a mind endowed with tranquility upon the life of living beings.
The life-force of people is the cause of the life of all living beings, according to the Vedic revelation: "By it, those that are born live. (20)
What is there here to be accepted that I should strive to accomplish?
Upon what object, free from destruction, shall I fix my steadfastness? (21)
What is the use of my being intent on action, or what is the use of my being inactive?
For there is nothing that has arisen which is not subject to destruction.
Alternatively, the word "effect" (kāryam) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. For indeed, whatever birth has arisen and been attained does not exist without destruction;
the meaning is that there is a necessary rule of destruction for any produced entity. || 22 ||
Whether this body be active or inactive, it arises from what is unreal;
for me, who am pure consciousness established in equanimity, what loss can there possibly be? (23)

For the consciousness that remains perfectly established—abiding in an identical state whether the body moves or is motionless, and whose very nature is pure consciousness—I do not desire what has not been attained, nor do I abandon what has been attained.
Abiding in the Self, I remain as I am; let whatever belongs to me remain mine. (24)

The meaning is: "Let there be only that which has been brought to me by my past karma (*prārabdha*), and nothing else. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Let there be only that internal state of mine which consists of unsurpassed bliss, and let there be no external thing whatsoever. || 24 ||
I have no purpose here in this world through what is done, nor any at all through what is not done;
whether by action or by non-action, that which is obtained is composed of unreality.

By "neglect through non-action," the word "some misfortune" is to be understood as the ellipsis. By "non-performance" or "indifference," one encounters suffering that is unreal, consisting of illusion; that is to say, it is merely false. || 25 ||
Whether I am acting or not acting, my deeds—whether appropriate or inappropriate—are such that there is nothing here desired by me that has attained the state of being worthy of acceptance. 26.
"Appropriate" means those prescribed by the scriptures; "inappropriate" means those prevalent in the world. || 26 ||
Therefore, having risen, let this body perform its natural activity as it has duly arrived;
for why should it wither away well while its limbs remain motionless? (27)

[This body] has reached its present state through the sequence of successive worldly transactions. Yet this body is wasting away with its limbs motionless; is that good? The meaning is: "Is it not necessary [to act]? || 27 ||
When the mind is steady, free from desire, equanimous, and devoid of passion,
the movement and stillness arising from the parts of the body are equal in their result.
The two effects, brought about by prārabdha-karma, are equal in their result, characterized by the non-arising of merit and demerit.
When the mind [perceives] itself as the agent and enjoyer regarding the fruits of fortune born of karma,
once that [mind] has attained peace, even what was done by men is as if undone.

To explain why that is so, he says: "In those born of karma. It should also be applied thus: even what has been done is as if undone, and even what has been experienced is as if unexperienced. || 29 ||
Whatever firm resolve is rooted within a person regarding actions, that very resolve attains identity with them;
my intellect has reached the state free from affliction.
I abandon the intermediate state of impatience. || 30 ||

The actual state of affairs is this: the internal resolve of a person—whether it be the conviction that "I am the doer" or "I am the enjoyer"—causes that person to attain identification with all activities of the body and so forth, consisting of the object determined by their own resolve. But now, for me, O wise one, the state of the Self has been struck down, being free from the disease of being a doer or an enjoyer.
"Disturbed" means being devoid of firm resolve. Therefore, within the mind,

there arises a doubt caused by the fear of obtaining rebirth and so forth due to the inevitable occurrence of the fruits of actions performed or left undone, as well as a doubt caused by the obstruction of attaining the desired or the undesired.
The meaning is: "I shall utterly abandon even this impure lack of fortitude. || 30 ||

Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "Janaka’s Resolution," in the Section on Quiescence (*Upaśamaprakaraṇa*) within the *Dehādvaita-mokṣopāya* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. || 10 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Janaka’s Resolution," in the *Upaśamaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Eleventh Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, Janaka performed the duties as they presented themselves.
He rose to act without attachment, just as the sun rises at the beginning of the day.
Now, after the king has performed his daily rites at the end of the night, his awakening of his own mind through many diverse discernments is described once more. (1)
Unattached means being free from attachment characterized by the conceit of agency and enjoyership. || 1 ||
Having himself abandoned, by means of his mind, all mental impressions regarding the desirable and the undesirable,
he acted according to whatever came to him, as if in deep sleep even while awake.

The latent impressions (*vāsanās*) are the causes of conceptualization, such as "this is desired by me" and "this is undesired by me. The phrase "as in deep sleep" implies that when there is an absence of identification with the gross and subtle bodies and so forth, there is no distinction between the waking state and deep sleep.

Having performed the duties of that day preceded by the honoring of the venerable ones—namely, the worshipful deities, Brahmins, and others—he spent the night alone in the playful absorption of meditation. (The reading *mekāntayaiva* is also found. "Honoring the venerable ones" refers to the worship and giving of gifts to the deities, Brahmins, and so forth.
The term *samādhāna* means "concentration" or "composing. The term *āhnika* refers to that which is to be done during the day. || 3 ||
Having made the mind equanimous and stilled the wandering toward sense objects, he thus awakened his consciousness as the night was waning: || 4 ||
Having made [the mind] of equal flavor and concentrated, in the manner that will be described hereafter. (4)
The flickering mind in saṃsāra is not for the happiness of the self;
attain tranquility, for from tranquility, the peaceful, essential happiness is obtained.
It is peaceful, free from distraction, the essential reality, and the bliss of the Self. || 5 ||
To the very extent that you effortlessly conceive floods of conceptual constructions,
to that same extent does this cycle of existence expand through your own thinking.
Just as a tree attains a hundred branches through watering,
so too do you attain infinite suffering through your desire for the enjoyments of the wicked.
You attain endlessness, you reach a state possessing countless afflictions, and you undergo delusion.
The creations of birth and saṃsāra arise from the play of the web of thought (or, according to another reading, "from the arising of conceptual construction").
Therefore, having abandoned this manifold thought, you should attain tranquility.
The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: since the creations of birth and saṃsāra arise from the conceptual constructions of the web of thoughts concerning sense-objects. || 8 ||
O handsome one, weigh this world against the instability of the creation of saṃsāra;
if you find any essence within it, then resort to that alone.

O beautiful discerning one, weigh this creation of saṃsāra against the bliss of tranquility (śama-sukha) as if placing them on a scale with your intellect; examine which of the two possesses true essence. By the word "taralām" (unsteady), it is indicated that because it is perishable and entangled with the suffering of distraction, there is no essence here. || 9 ||
Since you have abandoned all reliance [on the self] out of a longing for the seen and the seer, do not grasp this, nor let it go; wander according to your own will and desire.

Since this [world] is essence-less, therefore, having abandoned attachment to it, do not grasp what is dear out of a longing for vision— thinking "this visible object is fit to be seen"— nor release what is unpleasant out of aversion— thinking "this is unworthy of being seen. Rather, act solely through the desire for the Self alone, which is the witness of both.
Being one who desires the Self, sport at will according to your own desire. 10.
Whether this visible world be unreal or real, whether it arises or passes away,
O virtuous one, do not fall into a state of agitation because of its merits or demerits.

The meaning is: let that which was previously non-existent—the cause of pleasure and pain—arise now as something existing, or let it go to its end and perish; do not, on account of its coming and going, fall into an imbalance characterized by joy and dejection. || 11 ||
There is not even the slightest connection between you and an object of perception;
what kind of connection could this be with that which has no existing form? (12)
[Objection: But if there is a connection with that [world], how is it possible to avoid the inequality caused by it? To this he says:
"Even in the slightest degree" (manāgapi). || 12 ||

This non-existence [of the relation] belongs to two things that are either both non-existent or both existent; that there can be a relation between them—this is a truly wondrous and unprecedented string of syllables! (13)
"The mind is non-existent; and this visible world is also not existent. Here, the particle *eva* is used in the sense of "also.

Therefore, the statement that there is a relationship between these two—which are both non-existent like the son of a barren woman and a flower in the sky, and which lack any established nature—is a series of syllables expressing something unprecedented; the meaning is that it is truly marvelous. || 13 ||
