Even if this unreal thing were to become real, O handsome one, tell me nonetheless: what kind of association could there be between the existent and the non-existent, such as that between a mortal and life? (14)

If you think, "I am not non-existent; the Self alone is real, and the visible world is indeed non-existent," even so, there can be no establishment of a relationship between them. Thus he says: "Non-existent"—referring to the mortal and the living, who are always [alternately] dead and living. || 14 ||
If both the mind and the object of perception were truly existent and eternally established, then from what source could the expansion of joy and sorrow arise? (15)

Since both [existence and non-existence] are indeed existent and not non-existent for anyone, even in any conceptual construction (kalpa) there is never an absence of separation from what is desired; thus there is no possibility of joy or sorrow. He says: "O mind" (*citta*), with the word break being "he *citta* tvam" (O mind, you). || 15 ||
Therefore, abandon this great delusion; bring forth joy for the mute [the unawakened]. Abandon this wretched state, which has entered upon you like a turbulent ocean.

Bring forth great resolve and dispel despondency; bring forth the enthusiasm for remaining forever established in the true nature of the Self through the practice of meditative absorption (samādhi), and [calm] the ocean characterized by agitation—that is, distraction. 16.
O noble-minded one, do not, like a ball struck by a clod of earth, burn yourself in vain and fall into dullness by succumbing to the impurity of delusion. 17.

The *kandukālāta* is a fire-wheel shaped like a ball, constructed from combustible materials for the purpose of exciting the curiosity of the people during festivals; it indeed leaps up again and again while burning by itself. "Moha" means enough, or it refers to delusion (*moha*) as its characteristic, or impurity (*mala*). || 17 ||
There is nothing here that is so exalted and supreme by which you might attain ultimate perfection; therefore,
relying upon it, summon great fortitude by force.
Abandon your fickleness, O rogue mind! || 18 ||
In this world, among all that is visible, there is nothing whatsoever by which you may attain fullness. How, then, is fullness attained? He states the means for that:
"Therefore"—that is, by relying on extreme fortitude through the power of practice and dispassion.
Or rather, having relied upon that Brahman and attained extreme fortitude, abandon—cast off—your fickleness. || 18 ||
Thus ends the eleventh canto, titled "Instruction on the Mind," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki;
and thus concludes [the section] in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*, in the Section on Tranquility.
The eleventh canto, titled "Instruction on the Mind."
The Twelfth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
While King Janaka was thus reflecting there in his own kingdom,
The one of steady intellect performed all his duties and did not fall into delusion. || 1 ||
In this [work], the state of Janaka as one liberated while living is described, as well as the wonderful greatness of inquiry and wisdom at length. (1)
The meaning is that he was not deluded by the notions of "I" and "mine," as previously described. || 1 ||
His mind did not leap forth toward any objects of joyful experience;
it remained perpetually established, as if in a state of deep sleep.
"In states of bliss" means in occasions for joy; "in which there is a state like deep sleep" is a qualifier for the action of abiding, meaning a state of non-distraction. || 2 ||
From that time forward, he neither grasped at the visible world nor did he abandon it;
he simply remained established in the present, free from all doubt.
While the present object is manifesting, he remains steadfast, established with the conviction that it is sufficient. || 3 ||
Through that constant solitude, he immediately attained the eternal state;
he never again incurred any stain, just as the sky is never again defiled by dust.

By means of unceasing solitude and by being constantly engaged in inquiry, one attains the eternal [Self], which has possessed its beginningless nature. The stain—consisting of the impurity of the egoistic conceits of "I" and "mine"—is stirred up by the quality of *rajas* and by worldly dust. (4)
Through his continuous pursuit of self-discernment, that lord of the earth attained a perfectly realized knowledge of infinite luster, which reached a state of stainless purity.
It has infinite luster and the form of Brahman, which is without limitation. || 5 ||
The conscious self, free from disease and untouched by the rays of conceptual thought,
arose in the space of his heart like the sun in the sky.

He whose rays of light are unobscured by conceptual constructions (vikalpa) or masses of clouds, and whose illumination is free from the distinctions of coloring and differentiation; he from whom have departed the maladies of suffering caused by the obstruction of the distinctions of the body. || 6 ||
He, the infinite self, who is skilled in knowing the self of all beings, beheld all entities established within the power of consciousness as being identical with his own self.

[He perceives] those [objects] which are established within the power of consciousness (cicchakti) in the conscious self (cidātman), yet are not superimposed upon it; for this very reason, they are, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthadṛśā), identical with the Self. || 7 ||
He was neither elated nor deeply distressed at anything;
because worldly affairs are merely the functioning of nature (*prakṛti*), his mind was always equanimous.
Since all worldly transactions consist of *prakṛti*—that is, *māyā* alone—the Self is seen to be unattached and untouched; thus, he is even-minded.
From that time forward, Janaka, the giver of honor, became liberated while living; he was a sage of mature wisdom who had realized the higher and lower nature of the world.
"Jaraṭhajñānī" means one who is advanced in knowledge; that is to say, one who is old in wisdom. || 9 ||
While ruling the kingdom of the Videhas, Janaka, the life of his people,
was not at all tormented by joy or sorrow, for he was no longer subject to their sway.
That is to say, he was as dear to people as their own life. || 10 ||
It neither sets nor rises due to the fluctuations of virtues and defects.

He does not undergo setting—the concealment of his true nature—nor rising—the manifestation of it—due to mental activities involving virtues and defects; nor does he rejoice or despond because of external gains and losses arising from sovereignty. This is the construction of the sentence in reverse order. || 11 ||
He neither desponds nor exults because of gains or losses arising from his kingdom;
even while acting, he does nothing at all anywhere.
He remains forever and always established within the consciousness.
The meaning is that it performs no action whatsoever because its nature is that of a non-agent. He states this very point with the word "sa" (he). || 12 ||
In the state of deep sleep, all mental impressions of King Janaka, the lord of the earth,
had entirely set, having vanished from all objects whatsoever.
Cultivation refers to the latent predispositions of passion and so forth. || 13 ||
He does not connect with the future, nor does he dwell upon the past;
rather, he follows the present moment as it passes, even while laughing.
He states the fruit of the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) with the words "it will come to be.

Due to the power of latent impressions, there is a connection between the past and the future; by means of that, there arises aversion toward things that caused harm in the past, and attachment for the sake of what is pleasant in the future, from which follows active engagement (*pravṛtti*). Thus, there is the consequence of all manner of misfortunes.

However, because he perceives only the present and does not disregard suffering, he does not contemplate its unpleasantness; thus, the meaning is that he laughs while continuing in his innate bliss. || 14 ||
O lotus-eyed Rāma, by the power of his own inquiry alone, he has attained everything that is to be attained in its entirety; it was not through any other desire.

Recalling the seed that introduced the narrative, he concludes with the words "svavicāra" (by his own inquiry): "By him, Janaka, [the goal] was attained in its entirety—that is, without remainder—merely through knowledge, like a golden necklace found around one's own neck that had been forgotten. || 15 ||
To whatever extent the limit of analytical investigations is reached, to that same extent one investigates by means of one's own mind alone. (16)

And thus, he says "tāvat" (so long), meaning that the inquiry must be carried out until the attainment of the fruit and should not be abandoned midway due to despondency; "pravicāryate" means one should investigate thoroughly. || 16 ||

That state which is attained from a heart purified by inquiry arising from association with the virtuous—that state is not reached through a guru, nor through the meaning of the scriptures, nor through merit. (17)
The statement that the means of practice, such as the guru and so forth, are not true means is intended to demonstrate the primacy of inquiry, just as it is said:
"Other animals are indeed no-animals; only cows and horses are animals. || 17 ||
O Rāma, the state is attained through one's own beautiful intellect as if through a companion, and not by any other name or ritual action.
By means of that female companion, Wisdom (prajñā)— an intellect skilled in reasoning and refutation, refined by the discernment of the true scriptures— [she was accompanied] by Sundarī.
For one whose flame of wisdom—sharp-tipped and wandering through the past and future—is ever ablaze, the blindness of dullness never afflicts him. (19)
Dullness is ignorance; its characteristic is blindness, which is darkness. || 19 ||
O Great-minded One, those calamities which are difficult to cross over and are crowded with waves of suffering are crossed by means of wisdom, as if by a boat. (20)
It is well known that people cross over those waters, which have fallen leaves for boats, by means of the boat of wisdom. || 20 ||
Even a slight misfortune afflicts a fool who is devoid of wisdom,
just as even a tiny gust of wind destroys a sapless stalk of grass.
*Pelavā* means soft; *anilasya kalā* means a mere fraction of the wind; *ulapa* is a specific kind of grass. || 21 ||
O crusher of enemies, O Rāma, even one who is delicate may indeed cross over the ocean of saṃsāra, provided he possesses wisdom, even if he is without companions and lacks weapons.
"Without a companion" means devoid of assistance from a guru or others; "without scripture" means even one who is devoid of hearing the scriptures.

This too is an exaggeration solely for the sake of praise, because it contradicts such Vedic texts as, "Knowledge, once known from the teacher alone, reaches its highest perfection," and so forth. O Rāma, [from] the "tender"—that is, from that which is exceedingly delicate because it is sublatable by mere knowledge—22.
One who possesses wisdom reaches the successful conclusion of his task even without assistance;
but one of poor intellect perishes, even when undertaking a primary enterprise.

In the world as well, it is well known that one endowed with wisdom possesses greater strength than others who possess merely physical power; thus he says: *prajā* is the mental state (*vṛtti*) of final direct realization; its possessor, the Self (*ātman*), is the end—the sublation—of all the manifold effects (*kāryaprapañca*), and the end—the ultimate limit—of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) that must necessarily be accomplished, namely, the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*).

And he attains it. The meaning is that delusion (*moha*), characterized by the continuity of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), even though it is the primary cause since it is the root of the entire collection of effects, perishes through mere knowledge once that [knowledge] has been reached.
This may also be construed according to the distinction between the side of the knower and the side of the ignorant (or, as it appears in some versions, "the side of knowledge"). || 23 ||

One should first increase one's wisdom through the study of the scriptures and association with virtuous people, just as one nurtures a creeper toward the attainment of fruit by beginning its watering and protection. (24)
If so, by what means is wisdom to be attained? To this he says: "By the Teacher," etc. (24).
With the great root of the power of wisdom, the tree of virtuous action bears fruit that is exceedingly sweet in its proper time, like the reflection of the moon in the water.

One whose root is the great power of wisdom (*prajñābala*)— such a person is like a tree characterized by good deeds (*satkārya*), virtuous actions (*satkarma*), and past fortune (*prāktanabhāgya*). Just as the light of the sun (*bhāsaḥ sūryaprakāśaḥ*) enters the lunar orb during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) in due order and becomes full, consisting of nectar (*amṛtamaya*).

The lunar orb bears fruit in that same way. Alternatively, the meaning is that the lunar orb, as the agent, just as it bears forth the moonlight—splendors that dispel the darkness of the world—likewise bears forth the knowledge of the Self, which is capable of destroying fundamental ignorance. || 25 ||
The very same effort that people exert in acquiring external objects should first be applied toward increasing one's wisdom. (26)
Whatever kind of effort or exertion there is, it is of that same kind; thus, the meaning is that there is no excessive labor involved. || 26 ||
One should destroy the dullness of wisdom—the boundary of all sufferings, the supreme treasury of calamities, and the seed of the trees of saṃsāra. (27)
The ultimate limit and the supreme boundary of all sufferings and misfortunes. || 27 ||
Whatever is obtained from heaven or the netherworld, and whatever sovereignty is attained—that all is secured by the high-souled one from the treasury of wisdom. (28)

Thus, he shows that the treasury of wisdom (*prajñā-kośa*) is likewise the source of all prosperity—by the words "from heaven" (*svargāt*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "the happiness which is obtained. According to the statement of the Purāṇas: "Nārada, having returned from the nether worlds (*pātāla*), declared in the midst of the celestial dwellers: 'The nether worlds are even more delightful than the heavenly realm (*svarloka*'). Thus, [this excellence] exists even in the nether worlds.
The excellence of happiness is well known. || 28 ||
O Raghava, one crosses over that terrible ocean of saṃsāra through wisdom; neither by gifts, nor by sacred fords, nor by austerity is this achieved.
He states that even the ultimate destruction of suffering has wisdom alone as its fruit, using the words "by wisdom" (prajñayā).
The underlying sense is that acts such as charity and austerity have only the destruction of minor sins as their result. || 29 ||
That even men who walk upon the earth have attained divine prosperity is the sweet fruit that has arisen from the creeper of wisdom and merit. (30)
And whatever other fruit of actions such as giving exists—namely heaven and so forth—that too is indeed the fruit of wisdom; thus he says, "That which...
The meaning is: even those men who move upon the earth have attained divine prosperity characterized by moving through the sky and so on—that too [is the fruit of wisdom]. || 30 ||
By means of their wisdom, jackals have conquered lions whose leaders of elephant herds have been torn apart by their claws— just as lions [conquer] deer.
Even through common means, kingship has been attained by men through the power of wisdom;
indeed, it is observed here that the fitness for heaven and liberation belongs only to the wise man.
Through wisdom, all debaters—who revel in their own conceptual constructions—conquer even those men who are exceedingly timid, as if they were formidable warriors. (33)
"Resembling excellent warriors," that is to say, those who are brave in debate. || 33 ||
This wisdom is a wish-fulfilling gem residing within the heart-treasury of the discerning; like a celestial kalpa-creeper, it bestows the very fruit one has contemplated. (34)
The capable one crosses the cycle of existence; the inferior one is cast away by wisdom.
The trained person reaches the further shore, while the untrained person does not reach it with a boat.
A trained fisherman is one who possesses the skill of navigating a boat. || 35 ||
Wisdom rightly applied leads one to the further shore, while wrongly applied it leads to the stateless;
like a boat tossing in the ocean, it causes a man to wander in saṃsāra. (36)

If the intellect (dhī) is properly directed onto the true path of discernment, dispassion, and so forth, it leads one to the further shore; however, if it is improperly directed onto the wrong path of passion, hatred, greed, and so forth, it leads to—or brings about—calamity. This is the meaning. || 36 ||
Faults arising from the multitude of desires do not afflict the discerning man who is undeluded and wise, just as arrows do not strike one who is well-armored.

Hope and craving are its partisans; the hosts consist of greed, delusion, anger, anxiety, and so forth. From these arise the defects—hatred, sorrow, despondency, and the like. "Equipped" means armored. 37.
O dear one, when this entire world is seen correctly through wisdom, neither calamities nor prosperities come to one who has attained right vision. (38)
He for whom there is right vision—that which is seen through the correct discernment of the reality of virtues and defects—is a person of right vision. || 38 ||
The vast and dark cloud of ignorance, which is the ego, is the veil over the supreme sun; intoxicated by it, it is dispelled by the wind of wisdom. (39)
The Supreme is the Supreme Self; He is the "covering" (*pidhānam*)—that is, the concealer—of the Sun characterized by that [Supreme].

Due to the non-distinction between the letters *la* and *ra*, in the sense of "cloud" (*ambuda*), He is "watery" (*jala-ātman*). He is "extended" (*vitataḥ*), meaning vast. He is "black" (*asitaḥ*), meaning not clear and blue. || 39 ||
For one who desires to attain the peerless state of a Buddha,
this very intellect must first be cherished,
just as a farmer seeking a harvest must first tend to his seed.
Indeed, the earth itself is drawn forth first of all. || 40 ||

Like a child, one should be nurtured and gradually purified through the instruction of discernment (*viveka*). The fruit is the fruit of cultivation, namely the increase of grain. "Nanu" is used here to indicate what is well-known. || 40 ||

Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Majesty of Wisdom," in the section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition. 12.
Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Greatness of Wisdom," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, having thus investigated the self by means of the self, as Janaka did, [one attains liberation].
You attain, without obstacle, the state of those who have known what is to be known. || 1 ||
Taking that reflection of Janaka as an illustration, the means for the pacification of the mind are here proclaimed in detail through reasoned arguments. (1)
"Without obstacle" means by way of removing hindrances such as lack of confidence and so forth. || 1 ||
For those wise people who are born later and possess a predominance of *rajas* and *sattva*, they attain by themselves that which is to be attained, just like Janaka.

The sense is that because passion (*rajas*) arises from human effort and goodness (*sattva*) results in the cultivation of mental clarity, those who are both passionate and good (*rājasasāttvika*) alone are qualified for the attainment of knowledge through their own discernment—just as one reaches for a fruit in the sky by means of a ladder. || 2 ||
Having repeatedly conquered those enemies known as the senses,
he remains until this self, by means of the self alone, becomes serene within the self.

He explains how they attain that state with the words "to such an extent, to such an extent" (*tāvattāvat*). The meaning is: as long as the Self becomes serene within itself through the accumulation of virtuous qualities (*sattva*), to that same extent one repeatedly conquers the enemies that are the senses by means of the power of suppressing *rajas*.
"When the all-pervading God, the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Self, has become serene... (3)
When one has personally perceived [the truth], all false views are extinguished.
Since the Supreme Self—the Lord who rules over all the gods and the senses, and who is the master—is Himself beheld through the internal organ, [all else follows]. || 4 ||
When that Supreme and Immanent One is seen, the fists of the seeds of delusion, the showers of various calamities, and false views all go to destruction.
The handfuls of evil latent impressions, which are the seeds of delusion, grasp things firmly within like a closed fist; and when sown in the field of the mind,
they become showers of various calamities and sufferings, distinguished as internal and so forth.
Like rain, they suddenly pour forth from all sides.
Wrong views—characterized by notions such as "I" and "mine"—are the knots of the heart.
Higher [blisses] range from human bliss up to the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha; lower means inferior.
Because it is of such a nature; and thus says the Śruti: "The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder, and one's karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. (5)
O Rāma, like Janaka, always regarding the self through wisdom in all undertakings, become possessed of fortune and supreme.

The meaning is: by means of wisdom—that is, through the intellect of discernment—having perceived and directly experienced the Self as Brahman, which, like all undertakings, is the substratum for the origin and so forth of the entire world; thus, become possessed of the glory of the supreme human goal, the most excellent and preeminent among all.
For one who constantly reflects within and perceives the world as flickering,
the Self becomes serene of its own accord over time, just as it did for Janaka.
Now, he states that reflection alone is the primary means for attaining self-serenity, beginning with the word "constantly":
"It is restless, impermanent, and by nature prone to wandering. (7)
Neither destiny, nor actions, nor wealth, nor kinsmen provide refuge for men afflicted by worldly existence, except for their own effort. (8)
With the intention that the root of even reflection (*vicāra*) is indeed human effort, he says: "No" (verse 8).
O dear one, those who are devoted to fate and intent on harmful rites and the like possess dull intellects; their understanding is not to be followed, for it leads to destruction.

He censures those who think, "Surely knowledge will arise by itself in due course through the power of destiny; what is the use of our effort?"—the word "yaḥ" (those who) refers to them. "Kṛtiḥ" means effort.
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), discrimination, dispassion, inquiry, and the like are included. When destiny is adverse, what is the use of a thousand efforts of one's own?
"Success will come to many who strive, yet we see failure due to the affliction of fate and the influence of desire and anger"—thus they become devoted to such evil doubts. (9)
Relying firmly upon solitude and beholding the Self by means of the self,
one should cross the ocean of saṃsāra with an intellect intensified by dispassion.
This, O Rāma, has been described as the attainment of knowledge, which bestows happiness and fells the tree of ignorance, like the falling of fruit from the sky. (11)
This [truth] has been elaborated through the illustrative narrative of Janaka. || 11 ||
Like that of Janaka, for the one of true wisdom who perceives by himself,
this embodied being— this very deity— attains full bloom, like a lotus at dawn.
The embodied one, the God, the Supreme Self, resides within the heart of every body. || 12 ||
The manifold mental construction of saṃsāra dissolves through inquiry,
just as snow, once its melting touch is mastered, vanishes under the heat of the sun.
The reflection upon, the conceptualization of, or the contemplation of saṃsāra—its touch is mastered and its coldness removed. 13.
When the destruction of this night of the thought "I am this very [person]" has dawned,
there arises of its own accord the all-pervading, expansive self-luminosity.
He states that the very abandonment of the sense of "I" regarding the body is the primary means for the realization of the perfect Self: "This... (verse 14).
When this contraction of "I am this very person" has dissolved,
an expansion arises that pervades infinite worlds.
Just as the latent impression of egoism was abandoned by Janaka, so too you, O man of noble intellect, should abandon it after reflecting within yourself. 16.
When the cloud of egoism has perished, in the vast and stainless sky of consciousness,
the supreme sun of self-luminosity surely attains its full maturity.

"Nūnam" means certainly or necessarily—that is, inevitably. The sun, whose nature is its own light, has attained full maturity, like the autumn season, meaning it has reached a state of clear radiance. || 17 ||
The cultivation of the sense of "I" is the very height of darkness;
when that is brought to rest, light arises. (18)
"Exceeding darkness" means that it is the primary strength of darkness. || 18 ||
When it is cultivated that "I do not exist, nor does another exist, nor does [anything] not exist," the mind attains tranquility and no longer sinks into things to be grasped. (19)

There is no "I-ness" (*ahamahaṃtā*). Since even the *ahaṃkāra*—the referent of the word "we" (*asmad*)—is intended here as not being the inner self (*apratyaktva*), the first person pronoun is not employed to denote it. Having raised the objection that if both the meaning of "I" and its other [the *ahaṃkāra*] are negated, the consequence of nihilism (*śūnyatā*) would follow, it is said: "And yet, it is not non-existent. The sense is that [it exists] because there is a witness (*sākṣin*) of both.
Regarding objects that are desirable and worthy of being grasped. || 19 ||
O Rāma, know that the mind’s pursuit of what is to be accepted and its absolute avoidance of what is to be rejected is bondage, and nothing else. (20)
Attachment toward things to be accepted and aversion toward things to be rejected constitute the mental bondage of a person, and nothing else; thus he says: "Upādeya... (verse 20).
Do not indulge in grief regarding things to be abandoned; do not be intent on things to be accepted.
Having relinquished the views of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, abide in the remainder and attain clarity.

The two views of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted are mental modifications consisting of attachment and aversion. The remainder is their witness; remaining established in that [witness], being solely intent upon it, one attains clarity—freedom from the turbidity of distraction. (21)
Those for whom the distinction that "this is to be accepted" and "this is to be rejected" has dissolved, do not desire anything nor do they renounce anything here.

Thus, those persons for whom such a state of affairs has dissolved—due to their vision everywhere of the mere nature of the Self as being neither to be rejected nor to be accepted—are the ones [described]. 22.
As long as the mind’s discrimination between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted has not ceased,
equanimity does not shine forth, just as moonlight does not appear in a sky filled with clouds.
Equanimity is the state of being the self of Brahman, which is free from inequality. || 23 ||
For one whose mind is agitated by the thought, "This is non-substantial" and "this is substantial," equanimity does not arise, just as a flower-cluster does not appear on a śākhoṭa tree.

The meaning is that his mind is agitated within, having fallen into a state of restlessness—thinking, "This is a non-entity, an unpraiseworthy thing, therefore it is to be abandoned; this is an entity, a praiseworthy thing, therefore it is to be accepted. A *śākhoṭa* is a specific kind of tree, well known for its large flowers, fruits, and shoots, yet providing no useful shade. || 24 ||
Where there is the pursuit of what is proper and improper, delighting in gain and loss, how can there be equanimity or purity that shines with the light of dispassion? (25)

The longing for gain is the desire that "may this which is appropriate and favorable be mine," while the longing for non-gain is the aversion that "may this which is inappropriate and unfavorable never be mine"; these two, longing (icchā) and aversion (dveṣa), reside in whichever person [possesses them]. || 25 ||
While this single, stainless reality of Brahman exists, what is improper, and where is there any propriety, in its being eternally both manifold and non-manifold? (26)
Regarding that, he states the lack of contradiction in the possibility of both equanimity (*samatā*) and transparency (*svacchata*): "In one [entity]," etc.

By means of the conceptualization of difference and non-difference through multiplicity and non-multiplicity: if the unattached, non-dual blisses are non-distinct, then because they are the Self (*ātman*), all are necessarily agreeable. If they are distinct, even so, because they do not touch the Self, they are not agreeable. Nor are they disagreeable.
Or [if they are] contrary; the sense is that even then there is no opportunity for those two. || 26 ||
I suspect that the two monkeys—desire and aversion—are flickering upon the tree of the mind; since they are so restless, how can there be any tranquility in it? (27)
The gentleness and immovability of that tree of the mind. || 27 ||
Hopelessness, fearlessness, constancy, equanimity, knowledge, effortlessness, actionlessness, gentleness, and freedom from conceptual construction. || 28 ||

Now, he describes the fifteen qualities that constitute the characteristics of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) in two verses, beginning with "freedom from desire" (nirāśatā). Freedom from effort (nirīhatā) is the absence of mental restlessness. Freedom from action (niṣkriyatā) is the absence of the persistent attachment to being the agent of bodily actions. Gentleness (saumyatā) is constant serenity. || 28 ||

Fortitude, loving-kindness, intelligence, contentment, gentleness, and soft speech—these abide without any latent impressions in the knower who is free from what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted. (29)

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is friendliness toward all beings; wisdom (*mati*) is the disposition of contemplation. Anticipating the objection that if virtues remain, then one would be bound by the very latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those virtues, he says: "free from latent impressions" (*apavāsanam*).
The sense is that the seed of latent impressions, which is ignorance (*ajñāna*), has been destroyed. (29)
One should forcibly withdraw the mind that is running downward by means of *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal),
just as water falling downward is held back by a dam.
Now, he describes the means for Rāma to acquire those qualities, beginning with the words "dhāvamānam" (running):

[the mind] toward the lower objects, that is, base sense-objects; by means of *pratyāhāra*, which is the withdrawal of all the external senses from their objects; [like] water fallen downward or flowing toward a current.
Just as by a mountain range. || 30 ||
Having abandoned these external objects, whether standing, walking, sleeping, or breathing, investigate all internal things in every way and at all times. (31)

Since the delusion of selfhood does not arise with respect to external objects, the only remedy is their abandonment; however, since such a delusion does arise with respect to internal objects, one must always and in every way exercise inquiry into them, like the examination of the true nature of a jewel. Thus he says:
"External... Accordingly, the elders have said: "Whether walking or standing, whether waking or even sleeping..."
Or rather, he whose mind is not intent on discernment is said to be dead. || 31 ||
The turbid net of latent impressions (vāsanā), having seized the fish of craving,
has spread through the waters of saṃsāra and is stretched out with the threads of anxiety.

The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: "With this dart characterized by wisdom (buddhi) taught by me, or with a knife, cut the net characterized by latent impressions (vāsanā). [This net] has caught the fish of craving (tṛṣṇā), and it is spread out, extended, in the waters characterized by saṃsāra, which are turbid and fouled by the moss of delusion (moha).
It is stretched out and fashioned from threads characterized by thought. || 32 ||
O dear one, cut through [this] with this sharp probe of intelligence,
as a wind sweeping across the vast expanse cuts through a cloud at the proper time.
The phrase "moving in the vast, more extensive space" qualifies both the whirlwind and the arrow, referring respectively to the sky and Brahman.
The root of this tree of saṃsāra, which is the seat for the sprouts of defects, should be uprooted by one who is capable through steadfastness and with an intellect that is firm and resolute. (34)
O fortunate one, by means of a steadfastness of mind characterized by stability in the one Self— which has been made firm through long-term practice—
and which is therefore exalted and capable of uplifting the self submerged since beginningless time, [one attains] the intellect of immediate direct realization.
The meaning is: "Cut the root of the tree of saṃsāra, which is ignorance along with its latent impressions (vāsanā). || 34 ||
Having severed the mind with the mind itself, as one would cut down a tree with an axe, and having attained the state of purity, become steady this very moment. (35)
[Objection: But if there is a cause for distraction within the mind, how can there be a cutting off of its root? To this he says: "by the mind itself.

Just as a tree is cut down by an axe whose blade is made of wood from the very same tree, so too, the mind is cut by the mind itself—by means of the mind in which the consciousness of Brahman has been established as its function (vṛtti). This is the meaning.
Having severed the mind with the mind itself, and having forgotten the final mind,
and having severed even the present mind, attain the state of one whose saṃsāra is destroyed.

[Objection: "But even if the previously established mind (*manas*) is severed by the aforementioned means, how can there be a severing of future mental modifications (*bhāvi-manovṛtti*) or of the present mental modification that has the form of Brahman? To this, he says: 'By forgetting' (*vismṛtya*).

Forgetting (*vismṛti*) is the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanoccheda*); by that [forgetting], the final [modification]—that which would otherwise arise at a subsequent time in the form of a mental modification—is [severed] when it is absent.

Because even at the forefront of the latent impression (vāsanā), no further mental modification (vṛtti) arises; having severed it by its own means, according to the maxim of the clearing-nut (katakareṇu) which removes itself by itself, [it brings about liberation]. || 36 ||
When delusion is forgotten, saṃsāra no longer grows;
when the mind is forgotten, saṃsāra no longer grows. (37)

One might object: "Even so, for the sake of the continued life of one who knows reality, that delusion called ignorance—which serves as its material cause—must necessarily be admitted; and that very same [ignorance] will then cause saṃsāra to sprout once more.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Delusion" (moha). It "sprouts" (parirohati), that is, it grows.

The sense is that when there is forgetfulness characterized by the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the seed-potency of that [mind] ceases to exist. If it is then argued that cyclic existence might sprout of its own accord in that field of delusion, he replies with the word "citta":
when there is forgetfulness of the mind characterized by the eradication of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), the sprouting of the object of cognition (*cetya*) is not possible.
The meaning is that the mental formation (*cittasaṃskāra*) is also the seed for the superimposition of the object of cognition (*cetya*). || 37 ||
Whether standing, walking, sleeping, waking, sitting, rising, or falling—
having inwardly resolved that "this world is indeed unreal," abandon all attachment.
He says—“standing”—that when both the mind and its objects are forgotten, the very means is the abandonment of attachment to them. || 38 ||
Relying upon the purity of equanimity, O Rāghava, perform the duties that have arrived; likewise, without thinking of what has not yet been attained, dwell here indeed.

With the intention that equanimity is also accomplished through the relinquishing of all reliance, he says: "equanimity. Likewise, the word division is *tathā aprāptam* (and thus unattained). || 39 ||
Just as Śarva both bears and does not bear the lingas,
so too, O sinless one, you alone should here perform and not perform these actions.
Just as Śarva, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), does not bear the eightfold forms such as earth and so forth by means of the vision of pure consciousness alone,
yet bears them through mere presence because he is the substratum of the illusion that manifests in the form of the world, and is therefore the creator of all.

And it is so; thus, you too should perform the duties of kingship and other such tasks through mere presence with detachment, meaning that you should do so while maintaining the firm conviction that the Self is not the agent. || 40 ||
You alone are the knower; you are the unborn, you are the Self, you are Maheśvara.
Being non-different from the Self, this entire universe is thus spread out by you.

Furthermore, according to such scriptural passages as "There is no other seer than this, there is no other hearer than this," you alone are the knower and the perceiver within all bodies. The form *iḍ* is a Vedic (Chāndasa) usage; it is derived from the root *vid* in the sense of existence (*sattā*), with the suffix *tṛc*.

Thus, the meaning is "the ultimately real" (*paramārthasat*). You are unborn (*aja*), devoid of transformations such as birth and so forth; you are the Self of all, the essence of inward-facing consciousness (*pratyak-cit-rasa*).

And you alone are the Maheśvara mentioned previously; being non-different from your own self-nature, remaining indeed with an unswerving nature, it is by you—such as you are—that this [world] has been spread out and expanded through your own delusion and so forth, and not by anyone else—this is the meaning. || 41 ||

He by whom the cultivation [of the mind] has been abandoned on all sides due to the non-existence of the self and its objects of perception, is not seized by defects born of joy, resentment, and despondency. (42)
If this has been spread by me alone, then how can there be the arising of the defects of joy or resentment in me regarding this? To this he says:

"By whom... By that knower of reality (*tattvavid*), because of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) that the existence of the self's objects of perception is merely the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat-mātra*), the contemplation that "it is something other" has been abandoned—that is, relinquished. He [is the one].
Therefore, you too should abandon it; this is the meaning. || 42 ||
Freed from passion and hatred, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, the yogi who has abandoned the latent impressions of worldly existence is said to be "yoked" (yukta). || 43 ||
Whatever he does, whatever he eats, whatever he gives, or whatever he destroys— in all that,
his mind being liberated, there is equanimity toward pleasure and pain.

He who, having abandoned the mental construction of the desirable and the undesirable, engages in his duties with the thought that "what has come must simply be done," does not sink into anything whatsoever.
O high-minded one, the mind that possesses the certainty that "this [world] is merely the existence of consciousness," having abandoned the conceit of enjoyment, attains tranquility. (46)
This world and himself as well; he by whom the conceit of enjoyment and the thought of enjoyment have been abandoned. (46)
The mind, being insentient by its very nature, runs after the principle of consciousness (cittattva), just as a cat pursues the lord of beasts in the forest out of a craving for meat. 47.

He establishes what was stated—that this [universe] is merely the existence of consciousness—by means of the passage beginning with "the mind" (manaḥ). Since the mind is insentient (jaḍa), it is incapable of establishing itself or another;
therefore, for its own establishment and for the establishment of its objects, there must exist the ultimate reality, which is the self-luminous principle of consciousness acting as its own witness.
It pursues and follows after the object; the meaning is that it is just as a cat follows a lion for its own livelihood and for the sake of supporting its offspring and so forth. || 47 ||
The follower of the lion eats the meat obtained through the power of the lion's prowess;
likewise, the mind resorts to the visible world obtained through the power of the prowess of consciousness. 48.
It relies upon and subsists by means of its own visible object and its respective domain. || 48 ||
The mind, though unreal by nature, lives through the grace of consciousness;
even consciousness itself, becoming thought, imagines the entire universe as one.

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "The mind. The meaning is that this being the case, it is established that the mind is as if non-existent (*asatkalpa*), almost void (*śūnyaprāya*), and false (*mithyā*). How does it then persist? He says: "Contemplating.
Having forgotten the one, non-dual Self, it contemplates only the universe in the form of the world. This is a Vedic [usage].
There is a change of gender. The meaning is that it lives by becoming the world-form while imagining [itself] as real.

For this very reason, having attained—that is, reached—thought, which is the remembrance of the Self, it furthermore becomes consciousness once again; the meaning is that it abandons its state of being the mind.
That which is indeed inert and devoid of the power of the lamp of consciousness—
How can that mind, which resembles a corpse, arise without consciousness?

He states that just as the power of illumination belongs to the mind, so too the power of vibration is dependent solely on consciousness—thus: "The inert... Without the lamp characterized by consciousness, and without its radiance and strength, [the body] neither rises nor vibrates. (50)

The power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*), which consists of aesthetic relish (*rasa-mayī*) and is touched by the very nature of consciousness (*cit-svabhāva*), is described by those who see according to the scriptures as "mind" (*citta*) through the statement that it is "imagination" (*kalpanā*). (51)

For this very reason, there is also a tradition among the learned that the mind is nothing but the conceptualization of vibration within consciousness; thus he says: "The nature of consciousness... and so forth.
That which is the hissing of the serpent of the mind is called this very "mental fabrication" (kalanā).
Having realized that "I am consciousness alone," it dissolves back into that very consciousness. || 52 ||
He says that the mind and its fluctuations are merely the play (*vilāsa*) of the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*) itself—this is indicated by the word "ya" (that which).

The mention of "blowing" (*phūtkāra*) is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for poison. Thus, the meaning is that the triad beginning with the mind (*cittādi-tripuṭī*), when appearing in the form of the perceptible, is itself the mental construction (*kalanā*). [The sage attains] the state of the mind as pure consciousness alone (*śuddha-cinmātratā*). || 52 ||
That consciousness which is devoid of an object of thought is the eternal Brahman;
that same consciousness which is accompanied by an object of thought is called "kalana" (mental construction).
And thus, he states that the very abandonment of the object of consciousness by consciousness results in its culmination as Brahman: "By the object of consciousness... (verse 53).
That Brahman whose form is slightly touched [by manifestation] is the steady mind;
this conceptualization, being ever-existent, appears in the heart as if it were real.

He states that it is indeed *kalana* (the act of conceptualizing) that becomes the *manas* (mind) through the process of thinking—using the words "something" (*kiñcit*). That very Brahman, when its form is slightly touched upon as "something," is *kalana*;

it is always present in the heart as if it were real, and having become the conceptualization consisting of volition and doubt, it becomes this well-known, stable *manas*. This is the meaning. || 54 ||
As soon as this mental activity arises, which is conventionally known as "mind," it immediately forgets its own nature as consciousness and remains as if inert.

He says "the mind" (*cittam*) to show that when the nature of eternal experience is forgotten, the very act of conceptualization (*kalana*) attains the state of memory and becomes the mind. He further says "as if inert" (*jaḍeva*) to indicate that at that time, even its insentience (*jaḍatā*), which is fit for becoming an object of indirect perception (*parokṣatā*), has come into being. || 55 ||
It has become fully developed under the name of "mental construction" (kalanā), following after volitional thought (saṃkalpa);
it possesses limitations, is the foremost of speech, and is characterized by the qualities of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.

With the intention that she has attained the state of *citta*—as it were—through the conceptualization of the forms of past objects, and likewise the state of *manas* through the conformity to mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) and discursive thought (*vikalpa*) by means of the conceptualization of the forms of future objects, he says: "She has become [perfected] (*saṃpannā*).
Thus, being possessed of limitations, she is divided in two ways.

The meaning is that, having determined the similarity between past means of attaining the desired and the undesired, and having conceptualized the future status of being a means to the desired and the undesired, the primary consciousness itself has become the foremost [cognition] characterized by what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted. || 56 ||
This very consciousness, as if having entered the worlds through its own power,
does not perceive their form as long as it has not been fully awakened.

Having established through the passage beginning with "the mind by its very nature," etc., that this [universe] is nothing but the mere existence of consciousness, he concludes by summarizing this point: "She is this... By her own power—that is, by the force of her own *māyā*-power—[this world appears], until it is fully awakened by means of the teacher, the scriptures, and one's own inquiry; until then, it remains [merely] apparent.
The meaning is that the nature of non-dual, perfect bliss is not understood. || 57 ||
Therefore, through inquiry into the scriptures, through supreme dispassion,
and through the restraint of the senses, one should personally awaken to the nature of mental construction.

The meaning is that one should awaken [the mind] from the dream of the three states, which is characterized by the manifestation of the forms of insentient matter, and cause it to turn away from them. || 58 ||
The differentiation of all living beings occurs through consciousness and its cessation;
when awakened, one attains the state of Brahman, otherwise the world wanders in delusion.
By "consciousness" (vijñāna) is meant knowledge born from the scriptures; by "tranquility" (śama) is meant [the state] when there is no awakening through both consciousness and tranquility. || 59 ||
One should awaken only that mental construction which is intoxicated by the wine of delusion, wallowing in the pit of sense-objects, and fast asleep through the lack of self-awareness. (50)
Delusion is passion; ignorance is the non-perception of the self, which is sleep; by that, she is fast asleep. || 60 ||
For when this [intellect] is unawakened, it perceives nothing at all;
though appearing within as the fabrication of conceptual constructions, it is composed of unreality.

Now, if mental construction (*kalanā*) is asleep, how is the world perceived? Or, if it is awake, what excellence is there in that state beyond its well-known nature as consciousness? To this he says: "unawakened" (*aprabuddha*). That which you think perceives the world does not perceive anything at all, because the world is merely a manifestation of non-perception.
The meaning is that the state of the world, though being perceived, is composed of non-existence, like the construction of a palace created by mere imagination.
By that supreme vision residing within,
this mental construction shines forth among all objects, just as the power of fragrance resides within a flower cluster.
When it is stated that the Self is the residual cognition alone once the portions consisting of objects have been abandoned, one might mistakenly grasp this [cognition] itself as the Self.
To prevent this, the author distinguishes and shows the pure consciousness (*śuddhacit*) which is its witness and internal to it, beginning with the words "by that" (*tayā*).
This cognition, which takes the form of a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*), is [perceived] by that internal witness of all.
The meaning is that, being pervaded by the supreme vision, she shines—that is, becomes capable of illuminating—within objects, each within its own respective domain, and not by itself. || 62 ||
This subtle body, which is conceived as "intellection" (kalanā) throughout the three worlds,
indeed knows something, for it has the constant nature of pure consciousness.

If she is the witness of all, why does she manifest only the attributes of this or that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and not everything? To this he says: "The body is imagined" (*tanuḥ saṃkalpitā*). That which is the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicit*), whose sole attribute is knowledge and whose nature is eternal awakening, appears as a "body"—that is, as something limited and small—due to the influence of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the various circumscribed mental modifications (*vṛtti*). Thus, even throughout the three worlds, by those various [means]...
The meaning is that because they are fashioned by living beings, they perceive only a very small portion of each respective internal organ and so forth.
O Rāma, this insentient world, which consists of the form of the stone of mental construction, is awakened only by the Supreme, just as a lotus is awakened by the sun. 64.

But the mental construction (*kalanā*), which consists of the form of activity, becomes like a stone—insentient and resembling a rock—in the state of discrimination (*viveka*); for this very reason, it is awakened by the conscious witness (*sākṣin*). (64)
Just as a maiden made of stone does not dance even when urged,
so this mental construction within the body perceives nothing at all.

But those, such as the Naiyāyikas and others, who— being ignorant of the eternal witness— believe that the manifestation of an object belongs solely to a non-eternal cognition which is itself manifested by another, he ridicules them with many examples, beginning with the words "Just as... (verse 65).
Where has a battle with a gurgling roar ever been waged by kings who are but mere painters?
And where have medicinal herbs ever been awakened by the rays of the moon? (66)

With the intention that, for the insentient internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and its modifications (*vṛtti*), the very inclination toward objects would be difficult to achieve in the absence of the constant proximity of consciousness—let alone the capacity to illuminate them—it is said:
"By the acts of painting" (*lipikarmabhiḥ*). [This refers to] kings depicted in paintings; "awakened" means nourished or stimulated by them. || 66 ||
Where was there the leaping about of corpses with limbs smeared with blood?
Where was there sweet-sounding song from fragments of forest stone? (67)
Parivalgitam means running about. || 67 ||
Where is the darkness of night dispelled by the suns created by men?
And where can a shadow be produced by forests in the sky made of mere mental constructs? (68)
By men, through those things fashioned such as stone and so forth. || 68 ||
Where can any action be performed by these minds—which are as inert as stones, arisen from the weight of false delusion, and consisting of nothing but the mirage of desire? (69)
Just as a shimmering river of mirages appears in a vast expanse of heat when one is afflicted by it,
so too does this mental construction manifest within the Self as if it were truly real.

With the intention that, if an eternal conscious self were not accepted, the superimposition (adhyāsa) of mental constructs and so forth would simply not be established, he says: "Just as... (verse 70).
Know that this which is called "vibration" has been grasped by the crafty as the mind; understand it to be that power of the winds which has the vital breath (prāṇa) as its body.

It has been stated that the mind (*manas*) is merely the conceptualization of the movement of the discerning consciousness (*cita*). Now, when there is a distinction between the conscious and unconscious aspects, since the conscious aspect is nothing other than the Self (*ātman*), only the insentient aspect remains; and such a power of movement is precisely the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, to state that once this [breath] is restrained, there is no separate entity called "mind" to be restrained, [the author says]:

He provides the introductory context with the words "yadetad" (that which...). By the "deceitful"—those who are ignorant and self-deceptive—[the mind] is made to consist of the body of vital breath (*prāṇa*), that is, having the nature of the sheath of vital breath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*). || 71 ||
This supreme splendor of their own self, whose consciousness is not assailed by the determinations of even the slightest volition, possesses a form whose aesthetic flavor is never interrupted.

That vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) arises from volition (saṃkalpa); for yogins who are free from volition, it is nothing other than the conscious self (cidātman). He says "of those" to show that it does not exist separately. "Rasas" are the objects of experience because they are tasted; that [energy] takes their form. || 72 ||
That turbid conceptualization which takes the form of "this is I" and "that is mine" regarding the vital breath (prāṇa) and the principle of the self (ātman-tattva) is called by the name "jīva. (73)
When that very [consciousness] assumes the form of the "I" and "mine," its [innate] flavor being eclipsed, then— since such an eclipse would be impossible without vibration—

the principle of *prāṇa* (vital breath), which is essentially vibration, and the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is essentially consciousness, appear as if they have become separate. Due to this lack of discrimination, through the superimposition of identity, [consciousness] becomes turbid, a form of consciousness conjoined with the insentient.
The meaning is that, because it follows the root-meaning of "jīv" as "the maintenance of life-breaths" (prāṇadhāraṇa), the designation "jīva" is stated for that which lives. || 73 ||

"Intellect (dhī), mind (citta), and the individual soul (jīva)—these are considered names of the unreal mental construction (saṃkalpa). O Rāma, these designations are conceptualized by those who know that [reality], but they do not exist from the perspective of the ultimate truth."
He states that other designations for her are likewise well-known: "Wisdom" (dhī). || 74 ||
Neither the mind, nor the mental faculty, nor even this intellect, nor the body exists here in the ultimate sense;
only one's own Self exists here at all times.

To explain why that is not so from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), he says: "The mind" (manaḥ). For, in ultimate reality, this mere object of perception—characterized here as the mind, the intellect, the thought-organ, and the body—does not exist within the Self, according to hundreds of scriptural passages such as: "For He is without breath, without mind, pure; bodiless, woundless, without veins; neither gross nor subtle. etc.
The meaning is that [the opponent's position] is sublated by the experiences of the wise and by logical reasoning. || 75 ||
The Self alone is this entire world, and the Self likewise is the succession of time;
it is clearer than space, as if non-existent, yet it truly exists, stainless.
If the Self alone exists, then why does it not appear in the form of the world? Or, what else appears there? To this he says:
"The Self alone... (verse 76).
Because it is transparent, it appears as non-existent; yet, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, it is existent.
The Self, which transcends all categories, is experienced through one's own direct experience.
To provide certainty regarding how it is as if non-existent and yet how it is indeed existent, he says: "Because of its transparency" (*acchatvāt*).
Because of its transparency—due to the absence of grossness, blueness, and so forth, which are the conditions for being perceptible by the eyes and other senses—it appears as if non-existent;

thus, it is "an appearance of the non-existent" (*asadābhāsa*). However, because it is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), it brings about the manifestation of both itself and others, and is therefore existent. For this very reason...
The meaning is that it is experienced through one's own direct experience alone, and not by means of the sense organs. || 77 ||
The mind is completely exhausted there where the consciousness of the Supreme Self resides;
darkness is destroyed there where light prevails.

"Let other instruments not function there due to the absence of grossness and so forth; but why should the mind, which is well-known as the cause for determining objects by virtue of its subtlety, not function there? To this he says: "The mind.
It is true that the mind would function there, provided it did not itself perish at the time of that perception.
However, because the mind is an effect of ignorance, it perishes along with ignorance at the very moment that the function of seeing That arises;
therefore, the meaning is that the mind does not possess the power to see That. || 78 ||
Where the reflections of self-consciousness are considered to have arisen from volition,
there occurs the forgetting of the Self and the remembering of that which is born of the mind.

Where, then, is the active power of the mind? To this he says: "where. In which state, by the power of volition (*saṃkalpa*), external objects arise from consciousness—which is of the nature of the Self and exceedingly clear—by taking on the form of external objects.

The meaning is that it is well known that in that state, there is the forgetting of the ultimate Self—which is intended as the object of illumination—and the recollection and perception of false objects born of the mind. || 79 ||
The state of being composed of volition (saṃkalpa) is called the mind (citta) of another person;
liberation arises from that [state] through the absence of volition, which is the state of no-mind (acittatva). || 80 ||
He states that the mind also lacks the power to perceive the Self because it is contrary to its own origin—with the words "of another" (*parasya*).

The sense is: since the mind arises dependent on the nature of volition (*saṃkalpa*), how could it function toward the Self of liberation, which is characterized by the cessation of all volitions? || 80 ||
This much is the birth of the mind—the seed for the perpetuation of saṃsāra—whether it be the consciousness or the Self that has turned toward volitional construction (saṃkalpa). (81)
For this very reason, it has been stated more than once that the seed for the birth of the mind is volition (*saṃkalpa*); thus he says, "This much alone.

The grammatical connection is as follows: when the Self, having turned toward volition, undergoes a conceptualization (*vikalpana*)—characterized by a slight alteration—from its consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is of the nature of pure awareness (*cit-svabhāva*), this alone is indeed the birth of the mind. || 81 ||

The existence of the mind, when stained by the mark of conceptualization (saṃkalpa) due to its state of being free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), is called "differentiation" (kalanā); therefore, the mind is understood to possess masculinity, as it were.
Having clarified what was already stated, he says: "From the non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpāt*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "fallen from the non-conceptual.

Just as masculinity—the male organ—is perceived through the mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) of women and so forth, and manifests for the purpose of procreating offspring, so too does the mind [manifest] for the purpose of procreating the world; this is the meaning. And thus:
Bādarāyaṇa’s sūtra also states: "For it is like manhood and so forth in the world. (82)
O Rāma, when the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) is restrained, the mind dissolves;
for the mental [self], whose form is the vital breath, follows that vital breath just as a shadow follows its substance. 83.

He states the purpose of that which was introduced by the words "this so-called vibration" (*spanditam*) and so forth, with the phrase "in the power of breath" (*prāṇaśaktau*). Just as the reflection belonging to a substance such as a mirror dissolves when that substance has dissolved, following after it, so it is here. Why is that? Because, just as a reflected image—
Just as the form of a mirror is imagined [to exist within it], so too the mental faculty is merely a form of the vital breath (prāṇa); this is the meaning.
The vital breath, though situated in the heart, perceives the experience of other places;
that which [perceives] through the sensation of vibration is designated as "mind" (manas). || 84 ||

How is it known that the mental [perception] has the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)? To this he says: "In another place," etc. Since a living person, through the vital breath, perceives within the heart the mental experience of a distant foreign land—experiencing it as "I have an experience of that place within my heart"—therein [lies] the connection with that other place.

The meaning is that because the aspect of sensation cannot be established without vibration, and because vibration cannot occur without being conjoined with consciousness, the vital breath (prāṇa) itself is designated as the mind (manas), owing to its possession of both the powers of vibration and sensation. || 84 ||
Through dispassion, through the practice of the causes, through right application, through the destruction of vice,
and through the realization of the supreme truth, the vital breaths are restrained.

Thus, having established the unity of those two for the sake of achieving the restraint of the mind through the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he now states the means of restraint: "From dispassion" (*vairāgyāt*). The cause is *prāṇāyāma*; from its practice. Yoga is the application; [it is] *samādhi*. From that. The addiction of the mind is its habitual tendency to approach external objects; of that—
From destruction. || 85 ||
Stones may at times possess the power to move or burn;
however, minds do not possess the power to initiate motion or cognition.

Now, even according to the position that there is a distinction between the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*) because they have different material causes— as stated in the scripture, "For, my dear, the mind consists of food, and the vital breath consists of water"—
both of them are nonetheless dependent upon the conscious self (*prāṇacidātmā*), since the mind lacks its own inherent power of movement and lacks the power of consciousness.

With the intention that cessation arises from the cessation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he says: "of a stone" (*dṛṣadaḥ*). By the word *edhas*, which denotes firewood, its causal power of burning is indicated. Even in a stone, that is, a rock, there exists or might exist at some time the power of movement and the power of burning; however, this is not the case regarding the vibration of minds.
The meaning is that there is no capacity regarding the object of comprehension. || 86 ||
Vibration (spanda) is the power of the vital breath (prāṇa), which is by nature mobile and insentient;
whereas the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is the pure essence of one's own self, eternally all-pervading.
He states what those two powers of the body are: "Vibration" (spanda). || 87 ||
The mind is conceived as the connection between the power of consciousness (cicchakti) and the power of vibration (spandaśakti);
that which has arisen from them is purely false, and it is called false knowledge. || 88 ||
What then? He says that it is the mind (manas), [referring to] the power of consciousness (cicchakti). || 88 ||
This indeed is called ignorance; it is described as illusion (māyā).
This supreme ignorance bestows the poison of saṃsāra and other such states. || 89 ||
Avidyā is the effect of ignorance; māyā is the power of projection. This very mind is called ignorance because it carries out the entire essence of ignorance. (89)

If the conceptualization born of volition is not formed through association with the power of consciousness (cic-chakti) and the power of vibration (spanda-śakti), then these fears of worldly existence are utterly destroyed.

The "conception of volition" (*saṃkalpakalpana*) means, in other words, that which has the conception of volition as its cause. For this very reason, he states—“If it were not done”—to establish that when the cause is not produced, the effect (*naimittika*) necessarily ceases to exist. || 90 ||
When that power of vibration belonging to the wind is perceived by consciousness, it becomes an object of perception;
at that very moment, through its internal ideation and so forth, it attains the state of being the mind (citta).
"From Vāyu" means from the wind; the suffix *tasi* is applied after a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), functioning as all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). || 91 ||
This "cittatā" (the state of being mind) is falsely imagined by the conscious principle, like a yakṣa conjured by a child;
for it is consciousness itself that takes the form of a vibration appearing as an unbroken, circular shape.
The meaning is that consciousness itself, in which there exist no forms of vibration characterized by unbroken, circular shapes, is the ultimate reality (paramārtha). || 92 ||
How indeed can this very mind be obstructed by anything other than itself?
With whom could Indra, who possesses unbroken power, have a conflict? (93)

That which has been described as the characteristic of indivisible fullness—the nature of consciousness—is not obstructed or fragmented by anything else. The particle *kila* is used to indicate the impossibility of such a thing. Could it be by something dependent on it for its own establishment, or by something else?

Since nothing else is established independently, that which depends on consciousness for its establishment lacks the power to obstruct consciousness; thus, even an obstruction [of consciousness] is impossible.

The meaning is that since the establishment of the non-conscious (acit) depends upon the existence of consciousness (cit), it is impossible for the non-conscious to be established within the interval of consciousness without the fragmentation of consciousness.

However, if the reading is *tadvidante*, it should be construed as follows: "He knows that"—meaning he knows such a nature of his own as being consciousness—and "at the end," when ignorance along with its effects has been destroyed, by what could he be obstructed? [This refers to] Indra, the king of the gods.
Or [it belongs] to the Supreme Lord. || 93 ||
Therefore, due to the absence of related entities, no relation exists here;
without a relation, for whom is that mind established, and of what nature is it? (94)

Therefore, since the non-accumulation [of the mind] is impossible without contradiction with consciousness (*cit*), and because even if there were a contradiction, its existence would be sublated by the presence of consciousness— what kind of mind could it be?
Even if one were to say that the insentient [mind] is self-established in its own existence independently of anything else,
nevertheless, in the absence of another conscious being who experiences it or is connected to it, it cannot exist without a connection to consciousness.

To whom is that mind established, or of what nature could it be? The meaning is that since it does not ascend to [the level of] direct experience, its specific characteristics remain unestablished as something unreal. || 94 ||
In the unity of consciousness and its vibration, what indeed is called the "mind"?
What is an army without the gathering and clashing of horses and elephants? (95)

Having thus stated the unreality of the mind on the view that consciousness (*cit*) and its vibration (*spanda*) are distinct, he says—starting with "citspandayoḥ"—that on the view of their identity, it is even more so. Consciousness and its vibration cannot be said to be identical by means of the denial of consciousness, because that would entail the consequence of there being no proof for vibration. Therefore, by process of elimination, if identity is asserted through the denial of vibration:

The meaning is that, just as the very nature of an army cannot be established if one denies the elephants, horses, and so forth that exceed the king [in number], the mind is all the more unestablished. || 95 ||
Therefore, O Rāma, there is no such thing as a wicked mind in the three worlds;
this destruction of the mind arises from perfect realization. 96.

Therefore, since [the mind] is impossible in either of the two positions, the meaning is that the destruction of the mind is simply the certainty that "mind" and "intellect" do not exist at all, based on the knowledge of reality. || 96 ||
O sinless one, do not thus vainly resolve your mind toward what is harmful;
the mind has arisen falsely, for in the ultimate sense, this does not exist.
O high-minded one, do not form any mental construction whatsoever within yourself;
for the mind that constructs, O Rāma, does not exist anywhere at all.
The conceptual construction born of incorrect knowledge is like a mirage;
it has been completely stilled within the desert of your heart through right vision, O Sage. (99)

By the word "heart" (hṛt), the innermost self (pratyagātman) residing within the heart is meant; [it is situated] in the desert (maru) characterized by that [self]. "Produced by imperfect knowledge"—this is an address to Rāma, O Sage (mune), intended to enjoin him toward the practice of reflection (manana). || 99 ||
Because of its insentience and lack of intrinsic nature, the mind is always dead;
yet the world is killed by that which is dead—strange indeed is this cycle of folly! 100.

If death is the cessation of consciousness, or if it is the attainment of a state devoid of essential nature, both of these exist within the mind; thus, it is eternally dead. This wheel of folly is a succession of ignorance that revolves like a turning wheel. (100)
He who has neither self nor body, neither support nor even form—by him all this is consumed; wonderful indeed is this snare of ignorance! (101)
The self (ātman) is the essential nature; it is either the configuration of parts (ākṛti) or the genus (jāti). || 101 ||
He who is struck even by the mind, which is devoid of all physical instruments— I believe his head has been shattered by blows from the petals of blue lotuses.

"By one lacking the equipment"—that is, the equipment for battle consisting of weapons, missiles, body, hands, feet, and so forth—"he whose head was crushed"; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 102 ||
He who is struck even by the mind—which is dull, mute, and blind—I consider that fool to be scorched by the rays of the full moon. (103)
Even when a hero exists, he is overwhelmed by the world;
this [world] that does not even exist is slain through the delusion of ignorance. 104.
By that non-existent mind,

the existent world— though its people are heroic and endowed with every requisite for conquering their enemies— is overcome by the deluded; and by the discerning, through great effort, by means of such instruments as dispassion and the like.

The meaning is that this entire conceptualization—that even what is non-existent is destroyed by means of the practice and realization of yoga, meditation, and concentration—is merely a state of delusion and not ultimate reality. Thus have the Masters said regarding me, who am the sky of pure consciousness, in this innate, dense bliss: "It is the same as the world," "it is free from ignorance," and "it is equal to everything."
"Alas, this creeper of manifold conceptual constructions has indeed become fruitless! (104)
Composed of false conceptualizations and having attained a false state of existence, it is not seen even when sought; what power indeed can it possibly possess? (105)
The capacity to overcome; this is the ellipsis. || 105 ||
Ah! How truly wonderful is this illusory creation;
by means of it, even with a mind that is exceedingly fickle, this world is utterly overcome.
She is the fashioner and creator even of Maya, who is renowned for his great power of illusion. || 106 ||
When one is beset by calamities, what indeed does that person not consider a misfortune?
Behold, this entire creation is produced solely through ignorance and folly.

When there is folly, then that man is sought after, searched for, and resorted to by every kind of calamity (*sarveṇāpyāpadā*); here there is no disagreement, for since he is ignorant and foolish, what calamity could there not be? The meaning is that every single one indeed exists.

He who possesses no knowledge is "ajñānaḥ," a foolish soul; by means of that foolishness, through the gateway of evil actions and so forth, this creation—which is a treasury of all calamities—comes into being. However, if the reading is *āpadāṃ niṣṭhā*, the meaning is self-evident. 107.
Alas, what a tragedy! Even the creation of the evil-minded has fallen under the sway of folly, in that even by means of this non-existent life, something [false] is brought about. (108)

This creation, having fallen under the sway of ignorance due to the cause of the evil intellect consisting of mind, body, and so forth, is afflicted by that very ignorance; and even by this well-known *jīva*, which is itself unreal,
it is brought about for ever-increasing suffering solely through following the path of unreality— just like one who is blind and inert.

The meaning is that for one already afflicted by the natural ignorance of the mind and so forth, to be further tormented even by the *jīva*—which itself is well-acquainted with such suffering—is more painful than pain and is improper. || 108 ||
I believe this creation, consisting of ignorance, is exceedingly fragile;
it is shattered into fragments by the flow of the waves of speech. 109.

"Extremely fragile" means that because they are established merely through a lack of inquiry, they can be sublated by mere inquiry. Regarding this, he states examples that are to be discarded by mere inquiry, beginning with the word "water" (*vāḥ*). Just as water (*vāri*), being crushed by its own imagined flow of waves, is shattered into fragments.
The meaning is "like an illusion. || 109 ||
By the very mechanism of the basin of blue collyrium, it is ground to powder;
it faints at the touch of the rays of the full-orbed moon. (110)

That very water where there is a whirlpool is ground to powder by a grinding machine in the form of a basin with a central hole, appearing like the color of blue collyrium. That very water where it trembles is bewildered by the touch of the rays of the full moon through its expansive orb, and falls under the sway of madness.
The meaning is: "just as an error [is perceived], so too is that. || 110 ||
When seen by enemies released from their eyes, he is bound with threads;
he is overcome by the army of Saṃkalpa (volitions) belonging to Śūrasena. 111.

The meaning is that it is like the delusion [of the illusionist] wherein a man, as soon as he is seen by his enemies, is bound by threads released from their eyes—that is, created by their vision. Alternatively, [the verse beginning with] "I think" and so forth means:
can this creation be destroyed even by an illusory mirage, a wave, a current, or the like? No, it cannot.
Furthermore, one should connect the phrase "I think" with the words "by means of the scriptural method. || 111 ||
Therefore, it is said that this [intellect] is struck down by the mind—which, though not established anywhere, is falsely imagined as something else and is wretched—rendering it useless. (112)
Therefore, because it is so extremely frivolous, this creation consisting of the world of fools is destroyed; such is the connection with what follows.
This creation consisting of the world of fools arises from the mind alone as something unreal.
He who is unable to bring it under control is not instructed by Rāma. (113)
Therefore, one who is unable to bring the mind under control is not qualified for the inner science (adhyātma-śāstra); thus he says: "The mind alone," and so forth.
This wisdom is noble by its very nature; it is not capable of being diminished by analysis.
It is not fit for the words of instruction, yet it remains as if perfectly complete.

To the question "Why is it not taught [to her]?", he says: "Because she is *abhijātā*. Since this wisdom (*prajñā*) of hers has arisen all around (*abhito jātā*), being *abhijātā*, it is firmly rooted only in external objects; having become so, it remains as if fully satisfied, and is not intent upon the restraint of the mind. It is "without its own nature" (*asvarūpā*), meaning that such a wisdom lacks an internal essential nature.
The meaning is that she does not incline toward [worldly] objects. For this very reason, she is not capable of subtle investigations into minute matters;
she even fears the faint sound of the strings of a lute, and she is afraid of the radiance of the face of even her sleeping kinsman. (115)
For this very reason, because there is no cause for steadfastness, he says "he fears" [in verse 115], meaning that he fears from all sides.
