Even from a person who does not exist, she flees in terror when their song is heard loudly;
this ignorant woman has indeed been rendered helpless by her own mind alone. (116)

Even from an enemy who does not exist, she flees in terror when she hears him loudly proclaimed by deceivers and others as "that enemy has arrived. To say more: she is rendered helpless and terrified by her own mind alone;
what need is there for anyone else? This is the meaning. || 116 ||
Overpowered by a mere fragment of pleasure, as if scorched by her own heart dwelling within her breast,
her intellect is impaired and she does not perceive the truth.
How is it that even this has been so foolishly deluded? || 117 ||
Now, even if that foolish wisdom may indeed be afraid, it is nonetheless not proper for a person to be deluded by its power;

thus he concludes what was previously introduced with the word "sukha" (pleasure). For that wisdom, through a mere fragment of sensual pleasure—which is like the taste of a drop of water mixed with poison—is as if on the verge of death.

Helpless, as if struck by an enemy, her heart scorched and tormented by the mind alone, and thus her intellect— her faculty of discernment— distraught and void, she truly did not understand at all; yet even in such a state, that man was pointlessly deluded by her.

The sense is that delusion is appropriate from an enemy who possesses a pure mind, who does not distress his own kin, who is endowed with the intellect of discernment, and who knows the secret of the nature of truth; however, it is not so from its opposite, which is corrupted wisdom (*duṣprajñā*).
Thus ends the [chapter] in the holy *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of Vālmīki, in the [Section on] Liberation.

Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Restraining of the Mind," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*. Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Restraining of the Mind," in the Section on Tranquility. 13.
The Fourteenth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Being carried away by the insubstantial waves of the ocean of worldly existence,
O giver of honor to your mother, it was by that populace that the state of muteness was earned. || 1 ||
Those suffering in various states of existence who are indifferent and unworthy of instruction are disregarded; here, the means for purifying the mind is described for those who are worthy of it. (1)
In this regard, first of all, it is the mind itself that has arisen from the unreal. He who is not capable of bringing it under control is not taught by Rāma;

thus, with the verse beginning with "saṃsāra... and so forth, he describes those people previously introduced as being ineligible for instruction, on account of their being objects of neglect. [He speaks] of the ocean of saṃsāra...
By that multitude of people— who are carried away by cravings for sensual pleasures that are like insubstantial waves, and who are incessantly driven [by them]—

because of their lack of interest in matters such as the restraint of the mind, discernment, and dispassion, and because they do not offer questions or requests even when encountering a wise man, a state of mere muteness has been adopted by their intellect; such is that multitude whom I [address].

The connection between the two [sentences] is as follows: "In this world, it is not taught in this treatise by means of analytical discourses characterized by an abundance of excellent arts that serve as the means for attaining the Self. || 1 ||
In this treatise, that [reality] is not taught by means of these analytical statements, which consist of noble insights arising from the attainment of the Self.
For one who does not see at all—or for one who sees constantly—what indeed is the dull-witted person?
To him, the forest displays its wonderful blossoms and variegated beauty. (3)

While it would have been sufficient simply to say "he who is blind," the expression "one who never sees" is intended to indicate that it is likewise improper for even one who possesses sight to fail to see due to misfortune, hatred, or other such factors.

Who, being himself devoid of intelligence, would take as an authority a fool whose nose is wheezing from leprosy when it comes to discerning various fragrances, by means of his own instruction? || 4 ||

What person of little intelligence or lack of discernment would take as an authority—would rely upon as a determiner of the true nature of fragrance—a man whose nose is shattered by leprosy and makes a gurgling sound, for the purpose of investigating or examining various perfumes? This is the meaning. || 4 ||
Who would accept as authoritative for the determination of dharma a person whose senses are perverted, who is intoxicated, whose eyes are rolling from liquor, and who lacks discernment? (5)
Who asks hundreds of questions about a corpse lying in a cemetery, or who seeks to resolve doubts by consulting a fool? (6)
The assemblies are gatherings of people; therein lies a hundredfold discourse. (6)
How indeed can that evil-minded one be called a teacher, by whom the serpent of the mind—though dwelling in the cave of his own disposition, and though mute and blind—is not conquered? (7)
That in which one rests is the "āśaya," the heart; [the Self] resides within its cavity.
Know that the mind is already conquered in reality because it does not exist;
that which does not exist at all, such as a stone in the vicinity, has been gone for a long time.

If it be asked, "Is the conquest of the mind then impossible even for the discerning one? he says, "It is indeed conquered"—meaning that from his proximity, that is, from his own presence, [the mind] is already cast away, driven far off. || 8 ||
O Rāma, he of wicked intellect by whom the mind— which though non-existent— is not conquered,
dies from the stupor of poison, as if by having swallowed actual venom.
The phrase "by one whose poison has not been swallowed" is also an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the absence of snake bites and other such harms. || 9 ||
O Rāma, the Knower always perceives the Self; the vital energies perceive the throbbing [of the body], and the senses perceive their own respective objects—what more need be said of the mind? (10)

He establishes this point—that in reality, that which does not exist—by the word "the knower" (*jña*). Is it for the purpose of manifesting objects, or for the purpose of movement, or for the sake of accomplishing the functions of the organs of knowledge and action? For all three of these are impossible;
since the manifestation of objects brought forward by the senses, impelled by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), occurs solely through the witness (*sākṣin*).
The sense is that the mind has its own function to perform. || 10 ||
The power that causes the vital breaths to vibrate is the power of knowledge belonging to the Supreme Self;
it is the innate power of the senses—what single thing here can be bound? (11)

If it is asked, "Could the mind not be bound by all the powers [of the senses]?"—the answer is no. This statement is applicable in the context of discernment (*viveka*), for even through a collective assembly, worldly activity is accomplished, much like the sweet sound of a lute. With this intention, he says:
"Of the vital breaths" (*prāṇānām*). Thus, just as the activities of bathing, giving, singing, and praising performed by a community of outsiders (*tairthika*) do not [lead to liberation],...
The meaning is that this [individual soul] is likewise impelled by that single possessor of all powers. || 11 ||
All these rays belong to that Self who possesses all powers;
from where indeed has this distinction or this expressibility of yours arisen? (12)

If someone were to say that, because of the rule that a composite must exist for the sake of a unifier, some other entity must be required here as well, then [we reply]: since this composite too is included within the composite of the universe, all the functional capacities of all things are but portions of the Self, which is the Lord, the creator of all.

With the intention that even for this [mind], its being for the sake of that [the Self] would be established, and not its being an insentient object, there is no proof of a sentient mind distinct for each body; thus he says: "All... The state of being denotable means being denotable by words such as "mind" and so forth.
What indeed is called the "individual soul" (jīva), by which the world here has been rendered blind?
Know that the mind itself is indeed non-existent; what power can it possibly have?

If it is argued: "In that case, let the *jīva* be the conscious controller; and since he cannot control the horses of the senses without the rein called the mind (*citta*), the mind is also necessarily established," to this he says: "What indeed?"—that is, what indeed is this "jīva" and what is this "mind," both of which you have mentioned? Are they something distinct from the Self?

Is it another conscious entity or unconscious? Not the first, because the scripture—"There is no other seer than this; there is no other hearer than this"—prohibits any other conscious entity apart from Brahman. Regarding the second [option], he asks: "What is its capacity?
Since that which is unconscious must necessarily exist for the sake of a conscious being, [it cannot arise] from the sense organs...
Because there is no distinction [between them] and because there is no power to preside over them; therefore, the meaning is that you should know both of those to be non-existent. || 13 ||
O Rāma, seeing the succession of sufferings of those whose views have been consumed by their own minds, my heart, overcome with compassion, suffers like one who is deluded.

Those whose vision of ultimate reality has been scorched by their own imagined minds are deluded; they have fallen into a state of confusion because, despite searching for a means to avert that suffering for tens of millions of years, they have found none. 14.
Who indeed here, and from what cause, would feel distress, since it is only the fool who suffers?
For common people and young camels are born only for the sake of suffering. 15.

For suffering that has a cause can be warded off by removing that cause; however, for fools, suffering is indeed causeless, and therefore it is impossible to ward off—this is the intention with which he says, "Who indeed... (kaḥ kila). Camels (*karabha*) are donkeys, and they are the fools under discussion; thus, the meaning is that they alone are truly pitiable. Alternatively, these [others] are not to be pitied.
This statement is made with the intention that, upon seeing such countless beings born in foolish wombs, they are likewise worthy of being disregarded. || 15 ||
Only for destruction are born the dull-witted and the ignorant within bodies;
these sinners arise incessantly like bubbles from the ocean. 16.

In order to explain what has been stated and to provide illustrative examples of those suffering from the distinctions of various births, he constructs an introductory framework, beginning with the words "vināśāyaiva" (only for destruction). The word "pāpāḥ" means those who are doers of evil. || 16 ||
Behold, how many animals are slaughtered every day in every slaughterhouse by those who act like butchers; what lamentation can there be for this? (17)

He cites the various forms of suffering among the different wombs of the ignorant in order to strengthen their dispassion, beginning with the words "How many," and so forth. "In every circle" means in every region. "Slaughter-places" (sūnā) refers to sites of animal killing;
"by those [associated] with them" means by the persons presiding over them. (17)
The wind daily destroys the tumors born upon the earth among gadflies and mosquitoes; what cause for lamentation is there in this? (18)
Among the creatures born from the earth that arise from the soil, the wind destroys the countless tumors of gadflies and mosquitoes. || 18 ||
In every forest upon the lords of mountains in every direction, the Pulindas and others slaughter hundreds of thousands of deer; what lamentation can there be in this? (19)

"Towards every direction" means in each and every direction. Although the repetition [of the word] is optional due to the force of the commencement of the *avyayībhāva* compound for distributive emphasis (*vīpsā*), the absence of both [the prefix and the repetition] is Vedic (*chāndasa*), since one or the other must necessarily be present. || 19 ||
In the water, a large fish mercilessly tears apart swarms of tiny aquatic creatures for the sake of a meal; what lamentation can there be in this? (20)
The fly, emaciated by hunger, eats the minute particles of a louse;
the hungry silkworm eats that [fly], and the gadfly eats even that restless [silkworm]. (21)
Now, he demonstrates through a sequence how the weak are oppressed by the strong, beginning with the words "a louse" (likṣā) and so forth:

a fly devours a louse—a cloth-mite—emaciated like a minute particle out of hunger, that is, the desire to eat; or [it devours] a silkworm, which is a specific type of insect; or a gnat, which is a forest-fly. || 21 ||
The frog eats that gadfly, and the wild beast eats that frog;
the bird kills the fierce serpent, and the mongoose tears that bird to pieces. (22)
The *dardura* is a frog; the *khaga* is a bird such as Garuḍa; and the *babhru* is a mongoose that [kills] this serpent. || 22 ||
The cat kills the mongoose; the dog tears apart the cat;
the bear kills the dog; and the tiger tears apart the bear. (23)
*Ṛkṣa* means a bear (*bhallūka*). In the reading *riccha*, it refers to a particular species of wild beast. || 23 ||
The lion overcomes the tiger, and the śarabha devours the lion;
yet the śarabha meets its destruction when leaping upon a rutting cloud-elephant.

The meaning is that it is well known that when a roaring cloud, being intoxicated, attempts to overleap—that is, to pass above—it rises up out of intolerance for that [obstruction] and, by falling upon the surface of a rock, meets its destruction. || 24 ||
The clouds are scattered by the winds, the winds are overcome by the mountains;
the mountains are crushed by the thunderbolt, for the thunderbolt is under the control of Śakra.

They were crushed and shattered by the thunderbolt (*vajra*). Although the thunderbolt is "pavi," it is also under the control of Śakra; that is to say, it has been brought under his power by Śakra through force. || 25 ||
By Viṣṇu Śakra is created, and Viṣṇu enters the state of a living being;
he undergoes this condition of pleasure and pain, governed by old age and death.

The phrase "is made subject" (vaśaga) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. Regarding "the state of a creature" (*jantutām*): having formed the resolve, "Entering by means of this living self (*jīvenātmanā*), let me manifest names and forms," Viṣṇu himself enters by way of the individual soul (*jīvātman*). Thus, because he has all creatures as his body through the mode of being the individual soul, there is the state of being the self of all creatures (*sarvajantvātmakatām*). Therefore...
He specifies it thus: "pleasure and pain," [referring to] those protected for as long as life lasts by old age and death, like food intended for one's own consumption. || 26 ||
Even creatures of massive bodies, even those equipped with the weapons of magic spells, are indeed subsisted upon by lice clinging to their limbs. (27)
The mention of "lice" is an illustration intended to include mosquitoes, bedbugs, flies, carnivorous insects, and so forth. They are "subsisted upon," meaning they are eaten. || 27 ||
Thus, this forest of living beings is incessantly being torn apart and scattered;
out of delusion, they devour one another and likewise protect one another.

The forest of beings—the multitude of living creatures—is uncut by physical sufferings and shattered by internal and celestial miseries; it is devoured, that is, eaten, at a later time, and for the sake of being eaten now, it is protected.
By the use of the word "api" (even/also), it is implied that having eaten half, the other half is protected. 28.
Various kinds of living beings perish incessantly, and lice, bugs, and ants are born incessantly. (29)

"Anārata" means continuous. "Yūkāḥ" refers to lice born from the hair. Regarding the compound "likṣā-yūka-pipīlikāḥ," the failure to form a singular collective (ekavadbhāva) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Furthermore, it is not the case that every *dvandva* compound optionally forms a singular; for instance, in the rule "In a *dvandva* of lunar mansions, the dual number is obligatory for *tiṣya* and *punarvasu*," [the plural is used].

It is correct to say that [the desired result] is established by the inclusion of the plural number as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is because an indicator applies with respect to its own class (*sajātīya*);

thus, since that [indicator] pertains to an optional rule where [the default] would otherwise not apply (*aprāptavibhāṣā*), otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of optionality even in the case of a *dvandva* compound of parts of living beings, musical instruments, and so forth.
In the reservoirs of water, fish, elephants, sea-monsters, and others are born;
within the earth, swarms of insects, scorpions, and the like are produced. (30)
Having concluded the series of objections, the author returns to the subject at hand: "In the reservoirs of water.
This means in the bodies of water, that is, in pools and lakes. "Elephants" refers to specific aquatic creatures shaped like elephants. (30)
In the intermediate space, birds and other creatures of the sky are born;
in the forest paths, lions, tigers, deer, and others are born. || 31 ||

Regarding the birds of the sky— those specific types of small birds— it is well known by popular tradition that they always wander in the atmosphere alone; they procreate in mid-air, and having broken open the egg before it falls to the ground, the fledglings emerge with wings already fully formed and immediately fly up into the atmosphere to wander about.
From the word "etcetera" (ādipada), piśācas, bhūtas, vetālas, and so forth are to be understood. || 31 ||
Various [insects] are born even within the limbs of living beings in every direction;
even among stationary things, wood-boring insects such as the *jaghanaka* and others are born. (32)

Regarding the limbs of living beings, there are worms, lice, and so forth. "Toward every quarter" means in every direction. *Ghuṇas* are wood-worms; *jaghanakas* are wood-insects shaped like *bhramarikās*.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), various types of worms and mosquitoes originating from leaves, fruits, flowers, and the like are included. || 32 ||
Within stones, insects, frogs, woodworms, and the like are born;
likewise, various swarms of insects are born even within excrement. (33)
Thus, throughout these countless births and deaths, may those who possess compassion rejoice or weep incessantly. (34)

Having concluded [the previous argument], he applies it to the present topic with the words "evam" (thus). The sense is that since there is an absence of hatred, rejoicing in the suffering of others is improper; and since there is an absence of affection, even weeping is inappropriate—therefore, indifference alone is fitting. || 34 ||
In this whirlpool of saṃsāra, which is incessantly dying and incessantly arising, neither contentment nor sorrow is appropriate. (35)
He states clearly what has already been said: "Without ceasing," etc. (35).
In this very same way, these rows of beings, which arise from many origins, are like the clusters of leaves on a tree; having arisen again and again, they dissolve away.
"Rows of beings" means multitudes; the sense is that it is exactly thus, in vain. || 36 ||
He who has set out to wipe away the suffering of the evil-minded is compassionate;
yet the sky suffers, as its own rays are wiped away by the parasol held over him. 37.

He who, being compassionate, has set out to wipe away the suffering of those with impaired intellects, exerts himself—that is, he toils—to make the entire sky, the atmosphere, such that the rays of the sun are wiped away by his own parasol and the heat is dispelled. In the reading "khidyate na saḥ," however, the sense is: "Does he not exert himself? (i.e., he certainly does).
It should be applied with a change in intonation (kāku). || 37 ||
Men on this earth who possess the nature of animals are not to be instructed;
what purpose is served by explaining the meaning of a discourse in the presence of a tree stump in the forest? (38)
What indeed is the distinction between those with expansive minds and animals?
Animals are led by a rope; those of deluded mind are led by their own thoughts. (39)
"Of those with expansive minds" means those whose minds are spread out toward sense objects; "viśeṣaṇam" means a distinction. || 39 ||
Seeing the calamity of fools who are submerged in the mud of their own minds and have begun actions leading to their own destruction, even stones weep. 40.
Even stones and pebbles weep, how much more so those possessed of consciousness; this is an instance of hyperbole (atiśayokti). || 40 ||
For those who have not conquered their own minds, all conditions bring suffering from every side;
therefore, one of perfected wisdom does not engage with them. (41)

The meaning is that conditions which bring suffering exist everywhere in all places at all times; therefore, because it is as impossible as sweeping away the dust of the entire earth, one does not undertake [the task]. || 41 ||
O descendant of Raghu, the sufferings of those who have conquered their own minds are to be well-considered; therefore, having known what is to be known, proceed in this matter.

They are well-examined because of the non-difference between *ra* and *la*, and they are not easily shaken; the meaning is that they are easily cast off. For that reason, in this context of wiping them away, one who knows what is to be known is a knower of reality. 42.
The mind does not exist, O mighty-armed one; do not imagine it in vain. By this imagination, you are being struck down as if by a vetāla spirit. (43)
Having concluded the incidental reflection on the qualified seeker, he continues with the subject at hand, saying:
"O fool, as long as you remained ignorant of the reality of the Self, so long did the serpent of your mind remain aroused. (44)

If [it is argued that] it does not exist, then, fearing that there would be no occasion for negation due to the non-establishment of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), he says: "as far as" (*yāvat*). Thus, the meaning is that establishment is possible by taking into account the previous state of ignorance. || 44 ||
Now you have understood it as it truly is, O subduer of enemies: the mind grows from volitional thought; therefore, abandon that very thing immediately. (45)
The nature of the self as it truly is from the perspective of ultimate reality. || 45 ||
If you take refuge in this visible world, then you possess a mind bound by kinship;
if you renounce this visible world, then you possess a mind that has attained liberation.
He states the secret of bondage and liberation: "The visible," [verse 46].
This collection of qualities, when relied upon, leads only to bondage; when renounced, it leads to liberation. Do as you wish. 47.
What, then, is the reality of that which is perceived? He states this with the word "this" (ayam): the meaning is that it consists of Māyā, whose nature is the three guṇas.
Meditating that "I am not this" and "this is not [me]," remain as immovable as a mountain;
with a heart resembling the infinite sky, you are the Lord of the Heart.
Meditating that the internal object of perception, "I," and the external object, "this," do not exist at all; he is immovable like a mountain, steadfast, the Lord of the Heart, the Self. 48.
O Rama, my dear friend, having abandoned the impurity of conceptualizing this self and this world as consisting of duality, remain perfectly steadfast, abiding in the all-pervading reality.
The meaning is: having completely abandoned, by means of one's entire self, the conceptualization consisting of duality in the form of "I" and "this. || 49 ||
Within yourself and within the world, amidst the various states of the seer and the seen, remain ever contemplating your own Self in that which is called "vision. 50.
One might ask: "If both those [states] are abandoned, what remains wherein stability is taught? To this he says:

"of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*). When it is said "in the interval between the states of the seer and the seen," one might include *vṛtti-jñāna* (cognitive modification) as well, since it too occurs in the interim; so that this may not be the case, [he specifies] "of the Self."

"And within the world. Thus, contemplating your own Self as abiding in that which is called "vision"—the nature of the witness of the threefold division (tripuṭī), whose form is pure Being (sanmātra) permeating the threefold division—remain as you are. 50.
Meditating constantly on the act of tasting alone—devoid of both the object of taste and the taster, and situated between the object of taste and the taster—become one with the Self. 51.
With the intention that, just as in the triad of the visual organ, so too in the triads of the gustatory and other senses, that very witness of them is to be discerned, he says:
"Taking hold of the supportless middle between the object of experience, such as taste, and the experiencer himself, remain steady in that middle. (52)
With the intention that this should be understood in the same way regarding other experiences such as inference and so forth, he says "Rāma": "Without support.

The meaning is: the "support" (ālamba) is the triadic aspect consisting of the subject, object, and act of cognition; being distinct from that, one should become steady by taking hold of the "middle" (madhya), which is the inner heart-center. || 52 ||
Free from the contemplation of worldly existence, and abandoned by the states of both being and non-being—thus contemplating the Self, remain established in the Self yourself. 53.

The cultivation of existence (*bhava*) by the power of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) is what is meant by the "state of dreaming"; the state of existence (*bhāva-daśā*) is the waking state; and the state of non-existence (*abhāva-daśā*) is deep sleep. In the reading *bhāvābhāvadṛśojjhitam*, the meaning is that it is free from both those perceptions. || 53 ||
O Rāma, when you yourself contemplate this object of thought while abandoning the existence of the self, then you fall into the state of the mind, which brings extreme suffering.

The syntactical connection is as follows: when, through negligence, you abandon this self-existence whose nature is pure consciousness alone and instead contemplate an object of thought that is distinct from it, then you fall into the state of being a mind (cittatā). || 54 ||
O mighty-armed one, by means of the method of knowing its own nature, release the lion of your own self from this chain of the mind, from the cave that is the mind. 55.

The ellipsis "having broken" [is understood] through the reasoning that consists in the knowledge of one's own true nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*). From the mind—that is, from the cave characterized by the mind, or from the cage.
However, if the reading is *balāt* (by force), it means by the power of the firmness of knowledge produced through reflection (*manana*) and so forth. || 55 ||
When you abandon the state of the Supreme Self and fall helplessly into the realm of the objectified (cetya),
and when you give rise to volitional thought (saṃkalpa), then you perceive that which is an object of cognition.
"Saṃpaśyase" means "you see. The transposition of the word order is Vedic (chāndasa). || 56 ||
O dear one, through the consciousness that the mind is an entity distinct from the Self, the mind becomes afflicted by suffering; yet, when that [consciousness] is abandoned, it perishes.
And how does it not fall away? And by that, how does it proceed toward conceptualization, or how is that [conceptualization] destroyed?

To this he says: "Of the self," etc. O dear one, when the mind—upon the awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of objects experienced previously—becomes, as it were, consciousness itself having attained a slight degree of grossness;

When the mind, through the consciousness of its own existence as something distinct from the Self, becomes established, it then—through repeated reflection—becomes firm, capable of volition, and attains the state of the *manas*; it is that very [mind] which experiences suffering. But when that consciousness of a separate existence is abandoned, it perishes.
When the realization arises within that "this entire world is indeed the Self alone," where is the intellect and where is the mind; what is the object of thought, and what is consciousness? (58)

He states this very point clearly: "This is indeed the Self" (ātmaivedam). Consciousness itself [is perceived] by consciousness. According to the opinion of Bhāguri, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied to a word ending in a consonant (*hal*). When that [consciousness] arises, the cognizer (*cetā*)—the one who has cognized—is conditioned (*upahita*). The mind (*citta*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and the object of cognition (*cetya*) is that which is pervaded by its modifications (*vṛtti*). What then of the fourfold set, including cognition (*cetana*) as the modification? Nothing whatsoever remains.
This is the meaning. || 58 ||
"O Rāghava, the wise know that the mere notion 'I am the self' or 'I am a living being' is the mind; by this, beginningless and endless suffering is extended. (59)
Thus, I am the individual soul (jīva) possessing a body, senses, and so forth, as they are currently being experienced. || 59 ||
"I am the Self; there are no other beings called 'living souls' anywhere"—this very stilling of the mind is said to be supreme bliss. (60)
The Self is indeed Brahman alone; there are no other entities called "living beings" (jīvas) existing as ultimate realities apart from Brahman.
O Rāghava, when the certainty arises that "this world is indeed the Self," the non-existence of the mind occurs; of this there is no doubt. (61)
Since everything in the world exists as Brahman, it follows by implication that the mind contained within it also lacks independent existence; thus he says: "All this is indeed the Self. (61)

When this is so, know that through the realization of truth, the mind is completely dissolved— just as darkness is by the light of the sun— remaining established in the conviction that "this is indeed one's own Self."
He concludes the stated means for the dissolution of the mind with the word "evam" (thus). || 62 ||
As long as the serpent of the mind remains within the body, there is great fear;
once it has been expelled through yoga, how can there be any occasion for fear? 63.

Now he states the fruit of that [practice] with the words beginning "the serpent of the mind": "From yoga"— that is, from *samādhi*, or from the merging characterized by the oneness of the inner self (*pratīc*) with Brahman— "verily,
when he finds fearless support in this [Self] which is invisible, ungraspable, undefined, and without abode, then..."

He becomes one who has attained fearlessness; for such is the meaning of scriptural passages beginning with, "Knowing Brahman as bliss, he fears nothing from anywhere" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9). || 63 ||
O sinless one, this exceedingly powerful Vetāla has arisen in the mind from mere delusion;
let it be forcibly cast down by the mantra of perfect knowledge.
When the yakṣa of the mind has departed from the house of the body, O best among the powerful, remain free from mental anguish and devoid of agitation; there is no fear for you.
The mention of "seizing" (*ādhigrahaṇa*) is an indication of all forms of suffering. "Agitation" (*udvega*) is a state of being disturbed due to an inability to endure suffering.
By the mere realization that "I am indeed free from passion and free from acquisition," the existence of your mind has dissolved;
you have reached the supreme state, the highest station, which is devoid of suffering.
"Remain thus, O you whose supreme seeking has been stilled; this is the end. (66)

Because he has attained all desires through the acquisition of the Self, he is free from passion (nirāgaḥ); for that very reason, he is "devoid of acquisition" (nirupārjana), meaning he is empty of the effort to acquire external means of pleasure. And thus, since even the desire for liberation (mumukṣā) does not remain, there is no possibility of activity for its sake; with this intention, he says: "one whose supreme longing is stilled" (upaśāntaparamaiṣaṇa). || 66 ||

Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Examination of One’s Own Mind," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki according to the Seer’s tradition. || 14 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Description of One’s Own Mind," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, following this impure existence of the mind, [one falls].
The tiny seed-grain of saṃsāra, the snare that binds the living soul.
That craving by which the self, having attained the state of the mind, is bound in transmigratory existence, is described here as the seed of all misfortunes in its many varied forms. (1)

The attainment of the supreme human goal has been stated to result from the destruction of the mind; now, in order to demonstrate that following after the mind leads to a succession of calamities through the increase of craving, he prepares the introductory context with the words beginning "etām" (this):
"The Self, following this existence of the mind..."

Having abandoned the manifestation of his own true nature as Brahman-Ātman, he follows after that very mind which has fallen into ignorance— defiled, veiled by nescience (avidyā), and whose manifestation is dependent on the functions of the senses— and thinks, "I am merely a composite of the body and so forth, imagined by the mind."

It joins together [the mind] and it bears the impurity of the latent impressions of passion and aversion, which are occasioned by the conceptualization of various objects presented by the mind; such is the connection between the two [meanings]. || 1 ||
The self, having abandoned its own true nature, assumes a defiled appearance; it aligns itself with that vision of the mind and takes on the impurity of conceptualization.
Bestowing increasing great delusion and causing fear, craving—in the form of a poisonous creeper—brings about nothing but fainting. (3)
What is the point of its being called "Dhātrī" (the Nourisher)? To this he replies: "Vardhamānā" (The Increasing).

Because it is the cause of thousands of instances of death, fainting, and delusion, craving—which takes the form of a poisonous creeper—bestows only fainting upon this Self that bears the impurity of mental constructions (*kalanā*), and not even a trace of happiness; such is the meaning.
Whenever it arises, this craving— which bestows great delusion and causes infinite transformations of the self— is like the dark night.

He explains the phrase "bestowing increasing great delusion" with the words "when": the "dark night" is the gloom of the rainy season; for even that [night] undergoes many transformations, such as the flashing of clouds and rain, within the infinite self that is like the sky. || 4 ||
Hara and the other gods are capable of enduring the burning of the flames of the fire at the end of an aeon;
but none whatsoever are capable of enduring the burning of the flames of the fire of craving. (5)
He also explains the phrase "causing fear" with the words "for aeons" (kalpānala); the ellipsis is "no wise men at all [are able to endure it]. || 5 ||
Sharp, black, and very long, this terrible sword of craving always cleaves one's own limb; though cool, it results in unhappiness.

*Kṛpāṇikā* means a sword (*asi*). The words "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*) and so forth serve to establish its nature as a blade. It constantly carries its own body—that is, it continually cuts itself. Its *udarka*, or the time of its fruition, is unhappy (*asukha*). || 6 ||
O Rāghava, those fruits of the creeper of craving which are here so difficult to reach the end of, difficult to digest, and so exalted—these are indeed sufferings. (7)
He clarifies the phrase "poisoned food" with the words "yāni" (those which): "durjarāṇi" means incapable of being digested; that is to say, they are difficult to ward off. || 7 ||
Invisible, this craving— the hunting hound of men— dwells within the cave of the mind and devours the flesh, bones, blood, and other parts of the body from the person.
A female dog or a female wolf [is called] *vanaśunī*. || 8 ||
In one moment it attains exaltation, and in another moment it falls into emptiness;
the river of craving, though dull, swiftly shatters [all things]. 9.
"An instant's joy" means an increase. The adjectives are to be applied to both [the woman and the river]. "Dull" means cold and turbid.
"It shatters" means that having led one into entry upon rocky thorns, forests, and the like, it breaks him apart. "The monsoon river" is a river swollen by the rains. (9)
Seeing his own wretchedness, with his heart destroyed and his vigor gone, a person falls into degradation;
struck down by craving, he becomes deluded, cries out, and falls. (10)
He explains this very point—that it brings about fainting—with the verse beginning "dṛṣṭadainya" (10).
The vital breaths moving within the cavity of the heart remain healthy for that man in whose hollow the black female serpent of craving does not dwell. (11)
He says, beginning with "not remaining," that when craving is exhausted, the destruction of all suffering and the arising of all merit are accomplished. || 11 ||
Surely, wherever the dark night of craving has set, there meritorious deeds increase like moons during the bright fortnight. (12)
That tree of a man which has not been gnawed by the woodworm of craving always reaches a state of full bloom with the flowers of merit. (13)
In the forest of the heart, the river of men blinded by craving flows on, filled with endless and turbulent waves and crowded with eddies and whirlpools. (14)

In the forest characterized by such features, the river of craving— possessing waves marked by endless agitation and eddies marked by delusion— surely flows and surges through the hearts and minds of blind men who lack the vision of discernment. 14.
Driven by craving, all these people are whirled around, shattered, and repeatedly gathered together, like birds on the string of a mechanical puppet. (15)

Like a bird caught in a string-trap—held by a string and bound—a man is first made to wander about for the sake of acquiring wealth; then he is shattered, as if by the plucking out of his feathers, through anxieties regarding its protection, expenditure, and depletion, along with grief; and finally, he is gathered in and killed. || 15 ||
Even the most subtle roots, craving—harsh with its cruel intent—cuts away as it leaps about like the edge of an axe. (16)

The very subtle roots of knowledge of the Dharma, such as compassion and discernment, though only slightly sprouted, were struck by a harsh and merciless disposition; they were then violently shaken and fell away at that moment. (16)
The deluded person, pursuing craving, falls into a pit, just as a young deer, following a dark blade of grass or a branch, falls into a chasm. 17.
Into the pit, the dark well of hell; like a young deer falling after a branch of grass growing on the mouth of a chasm or a well—[the branch] which is blue and green. || 17 ||
Even one who is not intoxicated, old age thus withers the eye in an instant,
just as emaciating thirst, which dwells within the heart, causes decay.
Even when it has grown most intense, this madness of old age—the *rūpikā* demoness dwelling in the heart—wears out the eyes and blinds them. 18.
Through this deep-seated and inauspicious attachment to desire, which has taken root in his heart, this Blessed One Viṣṇu has assumed the form of a dwarf.
By that which has become inauspicious, having taken root and made its nest within the heart. || 19 ||
Driven by this very thirst, which is somehow knotted within the heart, one indeed wanders through the sky day after day, like the sun bound by a rope.

The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: he is bound, as if by a rope, by thirst (tṛṣṇā)—which is divine, impelled by the Lord (deva), or which has as its object the pleasures to be enjoyed by the gods. || 20 ||

One who has gone far away should abandon craving— which consists of the nature of all suffering, which cuts short the life of the world, and which is cruel— just as one would avoid a venomous female serpent.
By the word "jagatī," all living beings dwelling in the world are indicated. || 21 ||
By craving the winds blow; by craving the mountains stand firm;
by craving alone the earth supports all; by craving the three worlds are sustained.
With the intention that the entire existence within saṃsāra occurs solely through the power of craving, he says: "by craving" (tṛṣṇayā). || 22 ||
This entire course of worldly existence is strung together by the bowstring of craving;
no one is ever liberated from the bond of craving, just as one is not released from the bond of a rope.
A *varatrā* is a leather rope. || 23 ||
Therefore, O Raghava, abandon craving by relinquishing mental constructs;
for it has been determined through reasoning that the mind does not exist when there is no conceptualization. (24)
To explain how the abandonment of craving is accomplished merely by the relinquishing of volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*), he says: "The mind.

The mind that is free from conceptualization—that is, devoid of volitional construction—does not exist. The sense is: in the absence of the mind, whence could there be the possibility of craving? || 24 ||
O mighty-armed one, first fix this evil desire, consisting of darkness, within my heart—that very thought of "this is you" and "this is I. (25)
Do not form the false hope that "this body is you" or "I am this," nor the conceit which is the cause of all baseless hopes;
do not entertain this notion of selfhood in that which is not the self, for it gives birth only to suffering.
O Rāma, if you do not cultivate such thoughts, then you shall be counted among the knowers of Truth.
O fortunate one, having severed this unmeritorious state consisting of the sense of "I" with the very probe of the "non-I" state,
you shall reach the ground that marks the end of existence through your own natural disposition.
He whose fear for all beings has been overcome by the realization of existence. || 27 ||

Having severed this craving consisting of the sense of "I" with the knife characterized by the absence of the sense of "I," O fortunate one, [the meaning is: "abide in existence"—that is, in *brahman*, which is the end of worldly existence (*bhava*) and the cessation of affliction, or specifically in the seventh stage (*saptamabhūmikā*)—in that very state. || 27 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of Thirst," in the section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki according to the ancient seers. 15.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Thirst," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixteenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, these words of yours are profound by their very nature."
When you say to me, "Do not grasp at the thirst for egoism," [I reply: 1.

The relinquishing of latent impressions (vāsanā) is described according to the distinction between the object of meditation (dhyeya) and the object of knowledge (jñeya); by means of this, the characteristics of those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and those liberated after death (videhamukta) are established here. || 1 ||

Not grasping the intended meaning of the statement beginning with "Having cast off this thirst consisting of the sense of 'I'," which was spoken because it is impossible to abandon the sense of "I" while one is alive in the body and because it would be inappropriate for the Guru to have such an intent regarding the death of his disciple, Rāma asks with the words beginning "svabhāva... (by nature...).
O Lord, if I were to renounce the sense of ego,
then I would completely abandon this entire configuration known as the body.
"Without remainder" means:

since you yourself have stated that there is a state of oneness between the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), it is impossible to abandon the ego-sense while leaving the vital breaths remaining; therefore, the meaning is "by not leaving even the vital breaths behind. || 2 ||
Just as a great tree is supported by its massive trunk, so too, it is said, is this body supported by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). || 3 ||
By the "knee-pillar" (jānu-stambha), that is, by the obstruction caused by the binding of the root [channels] extending from the knees. || 3 ||
Upon the destruction of the ego-sense, the body surely perishes,
just as a great tree falls when its root is cut by a saw.
He confirms that very point through negation: "Egoism," etc. (Verse 4).
Therefore, O Sage, how may I abandon him and yet how may I live?
Having determined this matter, speak to me, O best among speakers. (5)

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O lotus-eyed Rāma, bestower of honor, the abandonment of latent desires (vāsanā) everywhere is described by the knowers of truth as being of two kinds: that which is to be known and that which is to be meditated upon.

It should be known that for the wise, during the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and in the state of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*), the Self— remaining as the substrate alone— is the object of meditation, being sublated by knowledge. Even though ignorance along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is sublated at the time of emergence (*vyutthāna*) by the undivided mental modification (*akhaṇḍākāravṛtti*) produced by the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*), [the Self remains the substrate].
In accordance with the scriptures on liberation while living (jīvanmukti), and because of the remaining portion of the experience of the fruits of prārabdha-karma that must be exhausted, one accepts—

either as a persistence of the sublated (bādhitānuvṛtti) or as the non-sublation of the aspect of projection (vikṣepāṃśa)— the residue of a trace of ignorance (avidyāleśa); thus, by means of the body, which is no longer superimposed as the "I" (anadhyastāhaṃbhāva).

The meaning is that [the ego-sense] is of two kinds: first, because worldly transactions for the sake of enjoyment are not established [as real], there is the persistence of a temporary appearance of the ego-sense; second, because it is based on the experience of the wise, it is like the object of meditation due to its being primarily meditative concentration—thus it is called "like the object of meditation" (dhyeya iva dhyeya). || 6 ||
"I belong to these objects, and these are my very life;
I am nothing at all without them, and they indeed exist not without me. (7)

Therein, he establishes the second [point] with the words "I am" (*aham iti*). From the perspective of one who possesses discernment (*vivekin*), two objects of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) are perceived here. One is the aggregate-self (*saṃghātātman*) which depends upon the body, senses, intellect, and mind, and which is characterized by the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatā*) toward sons, friends, wife, wealth, and so forth.

Another [reality] is of an indivisible, unitary nature, common to the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], as well as death, fainting, and other births; it is of the nature of pure consciousness alone, remaining as the residue after discrimination. Having first investigated and determined the nature of the former [the individual self], he says "I am," etc., regarding these—the body, senses, and so forth, as well as external food, drink, and so forth.

The meaning is that it is the aggregate of objects experienced by the self. These bodies and so forth, as well as food and so forth, are the cause for the establishment of my own existence as a living being. Therefore, having formed a firm internal conviction regarding the primary referent of the word "I"—namely, that without these [factors] I am not established as anyone at all within the sphere of worldly transaction—one [proceeds] together with the mind.

Upon discerning that the aggregate-self is in reality an absolute non-entity, when one meditates in the second stage upon the remaining subject of the "I" as pure consciousness— thinking "these objects do not belong to me"— through such an extracted realization; that abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) consisting of such meditation is what I have proclaimed as the object of meditation (*dhyeya*).
The meaning of the three [is as follows]. || 7 ||
Having thus made this internal resolve and deliberated with the mind, one contemplates:
"I am not the object, nor does the object belong to me. (8)
O Rāma, that which is truly the renunciation of latent impressions (vāsanā)— performed with ease by a mind that is cool within— is declared to be the object of meditation.

Having understood everything through equanimity and thereby brought about the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanā), one who is free from the sense of "mine" abandons the body; this is to be known as the exhaustion of latent impressions. || 10 ||

First, he establishes the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) with the words "all": having realized— that is, directly perceived— through the sequence of practice on the stages (*bhūmikā*), that the entire world is equal because it is identical with Brahman,
one effects the destruction of latent impressions and becomes free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, and established in non-conceptual samādhi.
The meaning is that when one abandons the body in every way through the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, that should be known as the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*).

He who, having effortlessly abandoned the latent impression consisting of egoism and renounced all objects of meditation, remains [in that state], is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 11 ||

Therein, he illustrates the second [type] with the words "ahaṃkāra" (egoism). He who remains through *līlā*—that is, through conduct appropriate for the purpose of winning over the world—is one who has abandoned the object of meditation, meaning he is one who has relinquished the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the object of meditation. || 11 ||

O descendant of Raghu, know that he who has attained tranquility by abandoning all rootless mental constructions and latent impressions, and who consists of the relinquishment of the knowable, is truly liberated.
He illustrates the first [type] with the words "nirmūla" (rootless) and so forth. The meaning is: having abandoned all mental construction (*kalanā*) along with root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).

This consists in the abandonment of the knowable (*jñeya*), and is primarily characterized by pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) remaining after all knowledge accompanied by latent impressions (*savāsanājñāna*) has been sublated by wisdom.
Having abandoned all latent impressions (vāsanā), those noble souls who are liberated while living—such as Janaka and others—remain at ease, absorbed in that which is to be meditated upon. 13.

He elaborates on what has already been stated with the words beginning "the object of meditation" (*dhyeya*), etc.; [it is] by way of sport (*līlayā*), that is, through worldly activity (*vyavahāreṇa*). || 13 ||
But those who, having abandoned all latent impressions (vāsanās), have attained tranquility,
remain as liberated-in-body (videhamukta) within Brahman, both supreme and inferior.
O Raghava, there are only two kinds of renunciation that are equal and established in the state of liberation;
both of these have attained the nature of Brahman, and both are free from the fever of worldly distress.
The particle *eva* is used in the sense of "also" (*api*). || 15 ||
O sinless one, when the mind is settled in the pure and solitary vital breath, one remains with a throbbing body, while the other remains with a tranquilized body. (16)
One whose mind is disciplined is established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*); one whose mind is undisciplined is engaged in the activities of the waking state.

Both of these—the disciplined and the undisciplined—abide with ease and find rest in that which is called "the pure breath" (*svāsa*), namely, in Brahman alone, which is stainless and free from the impurity of ignorance. What, then, is the distinction between them? He explains this:
"One" refers to one who has emerged from meditative absorption; "the other" refers to one who is absorbed in concentration. || 16 ||
One remains with the body, liberated and free from fever;
the other, having abandoned the body, exists as one who is emancipated and whose latent impressions are no longer knowable.
The analysis is: "the latent impression of the unknowable. || 17 ||
He who neither rejoices nor desponds when pleasure and pain arrive incessantly in their due time— he is called liberated.
He states the characteristics of one who is liberated while engaged in worldly activity with the verse beginning "Even when [calamities] befall," etc. (18).
He for whom neither desire nor aversion exists toward desired or undesired objects, and who moves about like one in deep sleep—he is said to be liberated. (19)

Desire and aversion consist of longing for what is desired and dislike for what is undesired. With respect to objects regarded as desirable or undesirable by the perspective of the ignorant, he is unattached, meaning he is like one in deep sleep. || 19 ||

He within whom the notions of "mine," "I," and "here" have completely ceased regarding the calculation of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
The construction is as follows: "here, in this body and its adjuncts, there are the conceptualizations of 'I' and 'mine'. (20)
He who is not internally touched by joy, resentment, fear, anger, desire, miserliness, or [wrong] views is said to be liberated while living. 21.
He who always dwells in a state of wakefulness with a mind whose mental fluctuations have been stilled as if in deep sleep,
remains forever filled with joy like the moon joined with its digits.
He who is served [by these] is remembered here as one who is liberated. || 22 ||

By that man whose mental fluctuations have been stilled as if in deep sleep, and who is characterized by a mind that has no attachment to worldly objects—even while awake, he remains forever established [in that state]. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of a state (*bhāve*). Furthermore, he who is always endowed with joy—that is, natural gladness—is like the full-orbed moon in its clarity.
He who practices this in this world is liberated; the meaning is that he is remembered as one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 22 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the sage had thus spoken, the day passed away, and the sun went to its setting for the performance of the evening rites.
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe;
and at the end of night, it returned along with the rays of the sun.

Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Treatment of Thirst," in the section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation, in the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 16.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Thirst," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eleventh day.
Seventeenth Chapter. 17.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, those who are liberated while in the body (videhamukta) are here within the range of my speech.
They do not remain at all; therefore, listen to this liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 1 ||
The specific determinations endowed with which one who is liberated while living is not bound, whereas the ignorant person is bound again—this distinction is described here. (1)

Having perceived through Rāma’s gestures his desire to know the characteristics of one liberated while living (videhamukta), [the sage]— by indicating that words become stumped due to the absence of such characteristics because of his uniform nature—
suggests that the definition of his true nature is the state where nothing remains but the unsurpassed, self-luminous plenitude of bliss alone.

He makes a formal declaration in order to state the specific features that must necessarily be adopted among the characteristics of liberation while living (jīvanmukti): "Those who are liberated while in the body" (vedehamuktāḥ). || 1 ||
When ordinary actions are performed even by one who has abandoned desire through craving, they know that state to be liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā). || 2 ||

Now, one might object: if those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) still possess a craving for the fruits of the various duties appropriate to their caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), then, like the ignorant, they would undergo bodily bondage again for the sake of experiencing those fruits. On the other hand, if such craving does not exist, then no activity would occur at all, according to the maxim that "even a fool does not act without aiming at a purpose. To avoid this objection:

He begins to establish the distinction between the impure craving that impels the ignorant and the pure [craving] that impels the wise, starting with the words "prākṛtāny eva" (only those which are natural), etc. "Prākṛtāni" means those obtained through the inherent nature of their respective caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama).
Desire is the enthusiasm for tasting sense objects. || 2 ||
The teachers declare that the state in which a living being remains with an attachment fixed upon external objects through craving is bondage—a firm shackle to the cycle of existence. (3)

That state of being in which the impulse for enjoyment has been firmly established by the conviction that worldly existence is real is called *baddha-utsāha*. (3) Indeed, when the latent impression (*vāsanā*) has abandoned its conceptual constructs within the heart yet continues to sport externally, it is said here to belong to one who possesses a body while liberated in life (*jīvanmukta*). (4)

The meaning is that for those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), desire— which is a latent impression (vāsanā) that has abandoned the intention for enjoyment in the heart through the certainty of the unreality of all objects of enjoyment, and which operates externally solely for the purpose of maintaining the world— rests upon the body alone. || 4 ||
"O Rāghava, craving that is swollen by the calamity of external objects is said to be 'bound';
craving that is liberated from the calamity of all objects is called 'liberated'. (5)
Intending to elaborate upon craving (tṛṣṇā) as it has been defined, he says [the following] in summary: "External," etc. "Calamity" (vyasana) means addiction (lāmpaṭya). || 5 ||
That craving for which there was previously an eternal state of freedom from suffering and partlessness, even while it exists in the present, is remembered by the wise as liberation. (6)

"Prior" means at the time before the attainment of the object; this also implies the period after the destruction of the object. "Freedom from suffering" means being devoid of the suffering caused by passion and its like. Even at the time of attaining the object, there is "lack of agitation," meaning an absence of swelling or excitement. (6)
"O Raghava, O high-minded one, know that this internal notion, 'let this be mine,' is craving; it is a chain and a mental construction. (7)
Having completely renounced this [notion] regarding all things, whether they exist or do not exist, at all times, the noble-minded one, supremely generous, attains the Supreme. (8)
The supreme state of liberation while living. || 8 ||

Having abandoned the hope for bondage and the hope for liberation, as well as the states of pleasure and pain, and even the hope for existence and non-existence, remain like the unagitated great ocean.
"Bonds" refers to the body and so forth, which bind; "hope for them" means hope for those bonds. "Liberation" is their cessation; "hope for that" means hope for liberation.

The point is that when there is the certain conviction of the falsity of bondage, its cessation cannot be hoped for, for one who is wide awake does not hope for the release from a dream-fetter. This applies equally to the states of pleasure and pain.
In this context, "renunciation" refers precisely to the certainty of falsehood.
O best among the wise, having realized yourself to be undecaying and immortal,
do not let your mind be troubled by fears of old age and death.
This reality of the categories of existence does not belong to you, nor are you this, O Rāghava;
that [reality] is something else entirely, and you, O Rāghava, are someone else entirely.
He states the means for abandoning hope: "The reality of objects," etc.

This visible world—the true nature of objects—is not yours; nor are you it. Therefore, the meaning is that it is something else entirely, a mere trifle, distinct from the ultimate reality (paramārthasatya). || 11 ||
When all that is non-existent has arisen [as appearance] and the existent has subsided into non-existence, and when you have transcended even that state—how can there be the arising of craving? (12)
Furthermore, O virtuous Rāma, in the mind of a discerning person, there arises a fourfold certainty of vast proportions. (13)
"O Rāma, listen further to what is about to be said regarding the fourfold division of certainty"—this is the ellipsis.
He explains that very point with the verse beginning "In the mind... (verse 13).
"From head to foot, I am created by my mother and father"—O Rāma, this is the singular conviction that leads to bondage through the perception of what is unreal. (14)
"I am subtler than even the tip of a hair, transcending all existing things"—this second conviction arises in the wise for the sake of liberation. (15)

It transcends and is distinct from all distinctions such as the body and the senses; "tanu" means subtle, that is to say, devoid of grossness. Its status as the cause of liberation arises through the process of purifying the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha). || 15 ||
"I am the very soul of all things in the web of the universe, the imperishable All"—this third conviction, O scion of Raghu, leads indeed to liberation. (16)

Regarding the third [category]: since its delusion regarding the limited nature of the internal self can likewise be removed through purification together with the referent of the word *tat*, it is useful for liberation. || 16 ||
"I or the entire world is always empty, like space"—this is another fourth conviction for the attainment of liberation. (17)

"I" is the limiting adjunct consisting of internal demarcation; "the world" is the limiting adjunct consisting of the celestial and so forth. Always—that is, throughout the three periods of time—this is the certainty regarding the Self, which consists in the sublation of all that is perceivable. || 17 ||
Among these four certainties, the first is said to lead to bondage; the other three, arising from pure contemplation, are declared to lead to liberation. (18)
Of these, the first is said to be the state of being bound by craving;
the three types of pure craving are clear and belong to those who sport as liberated while living. (19)
Regarding the question of what relevance this classification has in the investigation of the divisions of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), he says: "Of these...

The meaning is that since craving is a cause of bondage only when this [ignorance] exists, this alone is the cause of bondage. Those subsequent three certainties are characterized by pure—that is, faultless—craving. (19)
O Mahāmati, my mind, having taken hold of the certainty that "I alone am everything," does not again go toward despondency. (20)
Regarding that, he states the purpose of the third [verse]: "All," etc. (20).
The greatness of the Self pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards;
by the internal conviction that "all is the Self," one is not bound.
It is called the Void, its nature is Māyā, and it is also known as Brahman and Consciousness; it is likewise described as Śiva, Puruṣa, Īśāna, and the eternal Self.
Warding off the notion that the fourth [self] has entered the view of the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādin), he says: "It is empty.
The meaning is that it is the remaining self alone that is designated by the disputants with words such as "empty," and not a non-entity. || 22 ||
All this is always being alone; here, duality or anything else is never found anywhere. The world is pervaded by knowledge, and not by any other cognition. (23)
The world is pervaded—that is, swallowed—by knowledge, which is the vision of the nature of ultimate reality; not by the other, namely the deluded intellect as before. (23)
The ocean of waters, whose self is infinite, was filled with a pale-red hue;
the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, was pervaded by the Self.
The meaning is that it is just as the infinite-souled ocean, whose extent is immeasurable, is filled with waters reaching down to the very foundations of the earth (Pātāla). || 24 ||
Therefore, truth is eternal and immortal; falsehood exists nowhere at all.
Just as the entire ocean is nothing but water, waves and the like do not exist anywhere apart from it.

Let it be that [the world] is unfulfilled; what follows from that? To this he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). Therefore, the oneness with Brahman alone, which is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is the eternally real (*satya*). The meaning is that it is established that apart from that, the "unreal" (*amṛta*) world-form does not exist. || 25 ||
Bracelets, armlets, anklets, and so forth are not distinct from gold;
likewise, the millions of forms of trees and grasses are not distinct from the Self.
They are not separate from gold; they are not distinct from the self, that is, from the self which is earth. || 26 ||
Through the playful manifestation of the world via the emergence of duality and non-duality,
it is the power consisting of the Supreme Self that alone expands as non-dual.
How, then, is there the cognition of both difference and non-difference in the world, such as in water and the ocean? To this he says: "Duality and non-duality...

The meaning is that the power consisting of the Supreme Self, which is non-dual, is the very existence of Brahman itself; it unfolds through the various manifestations of duality and non-duality for those who are ignorant. || 27 ||
Whether it be your own or that of another, in all things at all times— whether they have perished or increased, whether they be effects, pleasures, or pains— do not grasp them.

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he replies: "In that which belongs to oneself. The meaning is: whether it be one's own or another's—regarding everything in the world, such as sons, friends, and so forth—whether they flourish or perish, you who are wise should not grasp at the resulting pleasure or pain. || 28 ||
Relying upon the non-duality of existence, consisting of the nature of the non-duality of being,
and disregarding the non-duality of action, become one who embodies both duality and non-duality.

If it is asked, "How then should I conduct myself? the answer is: "Just like Brahma, by relying precisely upon non-duality and duality. He explains this in detail: "The non-duality of existence. Just like Brahma, you, being in reality composed of the non-duality of pure existence (*sattādvaitamaya*), even during the time of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), should rely solely upon non-duality through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The meaning is: in the matter of bestowing the fruits of the respective actions of various living beings, and in the matter of establishing the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), you should act by completely disregarding non-duality (*advaita*) and, as is appropriate, be devoted to both duality and non-duality. For in non-duality, action itself is impossible, as everything would be of a single uniform nature everywhere.

The sense is that, since there would otherwise arise the contingency of contradicting the established order of the world, the treatises on dharma (dharmaśāstra), and so forth, it is more appropriate to rely upon duality in that regard. || 29 ||

Do not fall, like an elephant into the depths of terrifying caves filled with calamities, by means of the whirlwind of the cultivation of worldly existence within the fearsome stages of becoming. (30)

To the question, "Even if existence [is granted], what is the harm in resorting to duality?", he replies with the verse beginning with *bhava*. [The phrase] "filled with portents" refers to inauspicious omens. By the mention of a "cave" (*darī*), a pit (*garta*) is indicated. Thus, the intended meaning is that the very fall into the pit of saṃsāra is the harm in that case. || 30 ||

O Great-Souled One, duality consisting of the mind does not exist; nor does unity exist within the Self, for the nature of the Self has transcended both. Non-duality is devoid of unity; it is eternally manifest—
Therefore, they say that everything is not anything at all; such is its own nature.

He establishes the stated non-duality of the seven categories with the words "duality": Duality cannot exist as ultimately real, because it consists of the mind—that is, it is merely imagined by the mind and does not touch the reality of things.
This is because even according to others [the Naiyāyikas], duality is admitted to be produced by relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), and it is admitted that it perishes when that cognition perishes.

Thus, even the quality of number called "oneness" (ekatva) is not possible in the Self, because that too is merely a conceptual construct for the purpose of distinguishing it from duality and so forth; the Self is such that its very nature arises as distinct from duality and the like. Therefore, it is non-dual (advaita), being devoid of oneness.

The meaning is that even though it is self-established, because it is independent of anything else, Brahman—which is Being alone—is eternally risen; yet, because of the exclusion of oneness and the exclusion of all duality, it is also "not anything at all. Therefore, scriptural passages such as "That became all" and "There is no diversity whatsoever here," as well as those who experience That, speak of it by way of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). || 31 ||
Neither do I exist, nor indeed do the worlds exist; yet all this that appears is surely the unchanging.
It is mere consciousness alone that manifests, tranquil.
Know that this world is neither non-existent nor existent, yet it appears as if it were real.

The form distinguished as "you" (the object) within the self of "I" (the subject) does not exist at all; nor do the worlds of "you" and so forth, which are forms distinguished from the referent of "I. Rather, all this exists as nothing but changeless pure consciousness (*vijñānamātra*). This world appears through the mere direct realization of that [consciousness], yet it is eternally quiescent—neither existent nor non-existent.
"Sacca" means "viddhi," which signifies "know. || 32 ||
The supreme nectar, beginningless, the illumination of all illuminations, undecaying, unborn, inconceivable, partless, and changeless;
it is free from the web of the senses and is the life-force of the vital energy.
The cause of all causes, devoid of all parts and qualities.
Furthermore, he confirms that very certainty with firm resolve through two verses beginning with "param":
[He is] the life-force of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*), meaning the cause for the activity of breathing; for there is the Vedic scripture: "The breath of the breath," and so forth. (33)
The Lord, eternally joyful, abiding in the expansive light of consciousness, the seed of experience, to be taught as one's own essential nature—
Brahman is always everything, its tasting occurring within through the appropriate means.
"May you, I, and the world—let this be your internal certainty. (34)

The seed, which is the fundamental basis, of experiences such as visual perception and the like, is one's own self-nature—the abiding in one's own true form. By means of that, through the production of direct perception via words—just as in the statement "You are the tenth"—that which is to be taught is Brahman alone, whose essence is the singular flavor of internal bliss and inward relish; [it is realized that] "You, I, and the world are not [separate from that]."

"Following from that, may you possess the conviction that 'there is something else beyond this,' and may that [conviction] be firmly established within you"—this is both the blessing and the instruction. (34)

Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Instruction on Severing Thirst," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Tranquility) of the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 17 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Severing Thirst," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighteenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For those great souls whose intentions are disciplined, there is no concern with false views.
O mighty-armed one, this is the very nature of those who move about here in sport. || 1 ||
That state of being established in which a wise man, remaining in the world of transmigration, does not sink into despair—
that state is here taught in detail to Rāghava.

Listen to this nature and state of those whose intentions are disciplined, whose minds are concentrated, and who are uncorrupted and uninjured by false views such as desire, greed, and the like; this is the manner that will be described—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 1 ||
Even while dwelling in saṃsāra, the sage whose mind is liberated while living should laugh at the worldly courses of existence, which are tasteless in their beginning, middle, and end.

At the beginning, they are rendered tasteless by the sufferings of birth and so forth; in the middle, by internal sufferings and the like; and at the end, by the sufferings of death, hell, and so on. One should laugh—that is, look upon them with derision—recognizing their fitness for laughter.
Established in all one's worldly duties, one remains impartial toward all philosophical views.
One who is established by relying on the abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā) should meditate upon that [Self]. || 3 ||

He who stands firm (*stha*) in all duties appropriate to his nature and relevant to each particular time, and who is impartial (*madhyastha*)—that is, equal—toward all perspectives such as those regarding enemies and friends, is described in two ways: as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and as the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). The meaning is that, between these two, one should rely upon the abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā-tyāga*), which is the object of meditation. || 3 ||
Free from agitation in all circumstances, nourishing all goals,
having seen the Self through the light of discernment, he dwells in the grove of awakening.
He nourishes the desired welfare of all and does nothing displeasing to anyone; he whose dwelling is in the grove characterized by awakening.
Taking as his support the state that transcends all things, with an intention as cool as the full moon, neither agitated nor self-satisfied, he does not despair within saṃsāra. || 5 ||
Remaining impartial toward all enemies, endowed with compassion and courtesy,
and performing his duties as they arise, he does not perish in this worldly existence among the foremost of men.

"Equal" (*samaḥ*)—[according to the reading *mūlasthitapāṭhe*, this means being neutral toward all enemies by virtue of the state of neutrality, and likewise neutral toward friends; the meaning is that he is "equal" because he is devoid of both attachment and aversion toward both parties]. The reading "toward enemy and friend" (*śatrau ca mitre ca*) is clear. "Of the foremost" (*agryāṇām*) refers to teachers and the like.
He performs duties such as serving and protecting those who have attained their positions in accordance with the established rules.
He neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires;
established in silence, initiating only what is natural, he does not sink in the cycle of existence.
He remains silent and speaks sparingly; he undertakes what is appropriate and is not indolent in necessary duties. (7)
When questioned, he speaks of the matter at hand; when not questioned, he remains like a pillar.
Free from both likes and dislikes, he does not suffer in saṃsāra.
He says that very thing: "When asked," etc. (verse 8).
One who speaks what is pleasing to all, who is eloquent when exhorted,
and who understands the intentions of living beings, does not despair in the cycle of existence.
He speaks what is agreeable and pleasing; when urged or challenged, he possesses graceful speech and skillfully provides a resolution. (9)
Seized by the vision of what is proper and improper, his actions ruined by greed,
he perceives the example of the world as a bilva fruit within the hollow of a hand.

Through the vision of impartiality, one knows "this is appropriate" and "this is inappropriate," and sees with non-partisanship. For this very reason, it is said that [the truth] is as clear as a bilva fruit resting in the hollow of the palm of the hand;
for if one were to favor one side, then the defects of that side and the virtues residing in the other side would remain hidden due to being shrouded by attachment and aversion.
"They appear clearly," so it is said. || 10 ||
Having ascended to the supreme state, he looks upon the fragile condition of the world as if laughing, with an intellect that is inwardly cooled.
For this very reason, he says "the Supreme," indicating that He observes even the fruit of people's perception of inequality and so forth with indifference, as if smiling. || 11 ||
O Rāghava, you have been told that such is the nature of those great-souled ones who have conquered their minds and have perceived both the higher and the lower.
He summarizes: "Conquered," etc. || 12 ||
But as for us, we do not know the intended doctrine of those fools whose own minds are unsubdued and who are submerged in the mire of worldly enjoyments. (13)
