If it is argued that even the state of being bound should be described by revealing its underlying intention (āśaya) as if it were the state of liberation, [the author] says the following with the intention that such a description is impossible because the delusions of the foolish's desires, the evil deeds motivated by them, and the various sufferings resulting from them are infinite: [The verse: "O Lord, how can the state of bondage be described? It is like a dream, like a city of Gandharvas, like a mirage, and like a reflection; it is like a painting, like a shadow, and like a bubble on water. [The commentary: Just as the state of liberation is described through the realization of the ultimate reality, so too the state of bondage—which is characterized by the ignorance of the self (ātman), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and the mind (manas)—is difficult to describe. Why? Because it is like a dream and the rest. For example, a dream is a mental construction appearing as an external object despite having no objective basis; likewise, this world-appearance is a mental construction devoid of external reality. A "city of Gandharvas" refers to an illusory city perceived in the sky; likewise, this world is a mere appearance lacking substantiality. A "mirage" is a false perception of water in a desert; likewise, this world is a deceptive appearance arising from the heat of ignorance. A "reflection" is an image appearing in a mirror or water; likewise, this world appears as a reflection of the Self within the intellect (buddhi). It is "like a painting" in that it is a mere arrangement of colors and lines without intrinsic substance. It is "like a shadow" in that it follows the body and lacks independent existence. And it is "like a bubble on water" in that it is fragile, momentary, and subject to constant change. Thus, since the nature of bondage is as insubstantial as these illusions, it cannot be truly described. Furthermore, because the delusions of the ignorant, their consequent wicked actions, and the manifold sufferings resulting therefrom are endless, the state of bondage remains beyond full description.
The women desired by them were adorned with both beauty and its absence;
they were the very flames of the fires of hell appearing with the luster of gold.

The women desired by those fools— those women who are adorned by the absolute non-existence of discerning intellects (bhāva), by the non-existence through destruction of previously accumulated merits, and by the preservation of the antecedent non-existence of merits, austerities, self-restraint, and so forth.
They are adorned from head to foot; therefore, the meaning is that those very flames of the fires of hell possess a luster equal to gold. || 14 ||
Meanings are dense with purposelessness, consisting of futile and harmful afflictions; they point toward the intensity of suffering and cast forth calamities on all sides. (15)

Likewise, the objects desired by fools—wealth and riches—are a thicket of misfortune; for their acquisition, preservation, expenditure, and loss, they are the cause of great exertion and heaps of demerit. They are useless, meaning that from them arise the afflictions of strife, enmity, and the like, which result in calamity. Such is the sense. || 15 ||
We are unable to describe those karmas which possess connections with their fruits, consist of various modes of conduct, and are filled with pleasure and pain. (16)
One might object: "Could there not be salvation for them through the performance of virtuous acts such as sacrifices, even with such [limited] goals?

To this he says: "Those who have attachment to results. Those sacrificial and other rites performed by fools are indeed accompanied by an attachment to results; they are not free from such attachment.

The meaning is this: because they are filled with various kinds of hypocritical, arrogant, conceited, and envious behaviors as well as wicked conduct, and are consequently overflowing with the pleasures and pains attendant upon rebirth and so forth, we are unable to say anything at all that might serve as a cause for the deliverance of such fools. || 16 ||
Firmly grasping the perfect vision that delights in the relinquishment of all objects of meditation,
remain established in yourself through the state of liberation while living, and wander in the world, O Rāghava.
Therefore, he says "pūrṇām" and so forth, meaning that you too should conduct yourself solely according to the conduct of the wise, and not otherwise. || 17 ||
Internally having renounced all expectations, free from passion and devoid of latent impressions,
move about in the world, O Rāghava, while externally maintaining all conventional conduct.
Noble, of refined conduct, and following all proper behavior,
yet inwardly renouncing everything— wander thus in the world, O Raghava.

The sense is that one should follow the conduct of ritual action and so forth even among all those who are ignorant, because of the Lord’s statement: "One should not create a disturbance in the minds of the ignorant who are attached to action. (19)
Having investigated all the stages and having taken as your object through devotion that supreme state which is not trivial, wander in the world, O Rāghava.
All the states of saṃsāra, as well as the states consisting of the various stages of abiding in the nature of ultimate reality. || 20 ||
Having taken up inner hopelessness while directing your outward actions toward hope,
being scorched on the outside but cooled within, wander in the world, O Rāghava.

His activities were like those of people whose hopes are directed toward [attaining wealth], for by manifesting total despair, it would be impossible to gather followers such as Dhanamitra and others, and thus the maintenance of the kingdom could not be sustained—this is the sense. For this very reason, upon the loss of wealth and so forth, he was as if scorched on the outside; but within, he was unscorched, being cool in every respect. || 21 ||
Displaying artificial agitation outwardly while being free from agitation in your heart;
acting as an agent externally but a non-agent within—roam thus in this world, O Rāghava.
You have correctly understood the inner nature of all things;
therefore, O Raghava, wander in the world according to your will, with such a vision.

There is a gradation of essence and non-essence both from the perspective of conventional usage and from the perspective of ultimate reality. Therefore, he says "as you wish" (yathecchasi) to grant you permission regarding the practice of virtue. || 23 ||
Abiding in feigned exultation and joy, expressing feigned agitation and reproach,
and manifesting feigned zeal in your undertakings, move about in the world, O Rāghava.
Having abandoned egoism, with a mind at peace and as radiant as the sky,
wander through the world, O Rāghava, free from the stain of blemish.
The moon, however, has grasped the notion of being the sole illuminator during the night;

yet, due to his consumption by disease (the waning phase), his mind is unconfident, and he is marked by the stain of a spot. You, on the other hand, are not like that—this is the distinction (vyatireka). || 25 ||
Freed from hundreds of bonds of desire, equanimous in all conditions of life,
and remaining outwardly engaged in the duties of your natural state, move about in the world, O Rāghava.

"Nature (prakṛti) consists of the inherent character of one's respective caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), remaining engaged in duties appropriate to that, or engaged in activities for the welfare of living beings.
(26) In the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is neither bondage nor liberation for the embodied soul (dehin).
This revolving cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) is a false display of magic (indrajāla). (27)
Regarding what was stated— that [the Self] is equal in all states—
he establishes this by refuting the inequality of bondage, liberation, and so forth, with the words beginning "There is no bondage" (verse 27).
O Rāghava, this world is seen as mere delusion arising from ignorance, appearing vast and producing conviction, just like water in the intense heat of the sun. (28)
Water is like the water seen in a mirage. || 28 ||
How could there be bondage for the Self, which is unbound, uniform, and all-pervading? And in the absence of that [bondage], for whom could liberation be ordained? (29)

He states the reasoning as to why there is no bondage in that state with the words "of the unbound" (abaddhasya). This means "of the unattached" (asaṅgasya). "Is ordained" (vidhīyate) means it is accomplished through effort. || 29 ||
This vast delusion of saṃsāra arises from the lack of knowledge of reality;
it comes to an end through the knowledge of reality, just as the notion of a snake in a rope vanishes. (30)
In that case, is the knowledge of reality useless? No; he says: "Not [the knowledge] of non-reality," etc. (verse 30).
You have realized the truth by yourself through a single, subtle intellect;
you have become free from egoism, so remain stainless like the sky.
Since you are thus a knower, abandon all these latent impressions of friends and kinsmen; for what indeed can be the cultivation of thoughts regarding that which is unreal by nature?

Therefore, O Knower, you shall witness that the latent impressions of "mine-ness" regarding friends, kinsmen, and objects belong to that which is unreal by nature—that is, whose true essence does not exist. What indeed is the contemplation or thought of friends and the like? The meaning is that it is not proper [to entertain such thoughts]. || 32 ||
Moreover, you are inferred here to be a virtuous being distinct from that [other person];
this is the first conclusion reached even from the highest cause. (33)
Moreover, when the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been abandoned in the manner described by me, you are inferred to remain as the Witness (*sākṣin*),
distinct from them and possessing ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*), by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). First, prior to the abandonment of the latent impressions,
even though this [world] was eternally attained by you from the Supreme Cause, Brahman, during dissolution and deep sleep— this...

The meaning is that [the Self] has attained only the nature of limited unreality and not the nature of ultimate reality; therefore, the abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone is the cause for attaining That, and nothing else. Alternatively, *api ca* is used as a conjunction:
"And you are other than that"—other than that which is unreal by nature, you are the one whose nature is ultimately real.
By your very nature, you are inferred to be possessed of being and strength, standing in contrast to those things—ignorance and its effects—which are devoid of intrinsic nature (*asat-svabhāva*).

Therefore, even from this supreme primordial cause characterized as ignorance, you must likewise completely abandon this bondage, which has been attained since beginningless time, just like the latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This is the implied conclusion. || 33 ||
The self has no connection with enjoyments, kinsmen, the states of the world, or with auspicious and inauspicious actions; why then do you grieve for these? (34)

By enjoyments, by those who accomplish them, by kinsmen, by worldly objects such as garlands and sandalwood, and by auspicious and inauspicious karmas that serve as the causes for attaining them. || 34 ||
"I am the very essence of the reality of the Self"—for those who have conceived this thought, there is no connection with fears, O Rāma; why then do you fear the delusion of the world? (35)
One whose intellect has arisen such that "I am one whose sole essence is the reality of the Self, which is true and supreme bliss," [is freed] from fears—that is, from the causes of fear. || 35 ||
O Rāghava, since your kinsman was unborn, what connection do you have with the delusions of a kinsman's sorrow and joy, that you should mourn for these?

If it is argued: "While suffering does not arise for me, who knows the truth, by itself, the suffering resulting from the association with the suffering of my kinsmen—who suffer due to their ignorance—is difficult to avoid," the author replies with the words "of one unborn" (*ajātasya*). This means: when a kinsman is "unborn," that is, because he is unreal (*mithyātva*). The genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (*anādare*), according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare*. Alternatively:
The phrase "of you who are unborn" should be construed with "of the kinsman" by virtue of their relationship. || 36 ||
If you existed in the past, so shall you exist now;
you have understood with certainty that you stand here today. (37)

Thus, it has been stated that grief is impossible when one perceives the Self as unattached and non-dual. Now, however, let us assume for the sake of argument that the Self is attached; even so, is it eternal, or momentary, or perishable at some later time—like a jar or other objects, which possess prior non-existence?
Since grief for kinsmen is not logical under any of these positions, the author now seeks to provide a resolution through bold reasoning (*prauḍhi*) regarding the first case.

Regarding the eon (*kalpa*), he says: "If you... [and so forth]. If you have known with firm certainty that the Self is of such a nature—that you existed thus in former births (*purā pūrvajanmasu*), will exist thus in future births (*bhāvijanmasu*), and are situated here now in this present birth (*adyedānīmiha janmani*)—then...

The ellipsis to be supplied is "like your own life-breaths and so forth" regarding your immediate, present, nearby, and close relatives. Why do you not grieve for the very many past lives throughout endless births?

The sense is that, due to the lack of any determining factor [to prefer one over another] and because of the impossibility of grieving for everything, grief is not appropriate in any case whatsoever. || 37 ||
Why then do you not grieve for the many other kinsmen who have passed away—those such as Prāṇa and the rest who were situated nearby and followed immediately after him? (38)
O Rāma, if you were one thing previously, and have become another now, and will likewise become something else in the future, then why do you, who are the true reality, become deluded? (39)

Regarding the second [verse], he says: "Previously," etc. Even if you know yourself to be momentary—thinking, "I am one now, and I shall be another later"—nevertheless, why do you become deluded and grieve by clinging to a real nature? The meaning is that since the object of grief and the griever are non-existent in the second moment, there is no occasion for sorrow.
Even if you did not exist in the past, do not exist today, and will not exist again in the future, nevertheless,
since your cycle of existence (saṃsāra) has been exhausted, why do you grieve?
Regarding the third [point] as well, he says "pure" (in verse 40): "Nevertheless, by the very destruction of the self, saṃsāra is exhausted."
Therefore, it is not appropriate to be sorrowful regarding the ordinary course of worldly existence;
likewise, it is appropriate to be joyful, for it is proper to act in accordance with one's duty.

With the intention that, if grief is not appropriate even when the self is associated with birth and so forth, then what need is there to say that it is not appropriate when the self is unattached, indifferent, eternal, immutable, self-luminous, and of the single essence of perfect bliss, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). *Muditā* is the state of natural contentment. || 41 ||
Do not go to sorrow, O Rāma, nor even to happiness;
attain equanimity toward all things, for the Supreme Self is omnipresent.
You are infinite, the very nature of existence, with an inner expanse as vast as the sky;
you are eternal light, pure as the hollow interior of a flame.

Just as there is no room for darkness within a hollow filled with light on all sides from a flame, so too there is no room for darkness, suffering, and the like in you; such is the intended meaning. || 43 ||
To all things in the world, you are the unseen body within their bodies;
residing in the heart, you are spread out like the single thread running through the pearls of a necklace.

He says, "You alone are the innermost of all," with the words "of the worlds" (*jāgatānām*). His body—meaning his essential nature—is not perceived. "Body" (*tanu*) here means subtle; like a thread woven through pearls on a necklace, he is extended and pervasively interwoven. || 44 ||
This very state of worldly existence is such that, having come into being, one comes into being again;
this occurs only for the ignorant, not for the knower. O Rāma, you are a knower; be happy.
He wards off the fear of rebirth with the words "saṃsāra... etc.: having come into being, that is, having been born, one is born again. || 45 ||
"O noble-minded one, you have understood that this very nature of this world, which is constantly causing mental anguish, expands through ignorance. (46)
Its essential nature is its own-being; it is constantly afflicted and full of suffering. (46)
What else could form (rūpa) be, apart from mere delusion, except within delusion? For what other sequence could there be in a dream, apart from the dream itself? (47)

He says "rūpam" (form) to show that one should not think that its own nature (*svarūpa*) is the reality (*tattva*). The meaning is that since reality is not established in other delusions, it is likewise not reality here either. || 47 ||
O Rāma, this power of the All-Powerful is likewise composed of mere delusion; yet this exceedingly radiant manifestation is indeed perceived.

Now, one might ask: "How can that which is devoid of reality (nistattva) appear as real? To this he replies with the word "sarva" (all). "Ābhāna" means the manifestation in the form of the world; "atibhāsvara" means clearly manifest. || 48 ||
Subandhu may belong to someone; who here is not our enemy?
Yet, by the will of the Lord of All, everyone is always everything to everyone. (49)

In order to demonstrate that the world is mere illusion, he shows its lack of fixed nature with the verse beginning "subandhu" and so forth. The meaning is that for everyone, all beings are simultaneously enemies, friends, and neutrals. || 49 ||
This entire world, torn asunder and shattered, yet mutually dependent, flows incessantly like a mass of waves upon the water. (50)
Mutually dependent, they are the respective causes for one another. || 50 ||

Just as the rim of a wheel moves all around, so too in this ever-shifting cycle of existence (saṃsāra), one goes from the state of being above to the state of being below, and likewise from the state of being below to the state of being above. (51)
"Now," [he says]. The sense is that this is directly perceived both for the portions of the circle of light (the celestial sphere) and for the earth. || 51 ||
Those dwelling in heaven go to hell, and those in hell go to the third heaven;
people pass from one womb to another, and from one continent to another.
Thus, he states that increase and decrease are likewise indefinite: "Those dwelling in heaven," etc. (52).
The wise fall into wretchedness, while the wretched attain wisdom;
living beings flutter about in the confusion of hundreds of falls and rises. 53.
The steadfast are those whose nature is free from longing. || 53 ||
A wheel that is uniform, stable, transparent, and free from distress—
nothing such as this is found here, just as a particle of frost cannot exist in fire.
He summarizes: "of a single form. The *cakra* is the maṇḍala of the categories of existence (*padārtha*). || 54 ||
Whosoever indeed were those highly fortunate ones and many kinsmen,
they are all seen to have perished within just a few days.
He states that destruction, however, is certain everywhere: "Whichever [things]... (verse 55).
The conceptualization of otherness, selfhood, difference, yours-ness, mine-ness, existence, and so forth— O mighty-armed one, these are not real here, just like the vision of two moons and the like.
Let there be indeterminacy; what follows from that? To this he replies: "By another," etc. (verse 56).
"This one is a kinsman, and this one is a stranger; this is I, and this is you"—O Rāma, may such false views now fall away from you. 57.
Let them flow away; let them fall apart. || 57 ||
Remaining engaged in worldly affairs for the sake of play, sport with these [senses] whose vision has been destroyed—sport with ease, though they are severed from the root to their very core. 58.
By those whose views have been destroyed and whose persistent views have been refuted, [the afflictions] are cut off at their very root along with the latencies of ignorance. || 58 ||
O observer of noble vows, conduct yourself thus during this state of wandering in saṃsāra, so that you do not become exhausted by fatigue as if bearing the burden of latent impressions (vāsanā). 59.

Free from the burden of latent impressions (vāsanā), do not become weary with exhaustion like an ignorant man; rather, wander upon this path of saṃsāra in such a way that you do not come to exist [as a bound soul]. 59.
In whatever measure this investigation of yours arises, which brings about the exhaustion of latent impressions regarding all activities, in that same measure they are pacified. (60)

When, then, will there be a cessation of my worldly activity? To this he says: "In whatever manner... (yathā yathā). In whatever manner the inquiry that effects the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā) arises, in that same manner worldly duties and activities (vyavahāra) are pacified; the meaning is that they will come to an end. || 60 ||
"This one is a kinsman, this one is not"—such is the calculation of those with small minds;
but for those of noble conduct, the intellect is indeed free from all obscuration. 61.

The meaning is that she perceives equality everywhere, being characterized by the discernment that "this very [mind] is free from [duality]" and thus possesses the characteristic of having removed the obscuration of grasping at a relative distinction such as "this is a kinsman. || 61 ||
"There is nothing where I am not, and there is nothing that is not mine.
Having thus resolved, the intellect of the wise becomes truly free from all veils. (62)
He elucidates the very point already stated by adducing a reason: "Not that," etc. (62).
He who is as vast as space neither sets nor rises;
established in himself, he perceives everything, just as one standing on level ground sees the surface of the earth.
One who is self-abiding is established in one's own true nature, or possesses the well-being that consists in the cessation of the suffering of distraction. || 63 ||
For indeed, O Rāma, all these classes of beings are your kinsmen;
yet, O Rāma, none of them are ever truly joined with you.

"All" means that in this beginningless *saṃsāra*, one has experienced birth many times within all wombs. "Not at all joined as kinsmen" means that there are none with whom one has not been connected in some way, either sequentially or through everyone else; or alternatively, it refers to the connection through a continuous succession mediated by bodies.
The meaning is that because the relationship of direct identity with all living beings is internal, there is nothing whatsoever that is not absolutely united with that relationship. || 64 ||
In this world, where confusion has been accumulated through hundreds of diverse births, the perception of "this is a kinsman" or "this is not a kinsman" is merely the play of delusion; in reality—
Though he was not a kinsman, he became a long-standing friend to the three worlds. || 65 ||

Summarizing and elucidating the very point already stated, he concludes with the verse beginning "vividha": In this world, wherein there are disturbances produced by hundreds of births diverse through various wombs,
the perception of duality— the view that "this one is a kinsman" and "that one is not"— is merely the throbbing of a state of delusion.
It unfolds. In reality, however, from the perspective of the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*), the three worlds and all living beings dwelling within them are one's own kin;
yet from the perspective of the state of Brahman (*brahmabhāva*), everything is oneself alone, and thus even that which is not kin is indeed that very same self—this is the meaning.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberated while Living," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. 18.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation while Living," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Nineteenth Canto. In this very context, they cite this ancient history:
the dialogue between two sons of sages on the banks of the triple-pathed river (the Gaṅgā).
To achieve the goal stated here, the narrative known as "Puṇya-pāvana" is told;
for Puṇya enlightened Pāvana, who was afflicted by grief for his father. (1)
In this regard, concerning the subject matter already stated. || 1 ||
"This is a kinsman, this is not"—it was remembered from such a discourse.
O Rāghava, listen to this meritorious and wonderful history. (2)
In a certain mountain glade of this Jambūdvīpa,
there is a mountain named Mahendra, the great crest-jewel of the forest array.
"In the middle": the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The reading "puñjake" is clear. || 3 ||
He, whose high peaks reached out into the sky, surpassed it by providing rest for sages and kinnaras in the shade of groves of wish-fulfilling trees.
He has conquered—that is, pervaded—the vast and expansive sky with his peaks. || 4 ||
It seems to sing through the resonant *ghuṃghum* sounds of the Sāma Veda, produced by those dwelling in its peaks and caves who have reached the realms of Brahmā.
The expression "the world of Brahmā" is an exaggeration (atiśayokti). || 5 ||
He who shines with clouds thick with water, shimmering upon the tips of his peaks like locks of hair entwined with the flowers of climbing vines.
"With locks" means with hair that is dark, that is to say, as black as fresh butter; "with flashes" means shining with streaks of lightning. || 6 ||
Where, with the yawns of the śarabhas eager to leap from its slopes,
it thunders through the mouths of its caves as if laughing at the clouds of the cosmic dissolution.
On its banks, it thunders and roars with the outbursts of the sharabhas—eight-legged creatures—who are eager and longing to take flight. (In some recensions, "roars" is not read. || 7 ||
By means of the roar of its waterfalls flowing through the interior of the caves,
it has completely surpassed the playful splendor of the waves of the ocean's waters.
"By those moving within the mountain caves," meaning by the echoes; "the play of the waves" refers to their dancing accompanied by thundering. || 8 ||
On a portion of that delightful mountain-peak, spread out with jeweled summits,
the celestial Gaṅgā was brought down by sages for the purpose of bathing and drinking.
On the jeweled summit, in the region of the plateau, flows the Mandākinī, the celestial Gaṅgā.
On the bank of that triple-pathed river, where trees were in full bloom,
it shone against the slopes of the jewel-mountain, golden-hued and glittering.
Shining like the slope of Mount Meru, the king of jewels.
There was a sage named Dīrghatapas, possessed of exalted wisdom and noble intellect, who was a mass of asceticism, like another embodiment of penance itself. (11)
He whose supreme self-knowledge has arisen, who has assumed a physical form—that is, who has taken on a body. || 11 ||
That sage had two sons, as beautiful as the moon,
named Puṇya and Pāvana, who were like the two hairs on the head of Bṛhaspati.
"Like two locks of hair"—this is an *abhūtopamā* (impossible simile). [It refers to] Vācaspati, that is, Bṛhaspati. || 12 ||
Together with those two sons and his one wife,
he dwelt upon the bank of that river, which was lined with fruit-bearing trees.
Then, in the course of time, one of those two sons became possessed of knowledge;
O Raghava, he who was the elder was named Puṇya, and he was the most excellent in virtues.
He is possessed of knowledge and knows reality.
He became half-awakened like a lotus at the dawn of the morning twilight;
having reached the state through folly, he remained there, wavering and unattained.
The explanation of the term "half-awakened" is as follows: due to ignorance, he has entered [the path] but has not emerged;
regarding the state of the supreme reality, he has not attained it; he remains suspended, wavering in the intermediate space. || 15 ||
Then, as immeasurable time— whose cause has been determined—
flows on, a hundred years pass, during which his life-span exists as a withered, long vine of a body.

When the time—consisting of a hundred years—had passed away, unreckoned by living beings and unnoticed due to the exhaustion of their lifespan; and when that time, in which both the vine of the body and the lifespan had withered, was flowing on—that is, passing by—the sage abandoned his body. This is the connection with the distant [verb]. || 16 ||
Abandoning attachment for this cycle of existence, which is filled with fragile beings and terrifying with its hundreds of events, he whose life was worn out by old age [departed]. (17)

The sage Dīrghatapas abandoned his body— the nest of the bird of mental construction— within the dwelling of a mountain cave, just as a porter discards a burden, for that body was terrifying due to the hundreds of occurrences of birth, old age, death, falling from heaven, and rebirth in hell, and it was the source of attachment to worldly existence.
The meaning is: "just as a porter carrying a load sets down that burden at home.
The words *vivadha* and *vīvadha* both refer to a specific kind of wooden pole used for carrying loads on the shoulder, with loops of rope tied at both ends.

He attained a state free from passion, a locus of consciousness devoid of objects of thought and with the cessation of all mental constructions, just as the fragrance of flowers pervades the sky. (19)

That supreme state is the abode and foundation of all those individual living consciousnesses—the consciousnesses which are devoid of objects of thought (cetya) and from which the commencement of mental constructions (kalanārambha) has become utterly tranquil.
Just as the fragrance of a flower reaches the atmosphere, so too does it reach that space. 19.
Then the sage’s wife, seeing his body deprived of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the downward breath (apāna), lying tossed upon the ground like a lotus without its stalk, [fainted].
Through the practice of yoga cultivated for a long time and bestowed by her husband,
she cast off her unfading body, just as a female bee leaves a lotus.
By means of the yoga-technique bestowed and instructed by her husband, she abandoned her body, which was unfading— that is, free from the fading caused by disease, old age, and the like.
Having vanished from the sight of the people, she followed her husband alone,
like the light within the expanse of the sky following the moon that has set.

She herself followed her husband who had become one with Brahman, meaning that she too attained the state of Brahman. For those who know Brahman have no movement to another place; as the Śruti declares: "His vital breaths do not depart; they are merged right here. (22)
When his parents had passed away, he remained unperturbed and devoted solely to the meritorious funeral rites; yet, though purifying, he experienced sorrow.
Undisturbed and free from sorrow. || 23 ||
With his mind overwhelmed by grief, wandering through the forest paths and not seeing his elder brother, Pāvana indeed lamented.
"Without looking after his elder brother," that is to say, without maintaining composure in that manner. || 24 ||
Then, having performed the funeral rites for his parents, the noble-minded and meritorious one returned to the sacred forest, which was filled with those overwhelmed by grief.
Puṇya said:
"O son, why do you bring such intense grief to a state of blindness— the sole cause of which is the bearing of streams of tears— like a lotus in the terrible rainy season?"
According to the scriptures, the eldest brother is "equal to a father," hence the address "son. [The terms] *śoka* (grief) and *duḥkha* (suffering) refer to heat;

*ghanatām* (solidity) and *nibiḍatām* (density) refer to the state of a cloud (*meghatā*). Therefore, through paronomasia (*śleṣa*), the qualifying attributes are common to both, as it is said that [grief] is the sole cause of blindness, like a cloud bearing streams of tears (*bāṣpadhārādhara*).
"Āmbujam" means relating to a lotus, as well as relating to eyes that resemble a lotus. || 26 ||
O one of great wisdom, your father has gone together with your mother to that very state of the Supreme Self which is called liberation. (27)
That is the station of all living beings, that is the form of those who have conquered themselves;
since you have attained your own true nature, why do you grieve for your father? (28)

"Abode" (sthānam) means that which serves as the support throughout the three times, beginning with birth. "Of beings" (jantūnām) refers to living creatures characterized by birth. "Of those who have conquered the self" (vijitātmanām) refers to the knowers of Brahman. "Form" (rūpam) means one's own essential nature (svarūpam). For this very reason, he says "one's own nature" (svabhāvam) to show that there is no cause for grief regarding the father. || 28 ||
Such an illusion born of delusion has been formed by you here in this world, since even your father,
who ought not to be mourned, is being lamented by you within saṃsāra.

Such is this very one who is my mother, and such is this very one who is my father—this is the nature [of that perception]. By whatever such conception [is held], she is not truly your mother, nor is he truly your father;
you are not the son of those two, who have countless sons. (30)
They had sons who were beyond counting, impossible to enumerate.
O son, thousands of mothers and fathers have passed away for you,
like many watercourses flowing down through forest after forest.
They are like low-lying places, such as deep pits. || 31 ||
O son, you alone are certainly not the son of those two who have countless sons;
for the multitudes of sons belonging to men pass away like the waves of a river. (32)
He is the son of men and of others as well. || 32 ||
Countless hundreds of thousands of our parents' sons have passed away,
like the leaves, buds, and stalks of a creeper upon its branches.
By the mention of "branches" (viṭapa), the "branched tree" (viṭapin) is indicated; or alternatively, the reading may be "like two branched trees" (viṭapinoḥ). || 33 ||
In birth after birth, the multitudes of friends and kinsmen pass away for a living being, just as the fruits of a great tree fall season after season. (34)
O son, if parents and children are to be mourned out of affection, then why are those thousands who have passed away not mourned incessantly? (35)
The ellipsis "are not grieved by you" is to be supplied. || 35 ||
O illustrious one, this phenomenal world is seen within the delusion of worldly existence;
in ultimate reality, O wise one, you have neither friend nor kinsmen. (36)

The world-appearance is perceived only while the delusion and ignorance that cause the conceptualization of the world persist; from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, it does not exist for you. As it has been stated in the *Vārttika*:
"Saying 'ignorance exists,' one conceptualizes [it] by remaining within ignorance itself; but from the perspective of Brahman, this ignorance does not exist."
In no way is this tenable. || 36 ||
For destruction, my brother, does not exist in the ultimate sense, just as drops of water do not exist in a vast desert, even after it has been scorched for a long time. (37)
From the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), by virtue of its very nature as waves upon the ocean, drops of water do not exist there at all;

this is especially true when it has been heated for a long time. Likewise, because of its inherent nature as Brahman, destruction does not exist there at all within that realization of reality (tattvabodha).
It is for the purpose of illuminating this point that the word "api" (even/also) is used. || 37 ||
O man of great intelligence, these splendors that you behold, flickering with parasols and chowries, are merely a dream for three or five days. (38)
"Lakṣmī" refers to the riches of sovereignty and so forth; the ellipsis implies that these are merely dreams. || 38 ||
But with the ultimate vision, my son, investigate the truth:
neither you nor we are possessed of delusion; abandon it! (39)
"This one has gone," "this one is dead"—such false perceptions appear before [the ignorant], arising from the fever of their own mental constructs, but they do not exist in reality. (40)
The affliction characterized by one's own mental constructs, arising from the delusion of the humors' imbalance, is seen before one as [these visions].
In the vast desert of ignorance, it wanders,
filled with waves consisting of the flow of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
For those with latent tendencies (*savāsanānām*), this water in the mirage appears as a manifold form shimmering before them. || 41 ||
In the self, which is like a desert—vast and covered by the heat characterized by ignorance—there exists the water of a mirage, known as the latent impressions of one's own volitions. (41)

Thus ends the nineteenth canto, titled "The Purifying Enlightenment," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki;
and thus concludes the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The nineteenth canto, titled "Purification and Awakening."
The twentieth canto.
Puṇya said:
Who is a father, and what is a friend? Who is a mother, and who are kinsmen?
By one's own intellect alone, the dust of worldly people is shaken off, just as by a whirlwind. || 1 ||
Thus, the births of the Purifier (the Self) in various wombs are recounted here through merit for the sake of dispelling sorrow and delusion. (1)

Considering that grief is rooted in delusion (*moha*) and must therefore be removed only by the removal of delusion, Puṇya—having asserted the unreality (*mithyātva*) of his father and other objects of affection because they are indefinable—declares that they are to be dispelled by knowledge, saying: "Who is the father? That is, what is his true nature? In reality...

The meaning is that all [these things] are impossible to define. They are shaken off—that is, raised up—by one's own intellect, which is itself a delusion; or alternatively, the dust of one's own kin is shaken off and cast away by the whirlwind characterized by one's own discriminative intellect. || 1 ||
This phenomenal world is spread out by means of mere self-designation alone, consisting of the states of affection, hatred, and delusion toward one's kinsmen, friends, and sons. (2)
The "disease" is characterized by the states of attachment, aversion, and delusion; it is merely by means of one's own designation—that is, one's own convention—that it is so called. (2)
When cultivated as a kinsman, one becomes a kinsman; when cultivated as a stranger, one becomes a stranger.
In this world, one's state of being is dependent upon mental cultivation, just like the states of poison and nectar.

He provides a justification for what was stated in the verse beginning with "bandhutve" (in the state of being a kinsman): "bhāvitaḥ" means made manifest through firm contemplation (*dṛḍhabhāvanā*), that is, conventionally established.

"Paratve" means in the state of being an enemy. Just as poison, when firmly contemplated by those [who know its nature] as a cause of life, is seen as nectar by them, while for others it is seen as poison due to a contrary contemplation.
The meaning is that stability is likewise bound by cultivation (bhāvanibandhanī). || 3 ||
Since the Self, which exists as a single entity and is all-pervading, is indeed one, how can there be such a conceptualization as "this is a kinsman" and "that is a stranger"? (4)

Let the consideration of the reality of kinship rest; with the intention that for you, who grieve for them, they can be dispelled merely by reflecting upon your own true nature, he says: "In oneness" (ekatve). This means in the state of non-difference among all bodies. || 4 ||
"O son, reflect for yourself upon this: 'Who am I?'—regarding this very body, which is a mere collection of blood, flesh, and bones, a cage of bone. (5)

If it is asked, "How am I one in all bodies?", [the author] says— "Consider who this is"— meaning that you should investigate, "Who am I, whose nature is consciousness, and who is distinct from the body, which is a collection of insentient things such as blood and so forth?"— that very thing which is known through the notion of "I". || 5 ||
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is neither you nor am I;
it is only through false cognition that one exults, thinking "I am meritorious" or "I am pure."
You are that which is denoted by the word "pure," while the body and so forth are nothing at all; I am that which is denoted by the word "meritorious.
It is only false knowledge—the delusion that the body is the self—that flutters and expands.
Who is one's father, who is a friend, who is one's mother, or who is another? In the face of the infinite play of the Self, what is "this" and what is called "one's own"? Tell me. (7)
Thus, he says "Who? (kaḥ) to show that even the bodies of one's father and others are nothing but an illusion when subjected to inquiry.

However, if you consider that the space of consciousness alone—stripped of limiting adjuncts such as the body—is "I," "you," and "my father" and so forth, then a relationship characterized by distinctions such as "my father" or "my brother," involving notions of ownership and the like, simply cannot be established; thus he says:
"Of the void" means of the consciousness-space (cidākāśa). || 7 ||
If you were such [a person], then when all those others had passed away through many births, why do you not grieve for those who were your kinsmen and your riches? (8)

If it is argued that "I am indeed the subtle bodies (liṅgaśarīra), as are my kinsmen," he says in response: "If you... If you are that self whose subtle body is distinct from me, then why do you not grieve when they have gone, that is, passed away? Why for what purpose? || 8 ||
On the flower-laden plains and in the habitats of wild beasts, there were many kinsmen and paths; why do you not grieve for them?
He elaborates upon the kinsmen from other births with the words beginning "babhūvuḥ" (they became): "mārgāḥ" refers to living beings born from the womb of deer. || 9 ||
Those swans, the kinsmen of Haṃsa, lived upon the lotus-filled banks of the ponds; how is it that you do not grieve for them? (10)

In the lotus ponds, in the clusters of lotuses, and on the banks of rivers and other waters, those various swans who were renowned at that time became your kinsmen. In the reading "on the banks of the wives of the ocean," the meaning is "on the banks of the rivers."
They had many kinsmen in the form of trees elsewhere in the various forest groves; how is it that you do not grieve for them? (11)
In other births, others have likewise become one's kinsmen; enough of this excessive attachment. || 11 ||
On the most formidable peaks of the mountains, there were many lion kinsmen; why do you not grieve for them? 12.
In the rivers, lakes, and lotus ponds, you had many kinsmen in the form of fish; why do you not grieve for them? (13)
In flowing rivers. || 13 ||
In the Daśārṇas you became a brown forest monkey;
in Tuṣāra you were a prince, and in Puṇḍra a wild crow.
Now, specifically reminding [his brother] of the various births he has seen through the power of yoga, he says: "You have become...
etc. Daśārṇa, Tuṣāra, Puṇḍra, and so forth are specific regions. 14.
Among the Haihayas he was Mātaṅga, among the Trigartas he was Gardabha;
among the Śālvas he was Saramāputra, and in the Sarala tree he was a bird.
Saramā is a female dog; her son is a winged creature, that is, a bird, specifically among the Śālvas. 15.
Having become a Pippala tree on the Vindhya mountain, and having become a wood-boring insect in a great banyan tree,
and having become a cock on Mount Mandara, you were born as a Brahmin in a mountain cave.
A wood-boring insect [searches] for meanings within the caves and mountain clefts of Mount Mandara itself. || 16 ||
Having been a twice-born man among the Kosalas, and having been a partridge among the Vaṅgas,
you were born as a horse at the sacrifice of Brahmā in the Tuṣāra region.
At Puṣkara, in the famous sacrifice of Brahmā Prajāpati, he was born as a sacrificial animal—this is the sense; or the reading may be "yātaḥ" (gone). || 17 ||
He who was a worm within the *tāla* bulb, he who was a gnat in the *udumbara* tree, and he who was formerly a crane in the Vindhya forest— that very person is you, my younger son.
The bulbous root of the palmyra tree is its foundation; all three [of us] were born there within the Vindhya forest. (18)
That ant which, for six months, dwelt within the hollow of a knot on the thin bark of a birch tree in a cave of the Himalayas— this is you, my younger brother.
In a hollow, a cave formed by a knot in the bark of a Bhūrja tree—bark that is thin and soft—[he dwelt]. 19.
O virtuous one, that scorpion which remained for a year and a half in the cow-dung of the village of Sīmāntaka is this very younger brother of mine.
By implication, at the edge of the boundary of his own country, there was a wretched village, and in it was a heap of dry cow-dung.
He by whom you were embraced in the forest upon the breast-bosoms of Pulinda women, like a bee among lotuses—he is this very younger brother of mine. (21)
"Stagnant" means that it is understood from the sense [of the context] that this occurs upon obtaining the birth of a Pulinda woman's child. || 21 ||
O son, in these and many other births among living beings,
you have been born previously in this Jambūdvīpa hundreds of thousands of times.
Thus, with a subtle intellect purified by right vision, I behold the sequence of your own past latent impressions.
Many diverse wombs of mine, slowed by delusion, have passed away;
today, through the vision arisen from knowledge, I remember them.
Having concluded the words of his brothers, he begins to speak of the various births of himself: "Of me also...
[He describes those] who are slow with delusion, that is, rendered inert by ignorance. || 24 ||
Having been a parrot among the Trigartas, having been a frog on a riverbank,
and having been a quail in the forests, I have now been born here in this grove.
The *lāvaka* is a specific kind of small bird. || 25 ||
Having experienced the state of a Pulinda in the Vindhya mountains and having become a tree among the Vaṅgas,
I even attained the state of a camel on the Vindhya mountain, and now I am born here in this forest.
"Having attained the state of a tree" means having experienced birth as a tree. "The state of a camel" means birth as a camel.
Even if the reading is *nyubjatvam*, the meaning is that he was born here after experiencing the state of a camel with a hunched back (*nyubjapṛṣṭha*). 26.
He who was a Cātaka bird on the Snowy Mountain (Himavat) and he who was the king in the Pauṇḍra region...
"He who was the tiger in the thickets of the Sahya mountains is indeed I, your elder brother. [The reading here is "sa eveha" (he is indeed here).]
He who was a vulture for ten years, he who was a crocodile for five months, and he who was a lion for many years—he alone is your elder brother here. (28)
In this very birth. || 28 ||
I, the partridge of the village of Āndhra, the king among those with frost-like virtues,
the son of the teacher of Śrīśaila, speak this as if in jest.

In the snowy regions of the Himalayas, by one who shines like a king—that is, by a regional ruler (māṇḍalika)—there is a conceit: "I stand here like one who, though meritless, proclaims himself by the name of 'merit' for the sake of deceiving the world. However, in the reading "this is told by me to you," the meaning is clear.
All the various transmigrations, with their diverse modes of conduct and activities, and the pleasures of birth within this delusion, are remembered by me as belonging to the past. (30)
The manifestations of birth are the play of delusion, which takes the form of various distinct births. || 30 ||
This being the case, hundreds of kinsmen born within this world have passed away—fathers, mothers, brothers, and likewise friends. (31)
Having summarized [the preceding], he applies it to the subject at hand: "This being so" (evam sthite). || 31 ||
Whom do we grieve for together, and whom do we not grieve for at all?
We grieve excessively for our kinsmen; such indeed is the course of the world.

Whom among those former kinsmen do we grieve for? Having passed beyond those kinsmen, whom here do we grieve for? We grieve for no one at all; the meaning is that such indeed is the course of the world. || 32 ||
Infinite fathers pass away, and infinite mothers pass away,
like the leaves of the trees in a forest for men wandering here in this cycle of existence.
Therefore, my son, what measure is there here for either suffering or happiness?
Consequently, having abandoned everything and attained purity, let us remain thus.
What is the extent of the limit? Is it everything, or is it all that is perceived as sorrow? || 34 ||
Having abandoned the mental cultivation of conceptual proliferation and the "I" established in the mind,
go to that state— may it be well with you— which those skilled in the goal attain.
They are skilled in the [destinies of] rebirth and proficient in the realization of the self. || 35 ||
In this world, the wise do not grieve over the constant coming and going, consisting of falling and rising; they merely sport for a long time. (36)

Falling is downward motion, and rising is upward motion; that which consists of these is the state of constant flux (*ājavamjavībhāva*), an unceasing whirling. It is only through the absence of ego-inflation that they leap about and engage in worldly activity.
Free from existence and non-existence, devoid of old age and death—remember the Self with an undistracted mind; do not be deluded in spirit.
For you there is no suffering, no birth, no mother, and no father;
you alone are the Self, O Sage of Truth, for you are indeed none other than that. 38.
"You are the Self alone, not another; the meaning is that you are none other than the Self, distinct from the body and so forth which constitute the non-Self. || 38 ||
In this journey through saṃsāra, it is only the ignorant who provide various dramatic performances, while the wise remain endowed with the true sentiment.
Like dancers, their efforts of attachment consist of various dramatic gestures; those who provide them and perform them are indeed ignorant and deluded men.
"Possessing that" means possessing the notion that the nature of the virtuous assembly is the essence of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha). || 39 ||
Those with impartial vision, established in their own nature, perceive objects exactly as they are; those who know that [reality] are indeed observers, situated in the role of witnesses.
But those who know that [reality]—the knowers of truth—are bystanders, indifferent, and mere observers; for this very reason, they are established in the nature of a witness. (40)

Even though they are agents, they are not agents, just as lamps at the arrival of night [are not agents] with respect to the acts of illumination; so it is for those who know that [reality] regarding their existence here in the world.

When night arrives—that is, upon its coming—just as lamps are the agents of illuminating actions through their mere presence, yet are non-agents because they do not exert effort, so too are those knowers [non-agents] in the context of worldly convention; this is the meaning. || 41 ||

Just as mirrors, gems, and the like do not appear as reflections even when they are present within their own reflected images, so too do those of great intelligence not appear within their effects. (42)

He states another illustration: "In the reflection" (*pratibimbe*). Just as mirrors and gems located on the hands and so forth—which serve as the limiting adjuncts for a reflection—do not appear within the reflection produced upon themselves, even though they are accompanied by all the attributes belonging to the entire body that constitutes the original object (*bimba*), because those attributes of the original object are [already] present there.

In the same way, the meaning is that even those who act as agents toward an effect superimposed upon their own self do not themselves become attached to it, because they possess the wisdom of honey (madhu-dhi). || 42 ||

In the center of the heart-lotus, by this very Great Sage, who is free from the stain of all the diseases of craving and who possesses a self-existent nature, [the world is seen] as a son within the Self.
Abandoning all agitation, attain complete satisfaction.
O son, by that very self which is free from the stains of all cravings, which is a sage by its nature of contemplation,
and which has been realized as one's own inherent nature within the center of the heart-lotus—
having completely abandoned the delusion of saṃsāra— one remains by means of this very self alone, which is what remains.
The meaning is: "Be fully satisfied. || 43 ||

Thus ends the twentieth canto, titled "The Purifying Awakening," in the section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 20.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Purifying Awakening," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twenty-first Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus was Pāvana then awakened by that Puṇya.
He attained awakening and manifestation, just as the surface of the earth does at dawn. || 1 ||
The destruction of the noose of craving is indeed liberation; for the fluctuations of the mind are rooted in desire.
For one who is free from desire and full of the Self, liberation is said to be spontaneous. (1)
Awakening, which is the final certainty established within the self. || 1 ||
Then both of them, having attained perfection and having reached the further shore of knowledge and realization, wandered through that forest as long as they desired, blameless in their conduct.
"As long as desired" means until the exhaustion of *prārabdha* (the karma already set in motion). || 2 ||
Then, after some time, those two from Videha attained the state of nirvāṇa; free from attachment, they reached tranquility like two lamps that have gone out.
Those whose oil is exhausted are devoid of affection. || 3 ||
In this way, there has been an infinite succession of kinsmen and people throughout one's previous bodies;
alas, O sinless one, what can be grasped from them, or what can be abandoned?

Having concluded the narrative thus told, he applies it to the subject at hand with the words "In this way" (*evam*). "The circle of kinsmen of people" (*janabandhutā*) refers to the multitude of friends and relatives. *Āḥ* is an indeclinable particle used here to express astonishment. It is grasped—that is, taken up as an object of lamentation;
therefore, O descendant of Raghu, [be wary] of these endless cravings (*tṛṣṇā*).
Abandonment alone is the means; indeed, it is not preservation.

The nurturing of these [desires], which are the root of all sorrow and the like, infinite in number for each respective object, consists of their fulfillment through the acquisition of objects and their subsequent intensification. (5)
Thought increases through further thinking, just as fire grows with fuel;
it perishes by not being thought upon, like a flame without fuel.
With the intention that the non-consideration of sense objects is itself their renunciation, he says: "By not thinking... [it] increases, that is, it grows.
"Mounted upon the chariot of the abandonment of the object of meditation, looking upon the world with a gaze noble with compassion for those who are wretched, remain thus; arise, O Rāghava! (7)

"Abandoning the object of meditation" means the relinquishing of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding the objects of meditation previously described. "Compassion" is sympathy for all living beings. "Abide"—that is, practice—the worldly conduct under discussion; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 7 ||
This is the state of Brahman—transparent, free from desire, and devoid of affliction;
having attained this, O mighty-armed one, even one who was deluded is no longer bewildered.
Though deluded and unskilled in worldly affairs, he does not become bewildered.
Taking solitude as his only friend and a mature intellect as his only companion, he who wanders in this manner is not deluded even amidst difficulties.
Discernment is her friend and companion, characterized by discrimination; and wisdom, characterized by the awakening to ultimate reality, is her dear confidante. (9)
When all means of rescue have been blocked and kinsmen have cast one aside,
no one can lift one out of such a crisis except through one's own fortitude.
By whom all objects and riches have been warded off and abandoned;
by whom kinsmen have been cast aside—driven away as if pushed with the hand from the hump of an ox—due to the severance of internal affection;
he rescues [them] from distress, that is, he elevates himself [from it]. || 10 ||
Then, through dispassion, through the scriptures, and also by means of qualities such as greatness,
one should personally elevate the mind with effort for the sake of warding off calamities.
One should elevate it, lead it to excellence, or rescue it from the pit of sense-objects. || 11 ||
Neither from sovereignty over the three worlds, nor from a treasury filled with jewels,
is that fruit obtained which is attained from the mind when it is augmented by greatness.
That fruit is characterized by the attainment of unsurpassed bliss, marked by the pacification of all suffering.
Its greatness consists in the absence of desire for trivial objects; it arises from that which is nourished—that is, accumulated—by such [desirelessness]. 12.
In this belly of the world, through falls, rises, and oscillations,
those men who indeed fall— their minds are freed from the fever of distress.

Falls are downward movements; leaps are upward movements; and swings are the wanderings through the mortal worlds alone in a succession of births. For those who fall because of the desires for sense-objects which cause these states, their minds are never free from fever—that is, they are always possessed by distress.

The meaning is that [the mind] sometimes finds rest. Alternatively, by carrying over the word "not" (na) from the preceding verse, it should be explained as: "the fever residing in the minds of those who do not fall becomes free from distress. Or, if the reading is *punanti* or *yatante*, then those attachments to sense-objects which cause one to fall (*pātayanti*) or cause one to rise up (*utpātayanti*) are the "falling and rising" (*pātotpātana*); [it refers to being shaken] by the tossings and upward thrusts resulting from them.

It should be explained that for those who purify their minds or strive by means of the methods of sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra) to achieve steadiness within the self, the fever residing in the mind becomes pacified, as do the three kinds of affliction (tāpa). || 13 ||
When the mind is full, the entire world is filled with streams of nectar;
indeed, for one whose feet are covered by sandals, the earth is as if carpeted with leather.

Now, one might ask: "Since the causes of suffering—whether internal (ādhyātmika), celestial (ādhidaivika), or external (ādhibhautika)—such as disease, rain, heat, thieves, serpents, and so forth, actually exist, how can there be the cessation of all suffering through mere tranquility of the mind?
To this, he says: "In the Full One. All three types of suffering have their root solely in defects of the mind.
When the mind is filled with the nectar-essence of the pure Brahman, the entire world appears as nothing but fullness of bliss.

The meaning is that it is just as for one whose feet are covered by soft sandals, the whole earth—even though strewn with kusha grass, thorns, and the like—appears as if covered with the softest leather. || 14 ||
Through dispassion, the mind reaches fullness by following the power of its own dissolution; through desire, it reaches emptiness, just as a pond becomes free of mud in autumn.

The analysis of the compound is: "not following the sway of hope. "Emptiness" (riktatām) means being like the interior of a parched ocean. "With its mud and weeds" refers to the mud of a broken pond; or there is a reading, "with its water" (sarojalam). || 15 ||
The heart of those whose minds are helpless before their desires becomes empty, its hollow exposed, like the ocean drunk by Agastya.
He explains the phrase "it becomes empty" by means of an illustration: "the heart.

This refers to the clear manifestation of the hollow interior, as well as the defects such as greed and wretchedness contained within its leaves, and the presence of crocodiles, serpents, and other creatures. || 16 ||
He in whose expansive mind-tree the restless monkey of craving does not leap, for him that vast forest of the heart shines with splendor. (17)

In the vast tree of the mind—a mental forest abounding in the flowers and fruits of the knowledge of dharma, dispassion, tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth—the inner-sense forest is composed of four kinds of trees: the heart (hṛdaya), the intellect (manas), the ego (buddhi), and the consciousness (citta). || 17 ||
To those whose minds are free from longing, the three worlds are but the calyx of a lotus, a distance of a league is like a cow’s footprint, and a great aeon is but half a moment.

He praises freedom from desire with the verse beginning "O lotus-eyed one" (*padmākṣa*) and so forth. This means that even the three worlds (*trijagat*), the triple universe, is as insignificant as the interior of a lotus seed. This is because, when viewed through the vision of the bliss of Brahman which is unlimited, the fragments of happiness contained within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) are exceedingly small. Thus, it is by means of the vision of Brahman, who is eternal and omnipresent.

With the intention that even the power consisting of sovereignty and so forth, though delimited by place and time, is indeed trivial, he says: "It is but a cow’s footprint"—that coolness which exists not in the moon, nor in the caves of the snowy mountains, nor in rows of plantain trees and sandalwood, but rather in minds free from desire. (19)
Coolness is the joy of being free from heat; it arises from the rows of plantain trees and sandalwood trees in that forest, or from contact with them as appropriate. || 19 ||
Neither does the full moon shine thus, nor the full ocean of milk, nor the lovely face of Lakṣmī, as does the mind free from longing. (20)
Just as a streak of ink defiles the moon’s surface of nectar,
even so does the demoness of desire corrupt a man within.
A streak of clouds is a line of rain-clouds; ink is liquid soot; it defiles, that is, it makes dark. || 21 ||
The branches of the tree of the mind, known as hopes, cover the horizons;
when these are severed, the great tree of the mind returns to its true nature.
"Covering the horizons" means they shrouded the quarters of space. "Formlessness" refers to the state of being Brahman and the state of being an immovable pillar (sthāṇu). || 22 ||
When the mind, having become a trunk with its great branches of craving severed,
comes to rest, fortitude— which was previously of a single form— attains a hundredfold branching.
When the evil tree of cessation is cut down, the good tree that has grown beneath it subsequently attains the state of a hundred branches through fortitude; let it grow as far as it may. 23.
O Rāma, when the mind has reached its dissolution through that unflagging fortitude,
that state is attained wherein no destruction exists.
"Let there be an increase in fortitude; what follows from that? To this he replies: "By one whose fortitude has not set.
This refers to a person possessed of such fortitude as increased dispassion, mastery over the senses, and endurance of the pairs of opposites (dvandvas). || 24 ||
O Raghava, if you do not allow these mental fluctuations and longings to take root, then there will be no fear.
If you do not grant further growth—that is, the opportunity for rebirth—then there is no fear of birth and so forth; this is the meaning. || 25 ||
When your mind, devoid of fluctuations, has reached the state of no-mind,
then you attain that pervasive internal existence which consists of liberation.
That which is extended and full. || 26 ||
O Raghava, when the mind is agitated within by the bird-like female kite of craving, inauspicious things come forth in abundance.

By the owl-woman Kauśikī having entered the mind— it is well known in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* and other sciences that if an owl should ever enter a house, inauspicious events such as death, poverty, and calamities occur—
if she enters incessantly into the interior of the body within the mind and remains agitated during all activities, then:
The meaning is: "By her, all inauspicious things indeed become fully expanded; what more need be said? || 27 ||
Thinking is said to be the activity; the mind functions through its latent tendencies.
Therefore, having abandoned the hope of one who possesses mental activity, proceed toward the state of mindlessness.

One might object: "How can there be tranquility of mind merely by abandoning hope, since the sprouting of that [hope] is difficult to prevent through other mental modifications such as volition, doubt, steadiness, and lack of steadiness? He dispels this doubt by demonstrating that all mental modifications have their root in hope.

It was stated previously that since there is no possibility of the functioning of the visual and other senses [at that time], mental reflection alone remains as the activity of the mind (*citta*). Furthermore, the mind proceeds toward reflection solely by means of desire (*āśā*), because we observe that reflection occurs only upon objects that are desired.
Moreover, since activities such as volition (*saṃkalpa*) have as their object things already reflected upon, [desire is the primary driver].

The meaning is: having abandoned the mental modification called *āśā* (hope), which is rooted in thought because it is preceded by thought, one should attain the state of being without mind (*niścittatā*). || 28 ||
Whatever mode of existence one pursues, it perishes without that very same mode;
therefore, for the sake of the mind's tranquility, bring that mode to its complete cessation. (29)

He says—“he who by which”—that when the mental modifications cease, the subsiding of the mind is accomplished, just as the heat of fire ceases when its flame is extinguished. Without that [object], through the absolute cessation of those modifications, it perishes by a process of gradual decay.
O Great-Souled One, having pacified all desires and cast off the bonds of existence, you are liberated in mind; when will the fetters of hope ever again bind the mind?
And when those [impurities] have been completely dissolved, who is not liberated? || 30 ||

He summarizes the aforementioned point with the words "praśamita" (calmed): O Great-Souled One, having calmed all desires for son, wealth, worlds, and so forth, and having cast off the bond of worldly existence known as hope, become one whose mind is liberated—a *jīvanmukta*. For it is because base hopes existing in the mind [afflict] the self...
Iron chains and ropes are causes of bondage, like iron fetters and like cords. When these have fallen away, who is not liberated? The meaning is that every living being is indeed liberated. || 30 ||

Thus ends the twenty-first canto, titled "The Arising of the Yoga of Doubt regarding Thirst," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Arising of the Yoga of Doubt Regarding Craving," in the Section on Quiescence (*Upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Or rather, O full moon of the sky known as the lineage of Raghu!
Like Bali, attain stainless knowledge through the transformation of the intellect. || 1 ||
Beginning with the narrative of Bali, the netherworld (pātāla) is described here;
then the kingdom of Bali, and out of world-weariness, his contemplation upon the peak of Mount Meru.

Now, in order to demonstrate that even the sovereignty over the three worlds is insignificant—just as it was stated in the *Vivekodaya* that the three worlds are but the calyx of a lotus seed—Vasiṣṭha, wishing to relate the narrative of Bali, prepares the introductory context with the words "Or else" (*athavā*). [The phrase] "by a transformation of the intellect" (*buddhibhedena*) means by the sudden arising of inquiry. || 1 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, by your grace everything that was to be attained has been attained within my heart, and it rests in the stainless state.
The entire Brahman, which is the self of all, has been attained within the heart; it rests in that very same stainless state. || 2 ||
O Lord, like a cloud from the sky in autumn, that great darkness called craving has entirely departed from my mind.
That abundant and not insignificant darkness known as craving, which was well-known to me, has departed from my mind. (3)
Filled with nectar, stationed in the sky, cool-natured and of great luster,
I abide within, full of bliss, like the full moon at evening.
The epithets beginning with "filled with nectar" (amṛtāpūrita) are common to both himself and the Moon, the king of stars. || 4 ||
O autumn season for the clouds of all my doubts, yet I do not reach satiety with these words as you speak.

"O Teacher, you are like the autumn season that dispels all clouds characterized by doubt"—this is the address to the Guru. As you speak, I do not reach satiety or the sense of "enough" within the range of hearing these words of yours. (5)
O All-pervading Lord, tell me again of Bali’s attainment of wisdom for the sake of increasing my own understanding; for the virtuous do not feel weary toward one who is humble.

The attainment of consciousness and the manner of its acquisition; [this refers to] the instruction directed toward a disciple who has bowed down and approached with prostration—the ellipsis being "in the act of teaching. (6)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O Rāghava, I shall tell you the excellent account of Bali;
by hearing which, you will attain that eternal awakening to reality.

Such realization of reality (*tattvabodha*)—the ascertainment of reality preceded by inquiry—is eternal, having the attainment of the permanent Self as its fruit; or rather, it is the eternal, constant awakening to the true nature of the Self, which is the very essence of reality.
Within this treasury of the world, in a certain corner of the quarters,
there exists a realm situated beneath the earth, renowned as Pātāla.
In the treasury of the world, that is, in the cosmic egg; in a small bower characterized by the directions—that is, in a tiny grove. || 8 ||
In some places, with female elephants born from the Ocean of Milk who possess the radiance of the moon,
and in others with the daughters of the Dānavas, it shines with no gaps between them.

Born from the Ocean of Milk—that is, from the milky sea—and because it is well known that the Dānavas also dwell within the depths of that ocean, [the mountain] is as if smeared or augmented by the rays—which are its constituent parts—of the nectar produced therein; thus, it is delightful, being without any intervening gaps, that is to say, completely full. || 9 ||
In some places it was filled with serpents possessing hundreds of heads, their forked tongues flickering with the fierce sounds produced by the tips of their tongues.

With tongues numbering from two up to two thousand—twice as many as others—and with loud sounds arising from the exposition of grammar, prosody, and other sciences, [the mountain] is thus possessed of pairs of flickering tongues; by the "enjoyers," namely Śeṣa and the other serpent-kings. || 10 ||
In some places it was pervaded by the sons of Danu, who were like moving Mount Merus, voracious in their desire to uproot the entire universe encircled by the mountain ranges of their bodies.

The entire world is enveloped and pervaded by those whose bodies are like mountains; [it is pervaded] by those who are devourers—forcibly consuming—that which sustains the universe, namely dharma, or the sacrificial oblation (yajñahavis). This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. || 11 ||
In some places it was approached by mountain-like elephants of the quarters, whose trunks were like trees and whose peaks rested upon the surface of the earth like the summits of jars.
Those whose bellies— the middles— of the circle of the earth rest upon the tips of the peaks and summits characterized by their jar-like shapes;
by the mention of "bellies," it is implied that they extend downward to the very edges of Jambūdvīpa in all directions.
It is understood that the placement of the world-elephants (*diggaja*) for the purpose of supporting the earth is like that of the pillars of the central pavilion.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Pūrvarāmāyaṇa* that the sons of Sagara, while digging up the land of Jambūdvīpa, beheld the world-elephants in every direction. [The text continues: "By the mountains, of the trees characterized by their tusks..."
By those who have become supports like mountains. || 12 ||
In some places, there were circles of hells below, terrifying with foul-smelling spirits, while in others, there were successions of beings terrified by the great, crashing roar of *kaṭakaṭa*.

"Durgandha" (the foul-smelling) refers to that place where the appearances of hell-beings—manifestations produced solely by their own karma—are found. It is "below," meaning at the very bottom; for it is there that the hells are well-known in the Purāṇas. 13.
It was pervaded in some places by oceans reaching down to the surface of the earth and the seven circles of the netherworld (pātāla), appearing like openings into the subterranean realms.

In some places, it is pervaded by the foothills of Mount Meru and other mountains, which serve as mines for jewels and consist of seven layers of the Pātāla regions— studded like iron needles with seven apūpas— extending from the lower hellish regions down to the surface of the earth and reaching up to our own upper terrestrial plane.
And in some places it was pervaded by subterranean regions that were like openings, consisting mostly of narrow caverns, which were parts of the netherworld (pātāla). || 14 ||
In one place, it was purified by that Blessed One, Kapila, with the dust from his lotus feet which rested upon the heads of the gods and demons.
By him whose dust from his lotus-feet rested as if asleep upon the heads of both gods and asuras—that is to say, by him who is venerated by the three worlds. 15.
In one place, it was protected by that Lord Hāṭakeśa, who desired the worship and play of infinite beings brought forth by the Asuras.

By such a Hāṭakeśa— Śiva, renowned in the Purāṇas as being of the nature of a golden liṅga— who is characterized by the habit of desiring (eṣṭum) worship and amusements through the Asuras, Asura women, or armies, and through infinite and manifold articles of enjoyment. || 16 ||
In that realm, where the great burden was sustained by the pillar-like arms of the enemy of the Asuras,
there arose as king the Dānava Bali, the son of Virocana.

In that world of Pātāla, there exists a great burden—the burden of sovereignty—sustained by the pillar-like arms of the asuras. (The phrase "the burden of sovereignty" is not found in some versions of the preceding verse. 17.
Together with all the gods, Vidyādharas, and serpents, he was accompanied by Sākranda;
even the king of the gods longed to perform the massaging of his feet.
He describes his prowess with the words "sākrandena" (with crying). "Ākranda" means weeping; [the phrase means] accompanied by that.
The ellipsis is "forcibly [attained] what was desired. || 18 ||
He is the treasury of the jewels of the three worlds, the protector of all embodied beings, and the sustainer of those who sustain the universe—he whose guardian is Hari. (19)

To the question, "Whence does he have such power?", he says: "The treasury. He is like a treasury for the jewels characterized by the three worlds, preserved within his own belly. He is the sustainer—the foundational support—of those who sustain the world, namely Indra, Manu, Śeṣa, and the others. [Of] that Bali. || 19 ||
By the mere mention of his name, the temples of Airāvaṇa withered away; like the cries of a peacock, they caused the veins of the serpent's heart to go into distress and return in agony.
Of Airāvaṇa—that is, of Airāvata—the "wall-like temples" (kaṭabhittayaḥ) refer to the regions of the cheeks; the plural number is used to indicate all seven locations of rut-fluid.

The phrase "by the mere mention of whose name" is the ellipsis to be supplied. By that [name], the "arteries of the hearts of serpents"—that is, the veins of their hearts—reached a state of exhaustion, as if withered like the cries of peacocks.
And they became perspiring from fear. || 20 ||
By the fierce heat of his majesty, the seven oceans— like those at the time of universal dissolution— became prone to drying up before his wrathful form, as if they had become sevenfold.

The seven great oceans, on the verge of drying up through the fierce and unbearable heat—the warm touch—of his majesty when he was provoked to anger, became seven merely by way of counting their hollows, as if at the time of universal dissolution (kalpa); the meaning is that they were no longer counted by the volume of their waters. || 21 ||
The rows of clouds formed by the smoke from the foremost sacrifices, which encircle the oceans,
have always served as armor for this hollow of the cosmic egg.

The foremost of sacrifices, the Aśvamedhas, produced rows of clouds from their smoke; by these [clouds], the oceans were turned toward drinking water. By the word "cavity" (koṭara), the living beings residing therein are understood. Because they protect the world through rain and because they provide shelter, they possess the nature of armor and mail. || 22 ||
By the forceful impact of whose gaze the supporting kulaparvata mountains are driven down, so that all the directions bend like creepers weighed down by fruit. (23)
