The quarters of space were such that their supporting base mountains on earth were driven away by her glance, which was a firm blow and a sidelong look; thus, because the earth bent down and the quarters of space appeared in the region below, there is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding their bending. 23.
Having effortlessly conquered the entire expanse of the world and adorned it,
that Daitya indeed ruled the kingdom for one hundred million years.
By whom Indra and the others, who serve as the ornaments of all the vast expanses of the worlds and their various arrangements, were conquered effortlessly. || 24 ||
Then, as many ages passed away in their cyclical turnings, amidst the great floods of gods and demons leaping up and falling down; (25)
In the movements of whirlpools, whose inherent nature is like that of water eddies. || 25 ||
Bali, the leader of the Dānavas, felt a sense of revulsion toward enjoyments that were incessantly consumed and possessed the grandeur of the three worlds.
Even while enjoying the vast and sublime pleasures of the three worlds, which were his objects of experience, he felt a sense of agitation and distaste. || 26 ||
Once, standing at a window fashioned with jewels upon the peak of Mount Meru,
he reflected for himself upon the nature of worldly existence.
Standing and seated upon the peak, at the highest point of Mount Meru’s summit, in a window of a palace constructed of jewels. || 27 ||
"How much more of this universal sovereignty must I now exercise, and how long must I sport within these three worlds, while my power remains unimpaired? (28)
Nor has my power been crushed by others; it remains unimpaired, even though I am such as I am. || 28 ||
What is the use of my vast kingdom, which causes wonder throughout the three worlds and captivates with its manifold enjoyments, if it is merely consumed [by me]? (29)

What is gained by the kingdom being enjoyed? By abundant enjoyments that are exceedingly captivating and heart-stealing—sweet only at first sight but inevitably perishable—what indeed is this mere indulgence in pleasures that brings me happiness? (30)
The word "mere" (*mātra*) refers to the enjoyment of all objects of experience; or, the word "mere" is used to exclude any other purpose for the Person (*puruṣa*). (30)
Again there is the passing of a single day and the persistence of the night; again those very same actions [are repeated], leading neither to shame nor to satisfaction. (31)

These very things—bathing, eating, sleeping, and so forth; there is no new activity whatsoever that constitutes happiness. Therefore, in the presence of the great, greed leads to shame, not to satisfaction. // 31 //
"The beloved is embraced again and enjoyed once more;
this is the play of children, which brings great shame here to the wise. (32)
He clarifies what has already been stated with the words beginning "furthermore" (punar), etc. || 32 ||
Why does the wise man not feel ashamed as he performs day after day that very same flood of activities which have become tasteless once they have been experienced? (33)
Day after day, night after night, and again the succession of duties—over and over, I consider this to be a mockery for the wise man. (34)
To the wise person, this visible mockery is like a repeated imitation; the meaning is that it serves as a cause for derision. || 34 ||
Having reached the state of being wavy, it returns again to the state of being waveless;
just as water does, so too does this person undergo various actions.
He provides an illustration regarding the futile imitation [of the Lord]—namely, "the state of being wavy"—in verse 35.
This repeated activity, appearing like the behavior of a madman, repeatedly causes even the wise person to laugh, being ever comparable to the play of a child. (36)
What purpose would there be in this constant performance of ritual action, once it has been accomplished, by means of which no further karma would exist? (37)

What kind of goal could there be, such that once it is attained, no further action remains and one’s duty is fulfilled? Or for how long must this great display continue? What, then, is actually achieved here by us through our practice? (38)
The great clamor arising from the collection of actions whose fruits are both seen and unseen. || 38 ||
This endless play of children is in fact devoid of any real substance;
it is performed in vain through repetition by those who seek only the expansion of what is meaningless. (39)

The streams are endless because they are endless in their flow; yet, by their very nature of arising and perishing, this childish play is in reality empty of substance from the perspective of ultimate truth. Those who seek such things engage in it only to produce a proliferation of misfortune and to undergo a succession of sufferings. (39)
I do not see here any single, magnificent fruit;
there is no other purpose whatsoever for which one might obtain it. (40)
When that [state] has been attained, there remains no other task whatsoever to be performed; I do not see any such fruit or human goal (puruṣārtha) here in this world. || 40 ||
"Apart from enjoyment, what else could there be that is auspicious and indestructible?
Thinking thus, Bali quickly reflected, having reached this conclusion. (41)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Thinking, 'Apart from the enjoyment of momentary and trivial sensory pleasures, what other imperishable and eternal happiness could there be? Is it thus that I should contemplate? this Bali quickly meditated."
Then the lord of the Asuras said, "It is remembered," instantly reflecting upon the matter within his own mind with a frown.

Through meditation, due to the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), he demonstrates the recollection of the sequence of instructions previously received from his father and later from himself, accompanied by reflection—beginning with the word "atha.
Then, in an instant, he spoke within himself. The particle "āḥ" is an indeclinable used to indicate remembrance. What did he say?

Regarding this, he says: "It has been remembered" (*saṃsmṛtam*) means "it has been correctly remembered by me"; thus, while reflecting upon and examining the object of memory within the mind itself, the suffix *ṇic* is applied due to the sense of sending forth (*preṣaṇa*) or superimposition (*adhyāropa*). || 42 ||
It is said that in former times, the Blessed One Virocana— my father, who knew the reality of the self and had perceived the higher and lower worlds— was questioned here by me.
He states the remembered meaning in sequence, beginning with "In former times, it is said," and so forth. || 43 ||
O Mahāmati, that wherein all delusions regarding both all sufferings and all pleasures have subsided—what is that called the ultimate limit? (44)
To the question "What?", he replies with the words beginning with "yathā" (as). The word "yathā" serves to introduce that specific manner.

That in which all delusions of worldly activity—concerning the means for the avoidance of all sufferings and the attainment of worldly pleasures—are stilled, is called the end, the limit, the boundary of saṃsāra. What is it? It is said: [the Self].
The meaning is "by the wise. || 44 ||
Where has the delusion of the mind been stilled? Where have all desires passed away?
And where, O Father, is that long rest, free from cessation? (45)
Cessation is returning again; rest is being free from that, which is tranquility. || 45 ||
What man here would be satisfied with having obtained all that is to be obtained?
And what sight, once seen, would not be of great benefit to you, O Father, for all time to come? (46)
Having attained what happiness has the person obtained?

The sense is that he becomes possessed of that contentment—the fulfillment of all desires—which arises from the happiness obtainable from all objects, from the worldly realm up to the world of Brahmā;
it does not assist him by means of any other fruit. The meaning is that through the knowledge of one thing, the knowledge of everything is established.
For even though these enjoyments are exceedingly abundant, they do not bring happiness;
they agitate the mind and cause even the virtuous to fall into delusion.
To the question "Whence arises the desire to know that?", he says: "Excessively... To the question "Why do they not bring happiness?", he says:
"...agitating... (47).
Tell me of something that is beautiful with an unimpeded bliss like that [of yours], abiding in which I may find long-lasting rest. (48)

Having previously heard these words from my father— who, when I was carried off to heaven, planted the tree of the ocean in our courtyard— words spoken at his feet, where he was veiled by a mass of flowers falling from clusters that vied with the rays of the moon:
His speech, equal to a potent elixir of vast form, serves to pacify delusion.

In former times, due to the abundance of qualities such as being filled with the nectar-essence of beauty, there was a rivalry between the moonbeams of the night-maker, Candra, and the flower-clusters; from these clusters, which were vying for superiority, flowers and fruits fell in an overflowing abundance.

Thus spoke my father Virocana, who was seated at the foot of the ocean-born *kalpa* tree— the wish-fulfilling tree produced from the Milky Ocean— which had been forcibly brought from heaven and planted in his own courtyard (*ajira*), its base being covered with a veil.

Having heard his question in the manner previously described, [the Kalpataru spoke] words— fragrant, sweet, and capable of warding off the suffering of old age and death— which were equal to the nectars (*āsava*), essences (*makaranda*), and elixirs (*rasāyana*) of that vast Kalpataru tree, for the sake of quelling his delusion.
The meaning is that I have remembered what was said for the purpose of dispelling the delusion arising from my own ignorance. || 49 ||

Thus ends the twenty-second canto, titled "The Remembrance of Virocana," in the Section on Tranquility (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) within the Means to Liberation (*mokṣopāya*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki;
and thus concludes the Section on Tranquility in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-second canto, titled "The Recollection of Virocana."
The twenty-third canto.
Virocana said:
"O sons, there exists an exceedingly vast region with a wide hollow."
Wherein even many thousands of the three worlds find room. || 1 ||
To explain the conquest of the mind, the story of the royal minister is told;
therein lies the powerful and unrivaled prowess of that minister.

"When your mind, devoid of fluctuations, has attained the state of no-mind, then you reach that pervasive internal existence which consists of liberation. Thus, it is stated that liberation is dependent upon the conquest of the mind; and regarding the conquest of the mind, the abandonment of hope is said to be the ultimate means, yet that cannot be accomplished without the realization of the Self. [Objects...]
The cravings of the embodied being turn away when it abstains from food; even the craving for the essence of existence turns away for him upon seeing the Supreme.

Because of these words of the Blessed One, there arises the doubt that since the vision of the Self cannot be accomplished without mastery over the mind, this [process] involves a circular dependency and is therefore impossible; to dispel this doubt and to explain the various means— such as the simultaneous practice of the two methods and so forth— the following is stated within the narrative of Bali’s account.
He introduces the narrative of the royal minister through the mouth of Virocana, beginning with the words "There was a son... and so forth. The region is called Mokṣa. || 1 ||
Where there is neither the rising of the waters nor oceans, nor mountains;
neither forests nor sacred fords, nor rivers nor lakes.
Neither the earth, nor space, nor the sky, nor the winds and so forth;
neither the moon and sun, nor the world-protectors, nor the gods, nor the dānavas [are able to protect you]. (3)
Neither spirits, yakṣas, nor rākṣasas; neither shrubs nor the splendors of the forest;
neither things consisting of wood or grass, nor anything stationary or moving—[none of these exist]. (4)
Neither water, nor fire, nor the quarters, nor above, nor below, nor the earth;
neither the world, nor heat, nor I, nor Indra, Śiva, and the others. (5)
There is but one great king there, possessed of immense splendor;
he is the doer of all, the all-pervading, the All, and he remains established in silence.
The King is the Self; he remains silent, meaning that he is immutable (kūṭastha). || 6 ||
A minister so resolved, intent upon every wise counsel, quickly brings about what was impossible and thoroughly accomplishes what was already possible. (7)

The minister is the mind. It brings about for itself the state of being a transmigrating soul (*saṃsāritva*), which is impossible and utterly inconceivable. Even while bringing about that which is to be brought about, it destroys its own nature as the single flavor of perfect bliss; it denies it, saying "it does not exist" and "it does not appear. || 7 ||
He is unable to enjoy anything nor does he know anything at all;
yet, though ignorant, he always performs everything solely for the sake of the king.
Even though he was ignorant and dull-witted, || 8 ||
He alone was the sole performer of all the king's duties;
the monarch himself remained entirely at ease in private.
In solitude, in a state that is non-dual by nature. || 9 ||
Bali said:
O high-minded one, what is that land free from mental and physical afflictions?
How is it reached, and by whom has it been attained, O Lord? (10)
The questions regarding the offerings are explained by their very recitation. || 10 ||
Who is that such-like minister, and who is that king of great power, by whom even we have not been conquered, he who effortlessly tore asunder the nets of the world? (11)
"This narrative is unprecedented for me, a source of fear even for the immortals;
please dispel the cloud of doubt from the sky of our hearts. (12)
By our narration of omens regarding his invincibility. || 12 ||

Virocana said: "O son, that minister there is so powerful that he cannot be overcome even slightly, even by the hosts of gods and asuras combined, even if they were multiplied a hundred thousandfold."
There, at the beginning and at the end, he explains in detail the very cause for that non-conquest which was asked about, starting with the words "sa tatra" (he there) and so forth.
Even slightly (*manāk*) means even a little (*īṣat*). || 13 ||
He is neither the thousand-eyed Indra, nor Yama, nor the Lord of Wealth;
he is neither a god nor even an asura, if my son is victorious.

Is that minister a second Indra, or Yama, or Kubera, or some great-souled immortal or asura, such that he is impossible to conquer? To this he replies: "He is not. The meaning is that if he were someone like the Thousand-eyed One (Indra) or others, then he would certainly be conquered by you. || 14 ||
There, weapons such as swords, clubs, javelins, thunderbolts, discuses, and maces become blunted, like the striking of a lotus against a stone. (15)
"Do I have no weapons or soldiers? Let them indeed exist; however, he is not within their jurisdiction," he says:
"Therein" (verse 15).
He is not accessible to missiles or weapons, nor to the deeds performed by warriors;
therefore, all the gods and asuras have been brought under his control at all times. (16)
On the contrary, he says "by him" (tena) [in verse 16], meaning that you and others have been conquered by that very same person.
Even though he was not Viṣṇu, by him here the asuras such as Hiraṇyākṣa were struck down,
like the wish-fulfilling trees on Mount Meru by the wind at the end of an aeon.
With the intention that even our ancestors and others were slain by Viṣṇu after being brought under his control by that very same [power], he says:
"even by one who is not Viṣṇu. By the *kalpavāta*, that is, by the wind of universal dissolution (*pralaya-vāyu*). || 17 ||
Even the gods, beginning with Nārāyaṇa, though they were all-knowing,
were overcome by him and cast into pits at his will.

Even those who instruct all beings in discernment were attacked and brought under control by him alone through the instigation of causes such as Bhṛgu’s curse; he cast them into pits, that is, into womb-like chasms.
By his grace, Smara, possessing five arrows, strides with pride through these three worlds, leaping about like a sovereign emperor. (19)
Smara, the god of love, though possessing only five arrows, by her grace has pervaded these three worlds; having conquered them, he now exults and expands his power. || 19 ||
Though he is grasped by the hosts of gods and asuras, though devoid of virtue, evil-minded,
and of hideous form, Krodha expands through his grace.

By whom the hosts of gods and demons were made dependent and deprived of their independence; [the suffix] *kyap* is applied here according to the rule: "after the root *pad*, [the suffix *kyap* occurs] when meaning 'dependent,' 'external,' or 'belonging to a faction. (Pāṇini 3.1.119) 20.
The repeated conflict between thousands of gods and asuras is merely a play for that counselor who possesses such power of counsel.
O son, if that minister is conquered by that lord alone, then he is easily defeated; otherwise, however, he is like a mountain.
If [the opponent] is conquered by the Lord himself, then that which is to be conquered is easily won. || 22 ||
In time, that very same lord develops the desire to conquer his own minister; by that [desire], he is conquered without effort. || 23 ||
At the time when, through the ripening of abundant past merits, the state of seclusion arises, [liberation occurs] effortlessly through mere knowledge alone. || 23 ||
If you have the power to conquer the wrestler of the three worlds, who has caused the three worlds to gasp for breath, then you are truly possessed of valor. (24)

He who, by his strength, was the conqueror of the wrestler among all those who possess power in the three worlds; by whom the triple world was made to gasp for breath, like a living being on the verge of death—he, then, [is he]. 24.
When that sun has risen, these lotus-pools of the three worlds come into bloom;
when it has set, they dissolve away.
He states that he possesses not only the power of universal victory, but also the power to create the three worlds and so forth, by saying "in him":
*tasmin* (in him). This is a *vyastarūpaka* (a partial metaphor), meaning "in that sun. || 25 ||
If you, O steadfast one of noble vows, are thus capable of conquering that [mind] with a single intellect free from delusion, then you are truly wise.
By means of that which is certain and one-pointed; therefore, you are indeed steadfast. 26.
When that is conquered, even unconquered worlds will be conquered;
but if it remains unconquered, these remain unconquered, even if they have been held for a long time. (27)
Therefore, for the sake of infinite accomplishment and for eternal happiness, apply yourself to their conquest even through arduous effort. (28)

For the sake of those infinite accomplishments (*siddhi*); "infinite" (*ananta*) refers to death (*anta*), and its absence is "the infinite" (*ananta*), meaning the conquest of death; and for the sake of accomplishing that, even through arduous practices involving the abandonment of everything and so forth, [he conquered] the hosts of gods, demons, *nāgas*, and *yakṣas*.
Together with the gods, nāgas, and kinnaras, even the three worlds were brought under his control; indeed, by that exceedingly powerful one, all was accomplished with ease. (29)
Having restated that very power once more, he concludes with the verse beginning "sasure" (along with the gods). "Nāgas" refers to the elephants of the quarters;
"mahoragas" refers to Śeṣa and others. || 29 ||
Thus ends the twenty-third canto, titled "The Words of Virocana," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki;
and thus ends [the same] in the *Tātparya-prakāśa* commentary on the Section on Tranquility of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*.
The twenty-third canto, titled "Virocana’s Speech."
The twenty-fourth canto. Bali said:
"O father, by what means can that powerful one be completely conquered?"
Who is this one of such exceeding great heroism? Tell me everything quickly.
This method for overcoming that evil counselor is now proclaimed;
it consists of gaining access to the king's presence and being endowed with detachment and other such qualities. (1)
The question is clear. || 1 ||
Virocana said:
"O son, listen as I speak of the means by which even that son of a minister, whose position is eternally invincible, may be easily subdued. (2)
"Ease of accomplishment" means, in other words, the means for attaining happiness. || 2 ||
"O son, if he is approached with the proper method, he will come under control in an instant;
without the method, he burns like an arrogant, venomous serpent. (3)
Those who, having fondled this king like a child, restrain him through skillful means—having observed such a king, they attain their goal. (4)

Having indulged him by granting small objects of enjoyment and having deceived him by repeatedly proclaiming the defects of sense-objects, [he attained] the state—the rank of a king—by means of the skillful method known as *rājayoga*. || 4 ||
When that lord of the earth is seen, the minister comes under his control;
and when that minister is overcome, the king is seen once again.
The word "punaḥ" (again) serves as an ornament for the sentence. || 5 ||
As long as that king is not seen, the minister is not conquered;
and as long as the minister is not defeated, the king is not seen. (6)
When a king has a wicked minister, that [minister] bears fruit in extreme suffering;
when the minister is not subdued, the king becomes utterly invisible.
It bears fruit as extreme suffering through passion, hatred, and so forth. || 7 ||
Therefore, through practice, one should undertake both simultaneously:
the sighting of the king and the defeat of his minister. (8)
The two terms "manifestation" (saṃdarśana) and "defeat" (parājaya) refer to their respective means.
By means of human effort, diligent practice, and gradual perseverance,
having accomplished both with exertion, you shall reach that auspicious land.
The twofold [result] consists of the king's appearance and the defeat of the ministers. || 9 ||
O Lord of Daityas, when your practice has borne fruit, you shall go to that realm; if so, you will not grieve even slightly for it again.
When it has become a fruit, when it has become fruitful, or when it has transformed into the nature of the fruit of knowledge. || 10 ||
With all their exertions completely stilled and their intentions eternally joyful,
the virtuous dwell there, with every doubt entirely pacified.

Regarding this, he states who reside there: "perfectly tranquil" (saṃśānta). The meaning is that those virtuous ones in whom all misfortunes have ceased and who are filled with unsurpassed, eternal bliss reside there. || 11 ||
Listen, O son, as to what that country is; I shall reveal everything to you.
By the name of that country, I have described to you liberation (mokṣa), which destroys all suffering.
Now, in order to explain the hidden meaning, he says: "Listen," etc. (12).
But there, O Mahāmati, the Blessed One, the Self who transcends all states, made the wise one named Manas his minister.

He is "transcending all states" (sarvapadātiga) because he goes beyond all stages beginning from human bliss up to the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha; he is also beyond the range of all speech and mind. He is the "wise one" (prājña), the collective totality of all intelligence, by whose abiding in the mind this entire universe has undergone transformation.
Just as a lump of clay [is perceived] as a jar, and smoke [is perceived] as a cloud. (14)

"By being established in the mind" means by existing in the mind in a subtle state consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). "Transformation" (*pariṇati*) means grossness. "As a jar" means as the state of being a jar. "A lump of clay" refers to the portion of clay contained within the lump.
When that is conquered, everything is conquered; everything becomes attained. One should know that it is difficult to conquer, yet it is thoroughly mastered through skillful means alone. (15)
The meaning is that everything to be conquered has been conquered, and everything to be attained has been attained. || 15 ||
Bali said:
"O Blessed One, tell me clearly that method by which his mind may be overcome, so that I may conquer this formidable one. (16)
In "ākramaṇe" and "āskandane," [the meaning] is "in victory. || 16 ||
Virocana said:
"O son, regarding all sense-objects in every respect, this supreme lack of attachment is indeed the means for the conquest of the mind. (17)
Non-attachment is the absence of longing; the application is the means. || 17 ||
This alone is the supreme method; by this very means, the great rutting elephant of one's own mind is swiftly brought under control. (18)

"Drāk" means instantly or immediately. "Avadamyate" means being subdued after having been disregarded. This is according to the statement of the learned: "O dear one, if you desire liberation, abandon sense-objects as if they were poison. (18)
For this, O Mahāmati, is exceedingly difficult to attain and yet easy to attain;
it is very difficult to attain if not practiced, but when well-practiced, it is attained with ease. (19)
This is the method of application. || 19 ||
O son, this aversion to sense objects, when practiced gradually,
attains full manifestation in every respect, just like a creeper watered by irrigation.
Dispassion is the lack of attachment toward sense objects; it attains clarity through the manifestation of the expansion of the branches of tranquility and the other [aids to yoga]. (20)
For even by one of deceitful nature who desires it, that [attainment] is not reached if it has not been practiced, just like rice that has not been sown, O son; therefore, apply yourself to this. 21.
By one who is deceitful in nature and whose mind is greedy for enjoyments; "un-sown" means not planted in fertile fields; "collect" means stabilize it through practice. || 21 ||
So long do these embodied beings, dwelling in the wilderness of saṃsāra, wander amidst sufferings as they do not attain detachment from sense objects. (22)
Abstinence and dispassion. || 22 ||
Without practice, no embodied being— not even one of extreme strength— can attain detachment from sense objects, just as one cannot reach another country without travel.
Non-going is devoid of going. || 23 ||
By constantly abandoning the object of meditation while still possessing a body,
one should increase through practice the lack of attachment to enjoyments, just as one would grow a creeper.

The abandonment of the object of meditation means the relinquishing of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding the objects of meditation previously mentioned as the cause of *jīvanmukti*. O son, for one who meditates with desire and is devoid of the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), no auspiciousness is attained here;
nor can one, free from joy and anger, fully attain the fruit of ritual action. (25)

It is not possible to abandon all objects of sense simultaneously; rather, one should abandon them gradually, one by one. Having renounced each object for a long time, one may occasionally enjoy it once in a while, until finally, through the ripening of dispassion, one abandons them all. This occurs when there is firmness in human effort toward that end.
Furthermore, with the intention that [the practice] is necessary as a means of warding off attachment to joy, resentment, and greed, he says:

"Without the aim of man" (puruṣārthāt). Without the aim of man—that is, without human effort—one cannot obtain an auspicious means conducive to attaining the fruit of action, which is free from joy and resentment. || 25 ||

In the world, it is called "fate" (daiva), yet fate is nowhere embodied like a living being; rather, it is that which is known as "inevitability" (avaśyambhāvin) and "destiny" (niyati), arising from one's own past actions.
One might ask: "Could that attainment not occur through destiny alone? To this he replies with the word *daivam* (destiny).

His own inherent action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—impelled by necessity (*niyati*), is what is called "destiny" by men who possess a human perspective, but not by others who possess the divine, scriptural vision; such is the connection with the following verse. || 26 ||

It is said that by the word "fate" (daiva) it refers only to men and not to others; for whatever has been accomplished here, whenever, and wherever, once it has reached completion, it is called fate. (27)

[Objection: Is it not observed that for some people, the subsiding of joy and resentment occurs even without effort, solely by fate (*daiva*)? To this, he says "that which" (*yat*). The meaning is: when the karma that causes joy and resentment has been exhausted, whatever arises for the destruction of that joy and resentment is precisely what is called "fate" by people. || 27 ||
That which is called destiny (daiva) is for the destruction of joy and resentment; destiny, which takes the form of necessity (niyati), is sustained by human effort (puruṣārtha). 28.

"Let it be as you have said regarding destiny. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Destiny. The meaning is that destiny, which consists of necessity (niyati) as I have described it, is overcome by human effort—such as the firmness of dispassion and practice—in a very short time, just like the delusion of a mirage is dispelled by the realization of the true nature of the desert. || 28 ||
Just as the delusion of a mirage vanishes through the play of right knowledge, so too whatever is conceived by human effort comes to pass exactly in that way. (29)

If it is objected: "If destiny, known as *daiva*, is overcome by that which is known as human effort (*pauruṣa*), then since there would be no fixed rule regarding its fruit, it follows that destiny is non-deterministic"—we reply that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). For among all things born of mental resolve, provided there is no sublation, they are apprehended by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being fruitful; thus, they possess fruit.
He says "yathā" (as for example), because he accepts the restriction that [the word] "sukhaprada" (bestowing happiness) [expresses only the primary meaning]. || 29 ||
When it is grasped as possessing fruit, it bestows the happiness of possessing fruit;
for here, the mind alone is the agent, and whatever it conceives, that becomes so.

And there is no consequence of this being unregulated, because the designation "regulated" is established by the very conception of such a restriction [of action] by the mind as the agent; with this intention, he says: "The agent. In our view, the agent is the individual soul (jīva), which is indeed the mind itself. || 30 ||
Whatever kind of destiny this [power] intends, it becomes exactly so;
it renders some objects determined, others undetermined, and even those that were indeterminate.

He establishes how this [Will] conceives such a destiny (niyati) with the words "determined and undetermined. The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: it makes determined those things whose fruits are generally fixed; undetermined those things which fall within the scope of exceptions; and it makes undetermined those worldly objects whose fruits are not fixed, as well as even those illusory (prātibhāsika) objects whose fruits are absolutely non-existent. || 31 ||
It acts upon the mind; therefore, this mind is joined to destiny.
While acting with certainty within destiny, it sometimes bears the name of its own purpose.

For that reason, this mind is the "joiner" and "establisher" even of the determination of results (*phala-niyati*) in accordance with its own conceptualized objects; such is the meaning. Precisely for this reason, he says—with the intention that if an object were ultimately real, the cognition having that object as its domain would necessarily have a determined result, and would not have an undetermined result like fate (*daiva*) or karma—:
Regarding the phrase "in Niyati": this living being (jīva), whose essence is consciousness, at some point during a birth qualified for liberation, [attains] within the Supreme Self— which is Niyati,

characterized by an eternally fixed and singular nature— the Niyati known as one's own purpose, namely the stream of mental modifications (vṛtti-dhārā) of identical form known as direct realization (sākṣātkāra) whose object is the immediate, ultimate reality.

This means: while practicing the non-conceptual samādhi, he vibrates without attachment within this cosmic shell like the wind in the sky; the sense is that he shines forth in his own true nature. || 32 ||
Within this vessel of the world, the individual soul vibrates like the wind in the sky;
performing what is ordained by necessity, it sometimes moves beyond that very necessity.

At times, during the period of emergence from samādhi, while performing the duties prescribed by necessity (*niyati*)— which is characterized by the scriptures and appropriate to one's own stage of life—

for the sake of designation, that is, for the purpose of awakening ignorant people, he is known in the world as one whose name "Niyati" is established and renowned through such titles as "these ritualists," "the cultured," or "the promoters of right conduct."

Being of such a nature, it manifests; the meaning is that just as a mountain ridge, though its own nature is immovable, appears to move when the trees move due to the force of the wind, and appears to be still when they are still, so too does this [consciousness] manifest.
For the sake of conventional designation, the word "destiny" (niyati) shines forth like a mountain peak;
therefore, as long as the mind exists, there is neither fate nor destiny.
Therefore, he says "tasmāt" (therefore), meaning: "For this reason, you too should rely upon these two final modes of conduct for as long as you live."
O virtuous one, once the mind has set, let whatever happens be so;
for the individual soul is born as a person according to its own human effort. (35)

Regarding what will happen after that, he says: "In the mind" (*manasi*). A person who has been born—that is, one who has attained a body qualified for the practice of action and knowledge—whatever he intends (*saṃkalpayati*), that comes to be;
thus, since intention is within his own control, he should accomplish the means such as detachment (*vairāgya*) through human effort.

With the intention that one should contemplate only the state of being the Self which is Brahman—the nature of the supreme human goal—and not the state of being a transmigrating self, he says: "Apart from the human goal," and so forth. (35)
In this world, whatever one intends comes to pass exactly so for him and not otherwise;
O son, there is nothing here that exists apart from human effort.
Relying on supreme human effort, one should cultivate detachment toward enjoyments;
for as long as detachment toward enjoyments—which destroys worldly existence—does not arise. (37)
Supreme liberation, which bestows victory, is not attained as long as attachment to sense objects—which causes delusion—remains. (38)

As long as there is attachment to sense objects, the swing of one's condition—characterized by the constant oscillation of worldly enjoyments—is strung together with the heavy loads of serpents, namely the burdens of enjoyments; for this reason, it is painful and consists of baseless desires.
Without the practice of detachment, listening to the teachings, meditative absorption, and so forth, this swing of existence never, at any time, comes to rest.
"It does not turn back and cannot be restrained"—this is the connection with what follows. || 38 ||
O son, as long as the state of the mind’s swinging on the swing of worldly existence remains unsteady, it will never cease to cause suffering without the practice [of yoga]. (39)
When will the hope, pierced by the weight of enjoyments and enjoyers, ever turn back?
Bali said:
O Lord of all the Asuras, how does that very lack of attachment to enjoyments—which bestows long life—attain a stable state within the individual soul? (41)
Longevity is the persistence of the personal existence as something eternal. || 41 ||
Virocana said:
The creeper of self-realization clearly bears fruit;
it produces in the living being a distaste for enjoyments, just as a great vine does in autumn.

The *phalinī* tree, bearing the fruit of liberation, yields as its intermediate fruit a lack of interest in worldly enjoyments (*vairāgya*). Just as the great vine of grapes and other such plants bears unripe fruit in the autumn, so it is with this. (42)
Through the contemplation of the Self, this supreme detachment from sense objects takes its abode in the heart, like the goddess Śrī within the hollow of a lotus.
Śrī is Lakṣmī; in the hollow of the lotus, that is, within the interior of the lotus. || 43 ||
Therefore, with an exceedingly beautiful investigation through the whetstone of wisdom,
one should behold the deity and simultaneously extract delight from worldly enjoyments.
By means of investigation, which serves as the whetstone for the jewel of wisdom; simultaneously, at the same time. 44.

For one who has not yet attained proficiency in the noble method, one should fill two parts of the mind with enjoyments, one part with the study of the scriptures, and one part with service to the guru. (45)

In this context, wishing to explain the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmikā*) according to the distinctions in the maturation of the mind, he speaks of the first stage, beginning with the words "of the mind" (*cittasya*). By means of enjoyments—which serve merely as sustenance for the body—one should spend two parts of the day's duration in study, that is, in hearing the scriptures. This applies to one whose mind is unrefined, at the commencement of the true path (*satkrama*) within the noble way (*sanmārga*).
Or, [it means] "in the sequence taught in the scriptures. || 45 ||
One who possesses some degree of proficiency should fill one part with enjoyments, two parts with service to the teacher, and one part with reflection on the meaning of the scriptures. (46)

Regarding the conquest of that [state], he speaks of the stage that follows it with the words "something" (*kiṃcit*). This means for one who has attained the sense of wonder (*camatkāra*) in the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*).

Precisely because of this, through the arising of detachment from enjoyments (*bhoga*), there occurs a reduction in their portion; and through service to the Guru (*guru-śuśrūṣā*), there is an increase in another portion. When one remains in the presence of the Guru for a long time, on the appropriate occasion, regarding the Gurus...
The sense is that [this is said] because of the possibility of questions arising from one's own doubts. || 46 ||
For one who follows the path of thorough understanding, he should daily fill his mind:
two parts with the scriptures and dispassion, and two parts with meditation and the worship of the Guru. (47)

Regarding the conquest of that [mind], he speaks of the stage subsequent to it—namely, *vyutpatti* (mastery). Mastery is the definitive ascertainment of reality through long-term investigation, like the examination of a jewel. One should fill two parts of the mind following that mastery with the combined practice of the scriptures and dispassion (*vairāgya*). However, one should fill the other two parts respectively with meditations (*dhyāna*) and the worship of the Guru. || 47 ||
The soul that has attained goodness becomes fit for the sequence of discourse on knowledge;
like a cloth of pure form, it receives the highest dye.
He states that in all four stages, only one whose mind is pure is qualified, and no other—beginning with the words "sādhutām" (purity).
The meaning is that only a cloth of stainless appearance and perfectly pure form receives the finest dyeing with safflower, *kiṃśuka*, and so forth, and not one that is soiled. || 48 ||

One should protect the child of the mind by nurturing it very gradually through skillful means and purifying words, and by bringing about its transformation through the meaning of the scriptures. (49)
To the question of how this applies to one who is slightly impure, he says: "Gradually.

This means that through reasoning which demonstrates the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of suffering, and through purifying words—the teachings of the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and the preceptor—the transformation of the mind regarding the meaning of the scriptures occurs through long-term cultivation.
Therefore, its result is a state of uniform sweetness, like that of sugar and āmalaka fruit. || 49 ||
When the mind has matured in knowledge and its stubborn grasping has been loosened,
it shines forth coolly, like crystal devoid of moonlight.

That which has become relaxed and difficult to grasp—the grasping of external, impure, and inert forms—is like crystal that is not separate from the moonlight; that is to say, it is in a state of aesthetic fusion (*samarasa*) with the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*). In the reading *līna* (merged), the meaning is clear. It is cool, free from heat. || 50 ||
Then, with supreme and straightforward wisdom, one should quickly observe the form of the body as being exactly the same as that of a lord of enjoyments.
He demonstrates what that supreme transformation is like with the words "by means of wisdom" (*prajñayā*).

By means of supreme wisdom— which is straight (*ṛjvyā*), having shed the crookedness of differentiation, inequality, and deviation, and which takes the form of Brahman— one [perceives] enjoyments through the analytical understanding of the instruments, actions, and states [of the senses], as well as the sense organs, their objects, and their fluctuations, belonging to the Lord who is their master.

One should perceive the very nature of the foundational Brahman—which is non-dual, of one essence, and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss—as being equal and identical to the individual soul (jīva), the body, and the locus of experience; or rather, one should perceive that form of the foundation as being equal [to them] at the same time. || 51 ||
O son, by the power of wisdom and discernment, one should always bring about the simultaneous observation of the self and the abandonment of craving. (52)
With the intention that the absolute abandonment of the thirst for the fruits of deliberation occurs only then, he says: "Prajñā... (verse 52).
Freedom from thirst for other views and the supreme vision that exists when thirst is absent—these two views stand in mutual dependence, like light and the wick of a lamp. (53)

He states that the result of *vicāra* (investigation), which is the cessation of personal error, and the result of *jñāna* (knowledge), which is the cessation of root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), do not exist as separate entities: "In the vision of another" (*paradṛṣṭau*). Just as the state of heat of fire, the state of radiance of a lamp, and the state of the lamp's form are mutually the removers of both darkness and oil.
The meaning is: "it is like that" when they exist through mutual simultaneity. || 53 ||
When the multitude of enjoyments has lost its relish and the Supreme Lord, who is both transcendent and immanent, is beheld,
an eternal and infinite repose arises in the Supreme Brahman.
That which is tasted is "taste" (*āsvāda*), meaning flavor (*rasa*); the sense is that its flavor has departed. || 54 ||
An infinite bliss arises from the joy unconditioned by sense objects;
for living beings, this never occurs except through hearing of the Self. 55.
He says that for those who are greedy for the taste of enjoyments, there is no attainment of the bliss of the Self—beginning with the words "viṣaye" (in objects).

For living beings who savor [pleasure] in such a manner that joy is perceived and grasped as the essence within sense-objects alone, there is never—at any time whatsoever—*nirvṛti*, which is unsurpassed bliss. || 55 ||
Happiness arises through sacrifice, charity, austerity, and visiting sacred fords;
yet it is not produced by austerities alone, nor by charity, nor even by sacred fords. (56)

Regarding what was stated—that this supreme detachment from sense objects comes to abide in the heart through the contemplation of the Self—some do not accept it, arguing that detachment from sense objects arises solely through the purification of the mind by means of sacrifices and other such rites. To them, he says: [the phrase] "detachment is born" is to be connected with what follows. (56)
A person’s detachment from enjoyments occurs only through the contemplation of their true nature;
by no other means whatsoever can the intellect be directed toward the contemplation of the Self.

Thus, he says "by some [means]" (kayācit) to show that even by any other means whatsoever, the intellect does not proceed toward the perception of the Self without the effort of a person consisting in the practice of detachment from enjoyments. || 57 ||
O son, without one's own effort, it does not lead to the welfare of a person; nor does it do so without the attainment of the supreme goal through the renunciation of enjoyments. (58)
The supreme bliss of resting in the state of Brahman is not attained anywhere else in this world, from the realm of Brahmā down to a blade of grass. 59.
In that same way, one finds rest when the Supreme Cause shines forth, by relying on human effort and casting destiny far away. (60)
One breathes freely and finds rest in the Supreme Cause, the Supreme Self, which shines forth as one's own nature, fully manifested.
The wise man should revile worldly enjoyments, which are the firm bolts barring the door to the highest good; when revulsion toward enjoyments has matured, discernment arises.
Vicāra is the discrimination between the existent and the non-existent. || 61 ||
When the rainy season had passed, he was as stainless as the glorious autumn;
through reflection arose a revulsion for enjoyments, and from that revulsion came further reflection.
When the earth is "grown," meaning endowed with the increase of crops and the like, it is "prosperous" through the abundance of fruits such as rice.
Since the growth of both [the earth and the harvest] is mutually dependent, he says "investigation" (vicāra) to indicate that they must be made to flourish simultaneously.
These two mutually fulfill one another, like the ocean and the clouds:
the contemplation of the reproach of worldly enjoyment, and the eternal vision of one's own true self.

Just as the clouds are filled by the ocean through the gateway of its rays, and the ocean [is filled] by the clouds through the gateway of rain, so it is here. Now, he states that these three must be increased simultaneously: "by the longing for enjoyment," etc.
"The light of the Self" means the vision of the Self. (63)
Like very affectionate friends, they accomplish their purpose for one another,
having previously disregarded fate through diligent human effort.
Pressing his teeth against his teeth, he should cultivate a lack of attachment toward worldly enjoyments; this should be done in accordance with local customs and with the consent of his kinsmen.
First, he states that the very absence of attachment to enjoyments must necessarily be accomplished with great effort, using the words "with teeth" (dantaiḥ).

To that end, he states the means: "place" (deśa). The intention is that among the means such as accepting gifts prescribed for various castes, only those approved by the local people and one's kinsmen should be adopted, and no others. || 65 ||
In the beginning, one should acquire wealth through human effort and gradual means;
with that wealth, one should attract noble and virtuous people who possess excellent qualities.

One should acquire [wealth] through human effort—that is, by means such as receiving gifts appropriate for a person born into a particular caste—meaning that one should win over and bring under one's control [the king]. || 66 ||
From attachment to them, there arises a revulsion toward enjoyments;
from that, reflection follows, and subsequently knowledge, which is the synthesis of the meaning of the scriptures. (67)
Following that, after reflection (*vicāra*), there arises knowledge—the knowledge of the meaning of the sentences thus reflected upon.

Following that, through the consideration of the principle of the uniformity of purport (*gatisāmānyanyāya*), there occurs the summary of the meaning of the scripture: the determination of the intent of all the Vedas toward non-dual Brahman; such is the meaning. || 67 ||
Then, in due course, the attainment of the supreme state arises,
when, at the time of cessation, you have withdrawn from sense objects.

Then, through the sequence of reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), or by the process of ascending the stages (*bhūmikā*), this means for attaining the supreme state has now been described as consisting in detachment from sense objects.
However, if you are unable to renounce sense objects, then when youth has passed and you have ceased [from worldly activity], you should withdraw from sense objects at that time.
The meaning is that you shall attain the supreme state at that very moment through the power of inquiry, and not later. || 68 ||
Then, through the power of inquiry, you will attain the supreme state;
you will find perfect rest within the utterly pure Self.
With the intention that, since the cessation of sense-objects is thus necessary, it is appropriate for you to cease right now, he says: "Properly... (verse 69).
Furthermore, you shall not fall into the mire of conceptual construction to your suffering;
though you abide, you have no attachment—O Pure One, O Sadāśiva, let there be salutation to you forever! (70)

"O Śuddha, that [nature] is yours. Even though you are situated in the state of worldly enjoyment (bhoga), because there is an expectation of another time [for liberation], you are indeed Sadāśiva; therefore, let there be salutation right now to you who have become Brahman.
Thus, although a salutation from the perspective of a son would be inappropriate, it was performed here through the vision of Brahman. || 70 ||
O dear one, acquire wealth by traveling through various lands with little reproach, and thereby win over virtuous people with honor;
and do so without disregarding the objects of the senses that arise from their company.
Your attainment of selfhood occurs through the power of correct investigation.

He summarizes the stated meaning concisely with the word *deśa* ("instruct"): "Instruct [him] to acquire wealth" is the ellipsis; that is, in a manner not contrary to local customs. By means of that wealth, through the rejection of meager and most trivial enjoyment—that is, without expending wealth for the sake of enjoyment—one [should serve] the virtuous people, namely those who know Brahman.

Acquire [knowledge] preceded by proper honor, such as prostration, service, food, clothing, and so forth. However, if the reading is *śāstrapūrvam* (preceded by scripture), it means according to the method prescribed in the scriptures:

"For the sake of that knowledge, one should approach a guru alone, with fuel in hand, who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman. Thereafter, through the disregard for sense objects and the passions of attachment and aversion arising from association with the virtuous, [one attains realization].

The meaning is that, through the power of the correct investigation of the spiritual scriptures undertaken by you once you have attained the fourfold qualification, the realization of the Self will come to you like the recovery of a golden necklace forgotten around one's own neck.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Mental Doubt," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Tranquility) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Mental Doubt," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-fifth canto. Bali said:
"This was previously told to me by my father, who is possessed of beautiful discernment."
Now, by good fortune, I have regained my consciousness and remembered it all. || 1 ||
Here, for the sake of pacifying doubt, the auspicious rise of the moon of discernment within Bali is further described according to the desire of Śukra’s contemplation. (1)
Having concluded the intermediate narrative, he applies it to the subject at hand with the words: "This... (verse 1).
Today, this clear aversion to enjoyments has truly arisen within me;
by good fortune, I enter the pure bliss of tranquility, cool as nectar. (2)
Filling my hopes once more, bringing back my provisions once again,
and winning over my beloved once more— I am weary of this state of worldly existence.

"Punar" means repeatedly; it signifies "again and again. "Āvarjayan" means making favorable through entreaties and the like. "Vibhavasthitau" refers to the matter of maintaining prosperity; I am "khinnaḥ," that is, distressed. || 3 ||
Ah, how truly delightful is this cool inner ground of tranquility!
For in tranquility, all perceptions of pleasure and pain come to rest.
In tranquility, which possesses the quality of peace, all perceptions of pleasure and pain alike go to their destruction. || 4 ||

I am at peace, I am fully extinguished, and I abide happily in tranquility. [In printed editions, the reading *same* is generally found, but as that is inconsistent, the reading *śame*, which is supported by the author of the commentary, has been adopted from another manuscript. I remain established in peace.
Within, I rejoice like the reflection of the moon's orb set within.

"Abiding in tranquility, I am established; I am at peace"—this is a statement regarding the cessation of all suffering (*tāpa*). "As if placed within the lunar orb, I am completely extinguished" (*parinirvāmi*)—this is a statement regarding the mind's subjection to unsurpassed bliss. "I dwell in happiness"—this is a statement regarding abiding in the nature of the bliss that is its cause. The word "within" (*antar*) is to be understood as applying everywhere. This...
"I rejoice"—this is an exaggeration (atiśayokti) regarding the signs of joy, such as horripilation and so forth. || 5 ||
Alas, the acquisition of wealth is misery: it causes the body to waste away through the impetuous force of a mind in constant agitation, and it brings incessant turmoil.

From the word *uttāṇḍava* [meaning "leaping up" or "exultant"], by the rule that *kvip* is to be prescribed after all nominal stems (*sarvaprātipadika*) in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*), the suffix *kvip* is applied; then, for the present tense (*laṭ*), the substitute *śatṛ* is used. [The compound is explained as follows: in which [place] the broad (*uru*)—meaning principal or extensive—the body (*śarīra*) is "departed" (*proṣita*) or "consumed" (*dagdha*) by the velocities of the mind leaping up (*uttāṇḍavataḥ*) due to the longing for enjoyment (*bhogotkaṇṭhayā*), or which is characterized by wandering through various lands (*deśabhramaṇaśīla*). Alternatively, it means that in which the broad body is [so situated].
Thus, the acquisition of wealth, which involves incessant agitation, is nothing but suffering. "Hā" expresses grief. (6)
In the past, I was delighted when women pressed limb against limb and flesh against flesh; that was merely the manifestation of delusion.
Now, having analyzed even the nature of the enjoyment of women and other such fruits of that [action] as being essence-less, he laments with the verse beginning "The limb," etc. (verse 7).
Examples have been seen; what was to be enjoyed has been enjoyed without loss; the entire world of beings has been traversed. What, then, could possibly be considered auspicious? (8)
They have personally witnessed great displays of wealth that serve as examples for all forms of prosperity.

They have enjoyed the pleasures of sovereignty and the like, which are unimpaired and unopposed by others. Furthermore, they have overwhelmed every living being—the entire host of creatures—with their own power, bringing them under their sway; yet, even so, what indeed is truly excellent?

Eternal happiness has arisen. The meaning is that since, in this beginningless saṃsāra, such prosperity has occurred for everyone at some point, and because even for oneself a hundredfold misfortune has been possible in the past—even more so than a thousandfold—nothing [in this world] is truly auspicious. || 8 ||
Those very same things, those very same things, whether there, here, or elsewhere, moving from this place to that—there is nothing at all that is truly new. (9)

He says "again" (*punar*) because there is no perception of any other fresh wonder, and because worldly and celestial enjoyments are merely like the chewing over of what has already been chewed; thus, they possess no essential value. In that regard, "there" refers to heaven and so forth; "here" refers to this earth;
and "elsewhere" refers to the world of the *nāgas* and so on. || 9 ||
Having mentally renounced and cast aside everything by myself,
I remain established in my own true nature, like one who has emerged from the full into the full within the Self.

The phrase "as if full" is used to indicate the mere removal of the delusion of incompleteness upon attaining fullness from the nature of consciousness itself, rather than the attainment of some previously non-existent fullness; or else, it means that [the Self] is full like the Ocean of Milk due to the full moon as its cause. || 10 ||
In the netherworld, on the earth, and in heaven, there are women, jewels, precious stones, and the like;
yet even that essence is swiftly swallowed up by insignificant time. (11)

Even that which is perceived as substantial by the vision of the ignorant, though it is an object of enjoyment, ultimately results in suffering because of its perishable nature; with the intention that from their perspective it is likewise insubstantial, he says: "In the netherworld... (verse 11).
For so long a time in the past, I was utterly childish,
harboring hatred toward the immortals for the sake of this trivial worldly desire.
The meaning is that by my vain desire for sovereignty over the world and by harboring hatred toward the immortals, I was utterly childish and truly a fool. || 12 ||
What purpose could there be in abandoning this great affliction called the world, which is merely a mental creation? Indeed, what passion could a Great-Souled One have for it? (13)

The word "jagat" (world) refers to the great mental anguish (*ādhi*) consisting of the desire for sovereignty over the world; the phrase "not having abandoned" (*atyaktena*) is to be joined with the first half-verse to form the complete sense. The "goal" (*artha*) would be a human aim (*puruṣārtha*).
For it is only when there is passion that the notion of something being a human aim arises; since that very passion is absent here, he asks: "Who? (verse 13).
Alas! For a very long time, intoxicated by the pride of ignorance, I have pursued misfortune with the thought that it was a gain, serving my own self for so long. (14)
The meaning is that this misfortune was pursued by me myself—who had become my own death—at the [wrong] time, while perceiving it as a benefit. || 14 ||
Driven by ever-increasing craving, what in these three worlds have I, a fool, not done to further increase my remorse? (15)
Therefore, let me have enough of this trivial former anxiety;
human effort achieves its fruit through treatment directed toward the present.
Alternatively, thinking, "What is the use of my past grief? I shall now consider the means for making this human birth fruitful by treating my present delusion," he says: "By this... (verse 16).
Today, through the unity within oneself of the single cause of infinite forms,
happiness approaches from every direction, like an elixir in the ocean.

Today, just as the elixir of immortality (rasāyana) emerges from all sides through the churning of the ocean of milk, so too does the bliss that is entirely full within the Self— by virtue of its oneness with, and non-difference from, that Cause which is Brahman of immeasurable forms and unlimited nature— manifest itself today.
"I ask Śukra about the teachings of Uśanas"—this is the syntactical connection with what follows. || 17 ||
"What is this 'I', and what might the self be?"—this is the contemplation of the Self.
I shall surely ask the Lord, the son of Uśanas, for the sake of pacifying ignorance. (18)

"What is this phenomenal proliferation (prapañca)? What is 'I'—the reality of the individual soul (jīvatattva) known through the notion of 'I'? I shall ask, I will inquire, of the Lord who is like Uśanas, the master of the Kula, because he is the Guru of the Kula—the means by which the Self is beheld. || 18 ||
I contemplate the Supreme Lord Śukra,
whose grace is ever-ready; then, instructed by his words,
I abide by myself through the Self within the infinite glory [of the Lord].
The words of instruction bear fruit when their meaning has not been exhausted. || 19 ||

I meditate upon Śukra, the Supreme Lord, who is the master of all desires due to his perfection in yoga, and whose grace is swiftly directed toward those who take refuge in him. By means of that Śukra, I abide, and shall continue to abide, by myself alone within the Self, which possesses infinite glory as taught by the Word (Vāk).
[The present tense is used here to indicate proximity to the present moment.]
Regarding the reason for your confidence in remaining there, he says: "It is inexhaustible.
This means that the words of instruction from the great yield inexhaustible and imperishable results; they never fail to bear fruit. || 19 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Instruction on Yoga Concerning the Realization of Bali’s Reflection," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, belonging to the Holy Tradition (*ārṣa*). Canto 25.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Instruction on Yoga for the Realization of the Principles of Childlike Thought," in the Section on Quiescence (*Upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, the powerful Bali closed his eyes.
He meditated upon Śukra, whose eyes were like lotus petals and who had the sky as his abode.
Now, regarding the offering for the semen that has been emitted through mindfulness,
the instruction on the essence of reality (tattvasāra) and the movement through the sky are briefly described here.
He whose abode and place of rest is the very space of Brahman, which is indeed the ether (ākāśa). || 1 ||
Then Bhārgava, who was constantly meditating, perceived through his contemplation on all things that his disciple Bali, residing within his mind, was in the city seeking wealth for his teacher.

Then, the descendant of Bhṛgu (Bhārgava), who was constantly engaged in perpetual meditation, realized that his disciple Bali—who was situated within all things because he is the form of Brahman existing within everything—was dwelling in his own mind, seeking the Guru for the sake of knowledge and desiring to see him out of a desire to know the ultimate reality; such is the syntactical connection. || 2 ||
Then the lord Bhārgava, whose self is all-pervading and infinite consciousness,
brought his own body to Bali’s palace, which possessed jeweled windows.
Then that descendant of Bhṛgu brought his own body toward the jeweled window and the place of the jeweled lattice of Bali; that is to say, he himself arrived there. || 3 ||
With his body touched by the mass of light-rays from the preceptor’s form,
Bali woke up at dawn like a lotus awakened by the rays of the sun.
"Parimṛṣṭatanuḥ" means one whose body has been touched; "saṃbodhitam" means expanded or blossomed. || 4 ||
There, he honored that descendant of Bhrigu by offering precious gems and water for his feet, by scattering heaps of mandāra flowers, and by prostrating at his feet.
Then Bali spoke to his preceptor, whose limbs were adorned with jewels and offerings of honor, who wore a crown of mandāra flowers, and who was resting upon a costly throne.
Bali said: "O Blessed One, this intuition arising from your grace impels me to speak before you, just as the light of the sun impels one to perform a task."

*Pratibhā* is an intellect characterized by ever-new flashes of insight; just as the rays of the sun risen at dawn impel Brahmins and others to perform their duties such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*) through its mere presence, so too is this [pratibhā]. || 7 ||
I am dispassionate toward enjoyments that bestow great delusion;
I desire to know that reality which removes this great delusion.
That reality which, by its mere knowledge, removes great delusion—such is that reality. (8)
How vast is this web of enjoyments, or of what nature is it?
Who am I, who are you, and what are these worlds? Tell me this quickly. (9)

"To what extent" means that of which there is a limit of excellence. "The web of enjoyments" refers to the pleasure derived from sense objects. "Of what nature" and "of what essence" constitute the inquiry regarding the reality of enjoyment (*bhoga-tattva*). "Who am I? and "Who are you? constitute the inquiry regarding the reality of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-tattva*). "What are these worlds? constitutes the inquiry regarding the reality of the enjoyed (*bhogya-tattva*), based on the etymological derivation that "worlds" (*lokāḥ*) are so called because they are perceived (*lokyante*). || 9 ||
Śukra said:
O Indra among all the lords of the Dānavas, what is the use of speaking much here? I am striving to go to the sky; hear the essence in brief.

Intending to show that the answer to all three questions can be easily stated through a concise teaching on that very [reality], since the distinctions of the triad beginning with the enjoyer (bhoktṛ) are imagined within the one consciousness (cit), he says "not by many" (bahunā). "Kham" means the path of space (ākāśa); "sāram" means the essence of the three questions. || 10 ||
For here there is only consciousness; this is indeed composed of consciousness alone.
Consciousness, the state of being consciousness, I myself am consciousness, and these worlds are consciousness—this is the summary. (11)

In this world, consciousness (cit) exists. The word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to indicate that its existence is well-known as being independent of anything else. Therefore, this visible world, which is the collection of objects of experience whose establishment depends upon consciousness, is such that consciousness alone is its measure—the ultimate limit of excellence. This is because, according to the Śruti, "from which words turn back," it is only the full consciousness [that is thus described].

Because it is stated that [Brahman] is the ultimate limit of the excellence of all bliss; because consciousness alone, through the superimposition of the manifold variety of difference, appears as consisting of consciousness;
and according to the Śruti: "Of this very bliss, other beings live on only a minute portion.
Likewise, from such [Vedic] statements as "That thou art," "I am Brahman," "This is Brahman, this is Indra," and "There is no other seer than this, there is no other hearer than this."
Based on hundreds of scriptural passages such as "the hearer," he states that even the reality of the enjoyer (bhoktṛ), consisting of "I" and so forth, is indeed pure consciousness alone.

With the intention of explaining that the existence and manifestation of these are dependent upon consciousness, and citing such scriptures as "This entire universe is Brahman, the most excellent," he says: "And these... (verse 11).
If you are capable, then you will certainly attain all of this from this;
if not, then even though much has been spoken to you, it is like an oblation poured upon ashes.
One who becomes thus is "bhavya"—that is, one who possesses faith and is discerning. || 12 ||
The bondage of consciousness consists in the limitation of being an object of thought; liberation from that is called liberation.
"Consciousness is the non-object of thought, the self of all"—this is the summary of all established doctrines. (13)

Bondage is precisely the conceptualization of the form of the object of thought; [the state] free from the object of thought is devoid of the form of the object of thought. It is the universal self, the full self. 13.
Adopting this resolve, you look upon [the world] with ease;
by yourself, through your own self, you shall attain the infinite state.
"If you were to look" is the ellipsis; [you would see] by means of the internal self through a cognitive state (*vṛtti*) of undivided form that has ascended to the inner witness (*pratyak*). || 14 ||
"O sages, I am going right here where the seven seers have assembled; I must indeed dwell there for some purpose of the gods."
The sky is the world of the gods. It must be inhabited; it must necessarily be prepared. The suffix *tavya* is used in the sense of state (*bhāva*). || 15 ||
O King, as long as this body exists, even for those whose minds are liberated,
the abandonment of actions as they arise does not naturally appeal to them.
Now, one might object: "Since you possess a liberated mind and have accomplished all that was to be done, what loss is there for you in not going there? To this, he says: "O King," etc. (Verse 16).
When the descendant of Bhṛgu had thus spoken,
he leaped with great speed through the middle of the sky, which was darkened by swarms of bees and whose path was clearly marked by the ocean.
Agitated like trembling waves by the multitude of planets. || 17 ||

Then, after the descendant of Bhṛgu had thus spoken, the sky—already agitated by the multitude of planets and therefore variegated and speckled like a bee covered in pollen—was leaped across, that is, flown over, by the clear path of the mass of water, namely the clouds and the ocean, via its upper route with great speed like a trembling wave; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). || 17 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Instruction to Bali," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation, in the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, a work of the Seers.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Instruction to Bali," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Twenty-seventh Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When that son of Bhṛgu, the eldest in the assembly of gods and asuras, had departed,
Bali, the best among the wise, reflected thus in his mind.
For Bali, who reflected upon everything according to the path taught by Śukra, it is said that his long-term abiding here was due to his resting in the full bliss of consciousness (cit). || 1 ||
In the assemblies of gods and asuras, [he is] the eldest and most praiseworthy; in the word *jyāyas*, the substitute *jyā* occurs for the word *praśasya* when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied. (1)

What was spoken by the Blessed One is indeed appropriate: "This triple world is consciousness alone; I am consciousness, these worlds are consciousness, the quarters are consciousness, and this activity is consciousness. (2)
He stated what he had reflected upon with the words beginning "It is fitting," and so forth. || 2 ||
In ultimate reality, everything—both external and internal—is consciousness alone;
apart from consciousness, there exists nothing whatsoever here or anywhere else.
If this sun is not perceived as "this is the sun" because it is not cognized, then what distinction between light and darkness could possibly be apprehended here? (4)
He establishes its logical consistency with the passage beginning "This sun," and so forth. "Is cognized" means it is named.

The meaning is that if it were not manifested as being distinct from darkness, jars, lamps, and the like—[the reading *vyāvṛttatā* also occurs in some places]—then it would not be perceived. "Difference" (*bheda*) means distinction, separation, and dissimilarity. The word "as if" (*iva*)...
The purpose is for the ornamentation of the sentence. || 4 ||
If this earth, though it is called "earth," is not perceived as such, then what indeed is the "earth-ness" of the earth? O noble lady, that has become [merely] a state of being so designated.

What is the nature of "earth-ness" as distinct from water and the other elements? The same applies everywhere in what follows. It has reached, that is, attained, the state of being established or firmly rooted. || 5 ||
If these directions are not perceived as "this is this direction," then what indeed is the "direction-ness" of the directions, and likewise, what is the "mountain-ness" of the mountains? (6)
If even among mountains these [other] mountains are not perceived as such, this is understood by implication. || 6 ||
If this world is not perceived as "world" by the consciousness, then what is the world-ness of the world, or what is the sky-ness of the sky? (7)
The world consists of material substances possessing activity; space, however, is immaterial.
If this body, which has the form of a mountain, is not cremated on a funeral pyre, then what indeed can be called the "bodiness" of the bodies of embodied beings? (8)

Having spoken regarding the primary elements (*bhūta*), he speaks regarding the derivative elements (*bhautika*) with the word "body" (*kāya*). It has the form of a mountain; that is to say, it is gross. (8)
The sense organs are consciousness, the body is consciousness, the mind is consciousness, and the search of the heart is consciousness;
consciousness is within, consciousness is without, consciousness is the void, and the existence of all states and the stability of worldly life are consciousness.
Space is empty and non-existent; entities are its opposite and thus existent. The persistence of existence is a contingent being resulting from the conjunction of both.
Indeed, I perform all this preceded by the desire for touch;
I do not experience any contact with the body at all.

The "search for touch" (sparśanaiṣaṇā) is the desire for enjoyment; preceded by that, it is the contact with, or the enjoyment of, the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth. [The phrase] "by means of the body" is used because the insentient [body] cannot logically be the enjoyer—this is the intended meaning. || 10 ||
"What is the use of this body of mine, which is like wood or a clod of earth?
I am consciousness itself, the singular Self of the entire world, whose nature is pure awareness. (11)

If there is nothing [to be gained] by means of the body, then the conceit of identifying with the body is indeed in vain; therefore, it must be abandoned. With this in mind, he says: "What is the use of this? He further says: "Without remainder," with the intention that upon its abandonment, because there is no differentiator for the consciousness free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhiciti*), the realization of the single identity of all consciousness (*sarvacidaikātmya*) is achieved as an unsurpassed gain.

"Consisting of consciousness (cetanātmaka)" means that this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the reason: because the nature of being consciousness (cit) is without distinction everywhere. || 11 ||
I am the light in the sky of consciousness; I am the light in the cage of living beings; I am the consciousness within gods and demons, and in all things both stationary and moving.

In the sky, in the ether; in the sun, in the light of the sun and other luminaries; in the cage of the elements, in the remaining three elements; and in the bodies of gods, asuras, and others, both stationary and moving—that consciousness is indeed I, and I am that very same [consciousness]; such is the meaning. || 12 ||
Consciousness alone exists here; indeed, no second conceptualization is found.
Since duality is impossible in the world, who is an enemy and who is a friend? 13.

Thus, since in the unity of all consciousness there is no separate remainder for perceptions of difference and because of contradiction, duality is impossible; therefore, even the conceptualization of enemies, friends, and so forth is cast far away. Thus he says: "Consciousness exists" (cidasti). || 13 ||
When the radiant head of the body named Bala was severed, what of that [body] was actually severed, given that it remains filled with all the worlds? (14)

Or, let there be this duality of the body and so forth; nevertheless, for me, whose nature is that of unattached, pure consciousness alone, there is no injury whatsoever caused by that [duality]. Thus he says: "Of the one named Bala. (14)
Hatred accumulated through mental construction becomes hatred and nothing else;
therefore, all states such as hatred, whether existent or non-existent, are of the nature of consciousness. || 15 ||

Or, let it be that [the world] is indeed cut by consciousness alone; nevertheless, since the existence or non-existence of the objects to be cut, the act of cutting, and so forth, as well as the attachment, aversion, and other states directed toward them, are all conceptualizations dependent upon consciousness—and thus are not distinct from consciousness—nothing at all occurs that is contrary to consciousness. With this intention, he says: "By consciousness... (verse 15).
Even when thoroughly investigated, nothing whatsoever is found apart from consciousness, even within this vast interior of the three worlds. (16)
There is no hatred, there is no passion, and for him there is neither mind nor mental modifications;
for the utterly pure Pure Consciousness alone, how could there be any conceptualization? (17)
I am consciousness, all-pervading and omnipresent, consisting of eternal bliss; I transcend the construction of conceptual thought and am devoid of any second part.

With the intention that, when the disagreeable is not established, consciousness remains by its own nature as the essence of bliss—characterized by being eternally perceived as agreeable—the statement "consisting of eternal bliss" is made. || 18 ||
That which is called "consciousness" (cit) is not a name for that which is nameless;
this all-pervading power of consciousness, whose essence is sound, vibrates forth.

He states that even the conceptualization of its own name is merely a transformation (vivarta) of consciousness itself, just like the conceptualization of the names and forms of the world—this is expressed by the words "of consciousness" (citaḥ).

The meaning is that the all-pervading power of consciousness (cicchakti), which is the substratum for the conceptualization of all names and forms, manifests itself as if it were composed of the very sounds of its own name. || 19 ||
