Free from both the seen and the act of seeing, possessing a solitary and stainless form,
eternally risen and devoid of appearance— such am I, the Supreme Lord, the Seer.
And thus, he says—beginning with the word "dṛśya"—that even the answer to the question "Who am I? has been understood by me of my own accord.
Its form is devoid of conceptual construction; it consists of the subtle digit of the beautiful Time; arisen as mere appearance, it is free from eternal manifestation. || 21 ||

In me—who am of such a nature consisting solely of light—how can there exist that which is devoid of the manifestation of one's own eternal self? It is like a digit of the moon reflected in water, at the edge of a lock of hair, or on the tip of a strand; or rather, it is like the moon during the bright fortnight whose beautiful digits have increased, appearing as a partial form created by one's own imagination.
The meaning is that this state of being a limited individual soul which has arisen is merely a reflection, nothing but an illusion, and not real.
I am victorious in my own true nature within this Great Self, whose singular essence is light, which is liberated and devoid of the coloring of objects of thought. 22.

Therefore, by means of my very own nature, ignited by the final state of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-vṛtti*), I conquer—that is, I overcome—that state of being a limited individual soul (*jīvabhāva*). Having conquered the state of being a limited soul, I am the Supreme Lord, my very self; thus he pays homage to Him with the words beginning "cetya" (the object of thought), etc. || 22 ||
Salutations be to You, whose nature is immediate consciousness, who are the very essence of one’s own being,
who are pure awareness, who are free from the objects of thought, and who are joined with appropriate reasoning.

Salutations to You, the Brahman, who are of the nature of the inner self (pratyag-rūpa) for me; You who are endowed with the appropriate reasoning that establishes the non-dual, partless identity between the inner self and the external world; or rather, You who are endowed with the reasoning of reflection and meditative absorption (manana-nididhyāsana), which is capable of bringing about direct realization. || 23 ||

Salutations to you alone, who are the lamp illuminating all things—[the reading is "rūpāya"]—whose nature is consciousness free from the object of thought, and who fills the entire universe in every direction. (24)
I am the Great One, pure existence and consciousness alone, in which all that is perceivable has been completely stilled; I am infinite like space, yet more subtle than the subtlest, pervading all.
These perceptions of the states of pleasure and pain do not reach me; I am that pervasive consciousness, unperceivable by sensation and beyond the reach of thought.
Regarding the present object, consciousness is "unperceivable" (asaṃvedya); regarding past and future objects, it is "incognizable" (acetaya) yet conscious.

In both cases, the qualifiers "unperceivable" and "incognizable" are used for the purpose of excluding the functions of the eyes and other senses, as well as the functions of memory and so forth. || 26 ||
The states of existence and non-existence found in the world are not capable of defining me;
nevertheless, let these worldly states define this very me.
The meaning is that they are unable to delimit—that is, to establish a finite measure—either spatially, temporally, or substantially;

rather, existence and non-existence are, on the contrary, to be delimited by a witness (sākṣin). If one were to say: "We do not call 'delimitation' (pariccheda) the establishment of a finite measure, but rather the ascertainment of reality (tattvāvadhāraṇa)," [the response follows].

Furthermore, since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, which are conducive to that [liberation], truly determine the self as being within the cycle of worldly existence, he says regarding that:
"Now, moreover" (*atha ca*). The word *atha* is used for the purpose of indicating another perspective. || 27 ||
Just as they are intended by me, these are not distinct from me.
If [the reading "in me" is found somewhere], then an object is indeed led by an object that has become its own nature;
such a determination of mine is exactly as intended and agreed upon. For those [objects]...

The meaning is that, by the mere delimitation of my own nature, those things which are not distinct from me remain as nothing but myself; they become none other than I. And in the case of such a delimitation, whether there is the leading away of wealth held in the left hand by the right hand, its taking, or its being given back after turning around, [it is all] non-different from both hands.
He says "If... (verse 28) to show that just as there is no loss of wealth for Devadatta, who is distinct from his body, so too there is no loss whatsoever [for the Self].
Whether something is taken away or given, what loss indeed has occurred to whom?
I am always everything itself, the doer of all, and united with all. (29)

In reality, however, even prior to the awakening to truth, the world is itself [the Self]; thus, with the intention that even before that nothing has arisen or been destroyed, he says: "At all times" (sarvadā). || 29 ||
"I am this very consciousness; nothing at all has been enjoined here. What is the use of conceptualization and doubt? This consciousness is one and alone. (30)
I am alone, the very consciousness of that which has become consciousness; what can be accumulated, increased, or diminished by my own thoughts and doubts? || 30 ||
"I shall first cause agitation; then I shall find peace within my own purifying self"—thinking thus, the highly skilled Bali [proceeded]. (31)
Reflecting, "I am agitated by ignorance and I become tranquil through the awakening to reality," Bali—

awakening the consciousness that is conjoined with the gross and subtle agitations arising from the *oṃkāra* and with the ignorance regarding its seed-syllable (*bīja*)— set aside the three measures (*mātrā*) beginning with the letter *a*, and contemplated the fourth state (*turya*), the meaning of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*).
Experiencing it as his own self, he remained absorbed in that state. || 31 ||

Established in silence while contemplating the meaning of the half-mora of the syllable Oṃ, with all mental constructs completely stilled and the multitude of conceptualizations thoroughly pacified. (32)

Free from doubt, with thoughts entirely cast far away and no longer dwelling on the objects of thought, he is devoid of the meditator, the object of meditation, and the act of meditating; stainless, his latent tendencies are stilled.

"By whom thoughts that do not contemplate the 'it is' (asti) or 'it is not' (nāsti) have been cast far away"—this is an indication of the abandonment of the mere triad [of knower, known, and knowing].
The reason for this is stated: "the meditator," etc. (v. 34).
Bali, having encountered this great calamity, became like a lamp extinguished by the wind;
with his mind stilled, he remained there in that jeweled window for a long time, as if carved in stone. (34)
Like a man carved upon a stone, produced by the strokes of a chisel. || 34 ||
With this [state] in which all seeking had been stilled, which was fully perfected,
and which was free from the condition of the fault of conceptualization,
Bali shone with stainless being.
Like the autumnal sky, clear and free from clouds. || 35 ||

Bali, by means of this very existence— characterized by the attainment of the stainless state of Brahman, which is attained through the pacification of desires, and for that very reason is perfectly complete and entirely free from the afflictions of mentalizing sense objects— shone like the autumnal sky when it has become cloudless.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Resting of Bali," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, spoken by the Divine Messenger (*devadūtokta*). (Mokṣopāya) 27.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Resting of Bali," in the *Upaśamaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, at that time, those Dānavas who were the followers of Baleri there—
They ascended in an instant that lofty crystal palace. || 1 ||
Seeing Bali motionless, the dejected Dānavas called upon Śukra; having explained his condition, Śukra removed their grief here. (1)
His house was a palatial mansion that served as a place of refuge. || 1 ||
The wise ministers were Ḍimbha and others; the feudatories were Kumuda and others; the kings were Surādya and others; and the plunderers of the army were Vṛtta and others. (2)
He indicates the attendants themselves by their names, beginning with "Ḍimbha and the others," and so forth. || 2 ||
Hayagrīva and others were his soldiers; Cakra and others were his kinsmen;
Laḍuka and others were his friends; and Ballūka and others were his favorites. (3)
Kubera, Yama, Śakra, and other gods presented him with offerings;
yakṣas, vidyādharas, and nāgas awaited their turn for service.
And Rambhā, Tilottamā, and other excellent women who held chowries;
likewise the oceans, rivers, mountains, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate directions.
The cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, the presiding deities of those directions, and the people appointed over them. || 5 ||
At that time, many other Siddhas dwelling within the three worlds came to that region of Bali for the purpose of serving him.
The *siddhas* are a particular class of divine beings (*devayoni*).
Respectfully, the rows of crowns bowed down as they beheld Bali, who was established in meditative silence and samādhi, motionless like a figure depicted in a painting.
Those whose rows of crowns bend down as their heads bow; "attentive" means full of respect. || 7 ||
Having seen him, those great asuras, having performed their salutations with all duties fulfilled,
became faltering due to despondency, wonder, joy, and fear.

Those who had performed the necessary salutation reached a state of slowness due to sorrow if they were friends, slowness due to wonder if they were neutral observers, slowness due to bliss if they were knowers of reality,
and slowness due to both if they were those who lived off ignorance. Or rather:

The meaning is that they became slow due to the danger to their lives from the poison; slow with wonder upon seeing the appearance of ease and clarity; slow with bliss upon seeing the signs of joy such as horripilation; and slow with fear because they did not see any means of rescue despite their long failure to rise. || 8 ||
Having deliberated upon what had occurred there, the ministers, the Dānavas,
thought of Bhārgava, their preceptor and the foremost among all who possess knowledge.
Immediately after their thought, the Daityas beheld Bhārgava, who had assumed a radiant form,
appearing like a manifested city of the Gandharvas.
It was fashioned by Bhārgava, who, through the power of yoga, assumed the appearance of one of the Seven Sages and manifested it as if it were actually located within the palace of Bali.
Being honored by the hosts of asuras and seated upon a grand throne,
Bhārgava beheld the lord of the Dānavas absorbed in meditation and observing a vow of silence.
Having rested for a moment as it were, he looked with affection and,
observing Bali, perceived that his wandering through worldly existence had come to an end.
The word "iva" (as if) is intended to indicate that even [the state of] rest is merely imagined. || 12 ||
As if casting the ocean of milk with the radiance bestowed by hundreds of rays from his body, the Guru, smiling, addressed the assembly with these words: || 13 ||
"Scorning" means casting [the dice] or stretching them out; "reviling" means laughing at the assembly and the Daityas residing therein, in order to manifest his own ignorance. || 13 ||
O Daityas, this is truly extraordinary, that by his own discernment alone,
this venerable Bali has attained the state of a perfected being (siddha) and reached the stainless abode.

"O Daityas, this Bali has attained by his own discernment alone this stainless abode, which is Brahman as the substrate of all; such is he, and that state is beyond measure. The meaning is that there is an excellence in his repose in bliss. (14)
O best of Dānavas, let this one remain right here in that very same way;
let him attain stability within his own self and behold the state free from affliction.
Therefore, let this very person, remaining in a state of meditative concentration, attain a long-lasting abiding in his own self, which is unsurpassed bliss. || 15 ||
Exhausted, having attained rest, with the wandering of the mind through existence exhausted, and with the mist of saṃsāra stilled—he is not to be questioned, O Dānavas. (16)
"He is neither to be addressed nor to be spoken to; you must remain silent"—this is the meaning. || 16 ||
In this very crisis of ignorance, he has attained his own light;
now that this agitation has been stilled, it is like the mass of rays from the sun appearing by day. (17)
On this earth, when the confusion of night, darkness, sleep, and the like has been stilled by the day—
the sun’s mass of rays— by this powerful one, once the peril of ignorance has been stilled,
his own light has been attained. || 17 ||
For in due time, it will awaken by itself through its own self-awareness, like a sprout emerging from its seed-capsule after being in a state of sleep. (18)

From the seed-enclosure, that is, from the seed-sheath, by means of self-awareness through the departure from the state of swoon—that is to say, by the awakening of the ego-sense of the sprout. || 18 ||
"O leaders of the Dānavas, all of you perform the tasks of your master;
Bali will emerge from his meditative absorption after a thousand years."
The master's duties consist of the administration of the kingdom. || 19 ||
Having been addressed thus by the Guru, the Daityas there cast off the anxiety born of joy, indignation, and despair, just as trees shed their withered blossoms.

The mention of the *daityas* is also indicative of the gods. Therefore, the enemies abandoned the anxiety born of joy; the foes, that born of indignation; and those who lived off their friends, that born of despondency. (20)
Having assumed the form of Vairocani according to the previously established rule,
all the asuras then remained intent upon their own respective duties.
According to the prior arrangement, by means of the sequence of administrative procedures of the kingdom as previously established. || 21 ||
Men, the earth, the lords of the earth, the netherworld, the planets, the sky, the hosts of gods,
heaven, the quarters, the mountains, the guardians of the directions, and the caves— [in this verse there is a metrical variation].
The forest-dwellers and the sky-goers departed into the air.

Regarding what the visiting humans, *nāgas*, and others did at that time, he says: "The humans... The word "went" (*yayuḥ*) is to be connected with every term. The mountains—the presiding deities of the principal mountain ranges—and the lords of the quarters (*dikpati*), the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*), went to their respective quarters. The forest-dwellers—the leaders of the herds of bears, monkeys, and so forth—went to the caves of Kiṣkindhā and other such places.
The sky-dwellers, such as Garuḍa, Sampāti, Jaṭāyu, and others. || 22 ||

Thus ends the twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Description of Bali’s Meditative Absorption," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Bali’s Attainment of Samādhi," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, after a thousand divine years, that bull among the Asuras—[the reading "sattama" is found in some versions]— [The text continues with the description of his penance.]
The Blessed Lord Bali was awakened by the sounds of celestial drums.
In this [work], the royal glory of one liberated while living, the imprisonment of Bali in Pātāla,
and Rāma’s complete establishment there like Bali are taught.
"By a thousand years": the instrumental case is used here because liberation (apavarga) results from an absolute connection with meditative absorption (samādhi) lasting for a thousand years. || 1 ||
When Bala was awakened, that city then shone like a bed of lotuses when the mass of sunbeams has risen from Brahmā. || 2 ||
This city of Balarīda has become as glorious in its blossoming as a lotus-pond when the mass of the sun’s rays has risen in the sky— the very abode of Brahmā (Viriñci).
In the alternative readings *sargaughe* and *sarvaughe*, the meaning is that it causes the entire collection of created things (*sarva-padārthajātam*) or the creation itself (*sargam*) to flow forth.
By the etymological derivation *samarthayati* ("he empowers"), it is the sun alone that should be understood; the meaning is "when that [sun] has risen.
This is derived from the root *o-ghṛ* in the sense of "capacity" (*sāmarthye*), with the suffix *ṇiC* added and then the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). || 2 ||
Bali was already fully awakened; until the Dānavas arrived, he reflected for a moment in his meditation chamber.
In the abode of samādhi, that is, in the previously mentioned place for practicing samādhi. || 3 ||
Oh, how delightful is this ultimate path, so cool!
Having stayed upon it for but a moment, I have attained supreme rest. (4)
For one immersed in the bliss of samādhi, even a thousand divine years pass like a single moment; thus there is the expression "having remained for a moment. || 4 ||
Therefore, following this very path, I shall act;
what need have I for external splendors enjoyed here by you? (5)
The ellipsis "I attain rest" is to be supplied. What does it matter to me that external riches have been enjoyed? The meaning is: nothing compares to such happiness of rest. || 5 ||
Even from the lunar orbs, the waves of bliss do not gladden the inner self as much as the prosperity arising from the attainment of perfection.
He says that very thing: "In the lunar [worlds]," etc. *Saṃsiddhi* is the ripening of *samādhi*;

the *bhūtis* (prosperities) arising from that are the *ānandas* (blisses). Because they are not delimited by any measure (*iyattā*) even within a single [state], the plural number is used through the conceptualization of multiplicity.
Thus, as his mind again became slackened in its effort to find rest,
the Daityas obstructed Bali, just as clouds shroud the moon.
Having arrived, they warded him off and surrounded him.
Beholding them, his eyes agitated by the desire to bow before them, he meditated once more;
his body was thus surrounded by those who resembled the great boundary mountains.
The word "again" (punaḥ) is intended to indicate a turning away from the previous resolve regarding meditative absorption (samādhi). || 8 ||
For me, whose mind is gathered and whose conceptual constructions are exhausted, what is there to be accepted?
Since the mind falls toward that [reality], it becomes purely of the nature of its essence.

The meaning is that when one perceives external objects with the thought of them being desirable, the mind—because it falls upon them—incurs the impurity characterized by attachment to them, and not merely by the act of perception itself. || 9 ||
"I desire liberation; why am I bound? By whom was I bound in the past?
Being unbound, I desire liberation—what kind of childish mockery is this? (10)
[Objection: "Surely, let there be a rule for relying on meditative absorption (samādhi) out of a desire for liberation. To this he replies with the verse beginning "mokṣam" [v. 10].

The sense is that when ignorance and its effects are sublated by knowledge throughout the three periods of time, bondage itself is no longer perceived. The term *viḍambanā* refers to the imitation of the actions of fools—that is, of the ignorant. || 10 ||
There is no bondage, there is no liberation; my ignorance has come to an end.
What use have I for the play of meditation, or what could I gain from meditation? (11)
Having abandoned the delusions of meditation and non-meditation, look at your own true manhood;
let that which comes come, for there is neither increase nor decrease for me.

One's own fresh form—masculinity and the reality of the Self—perceives even external objects with equanimity by its very nature as pure consciousness; let whatever object comes toward it come, and let it manifest.
Nevertheless, unlike those who are ignorant, I am not subject to the increase or decrease [of merit or demerit] resulting from the superimposition of identity with the body and so forth.
The meaning is that there would be disadvantage because of increase and decrease. This verse exists only in some [versions] and not everywhere. 12.

I desire neither meditation nor non-meditation, neither enjoyment nor the state of non-enjoyment [the reading "bhogitā" is found for "abhogitām"]. Free from all feverish distress, I remain in a state of perfect equanimity.

I have no desire for the supreme reality, nor do I have any desire for the maintenance of the world; I have no task to be accomplished through the state of meditation— [here "dhyānadṛśā" is preferable to "dhyānadaśā"]— nor do I have any task to be accomplished through worldly power.
I am neither dead nor do I live; I am neither existent nor non-existent, nor am I composed of existence.
This is not mine, nor is anything else mine; salutations to me, for I am the Great One.

Because of the absence of connection with a body, I am not dead; because of the absence of connection with vital breaths, I do not live. I am of the nature of Being (*sat*). That which is composed of Being is its modification—namely, this body, world, and so forth.
Other than that are other bodies, other worlds, and so on. 15.
"Let this kingdom of the world be mine; I shall remain established here.
Or rather, let there be no kingdom of the world here; I shall remain cool within the Self. (16)
What use have I for the vision of meditative absorption, or what use for the glory of royal power?
Let whatever comes come; I am nothing, and nothing belongs to me anywhere.
Even if there is indeed nothing at all that must be done by me now, why then do I not perform this particular action that is currently at hand? (18)

That which is to be done must be accomplished through the conviction of being the agent. Therefore, why do I not perform that specific duty at hand—the protection of the kingdom—which is something that can be achieved even by one whose efforts are devoid of such conviction? (18)
Having thus resolved, Bali, the perfect soul and best among the wise, looked upon the Daityas as the sun looks upon lotuses. (19)
Through the distinction of his penetrating gaze, he received the prostrations of all the Danavas as the wind gathers the fragrance of flowers from their heads.
Through the classification of the various ways of looking, according to the diversity appropriate to each. || 20 ||
Then Vairocani,
through his mind which consisted of the abandonment of meditation, carried out all the affairs of state.

The object of meditation is the relinquishment of latent impressions (vāsanā), as previously described; [this is to be done] by one whose self is absorbed in that [relinquishment] and who abounds in its manifestation. || 21 ||
He honored the twice-born, the gods, and his teachers with worship;
he paid due respect to friends, kinsmen, vassals, and virtuous men.

There is a distinction between *pūjā* (worship), which consists of offerings such as water for the feet (*pādya*) and respectful water (*arghya*), and *satkāra* (hospitality), which consists of honoring through the giving of appropriate gifts and marks of respect; this is *saṃmānana* (reverence).
In that manner, he satisfied the hosts of supplicants with wealth and prosperity, and he doted upon the women by bestowing upon them various riches.
Thus he grew up in that kingdom under complete governance;
then, at one time, his mind became inclined toward sacrifice.
This Bali grew in sovereignty—that is, in the domain of command and authority over all the gods, asuras, and others;
the meaning is that he attained the full prosperity of the constituent elements of kingship. Then, at one time, his mind and desire were directed toward performing a sacrifice. (24)
Having gratified the entire world and being honored by the hosts of gods and sages,
he performed a great sacrifice together with Śukra and other eminent figures.
The great sacrifice, the horse-sacrifice. || 25 ||
Having determined that Bali was not seeking the burden of enjoyments, Mādhava,
the bestower of success, went to Bali’s sacrifice for the sake of accomplishing Bali’s desired goal.
Knowing what must be done, he gave this forest tract of the world to Śakra, who was the eldest by age but pitiable and solely miserly for worldly enjoyments.
To the miserly one—so called because of his attachment to wealth alone—and therefore to the pitiable one;
to the "knower of what must be done" (*kāryavit*), that is, one who knows how to bestow the fruits of Indra’s good deeds, being learned in the art of begging. || 27 ||
Moving here by his power and having deceived Bali, Hari bound the monkey within this subterranean dwelling at the bottom of Pātāla.
"Traversing the three worlds by means of his power and the power of illusion"—this is the ellipsis. || 28 ||
Today, O Rāma, he has established himself once more for the sake of attaining the status of Indra;
with his body liberated while living, he remains self-abiding, his mind perpetually absorbed in meditation.

Even today, that Bali remains in Pātāla, characterized by the prārabdha karma [intended] for the sake of regaining the status of Indra; his intellect has become dejected—that is, dissolved—in meditation, which is the state of non-conceptual absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi). || 29 ||
Dwelling in the cavern of the netherworld, Bali, having attained the state of one liberated while living,
views both adversity and prosperity with an equal eye.
That wisdom neither sets nor rises in the face of pleasure and pain;
it is even, steady-making, and variegated like a row of suns in a painting.

"Even" means devoid of rising and setting. "Steady rays" refers to those whose beams are constant. "Citralekhyā" means the act of painting a picture; the meaning is that it is like the solar disc (sūryamaṇḍala) belonging to such a [painting]. || 31 ||
Having long observed thousands of appearances and disappearances of living beings here, his mind has turned away from these terrifying things.

Having long observed the thousands of appearances and disappearances of living beings— who possess the hope for life, are greedy for enjoyments, and are full of worldly power— as well as the births and other transitions of existences, the mind of that Bali attained detachment and dispassion.
Having ruled over the three worlds for ten billion years,
at the end, Bala’s mind attained detachment and became completely pacified.
Thousands of conjectures and refutations, and hundreds of affirmations and negations have been scrutinized by the Mighty One; where, then, can he find consolation? (34)

There are thousands of instances of pleasure and pain, of acquisition and rejection, of arrival and departure; hundreds of instances of existence and non-existence, of prosperity and adversity. The words "thousands" and "hundreds" here refer to an incalculable number.
Having completely renounced his desire for enjoyments, Bali, with a fulfilled mind,
remained eternally established in self-delight within the depths of the subterranean realm.
He remained within the cavity of Pātāla known as Rasātala, situated in the midst of the seven netherworlds, until the destruction of his calamity. || 35 ||
Furthermore, O Rāma, this powerful one shall rule over this entire world as its sovereign for many groups of years.
The meaning is that he will be one who is to be instructed as a master and one who is to be commanded. || 36 ||
No satisfaction arises in him from attaining the station of Indra, nor does any agitation arise in him from falling from his own station. (37)
Equanimous toward all states of being, with his disposition ever-arisen [in its natural state], taking what comes to him, he remains established in himself like space. (38)
With his aspirations fulfilled and his mind contented, he partakes of and enjoys whatever has come to him, brought forth by the force of past actions (prārabdha). || 38 ||
This attainment of consciousness by Bali has been described to you by me;
having firmly grasped this view, may you also rise up. (39)

Having concluded the account of Bali’s life, he instructs Rāma with the words beginning "of Bali" and so forth: [Bali] was "prosperous," meaning endowed with the excellence of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 39 ||
O Rāghava, by means of solitude like that of a bull and through the certainty that "I am eternal," one should attain the state of non-duality solely through human effort.
Through seclusion and through one's own reflection. || 40 ||
Having enjoyed the three worlds for ten million years— specifically eighteen crores—
at the end, even Bali, the best among the Asuras, fell into a state of weariness.
Two and eight; that is to say, ten koṭīs. || 41 ||
Therefore, O subduer of enemies, having utterly renounced the burden of enjoyments which inevitably leads to bitterness,
proceed toward that state of true bliss which is free from all bitterness.
That which necessarily results in enmity culminates in suffering; that which is free from enmity is free from suffering. 42.
O Rāma, these perceptions of the visible world, which produce various forms and transformations, should not be regarded as beautiful here, for they are like mountain rocks seen from afar. (43)
By way of its loveliness and beauty; in this regard, he provides the well-known illustration that "mountains are beautiful when situated at a distance," stating: "from afar... (43).
Bind this mind, which runs hither and thither and wallows amidst worldly activities, and establish it within the hollow of the heart. 44.
Here, it runs after worldly enjoyments; there, after enjoyments of the next world; it wallows and is engaged in the ways of the world, in the conduct of the vulgar. (44)
You alone are the sun of consciousness, present everywhere in the world;
who is another and who is one's own? Why do you stumble in vain? (45)
Now, one might ask: how can there be an equal vision toward both enemy and friend? To this he says: "The sun of consciousness" (cidāditya).

Just as the sun illuminates everything, so too consciousness—which illuminates all—is the "sun of consciousness. Thus, the meaning is that you alone are the Self, the illuminator, even within the bodies of enemies; therefore, there is no ground for partiality. || 45 ||
O mighty-armed one, you are infinite; you are the primordial Puruṣottama.
You, whose body is consciousness, manifest yourself in the forms of hundreds of objects.
Now, one might ask: "How can there be for me, a living soul (jīva), the vision of the equality of the self with the Lord? To this he replies: "Thou" (tvam).

With the intention that even the disparity caused by insentience (jaḍa) is not to be suspected because of [the Lord's] very infinity, he says: "In the forms of hundreds of objects denoted by the word 'thou'. (46)
All this world, both stationary and moving, is strung upon you, who are eternally awakened and pure, just as clusters of gems are threaded on a string. (47)
To express the possibility of that, he says: "In you... (verse 47).
You are not born, nor do you die; you are the unborn, universal Person (Puruṣa).
O Pure Consciousness, let the delusions of birth and death not be yours. 48.
He says "na jāyase" (you are not born) in order to avoid even those inequalities caused by time. || 48 ||
Having deliberated upon the relative strength and weakness of all the diseases of birth, abandon craving for enjoyments and become merely an enjoyer. 49.

The meaning is that one should investigate through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that when craving increases, the diseases of birth and so forth become powerful, and when craving diminishes, they become weak.
Abandoning craving for enjoyments, remain as the enjoyer who is pure consciousness alone, the witness of enjoyment. (49)
While you, the Lord of the World, the sun of consciousness ever-risen, abide, all this— the ornamentation of the dream of saṃsāra— shines forth.
He states that the world is established solely through the power of your consciousness: "In you... (verse 50).
Do not indulge in futile despair; this longing for pleasure and pain does not belong to you.
You are pure in mind, the self of all, and the illuminator of all things.
One whose mind is pure, one whose mind is awakened. || 51 ||
Having first conceptualized what was desired as undesired and what was undesired as desired, abandon even that through the practice of such [equanimity]. 52.

He says, "First," meaning: even if you are of impure mind, listen to the means for its purification in due order. Whatever is desired—that which is pleasing to the mind—and whatever is undesired—that which accomplishes misfortune and is displeasing to the mind, such as austerity, hardship, restraint of the senses, breath control (prāṇāyāma), and so forth.

Having first conceived the thought, "All this is desirable and necessary for me," when mastery over that [thought] is achieved through its repeated practice up to the full maturation of the seventh stage, one should then abandon even that conception; such is the meaning. || 52 ||
When the perception of the desirable and the undesirable is abandoned, eternal equanimity arises;
by means of that which dwells within the heart, a living being is not born again.

He states the fruit of that abandonment in the verse beginning with "iṣṭa": "by means of that which resides in the heart," meaning by that which has been made stable in the heart through practice. || 53 ||
From whichever objects the mind sinks like a child, withdrawing it from each and every one of those, one should indeed apply it to reality.

In reality, [it is] that very consciousness which is the substratum of each respective object. And so it has been said by the Blessed One: "From whatever cause the mind wanders, restless and unsteady, from that very cause one should restrain it and bring it under control within the Self alone. (54)
Having thus bound with one's entire being the intoxicated elephant of the mind through the practice of constant application, the supreme good is attained. (55)
With all one's being, with every effort, and with one's entire self—having bound and restrained [the mind]. || 55 ||

Do not attain equality with those fools who know only the physical body as the reality, whose intentions are destroyed by false views, who are rogues sold by their own desires, and who are utterly deluded. (56)
By those who perceive the body itself as the true reality and the ultimate goal, they have become subject to it, as if sold into servitude by their own desires for enjoyment. (56)
In this world, there is nothing more painful than the state of being destitute when one’s own judgment falters and one must rely on the words of others due to ignorance. (57)

He states that for those whose wisdom is dependent on others and who are incapable of independent inquiry, ignorance itself is a great calamity—beginning with the words "akiṃcanāt. Regarding the determination of one's own true nature (*ātmatattva*), [the ignorant] are destitute of the means such as discrimination and dispassion; thus, they rely upon the words of others—both deceivers and fools.
Because it is being supported by the maxim of the blind man and the baboon. || 57 ||
O high-minded one, quickly drive far away from the sky of your heart this cloud of non-discrimination that has arisen by means of the wind of discrimination. 58.
This is the characteristic of folly: the delusion of non-discrimination arising from the burden of non-discrimination. 58.
As long as one does not bestow grace upon oneself through one's own effort for the sake of self-realization, so long will there be no arising of discernment.

He states that inquiry is the cause for the removal of ignorance, and that it arises only from the grace of the Self, which results from the ripening of merit accumulated over many lifetimes—expressed by the words "by the Self alone.
[This occurs] through effort, meaning through human exertion such as hearing [the scriptures] and cultivating detachment. || 59 ||
Even through the insights of logic regarding the meaning of the Vedas, Vedānta, and the scriptures,
this Self does not become manifest until it is perceived by oneself.

Even when there is detachment, reflection, and hearing [the scriptures], knowledge does not arise for one whose vision is directed outward; therefore, with the intention that inward vision is also necessary, he says:
"For the liberation of those with inward vision, and for the obstruction of those with outward vision. (60)
O Rāma, you have established yourself in tranquility within the self by means of the self;
you have attained expansive awakening and perceive it through my words alone.
If it is then asked, "In that case, let the inward vision alone suffice for knowledge; what is the use of the teacher's instruction?

he says: "Only upon my word. This means: only when my instruction is present. For, according to the maxim, "Even for those who are highly trained, the mind lacks conviction regarding the Self," conviction in one's own realization occurs only when there is corroboration by the words of the teacher and the scriptures.
The particle "eva" is used precisely to indicate that the attainment of non-doubting realization results from faith alone. || 61 ||
By my word, you have grasped this expansive pervasiveness of the Supreme Self, the Sun of Consciousness, which is devoid of any portion of conceptual construction.
He states this very point clearly with the words "vikalpa" (conceptual construction) and so forth.
The meaning is: of that which has not been made an object by mental conceptual constructions such as doubt and the like. "Vitatā" means pervasion; it is a threefold state of being unlimited. || 62 ||
With all mental constructs dissolved, with the delusions of doubt stilled,
and with the mist of curiosity exhausted, you have become free from the fever of worldly affliction.
Curiosity consists of the eagerness for the wonder of external objects and the eagerness for the desire to know the reality of the Self; that very thing is the mist or frost. || 63 ||
O Sage, whatever you approach, protect, destroy, drink, marvel at, or cause to increase— let that [be determined] by that [very thing] at that time.
Free from the suspicion of any stain upon his awakening. || 64 ||

O sage Rāma, you who are by nature contemplative, when you become one whose stains— the veils of ignorance— and whose doubts and distractions have vanished due to the state of oneness with pure consciousness and the reality of the Self,
then you will attain that knowledge which was previously unattained, as well as its means, such as inquiry, the guru, and the instructions of the scriptures.
That which you accept for the sake of liberation—discrimination, dispassion, and so forth; that which you protect with effort;
that which you destroy with effort—the host of defects such as laziness and negligence; that which you conquer;
that which you drink—the nectar of the bliss of *samādhi*; and that by which you marvel through ascending to ever-higher stages.

Through resting on the seventh stage, you increase because of the progressive excellence of bliss over each preceding state; however, even that should not be so at that time, but rather remain as Brahman itself, exactly as it is—this is the meaning. || 64 ||

Thus ends the twenty-ninth sarga, titled "Bali’s Attainment of Knowledge," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Seers (*ārṣa*).
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Bali’s Attainment of Gnosis," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirtieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, O Rāma, listen to this supreme method for attaining true knowledge.
Listen, O Lord of Daityas, to how Prahlāda attained perfection through his own self.
The prowess of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the birth of his sons beginning with Prahlāda, his slaughter by Nṛsiṃha, and the post-mortem state resulting from grief are here described. (1)

Thus, the sequence of the arising of knowledge has been described as occurring solely through one's own inquiry— which proceeds by way of the "crow-and-palm-fruit" maxim— and as being assisted by the instructions of the scriptures and the teacher.

Now, wishing to narrate the story of Prahlāda in order to describe the manner in which knowledge arises from inquiry born of the grace of the worshipped Lord, Vasiṣṭha directs Rāma’s attention toward hearing it with the word "atha" (now).
"In the attainment of higher knowledge" (*vijñānasyābhigame*) means in its direct acquisition; that is to say, in its attainment free from obstacles.
And so it has been said by the Blessed One himself: "Those who strive, taking refuge in Me for liberation from old age and death, they know that Brahman in its entirety. (1)
In the cavernous depths of the netherworld (pātāla) there was one named Hiraṇyakaśipu, whose prowess equaled that of Nārāyaṇa, who had put to flight both gods and demons.

In the sense of "like the prowess of Nārāyaṇa," the first member of the compound functions through metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā). It should be understood that in expressions such as *uṣṭramukhaḥ* ("camel-faced") or *kharamukhaḥ* ("donkey-faced"), the word *uṣṭra* signifies something similar to its face.
Alternatively, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopa*), functioning in the sense of "like" (*iva*).
Having pervaded the entire expanse of the world, he seized the universe from Hari,
just as a royal swan plucks a lotus with its broad petals from a bee.
The qualifying phrase "having pervaded the expanse of the worlds" serves to establish his prowess equal to that of Nārāyaṇa. By the word *bhuvana*, all three worlds are intended.
That Hiraṇyakaśipu, having seized it from Hari, Indra, and others, took away the sovereignty over the three worlds of the universe. [End of] the verse on the six-footed bee.

At night it is like a house-dwelling being, but in the morning, with its blossoming, it is a lotus of broad petals; the term "royal swan" (rājahaṃsa), like the terms for gods and demons (surāsura), refers to various sovereigns. || 3 ||
Having overwhelmed the hosts of gods, he ruled over the worlds,
just as a rutting elephant, having driven away the multitude of swans, rules over a lotus pond devoid of its beauty.
In the lotus pond, the kingdom of the bees (alinām) is such that the swarms of swans have been driven away;
by following this comparison with "like an elephant" (dantīva), his quality of causing terror to the world is understood. || 4 ||
Then that lord of the Asuras, exercising sovereignty over the three worlds,
in the course of time begot sons just as Mādhava produces sprouts.
Mādhava is the spring season.
Those boys of powerful splendor grew up in no time at all,
like a thousand rays of ten suns sporting as they pervade the sky.
In their splendor and vigor, they were like ten times ten hundred rays of the sun;
they were playful in their traversing of the sky, that is, in their pervasion of space and their ascent to the realm of the gods.
Among those most worthy ones, there was indeed one named Prahrāda, powerful and the foremost of them, like the Kaustubha gem among precious jewels.
Among them, the eldest, named Prahrāda, became the crown prince; this is according to the *Haitihya*. (7)
With that son, who was endowed with every beauty, Hiraṇyakaśipu shone intensely, like the year with the spring season.
Then that Daitya Mada, accompanied by his sons and endowed with an army and a treasury, arrived like an elephant from which ichor was trickling from three temples.

Like an elephant whose three temporal streams have flowed down from its face marked by three temples; although seven locations for rut are well known, nevertheless, only three are mentioned here due to their predominance. It is said that the elephant which has three streams flowing from its temples is sixty years of age.
Or rather, according to the statement of the learned, it occurs at sixty years of age. || 9 ||
With the splendor of his rays, which were ever-new and blossoming across the three worlds, he scorched them with the heat of his majesty, like a multitude of suns at the end of an aeon.
By means of its blossoming, that is, its unfolding; by the heat—that is, the affliction—induced by its onset or assault;

and by the splendor of its rays—that is, the beauty of its beams—which is both fresh, being young, and eternally new, as well as by the excellence resulting from the act of grasping with the hand. || 10 ||
Then the gods, headed by Sūrya and Indu, were not distressed by him,
just as kinsmen are not troubled by a child who is restless with wicked playfulness.
By that heat of being overwhelmed. || 11 ||
Then they prayed to the Unborn One for the slaying of the lord of the Daityas, who was like a rutting elephant;
for even great beings do not tolerate repeated wrongdoing.
A misdeed or offense committed repeatedly, through repeated occurrence. || 12 ||
Then there arose a deep, gurgling roar like that of the world at the time of dissolution,
produced by the thundering of vajra-claws resembling the tusks of the elephants of the quarters.

Then, immediately after that, Mādhava assumed a Nārasiṃha (Man-lion) body characterized by such attributes as "tossing the universe at the time of dissolution" and so forth, and slew the great Asura Hiraṇyakaśipu; this is the connection with the seventh [verse].
That [body] was one in which there was a yawning—a bending of the limbs—accompanied by a gurgling roar, like the world tossed about at the time of dissolution.
Wherein [the lion] has expanded with claws resembling the tusks of a celestial elephant, as if they were made of diamond and other precious gems.
The circle of his teeth shone like a dense network of steady lightning flashes,
while his earrings were like blazing fires flickering within the hollows of the ten directions.

He whose circles of teeth are firm, unshakable, and radiant like clusters of lightning; and whose [earrings] are like blazing fires wandering within the hollows of the ten directions, for he has made the quarters of space his ears. 14.
Its vast belly was formidable, containing the entire mass of the great mountain ranges as its seat;
with the hollow shell of the universe quivering, it was shaken and tossed by the trees of his arms.
His belly was formidable and terrifying, appearing like a single mass-pedestal formed by all the lords of the great mountain ranges; and by the shaking movements of his tree-like arms,
the shell of the cosmic egg was shaken, and thus it trembled, quivered, and split asunder.
Of whomsoever || 15 ||
He drove away the mountains with the wind issuing from his mouth and belly;
he was proud of the fire of the cosmic dissolution, which arose from his wrath as it prepared to consume the three worlds.
He by whom the mountains were driven away by the winds of his breath issuing from his mouth and belly. || 16 ||
The sun was driven away by the movement of his thick, formidable,
and hairy shoulders, while the mountains were turned tawny by the masses of fire flashing from the pores of his skin.
The edges of the quarters were made formidable by the construction of great walls of mountain ranges, while pattishas,
prāsas, and tomaras protruded from every part of its body.

In which [battle] the horizons were prepared as if for the construction of great walls by means of uprooted mountain ranges; and from whose every limb there issued forth *paṭṭiśas*, *prāsas*, and *tomaras*—specific types of weapons. 18.
Assuming the form of a man-lion, Mādhava seized the great asura, who was uttering a terrifying *kaṭakaṭa* sound, just as an elephant seizes a horse. || 19 ||

The meaning is: "having assumed such a body in the form of Narasiṃha. He "slew" (ahan), having killed; this is from the root *han* in the *laṅ* tense, with the elision of *tip* according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* [Pāṇini 6.1.68]. "With a resounding *kaṭakaṭā* sound" is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). By this, it is understood that he slew [the demon] after tearing him apart.
It is well known in battles that even a horse is torn apart by an elephant. || 19 ||
He consumed the hosts of Pauras and Āsuras with the flames vomited from his eyes,
just as fire at the end of an aeon consumes the web of the universe and all its beings.
The demonic city, all the beings dwelling within that city, and the city's equipment,
he consumed with the fires of his gaze— the flames from his eyes.
When that Nṛsiṃha-māruti had become intensely agitated,
he was like the single ocean in turmoil with the crashing of thundering clouds.

With the slapping sounds of his arms, which were like the crashing of thunderclouds—resembling the roars of the *saṃvarta* clouds at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*), during the single ocean of the watery deluge. || 21 ||
Those hosts of Dānavas fled like gnats before a blazing fire;
they vanished from sight like lamps whose light has faded.
Blazing in all directions like gnats. || 22 ||
Then, with the lords of the Daityas having fled and the circles of the inner apartments burnt,
the surface of Pātāla became like the world crushed at the end of a kalpa.
It is equal to that world which has been crushed and pulverized by the time of universal dissolution at the end of a kalpa.
When the Lord, having slain the Daitya in the manner of an untimely dissolution of the world, had slowly departed elsewhere,
he was worshipped by the gods who were recovering from their agitation.

When the Lord Nṛsiṃha— who is beyond the reach of words— had gone to his own abode after slaying the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu in a battle resembling the dissolution of the eon at an untimely hour, and had been worshipped with intense fervor and profound respect by the gods who were now comforted; || 24 ||
The surviving sons of Danu, protected by Prahlāda,
came to that burnt region like birds to a dried-up lake.
Birds are egg-born. || 25 ||
There, having performed their lamentation for their own loss as was appropriate for the occasion,
they offered the funeral honors to their deceased kinsmen among the spirits.
Lamentation and wailing caused by the destruction of one's own kinsmen and relatives. || 26 ||
They gradually consoled their own surviving people, whose kinsmen had been slain and whose circle of relatives and friends had been consumed by fire.
The circle—that is, the assembly—of kinsmen and their relatives was scorched, burnt, along with their very lives. || 27 ||
With forms as wretched as figures depicted in a painting, devoid of effort and dejected in spirit,
those leaders of the asuras resembled great lotuses scorched by grief.
They remained without any change of expression, like trees consumed by fire.

Devoid of effort and rendered motionless by anxiety, they were like figures depicted in a painting; those leaders of the asuras, such as Prahlāda and others, whose forms were distressed, remained motionless and free from all agitation like trees with scorched leaves and branches. It is well known that there is an absence of movement in tree trunks when struck by the wind. || 28 ||

Thus ends the thirtieth sarga, titled "The Slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu," within the section on Tranquility (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Mokṣopāya* in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki. 30.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu," in the Upaśama-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, his soul overwhelmed with grief because the Dānava had been slain by Hari, [the sage spoke].
The silent Prahlāda reflected thus within the cavern of Pātāla.
In this [chapter], the anxiety regarding Hari’s strides and the concern for the welfare of his own kin are described;
furthermore, the state of mind of Prahlāda arising from his devotion to Hari is depicted. || 1 ||
In such a cavernous hollow of the netherworld (pātāla), where the Dānavas had been slain.
"What indeed might be our remedy, for this sprout of the asuras that grows here with its sharp tip is devoured by every monkey, Hari? (2)

*Upāya* (means) is that which approaches; it is an ally. That radiant one who is born—sharp-tipped, capable of producing the sprouting of the foliage of prosperity, and resembling the shoots of these asura-trees—devours each and every one of them. This is indicated by the term *śākhāmṛga* (monkey) applied to the foot of Hari.
And [this] commentary is for the purpose of establishing that [the opponent's position] causes the destruction of the sprout, and because [the opponent] is distressed by the censure.
Never again did the Daityas, though possessed of mighty arms, remain firm in Pātāla;
they were shattered like lotuses upon the Himalayas.
They have sprouted, germinated, or blossomed through vigor. || 3 ||
Arising again and again, they perish— brilliant in form yet gurgling—
like the waves of the ocean whose surging movements have subsided.
"The Asuras perish"—this [phrase] is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. || 4 ||
These enemies, who rob the entire world of light, have reached full maturity; they cause suffering both externally and internally, appearing as an unprecedented delusion of darkness.

"Kaṣṭam" expresses distress. "Ālokāḥ" refers to those things which are looked upon—namely, external riches such as kingdoms and the like, as well as internal riches such as enthusiasm, joy, clarity, happiness, and repose; these very things are "ālokas" in the sense of illuminations.

Those who have the nature of seizing (*hāriṇaḥ*) or stealing away these illuminations are, for that very reason, enemies (*ripavaḥ*) characterized by an unprecedented delusion of darkness (*timira-bhrama*); such are the gods.
Maturity means excellence. || 5 ||
With hearts filled with darkness and their wealth of petals closing,
the lotus-pools— their friends— fall into sorrow at midnight.

With hearts filled with the darkness of dejection by *tamas*, those who possess prosperity like leaves that shrivel— such friends, resembling night-lotus ponds, surely come to grief because of my father’s dark feet, which act as the trampling stones upon their lotus-thrones.
The realm was overrun by the gods, as a great forest is overrun by wild beasts.

In the conjecture that "surely the region of the gods has been invaded by those who, though once pure, have now become defiled by hatred and are trampling upon their father’s footstool at the time of his prostrations," [he entered] the great forest, the forest of lions. || 7 ||
Devoid of effort, their fortune departed, wretched and with their inner intentions laid bare,
kinsmen do not shine, like lotuses whose petals have been scorched.
With their inner intentions revealed and the sorrow of their hearts made known, they were like trees with scorched leaves, their foliage burnt by the summer heat.
In the houses of the heroic Asuras,
the ashen mists stirred by incessant winds flickered like dense clouds of incense smoke.
Scattered by incessant winds with destructive blasts, the mists, appearing like ashes, shimmer as if they were the remnants of the masses of incense smoke from former times. || 9 ||
In the walls of the inner apartments of the Daityas, where the door-panels had been torn away,
new sprouts of barley appeared like the luster of emerald.
Just like the luster of an emerald from the east, new sprouts of barley have now appeared. || 10 ||
Even the Dānavas, who were like intoxicated elephants in the lotus-pond of the three worlds, fell into such wretchedness as the gods; oh, what indeed is impossible for Fate?
The lotus-navel of the three worlds [is situated] on Meru; even the Dānavas, who were like intoxicated elephants in crushing it, have fallen into a state of wretchedness, just like the gods of old.
"Why? is used here as an interrogative particle (ākṣepa), meaning that there is nothing impossible. || 11 ||
Even at the slightest movement of a leaf, they tremble with the fear of seeing an enemy;
utterly shattered, these young women flee like does that have strayed into a village.
The wives of the Daityas tremble and are agitated.
The jewel-clusters, once in full bloom for the purpose of adorning the ears of the Asura women, have become like withered stumps, their trees severed by the hand of Narasiṃha. (13)
Divine trees are those whose clusters and bunches consist of jewels. || 13 ||
There, the celestial wish-fulfilling trees were replanted in the Nandana grove, possessing leaves that were like divine garments and bristling with clusters of jewel-blossoms.
Those [trees] which possessed divine garments, as well as creepers, branches, and leaves of that same nature;
they were jagged with clusters of jewels. The word *danta* means "prominent" (*unnata*). By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), it is understood that they had previously been brought from there. 14.
Formerly, the faces of the captive goddesses were praised by the asuras;
today, the faces of the captive asuras are gazed upon by the gods.
"Of the female captives" refers to the women taken as prisoners; "seen with praise" means beheld with commendation. || 15 ||
I think that the great rivers of charity, having flowed over the flanks of the celestial elephants' temples, will become like mountain streams upon the ridges of the peaks.
The great rivers have the streams of my gifts as their characteristic; I think thus, "iti" being used in the sense of deliberation. 16.
Upon the temples of our elephants, the splendors of the flow of ichor shine like dust upon parched desert tracts. (17)
The burning away of pride through giving—that is, the splendors resulting from such practice—are but ashes.
Those Daityas, who were like the peaks of Mount Meru and who possessed winds reddened by the nectar of the blooming white Mandāra flowers, have now become difficult to find.
Their breezes, touching the body, were reddened by the pollen-laden nectar of blooming white mandāra flowers; for this very reason, they were equal to the peaks of Mount Meru. || 18 ||
The beauties of the gods and gandharvas, who were accustomed to the inner apartments of the dānavas,
have today taken up residence on Mount Meru like blossoms upon a tree.
Alas, father! The graceful charms of housewives, now as withered as dried lotuses and devoid of essence, are mocked by the celestial nymphs with their playful dances.
With the playful grace of dance, and with the playful mimicry in his movements. || 20 ||
Alas, by those very same chowries with which my father was formerly fanned in heaven, the thousand-eyed Indra is now being fanned! (21)
This calamity, which brings us wretchedness, has come upon us as well,
solely through the favor of that one Hari, whose course of manly prowess is difficult to fathom.
Even for us of great power, the course of human destiny is painful, such that even the memory of our own valor [is lost]. (22)
Having found rest in the dense shade of the forest of his arms,
the gods are never tormented, just like the peaks of the Himalayas.
They suffer; they are tormented just as we are. || 23 ||
Taking refuge on the summit of the pinnacle of Śauri’s valor, they have attained prosperity;
yet they now obstruct us like dogs blocking monkeys from a branch. 24.

Just as gods who have taken refuge on the peaks of mountains or the tops of trees— having attained prosperity by resorting to those summits— restrain even powerful men, so too do monkeys and dogs restrain us, despite our strength, by taking shelter upon the mountain-like Śauri Hari’s very peak of valor and prowess.
They cast them down into the netherworld. || 24 ||
Therefore, it was a constant ornament for the adornment of the wives of the asuras,
like frost upon the lotus-faces of the water-lilies.

In the lotus-face, which is itself the ornament of ornaments, tears remained constantly due to that prowess of Śauri; it was like a drop of frost upon a lotus, which is the very face of the night-lilies. || 25 ||
This world, like a dilapidated pavilion with crumbling, broken, and collapsing walls, is supported solely by the pillars of sapphire that are his arms. (26)

By implication, this ancient hall— the world itself— which has been shattered and split asunder by the prowess of the Asuras, and whose walls are now crumbling, is supported and held up solely by the arms of Śauri, which are like pillars made of sapphire. || 26 ||
He is the upholder of the celestial army as it sinks in the ocean of calamity,
like the tortoise supporting Mount Mandara when it was submerged in the belly of the Ocean of Milk.
Like the tortoise in the Kacchapa incarnation, that Śauri is the supporter, the one who upholds. || 27 ||
All these, beginning with his father, those best of Asuras, were struck down by him alone,
like the principal mountain ranges by the turbulent wind at the end of a kalpa.
He alone is the glorious Madhusūdana, whose arm-fire is capable of the act of universal destruction; he is the incomparable teacher of the assembly of gods. || 29 ||
That is to say, it is "uneven" in the sense that it is impossible to step upon. || 29 ||
By the prowess of that one who is an axe to the staff-like arms of the Daityas,
the heroic Śakra oppresses the Dānavas as a monkey torments young children.
He was like an axe for the shattering of the staff-like arms of the Daityas; just as a powerful monkey, possessing the prowess of a great ape, torments children, so did he [torment them]. || 30 ||
The lotus-eyed one is difficult to conquer; even when his weapons have been cast aside, he—whose essence is as hard as a diamond—is not shattered by the severing of missiles and arms.
Though subjected to severing and fragmentation by means of weapons and missiles, it is firmer and more solid than even a diamond.
By him, many terrifying battles have been practiced in mutual provocation, with mountains hurled against one another, equal to those of our grandfathers.

An imaginative conceit (*utprekṣā*): such mountain-like battles, characterized by the fury of combat, were practiced and mastered by our grandfathers through fighting with them [the mountains] when they were hurled forth by the gods. || 32 ||
In those various, most terrible, and extensive battles—[the reading *arirājiṣu* is more appropriate]—he who was not afraid now, what need is there to speak of his fear? (33)
"What talk can there be of fear arising? What occasion for it could there be?"—this is the meaning. || 33 ||
I consider this to be the only clear means for attacking Hari;
apart from that, I believe there exists no remedy.
Regarding "assault" (ākramaṇa) and "subjugation" (vaśīkaraṇa): "counter-action" (pratikriyā) refers to the remedy against the suffering caused by those acts. || 34 ||
With one's whole being, with all one's intellect, and with the full force of all one's exertion—that Lord alone is the refuge and the goal here; it cannot be otherwise. (35)
To explain why [no other refuge] exists there, he says: "by every means" (*sarvātmanā*).

The meaning is that in this world, by way of the nature of all things (*sarvavastusvabhāvena*), by every form of intellect (*sarvadhiyā*), by every distinction of consciousness (*sarvabuddhibhedena*), by the force of every exertion (*sarvasaṃrambharaṃhasā*), and by every effort in action (*sarvakriyodyogena*), He alone is the refuge for those seeking shelter; there is no other way of going.
There is no one superior to him within the three worlds;
Hari has become the cause of dissolution, maintenance, and creation. (36)
To the objection, "Why then should others not be a refuge?", he replies: "No. (36)
From this very moment onward, I have eternally taken refuge in the unborn Nārāyaṇa; for everywhere, I am indeed permeated by Nārāyaṇa.

Having thus resolved, he forms the intention to practice that with his whole being, saying "from this. He asks: "Do you approach [it] through distinctions of place, time, and substance? and answers "no," saying "everywhere":
"In all places, times, and substances, I am composed of Nārāyaṇa. (37)
The mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" accomplishes all purposes;
it does not depart from the treasury of my heart, just as the wind does not depart from the sky.

Having recollected that mantra which is revealed in scripture—the means for the practice of uninterrupted realization, retention, recollection, and recitation—one forms the resolve to recite it continuously: "Namo nārāyaṇāya.
This [mantra], together with the *praṇava* (OM), is fit for recitation only by one who is pure, in a pure place and so forth, but not at all times.

The inclusion of the syllable *praṇava* [is for the sake of indicating] that the recitation performed within the cavity of the heart (*hṛtkośa*) is intended as the primary form of mental recitation (*mānasajapa*). || 38 ||
Hari is the quarters, Hari is the sky, Hari is the earth, and Hari is the world;
I am Hari, the immeasurable Self, for I have become identical with Viṣṇu.
He clarifies the statement "I am indeed composed of Nārāyaṇa everywhere" with the verse beginning "Hari. "Āśās" means the directions.

"Viṣṇumayaḥ" means predominantly Viṣṇu through meditative cultivation (bhāvanā). The suffix *mayaṭ* here denotes abundance characterized by the state produced by such cultivation, as in the expression "a wretch [who is] full of women" (*strīmayaḥ*). || 39 ||
One who worships Viṣṇu while not being Viṣṇu himself shall not partake in the fruit of that worship;
having become Viṣṇu, one should worship Viṣṇu, for I abide as this very Viṣṇu. (40)

To the question "For what reason do you imagine this?", he says: "Not being Viṣṇu... The meaning is that it is in accordance with the injunction: "One who is not Viṣṇu should not worship Viṣṇu; one who is not Śiva should not worship Śiva. || 40 ||
Hari, who is named Prahlāda, is not other than me; there is no Hari separate from me.
Thus possessing this certainty, I am the all-pervading one within, everywhere. (41)

He who is Hari is indeed the one named Prahlāda; for according to such scriptural passages as "There is no other seer than He," there is no Hari distinct from me or from the inner self (pratyañc), existing as a separate individual soul. 41.
Having filled this infinite space, this son of Vinatā,
with his golden limbs, has become the seat for my own limbs.

Now he imagines for himself the vehicle, weapons, death, body, and so forth of Hari, beginning with the words "Ananta" and so on. The phrase "remaining after filling [the space]" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Whose limbs are like gold" means that his complexion is golden. || 42 ||
With all their weapons resting upon the branches of his hands,
his nails— like great emerald trees— are strewn with the blossoms of the rays of light.
Upon the branches of their hands—that is, upon their limbs—all weapons characterized as discuses, maces, lotuses, and so forth, rest eternally; these are like birds perched there.
Because they are strewn with the clusters of blossoms that are the luster of their nails, they have become like great emerald trees.

The grammatical connection of the two [verses] is as follows: "These four arms of mine, Hari's, whose root-regions have their shoulder-mounds smeared with garlands of soft Mandāra flowers and whose armlets were rubbed by Mount Mandara at the time of the churning of the ocean. (43)
These are my four arms, their shoulder-regions smeared with garlands of soft mandāra flowers, and their armlets rubbed by Mount Mandara.
This Lakṣmī, who emerged from the depths of the Ocean of Milk, stands by my side holding a beautiful chowrie that resembles the shimmering flow of the crescent moon. 45.
This fame of mine, which delights the world with its grace, is like a cluster of blossoms on the tree of the three worlds; it remains by my side, steadfast and shining with purity. (46)

She by whom the worlds—and the people dwelling therein—have been effortlessly and without exertion enticed, captivated, and made to long for her with their ears; therefore, like a blossoming cluster on the tree characterized by the three worlds, the Fame of Hari stands before me in embodied form. 46.

This illusion (māyā) by my side, who performs the incessant creation of the new web of the world—[or, according to another reading, the web of old age]—is like one sporting with her own magical trickery (indrajāla). 47.
Jayā, the companion of Lakṣmī, stands at one side, positioned on the opposite side. || 47 ||
This is she, who effortlessly tramples upon the groves of trees that are the three worlds;
she, Jayā, flashes at my side like a creeper from the wish-fulfilling tree.
These two gods, the Moon and the Sun, who are eternally cool and hot respectively, have manifested the cycle of worldly existence as my eyes within my face. (49)
This lotus-dark woman of mine, as beautiful as a full rain-cloud,
has a spreading bodily radiance that darkens the circle of the quarters.
The radiance of the body is the splendor of the physical form. || 50 ||
This conch Pāñcajanya, with its throbbing sound, is in my hand;
it is like the sky personified as the essence of sound, standing there like the Ocean of Milk.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "as white as the Ocean of Milk. || 51 ||
This glorious lotus, with Brahma as its bee dwelling within the calyx of its pericarp, has arisen from the hollows of my own channels upon the palm of my hand.

One's own hollow channel is the navel, and that [channel] originates from it; thus, it is understood that the navel-lotus itself is sometimes held by the hand and sometimes [held] at the navel. || 52 ||
This heavy mace of mine, adorned with jewels, resembling the peak of Mount Sumeru, encircled by golden bands, is the crusher of Daityas and Dānavas. 53.
The mace has golden armlets and is bound with gold. || 53 ||
This Sudarśana of mine, appearing like the sun, rises with its rays;
its edges are matted with flames, turning the quarters of the sky a deep crimson.
Since the horizons on all sides are the color of trumpet-flowers (*pāṭala*), by this it is understood that they are smeared with the blood of the asuras. || 54 ||
This dark, blazing axe of mine, beautiful as a banner-bearing fire,
stands ready as Nandaka, bringing joy and felling the trees that are the Daityas.

Ketumān is beautiful like fire, possessing streaks of smoke; for this very reason, he is dark blue. He is the cutter of the trees that are the Daityas, like an axe. Nandaka is the sword of the Blessed One, which gladdens the gods. || 55 ||
This Śārṅga bow of mine, resembling the Puṣkarāvarta cloud for discharging showers of arrows,
has the luster of the king of serpents and is as beautiful as Indra’s rainbow.
Beautiful like Indra’s bow, variegated with various jewels. || 56 ||
Within my belly, I have long borne these infinite worlds—those that have perished after being born, and those existing now in their many varieties. (57)
This [verse] is an illustration of those things born at present—whether long lost, long arisen, or currently existing—as well as of those yet to be born. || 57 ||
These two are my feet, O Earth; this is my head, O Sky;
this body of mine is the three worlds; and these directions are my flanks. (58)

Now he says that even the cosmic form (*virāḍ-rūpa*) of Hari belongs to himself alone—beginning with "These two": the grammatical connection is "The earth is these two feet of mine. The plural number in "bellies" (*kukṣayaḥ*) is due to the plurality of the directions, just as in the expression "Aditi [is the mother] of the fetters" (*aditiḥ pāśān*). || 58 ||
"I am this very Viṣṇu in person, with the luster of the interior of a dark cloud, mounted upon the mountain-like Garuḍa, and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace. (59)
All these evil-minded ones are fleeing from me, like heaps of straw with flickering movements before the wind. (60)
Heaps of grass means heaps of dry grass. || 60 ||
This one, dark as a blue lotus, clad in yellow garments,
bearing a mace, endowed with Lakṣmī, and mounted upon Garuḍa, is I myself, Acyuta.
"Who is this hostile being that seeks me out, like a moth rushing toward the fire of time—agitated and capable of burning the three worlds—for its own destruction? (62)

"One of hostile nature" means one who comes as an enemy, arriving for the purpose of battle. The meaning is that whoever comes thus comes solely for his own destruction; there is no other fruit to his arrival. || 62 ||
These gods and asuras standing before me are unable to obstruct my fiery creation, just as those with weak eyes cannot withstand the glare of light.
To restrain, pacify, or endure the fiery creation—the spreading radiance of flames. || 63 ||
Brahmā, Indra, Agni, Hara, and the others praise me, this very Lord Viṣṇu, with infinite speech issuing from their many mouths.
I have become one whose sovereignty is fully manifested, possessing an unconquerable form; indeed, by my supreme majesty, I have transcended all states of duality.
Ajita Viṣṇu possesses that form through supreme majesty, power, and the nature of the ultimate reality, according to the Vedic revelation: "This is His eternal majesty. (65)
The singular form within the interior of the abode of the three worlds, who forcibly destroyed all wicked beings,
and who dwells amidst thick mountains, grass, and forests—
I bow to that form which removes all fears. || 66 ||

That which possesses a single form such that the abode of the three worlds exists within its belly; that which resides within the inner state as the substratum of all things—such as clouds, mountains, grass, and forests—and which, for this very reason, removes all fear through the mere direct realization of its true nature: that is the Vaiṣṇava [reality].
The meaning is: "I alone am the body in the form of Virāṭ, the body of the deity, and the nature of the Supreme Brahman; thus I bow to myself. || 66 ||

Thus ends the thirty-first canto, titled "The Attainment of the State of Nārāyaṇa," within the "Nirvāṇa of Prahrāda" section of the "Upaśama-prakaraṇa" (Chapter on Tranquility) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the Sage Vālmīki. 31.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Attainment of the State of Nārāyaṇa," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, he assumed the form of Nārāyaṇa and became known as Prahlāda.
Once again, he reflected upon the means for the worship of the enemy of the asuras.
Herein is described Viṣṇu’s mental worship, as well as his external worship along with the Asuras;
and having heard this, the astonishment of the gods and their inquiry regarding Hari are recounted.
Having made her own body into Nārāyaṇī, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, through meditative cultivation. || 1 ||
From this body of Viṣṇu, let there not be another form, higher or lower;
for here is another Viṣṇu stationed outside by means of the flow of vital breath. || 2 ||

Let there be no other supreme form of Viṣṇu conceived by me as distinct from these three types of bodies— neither in the form of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) nor in the form of individual deities (*vyaṣṭi*); rather, let this very Viṣṇu, who is my own self,
be invoked outwardly from the heart through the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of the mental visualization of a handful of flowers.
The meaning is that he remains as if he were another person until the time of worship. || 2 ||
Mounted upon Vainateya, possessing four flashing powers, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, he has dark-complexioned limbs and four arms. || 3 ||

He describes what that [Lord] is like with two verses beginning with "Vainateya": he is one whose fourfold power—consisting of activity (*kriyā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), will (*icchā*), and grace (*anugraha*)—is throbbing. (3)
The glorious one, whose eyes are the moon and the sun, who delights Kānta, Nandaka, and Nandana;
he who holds a lotus in his hand, possesses large eyes, wields the Śārṅga bow, and is of great splendor.
With his beloved sword Nandaka, he brought joy to his own people and caused delight to the Nandana grove.
Therefore, I shall quickly worship him, together with his retinue,
through a mental worship delightful with every necessary offering.
He was accompanied by his retinues, including the divine manifestations such as Saṃkarṣaṇa and Pradyumna, as well as his attendants.
"Therefore, I shall worship this Mahādeva once again with a great external offering consisting of many jewels."

Having worshipped Mahādeva, the adorable deity who is non-different from Śiva, the tutelary deity of one's own lineage, with external enjoyments and abundant provisions on a grand and extensive scale.
Thinking, "This is Prahlāda," he worshipped Mādhava, the husband of Kamalā, with a mind laden with the weight of his accumulated spiritual provisions.
Kamalā is Lakṣmī; her husband (dhavam) means her lord (patim). || 7 ||
With heaps of vessels made of jewels, with ointments such as sandalwood, with various incenses and lamps, and with diverse ornaments of great wealth; || 8 ||
With multitudes of vessels inlaid with heaps of jewels—the word "with" (abhiṣecanaiḥ) implies "with consecrations"—and with various riches, ornaments, and decorations. || 8 ||
With garlands of Mandāra flowers, clusters of golden lotuses, thickets of Kalpa-tree creepers, and circles of jewel-like blossoms; || 9 ||
With the shoots of divine trees, with garlands of various flowers—
kiṃkirātas, bakas, kunda, campakas, and blue lotuses— (10)
Should the Kirātas and others be understood as various species of flowers according to their respective applications? || 10 ||
With kahlāra lilies, water-lilies, kāśa grass, date palms, mangoes, kiṃśuka trees, aśoka trees, madana trees, bilva trees, karṇikāra trees, and kirātaka trees; || 11 ||
With clusters of kadamba, bakula, nimba, sinduvāra, and yūthaka trees, and with heaps of blossoms from pāribhadra, guggulu, and binduka trees; || 12 ||

With clusters of *priyaṅgu*, with trumpet-flowers (*pāṭala*), with minerals that are crimson-red, with mangoes, hog-plums (*āmrātaka*), products of the cow, and with *harītakī* and *bibhītaka* fruits. || 13 ||
With the creepers, flowers, and tender sprouts of the *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees; with clusters of buds; and with *sahakāra* mango trees laden with saffron. (14)
With saffron, smeared with liquid from Kāśmīra.
With ketaka flowers, śatapatra lotuses, and clusters of cardamom blossoms—
with all honors of beauty, even through their own self-offering— (15)
