With all honors and services endowed with beauty, such as incense, lamps, food offerings, betel, mirrors, umbrellas, chowries, the waving of lights (nīrājana), the offering of flower-petals (puṣpāñjali), circumambulation, prostrations, and so forth. || 15 ||
With supreme devotion, which was as magnificent as the splendor of the universe,
Prahlāda mentally worshipped Hari, his lord, within the inner apartments.
With whatever worldly riches are renowned, by making each of them an offering through noble devotion, one [worships] the Lord of the World, who is one's own master. || 16 ||
Then, in that temple, the lord of the Dānavas worshipped Janārdana with an offering complete with all external requisites.
Then, after the mental worship, while he was staying in that inner apartment within the temple of the deity. || 17 ||
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord again and again with external substances in this very sequence, the Dānava became filled with satisfaction. || 18 ||
By this very sequence described for the mental worship. || 18 ||
From that time forward, Prahrāda worshipped the Supreme Lord every day with complete devotion in that very same manner. (19)
Then, from that time forward, all the Daityas in that city became Vaiṣṇavas; indeed, they were all auspicious, for the king is the cause of conduct.

"Indeed, the king... means that according to the maxim: "When the king is righteous, [the subjects] are most righteous; when he is sinful, they are sinful; when he is neutral, they are neutral; they follow his nature, for as is the king, so are the subjects. || 20 ||
Then the slayer of enemies sent word to the celestial realm in the sky, saying:
"The Daityas have abandoned their hatred for Viṣṇu and remain as his devotees. (21)
And news arrived by way of a spy; this is understood from the sense of the passage. || 21 ||
O Rāghava, Śakra and the other gods, together with the hosts of Maruts, were filled with wonder, wondering:
"How is it that the Daityas have indeed taken up devotion to Viṣṇu? (22)
Why, for what reason, was it taken? || 22 ||
In the Ocean of Milk, seated upon the coils of the serpent, the gods, overwhelmed with wonder,
abandoned the sky and approached Hari, who was resplendent in battle.
Ambara is Amarāvatī. || 23 ||
There, they related this account of the Daityas to him,
and as he sat there filled with unprecedented wonder and amazement, they questioned him.
For this, for this Hari; him, Hari. || 24 ||
The gods said: "O Blessed One, what is this? Those Daityas who have always been our adversaries have indeed attained identity with that [Māyā]; it is perceived as being Māyā itself. (25)
"Those who are hostile" means those who hate you; "identification with that" means identification with you. || 25 ||
Where, indeed, are the utterly wicked Dānavas who have shattered the mountains, and where is devotion to Janārdana, which is obtainable only through a great birth in the West? 26.
By whom mountains, the dwellings of your devotees, gods, and sages, were shattered out of hatred. || 26 ||
"O Blessed One, this report that a common man has been born with such virtues is like a garland of out-of-season flowers—pleasant at first, yet causing distress. (27)
A commoner is a vulgar person. This story is like a garland of flowers out of season—an omen of ill fortune. || 27 ||
For that which is not appropriate in a certain place shines forth there;
it is like a highly precious gem in the midst of a heap of glass. (28)
It is neither logical nor reasonable. || 28 ||
Whatever kind of qualities a living being possesses, he attains that very same state;
even among unborn beings who are similar in nature, a dog never finds delight in their midst. (29)

If it be argued that "since they belong to the lineage of Kaśyapa, they must indeed be like you," they reply with the verse beginning "yo yaḥ" (whoever he may be), intending to show that this is not so because of the disparity in their qualities (*guṇa*). The meaning is that it is logical that one who is *tāmasa* attains a *tāmasī* state, one who is *rājasa* attains a *rājasī* state, and one who is *sāttvika* attains a *sāttvikī* state. || 29 ||
Diamond needles, even when plunged into the limbs, do not cause such pain as these views of real entities, which are bound by way of dissimilarity. (30)

By way of dissimilarity and impropriety; as it has been said by Hari: "The moon is grey as day, the passionate woman has lost her youth, the lake is devoid of lotuses, and one’s own face is lacking in eloquence;
the lord is devoted to wealth, the virtuous man is in constant distress, and the villain has taken his place in the king’s court—in such thoughts, the mind [is troubled]."
"These are my seven thorns. (30)
Whatever is obtained here in its proper sequence, appropriate, and irreproachable— that alone shines forth there, like a lotus in water and not on dry land.
The sequence is suitability; by that, it is attained. || 31 ||

Where is this base, vulgar undertaking, always delighting in inferior deeds—the wretched Dānava (or, according to a variant reading, "the Dānava of low birth")? And where indeed is Vaiṣṇava devotion, which belongs to a noble lineage? 32.
One of low birth has a womb characterized by darkness (tamas). || 32 ||
Just as a lotus plant growing on harsh, saline soil does not bring happiness here because it has taken refuge in an unfavorable place,
so too even a son of Diti who possesses devotion to Mādhava—
O Lord, stories of worldly policy do not bring us such happiness. || 33 ||

Just as the story that the lotus-pond has gone to a parched and saline wasteland does not please the listeners, so too, O Lord, the report that even the son of Diti possesses devotion toward Mādhava does not bring us joy; the meaning is that even a tale concerning a base refuge is likewise not for our pleasure. || 33 ||
Thus ends the thirty-second canto, titled "The Words of the Wise," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation, in the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Words of the Wise," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then the slayer of enemies [Rāma], toward the gods who were roaring with extreme fury, spoke.
Mādhava spoke these words, like a cloud to a flock of peacocks.
Through devotion to Hari, the demon's virtues such as discernment and others arose;
having seen Hari pleased before him, his hymn of praise is now described. (1)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: Mādhava then spoke to the one who, having seen the unaccustomed sight, was exceedingly agitated and enraged, and who, roaring for that very reason, was questioning the world of the gods after shouting out loudly in the manner previously described. || 1 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
"O wise ones, do not be despondent; Prahlāda is possessed of devotion.
This is his final birth; this subduer of enemies is worthy of liberation."

The Daityas are powerful by their very nature, and being further strengthened by devotion to you, they will become even more powerful; why, then, is there no despondency? To this he says: "He is worthy of liberation. Since he is worthy of liberation, he does not desire the trivial pleasure of sovereignty; such is the meaning. || 2 ||
Therefore, he must not conceive an offspring by this one born of the Danujas,
just as a burnt seed cannot produce a sprout.
Therefore, by this birth of a Dānava, he shall not undergo the state of being in a womb—that is, dwelling within a mother’s womb—after this birth. || 3 ||
They know that "the virtuous one has become devoid of qualities" is an unfavorable sequence;
they say that "the one devoid of qualities has become possessed of qualities" is the sequence that grants success.
He dispels the fault of impropriety regarding his devotion to the Blessed One as stated by the gods with the words "he is virtuous" (*guṇavān*).

The word "and born" (*jātaśca*)—or alternatively, the reading "if" (*cet*)—is the remainder [of the sentence]. And the wise say that "the sequence of misfortune" (*anarthakramam*) is a sequence that results in misfortune and obstructs the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
"O best of immortals, go to your own various worlds;
this daughter of Prahlāda has not been acquired by you here for the sake of unhappiness. (5)
The lineage of Prahlāda, connected with Prahlāda and multiplied by my devotion and other virtues, shall not lead to your misfortune. || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to the gods there amidst the waves of the Ocean of Milk,
the Lord vanished like a cluster of *tāpiccha* blossoms upon the shore.
Just as the dark cluster of a Tāpiccha tree growing on a bank vanishes from view when obstructed by rising waves, so it is in this case. || 6 ||
That host of gods, having worshipped Hari,
ascended into the sky like a spray of droplets shaken from the ocean by Mount Mandara.
It was like a mass of spray that had previously fallen from the sky into the ocean, now returning from the ocean— stirred up by Mount Mandara— back to the sky once more.
Thereupon, the gods felt affection toward Prahlāda;
for where the great are not agitated, there the mind becomes full of trust.

Affection (*snigdhatvam*) means friendship (*sauhṛdam*). The meaning is that in whatever person or object great ones—such as one's own elders, father, teachers, and so forth—are not troubled, it is well known that even the minds of children possess trust toward that very thing. || 8 ||
The devoted Prahlāda worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, every day with his mind, his actions, and his speech.
Then, as he was devoted to worship, his virtues—foremost among them being discernment, bliss, and dispassion—increased over time. (10)
Joy is contentment with what has been obtained. || 10 ||
He did not delight in the multitude of enjoyments, as one does not in a withered tree;
nor did he take pleasure in his beloveds, like a deer among the inhabitants of the world.
As if in the great cities of the world, in lands crowded with people. || 11 ||
He found no delight in worldly activities except for explaining the meaning of the scriptures;
no pleasure arose in him for visible objects, just as a lotus does not thrive on dry land.
In worldly activities—that is, in the conduct of people that is not in accordance with the scriptures—and in spectacles worthy of being seen, such as the curiosities of social festivals and the like.
His mind found no rest in the attachment to the diseases of worldly enjoyments,
remaining like a detached pearl within a pure pearl-oyster.
Regarding diseases in the form of enjoyments, when one practices what is favorable by indulging in the unwholesome objects of the senses;
[the remedy is] that which is unattached, unstrung, or unpierced. || 13 ||
His mind, having abandoned the calculation of enjoyments and the like yet not having attained rest, remained as if fixed upon a swing. (14)
How, then, was his mind at that time? He says: "abandoned" (*tyakta*). The meaning is that it was as if suspended on a swing, not resting on either side, but hanging in between. || 14 ||
From his abode in the Ocean of Milk, the god Viṣṇu perceived that state of Prahlāda through his all-pervading and supremely beautiful intellect.
With a most beautiful intellect whose essence is pure being—that is, with the power of gnosis—he perceived; he understood. || 15 ||
Then, having been delighted by Viṣṇu at his front, he arrived at the temple of Prahlāda’s deity via the path to the netherworld (pātāla).

He who gladdens his devotees is *Āhlādita*; or rather, he is the creator of all bliss, according to the Vedic scripture: "By his bliss alone do other beings live upon a mere fraction. Having gone to the temple of the deity for worship, he arrived before Prahlāda. || 16 ||
Having recognized that the god had arrived, the lord of the Daityas honored the lotus-eyed one with a twofold increase in his luster and worshipped him with great reverence.
With a twofold provision of requisites, [she was] prosperous and radiant. || 17 ||
Prahlāda, filled with supreme joy, praised Hari— who was present in person within the sanctuary of worship— with words that were full of devotion.
By nourishment augmented by joy. || 18 ||
Prahlāda said:
[I bow to] that supreme light, the treasury beautiful within the palace of the three worlds, which removes every blemish.
I take refuge in Hari, the unborn and infallible Lord, the worthy refuge, the master, the protector of those without protection. || 19 ||
The treasury of the three worlds is a beautiful abode where its contents remain well-guarded;
for it protects by itself the entire universe— both external and internal— situated within it,
and it is the supreme remover (*hara*) of all stains and darkness.

It is a self-luminous light superior even to the illumination of the sun, moon, fire, and speech; it is the refuge and protector for those who have no other shelter, and because it is imperishable, it is "śaraṇya," worthy of being sought as a refuge. It is the Lord (Īśa), endowed with all powers; therefore, by means of *rajas*...
The meaning is: I take refuge in You—the Unborn, who is not fallen by passion (sattva), the Lord because of being untouched by darkness (tamas), and Hari because of removing all suffering. || 19 ||
Resembling the dark blue petals of a water lily, comparable to the hollow of the cloudless autumn sky, and possessing the luster of bees, darkness, and collyrium ointment—
I take refuge in the one who holds a lotus, a discus, and a mace. || 20 ||
It resembles, and possesses a luster equal to, the petal of a water-lily, a blue lotus, and a sapphire. || 20 ||
His limbs are as tender as a cluster of stainless lotus filaments; his conch-like [throat] possesses the luster of a white-petaled lotus bud;
and he is the bee to the Brahmā who resounds through the Vedas.
I take refuge in that which rests upon the petals of the lotus of my own heart. || 21 ||
He whose limbs are as tender and beautiful as a cluster of *alika* flowers;
he who possesses a conch shell that shines like the bud of a white-petaled lotus (*puṇḍarīka*);
and he who is the bee named Viriñci, whose humming sounds are the very Vedas themselves.
He whose bee [resides] in the navel-lotus; him who is the refuge and support for the petals of the heart-lotuses of his own people, that is, his own devotees. || 21 ||
The moon-like orb of his full face was white with a smile, studded with stars that were his rows of white teeth;
it was the Gaṅgā for the rays of light from the jewel upon his heart.
I take refuge in the autumnal sky spread across by Hari. || 22 ||
I take refuge in the autumnal sky, which has Hari as its characteristic mark—that is, the autumnal atmosphere.

To establish its nature as the autumnal sky, the author qualifies it with the words beginning "sitana-kha" (white-nail): he whose face, marked by a smile, is white, and whose full orb of the moon is plump; [he is] the jewel of the heart.
The multitude of rays from the Kaustubha gem itself is the Gaṅgā Mandākinī where [he resides].
Constantly absorbed in all that was created by his incessant emanation, unborn, unincreasing, and vast,
with a body matured by hundreds of qualities and noble birth—
I take refuge in the child lying upon the leaves of the tree. || 23 ||

In whom the entire creation—dense and compactly formed—is contained without crowding; who himself is eternally unborn and unproduced, and for that very reason undecaying, being devoid of modifications such as growth and the like. To the question of how he can possess a body, he says: "by the qualities," etc.

The meaning is: "I take refuge in that infant who, at the time of universal dissolution, was lying upon the leaf of a banyan tree—one whose body is ancient and venerable, yet beautiful, and which is matured by hundreds of qualities such as goodness and the like, employed through the power of illusion (māyā), and endowed with infinite auspicious attributes. (23)
Fair as the pollen of a newly blossomed lotus,
his limbs adorned by the form of a blooming lily,
with the glow of dawn at the close of day as his bodily unguent—
I take refuge in him who is beautiful with garments resembling gold. || 24 ||
Whose limbs— whether his chest or his beautiful thighs— are fair with the pollen from the newly blossomed lotus of his navel (which implies a yellowish hue on the region of the belly),

and whose body is adorned by the clearly manifest form of Kamalā, Lakṣmī; who is as ruddy as the time of day’s end, the evening, with the application of saffron and other cosmetics upon his face and limbs.
Of whomsoever. || 24 ||
A frost-fall for the lotus-pond of the sons of Diti,
a sun-disk ever-risen for the lotus-pond of the gods,
and a flood of water for the lotus-pond of Brahmā.
I take refuge in the All-pervading Lord, whose abode is the lotus in the heart. || 25 ||
Brahmā, born from the lotus (*kamalaja*), was filled with the water of that lotus-pond; thus, it is "filled with water" (*jalāvapūra*), meaning a lake.
The lotus well-known in the heart is, in other words, the heart-lotus (*hṛtpadma*). || 25 ||
The white lotus of the lily-pond of the three worlds, the foremost lamp for dispelling the darkness of delusion,
the most clearly manifest, non-inert reality of the nature of consciousness—
I take refuge in Hari, who removes all the afflictions of the world. || 26 ||

The sun-like one in whose hand there is such a white lotus belonging to the lotus of the three worlds; for this very reason, it is a lamp for delusion which resembles darkness. It is the foremost, the most excellent. Is this a physical light? No, he says: "most clearly" (*sphuṭataram*). Most clearly means eternally self-luminous, and therefore non-inert.
Therefore, the reality of the Self is of the nature of consciousness; by its mere direct realization, it removes all suffering for the worlds and for the living beings within those worlds. (26)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus praised with words abounding in virtues, that Hari, the destroyer of asuras, whose shoulder was adorned by the seat of Śrī, [remained there].
Like a cloud to a peacock, the one with the hue of a blue lotus petal, full of affection for the one who was being pleased by him, replied to the lord of the asuras.

Thus honored with words of praise abounding in the aforementioned qualities, Hari— whose shoulder was embraced and occupied by Śrī— replied to Prahlāda, the lord of the asuras, just as a rain-cloud addresses a peacock. || 27 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third canto, titled "The Arrival of Nārāyaṇa," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. 33.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Arrival of Nārāyaṇa," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-fourth canto.
The Blessed One said:
"O treasure-house of virtues, O great crest-jewel of the Daitya lineage, choose a boon."
Take another birth as you desire for the sake of pacifying suffering. || 1 ||
Having obtained the boon from Hari and through profound reflection,
Prahlāda cast aside the category of non-self and beheld his own self as the non-dual consciousness that is existence.
O great crest-jewel of the Daitya lineage, choose a boon! || 1 ||
Prahlāda said:
O bestower of the fruits of all intentions, you who abide within all worlds; O All-pervading Lord, instruct me in that which you know to be the most sublime.

He who dwells within the heart of all worlds and all living beings—meaning, he who is most noble and the dispeller of all wretchedness—[I entreat you] with humble words: "Command me! [This is the request. || 2 ||
The Blessed Lord said: O sinless one, may your inquiry lead to the ultimate fruit and the complete pacification of all agitation, culminating in rest in Brahman.

Thus entreated, Viṣṇu, considering that there can be no cessation of extreme wretchedness without the repose found in the direct realization of the reality of Brahman as one's own self— which arises from his own deliberation— bestows a boon accordingly, beginning with the words "All... (sarva...).
The complete pacification of all agitation and the cessation of ultimate misfortune; the supreme fruit is the attainment of unsurpassed bliss. (3)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to the lord of the sons of Diti, Viṣṇu vanished,
like a wave of the ocean subsiding after its gurgling roar has ceased.
When the god Viṣṇu had vanished, the Dānava cast aside the handful of flowers intended for worship,
which was adorned with jewels and gems.
Seated upon the lotus posture on that excellent seat with great joy,
he sat down and reflected within his mind upon the procedure for reciting the hymn of praise.
Having sat upon an excellent seat in the lotus posture (padmāsana), at the time of performing the recitation of the hymn of praise, he meditated in the manner that will be described below.
"I have been told by the Lord, the enemy of Bhava: 'May you indeed be possessed of discernment. Therefore, within myself, I perform the investigation of the Self."
"Bhava" means saṃsāra; "tadariṇā" means by that which wards it off. By that reason [it is so called]. || 7 ||
What indeed am I in this grand display of the world, such that I speak, go, stay, and strive to acquire things? (8)

In this regard, having determined that the self alone is primary because everything visible exists for the sake of the self, he investigates what that very self might be in this context, beginning with "What am I? and so forth. With effort—that is, with every exertion—he "brings forth," meaning he experiences sense objects. (8)
This world, including its trees, grass, and mountains, is not "I";
since that which is external is utterly impure, how indeed could I be it? (9)
Regarding this, he states that the Self is not external to the body: "The world," etc. (Verse 9).
Non-existent, yet arisen; mute, yet flickering for a moment with the vital winds;
destined for dissolution in a short time—this body is not I, for it is insentient. (10)
He says that even the body is not the "I" with the words "asat" (non-existent). A mute person is incapable of speaking precisely because of a lack of understanding.
By the winds—that is, the vital breaths (prāṇa)—it is made to quiver or move for a moment at the time of its own circulation. || 10 ||
Being produced by the inert auditory canal, momentary, formless, and born of emptiness, sound is insentient; it is not I. (11)

In this way, he states with the words beginning "by the insentient" that objects such as sound and so forth are also not the Self: "being conceptualized by the insentient—that is, by that which is of the nature of non-consciousness—and being supported by distinctions such as high-pitched, low-pitched, word, or sentence; because of its perishability, it has the form of emptiness. It is called 'bhava' because it arises from the void, namely space (ākāśa). Even though space..."

Although it does not have emptiness as its intrinsic nature, nevertheless, because it is distinct from the existence of a self, it is called "empty" on account of being devoid of its own form. || 11 ||
Whether attainable or unattainable by the skin that perishes in an instant,
I am not insentient, for I have attained the touch of the Self through the grace of consciousness.
That which is to be attained may sometimes be unattained; [for example], touch, heat, and so forth. The sense is that the self cannot have the nature of being eternally attained. || 12 ||
I am not the insentient taste, which is bound by the tongue, trivial, fickle due to its restless nature, possessing only slight movement, and dependent upon material objects. || 13 ||

One whose self is bound by the restless, impermanent, fickle, and wavering tongue— meaning, one whose very nature is fettered and whose accomplishment depends upon the organ of taste— is such that his slight vibration, the spreading of tasting, extends from the tip of the tongue to the throat. 13.
Dissolved in the seer and the seen—which are subject to destruction and momentary perishing—the form is extinguished in the solitary witness; I am not that insentient thing.
It means that [the intellect] is dissolved in both the object to be seen and the instrument of seeing, the eye; its establishment depends upon both of these.
It is momentary and perishable, being non-eternal. In the solitary Seer (Puruṣa), it becomes exhausted—that is, utterly spent—by producing experience.
I am not the insentient fragrance, which is imagined by the nose—blind, dull, and perishable—and which is fragile and of indeterminate form. (15)
By the blind and dull nose, which is without light; by the sense of smell (nāsikā); and by time, its form is indeterminate due to transformation into something else. || 15 ||

Free from the sense of "mine," devoid of mental constructions, peaceful, and with the delusion of the five senses gone, I am indeed pure consciousness alone, stripped of all parts and their manifestations.

The statement that sound and other sense-objects are not the Self applies equally to speech, grasping, and so forth; thus, due to the uniformity of the underlying logic, it serves as an illustration of the non-Selfhood of all threefold groups (*tripuṭī*).
By this, the threefold groups of ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and consciousness (*citta*) are also excluded from being the Self.
With the intention that only pure consciousness is the remaining self, he says: "free from the sense of 'mine'" (nirmama). || 16 ||
I am this pure consciousness alone, devoid of the object of thought; I am the illuminator, pervading both the external and the internal, partless, stainless, and composed of light. || 17 ||
Lest there be the inclusion of even an insentient object that possesses volition by means of the term "cetanā," he says this to exclude such a possibility:
"By this sentient [Self], all these things, from pots and cloths up to the sun, are illuminated, just as by a lamp of supreme brilliance. (18)

Having thus investigated the meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (you) as purified, he begins to investigate and ascertain the meaning of the term *tat* (that) by means of that very [term], starting with the words "by this" and so forth.
By means of the lamp of consciousness, which is supreme light because it is independent of anything else. || 18 ||
Now I have truly remembered all of this:
I am this all-pervading Self, the manifestation of non-conceptual consciousness. (19)

This Self is non-conceptual, devoid of concepts such as space and so forth, characterized by consciousness, a manifestation, and light; "I am this" [is the realization], which excludes any other Lord. || 19 ||
By this, these various fluctuations of the senses flash forth here— [the reading "rows" (paṅktayaḥ) also exists]—
just as rows of sparks flash forth by means of internal heat and light. || 20 ||
The meaning is: "just like rows of glowing embers that have become fire. || 20 ||
By this, these various rows of sense-faculties flash forth here,
like mirages in the desert by the all-pervading heat of summer. (21)
By this, the substantiality of these categories is established, just as the possession of qualities such as whiteness is revealed by a lamp for garments. (22)
He states that even existence (*sattā*), like the manifestation (*sphūrti*) of all objects, is dependent upon this [Brahman] alone—by the words "by this" (*anena*).
The illustration of the lamp (*pradīpa-dṛṣṭānta*) in establishing existence is intended to illuminate the non-difference between manifestation and existence. || 22 ||
For this very Self alone, like a mirror, stands as the ground of experience for all beings who are awake. (23)

"For those who are awake" means for those who possess consciousness. All these—body, senses, mind, intellect, and so forth—are "experiencers," meaning they possess experience; they are the ground, the supreme place of rest, for the experiences of those states [of waking]. Just as a mirror is the ground where the reflections of all objects come to rest, so it is with this.
By the grace of that one non-conceptual lamp of consciousness, the sun becomes warm, the moon becomes cool, the mountain becomes solid, and water becomes fluid. (24)
He states that even the diverse intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of entities have their establishment dependent upon this, using the words "of that" (*tasya*).
"Solid" (*ghana*) means hard; "melted" (*vidruta*) means liquid (the reading *druta* is also found). || 24 ||
This is the primordial cause of all things experienced continuously in the maintenance of the world; there exists no cause for it.

This is the primary cause for the established order of the origin and so forth of all objects in the world—objects experienced through scripture, direct perception, and other means, according to the sequence beginning with "from space comes air, from air comes fire, from fire comes water.
It is called *tat* because it extends (*tanoti*); that is, it pervades all effects by way of its nature as Being (*sat*). || 25 ||
Through this [cognition], the status of being an object arises intensely for those things experienced continuously,
just as the state of being heated arises from heat.
That well-known state of being objects such as space and so forth [is attained] by his majesty, just as the earth and other elements are heated by the heat of the summer sun. || 26 ||
From this causeless cause, the cause of all causes,
this world has arisen, just as coldness arises from ice and the like.

From this Brahman, which is in its ultimate sense formless, devoid of such forms as causality, and which, through ignorance, acts as the cause, this world has arisen from that very Brahman— the innermost Self— which is the cause of all causes, beginning with Brahmā. || 27 ||
Of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Rudra—the causes for the maintenance of the world—this is the primordial cause;
there exists no cause for it.
He explains this [phrase] "the cause of all causes" as follows: "Brahmā-Viṣṇu... (verse 28).
Salutations again and again to this Self of mine, which is devoid of names such as "citta," "thinker," "seer," and "seen," and which shines forth by itself all at once. (29)
To Him who shines forth once and for all, who is eternally self-luminous. || 29 ||
In this Lord of beings, whose nature is non-conceptual consciousness, all beings abide and enter as subordinate elements.
Because it is the cause, just as it is the cause of creation, it is also the cause of maintenance and dissolution; thus he says, "In this...

The [elements] enter—that is, they penetrate—into that which is subordinate (guṇabhūta), being themselves primary (pradhānabhūta) or having an existence not separate from that which possesses qualities (guṇavat).
And so, the definition of Brahman stated in such scriptural passages as "from which indeed these beings are born" applies to this very [Being].
The meaning is "concomitance" (samanvaya). || 30 ||
Whatever indeed is conceived by this conscious inner self, that alone comes to be everywhere; nothing else exists, even though it may be present.

The meaning is this: whatever exists now as a reality, though abiding in its cause in a subtle form, is determined and willed by this conscious Lord, the inner self, thinking "let it be" in the subsequent moment; that very thing comes to be in the subsequent moment, and nothing else. || 31 ||
Whatever little is grasped by the mind, that attains its own true state;
but whatever is not grasped by the mind here, even though it be real, comes to an end.
"Kalitam" means revived by being granted its own existence and manifestation; "nijam" refers to the pot itself, which is the locus of such worldly transactions as "the pot exists" and so forth;
"antam" means having reached destruction, characterized by non-existence. || 32 ||
These hundreds of rows of objects, appearing as jars, cloths, and so forth, belonging to the world, are indeed reflected in this vast mirror of the sky. (33)
This [world] arises as increasing in that which is more increased, and as decreasing in that which is decreased;
it exists as both real and unreal in the objective entity, like the reflection of the sun. (34)
He says "this" (etad) to show that modifications of existence such as increase and so forth are likewise superimposed upon this very [Self].

The meaning is: just as decrease and increase are superimposed upon the reflected sun—which remains in its own form—yet they are perceived as if they were occurring in something else, so it is here. || 34 ||
Invisible to all beings, yet attainable by those whose minds have dissolved,
this supreme, utterly stainless void is beheld by the virtuous.
For all beings who are ignorant and whose minds have dissolved, the term "to be attained" (*prāpya*) is used where "the visible" (*dṛśya*) should be said;
this is explained with the intention of indicating that there is no difference between seeing and attaining: "This is That. || 35 ||
This woman, rich with various visible clusters of blossoms and abounding with bees of virtuous conduct, attains prosperity from this tree of causes. (36)

However, with the intention that the conceptualization of those who imagine that the world is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) occurring in only one part of the cause also applies to this very [system] and not to any other, he says "this" in two verses. || 36 ||
From this [Self], this unstable structure of saṃsāra arises loftily, rich with various trees and shrubs, like a range of forests from a mountain. (37)
This self-luminous conscious Self is undivided among all those existing within the belly of the three worlds, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. (38)

If it is asked, "How is it known that this very [world] is a mental construction (kalpanā)? he says, "Of all [beings]," because the world possesses a non-differentiated manifestation (abhinnasphūrtika). || 38 ||
I am that one, without beginning or end, possessing all forms;
I abide within all moving and non-moving beings as my own self-experience. (39)
Of that very me, these many bodies— both stationary and moving, beyond all counting— have come into being.

The determination of number and calculation is the ascertainment of the specific quantity [of individuals]. By the word "etcetera," the determination of spatial extent and temporal extent are included.
This one is of the nature of pure experience; by virtue of its own self-experience, it is itself the witness of all seeing and the seen, possessing a thousand rays and eyes. (41)

The meaning is that this [Self] is of the nature of self-luminous experience, because, by virtue of its own experience, it cannot be joined with another experience due to the contradiction of an action operating upon itself; and even in the illumination of others,
it remains as the witness of all seeing, seers, and seen, being free from contraction and thus never becoming an object of illumination for itself.

Since the distinction between selves in each individual body is not established because they are of such a nature, this very one is the thousand-rayed and thousand-eyed for all; this is the meaning. || 41 ||
Here I am, moving through the sky with my beautiful solar body,
and also with my other body, the wind, as the wind itself.
He speaks of each of his own entire embodiments individually, saying: "This is that.
This one, manifest before my eyes, being the Lord, I am existing as the sun and move about with a solar body; likewise with the wind, I exist with a windy body. 42.
This body of mine, dark-blue in hue and bearing the conch, discus, and mace, dances within this world as the very pinnacle of all auspiciousness. (43)
It moves and engages in worldly activity. || 43 ||
I am born here, always seated upon the lotus throne;
established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, I have attained supreme bliss. || 44 ||
In the form of the three-eyed one, a bee at the lotus-face of Gaurī, I withdraw this universe at the end of creation, just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs.
By means of form and by means of shape. || 45 ||
In the form of Indra, I protect this entire triple world as my own inheritance,
just as an ascetic guards his small hut.
"Successively attained" means attained through the sequence of the Manvantaras. || 46 ||
"I am indeed this woman, and I am this man; I am also this youth.
Because I bear a body, I am old; I am born, facing in every direction. (47)

"You are woman, you are man; you are a youth or even a maiden; you are an old man tottering with a staff; you are born, facing every direction"—with these words of the Śruti, he brings it into harmony with his own experience within himself: "Woman," etc. (47).
I exist as the sap within the network of grasses, creepers, and shrubs; I cause them to rise up from the ground of consciousness, just as a well draws up a subterranean creeper.
By its essence, by its being the core of life, and by its nature as water; "kūpa" refers to a dilapidated well. || 48 ||
This beautiful and vast display of the universe was spread out by me, as a noble child, for the sake of my own play, like a toy made of mud. (49)
By a noble child, skilled in the creation of toys. || 49 ||
All this is obtained by me; existence comes to me when it reaches me.
And this, once abandoned by me, is nothing at all, even though it exists.

It is attained by way of being its cause; and through the dissolution of the existence of the effect, it reaches me and vanishes. This world, abandoned by me through the vision of my own true nature, is nothing at all, even though it exists within the worldly conduct of one liberated while living.
Whatever reflection has come into me, the expansive mirror of consciousness, that alone exists and nothing else; for apart from me, not even an atom is found here.
In flowers I am the fragrance; in flower petals I am the luster;
in lusters I am the art of form; and in forms, I am even the experience itself.
Now, he describes another experience through the enjoyment of the expansion of his own manifestations as the Supreme Lord, beginning with the words "In flowers" (kusumeṣu). || 52 ||
Whatever is seen here, this world of moving and unmoving beings—
free from all conceptual construction— that is the supreme reality of consciousness, which is I.

Whatever is visible and worthy of being seen—whether stationary or moving, possessed of power, splendor, or might—the cause of the excellence of all that is the reality of the conscious Self (cidātmatattva), which is none other than I myself. Why then am I not perceived in the form of a living being (jīva) defiled by volitions and the like? To this he replies: "devoid of all volitions. For this very reason, it is supreme.
The primordial Śakti consists of essence (rasa), by whom the flood of essence is spread;
as she is present in wood and walls, so am I in all things. (54)

The primordial power consists of *rasa* (taste/flavor), being the subtle element of *rasa*. Just as the flood of water from oceans, rivers, lakes, wells, and so forth, though being a mass of water, spreads out; that very same power, having become water, exists within wooden trees as the cause for the emergence of branches, shoots, and the like, and likewise within walls.

The meaning is: just as [the earth] has extended itself as the cause for the emergence of grass, barley-sprouts, and so forth, so too have I extended myself among all things as the cause for the emergence of their respective effects. || 54 ||
Having attained that supreme state of existing within all other entities,
I manifest the diversity of consciousness by my own will.

He states that, even amidst the diversity of the individual soul's consciousness (*jīvasaṃvit*) through its entry into various effects created by itself, it is the Self alone that is the cause: "Just as butter exists within milk, and as the power of taste exists within water, so too do I, as the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), abide within all beings. (56)
This entire world, existing throughout the three periods of time, is situated within consciousness,
devoid of any objective mental constructs, just as a collection of objects rests upon the earth.

The manifestation of objects (*cetyopacāra*) is the appearance of objects; that which is devoid of this is the insentient (*jaḍa*). This entire world—existing in the three times as past, present, and future—is situated within me, who am consciousness (*cit*), within my own singular aspect, just as a collection of things such as grass, wood, and clods of earth are situated upon the earth. (57)
Having filled the belly of all directions, having abandoned the delusion of limitation,
I stand as the Virāṭ, the sovereign emperor, existing in all things and the creator of all.

He is called *virāṭ* because he shines (*rājate*) in various ways through his individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*). He is called *samrāṭ* because he shines perfectly through his collective totality (*samyak-samaṣṭi*).
Alternatively, he is *virāṭ* because he shines preeminently (*viśeṣeṇa*) above other kings. A *samrāṭ* is the one who issues commands to all kings. || 58 ||
This vast sovereignty over the world has come to me unbidden—an unprecedented state in which Indra is no longer bound and the gods have been crushed by my weapons. (59)
To the question of how he attained the status of a sovereign (*samrāṭ*) before attaining a kingdom superior even to that of Indra, he says: "Unprecedented" (*apūrvam*). || 59 ||
Alas! I am indeed so expanded that I cannot even measure myself by myself, like the single ocean tossed by the winds at the end of an aeon.
I do not enter into [the Lord] as grain is placed in a granary; rather, I am like the ocean within the ocean of primordial measure. 60.
I find no end within myself, though it is well-established and self-savored within;
like a crawling cripple quivering in the ocean of milk and water. 61.

Within, while it is being relished by itself through its own unsurpassed nature of bliss; the cripple is one whose movement is obstructed, and the serpent is a crawling creature that moves about. (61)
"This small Brahma-hermitage named Jagat is very cramped;
his vast body cannot fit within it, like an elephant inside a wood-apple fruit. (62)
The Brahma-maṭhikā is the cosmic egg; it is extremely narrow with a constricted interior. My vast and expansive form does not fit within it, nor can it contain me. || 62 ||
Beyond the abode of Viriñci, even at the end of the principles (tattvas), it has established its station;
my form continues to expand even now and does not turn back.
Beyond the abode of Viriñci, which is characterized as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and enveloped by the coverings of earth and the other elements, each ten times greater than the preceding;
and beyond that, the twenty-four principles well-known in the Sāṃkhya, Vaiṣṇava, and other Tantras, numbering thirty-six.
Or rather, it means that as He proceeds, He takes His place even at the end of the categories (tattvas) favored by the Śaivas and Pāśupatas;
that is to say, "my form indeed spreads forth. This is a conceptualization of the very expansion of reality as a process of spreading out. || 63 ||
How could this internal notion "I am named so-and-so" be without support?
For this [notion] of mine was indeed limited, despite having an infinite form. (64)
The meaning is: from where did this conceptualization of "I" with respect to the body and so forth arise for such a long time? || 64 ||
The delusion that "this one is you" and "this one is I" is utterly false.
What is the body, or what is the bodiless? Who is dead, and who lives? (65)
If the body itself is not established, who is "bodiless"? For just as the son of a barren woman is unestablished, so too is his slayer.
Likewise, if the vital breath (prāṇa) itself is unestablished, who is dead—that is, who is separated from it? And who lives—that is, who sustains the vital breaths? || 65 ||
My grandfathers were wretched men of feeble intellect,
who abandoned this empire and took delight in the realms of worldly existence.
He now laments his grandfathers and others who were attached to a false empire, calling them "wretched"—that is to say, those of feeble intellect, meaning those of mean intellect. || 66 ||
Where, indeed, is this great vision, filled with and expanded by Brahman;
and where is this terrifying sovereignty, with its fearsome royal splendors? (Or, if the reading is *vibhūtayaḥ*, it would mean "where are these manifestations of power...")
Like crawling serpents, they were terrifying due to their fearsome directions.
This pure vision, consisting of consciousness, which possesses infinite blissful enjoyment and is characterized by supreme tranquility, triumphs over all other visions. (68)
Salutations again and again to me alone, who am the inner conscious self, free from the object of thought, abiding within all beings, and whose nature is inward awareness.
I, the unborn, having been born, have conquered the cycle of the decayed saṃsāra;
this great-souled one has attained all that is to be attained, and thus I live and I conquer.

Since I am one by whom the wandering of saṃsāra has been digested like food long consumed, and have thus become unborn (aja), I therefore conquer; that is, I have attained the fruit of victory over all that is to be conquered—the cessation of all misfortune. Furthermore, being one by whom all pleasures yet to be attained have been attained, I live; that is, I have achieved the fulfillment of life.
I have attained it; therefore, the meaning is that I am victorious and I abide in supreme excellence. || 70 ||
Having renounced this supreme, eternal sovereignty of awakening, I find no delight in the unpleasant opulence of royal power, which is nothing but suffering.
Fie on that wretched, ignorant insect among the wicked Danavas, who was tossed about upon the surface of the earth as if it were merely a piece of wood, water, or stone! 72.

In a forest-fortress, wood is the refuge; in a water-fortress, water; and in a mountain-fortress, stones—the very elements that crush one's pride. On such a surface of the earth, he who has become agitated and fickle through the conceit of lordship is but a worm characterized by wickedness. Even among worms, it is the wood-worms—

The meaning is that because one observes protection by means of wood against water-dwelling insects, by water against insects such as scorpions situated within the joints of stones, and by stones [against others], the capacity for self-protection is equal in each case. || 72 ||
What indeed has been accomplished by that ignorant teacher who, with substances consisting solely of ignorance, has satisfied his disciple with a limb made of ignorance? (73)

Because of the non-difference between cause and effect, [he was nourished] by substances consisting of food, drink, and other objects which are of the nature of ignorance, and by his father, the preceptor. || 73 ||
Having spent a few years in this illustrious Maṭha of the world, what indeed was it that Hiraṇyakaśipu obtained as his due? (74)

The three worlds are that monastery, endowed with prosperity and characterized by such qualities; it is appropriate for the lineage of Kaśyapa and conforms to the highest human goal as befits his birth.
Without tasting this bliss, even one who tastes hundreds of world-kingships would have tasted nothing at all in this world. (75)

This very Self, O Ānanda, is this Ānanda. Or rather, it is called "this Ānanda" because even this [world], though consisting of insentient matter and suffering, causes delight (ānandayati) through its own nature as bliss, or causes it to be experienced as having the form of bliss. Thus, it is "this Ānanda."
Nothing has been attained by that through which this supreme nectar is attained;
for one who is filled within by its attainment, everything is attained as an undivided whole.
He speaks of the attainment of the bliss of all objects through the attainment of the One alone, even without an object, saying: "Nothing whatsoever... [and so on].
It is unbroken and continuous. || 76 ||
Having abandoned this position, the fool moves toward what is limited, but the wise man does not;
for the camel, having abandoned the excellent grass, goes toward the thorn, and no other.
Having abandoned the excellent creepers, such as grapevines, which were bent down by the weight of their fruit; being one who had done so—thus he is described. (77)
Having abandoned this supreme vision, who would delight in a burnt kingdom?
What wise man, having discarded the juice of sugarcane, would drink bitter neem water? (78)
The milk of the nimba tree is the juice of the leaves of the picumanda. || 78 ||
Indeed, all those grandfathers of mine were fools;
having abandoned this vision, they took delight in the perils of sovereignty. (79)
The word "remire" (they saw) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 79 ||
Where is the blossoming grove of Nandana, and where are these scorched desert lands?
Where are these peaceful visions of awakening, and where is the notion of selfhood in sensual enjoyments? (80)
Regarding enjoyments, such as the body which is the locus of enjoyment, and so forth. || 80 ||
There is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that one desires even as a kingdom;
everything already exists within the nature of consciousness (cittattva), so why is it not experienced? 81.
The ellipsis is "not even the slightest happiness"; the ellipsis is "even having attained sovereignty. || 81 ||
By means of consciousness— which abides in all things, is established in its own state, is changeless, and is itself everything—
one rightly attains everything, at all times, from every source, and in every way.
All happiness and its means. || 82 ||
The radiant power is Taijasī; the attainment of immortality is Aindavī;
greatness is Brāhmī; and the sovereignty over the three worlds is Śākrī. || 83 ||

To explain why that is so, he says "bhāsinī" and so forth. Since the various powers (*śakti*), such as Bhāsinī and the rest, which are the causes of those respective pleasures, are produced by the Supreme Consciousness (*parā cit*)—this is the connection with the eighth [verse]. Brāhmī is [the power] belonging to Brahmā; Hairaṇyagarbhī is [the power] belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha. *Mahattā* means greatness or venerability; *mahatī* means most excellent. || 83 ||
The supreme fullness belongs to Śarva, and the fortune of victory belongs to Vaiṣṇava; the mental power belongs to Mānasa, swift movement to Śīghragati, and strength to Vāyava. (84)
Śarva is Śiva; that which relates to him is the supreme fullness—the state of being completely filled with unsurpassed power, sovereignty, bliss, and knowledge. || 84 ||
The Āgneyī is the power of burning; the Pāyasī is the satisfaction of taste;
the Maunī is the perfection of great austerity; and likewise, the Vidyā is that of Bṛhaspati. || 85 ||
The accomplishment of taste related to milk is the state of nourishment;
the accomplishment of speech related to the sages such as Bhṛgu is mastery over words. || 85 ||
The celestial movement of the Vaimānikas, the stability of the mountains, the depth of the oceans, and the great height of Mount Meru; || 86 ||
The glory of tranquility belongs to the Sugata; it is gentle like wine, yet intoxicated with passion;
it consists of the blossoms of spring (mādhavī), and it is called "the cloud" because of its dense harvest in autumn.
The "glory of peace" (*śamaśrī*) established by the Sugata’s doctrine is characterized by emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and is the cessation of all afflictions.
Alternatively, a "good state" (*sugati*) is the direct realization of Brahman; the glory of peace associated with that possesses the power to extinguish all misfortunes. (87)
There is the illusory nature of a yakṣī, the stainlessness of the sky,
the coldness of frost, and the heat-torment of summer.
The state of being composed of illusion is the abundance of illusion; stainlessness is the state of being untainted. || 88 ||

These and many others likewise—consisting of place, time, and action; arising from various forms and transformations; and situated within the belly of the three times (past, present, and future)—[are all contained therein]. || 89 ||
"Abiding within the womb of the three times" means those that are past, future, and present. || 89 ||
The diverse powers, established in their own state by the changeless Supreme Consciousness, are brought into being through that which is joined with the process of manifestation and withdrawal.

By means of consciousness (*cit*) that is established in its own state—meaning not fallen from its essential nature—and for that very reason, equanimous (*samayā*), i.e., uniform; or rather, changeless, being devoid of any real modification; and which is joined with the "reckoning of parts" (*kalākalana*), that is, the continuous engagement with the effects of its own powers. || 90 ||
Devoid of conceptual construction, the entire consciousness falls equally upon the perception of hundreds of objects, just as the light of the sun falls [upon all things]. (91)
Now, since one observes a diverse manifestation of various objects, how can there be equanimity for the consciousness? To this he says:

"By conceptualization," and so forth. Even though it enters into all or no mental modifications whatsoever, the consciousness is not stained by the diversity of conceptualizations residing within those mental modifications.
The meaning is that it is just like the light of the sun, which is not affected by the conceptualizations of a post or a person produced by those modifications.

Just as one experiences in an instant the entire earth—the mass of objects resting within the treasury of all desires, and encompassed by the activities of the three periods of time—so too [does he experience the Self]. || 92 ||

He states that there is no inequality in her even as it might be occasioned by differences of space and time, saying "sarvāśa" (in all directions). Just as the solar radiance pervades—that is, illuminates—the vast earth, so too does Consciousness perceive—that is, expand—[all things]; this is the connection with the following verse. || 92 ||
In the same way, the stainless consciousness, being of that very nature, perceives the splendor of the vast state of the entire objective world throughout the three periods of time.
The pure consciousness, touched simultaneously [with all things], is entirely full— comprising hundreds of calculations of the three times and the infinite expansion of worlds.
He states that differences of place and time are manifested by Consciousness as if they were non-distinct in time, just as the duration of one's own dream-place and time [is experienced as such];

thus he says, "of equal time" (*tulyakāla*). The word *tulya* (equal) refers to non-difference (*abheda*). And so, while the pure Consciousness remains entirely full and undivided, being perceived as non-distinct in time, it appears as if divided by hundreds of calculations of the three times—past, present, and future.

The meaning is that it appears as if it were the very expansion (ābhoga) of the infinite means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and types of persons, such as perception, inference, comparison, and so forth. || 94 ||
For consciousness, which has grasped the three times and perceives the infinite,
nothing remains but fullness, which is synonymous with equanimity.

Therefore, even when there is a difference in time and a difference in the modes of functioning (*vṛtti*), there is no difference in the consciousness that is their witness; thus, its fullness remains intact.
He states this in the verse beginning with "parāmṛṣṭa" (95).
When perceived at the same time, even by that which is sweet or pungent, consciousness attains a state of equality, just like the simultaneous experience of honey and the neem tree. (96)

For this very reason, he states—“at the same time”—that when two sweet things or two bitter things are tasted simultaneously, there is no difference in experience despite the difference in objects; thus, a difference in objects and so forth is not the cause for a difference in consciousness. [The phrase] “with equal” means with two sweets of identical taste and flavor. In that case:
"Just as in the case of the individual experience of honey, neem, and so forth"—this is the illustration for the non-difference of consciousness. 96.
By means of a subtle state of consciousness that has abandoned all mental constructs,
which pervades all existents and consists solely of the non-dual nature of pure being.

Even the manifold splendor of objects such as jars and cloths, when experienced simultaneously by the subtle cognitive state— which is of the singular nature of the non-dual existence and which has abandoned the mental construction of mutual exclusion and difference—
is experienced through equality alone, not through differentiation or disparity; thus, the distinction between objects and so forth does not constitute a distinction within consciousness.
The meaning of the two [is as follows]. || 97 ||
Even though the splendor of various objects has their internal natures intertwined with one another, they are experienced through equality, as their perception occurs at the same time. || 98 ||
By relying on non-existence through existence, existence abandons its state of suffering;
by perceiving existence through non-existence, existence abandons its state of corruption. (99)
He states the means for abandoning even the subtle trace of the conceptualization of difference with the words "by means of *bhāva*.

By means of *bhāva*—that is, by the mind (*citta*), by the scriptural texts such as "beginning with speech" (*vācārambhaṇam śrutyā*) and "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), and by the teacher’s instruction, one's own inquiry, and so forth—one relies upon the non-existence of the entire class of perceived objects; thus, that mental state (*bhāva*) which is the nature of the mind [ceases its] state of suffering.

One immediately abandons the transformation consisting of grief, delusion, and so forth; nevertheless, because it is defiled by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of passion and the like, grief and other such states may arise again at a later time. Therefore, one [should abandon] existence by means of non-existence characterized by the negation of all objects of perception.

Having perceived the Self, whose nature is the non-dual bliss of ultimate reality, that state characterized by the mind abandons even its corruption by passion and the like; for there is the word of the Blessed One: "Even his taste ceases upon seeing the Supreme. Therefore, the meaning is that the abandonment of the slightest trace of conceptualization regarding duality is established due to the absence of the seed [of such corruption]. || 99 ||

For the consciousness that does not perceive the three times, that is devoid of the bonds of the object of thought, and that is indifferent toward the object of thought, only equanimity remains. (100)

He establishes the stated point by means of a different formulation—“the three times. For consciousness (*cit*), which disregards the present object of thought (*cetya*) or visible world, and which is devoid of the bonds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from past objects of thought, and which does not perceive even the three times as a support for objects of thought, there can be no connection with an object of thought, even in the future; thus, there is only equanimity (*samatā*).
The meaning is that it remains. || 100 ||
Because it is beyond the reach of words, it goes as if into eternal non-existence;
it remains as if having attained the state of the established doctrine of selflessness. 101.
"It has approached," they say; however, in reality, it has not approached, because that which exists cannot be joined with non-existence—this is the intended meaning. || 101 ||
The self is thus Brahman—neither nothing nor the whole;
merged in supreme tranquility, it is designated by the name "liberation" (mokṣa).
That which remains is the Self (*ātman*) because of its inwardness (*pratyaktva*) in the context of scriptural usage, and it is Brahman because of its vastness (*bṛhattva*).

However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), nothing exists at all due to the absence of the operation of words. And if it is argued that the application of words occurs through the conceptualization of grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), then—

The meaning is that it is described in two ways in the Śruti: first, because there is no cause for its contraction and because it is the imagined ground (nimitta) for all activity, as in "and from which everything arises";

and second, as in "from which words turn back, unable to reach it along with the mind, therefore it became all. Thus, when all objects of perception have reached supreme cessation, [the Self] remains as their ultimate limit, being unabsorbed.
The meaning is that supreme equanimity is designated by the name "liberation. || 102 ||
But this world, fashioned by conceptual construction, is seen only dimly; thus the vision of consciousness does not perceive it correctly, just as an eye affected by a cataract does not see clearly.

Thus, the abandonment of the mental construction of duality, along with its means, has been described. Now, he explains the process by which the mental construction of consciousness gradually becomes dull, beginning with the words "In the mental construction" (saṃkalpe):
[the subject] does not see the world correctly, that is, in its ultimate reality; [it is] "paṭalinī," meaning possessed of a veil like a cataract. || 103 ||
Enveloped by impurities consisting of both effort and lack of effort, that consciousness is indeed unable to fly upward, like a bird bound by a snare. (104)

By means of impurities consisting of the conceptualization of the desirable and the undesirable—whether characterized by effort or lack of effort—to fly up, to pervade the entire sky, and to travel through the sky; || 104 ||
By the very movement of their own volitions, these people have fallen into the snares of delusion, like birds caught by a hunter. 105.
Ensnared by the web of volitions and falling into the pit of sense-objects, this path free from obstacles was not seen even by my ancestors.
This state, free from affliction and devoid of suffering, the undivided domain of the Self, has not been seen. || 106 ||
Within just a few days, they quivered upon the surface of the earth;
by that [force], those wretched ones perished like gnats in a cave.
By that vision of the path of the Self, they became my grandfathers. 107.

If these beings had known this reality, then, though seeking the pleasures of enjoyment, they would not have fallen into the blind wells of existence and non-existence with their intentions destroyed. (108)
"Deprived of hope and evil-minded, these grandfathers of mine would not have fallen [into this state] had they known the reality of the self.
[This is an example of the conditional mood (lṛṅ) used when there is a cause and its effect, with the conditional marker (liṅ) as the cause, denoting the non-occurrence of an action. 108.
Through the delusion of dualities arising from desire and aversion, living beings have attained the same state as worms submerged in crevices of the earth. (109)
By the delusion of duality, that is, by the persistent attachment to the acquisition and remediation of pleasure and pain, cold and heat, and so forth. || 109 ||
He alone truly lives whose mental thirst for conceptualizations—appearing in the forms of the desired and the undesired—is stilled by the cloud of the realization of reality. 110.
They are peaceful through the cessation of the heat of dualities by means of the cloud of the realization of truth; that is to say, he alone lives a life that is truly meaningful. || 110 ||
Whence indeed could there be these slightly warm stains, products of imagination, upon this pure moonlight of unbroken and stainless form? (111)
If it is asked how there can be peace through the mere realization of truth, he says "because of its non-existence" (asattvāt). [The questioner asks] "Why?
[The answer is: "Koṣṇāḥ" means slightly warm; "kalaṅkāḥ" means dark spots. || 111 ||
Salutations to myself—salutations to me, whose nature is the uninterrupted consciousness!
O Lord, jewel of the world and its beyond, alas, you have been attained by me only after a long time! 112.

Now, having directly realized the meaning of the sentence as an indivisible whole (*akhaṇḍavākyārtha*), he pays homage out of affection to that extremely rare Self which has been attained and established in that state, with the words "to the Self. [He describes it as] the light of the world—the illumination of knowledge—and the jewel that is its cause. [He adds] "after a long time."

And so it has been said in the *Svārājyasiddhi*: "Even when countless Brahmās, as numerous as the atoms of the earth, have passed away, there is no gain superior to the attainment of one’s own Self—the ocean of infinite bliss free from suffering. (112)
You have been grasped, you have been found, and after a long time you have arisen;
you have been lifted out from conceptual constructions—whatever you are, to you be homage! (113)
"Manifested" means revealed in its own ultimate nature. || 113 ||
Salutations to me and to you, the infinite; salutations to me and to you, whose nature is auspiciousness. Homage to the God of gods, the supreme, the Supreme Self.

In the first [mantra], the words "to me" and "to you" serve the purpose of purification through mutual qualification; for this very reason, it says "to Ananta. In the second, however, it serves the purpose of attaining the meaning of the sentence, which is characterized by indivisible, uniform essence (akhaṇḍaikarasatā);
for this very reason, it says "to the Self of Śiva," the presiding deity over all the senses, vital breaths, and minds of the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
Having empowered it for the sake of illumination. || 114 ||
The lunar orb, freed from the dense clouds that once filled it, is its own true form;
when one’s own body is gladdened, it is itself established within itself.
I bow down to that which has arisen by itself, which is self-dependent, and which is itself. || 115 ||

The phrase "like the full orb of the moon" implies that it is like the lunar disk when the clouds have passed away and the veil of mist has been dispelled. It is "established in its own body," that is, in its own self which consists solely of the essence of bliss; it is established by itself, without dependence on any other support, in its own ultimate form—meaning, it is without a substratum. It is "self-arisen," meaning self-luminous.

I, who am myself non-different [from Him], bow to that which is self-dependent and whose bliss is under its own control; the meaning is that I contemplate it as being preeminent in all respects. || 115 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Yoga of Instruction on the Self of Prahlāda," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. || 34 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Instruction on the Self by Prahrāda," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-fifth canto.
Prahrāda said:
"Om"—this is the single appropriate form, entirely devoid of modification.
This Self alone is all this, whatever exists within the world.
Having directly realized the Self here and having praised it within while bowing down,
he rejoices, reflecting upon his kinsmen who have been conquered through its power.

"Om. "Om is Brahman; Om is all this. Indeed, Satyakāma, this syllable Om is both the higher and the lower Brahman"—from such scriptural passages as these, it follows that the single syllable "Om" alone is appropriate and corresponds to its own nature, as it indicates Brahman through the superimposition of all [attributes] and indicates it by the exclusion of all [superimpositions].
That whose form is the expression [of all things]: the world (*jagat*) is that which moves; whatever exists therein, all that is this very Self (*ātman*) being experienced. || 1 ||
This conscious being transcends even fat, bone, flesh, marrow, and blood;
for like a lamp situated within, it illuminates the sun and other luminaries.

If it is asked, "How can this [Self], which is contained within the mere body, be all this external world, such as the sun and so forth? he says, "Because it is its illuminator"—namely, "It is fat" (medaḥ). This "fat" is not limited to the body consisting of bone and other elements; rather, it transcends that, because it resides within the sun and other luminaries. || 2 ||
It makes fire hot, it tastes the nectar-like essence, and it experiences the perceptions of the senses, just as a sovereign enjoys his pleasures. || 3 ||

To the question, "How is it that by the mere fact of being manifested by that [consciousness], everything is of the nature of that [consciousness]? he says: "It makes the fire hot. Since the nature of heat and so forth in fire and other things depends upon the manifestation of heat which is dependent on consciousness (*cit*), therefore the conscious Self alone, by its own existence, makes the fire hot. In the same way, water, which is essence (*rasa*), makes itself nectar by its own existence alone.

It relishes that which has attained existence by means of its own essence as "taste" (rasa) and manifests it; in this same way, it also brings about other objects whose nature consists of tactile sensations and so forth through its own existence alone, and then experiences them. || 3 ||
Though standing, he is not seated; though walking, he does not go. Though engaged in worldly activity, he remains peaceful; though acting, he is not defiled.

Though always remaining inactive while standing, he does not appear as if seated or withdrawn from activities such as running, because he is in constant motion through his nature as wind and sun. Likewise, though always moving through his nature as time, he does not move even a sesame seed’s breadth elsewhere, like the wheel of a potter. Thus, though peaceful and devoid of worldly activity, he remains.
He abides in all worldly conventions. || 4 ||
Whether performed previously, today, or now, in this world or the next, or in both— this [dharma] is equal in all modes of livelihood, whether it be prescribed or even unprescribed.

[Objection: Is one not indeed stained by the pleasure and pain resulting from what was done previously today? And will one not be stained in the future by what is done now in this world? How then can it be said that "even while acting, one is not stained"? To this, he says: "Previously," etc. [The action] performed here in this world, there in the next world, and in both—namely, in the intermediate state (*saṃdhi*) between this world and the next, which is one's own transition—is what is enjoined.

One who does not experience the fruits of auspicious actions prohibited by the scriptures, and who, though experiencing the fruits of inauspicious actions prescribed by the scriptures, remains the same in all modes of enjoyment—
the meaning is that no modification of the Seer (dṛk) is established by visible objects of enjoyment. || 5 ||
He brings forth fearless existence from here and there;
he remains pervading the world, revolving it from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
To the question of how there can be the fruition of actions through enjoyments that do not touch the enjoyer, he says: "It arises.

In reality, the Self, though entirely fearless, itself arises in accordance with various actions; and having arisen, it manifests as the state of enjoyer and enjoyed, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, along with their respective substrates.
And by causing the fourteen worlds to revolve through his mere non-presence, he remains;
the meaning is that this itself is his fruit of action. || 6 ||
He is eternally composed of constant vibration due to his divine nature as the Ever-Moving One;
yet he is eternally inactive even as a pillar, and more stainless than space itself.
Now, one might ask: how can that which is motionless cause a turning back? To this he says: "eternal," etc.
Since the existence of eternal selfhood itself is the existence of motion, it is eternally composed of motion, eternally inactive, and eternally untainted. || 7 ||
He agitates the minds just as the wind stirs the sprouts;
he drives his own row of senses like a charioteer driving a team of horses.
Now, it may be argued that it is the mind or the senses that set the body and so forth into motion, not the Self; to this he replies with the words "the minds" (manāṃsi).
He refers to the "row of the senses" (akṣapaṅktim) as the row of the faculties. || 8 ||
Always engaged in action within the house of the body— which is as difficult to manage as that of an extremely wretched person—
he remains established in his own self like a sovereign emperor, an all-pervading enjoyer of experiences.

[He was] like one whose condition is extremely wretched and difficult to behold; the word "iva" (like) is intended to indicate the falsity of that wretched state, and it should be applied even to his previously contradictory conditions. || 9 ||
This very one must always be sought, praised, and meditated upon;
by means of him, one transcends old age, death, and delusion and proceeds [to liberation]. (10)
The phrase "by this being sought" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 10 ||
This [Self] is exceedingly easy to obtain and easy to attain like a trusted kinsman;
it is the bee within the lotus-cavity of the body for everyone. (11)
It is easily obtained, meaning it can be attained through mere knowledge; it is easily mastered, meaning it is fit to be brought under control through mere mindfulness. || 11 ||
Even when not reviled and even when not summoned, he is obtained from his very own body;
even when merely slightly invoked, he appears face-to-face in an instant. (12)

The sense is that there is gain from the calling out and addressing of a friend or the like who is at a distance; however, for one who is slightly distant, there is gain merely from being called, whereas for this [deity], it depends upon both. He is "invoked" (upahūta), meaning remembered through the utterance of the syllable Om (praṇava). || 12 ||
Even when being attended upon, he who possesses every prosperity does not experience pride or arrogance, just as one who is a lord of wealth [might]. (13)
The meaning is that, unlike the case of a lord or a wealthy man for whom pride, arrogance, haughtiness, and the disparagement of others might be expected, such things do not exist in him. || 13 ||
As fragrance resides in flowers, as oil in sesame seeds, and as taste in various flavors, so does the Divine abide within bodies. (14)
He explains how this exists in the body: "Fragrance" (āmoda) [is the scent], and "taste" (āsvāda) is sweetness (mādhurya). || 14 ||
Due to a lack of discernment, this conscious being, though residing within the heart,
is not recognized for a long time— just like a kinsman seen before one's eyes after a long absence (or, according to another reading, "seen after a long time"). || 15 ||
Having not been seen for a long time, he is now seen before me like a kinsman, such as a father or other relative.
When this Supreme Lord is fully known through investigation,
supreme bliss arises, just as it does when a beloved person is found.
When this supreme kinsman, who bestows unrestrained bliss, is beheld,
various perspectives arise through which all fragmentation dissolves.
Destruction (bhaṅga) is the severance [of existence] such as death and so forth. || 17 ||
All bonds are severed on every side, and all enemies are destroyed;
hopes do not cut into the minds, just as wicked rats do not gnaw at houses. (18)
The snares are affection and the like; the enemies are desire and the like; the hopes are thirst. || 18 ||
When this is seen, the world is seen; when this is heard, everything is heard;
when this is touched, the world is touched; and when this is situated, the world is situated.

He states that through the knowledge of this one, there is the knowledge of all: "In this" (asmin). The meaning is that while this [Self] exists, the world has its existence dependent upon His existence. || 19 ||
This one keeps watch over those who sleep; he strikes down the undiscerning;
he removes the calamity of the distressed; and he bestows [virtue] upon the high-souled. (20)

Relying on the Śruti text, "This Person remains awake while others sleep, fashioning every desire," he says, "This. For those of small minds—those who worship a limited Lord—for the afflicted, He removes their distress and bestows what they desire; this is the sense. || 20 ||
This very life-force (jīva) wanders through the worlds for the maintenance of the universe;
it indeed delights in enjoyments and vibrates within all objects. || 21 ||

In the maintenance of the world, this very Self, having become the individual soul (jīva), wanders about, revels in enjoyments, flashes forth, and shines amidst objects such as garments, ornaments, social gatherings, and festivals. 21.
Therefore, the worldly being, experiencing the self by means of the self through tranquility,
abides within all bodies like pungency resides in black peppers.

He says—“by the Self”—to show that even during the state of delusion regarding the distinction of individual souls, which is uncommon [to the enlightened], there is no impairment of the manifestation of the common, singular identity. || 22 ||

Consisting of volition and the faculty of calculation, formless, and resting upon both the external and the internal, it abides as the universal existence within the multitude of objects in the world. || 23 ||
He is the synthesis of the preceding and the succeeding, consciousness, the perception of the present, and the mental construction;

he is that very form which rests upon all external and internal adjuncts of consciousness. Within the totality of the objects of the world, however, he abides as the nature of the mere universal existence that underlies them all, pervading everything. (23)
This is emptiness in space; this is the movement in the ever-moving wind; this is the radiance in fire; and this is the supreme essence in water. (24)
Just as hardness resides in the earth, heat in fire, coolness in the moon, and existence in the multitude of worldly beings; so too does he reside [in all]. || 25 ||
Just as blackness is in a lump of ink, as coldness is in a particle of snow,
and as fragrance is in flowers, so the Lord of the body resides within the body.
Likewise, the meaning is that the self, as the lord of the body, shines within the body. || 26 ||
Just as existence is all-pervading, just as time is all-pervading, and just as the power of sovereignty belongs to him who is present in every place, so too is the earth. || 27 ||

He demonstrates, by means of two verses beginning with "Just as," that luminosity itself—which is distinct from the mind, the senses, and so forth, and is common to all fields—is illustrated through examples. || 27 ||
This Great God (Mahādeva), who is eternal and the awakener of the gods themselves, exists as a being endowed with form, light, and mental attention, both for others and for himself. || 28 ||
Just as these examples illustrate,
