so too that which manifests external and internal objects through the operation of the eyes and other senses, through forms and light, and through mental attention and the functions of the mind, is the activity of the Self; thus, its essential nature is pure luminosity.

This is the meaning. Thus, with respect to the divine realm (adhidaiva), the connection is through love: "I alone am this well-known Mahādeva, the awakener even of all the gods, such as Sūrya, Indra, Candra, and others. || 28 ||
I alone am; indeed, no other mental construction exists for me, just as the sky is untouched by a particle of dust or a lotus leaf by water. (29)
By means of a minute, most subtle particle of dust. || 29 ||
Just as there is no connection with others in me regarding a stone out of agitation,
so let the fortunes of pleasure and pain not fall upon my body, or let them fall.
With agitation, such as trembling from fear and so forth. || 30 ||
What harm has befallen us by these streams falling upon the gourd?
It is like a lamp that, having passed beyond its wick, cannot be tied down by its cord. || 31 ||

*Tumbaka* means a gourd (*alābū*). The particle *ca* is used in the sense of *iva* (like). Thus, the meaning is "like a stream of water. The intention is: "for us who are like the empty space within a gourd. Just as the light of a lamp, having emerged after passing beyond its components—the oil, the wick, and the vessel—is not bound by the cord [that holds it], [so too is the Self]. || 31 ||
Likewise, I am not bound, for I transcend the entire multitude of existents;
what connection can there be between me and desires, states of being and non-being, or the sense organs? (32)
With what is the sky connected, and with what is the mind obstructed?
When the body has been shattered into a hundred pieces, what injury is there for the embodied soul? (33)
It is compressed and struck; the sense is that this is because it is formless (amūrta). || 33 ||
When the jar is broken, pierced, or worn away, what loss is there to the space within the jar?
Like an invisible ghost, the mind has arisen in vain.
When it is broken into pieces like skull-bowls, when it is perforated by the state of having holes, when it is wounded, and when it is diminished by the depletion of its clay. || 34 ||
When that inert thing is destroyed through awakening, what loss has befallen us?
That which consists of the latent impressions of pleasure and pain—that is my mind.

Because of the realization of the Self as distinct from the mind through awakening; the meaning is that for one whose latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of pleasure and pain was such a mind previously during the state of ignorance, it no longer exists now. || 35 ||
Formerly there was only one, who has today attained immense bliss;
yet one person enjoys, another takes [the fruit], while another faces the calamity of misfortune. (36)
The bodiless, undivided bliss is the repose of happiness. || 36 ||
Another observes: "Oh, what folly! To whom indeed does this wheel belong?
Nature experiences it, while the mind and body suffer its distress. (37)

The meaning is: due to the identity of these—the enjoyer and so forth—this foolishness characterized by superimposition is like the skill of a magician’s wheel in its circular revolution. He shows the distinction between the enjoyer and the rest with the words:
"He enjoys" (bhuṅkte). || 37 ||
The evil-minded one here possesses only folly; there is no other harm at all.
I have no desire for the persistence of enjoyments, nor do I have any desire for the abandonment of enjoyments. (38)

The self is defiled by nature and so forth, and defects are superimposed upon it; however, through critical inquiry (vimarśa), there is some degree of ignorance [removed], and thus there is no injury [to the self]. This is the meaning. || 38 ||
Let that which comes, come; let that which departs, depart.
I have no longing for pleasures, nor do I have any aversion toward states of suffering. (39)
Let pleasures and pains come or let them go; who am I in relation to these?
Whether there be various latent impressions (vāsanās) in the body or their cessation, [it is all the same]. (40)
"Let them go; I am not among them, nor do they belong to me in any way.
For all this time, I have been struck down by the enemy that is ignorance. (41)
These are indeed the latent impressions (vāsanās). || 41 ||
Having seized the entire essence of discernment and utterly crushed it in solitude by means of the beautiful grace of Viṣṇu arising from within himself, [he remained]. (42)
"Crushed" means destroyed by the enemy that is ignorance (*ajñāna*). In the reading "avabodhitam," the analysis of the compound is *aviveka-sarvasvam* (the entire essence of non-discrimination).

By the grace (*prasāda*) and favor (*anugraha*) of Viṣṇu, having taken away my entire essence of non-discrimination, Brahman—which is solitary and possesses a single, constant nature—has been made known to me. || 42 ||
Now, having fully understood it, I have robbed this demon of egoism from the hollow of the tree that is my body. (43)
"Parimoṣitaḥ" means robbed or plundered. || 43 ||
By means of the mantra of awakening others, I have now driven away this yakṣa of egoism from the great tree that is my body. (44)
Now, since the yakṣa of egoism has emerged from this great tree that is my body, it has thereby attained a state of sanctity. || 44 ||
Having attained the stainless state of merit, he shines as if in full bloom;
with the poverty of delusion stilled, he exists upon the exhaustion of the fault of evil desires.
I stand as the Supreme Lord, having accumulated the wealth of discernment;
all that is to be known has been known, and all sights to be seen have been beheld.
"Having obtained the accumulation of the wealth of discernment"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 46 ||
That has now been attained by me, through which nothing remains unattained;
by good fortune, I have cast far away misfortunes and am freed from the serpent of sense-objects.
It has its delusive frost completely stilled, its mirage of hope extinguished;
it is free from the dust of all directions, and possesses the cooling tree of tranquility.
Through praise, prostration, petition, tranquility, and self-restraint, I have reached the vast and exalted ground of ultimate reality.
It was obtained through the praise, prostration, petition, and prayer of Viṣṇu, by means of the mouth of Vara. || 49 ||
This Lord, the Self, has been obtained; He has been clearly seen and realized.
Having transcended the state of egoism, He has finally come within the range of my recollection after a long time. (50)
By its very nature, the Blessed One is the Self, the eternal Brahman of Viṣṇu;
[yet others fall] into the pits of the serpents of the senses, upon the ground of the chasms of death. (51)
The connection with the preceding verse is: "By the grace of Viṣṇu, Brahmā regained his memory.

The connection with the fourth verse, beginning with "indriya," is: "I was utterly deluded. In these compounds, the sense organs themselves are the "snake-holes" (uraga-gartāḥ), meaning the burrows of serpents; the same applies to the subsequent bahuvrīhi compounds as well. || 51 ||
In the thickets of the *karañja* trees of craving, amidst the clamor of desire, within the forest-nets of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and inside the wells of rebirth; || 52 ||
"In the nets born of latent impressions" (vāsanāvanajāleṣu) is the qualifier for all the locative endings [in the preceding verse]. || 52 ||
Amidst the burning of the forest fire of suffering, which extinguishes that very fire of suffering,
there are hundreds of thousands of states of rising and falling, accompanied by the delusions of sinking and emerging.
Where there is only the burning of forest fires of suffering; where there are thieves like forest fires—captivating, yet seizing the wealth and lives of others;
and where there are hundreds of thousands of states of calamity and prosperity that resemble falling and rising.
By those whose downward courses consist mostly of immersion, and whose upward courses consist mostly of emergence. || 53 ||
For a long time, I have been utterly deceived by my enemy, egoism, through its manifestations and concealments, and through its various maneuvers like the snares of desire. (54)
For a long time, I have been thoroughly deceived by the enemy characterized as the ego-sense, and I have been tormented by this self-bewilderment.
Just as one of feeble strength in the forest might be overcome by a *piśāca* during the night,
so now, indeed, by his own power of action alone, [he shall be subdued] by himself.

Under the pretext of Śauri—that is, by means of the guise of a gracious Viṣṇu—Vivekaśrī herself was awakened and inflamed by him. When she, Vivekaśrī, has become awakened within the Lord, the Sovereign, that is, within one's own self (svātman), then [all is attained]. || 55 ||
Through the mediation of Śauri, the glory of discernment was awakened;
now that the Lord Īśāna has been awakened, I shall [confront] that demon of egoism.
Just as one does not see darkness when the lamp of the sky is blazing, so I do not see that yakṣa of egoism which dwells in the hollow of the mind.
"O Lord, like an extinguished lamp, I do not know your destination; yet even as you were seen by me, O Ishana, you became intent on flight. (58)
When that false egoism has arisen like a demon, my perfected pride is like a thief at the rising of the sun. (59)
It was like a grove (ārāma) containing trees (druma), from which a great serpent (gonasa)—having previously arisen from ignorance regarding what is non-existent and having now departed—had gone out;
for the word *dru*, denoting a tree, takes the suffix *ma* in the sense of possession according to the rule *dyudrubhyāṃ maḥ*. || 59 ||
When it has gone, I remain established in my own well-being like a tree devoid of serpents;
being fully awakened, I am at peace and I am extinguished within this world.
"I have been abandoned by the thief; I am at last at peace for a long time to come. I have attained inner coolness, and the mirage of my desires has been stilled. (61)
By the thief, by the ego-sense which steals away one's true self. || 61 ||

Having bathed in the abundance of rain-clouds of the monsoon, like a mountain whose forest fires have been extinguished, one should wipe away this notion of "I" through reflection upon one's own true nature. 62.
With the forest fire of his afflictions extinguished, he is like an immovable mountain, a fireless forest conflagration. || 62 ||
What is delusion? What are the sorrows? What are the evil desires? What are the anxieties?
The delusions of hell, heaven, liberation, and so forth exist only when the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) is present. (63)
What are anxieties? They are mental agonies. To the question of why there would not be anxieties arising from thoughts of suffering in the next world and so forth, he says: "Hell... (verse 63).
Just as paintings proceed only upon a wall and not in the expanse of the sky,
so too the wonder of knowledge does not shine in a mind tainted by the subtle element of egoism,
just as the coloring of saffron does not shine on a faded garment.
One might object: "Even while egoism (ahaṃkāra) exists, why could there not be the wondrous pacification of delusion and other afflictions?
To this, he says: "Ahaṃkāra... [etc.]. This refers to the state of being afflicted by the bile (pitta) characterized by a portion of egoism—that is, when there is madness born of bile. || 64 ||
In the autumnal sky of the mind, which is a cloudless mass of water devoid of the showers of craving, there shines a splendorous clarity.

Now, manifesting himself through various forms such as lakes and oceans, he pays homage with the words beginning "nirahaṃkārā" (free from ego): "kāntiśālinī" means possessing the splendor of the moon of the Self; "svacchatā" means purity. || 65 ||
Obeisance again and again to you, O Self, whose mud of egoism has been washed away, whose inner being is perfectly serene, and who are a lake of the nectar of bliss.
To me, who am the innermost self; to you, who are Brahman. The same applies hereafter as well. || 66 ||
Salutations again and again to you, O Self, who are the ocean of bliss, whose fierce crocodiles are the tranquil senses, and in whom the forest fire of the mind has been extinguished. 67.
Salutations again and again to him who has gone beyond the clouds of egoism, for whom the forest fire of desire has been extinguished, who is a mountain of bliss, and who is at rest.
To the one who is rested and immovable. || 68 ||
Salutations again and again within to you, O Self, who are like a lotus of blossoming bliss, whose nature is a wave of peaceful contemplation, and who possess a noble mind. 69.
To the True Brahman, characterized by that [nature]; to the mental lake of the gods. 69.
Salutations again and again within to my own Self, who dwells in the hollow of the lotus, who is the swan of the entire mind, and who belongs to the side of the manifestation of consciousness.

That which has as its two wings consciousness and appearance—namely, the consciousness that is the reflection in the intellect and the consciousness that is the reflection in its modifications. || 70 ||

Salutations again and again to you, the Moon, who assumes forms through the divisions of time (kalās) yet remains partless, whose essence is nectar, who is eternally risen, and whose nature is fullness.

By the "parts" (kalāḥ) either those mentioned in the Śruti, "From this [Being] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses," numbering seventeen, or those indicated by the Śruti, "O gentle one, the person consists of sixteen parts"; or, in the case of the moon, by its well-known [sixteen] digits. To the partless, the one without limbs; or, in the case of the moon, to the divine self distinct from the digits.
Salutations again and again to the sun of consciousness, which is eternally risen, peaceful, the dispeller of the great darkness of the heart, all-pervading, yet invisible.

The distinction [of the inner sun] from the well-known [external] sun is shown by such qualifiers as "ever-risen" (*sadodita*) and so forth; it is for the peaceful one (*śānta*), the non-heating one (*atāpaka*), and for the invisible one (*adṛśya*), who is distinct from the visible. || 72 ||

Salutations again and again to the lamp of consciousness, which is without oil yet kindled by its own luster, whose wick has emerged from the [ordinary] state of existence, and which is steadfast, resting upon its own intrinsic nature as its support.

"Free from attachment" (asneha) means devoid of oil; "lamp of attachment" (snehadīpa) means that which illuminates supreme love (sneha). Alternatively, ascetics are those who have no attachment to sons, friends, wealth, and so forth, and [the Lord] shines by their devotion.
[Salutations] to the support of the intrinsic nature of all things, to the steadfast one, and to the illuminator of the intellect. || 73 ||
My mind, scorched within by the fire of passion, has been forcibly broken by my cool heart,
just as heated iron is shattered by cold iron.

Now he rejoices that his own human effort has borne fruit, with the verse beginning "Madana... and so forth. Just as iron is broken by a heated iron hammer, so too has my mind—which was scorched by the fire of passion—been broken by me through a mind cooled and endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and other virtues; this is the meaning. || 74 ||
Having repeatedly severed sense-faculty by sense-faculty, and having severed mind by mind, and having severed egoity by means of egoity—I remain as the Residue; thus do I conquer.

Having severed that very [mind] which is directed outward by means of the senses, such as the eyes, which are directed inward; the same should be understood for the mind (manas) and the ego (ahaṃkāra) as well. I am the remaining, residual pure consciousness alone. || 75 ||

Having severed non-existence by means of existence, and having abandoned craving through non-craving; having crushed ignorance with wisdom, you are the Knower who has become the Unknowable—you are the Truth, homage to you! || 76 ||

With *bhāva* means with faith. *Abhāva* means lack of faith. *Prajñā* is the intellect endowed with the capacity for reasoning and refutation; by that, one abandons *aprajñā*, which is characterized by a lack of inquiry, doubt, and so forth. One who is ignorant (*ajña*) is devoid of the conceit of being a knower, whereas one who is wise (*jña*) has the nature of pure consciousness alone. You are truly such; to you—[here, "to me"]—[I bow].
In some places it is recited: *namaḥ* || 76 ||
When the mind has been severed within the mind and egolessness has been attained, and when all mental states have dissolved through pure being, I remain as the pure, absolute Self.
Through the state of being as Brahman, when the ego-identification with the body and so forth has dissolved.
Free from objective manifestation, free from ego, free from the mental faculty, and free from desire,
my body remains established solely within the pure Self that is mere vibration. (78)

"Free from becoming" (nirbhāvam) means devoid of the intellect that is the cause of mental cultivation. "Without effort" (anīhitam) means devoid of the mind that is the cause of desire. "Pure by mere vibration" (spandamātraśuddha) refers to one whose self is purified by that alone; he abides, that is, lives, as a liberated-while-living (jīvanmukta) in such a state. And thus says the Śruti: "Therefore, one should observe only this single vow: one should breathe in and one should breathe out. (78)
This supreme bliss has arisen within me, surpassing even the infinite Lord of the Universe who is compassionate by nature, and it is endowed with the highest tranquility. (79)
From that Lord of the Universe— who effortlessly shows compassion and bestows enjoyment and sovereignty upon His infinite devotees—
there arises a supreme bliss, an unsurpassed repose in absolute joy, which excels even that of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others. || 79 ||
With the vampire of delusion stilled and the demon of egoism departed,
I have become free from the fever of worldly distress, liberated from the form of the wicked man-eater.
He is liberated from that Rūpikā Piśācī; for this very reason, he is free from fever. || 80 ||
Having severed the cord of the rope of craving from the cage of my own body,
I know not where the bird of wicked egoism has flown away.
In this tree of the body, whose nest of dense ignorance has been shaken loose, I know not where the bird of egoity has flown away. (82)
It has been raised up by the grinding of the practice of knowledge, turned to dust, and cast upward. || 82 ||

By good fortune, my numerous latent impressions (vāsanās)—which were soiled by the long-standing wickedness of evil desires and by the ashes of worldly enjoyments, and which were nourished by the serpents of fear—have been destroyed. 83.

She is grey and soiled by long-standing evil desires and by the false identifications with the body and other things as the self; she is the refuge of the serpents characterized by fear. She is the "ashes of enjoyment" (bhogabhasma), because she reduces enjoyments to ashes—that is, she is the meditative absorption (samādhi) by which the numerous bad latent impressions have been destroyed and eradicated. || 83 ||
For how long have I existed? What is this strange phenomenon, by which I have fallen into such false and firm identification with the ego? (84)
Now, upon the waning of sleep, as if remembering a former nightmare from a dream, he is struck with wonder, saying: "For so long... This is marvelous and astonishing. || 84 ||
Today I am truly born; today I have become one of great intelligence, since I have been completely released from the great cloud of egoism by Kṛṣṇa.
Today I have become, I have manifested, as one whose very nature is the unsurpassed bliss being experienced here and now;

for I am one whose great intellect—the cognitive modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of direct realization—has taken the form of the unlimited Brahman, and thus I have completely, utterly abandoned the great cloud of egoism. The meaning is that I am liberated.
This Blessed One, the Self, has been seen by me; likewise, He has been realized, grasped, experienced, and, O dear one, established within my own direct experience. (86)

He clarifies this term "Mahāmatis" as follows: "Seen" means perceived through the authority of scripture (*vākya-pramāṇa*), realized through reflection (*manana*), and experienced through the mind in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) after attaining long-term union with it; such a one is always present within his own experience, like his own body.

Thus they have said: "The knowledge that [the self] is the body is sublated by the knowledge that [the self] is not the body; he in whom this knowledge arises regarding the Self alone is liberated, even against his will. (86)
It has lost its foothold, is free from mentation, and devoid of longing; it is set aside by the delusions of clever egoism;
it is desireless and stripped of the coloring of passion.
This mind has attained tranquility, free from curiosity. || 87 ||
He says that his own mind has now attained tranquility, free from fault and distraction—expressed by the words "having lost its foothold" (*gatāspadam*).
"Having lost its foothold" means being devoid of objects; for it is well known that desire for objects arises from the mental processing (*manana*) of them.
Thus, through the uprooting of its foundation, it is free from mental processing and free from desire. It is "skillful," meaning it has utterly cast aside [distraction].

"Rejected" means abandoned; for this very reason, it is "inactive," meaning motionless. It is "devoid of curiosity," meaning free from the longing for enjoyment. For this very reason, the sense is that it has attained tranquility like a fire without fuel. || 87 ||
The great calamities— difficult to cross, both even and uneven, most hard to endure, and productive of long-lasting faults—
have come to an end; Maheśvara has attained [liberation].
The non-mind-state exists within the river of non-dual consciousness.

Concluding by stating that through the tranquility of the mind alone there occurs the cessation of all calamities and the attainment of the self which is unsurpassed bliss, he says: "Difficult to cross. The "sources of power" are the successions of births in various wombs;
the "long-lasting defects" are desire, greed, delusion, and so forth; and the "equalities" are those which bestow such [defects] and consist of uniform suffering over a long period of time.

The uneven great calamities, consisting of various sufferings at every moment, have gone to destruction; the Great Lord, who is non-dual consciousness and whose nature is perfect bliss, has been fully realized and attained. Why is that? Because within—the innermost self (pratyagātman)—the state of being non-consciousness, which is the dullness born of ignorance, has departed, meaning it has been sublated by knowledge. || 88 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fifth canto, titled "Contemplation on Brahman and the Self," in the section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (Sage) tradition. 35.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth canto, titled "Contemplation on Brahman and the Self" (or "Contemplation on the Attainment of the Nature of Brahman and the Self"), in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-sixth canto.
Prahlāda said:
The Self, which transcends all states, has finally come back to my recollection after a long time.
By good fortune you have been found, O Blessed One; salutations be unto you, the Great-Souled One. || 1 ||
Having attained the Self which is so difficult to find, Prahlāda bows down again and again;
he praises it and rejoices, delighting in solitude like a beloved woman with her lover. || 1 ||

The Self (Ātman) is the inward-facing reality, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss, transcending all states beginning from human joy up to that of Hiraṇyagarbha—all those levels which are stations of increasing excellence in happiness. To the Great-Souled One (Mahātmane), whose nature is unlimited. || 1 ||
Having saluted you and gazed upon you for a long time, I embrace you;
O Blessed One, who else in the three worlds could be my kinsman other than you?
You are embraced for a long time with a state of equal flavor like the waters of the milk-ocean, and you are experienced within meditative absorption as the most beloved kinsman. || 2 ||
You kill, you protect, you give; you praise, you go, you leap about.
You have arrived, you are seen; what do you do? Where are you going? (3)
As long as You have not been attained and seen, You become Death and strike down those who are not Your devotees;
You protect Your devotees. Worshipped through the acts of adoration, You grant [boons]; You praise [them] in the form of a panegyrist and the like;
You go in the form of a messenger; and You sport and act in every possible form. But by me, this...

My nature is eternally immediate; it has been attained and seen. Beyond this, what can you do for me, or where can you go? The meaning is that you are no longer able to go elsewhere or to act as you did before. || 3 ||
O you who fill the entire universe with your own existence, O friend of all people!
You are perceived everywhere at all times; where can you flee now? (4)
Beneficial for all people, it is "viśvajanīna. || 4 ||
The vast interval between our two births has today, by good fortune, become no distance at all; for you have been seen, O kinsman! (5)

The "interval" is the veiling ignorance; the word "was" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Today, through the destruction of that [ignorance], there has been attained an extreme proximity characterized by absolute non-difference, which is not far off. || 5 ||

Salutations to you who have accomplished all that was to be done; salutations be to you, the creator and the sustainer. Salutations to the one who is the stalk of worldly existence, the eternal, and the pure-souled one.
For the stalk of the leaf that has the characteristic of saṃsāra. || 6 ||
Salutations to the one who holds a discus and a lotus in his hands; salutations to the wearer of the crescent moon;
salutations to the lord of the wise; salutations to you, the one born from the lotus.
To the Lord of the Gods, who has the form of Indra. || 7 ||
This distinction between us here, which exists solely through the perception of the signified and the signifier,
is a false conceptualization, like that between a wave and the water of the wave.
From the perspective of the signified and the signifier, and from the perspective of conventional usage; this is the perspective of conventional usage, and it is also differentiation. (8)
You alone, through your infinite form consisting of the manifold variety of endless objects, ever-expanding and sporting with both existence and non-existence, manifest yourself eternally.
The remainder of the phrase is "by infinite conceptualization. It is eternal, beginningless in its stream [in some places it is also read as "by the river of the stream"]. (9)
Homage to the Seer, homage to the Creator, homage to the one of infinite expansion;
homage to the essence of all things, homage to you, the soul of all. 10.

First, to the Seer of the objects to be created; then, to the Creator; and to Him who, having created, expands through infinite forms; for this very reason, to the one whose nature is all things; and to the Universal Self as the underlying substratum. || 10 ||
Throughout many births, for a long time, I have endured manifold and protracted sufferings—
burnt and robbed of my vital energy by you, as instructed by me.

He says, "Throughout this much time, you yourself, by following my will, were peaceful in the form of 'I'; now, by you alone, you have been obtained for rest"—this is expressed in the verse beginning with "In every birth. By me—who has attained my own state and become the individual soul (jīva)—you were instructed by me through the wrong path according to the defects of your own desires and so forth.
Because it has come into operation, it is burnt; for that very reason, its power being destroyed, the state of the Lord is concealed. || 11 ||
The ways of the world have been looked upon, and the views of illustrative examples have been seen;
yet by this, you have not attained reality—nothing at all has been acquired. (12)

By you, the delusions of wandering through the upper, lower, and middle worlds as perceived by worldly vision were observed, as well as the perspectives of illustrative examples conducive to discernment regarding them. Therefore, from that observation of external worlds, nothing at all— not even the slightest— was attained by you through this viewing of the three worlds.
The meaning of the two [statements] is that the form of the human goal would not have been attained, nor did it exist [in the past]. || 12 ||
This entire world consists of nothing but earth, wood, stone, and water;
O Lord, there is nothing here apart from you that one does not desire to attain. (13)
To explain why it was not [found] there, he says: "all. One does not desire that which is such a thing for which the desire for human goals (puruṣārtha) is fulfilled;
the meaning is that, apart from you (tvadṛte), there is nothing else like that in this world. || 13 ||
O God, today you have been found, seen, and attained;
you have been reached and grasped. Salutations to you, for you do not become deluded.
"You are not deluded; that is to say, you have crossed over delusion. || 14 ||
O Lord, he whose body is interwoven by the network of rays from the pupils of his eyes, abiding here in the form of vision—how is it that he is not seen here? 15.

If it is asked, "How am I seen?", he says "He who" (*yaḥ*), referring to the means shown in the scripture: "That which is known through awakening" (*pratibodhaviditam matam*). This occurs when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) goes out toward the location of the jar and other objects by way of the eye, assuming the form of the manifestation of all functions such as vision.
The meaning is that its essence is the consciousness delimited by that [object], and it exists with its form woven into the network of rays from the pupil of the eye;
this should be inferred in the same way for what follows as well. || 15 ||

Since this [consciousness] touches everything—touching both skin and touch, as well as scent—just as oil exists within the sesame seed, and since it brings touch into its own interior, how is it that it is not perceived? (16)

Touching the skin, the sense of touch, and qualities such as heat by means of its tactile function and pervading them, it internalizes and perceives touch—such as cold and so forth—just as oil within a sesame seed internalizes and grasps the fragrance of a flower joined with the sesame; likewise, having pervaded them, it internalizes and illuminates touch. || 16 ||
How can he who, upon hearing a sound, internally contemplates the supreme power of that sound and causes his body's hair to stand on end, be considered distant? (17)
Reflecting upon and manifesting the power of sound and the aesthetic wonder of the qualities of song, poetry, and so forth. || 17 ||
To whom would he not be pleasing—he whose tongue, like a sprout, relishes things even before they have been tasted? (18)

Objects such as sweet, sour, and so forth, taste well even before—that is, prior to—the tasting of that which is the natural object of affection. "Tastes well" means it manifests as a state of happiness. 18.
Who does not hold within their grasp that body which one gazes upon with affection, taking up its flower-like fragrance with the hand of the nose? (19)

By means of the nose, which functions as an instrument of grasping just like a hand, he perceives—that is, clearly beholds as if it were directly before his eyes—the fragrance of the flowers from the garland held at his throat, and thus views his own body as adorned with a wreath. This is the meaning. || 19 ||
How indeed can that Self, which is sung of through the Vedas, Vedānta, established doctrines, logic, Purāṇas, and hymns, be forgotten once it has been realized? 20.
This very same series of bodies and enjoyments, though once so delightful, no longer tastes sweet within me today,
now that you— the supreme and the inferior— have been beheld in your pure self.
By you, as a stainless lamp, the sun has been made manifest;
by you, with your cool frost, the moon has attained its chill.
He also says "by you," based on the vision of such scriptural passages as, "By whose splendor the sun blazes, kindled with heat. || 22 ||
By you these mountains, these teachers, have been supported; by you these sky-dwellers have been sustained.
By you alone this earth is made firm, and by you alone the sky is held aloft.
Those that move by day and those that move through the sky, such as the winds and so forth; the wise are immovable; the atmosphere provides space. 23.
By good fortune you have attained me; by good fortune I have gone to you.
O Lord, I am you and you are I; by good fortune there is no difference between us.
"By good fortune" means by luck. Through the exchange of "I am you" and "you are I," non-duality has been firmly established. || 24 ||
Salutations again and again to the Great Soul, who is joined with the two synonymous words "I" and "you," whether belonging to you or to me. (25)

Now, he pays homage to the two words "I" (*aham*) and "Thou" (*tvam*), which have become the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the non-limited sense (*akhaṇḍārtha*): "I. These two synonyms serve to indicate the Great Self (*mahātman*), the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*).

[He does so] by referring to "Thee," whose denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) is qualified by the causal adjunct (*kāraṇopādhi*), and "Me," whose denoted meaning is qualified by the effected adjunct (*kāryopādhi*).

Or, because of the conceptualization of difference through two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that are like branches—being partial manifestations—which are conjoined, expressed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and linked by the two words "I" and "thou"; the repetition "namo namaḥ" is out of reverence; or there are two *vā* (or) particles.
These two [words] are intended to indicate the falsity of the connection with both branches. || 25 ||
Homage to me, the infinite one, whose nature is free from ego;
homage to me, the formless one; homage to the Self who is perfectly equal.

Now, having offered salutation to the partless reality (akhaṇḍārtha) by emphasizing its aspect as the inner self (pratyak), he demonstrates that very [self] as Brahman with the verse beginning "namaḥ" and so forth. || 26 ||
Abide right here in your own Self— equal, pure, the witness, free from all attributes, and unconditioned by space, time, and the like.
O Brahman, you abide within me as the very nature of the inward-facing Self (pratyak-svabhāva), never in the outward-facing state (parāgbhāva);
such is the meaning. || 27 ||
The mind becomes intensely agitated, the functions of the senses throb,
and the expansive power that flows through the prāṇa and apāna breaths surges forth.

How is this known? To this he says: "By the mind. The meaning is that it is known through the fact that the mind and the other senses are the movers [of their objects] like a magnet, as shown by such scriptural passages as, "Impelled by whom does the mind fly forth, sent forth? (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.3). || 28 ||
The machines of bodies, smeared with skin, flesh, and bone, and possessing the mind as their charioteer, are drawn along by the reins of desire. (29)
I am this very embodiment of consciousness; I am not anything whatsoever, nor do I have any fixed abode. Let the body fall or rise according to whatever desire it pleases.

In that case, are you the power of vital breath and so forth, or are you the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and the like which have made their abode in the body? He says "no"—"This one" (*ayam*). This one is the very body of consciousness (*saṃvid-vapuḥ*), and not some power, nor is he one who has made his abode in the object of meditation [the reading *deha-kṛta* is preferred]. If it is asked, "Then what do you have to do with the body?", he says, "Nothing at all."
"The body," thus [ends the section]. 30.
After a long time, I have been born as "I," and after a long time, this attainment of my own self has occurred;
after a long time, it comes to rest, just as the world does at the end of a kalpa.
The delusion comes to rest; this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 31 ||
Having traveled for so long upon the extended path of saṃsāra,
I am weary and have long been resting, like a fire at the end of a kalpa.
Because it leads to saṃsāra and because its nature is to wander within saṃsāra; for so long a time I have been weary on the path of saṃsāra, but now I am at rest. || 32 ||
Salutations again and again to you who transcend all and encompass all;
salutations also to those who speak of me and of you.
Those who are the gurus and the Vedantas proclaim you and me to be indeed my very own form.
Victorious is the witnesshood of the Supreme Self, which possesses all infinite enjoyments, is untouched by the functions of defects, and is free from any exertion.

She whose infinite and complete enjoyments are thus made manifest, yet who remains untouched by the functioning of faults that lead to manifestation; she by whom no agitation or obsession has been created—meaning she is indifferent—and for this very reason, she is victorious. 34.
Like fragrance in its flower, like wind in a bellows, and like oil in sesame seeds, you abide everywhere within this body. (35)
He says, "In yourself," [implying] that you alone are the essence everywhere. || 35 ||
You laugh, you watch, you give, you thunder forth, and you leap;
though your nature is free from egoism, this illusory power of yours is truly wondrous.
He says "Thou art the Haṃsī" to show that Thou alone art the creator of all. || 36 ||
I conquer, with the blazing radiance of my sovereign power, opening wide the entire world; I conquer again, with all undertakings stilled, closing the world once more.
At the time of creation, by You, the Lord and the conscious Self,

whose blazing radiance illumines all things both within and without, I was kindled; having entered as the individual soul (*jīva*), I manifest and unfold the entire universe consisting of name and form, and thus I triumph through Your very self.

Having brought [the world] under my control, I protect it; and at the time of dissolution, having ceased all activity and closing the world once again, I withdraw it and conquer—that is, I overcome it—by means of my own self alone. || 37 ||
Within a single atom of yours, this entire circle of the world-system exists; just as the state of being a banyan tree arises from a banyan seed, so it has been, is, and will be.

Of the atom (*paramāṇu*), which is extremely subtle; that is to say, difficult to perceive. "Vaṭa-ness" (*vaṭatva*) is the universal (*jāti*) conjoined with the individual instance (*vyakti*) of a banyan tree. || 38 ||
O Lord, just as a cloud in the sky appears in the forms of horses, elephants, and chariots, so too are you perceived through the delusions of hundreds of diverse objects.

For the sake of the non-existence and existence of entities that undergo manifold transformations, become one whose self is liberated from becoming and who stands outside both existence and non-existence. (40)
Now, being himself one whose self is liberated, he teaches the means of liberation to the bound self who is non-different from him,
beginning with the words "of entities" (*bhāvānām*). [This is] for the sake of the cessation— that is, the sublation— of "entities" which have the nature of manifold transformations (*bhaṅga*),
and for the sake of their arising— that is, the manifestation of the nature of unsurpassed bliss— by means of the vision of the unattached Self.
Excluded from both existence and non-existence, being thus solitary, always remain one whose self is liberated by that very state; do not again incur bondage—this is the meaning. || 40 ||
Abandon pride, great anger, turbidity, and likewise cruelty;
the great do not sink into the common mire of worldly qualities.
He teaches the introductory section (pūrvapīṭhikā), which serves as the means for that [realization], beginning with the words "abandon" (jahī) and so forth. || 41 ||
Remembering again and again his former state of long-standing wickedness, he laughed—a laugh as white as a shower of pearls—thinking, "Who am I? What was that which occurred? (42)

The phrase "having thus reflected" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Laughing so that it is white and bright like a mass or cluster of pearls, he abandons his former state of long-standing wickedness; this is the connection with what precedes. || 42 ||
Those undertakings have departed;
those days have passed in which you were strewn with the mass of flames from the fire of anxiety. (43)
Today you are the king in the city of the body with expansive desires;
you are not seized by sorrows nor by pleasures, just as the sky cannot be grasped by hands.
With his hands and fists, as if with the sky. || 44 ||
Having today conquered the horses of the senses and subdued the elephant of the mind, and having utterly shattered the enemy of worldly enjoyment, you now preside over universal sovereignty.
You are the traveler across the shoreless sky, forever setting and rising;
you are the sun that eternally bestows light both externally and internally. 46.
He whose setting and rising occur incessantly—respectively, in the perception of ignorance externally and in the perception of one's own true nature internally;

or rather, the meaning is that from whom the incessant (ajasram), that is, frequent, setting and rising of the world—its dissolution and creation—proceed. This is clear in the case of the Sun. || 46 ||
O All-pervading Lord, you are eternally asleep, yet you are awakened by Śakti for the sake of the play of perceiving enjoyments, just as a lover is awakened by his beloved.
If this is so, then why do I not perceive it as such everywhere? To that he replies: "Always.

You have been asleep from beginningless time. By *śakti*—that is, by the power of the impelling *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force)—you are awakened only to that extent for the sake of the play of observing enjoyments, and not in your form as the full Self; this is the meaning. || 47 ||
The honey of form brought from afar by the small bees of sight is drunk by you, having accepted it with your power while stationed at the window of the eyes.

He clarifies the very play of observing enjoyments with the words "by the minute bees of sight" (*dṛkkṣudrābhiḥ*). "Sights" refers to the functions of the senses, characterized by which are the "minute ones"—specific types of honey-bees.
"Honey" refers to the nectar characterized by forms and so forth. [This occurs] through the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) situated in the windows of the eyes and other sense organs. (48)
By you, through the constant movement of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, the darkness within the hollow of the cosmic egg is observed every moment as it goes and returns to the city of Brahmā.

He states that even the illumination of the path beginning with the *suṣumnā* at the time of the yogis’ departure is entirely dependent upon you—beginning with the words "Brahmāṇḍa. By the terms *prāṇa* and *apāna*, the practice of their restraint (*nirodha*) is indicated.
In the body, which is the city of Brahman (*brahmapura*) because it is the locus for the attainment of Brahman by those yogis intent on that [practice],...
By means of movements consisting of the repeated practice every moment of the vital breaths— concentrated within the heart and conducive to exiting the body,
entering another's body, wandering to other worlds, and so forth— through the coming and going in various channels (*nāḍī*),
one may travel to another cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) or proceed to the solar orb (*sūryamaṇḍala*) by way of the path beginning with light (*arcirādimārga*).

The stages of the path belonging to the cavity of the universe and the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra)—namely, the stages of the channels such as the suṣumṇā—are clearly perceived and seen by you alone, through your own self-luminous instrument. For it is said: "The tip of the heart shines forth; by that light, this Self departs."

Although, according to scripture, for all beings at the time of death the manifestation of the channels as gateways is indeed dependent upon the light of the Self, nevertheless, because non-yogins are unable to attend to it due to being overwhelmed by pain and other such factors,
whereas yogins are attentive both during the time of practice and at the time of death; therefore—
Thus have they been illustrated. || 49 ||
In the flower of the body you are the fragrance; in the moon of the body you are nectar and ambrosia; you are the sap in the tree of the body, and you are the coolness in the ice of the body.

*Ṛta* is that which has become the ultimate truth, the immortal [the reading is *satyamṛtāmṛtam*]. In the tree characterized by the body, it is the sap that serves as the cause for the emergence of the sprouts of passion and the like on its branches. (50)
In you there is a wondrous affection, like clarified butter within the milk of the body;
you abide within the inner self like fire within wood.

The affection that exists in the bodies of all living beings as the cause of pride and arrogance—that very affection resides only in you, who are like the essence of ghee (*sarpiṣ*) within the milk characterized by the body. The meaning is that when you abandon that conceit, no such affection is observed. || 51 ||
You alone are the unsurpassed taste; you are the manifestation even of splendors. You are the knower of all objects, and you are the illuminator of all lights.

It is of unsurpassed flavor, exceedingly sweet, and, in short, of the nature of nectar. Among the luminaries such as the sun and others, it is the supreme divinity (adhidaiva), the source of illumination. And with respect to the self (adhyātma), it is the illuminator of the lights—the sense organs such as the eyes. || 52 ||
You are the vibration of all winds; you are the rut of the elephant that is the mind;
you are both the radiance and the sharpness of the flame of the fire of wisdom.

It is called *spanda* because it causes the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the winds to vibrate. It is the cause of delusion, like the rutting state of an elephant characterized by the mind. Its sharpness is the cause of heat. || 53 ||
Under your influence, this speech of mine dissolves away;
yet, like a lamp, it arises again from somewhere else.
"Vācā" means speech (*vāṇī*). According to the opinion of Bhāguri, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied because the word ends in the consonant *h* (as in *āpah*).
"By your power"—that is, through your withdrawal—everything dissolves and subsides, as occurs in death, fainting, and sleep;
elsewhere, that is, in other bodies. (54)
Likewise, the circles of objects existing within the cycle of transmigration reside in you,
just as the arrangements of bracelets, armlets, and upper-arm ornaments reside in gold.
The phrase "the circles of objects arise" is to be supplied by way of ellipsis. || 55 ||
By means of such words as "you," "this one," and "I" or "you," you yourself praise and speak of the Self by means of the Self for the sake of sport. (56)

He says, "It is you yourself who, within your own self, employ terms such as 'I' and so forth; there is no one other than you," with the words "Bhavān" (You). You praise [yourself] by means of qualities, yet you speak of another. 56.
Just as a cloud driven by a gentle breeze is perceived in the sky by the sight of elephants, horses, and men,
so too are you perceived by the sight of all living beings.
Abda means a cloud. || 57 ||
Just as flame shines within fires in the forms of horses and elephants,
so too are you seen in the creations upon the earth as non-different from them.
When each of the pieces of wood is burning, the form of horses and other such things is sometimes seen in some of the flames. || 58 ||
You are the unbroken thread stretched across all those liberated from the cosmic egg;
you are the field for the crops of living beings, nourished by the elixir of consciousness.

Just as the true nature of cooked meat is perceived through its flavor, so too is the reality of all things— whether they be the characteristics of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), liberated souls, pearls, water, fire, or ether— which were previously unmanifest, revealed by you. (60)

He establishes its nature as a field with the words "by you": "By you, the unmanifest nature is revealed through creation. Just as by the act of cooking, the sweetness of meats—which is worthy of being tasted—is revealed through the perception of its flavor, so it is here. || 60 ||
Even though the splendor of an object exists, it does not abide when you are not present, just as the beauty of a woman’s form does not exist for one whose eyes have been removed.
Thus, he says that although it exists, it is as if non-existent because it is not grasped by the light of consciousness—using the phrase "vidyamāna" (existing) and so forth.
It is like the existence of beauty and charm belonging to a woman [when she is not perceived]. || 61 ||
Even though it was present here, you did not take notice of that object;
your own beauty, reflected in a mirror, did not satisfy you. (52)

The meaning is that what is not "inclined"— that is, not assisted by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*)— is not capable of either existence or causal efficiency, even if it is correctly perceived. For example, the beauty of one's own face— the splendor of one's own countenance— which is reflected from a mirror (*mukurāt*), the instrumental cause, by women...

The meaning is that [this] is not sufficient for the satisfaction resulting from the performance of purposeful actions such as kissing and tasting the lips, nor for the pacification of desire. || 62 ||
Without you, this body rolls upon the ground like a piece of wood or a clod of earth;
though existing, it is as if non-existent, its height lost, like the sun in the dark nights.
The height—the vertical elevation—of the city, the mountain, and the tree, though existing, appeared as if non-existent due to its lack of visibility in the dark nights. || 63 ||
The sequence of pleasure and pain, having reached you, perishes, just as darkness, light, or frost vanishes upon encountering the sky. 64.
Having attained and directly experienced manifestation— the radiance of the sun— these qualities such as pleasure and the rest attain their very existence through your light alone,
just as colors such as white and others appear in the morning through the light of the sun. || 65 ||

Since pleasure and the other [mental states] have acquired their very existence solely through the perception of You, they perish at the very moment of connection with You when You are kindled by the final direct realization; that is to say, they depart and vanish only when You have seen them, and not by any other means. || 65 ||
Having attained their own being, they perish at the very moment of their connection; like the darkness before a lamp, they vanish completely as soon as they are seen. 66.
That darkness, which has become manifest through the absence of a lamp, perishes as soon as it arises at the moment of contact with the lamp. (67)
When the lamp is absent—that is, no longer present—the darkness that had become manifest becomes dense;
at the moment of contact with the light of the lamp, that very [darkness] arises and, having separated from its own substrate, perishes.
However, the meaning is that the substrate itself, whose nature is pure existence, does not perish. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of emphasis (*evārthe*). || 67 ||
Thus, having seen you free from affliction, the fortune of pleasure and pain arises;
yet, as soon as it is born, it perishes through total destruction.
He applies what was stated in the example to the subject of the illustration with the words "tadevam" (thus, in this way). Regarding the phrase "by total destruction":
the meaning is "together with its state as a seed. || 68 ||
Because it is subject to decay, it is not capable of remaining here for even an atom of time,
just like the subtle fraction of time known as a nimeṣalakṣabhāga.

The fortune of pleasure and pain, being fragile by its very nature upon the departure of sense objects, is not capable of remaining here for even an atom of time, nor for even a single moment, within the Self which is the manifestation of eternal and unsurpassed bliss—
just as a subtle and extremely minute fraction of time is known to be a hundred-thousandth part of the duration of a blink of an eye.
The meaning is that it perishes by itself alone, just like that. || 69 ||
The slender city of the Gandharvas— the conceptualization of pleasure, pain, and so forth—
manifests by your grace, yet it dissolves when you are beheld.

Thus, because it is of such an extremely subtle duration, the cultivation of pleasure, pain, and so forth—though false like a city of the Gandharvas and impossible to perceive—is, due to the power of ignorance, manifested as if stable and real; yet when You are seen, it dissolves and perishes—this is the meaning. || 70 ||

Born from the sight of you and perishing at the sight of you—neither perceived as one who has died like being born, nor perceived as one who has been born like being dead—by whom can she be recognized? (71)

This [ignorance], which arose from the eye of the defective vision characterized by the light of non-knowing, perishes through the eye of the light of perfect knowing. Thus, this ignorance is as if dead in the dream and born again upon waking;
it is as if born in the dream and dead again upon waking—this is the meaning. || 71 ||
How could an object that is unstable even for a moment perform a causal function?
How can a garland be perceived [as such] when it consists of waves having the form of lotuses? (72)
Since it is difficult for false objects even to endure for a single moment, their capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is truly marvelous; thus he says: "even for a moment.
[This refers to] forms imagined through the cognition of a lotus by means of the shapes of lotuses. (72)
Or rather, when a thing that has already arisen and perished were to perform an action, then this world would take delight in making garlands out of flashes of lightning. (73)
[Objection: "But why should causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) not occur here as well through momentary [entities], just as it does in the Buddhist view? To this he replies: "Or when...
The sense is that even by the Buddhists, causal efficiency cannot be established as being grounded in valid cognition (*prāmāṇikī*). || 73 ||
Abiding within the minds of those possessed of discernment, you grasp this fortune consisting of pleasure and the like; yet you do not abandon your state of perfect equanimity.

In this manner, although prosperity such as pleasure, pain, and so forth is difficult to reconcile [with the nature of the Self], you indeed grasp it while abiding in the minds of the discerning who recognize its inherent difficulty.
He states the distinction between the non-discerning and the discerning with the words "you do not abandon": || 74 ||
O you who dwell by chance within the innate self of those lacking discrimination— enough of describing that form of yours to me, for it is the abode of no small words.

To the question "What am I? among those who lack discrimination (*avivekin*), there is no answer, because the conceptualizations of the undiscriminating are infinite and irregular; thus he says, "Among those who lack discrimination. By "chance" (*yadṛcchayā*)—meaning by the cause that is the spontaneous awakening of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—the remainder of the sentence is "my speech. [Such speech] is "not capable" (*nālam*), meaning it is not competent [to provide an answer].
"He is the locus of not a few, but infinite, varieties of forms and names of words"—this is an address intended to establish his capacity [for such expression]. (75)
By you—who are effortless, partless, and devoid of ego—agency has been accepted, whether you exist or do not exist. (76)
And with the intention that the superimposition of agency (*kartṛtva-adhyāsa*) is the root cause for being the locus of many words, he says: "by the inactive one" (*nirīheṇa*).

[The agent acts] by means of the existent, which is the adjunct of the gross embodied form (*mūrta-sthūla-deha-upādhi*); and by means of the non-existent, which is the adjunct of the subtle unembodied form (*amūrta-sūkṣma-deha-upādhi*). The word *vā* is intended to indicate the independence of the subtle body in dreams; the word *api* serves to include both bodies together in the waking state.
The purpose is to indicate agency. || 76 ||
Victory to you of fierce and formidable form! Victory to you who are devoted to peace!
Victory to you who transcend all scriptures! Victory to you who are the abode of all scriptures! 77.

Now he praises [the Lord] by means of two verses beginning with "Jaya," using the two well-known forms, the discriminative and the non-discriminative: "Victory to You!"—[this is the first of the two].
He whose form is "proḍḍāmara," meaning exceedingly vast, extending beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and so forth.
The mention of "āgama" (scripture) is an indication for all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). [Thus, the meaning is: O Abode of all scriptures, known through all means of valid cognition. (77)
Victory to you, O Born! Victory to you, O Unborn! Victory to you, O Wounded! Victory to you, O Unwounded! Victory to you, O Being!
Victory to you, O Non-being! Victory to you, O Conquerable! Victory to you, O Invincible! 78.
That which is to be conquered by means of the form of ignorance should be employed for conquest; however, that which is naturally unconquerable cannot be conquered. 78.
I exult, I am pacified, I abide, and I have attained my goal;
I am victorious and I live for victory—salutations to me, salutations be to you!
Therefore, because I possess victory over the form born of ignorance, I am the victor; I live even for the sake of conquering the remainder of my *prārabdha* karma.
While you abide in me— whose self is free from affliction,
established in its own nature, and unstained by passion—
where is bondage, where are calamities, and where are prosperities?
Where are existence and non-existence? I attain eternal peace. || 80 ||

He concludes by stating that, "Abiding in Your true nature, the accomplishment of the removal of all my misfortunes has been achieved"—where, then, are existence and non-existence, birth and death? Therefore, the meaning is: "I attain, I reach, eternal peace, which is the repose of bliss. (80)

Thus ends the thirty-sixth canto, titled "The Self-Praise," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Seers.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Self-Praise," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
While reflecting in this manner, Prahrāda, the slayer of enemy heroes—
He attained the meditative absorption of non-conceptual supreme bliss. || 1 ||
Furthermore, while Prahlāda remained absorbed in meditation here, the city of the Dānavas was seen to be leaderless,
ravaged by bandits, and fallen into a state of wretchedness.
Thus reflecting upon himself in the manner described, || 1 ||
Established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, he remained motionless like a figure depicted in a painting;
abiding in his own true state, he shone as if carved out from a mountain.
One's own station is the sovereignty of one's true nature. || 2 ||
As he remained thus engaged in his practice at home, a great deal of time passed for him, who was situated in the world like the mountain Meru, the enemy of the gods.
As Prahlāda, the enemy of the gods, remained thus in meditative absorption within his own home,
a vast period of time passed, like that of Mount Meru standing in the midst of the world.
Even though the lords of the asuras were awakened, they did not perceive the one of great intelligence,
just as a sprout does not emerge from its seed-vessel despite abundant watering at the wrong time.
From the seed-capsule, from the seed-pod. || 4 ||
Thus, for thousands of years, he remained with his body full and his gaze fixed on a single point;
perfectly tranquil in the city of the Asuras, like the sun reflected upon a stone.

The "plump" (*pīna*) one is the Self, which is Brahman in its state of supreme expansion. If the reading is *pīnāṃsa*, it is clear [in that sense]. "Single-eyed" (*ekadṛk*) refers to the external eye; that is to say, like the sun carved upon a stone—that is to say, being motionless through the transformation into the exclusive state of supreme bliss (*parānanda*).
Devoid of bliss, he has entered a state of appearance that is like a supreme radiance yet devoid of light.

By that [state], the Supreme Bliss (parānanda), known as the stage of Bhūman—which in that condition is exclusively of a single flavor and has transformed into suchness—is not manifested; nor does the Supreme Self (para), in which bliss is absent and is virtually non-existent, shine forth. Thus, he has reached a state resembling death.
Having reached the state of appearance where only the body remains, he has become fit for the perception of the people who see him.
After such a length of time,
that realm of the netherworld became kingless, harsh, and oppressed by the law of the fish.

The "law of the fish" (mātsyanyāya) refers to the groundless killing and other forms of mistreatment of the weak by those who are stronger—whether of their own kind or others—by which they are harassed and oppressed. || 7 ||
When Hiraṇyakaśipu had perished and his son remained absorbed in meditative concentration (samādhi),
there was no other king left in the abode of the sons of Danu.
To the question "Whence [did he come] there?", he says: "In Hiraṇyakaśipu's [abode]," that is, in the Daitya-city, the dwelling place of the sons of Danu.
Despite the efforts of those lords of the asuras seeking him through meditation and even with the greatest exertion, Prahlāda did not wake.
Even with the greatest effort, Prahlāda could not be awakened from his meditative absorption by the Dānavas.
The enemies of the gods did not attain their blossoming form— that lord—
just as bees at night do not reach a lotus with its shimmering web of petals and stalks.
"Of blossoming form" means, that is to say, being awakened; "they did not reach" means they did not see. || 10 ||
The doctrine of consciousness was not understood within him by those of unawakened intellect,
just as the sequence of human activity on earth is not perceived when the sun has set.

Even the discourse on consciousness, the very talk of awakening, is for one who is senseless, whose mind has dissolved— just as the sequence of human activities such as bathing, giving, setting out, and running belongs to the earth when the sun has set from its presence, that is, to the earth in a state of deep sleep. 11.
Then, while the Daityas had departed in their desired directions in agitation,
the city formerly wandered about at will without a king.

The syntactical connection with the following verse is as follows: while the Daityas were anxious and weak, and while other powerful Daityas were roaming and acting according to their own whims like robbers, Pātāla remained for a long time overturned by the law of the fishes (mātsyanyāya).
For a long time, Pātāla became devoid of kings due to that lack of rulership; it was overturned by the law of the fishes (mātsyanyāya), and the succession of virtues had set.
The city of Bali was stripped of its strength [the reading *bhuktābala* is required], devoid of all order and restraint,
with every woman afflicted by distress, and with their garments snatched away from one another.

He establishes the very principle of the "law of the fish" (mātsyanyāya) there with the verse beginning with "balibhiḥ": "Where the cities of the weak have been abandoned—that is, seized—by the powerful; where all women, being distressed and oppressed, [are left] without exception. (14)
The city’s interior was filled with men wailing and lamenting; its gardens and streets were strewn about in disorder, tormented by futile calamities and misfortunes. (15)
"Distorted" means with its layout destroyed; by the two terms "garden" and "city," the trees and people residing therein are indicated. (15)
The hosts of gods were overcome with anxiety, their kinsmen were deprived of food and fruit;
they were rendered helpless by an untimely calamity, and the entire circle of the quarters was destroyed.
Wherein the faces of the quarters of the sky were destroyed and overspread with dust.
It was humiliated by the children of the gods, overrun by outcaste spirits,
emptied of its elemental beings, devoid of prosperity, and its hollows were almost entirely destroyed.
It was humiliated and treated with contempt even by the children of the gods;
it was overrun by low-born beings of dark nature, such as Caṇḍālas, dogs, jackals, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and the like.
A battle of words with women of uncertain character, crying out on all sides for their stolen wealth and husbands,
resembling the fierce onset of warriors at the start of the Kali Yuga.
Then that host of Asuras became agitated. || 18 ||

For whom women, wealth, riches, mantras, the conventions of friendship, battles, and enmities born of those causes were no longer constant or regulated; at the time of the Kali Yuga, it became agitated and terrified by fear on all sides, resembling those fierce, cruel bandits who are bold and skilled in seizing the property of others.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh canto, titled "The Disturbance of the Asura Host," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 37 ||
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Disturbance of the Asura Host," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirty-Eighth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, he who delights in maintaining the sequence of the entire web of the worlds—
In the city of Kṣīrodana, Hari was seated upon the couch that is the serpent Śeṣa. || 1 ||
The thought of Hari is described here for the sake of establishing the order of the world, in order to protect the race of Daityas through the awakening of Prahlāda. (1)
He whose very play and sport consist in the preservation of all the sequences and laws pertaining to the entire web of the universe. || 1 ||
When the sleep of the rainy season had ceased, the destroyer of enemies, for the sake of the gods,
once surveyed with his intellect the course of the world.

Upon the departure of the sleep of the rainy season—that is, at the end of Kārtika—the remainder [of the sentence] being "in order to accomplish the purpose of the gods. By this, it is understood that he was awakened by the gods through praise at that time. [She saw] her, who knew the course pertaining to the three worlds—the state existing at that moment. || 2 ||
Having mentally surveyed both heaven and the earthly realm,
he quickly proceeded to Pātāla, which was protected by his enemies.

Having analyzed the very sequence of his observations, he says "triviṣṭapam" and so forth. "Pārthiva" refers to the conduct pertaining to the earthly realm (bhūloka), namely the performance of auspicious and inauspicious deeds by people. "He went to Pātāla with his mind" means that he reflected upon the conditions existing in Pātāla. || 3 ||
While the Dānava Prahlāda remained there with steady concentration,
he beheld the prosperity in Indra’s city that had reached its full maturity.
There, while the Dānava Prahlāda remained steadfast in his firm meditative absorption (samādhi) in the netherworld (pātāla), Indra,

having seen the prosperity that had attained full maturity and increase in the city of heaven, [reflected] upon the Lord who formerly lay upon the ocean of milk and later awakened, even while remaining there upon his serpent-couch.

The connection of the three [verses] is as follows: Viṣṇu—seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), holding a conch, discus, and mace in his hands—reflected upon this matter to be performed in the manner about to be described, with his own body conceived by his mind as a great bee (*alin*) for the lotus of the three worlds, which was exceedingly radiant. 4.
Of him who dwells upon a couch of serpents, who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, whose hands hold the conch, the discus, and the mace, and who moves within his own body; || 5 ||
Seated upon the lotus posture, with a body exceedingly radiant, he whose great abode was the lotus of the three worlds reflected thus within his mind.
Now that Prahlāda has found rest in his station and the leader has gone to the netherworld (Pātāla),
alas, this creation has for the most part become devoid of Daityas.
The state is the state of the sovereignty of meditative concentration; therein [the mind] finds rest. || 7 ||
In the absence of the Daityas, the host of gods will reach a state of desirelessness and attain tranquility,
like a river among unseen masses of clouds.
Peace consists in the absence of passion and hatred; it was not seen during those periods of drought when the masses of clouds did not appear.
Then, free from the pairs of opposites and known as liberation, it will go to that state,
becoming withered like a creeper whose sap has been exhausted by the loss of its pride.
Then, through tranquility (*śama*), she emerged from duality—that is, free from the affliction of dualities such as cold and heat—or she became non-dual.
She was "flavorless" (*virasā*), meaning detached from the pleasures of heaven, and devoid of the sprinkling of water. || 9 ||
When peace has come to the flood of the gods, all sacrificial and ascetic rites on earth will undoubtedly attain tranquility, bearing as their fruit the state of the deity that is consciousness.

When the host of gods attained a state of tranquility—due to the absence of anyone to hate, the observation that the happiness of heaven is difficult to obtain, the resulting indifference, and their own inherent goodness—the gods, fearing liberation, even through delusion caused men to fall [into worldly attachment]. Therefore, it is not pleasing to them that humans should know this; for that reason, they are called *asuras*.
They create obstacles and utter curses; though they are renunciants, they are seen to be negligent, outward-minded, malicious, and eager for quarrels, their intentions corrupted by the gods.

The meaning is that, since it is established by such scriptural, traditional, and philosophical (vārtika) authorities that even humans possess minds corrupted by the gods, when tranquility and the like occur, sacrificial and ascetic acts on earth— even if they are true— will result in the fruit of non-divinity and will lead to the destruction of tranquility. || 10 ||
Then, when ritual actions have subsided, the world of earth will come to its end;
upon its destruction, there will be no further connection to saṃsāra.

"Let there be the destruction of ritual action; what is the harm in that? To this he replies: "In ritual actions... The mention of the *bhūrloka* refers to the sphere of action (*karmabhūmi*). "Astaṃ" means futility. The meaning is that if it [the world] were destroyed—that is, if it were futile—there would follow the consequence of the cessation of saṃsāra, which is dependent upon karma. || 11 ||
This triple world which has been fashioned by me shall perish prematurely before the end of the kalpa, like a drop of frost in the heat.
"Let it be so; what harm does that do you? To this he replies: "Until the end of the aeon," etc. (verse 12).
"What have I done here by dissolving myself into this mental effort (*ābhoga*) until it has reached exhaustion, thereby causing the destruction of my own play? (13)

When this vast expanse of the world's structure has dissolved and reached its end, what would be considered an appropriate act on my part—by me, who am bringing about the cessation of my own sport? The meaning is: nothing at all. || 13 ||
Then, in this void where the moon, sun, and stars have perished, I too,
having brought my body to rest, shall abide in that state.

Then, through the exhaustion of my own sport, I too, having brought about the cessation—the withdrawal—of this body intended for sport, shall attain and abide in that state of the perfect Self, so as not to arise again in saṃsāra. Even though there is an abundance of certainty (saṃbhāvanā), the *lṛṭ* (future tense) suffix alone is used. || 14 ||
Since the world has thus come to such an untimely end, I see no good in this; I think it better that the Dānavas should live. (15)

Thus, when the world has come to rest unexpectedly and at an untimely moment through these various kinds of distinctions you have described, I do not see any welfare here for this multitude of living beings, including gods and humans; rather, I certainly do see it.
For, according to the traditional teaching that "through dispassion there is dissolution into primordial nature" (*prakṛti*), there is a dissolution into *prakṛti* as if in deep sleep.

Because the attainment of the supreme good, characterized by the cessation of all suffering, is achieved [through this], [the seeker] desires to know that very [Self]— as established by such scriptural and traditional texts as "Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas" and "One who has been perfected over many births then goes to the highest goal"— by means of the desire-to-know (*vividiṣā*) which is accomplished through disinterested action (*niṣkāma-karma*) performed over many lifetimes, leading to the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*).

I believe that because there is an absence of the sound "ṣāt," and because the obscuration of root-ignorance has not ceased, there remains the possibility of recurrence as long as the seed exists; thus, the supreme good characterized by the attainment of unsurpassed bliss is not established for anyone. Therefore, for the sake of all attaining that [bliss] gradually, [the means is] giving (*dāna*).
The meaning is "may they live. || 15 ||
Then, due to the exertion of the Daityas, the gods’ performance of sacrifices and austerities was obstructed by him;
otherwise, the structure of the world and the course of worldly existence would not have been altered.
He states that same sequence again in brief: "Daitya... and so forth. *Vibudhāḥ* means the gods. Therefore, from those *vibudhas*. || 16 ||
Therefore, having gone to Rasātala, I shall restore the lord of the Dānavas to his own position exactly as he was, just as the season restores a tree.
"Yathāvat" means as it was before; "ṛtu" refers to the seasons, beginning with spring. || 17 ||
Now, unless I kill another lord of the Dānavas besides Prahlāda, I think he will reach the gods. (18)
This final body of Prahlāda is great and purifying;
he must dwell here with this very body until the end of the kalpa.
For such is the decree of the Goddess Destiny, determined by the Supreme Lord:
that an embodied being must remain here in this world according to its own lot, just as Prahlāda did.
Therefore, I shall go to that very lord of the Daityas and awaken him,
just as a cloud awakens a peacock sleeping by a mountain stream with its thundering roar.
The thundering rain-cloud. || 21 ||
Established in the samādhi of one liberated while living, he may exercise lordship over the asuras,
just as a gem, free from mental effort, reflects images.
He is established in that eternal samādhi of those liberated while living, which is characterized by non-attachment;

he is one whose mental activity has ceased, being devoid of both the mind and its functions; and he performs the action of reflection, which is the bearing of the reflections of objects present before him within himself. 22.
This creation, along with the gods and asuras, shall not perish;
that conflict will come to pass, and it shall be my sport.
That is well known. By the word "pair" (dvandva), the battle consisting of their mutual action is indicated. || 23 ||
Although these two—the destruction and the emergence of creation—are perfectly equal to me, nevertheless, let this proceed according to its established order; what does it matter to me otherwise?

The dissolution and emergence of the world—that which is to be created—occur without transgressing the arrangement of the previous creation; that is, according to their established order. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "not exceeding" the objects [of the prior state]. (24)

That which is equal toward both existence and non-existence, whether in their destruction or their persistence—effort directed toward that, due to the absence of [discriminating] intellect, constitutes the attainment of union with it. (25)

Now, one might object: "Is it not improper for you to go to the city of the Daityas, rather than proceeding to the bliss of your own true nature through yogic sleep? Anticipating this doubt, he says: *bhāva*... etc. Because of the absence of intellect (*abuddhitva*) and the lack of attachment (*abhiniveśaviraha*), whatever effort there is toward going and so forth, that would indeed be a movement within yoga itself, and not a movement elsewhere. For...

The meaning is that it is "equal" (sama) with respect to the attainment of the bliss of yogic sleep, with respect to the presence or absence of effort in movement and so forth, and with respect to the arising or non-arising, as well as the destruction or persistence, of those states. || 25 ||
Therefore, I shall go to Pātāla to awaken the Lord of the Asuras;
I shall attain steadfastness and no longer engage in the worldly play of saṃsāra. || 26 ||
Even while moving, I attain steadiness and immovability; that is to say, because I do not engage in the worldly play like one who lacks self-knowledge. || 26 ||
Having reached the city of the Asuras, which is terrible with its arrogant conduct,
we shall awaken the Daitya like the sun awakening a lotus;
we shall bring this entire world back to its own stability.
Like a dense ritual upon a mountain, it is as fleeting as a mass of clouds.

Having reached the terrible and fearsome city of the Asuras through the conduct of those arrogant and lawless bandits, we awaken the Daitya Prahlāda from his meditative absorption, just as the sun, Vivasvat, awakens a lotus; and by him, this entire world [is restored] according to the manner previously described.

We bring about stability. Just as "the ordinance of clouds" (ghanavidhi)—meaning the rainy season—brings the flickering mass of clouds to a state of stability upon mountains such as Himavat; that is the meaning. || 27 ||
