Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Reflections of the Supreme Lord," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki according to the Seer’s tradition.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Discursive Inquiry into the Supreme Lord," in the Section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, the Soul of All [emerged] from his own city within the Ocean of Milk.
He moved along with his retinue like a mountain with its peaks.
Hari, having gone to the city of the Daityas, awakened Prahlāda with the sound of his conch and said,
"Let the kingdom be protected until the end of the kalpa."

From his own city, which is within the White Island (Śvetadvīpa) situated in the midst of the Ocean of Milk—the word "together with his retinue" being understood as the ellipsis—he [came], like Mount Mandara together with its ridges or plateaus; or rather, "immovable" (acala) means that in the ultimate sense he is devoid of movement. || 1 ||
Through that very opening in the surface of the Milk Ocean, whose waters were solidified,
he reached the city of Prahlāda, which was like another world of Śakra.
In which [ocean], the waters were rendered motionless by the mere resolve of the Creator (Dhātṛ) so that they did not enter the hollows of Pātāla;
thus, by means of such a subterranean opening—the lower cavity of the Ocean of Milk—it was as delightful as the world of Śakra (Indra). This is the meaning. || 2 ||
There Hari beheld the Asura situated within the treasury of a golden palace,
like the lotus-born Brahmā hidden in a mountain cave and absorbed in meditative concentration.
Then, there in the city of Prahrāda, [he saw] the Asura Prahrāda, hidden in a cave of Mount Meru like the lotus-born Brahmā.
There, those Daityas, shaken by the Vaiṣṇava splendor,
fled far away like owls terrified by the rays of the sun.
"Avadhūlitāḥ" means shaken off like dust; "kauśikāḥ" means owls. || 4 ||
Accompanied by two or three principal asuras and surrounded by his retinue,
Hari entered the abode of the asura, just as the moon enters the sky with its stars.
Seated upon the throne of Vainateya (Garuḍa), with Lakṣmī waving chowries for him,
surrounded by his own weapons and attendants, he is saluted by divine sages and holy ascetics.
"O Great-souled One, awaken!"— uttering these words, Viṣṇu blew his conch Pāñcajanya, making the quarters of the sky resound.
Of the quarters, the cardinal directions. || 7 ||
By that great sound, born from the breath of Viṣṇu,
the world was simultaneously agitated with the force of the clouds and the ocean at the end of an aeon.

The vital breath is strength; by its birth, the clouds of dissolution and the oceans of dissolution were simultaneously agitated by its velocity. By the word "secret" (rahas), the sound produced by that [birth] is indicated. || 8 ||
The host of Asuras fell to the ground in utter confusion,
like a flight of royal swans by the sound of a cloud rumbling with the playful grace of a rutting elephant.
Overcome by sudden agitation, she fell into a swoon born of intense fear.
The Vaiṣṇava multitude, having attained joy and being free from agitation,
rejoiced like a row of *kuṭaja* trees blooming at the roar of a rain-cloud.
The lord of the Dānavas gradually became fully awakened in spirit,
like a kadamba tree in full bloom in the forest at the onset of the rainy season.
Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas. || 11 ||
Then the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti), having ascended from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
gradually overwhelmed the demon as the Gaṅgā overwhelms the entire ocean.
He elaborates on the sequence of awakening with the words beginning "brahmarandhre" and so forth; "ākramayāmāsa" means he filled [it]. || 12 ||
In an instant, the splendor of his vital breaths overcame the asura from every side,
just as the solar radiance pervades the interior of the world immediately after its rising.
Then, as the nine apertures of his vital breaths began to function,
his consciousness became oriented toward objects of thought within, reflected upon the mirror of the vital breath.
In the vital breaths, that is, in the sense organs; "vital breath" (prāṇa) refers to the subtle body (liṅgadeha), and she is reflected—that is, mirrored—in the mirror characterized by it. || 14 ||
O Rāghava, the consciousness, turning toward the object of thought, attained the state of mind as the object of thought, just as the beauty of a face reflected in a mirror appears as a duality.

The consciousness (cit), directed toward an object capable of being willed, became as if the object itself through the awakening of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the form of that which is to be thought; thus it attained the state of the mind (manas), characterized by the nature of being both conscious and insentient. || 15 ||
As his mind began to sprout slightly and his eyes were about to open,
they gradually became like two blue lotuses at dawn.
His eyes gradually became ready to open. || 16 ||
As his consciousness was touched by the openings of the channels through the movement of the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
a throbbing arose within him like that of a lotus afflicted by the wind.
Due to the cause of consciousness being stirred up and awakened within the openings of the channels on all sides by the inhaled and exhaled breaths that had entered inside,
a slight movement— a vibration— arose in this body of his, like that of a lotus struck and shaken by the wind. || 17 ||
In the mere twinkling of an eye, the mind attained fullness,
as if it were a wave in water when that [ocean] is filled by the force of the vital breath.
Then he shone with his eyes, mind, breath, and body blossoming,
like a lake with quivering lotuses when the sun has half-risen.
At this moment, as soon as the Lord said,
"Awake!", he became fully conscious, like a peacock at the sound of thunder.
The peacock (barhin) [is so called] because of its tail-feathers; [the term] *ghanarava* refers to the sound of clouds (*meghaśabda*). || 20 ||
To him, whose eyes were blossoming, whose pride was born, and whose memory was robust,
the Lord of the Three Worlds spoke as he had formerly spoken to the one born from the navel-lotus.

He whose self-recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—consisting of the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) and joy (*prahrāda*)—had arisen, and who possessed a full and properly developed memory of his former state and so forth. (21)
"O virtuous one, remember Mahālakṣmī; remember your own form!
Why do you bring about the end of this body so abruptly? (22)

Remember your own great fortune—the splendor of the kingdom of the Daityas—as well as your own form, the very shape of your body. Why, why do you bring about the cessation and end of your body so abruptly and without occasion, by means of this forgetfulness of your physical self? || 22 ||
For you who are devoid of the conceptualization of what is to be rejected or accepted, what purpose do the existence and non-existence of things belonging to the body serve? Arise, arise now! (23)

If it be argued that— on account of the Vedic scripture stating, "Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no cessation of the pleasant and the unpleasant," and because all people experience it as such— the remembrance of the body is a cause of misfortune— to this he replies with the word "heyā" (to be abandoned):
even when the mental constructs of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted have been abandoned, you have no concern regarding the presence or absence of pleasure and pain within the body.
The meaning is that there is no possibility of an undesirable consequence. || 23 ||
"You must remain here with this body for as long as one kalpa;
for we know the blameless destiny exactly as it truly is. (24)
He then states for how long the maintenance of the body must continue there: "sthātavyam" (it must remain). "Niyatim" refers to the regulation of your lifespan. || 24 ||
Remaining here in this very kingdom as one liberated while living, you should carry this body until the end of the kalpa, free from all anxiety. (25)
They are to be cast out in legal proceedings; they are to be driven away. || 25 ||
O sinless one, when your body has been shattered at the end of the aeon, you must abide within your own majesty,
just as the space within a jar remains in the sky when the jar has broken.

Then, as to how I should remain at the end of the kalpa, he says: "In my own body" (tanvām). That is, in my own glory—my own self-nature, which is unsurpassed greatness; in my own great space (mahākāśa). || 26 ||
Abiding until the end of the eon, pure, and having perceived the higher and lower worlds,
this body of yours has become a playful manifestation of one liberated while living.
The twelve suns have not arisen, nor have the mountains dissolved;
the world has not been consumed by fire, O virtuous one—why do you abandon your body in vain? (28)
If so, is the end of the aeon (kalpānta) imminent? He says "no," with the words beginning "not arisen" (noditāḥ). || 28 ||
The wind blows, not mad, grey with the ashes of the three worlds;
why do you vainly cast off your body, which bears the mark of the skull of the fickle goddess Amarā? 29.
One whose lap bears as a mark the trembling skull-bones of the gods. || 29 ||
Like blossoms on an *aśoka* tree or the lightning of the Puṣkarāvarta clouds, they do not flicker within the vessel of the world; why do you abandon your body in vain? (30)
In the clouds known as Puṣkarāvarta, which bring about the dissolution of the world, the lightnings and flashes of lightning do not flicker; "now" is to be understood as applying everywhere. || 30 ||
The mountains, with their torrents of rain and roaring rivers, and the quarters of the sky, blazing with flaming fires, do not shatter; why then do you abandon your body in vain? (31)

In these [clouds], the mountains resound as they are rent asunder by the *sāra*—the pervasive trembling—of the earth (*dharā*) being consumed and shaken on all sides. "The quarters" (*kakubhaḥ*) refers to the directions; since formless things cannot disintegrate, the walls of the cosmic egg situated at the ends of the directions are understood here. || 31 ||
This world remains as nothing other than the triad known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; why do you vainly cast off your body, which is like a withered cloud? 32.

This world, in which the mature and fully grown clouds—that is, the clouds of universal dissolution—have subsided, has not remained as such once it has become nothing more than the triad of deities known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. || 32 ||
Nor have the quarters of the sky here reached a state of decay, their intervals inferred merely by the rows of mountain peaks; why then do you abandon your body in vain? (33)

The directions, which are like the walls of the cosmic egg, are such that their divisions—distinguished by the peaks of the Lokāloka mountain, which resembles the petals of the earth-lotus—are not determined by the rising of the sun and other such phenomena. || 33 ||
The solar rays wander in the sky with the thunderous roar of splitting mountain peaks;
the clouds of the kalpa do not roar—why do you abandon your body in vain? (34)

The negative particle *na* is to be supplied [to the verb], meaning that the rays (*karāḥ*)—the beams belonging to the twelve suns (*saurā dvādaśādityasaṃbandhinah*)—do not wander among those [rays] whose loud sounds (*ṭaṃkārā dhvanayaḥ*) are like those of the great mountain Meru as it is splitting and bursting apart. || 34 ||
I, whose banner is the bird, sport in all ten directions amidst the worlds filled with living beings; do not disregard my body. (35)

"I, Viṣṇu, sport within these regions teeming with beings—that is, pervaded by the four kinds of living creatures such as those born from eggs; do not disregard me, abandon [this intent]. For if you do so, your death now would not be glorious; this is the meaning. || 35 ||
We are these, these are the mountains, these are living beings, this is you;
this is the world, this is the sky—do not disregard the body.
For one whose mind is agitated by the force of excessive passion, sufferings cut him down; for such a person, death is preferable.

To whom, then, is death appropriate? He states this with the verse beginning "pīvare" (for one who is stout...). Death is fitting for one whose mind is being cut by sufferings through the application of ignorance;
the meaning is that the cause of death established in the Smṛti—that a soul excessively tormented relinquishes the gross body—is applicable here. || 37 ||
"I am emaciated, deeply distressed, and deluded"—these and other such thoughts rob one's intellect; for such a person, death is preferable. (38)
For one who is bound by the snares of desire and led hither and thither by the flickering movements of the mind, death alone shines forth as the only relief. (39)
For one whose heart is shattered by cravings that have carried away his spiritual cultivation, death shines forth like sprouts from among the greedy. (40)
Craving destroys and crushes the heart of one whose cultivation [of virtue] has been stolen away and whose sprouts of discernment have been snatched off—
just as fools, out of greed for great fruit, destroy the emerging shoots of rice and other crops belonging to those who desire them, such as cattle and the like. (40)
For him whose creeper of mental fluctuations has grown as high as a palm tree in the forest of his mind, death shines forth when it bears fruit through pleasure and pain. (41)
In the forest characterized by the mind, which is as lofty as a palmyra tree and possesses the height of passion and other afflictions. || 41 ||
For one whose body is this wretched tree, with its network of foliage being the line of body hair,
death shines forth as the supreme destroyer of the flood of misfortunes.

The flood characterized by desire and other misfortunes, like a torrent of fierce winds, carries away that tree of evil— the body— which possesses a network of creepers in the form of the line of body hair and a mass of branches in the form of its various limbs. || 42 ||
For one whose forest of his own body is being consumed by the forest fires of mental anguish and physical disease,
death shines forth like a flickering creeper.
For him upon whose body the pythons of lust and anger writhe, death shines forth like that of a tree withered within. (44)
Within the interior of the hollow. || 44 ||
This abandonment of the body is known in the world as death;
it is neither existent nor non-existent, and for that reason, it is not the cause of the perception of the knowable.
He says, "This which... [and so forth], to show that even when one reflects upon the true nature of death, it does not occur for the knower of reality (*tattvavid*).

"Smṛtam" means well-known. Furthermore, that [death] cannot be brought about by the existent Self (*ātman*), nor can it be brought about by that non-existent body; this is because the Self, being eternal, is devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*).

Because of the impossibility of the act of renunciation; because attachment to the body is not established for one who is non-attached; and because the renunciation of that which is non-existent is utterly dismissed. Now, what is the reason for the non-existence of the body? He states it: "The cause.
The realization—that is, the knowledge—of one's own Self, which is the object of cognition and necessarily worthy of being known through the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The reason for the non-existence of the body and so forth is that the cognition of the existence of the body and so forth is based on ignorance; this is the meaning. || 45 ||
The life of that wise person who does not turn away from the contemplation of the reality of his own self, and who perceives things as they truly are, is truly glorious.

Whose life, then, is truly splendid? To this he replies with the words beginning "of whom" (*yasya*). Thus, there is no departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) from the body, but rather a departure of the intellect (*mati*) from the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*); and since that [departure] does not exist at all for the knower, his life is always splendid. But for the ignorant person, the intellect is always...
The sense is that because he does not depart from his own essential nature, he is of the nature of eternal immortality. || 46 ||
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not defiled,
and who is equanimous toward all things— for him life truly shines.

Furthermore, for one who identifies with a single body, the abandonment of that body would constitute death; however, for one who does not have such identification, whose intellect is not tainted by its own likes and dislikes, and who is equanimous—possessing a common self—toward all states of being, bodies, and sense objects, there is no possibility of death for him, and thus his very life shines forth. This is the meaning.
In the same way, this should be inferred for fire as well. || 47 ||
He who, with an inner mind cooled and free from passion and hatred, beholds this life as a witness—his life indeed shines forth. (48)
For one who, having correctly understood through thorough discernment, abandons both what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted,
and has placed the mind within the mind— that person’s life is truly radiant.
Having thoroughly understood [the world] as being truly without essence, [one rests] in the Witness, who is at the end of the mind—that is, in its final state. || 49 ||
The life of one who has dissolved the mind— which is unattached to objects that resemble non-entities and free from the impurity of conceptualization— is truly radiant.

The meaning is that the mind— which, when unattached to the impurity consisting of the conceptualization of external objects, is not fixed upon unreal things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell appearing as a real thing when it is actually a similar object— becomes dissolved in Brahman alone, just as the hardness of ghee melts away. || 50 ||
Firmly grasping the true vision, this activity of the world is performed with ease; he by whom life is lived without latent tendencies (vāsanā) truly shines.
Jagatkriyā is the worldly activity of the universe. || 51 ||
The life of one who, even while moving about, feels neither internal satisfaction nor agitation upon encountering what is to be rejected or accepted, is truly radiant.

Upon encountering that which is to be abandoned—the cause of suffering—he does not feel agitation; upon obtaining that which is to be accepted—a means to happiness—he does not feel inward satisfaction. (52)
Like a flock of swans from a pure lake belonging to the bright fortnight, he from whom a stream of virtues flows—his life is truly radiant. (53)

He whose own wings—meaning his followers—are pure knowers of reality, and who himself is pure; in the case of the lake, he whose wings are pure white swans, cranes, and the like. He is naturally pure, stainless, and holy.
His qualities include tranquility, forbearance, sweetness, and so forth, as well as coolness, fragrance, and so on. (53)
When he enters the path of hearing, is seen, or comes to mind, all beings attain joy; his life is truly auspicious. (54)
The two ears are the "śrutīs," and that is their path. || 54 ||
In whose risings all the lotus-hearts of people, possessing swarms of living beings, become full of joy;
of him alone, the imperishable moon, shines forth the complete life.
O Lord of the Danujas, it is like the fullness of the moon; it does not belong to anyone else.

Upon whose rise— that is, upon his prosperity and emergence— the lotuses characterized by people, which possess bees in the form of living beings, become playful and joyful; the life of that very knower of reality shines like the fullness of the imperishable moon, which is free from the disease of waning.
The meaning is that this does not apply to the other, the ignorant one. || 55 ||

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Renunciation in the Words of Nārāyaṇa" within the *Prahlāda-Nirvāṇa*, in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus [ends] the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-ninth canto, titled "The Presentation of Nārāyaṇa’s Words. || 39 ||
The Fortieth Chapter.
The Blessed One said: "The stability of the visible body is called 'life' by people."
The abandonment of the body for the sake of another body is known as death. || 1 ||
Whether possessing a body or bodiless, whether remaining as the immutable witness (kūṭastha) or engaged in action—
just as a man of knowledge conducts himself in worldly affairs, that sequence is described by Hari.

Desiring to instruct Prahlāda— even though he was liberated while living— on the means for successfully carrying out the protection of his kingdom through mere proximity [to the Lord], the Blessed Vāsudeva sought to declare that, despite the presence of the body,
there is no real connection [between him and it]; thus, the previously mentioned "living" and "dying" are merely figurative and not primary.

He states the nature of life and death as they are well-known in the world, beginning with the word "stability": Death is traditionally understood as the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), which is the relinquishing of the previous body and the transition to another body for the sake of taking up yet another body; this is because the meaning of the verbal root *mṛ* is established as "the abandonment of the vital breaths. || 1 ||
O Great-minded One, you are now liberated from both these two sides;
what death can there be for you here, or what life remains for you? (2)

The meaning is that this refers to two alternatives: the stability of the body or the departure of the vital breaths (prāṇa). This is based on the Vedic scripture which states: "Bodiless among bodies, his vital breaths do not depart; they are merged right here. || 2 ||
O crusher of enemies, I have spoken this merely for the sake of illustration;
you do not die, O omniscient one, nor will you ever die.

To the question, "How then is it that you said, 'Life is auspicious for you, death is not auspicious'? he replies: "For the sake of illustration. This means: for the purpose of elaborating upon the qualities and defects of knowledge and ignorance. || 3 ||
Though residing in the body, you are bodiless because of your lack of embodiment; you are the seer who perceives beyond the body.
Though residing in space, you are like the wind in the sky, for you are unattached.

The reason for being "without a body" (*adehatva*) is "the vision of one who is bodiless" (*videhadṛk*), meaning the vision that is free from the perception of a body; this is because of non-attachment, due to the absence of clinging. || 4 ||
O observer of noble vows, because it brings about the perception of touch, the body alone exists [as the locus];
for by obstructing the upward expansion [of breath], space is the cause of that expansion.
To explain how it is known that [the Self] resides within the body, he says: "Touch," etc.

Because it is the cause for the perception of touch—such as cold, heat, and so forth—within the body, and because such perception is not observed elsewhere, the remainder of the sense is: "You exist only in the body.
[In some versions, it reads "tvaci" (on the skin). If [you ask]: "How can the unattached Self [be the cause] of the perception of touch on the skin?"

Regarding the term "cause," he provides an illustration therein with the words "height" (utsedha). The meaning is as follows: just as space is called the cause of the height of a tree because it does not obstruct it, so it is in this case. || 5 ||
Where is there room for a body here for those who have attained tranquility, since they have awakened to the true nature of reality?
This single, limited form, however, remains poorly situated among the ignorant.
To the question of how, then, there can be bodilessness in that state, he says: "Awakened. Because you have realized the truth, you are awakened;

and when awakening has occurred, where does the body exist for the *śamins*—those who possess the cessation of all duality? Indeed, when a dream ceases, the dream-body no longer exists. This [body], however, is a single, limited entity.
The meaning is that the form of the body, though unstable and inconceivable, exists among the ignorant who lack awakening. || 6 ||
At all times, you are indeed everything—the supreme singular consciousness that is the light of the intellect.
What is the body, and what is even the bodiless state, which you grasp and then abandon?

If the sacrificial fire, by remaining in the body, is called the "embodied one" (dehin), then why should I not likewise be so, since I too reside in the body through the perception of touch? To this he replies: "Always. His abiding as the illuminator is equal at all times and toward all objects; thus, you are everything, and not merely the body like an ignorant person. And in this way, what object could possibly be your body?

That which you grasp with the notion of "I" (aham-buddhi), you might grasp; that which you abandon with the notion of "not-I" (an-aham-buddhi)—meaning you would relinquish—it would be bodiless. What could it be? || 7 ||
Whether spring arises or the wind of dissolution blows, what has come upon the Self, which is devoid of both existence and non-existence? (8)

[Objection: "Is there not a distinction such that the body is that whose increase leads to an increase in one's own joy, and from the perception of whose destruction arises despondency, whereas the other is the non-body? [Reply: No, because for the knower of reality, the causes of joy and despondency are impossible. This is stated in the passage beginning with "samudetu" (may it arise), etc. It is cultivated through affection (*prīti*).
The meaning is that what is remembered is "existence" (bhāva), which is pleasant; what is not brought to mind is "non-existence" (abhāva), which is unpleasant;
thus, the sense is "of one who is devoid of both. || 8 ||
Even while mountains are crumbling, even while the fires of cosmic destruction are burning,
and even while cataclysmic winds are blowing, he indeed remains established in his own self alone.
"The Knower of Reality remains"—this is the ellipsis. || 9 ||
Let all beings remain, or let everything pass away;
whether they perish or increase, [the Self] abides firmly within itself alone.
The Supreme Lord does not perish when [the body] reaches destruction, nor does He increase when it increases;
He does not quiver even while this body is quivering.
When the mental delusion that "I am the body" or "I am the embodied one" has perished, why is this vain conceptualization raised: "Shall I abandon [the world] or shall I not abandon it? (12)

When the mental delusion—characterized by the superimposition of identity as "I am" with respect to the body, and characterized by the superimposition of association with its attributes as "the embodied one"—has been extinguished, how could the vain, causeless, and fruitless notion of "I shall abandon" or "I shall not abandon" arise? The meaning is that it does not arise at all. || 12 ||
"Having done this, I shall do that; having abandoned this, I shall take up that"—O dear one, such volitions have utterly perished for those who know the truth. (13)
"Having abandoned this, I shall abandon that"—this is the remainder [of the thought]. || 13 ||
Those who are awakened and are the agents of all things will perform some action here;
they do not, by failing to act, eternally fall into the state of being non-agents.
The connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the first half of the verse is as follows: "Even though they are the doers of all things, they will not do even the slightest thing.
The meaning is that if they never perform any action at any time, they remain forever established in the state of being non-doers (*akartṛtva*). || 14 ||
From the absence of agency, the absence of being an enjoyer follows by logical necessity;
indeed, who in these three worlds has ever gathered what was not sown? (15)
He states the result of that [argument] with the words "because of non-agency": grain and so forth that have not been sown—that is, not produced by planting and other such means. || 15 ||
When agency and enjoyership have subsided, only peace remains here;
that very state, having reached full maturity, is called liberation by the wise. (16)
Peace is the state of being free from distraction; maturity is the state of being firmly rooted through the eradication of the root of agency. (16)
Awakened, consisting of consciousness, and pure, they abide pervading everything;
what should they abandon that they have not already taken up, or what should they take up that they have not already abandoned? (17)
He establishes what has been stated by means of the verse beginning with "prabuddhā" (awakened).

Having ascended—that is, having overcome—by means of the manifestation of their true nature as the ultimate reality, what worldly fruit that was abandoned or not yet attained could they possibly grasp? || 17 ||

Devoid of the sequence of parts consisting of the object of cognition, the subject of cognition, their relation, and the means of valid cognition, what could it grasp as an object of knowledge, and what could it abandon? (18)

The immutable Self is devoid of the characteristics of the grasped, the grasper, and their relationship; it is free from the constituent stages of the great sentence—namely, the sequence of parts characterized by the meaning of intermediate sentences consisting of the construction of the relationship between action, factors of action, and objects as measured in the state of ignorance; and it is devoid of the modifications characterized by the entire complex of primary and secondary actions.

The meaning is: what [agent] could grasp or abandon that fruit of the hereafter, such as heaven and so forth, which is to be accomplished by the performance of the primary and auxiliary actions connected with that [sacrifice]? || 18 ||
When the relationship between the grasped and the grasper has been exhausted, peace fully arises;
that peace which has attained its stable state is designated by the name "liberation. (19)

The conclusion of the established argument is stated as follows: that state which has arrived at the condition of being free from the distinction between the grasped and the grasper—the causes for the acquisition or rejection of what is desired or undesired in this world and the next—is called by the name "liberation" (mokṣa). || 19 ||
Established therein, always tranquil, such supreme persons as you move about indeed by virtue of a similarity to the movement of limbs in deep sleep.

Even for those established in this state, as long as the *prārabdha* (the momentum of past actions) has not been exhausted, there is the accomplishment of worldly activity. Regarding this, he provides an illustration:

"Just as [the body] performs the movement of breath, the digestion of food, the flow of bodily fluids, and so forth, by the mere presence of the Self through the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) that sustains life—so too do those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) act. The meaning is that they engage in worldly affairs. || 20 ||
With your latent impressions stilled by the awakening of others, observe this state of existence in the world with a mind established in the Self, as if you were half-asleep. (21)

With the intention that he should likewise practice the protection of the kingdom, [the author] says: "parāvabodha... [etc. He is "half-asleep," situated at the junction between deep sleep and waking. || 21 ||
For those whose intentions are resolved within their own self do not take delight in pleasant things;
nor are they distressed by the sufferings of others, as they find their singular elixir within their own self. (22)

The phrase "in things that are delightful" implies "in things that are not the Self. [They dwell] in sufferings that are other than the Self and untouched by the Self. For them, there is only within their own Self a singular happiness, as sweet as an elixir (*rasāyana*). Thus it has been said in the *Vārttika*: "If the witness were to be subject to suffering, who could be the witness? One who is suffering cannot be a witness; for the witness..."
"Why are you suffering? || 22 ||
Those who are eternally awakened and free from attachment undertake these activities just as mirrors reflect images—exactly as they occur, without desire. (23)
To the question of how they undertake actions for the sake of attaining pleasure or avoiding pain when such states do not exist [in reality], he says:
"While awake in their own self, they remain established in themselves; yet while situated in the cycle of worldly existence, they sleep.
Like children, they tremble, possessing a disposition that perceives the state of deep sleep as real. (24)
In that case, are they devoid of conviction even regarding their own self? He says "no": "while awake," and so forth.

Thus, as the Blessed One also showed them conviction in the Self by saying, "That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled one is awake," [the ignorant] tremble, meaning they shake; that is to say, they engage in worldly activity. || 24 ||
Having entered the path of the Unconquered and having experienced for but a single day the life of the lotus-born Brahmā,
you have attained here itself the prosperity endowed with a multitude of virtues.
O great-souled one, go to Acyuta, the supreme refuge.

He summarizes the intended meaning in brief with the word "thou": O Great-souled One, having entered— that is, attained— the station of the unconquered Viṣṇu, the state of the Supreme Self, thou hast [enjoyed] for a single day of Brahmā, until the end of the Kalpa, the royal splendor endowed with a multitude of virtues right here in Pātāla.
The meaning is: having enjoyed [the bliss of] Acyuta, go to the supreme abode, the highest station, known as disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya), which is free from falling away. || 25 ||
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Enlightenment of Prahlāda," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 40.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Enlightenment of Prahlāda," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
By that vessel for the jewels of the world, which beheld the wonders of the three realms, [the ocean was seen].
When this was said by Padmanābha in a voice as cool as moonlight, || 1 ||
Having received worship from the Daitya who had accepted his command, Hari, together with his followers,
consecrated him in the sovereignty of the Daityas and gratified him with boons.

When it was stated in the manner previously described—that at the time of dissolution, because the jewels characterized by the world were drawn into his own interior, he is like the ocean acting as a casket; and at the time of creation, he is Viṣṇu in the form of Padmanābha, whose nature is to manifest the wonders characterized by the three worlds—[the following occurs]. || 1 ||
This body named Prahlāda, whose lotus-eyes were blossoming,
spoke these words with joy, remaining steadfast and having mastered the process of reflection.
That body previously mentioned by the name Prahrāda, having assumed the process of mental cognition, spoke joyfully;
[he did so] for the purpose of establishing the state of being an agent within the Self, despite the absence of bodily appropriation. (2)
Prahlāda said: "O Lord, through the deliberation of what is beneficial and harmful, and by means of hundreds of royal duties,
I have become exceedingly exhausted and have now attained a moment of rest."
He was exhausted—meaning he had reached a state of fatigue—by the deliberation: "What is beneficial for the Asuras? What is harmful to the gods?
The word "for a moment" (kṣaṇam) is used because, within meditative absorption (samādhi), there is no perception of the passage of time. || 3 ||
O Blessed One, by your grace, my stability has been perfectly attained;
whether in meditative absorption or non-absorption, I am always equal in form.

Stability is abiding in one's own true nature through the awakening to reality; by means of that form, which is the ultimate true nature, at all times, whether in meditative absorption or non-absorption, and whether in liberation with or without the body. || 4 ||
O Mahādeva, after being beheld for a long time within by my stainless intellect,
you are now, by good fortune, seen again externally by my sight, O Lord.

These two verses are found in some manuscripts only: "You were seen through inner vision—that is, by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of the direct realization of the indivisible Self; you are now beheld by outward vision—that is, by the eye—by good fortune, through the power of merit. (5)
O Maheśvara, I existed within this infinite vision,
which is free from all conceptual constructions, like space within pure space.
In this internal view. || 6 ||
Neither by grief, nor by delusion, nor by thoughts of dispassion, nor by the act of abandoning the body, nor by fear of saṃsāra. (7)

In this regard, he says "not out of grief" (verse 7) to show that he did not resort to samādhi under the influence of causes such as sorrow and delusion, by which there might have been the possibility of his abandoning the body.
For when that One alone exists, whence can there be sorrow? Whence can there be injury? Whence the body? Where is the cycle of existence? Where is stability? And where is fear or fearlessness? (8)

"You have indeed witnessed the destruction of your father's kingdom and other such causes for grief; how then can you deny them? To this he replies with the verse beginning "In one... (ekasmin). The meaning is: it is true that these were seen here [in the world], but they were not seen in the non-dual Self; therefore, my composure is not caused by those [worldly events]. || 8 ||
Just as by pure will alone, arising spontaneously,
so indeed did I dwell in that vast and holy state.
If it is asked, "In that case, what is the cause for this samādhi? he says: "It is the very desire for rest born of inquiry," as expressed by the words "according to one's wish.
Thus, it occurs precisely without any intention such as the abandonment of the body. || 9 ||
"Alas, I am detached; I shall renounce worldly existence"—O Lord, such is the thought of those with unawakened vision, which brings about the transformations of joy and sorrow. (10)

If it is argued that the denial of dispassion (*vairāgya*) is not tenable because one does not think "I am dispassionate," since such [thinking] is conducive to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) preceded by inquiry (*vicāra*), he says in response: "Alas, you are dispassionate! (10).
"In the absence of a body there are no sufferings; my view is that sufferings reside in the body"—this serpent of the poison of thought devours only the fool. (11)

If dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the cause of *samādhi*, then since the body is experienced as a cause of suffering just like passion (*rāga*), the abandonment of the body would also be a means for *samādhi*. [The author] says "the absence of the body" (*dehābhāva*) [in verse 11] to show that even this [abandonment of the body] is desired only by one who does not know reality, but not by me.
"This is happiness, this is suffering; this does not exist for me, this exists for me"—a mind thus oscillating is indeed deluded, not wise. (12)
For this very reason, he states that there is no concentration (samādhi) even through the desire for happiness or the desire for the cessation of suffering—namely, "this [is what]...
The phrase "it snatches away only the fool" is carried over from the previous verse. || 12 ||
The latent impression of those ignorant ones who think, "I am one, and this [other] is another," prevails here among living beings whose self-awareness has been cast far away. 13.

"In that case, let it be so; [the author] speaks of meditative absorption (samādhi) with the desire for the exhaustion of the latent impressions of difference: 'I am another'. The meaning is: "Victory belongs only to those ignorant ones whose self-awareness (*ātmabuddhi*) has been cast far away by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and not to those who know the truth";
[this refers to] "living beings" (*asumatām*). || 13 ||
The false mental delusion that "this is to be abandoned" and "this is to be accepted" does not lead one who knows the inner reality to madness,
as it does the ignorant person of wicked intellect.

If it be argued, "In that case, let there be meditative absorption (samādhi) for the sake of abandoning saṃsāra or for attaining liberation," he says in response to that: "This... The syntactical connection is as follows: this well-known delusion belonging to the dull-witted does not lead even the wise man to madness, just as it does the ignorant one. || 14 ||

O lotus-eyed one, when you, the Self, are spread throughout everything, how can there be a second conceptualization consisting of the categories of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted? (15)
To explain why that is so, he says "in everything," and so forth. || 15 ||
The entire world, whether existent or non-existent, has arisen as a manifestation of consciousness;
what here is to be rejected, and what is to be accepted, since nothing at all is ever abandoned? (16)
It is called "appearance as consciousness" because it appears within deluded consciousness like mother-of-pearl silver and the like, but not in ultimate reality;
it has arisen from the coupling characterized by the mutual superimposition of identity between the existent Self and the non-existent māyā. || 16 ||
Investigating the seer and the seen solely through their own intrinsic nature,
he rested for a moment within himself by means of the Supreme Self.
For this very reason, he says "only" (kevalam) to indicate that my very rest in the investigation of reality has become samādhi.
Freed from existence and non-existence, and devoid of that which is to be abandoned or accepted;
thus have I existed previously, and now I am established in this very way. (18)
Previously, at the time of meditative absorption; now, at the time of emergence from it. The meaning is: "I am thus established in the fitness to undertake the task commanded by you. || 18 ||
"O Mahādeva, everything that has come under my own control has become my very self; I shall do for you whatever pleases you. (19)

Having attained his true self-nature (*ātmatā*), he says, "I am the Self; by me, that which has become my own duty—every task commanded by you—I shall perform. He asks, "What will you do with your own passion? and answers, "No," saying "for you" (*tubhyam*); the meaning is: "by acting in accordance with your will. || 19 ||
O lotus-eyed one, you are indeed worthy of worship throughout the three worlds;
therefore, you ought to accept from me this honor offered according to my nature.

"Just as I accept this kingdom, which has come to me by necessity (*niyati*) as commanded by you, so too, because you are the Lord of All, accept the worship offered by me, which has come to you by necessity. Thus he says: "You...
*Prakṛti* refers to necessity (*niyati*), as it is well-known in both the scriptures and the world. (20)
Having spoken thus before the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, the lord of the Dānavas took up the vessel of the full moon like a king of mountains.
The lord of mountains is the mountain of sunrise (Udayādri). || 21 ||
Then he worshipped Govinda, who stood at the forefront of the three worlds, together with his weapons, the host of Apsarases, the gods, and the lord of birds.
Together with the three worlds, accompanied by the three worlds situated within his belly; "foremost" means standing before him. || 22 ||
Having worshipped the Lord of the Worlds, who dwells within all worlds— both external and internal— the Lord of Kamalā then spoke to Him as He stood there.

He is one in whose [body] there exist worlds that are delusive and revolving within the external [parts] such as the pores of the skin, and within the internal [parts] such as the bladder, the belly, and the heart. || 23 ||
The Blessed Lord said: "Arise, O lord of the Dānavas, and take your place upon the throne;
I myself shall soon bestow the consecration upon you."
May those Siddhas, Sādhyas, and hosts of gods who have gathered here upon hearing the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch, grant you auspiciousness. (25)
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one seated the worthy Dānava upon the lion-throne, like a cloud upon a peak of Mount Meru.
Upon the lion-throne, the seat of a lion. || 26 ||
Then Hari [anointed] him with the waters of the great oceans, such as the Kṣīroda, summoned there,
as well as with the floods of rivers such as the Gaṅgā, and likewise with the waters of all sacred fords (tīrtha).
Together with all the assemblies of brahmin-sages and all the hosts of siddhas,
he was again joined by the vidyādharas and accompanied by the world-protectors.

By the natural force of the word "again" (punaḥ), it is understood that he had previously consecrated himself alone, and now, out of an excess of enthusiasm, he consecrated himself once more along with the Vidyādharas and others. || 28 ||
The one of immeasurable soul consecrated the great Asura in the sovereignty of the Daityas,
while he was being praised by the hosts of Maruts, just as Hari was formerly praised in heaven.
Hari, Indra. || 29 ||
While being praised by the gods and demons, Madhusūdana spoke these words to Prahlāda, who was himself being praised by the gods and demons and had just been consecrated.

The Blessed Lord said: O sinless one, as long as Mount Meru endures, as long as the earth remains, and as long as the orbs of the moon and sun exist, so long shall you remain a king, praised for your unbroken virtues.
Dharā means the earth; or alternatively, it refers to other mountains as well. || 31 ||
Having abandoned the fruits of both the desirable and the undesirable with a mind of equanimous vision,
protect the kingdom, free from passion, fear, and anger.
"In this kingdom, which is filled with enjoyments and where the unsurpassed earth has been seen, you must not feel agitation whether regarding heaven or the human world. (33)

By you, who have seen that unsurpassed state of incomparable bliss, no agitation characterized by dissatisfaction should be felt toward the kingdom; likewise, no agitation should be felt, nor should it be allowed to arise, toward heaven—the world of the gods—nor toward Mānava, the world of men, as you would toward your father and other elders. || 33 ||
Regarding the views obtained according to place, time, action, and circumstance, attend to the matter at hand; O sir, remain with a mind free from attachment! 34.

Regarding the views on the restraint and favor of subjects and enemies as they arise, carry out and perform the relevant tasks— such as execution, imprisonment, or punishment— in accordance with the specific person, place, time, and manner; however, do not harbor mental imbalance such as passion and the like.
Having abandoned [it], remain. || 34 ||

By transcending the body, being free from the notions of "this-ness" and "mine-ness," and performing action with equanimity toward existence and non-existence, you are not afflicted here in this world.

By virtue of being beyond the body—that is, by means of the state of the self as distinct from the body—[one remains unaffected] in the presence or absence [of things], that is, in gain or loss. || 35 ||
Having perceived the various states of saṃsāra and having weighed the incomparable state of the Tathāgata, you know everything everywhere; what else remains to be taught? (36)
He says, "Dṛṣṭa" (verse 36), meaning: "Since you alone are proficient in both conventional practice and the ultimate truth, there is nothing further to be taught to you."
While you, free from passion, fear, and anger, reign as king,
this painful knot of suffering shall no longer crush the Asuras.
He says, "By this, even your former desire shall be fulfilled"—namely, "vīta...
(verse 37). The meaning is that the hard knot of suffering among the asuras shall no longer remain, and that [knot], residing within the god, shall shatter the asuras through me.
The beauty of her tears will drench the clusters on the ears of the Asura women,
just as a river of broad waves, flowing wildly, floods a row of forests.
The river, maddened and swollen by the rains, possessed ever-higher billows and massive waves. || 38 ||
From this day forward,
the world shall remain as if at peace, like the ocean after the churning by Mount Mandara has ceased, no longer witnessing the conflict between demons and gods.
He says that the well-being of the world will also be established: "Now," etc. It is like the ocean which, when the Mandara mountain has been removed, is free from the churning mountain. || 39 ||
May the wives of the gods and asuras, having been brought together, place their mutual trust solely in their husbands and within their own inner apartments. (40)
They were brought there by one another, having been made captives by their mutual husbands. || 40 ||
Having dispelled the darkness of the deep sleep of the long night of worldly existence, and possessing the splendor of an ever-arisen intention,
[he beheld] that which is delightful with the playful charms of the daughters of Danu.
Enjoy for a long time the royal fortune that has not yet been conquered. || 41 ||
O son of Danu,
having dispelled the blinding darkness of ignorance— which is like the extreme sleep and gloom found in the nights of the dark fortnight—
you are one whose splendor of intention (āśaya-śrī) is ever-risen, consisting of the manifestation of the self as the self-luminous Brahman.

May you long enjoy the royal splendor—which is not conquered by enemies nor defeated by the six passions such as desire—and the splendor of sovereignty itself, which is delightful through the charms of women, the wives of the Asuras, and the graces of peace and other virtues; this is the benediction. (41)
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Coronation of Prahrāda," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. 41.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Coronation of Prahrāda," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one [Viṣṇu], together with men, gods, and kinnaras—
Like a second cycle of worldly existence, it shook from the palace of the Asuras.
The supreme fruit of the narrative regarding Viṣṇu’s journey to the Ocean of Milk is told, as well as the cause for his emergence from meditative absorption. || 1 ||
Because it contained humans, gods, and *kinnaras*, it was as vast as a second cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*); it moved, it went. || 1 ||
He was being filled from behind by multitudes of handfuls of flowers released by Prahlāda and others,
and by heaps of feathers from the wings of the lord of birds.
By means of heaps of handfuls of flowers, gathered like a mound upon the feathers on the back of Garuḍa, the lord of birds; || 2 ||
Having reached the Ocean of Milk in due course and dismissed the celestial river,
he sat upon the seat of the serpent’s coils like a bee upon a white lotus.
Viṣṇu remained upon the seat of the serpent’s coils, Śakra in heaven with the immortals, and the lord of the Dānavas in the netherworld; thus they all stayed, freed from their feverish distress.
This attainment of awakening belonging to the daughter of Prahlāda, which destroys all impurities without exception and is as cooling as the essence of the moon, has been told to you, O Rāma.
The lunar fluid is as cooling as nectar.
Indeed, those men in the world who, even if they have committed many evil deeds,
shall contemplate her with their intellect, will attain that state without delay.
By general inquiry, evil action comes to an end;
by inquiry into the words of Yoga, who does not attain the supreme state? (7)
By the term "misdeed" (duṣkṛta), evil and its root, which is ignorance, are meant. || 7 ||
Ignorance is said to be evil; it perishes through inquiry.
Therefore, one should not abandon inquiry, for it cuts away the very root of evil.
I said that it is not merely sin; he states this with the words "ignorance. || 8 ||
For those men who contemplate this perfection of Prahlāda,
the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes undoubtedly go to destruction.

The statement that "it is committed over seven births" is the result of a superficial investigation; however, according to an investigation culminating in the fruit of knowledge, it is well-established that all sins—excluding those whose fruits have already begun (prārabdha)—are destroyed. || 9 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, how was the mind of the high-souled Prahlāda awakened when it had become absorbed in the supreme state by the sounds of the Pāñcajanya conch?

Rāma asks—"In the case of one liberated through samādhi who has attained a state of rest and bliss equal to that of one liberated while in the body (videhamukta)—desiring to know the cause for his subsequent re-emergence from that state—he asks: 'In the supreme...
The implication is: since even hearing the sound of the conch Pāñcajanya is difficult to achieve when the mind has dissolved, how can awakening occur by means of it? || 10 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, two kinds of liberation exist in this world: one with the body and the other without the body;
hear now this distinction between them.

To state the specific distinction—that the very will of the Lord, accompanied by pure latent impressions (vāsanā) awakened by the remainder of prārabdha karma, is the cause for that awakening—he demonstrates the division between liberation with the body (sadeha-mukti) and disembodied liberation (videha-mukti) through the verse beginning with "dvividhā" and so forth.
"Vibhāga" means the difference consisting of the defining characteristics that distinguish them; this refers to the manner about to be described. || 11 ||

Know that the state of one whose mind is unattached to the taking up or casting aside of actions, and who is free from longing— that state is what is called liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā) in this world.
In the case of desirable and undesirable actions, there is no longing or passion regarding their acceptance or rejection; know that state of his to be liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā). || 12 ||

O Rāma, that very state, when the body perishes, is called videhamuktatā (liberation without a body), which is devoid of rebirth; those established therein do not come within the range of the visible.

By the word "body" (deha), the remainder of *prārabdha* karma, which is the cause for its maintenance, is indicated; the meaning is: when that [remainder] has been exhausted through experience. || 13 ||
Like seeds that have been sprouted yet are further devoid of the sprout of rebirth— [the reading "in another birth" (janmāntare) is also found]—
the pure latent impression (vāsanā) resides in the hearts of those liberated while living. 14.

"Seeds that have been parched" (*bhṛṣṭāni*) means roasted; this qualifying term contains a reason for the non-attainment of further visibility [of the body]. He states that for those liberated while living (*jīvanmuktas*), there is a cause for the visibility of the body again through emergence from meditative absorption (*samādhi-utthāna*), by saying "in the heart" (*hṛdi*). [The word] *śuddhā*...
Free from the garland of attachment. || 14 ||
Purifying, supremely noble, and following after pure being, she who consists of self-meditation remains eternally as if in deep sleep. (15)
The contemplation of the pure Brahman-self is purifying, sacred, supremely noble, and free from the wretchedness of craving.
Regarding the state of latent impressions (vāsanā) remaining within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) even while [the self] abides as Brahman, he provides an illustration:
"as if in deep sleep" (suṣuptasyeva). || 15 ||
Even at the end of a thousand years, O descendant of Raghu, those liberated while living awaken with that very same intermediate state as long as the body remains.
Here too, by the word "body" (deha), the remaining portion of *prārabdha* karma, which is the cause for maintaining it, is indicated. || 16 ||
O mighty-armed one, Prahrāda attained awakening through his own internal latent impression of pure being (sattva), awakened by the sound of a conch shell.
He states that this very [realization] is also the cause for Prahlāda’s awakening: "Prahlāda," [it says]. || 17 ||
For Hari is indeed the self of all beings; whatever appears to him becomes exactly so immediately, for the Self alone is the cause of everything.

Anticipating the objection that if the sense of hearing were withdrawn, even the sound of a conch shell would not be perceived, so how could there be cognition by means of that alone, he says "Hari" to dispel it: the Self is the causal Self; that is to say, one whose resolve is true. || 18 ||

When it was thus reflected: "May Prahrāda attain awakening," then, for the sake of creation, he whose self is Vāsudeva assumed a body through no cause other than himself, yet as the cause of all beings. (20)
Without any external cause, by means of his own pure self— which is the unmanifest cause of all beings—

and by means of desire, karma, and so forth (indicated by the word "ca"), he assumed a mere body (*vapuḥ* = *śarīramātram*) consisting of Vāsudeva for the purpose of creating the world within himself; the word "hi" indicates that it is indeed so.
This is for the purpose of indicating the well-known status [of this matter] in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas. || 20 ||
Through the contemplation of the Self, Mādhava is swiftly perceived;
through the propitiation of Mādhava, the Self itself is swiftly beheld.

For this very reason, he says "The Self" (ātma), meaning that upon seeing its form, the vision of the Self is established, and upon seeing the Self, the vision of that [form] is easily attained. || 21 ||
Holding fast to this view for the sake of perceiving the Self, O Raghava, quickly sport with a mind of inquiry; you shall attain the eternal state.
Dwell and exert yourself. || 22 ||
O Rāma, the pervasive monsoon of saṃsāra, fraught with the downpour of suffering, brings about extreme dullness in those who do not behold the sun of inquiry. (23)
Sufferings alone are its banks; it possesses downpours that are like torrents [of misery], as well as dullness, folly, and disease. || 23 ||
By the grace of Viṣṇu, his own self, this exceedingly radiant illusion does not afflict the wise, just as a yakṣī cannot harm one who possesses the protective mantra.

The mention of *yakṣīs* is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all *piśācas* and the like; [the term] "those possessing mantras" refers to those who have attained mastery over mantras (*mantrasiddhas*). 24.

This infinite illusion, which weaves the net of saṃsāra, attains density solely through the will of the inner self, and in due course, it likewise reaches dissolution solely through the will of the inner self.
These flames here are like the circle of wind surrounding a fire. || 25 ||

This Māyā of the infinite Viṣṇu, characterized by the construction of the web of saṃsāra, has attained density— the state of the manifold misfortunes of the body and so forth— solely through the will of that very Self. And she [is withdrawn] solely through the will of that Self when He has been propitiated by means of sincere devotion, meditative concentration, and the like.

At the time of the arising of discernment (*viveka*), inquiry (*vicāra*), and so forth, [the veil] undergoes attenuation, that is, diminution. Just as the flame of a fire becomes dense due to the very presence of a circle of wind, and at the end, by the power of that same wind, it becomes attenuated; so it is here.
Therefore, the purport of this narrative is that the attainment of knowledge necessarily occurs only through inquiry and other means produced by the grace of the Lord (*īśvara*).

This is the meaning. And thus is the aphorism of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa: "But [the Self] is concealed by the meditation on another; for from that [concealment] come its bondage and the opposite [liberation]. And there is the word of the Blessed One: "From Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. This is the meaning. || 25 ||

Thus ends the forty-second canto, titled "The State of Prahlāda," in the Section on Tranquility (Upaśama-prakaraṇa) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Valmīki and spoken by the Divine Messenger (Devadūta). 42.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The State of Prahrāda," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-third canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, by the pure rays of your words..."
We have attained peace, just as medicinal herbs do by the rays of the moon.
Even though [liberation] is obtainable through the grace of the Lord, one should not place the entire burden upon the Lord;
it is said that knowledge is to be achieved through human effort by mastering the senses. (1)
We have attained peace; we are gladdened. || 1 ||
Your words, which are pure and gentle, and which people long to hear with their ears, bring delight when received, just like flowers.

Like flowers such as the blue lotus (*utpala*), which are desired for the ears both for hearing and for adornment, these [words] are pure because they remove sin by being, in the case of flowers, the very grace of gurus, deities, and others. || 2 ||
If everything is attained through human effort, then why was Prahlāda not enlightened without the grace of Mādhava? (3)

In that case, why did Prahrāda not awaken even without the boon from Mādhava, but solely through his own human effort? Therefore, the meaning is that the previously stated rule—that the attainment of knowledge occurs everywhere only through one's own human effort—is violated. || 3 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, whatever was attained by the high-souled Prahlāda, all that was achieved by him through human effort alone and from no other source.

With the intention that even the supreme Mādhava is merely a specific means (*dvāraviśeṣa*) for the attainment of human goals—which are themselves to be accomplished through one's own human effort—and is not independent, he provides a concise answer, saying "Whatever...":
"The Self and Nārāyaṇa are indeed not different, like sesame and its oil. (4)
In the same way, it is like the whiteness of a cloth, and likewise like the fragrance of a flower. (5)

Alternatively, with the intention that the resolution here is easily found—namely, that because there is no difference between Viṣṇu and Prahlāda’s self, the boon obtained through Viṣṇu’s effort was in fact obtained through Prahlāda’s own effort—he says "the Self," and so forth.
Just as oil within sesame seeds is not different from the oil extracted from them, so it is here. But if this is so, [one might object]:
Lest there be the charge of modification (*vikāritā*), he states another illustration: "like whiteness and a cloth.
Or, he says "like flowers" [to show] that non-difference is to be understood, meaning that just as fragrance is the essence of flowers, so too Viṣṇu is the ultimate essence of living beings. || 5 ||
For he who is Viṣṇu is indeed the Self (Ātman), and he who is the Self is Janārdana;
the words "Viṣṇu" and "Ātman" are synonyms, just as "viṭapi" and "pādapa" are.
Alternatively, he states that when the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of cause and effect are discarded, there remains only pure consciousness (cinmātra), which is absolutely non-different;
thus, the two words "Viṣṇu" and "Ātman," which refer to the object of definition (lakṣya), are indeed synonyms. He says:
"He who... Even though there is a difference in limiting adjuncts—such as being a branch, a root, or an instrument for drinking—there is no difference in the nature of the indivisible tree itself.
The meaning is that it is just as there is synonymy between the words *viṭapi* and *pādapa*. || 6 ||
First, he himself, by his own self, was appointed to devotion toward Viṣṇu by his own supreme power, under the name Prahrāda.
For Prahrāda himself had personally obtained this boon;
having brought it under his own deliberation, he had understood its nature by himself.
The meaning is that by means of Viṣṇu, who is his very own self, having himself made his own mind the object of inquiry, he came to know his own self by himself alone. || 8 ||
Sometimes the Self awakens itself by its own power;
sometimes it is awakened through the body of Viṣṇu, which is attainable through devotion.

"By power" means by the force of inquiry performed through one's own effort; that is to say, by means of the gateway of Viṣṇu’s body, which is attainable through the effort characterized by devotion. || 9 ||
Even though he has been propitiated for a long time and is exceedingly pleased,
Mādhava is unable to bestow knowledge upon one who lacks discernment.
Having demonstrated the point through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he strengthens it by showing negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as well: "For a long time... (verse 10).
"In the realization of one's own Self, the primary cause is inquiry arising from human effort;
causes such as [divine] grace are secondary. Be intent upon the primary cause. (verse 11)

With the intention that "let inquiry culminate in the realization of the Self"—and not that the boon granted by Hari (Viṣṇu) is the primary thing desired, but rather that inquiry arising from human effort alone is considered primary; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of granting a boon simply saying "let there be knowledge"—he says: "primary" (mukhya). || 11 ||
Therefore, having first forcibly subdued the five senses,
practice with every effort and make the mind possessed of discernment.
He shows that object of effort from which the arising of inquiry occurs with the words "previously" (*pūrvam*). The mention of the group of five is an indication for the group of ten. || 12 ||
Whatever is attained by anyone, anywhere, is indeed obtained through the operation of one's own power; it is never obtained from any other source.
By one's own power and effort, through the engagement prompted thereby, and by the performance of auspicious conduct. || 13 ||
Relying on human effort and having leaped over the mountain of the senses,
cross the ocean of saṃsāra and go to the further shore, the supreme state.
If Janārdana were visible without human effort, why then does that unborn Lord not deliver the multitude of beasts and birds? (15)
"It is seen" means it is perceived in its true nature (*tattvataḥ*). "It does not rescue" means it does not reveal the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*).
The intention is that the very perception of the self constitutes liberation (*uddhāra*). || 15 ||
If a guru can rescue an ignorant person without relying on his own human effort, then why does he not likewise rescue a trained camel or a bullock? 16.

Since it is established in the Yogaśāstra and other texts that the Guru uplifts the disciple through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and so forth even without the disciple’s own effort, one might suspect a lack of invariable concomitance (*anaikāntya*) there; therefore, he says: "If [there were] a Guru...

The sense is that even in that case, it is precisely the effort consisting of devotion to the Guru and so forth that serves as the medium for the Guru's grace (*anugraha*) in the production of knowledge. || 16 ||
Nothing great is obtained from Hari, nor from a guru, nor from wealth;
for that which is attained by one whose mind is overcome by its own self is attained from the Self alone.
"From wealth"—that is, from riches; the sense is that according to the Vedic scripture, "There is no hope for immortality through wealth.

For one whose mind is overcome—whose mind has been sublated by the firmness of knowledge—that which was attained from the Self, from oneself, is the Great, in the form of the supreme human goal. || 17 ||
That which is not attained by the self when the serpent-like senses have been subdued through the union of practice and dispassion, cannot be attained from anywhere in the three worlds.
That which consists of the supreme human goal. || 18 ||
Propitiate the Self by means of the self; worship the Self by means of the self;
beholding the Self by means of the self, abide in the Self by means of the self. 19.

Propitiate Him with a superior intellect through hearing [the scriptures] and other means; accomplish Him; and once He is accomplished, worship Him with uninterrupted contemplation. Having perceived Him in reality—that is, having realized Him directly—remain established in that very state;
abide perfectly therein. The meaning is: do not fall away from that state of being. || 19 ||

For the sake of engaging fools who flee from the study of scriptures, effort, and inquiry in a state of auspicious stability, Vaiṣṇava devotion has indeed been fashioned as a conceptual construct. (20)

If knowledge arises solely from inquiry conducted through one's own effort, then for what purpose is devotion to Viṣṇu and others enjoined in the scriptures? To this he replies with the word "śāstra":
[it is] because of the intensity of attachment to sense-objects, [which obstructs] the spiritual treatises, the efforts toward the conquest of the senses and so forth, and the inquiries.
The meaning is: for the sake of leading those fools who have fled and become estranged toward the true path, so that they may somehow attain a state of auspiciousness. || 20 ||

Practice and effort are declared to be the primary method at the outset; in their absence, however, the secondary method consisting of the sequence of worshiping the worshipful should be employed. (21)
He strengthens the very point already stated by means of logical arguments, beginning with the words "through practice" (abhyāsa) and so forth. || 21 ||
If there is no mastery over the senses, what fruit can be obtained through worship?
If there is no mastery over the senses, what fruit can be obtained through worship? (22)
For Hari is not attained without inquiry and tranquility;
and for one who is liberated through inquiry and tranquility, what need is there for the Lotus-handed One? (23)
"It is attained" means it is truly acquired as one's own essential nature. Hari is the self whose essence is perfect bliss (*pūrṇānanda*).

The meaning is: for one who is liberated through inquiry and tranquility and has attained the supreme human goal, what further thing remains to be obtained by means of the lotus-handed body of Hari? Alternatively, [it may be understood] through inquiry and tranquility...
The meaning is: what benefit can even the Lord with lotus-like hands (Viṣṇu) possibly provide for one who is liberated, detached, and yet attached to sense objects? || 23 ||
Cultivate your own mind so that it is endowed with discernment and tranquility;
when that is perfected, you are perfected, otherwise you are but a wild donkey in the forest. (24)
Propitiate him; make him gracious. When he is accomplished and pleased, you too will be accomplished, having attained the perfection characterized by the supreme human goal. || 24 ||
A request out of affection is made by Mādhava and others themselves;
why then is it not likewise made to one's own mind? (25)
The phrase "how it is done" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 25 ||
Viṣṇu resides within every single person;
those lowest of men who go outside, abandoning him there, [seek Viṣṇu externally]. (26)
He states that devotion of the mind alone is the primary devotion to Viṣṇu, and not external devotion, by means of the verse beginning with "sarvasya" (of all). || 26 ||
The reality of consciousness dwelling in the secret cave of the heart is the primary, eternal body;
the form with conch, discus, and mace in hand is merely the secondary form of the Self.
The true characteristic of the Self is reality, the uncontradicted entity, which is eternal; it is the very primordial, everlasting, and constant body or essential nature.
That which is secondary—constructed from the qualities of *māyā*—is adventitious, so to speak. (27)
For he who, abandoning the primary, pursues the secondary,
is like one who, having discarded a perfected elixir, strives instead for something that must still be accomplished.
The elixir is nectar; it accomplishes what is to be accomplished, such as cooked rice and the like, and produces it through agriculture and other means. || 28 ||
But he who, O descendant of Raghu, does not attain stability in this wondrous state of self-knowledge, his mind remains intoxicated with delusion.
Who, then, is qualified for external devotion to Viṣṇu? He states this in two verses beginning with "He who":

the syntactical connection is that he who does not attain stability at all in the wonder of the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) should worship the Supreme Lord who holds the conch, discus, and mace in His hands. || 29 ||

One who has not yet attained discrimination regarding the self, and whose internal mind is not yet mastered, should worship the Supreme Lord who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace in His hands. (30)
In due time, the mind attains purity through that which produces dispassion.
By means of austerity that produces dispassion. || 31 ||
Through constant practice and discernment, the mind quickly becomes serene; it gradually attains the state of being possessed of self-mastery, just as a mango tree reaches its full maturity.

The inclusion of the word "swiftly" (āśu) is for the purpose of indicating the inevitability of [the Lord's] grace. "Sahakāra" refers to the mango tree, which possesses an exceeding fragrance of flowers, fruits, and so forth; it denotes the state characterized by that very nature. || 32 ||
O destroyer of enemies, this very self also attains the fruit that has been described by means of the cause known as the sequence of Hari’s worship.
The meaning is that whatever fruit is declared in the scripture by means of the procedure for the worship of Hari, one attains that very same fruit through one's own volition alone. || 33 ||
Even he who obtains a boon from Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor has thereby obtained for himself the fruit of the tree of practice.
Even he who obtains a boon from Viṣṇu has, by that very means, obtained the fruit of his own personal tree of practice; it is not accidental—this is the meaning. || 34 ||
The restraint of one's own mind is the ground for all supreme states and for all long-enduring prosperities, just as the soil is the ground for the beauty of the harvest.

The meaning is that the restraint of one's own mind alone is the ground and the place of origin for those in the highest state, who are intent upon the praiseworthy goals of human endeavor, whose prosperity is long-lasting, and whose wealth— such as lineage and so forth— is to be enjoyed for a long time. || 35 ||
Even for one who causes the earth to roar and drags away a mountain,
there is no other means here than the restraint of one’s own mind.

The intention is that for those such as the sons of Sagara who were intent on digging the earth, or for the gods and asuras who were dragging Mount Mandara as a churning mountain, or even for one intent on digging the earth for the sake of obtaining treasures and jewels— no great undertaking can be accomplished without one-pointedness of mind (aikāgrya). || 36 ||
Human beings wander upon this earth for thousands of births as long as the great ocean of the intoxicated mind does not reach tranquility. (37)
Even though they have been worshipped for a long time, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the others—
despite being affectionate— cannot protect one from the calamities of mental affliction.
Even Brahmā and the other gods, though affectionate and compassionate, cannot protect one from the afflictions of the mental disease. || 38 ||

Having abandoned that which is radiant with forms, whether external or internal, and which is unborn, quickly perform the contemplation of pure consciousness alone for the sake of the destruction of birth. (39)

The meaning is: having abandoned the external form of objects—which is radiant with various shapes and perceivable by the external senses—and the internal [form]—which is perceivable by the internal organs; contemplate instead that which is unborn, devoid of transformations such as birth and the like, and the single, indivisible form of pure consciousness alone. || 39 ||
Taste that which is the essence of all— pure existence alone, whose form is infinite, consisting of the savor of the one, stainless consciousness that is liberated from the object of perception.
You shall reach the further shore of the river of birth.

He concludes by restating what has already been said with explicit words: "That which is experienced," and so forth. O Rāma, that pure Being (sanmātra) which, being free from all objects of experience—whether external or internal—tastes itself as consisting solely of untainted consciousness, and thus flashes forth as the nature of unsurpassed bliss; such is it.

Relish it continuously through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that takes on its form; by relishing it in this way, you will reach the further shore of the river of birth—this is the meaning. || 40 ||
Thus ends the forty-third canto, titled "The Resting of Prahlāda," in the section on Peace within the Means to Liberation, in the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, the work of the Sage. 43.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Resting of Prahrāda," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, this illusion called "transmigration" has no end.
Only through the conquest of one's own mind does it come to an end; not otherwise.
In this commentary, the illusory nature of the perceived world as suffering will be demonstrated in detail for the sake of achieving freedom from desire in the mind. (1)

In that regard, it is prescribed that for one who has died at home or been taken to a cremation ground, the burning should take place in the water of the Gādhi after Viṣṇu has been beheld through his illusory power (māyā). || 2 ||
That is to say, it is endless and the cause of immeasurable delusion. || 1 ||
O sinless one, listen attentively as I relate this history for the purpose of understanding the manifold variety of the world’s illusory expansion.
"Attentive" means one whose mind is focused. || 2 ||
On this surface of the earth, there is a province named Kosala;
it is like a forest of wish-fulfilling trees on Mount Meru, and a source of multitudes of jewels.
A maṇḍala is a particular region, like the grove of Kalpa-trees in Nandana and other such places on Mount Meru. || 3 ||
There lived a certain virtuous Brahmin known as Gādhi,
who was a supreme Vedic scholar, wise, and stood like the very embodiment of Dharma.
There, in that maṇḍala. || 4 ||
