From his childhood, he shone with a mind free from passion,
just as the world is illuminated by a stainless and pure sky.
The phrase "stainless and pure" is an epithet for the sky as well.
Having fixed some desired undertaking within his own mind,
he departed from the circle of his kinsmen and went to the forest to perform austerities.
The task is the purpose of austerity. || 6 ||
There, that king of brahmins reached a lake filled with blossoming lotuses,
just as the moon reaches the sky, which is bright and pure and filled with the essence of stars.
In that forest, Tārā and Aśvinī were the most beautiful and worthy of being seen.
Seeing that lake, the twice-born man entered it for the sake of penance;
submerged up to his neck in the water, he became like a lotus in the rainy season.

From the sight of Āśauṅgiri until the sight of Viṣṇu, for the sake of penance, he entered—that is, remained after having entered—the lake, submerged up to his neck like a rain-lily in the monsoon season. || 8 ||
Eight months passed for him as he remained submerged in the waters of the lake,
his facial luster only slightly diminished by the closing of the lotuses that served as his dwelling.

His facial luster was slightly dimmed by the affection he felt for his fellow lotuses dwelling there, as they had closed up due to their separation from the sun—the very abode where they resided. || 9 ||
Then, one day, Hari approached him who was scorched by asceticism,
just as a dark cloud approaches the earth when it is distressed by the heat of summer during the rainy season.
"Śyāma" is also an epithet for Hari. || 10 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Brahmin, arise from the midst of the milk and take your desired boon;
the tree of your religious observance has borne the fruit you longed for."
The tree of self-restraint is the tree of asceticism; "endowed with the desired fruit" means that it has become fruitful. || 11 ||
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Salutations to Viṣṇu, who is like a bee within the hollow of the heart-lotuses of the countless beings of the worlds, and who is the lake for the single lotus-plant of the three worlds. 12.
To the bee that is dark like a bee (alini), residing within the hollow of the heart-lotus of the countless beings and living creatures existing in the world. || 12 ||
O Blessed One, I wish to behold this supreme illusion fashioned by you, which is known as saṃsāra and causes sole blindness.
The supreme self-nature superimposed upon the Supreme Self. || 13 ||
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
"O unborn one, you shall see this illusion and then abandon it";
having spoken thus, he became invisible, like a city of the Gandharvas.

The second boon was granted by the Blessed One even though unasked: that you shall abandon [the world] because you will obtain the meaningfulness of your own penance for worship—which yields the fruit of the supreme human goal—merely by seeing the Māyā;
this is "invisibility," meaning disappearance. || 14 ||
When Viṣṇu had departed, that lordly Brāhmaṇa rose up from the water,
his form cool and stainless like the moon emerging from the waters of the Milky Ocean.
His soul became completely satisfied by the sight of the Lord of the World,
like a white water-lily blossoming at the sight and touch of the moon.
From the statement "by seeing and touching," it is understood that even stationary beings possess visual and other forms of cognition.
(16) Then, for him who was filled with the bliss of beholding Hari, some days passed in that forest while he performed the duties of a Brahmin. (17)
By means of the duties of a Brahmin, such as austerity, Vedic study, and the honoring of guests.
Once, he began his bath in a lake filled with blooming lotuses,
reflecting in his mind upon the words of Viṣṇu like a great sage.
When the lotus has risen—that is, when the lotus has blossomed—just as a great seer, by the power of yoga, contemplates in his mind that which is past and future, so it is here. || 18 ||
Then, during the ritual of bathing, he performed a submersion within the water for the sake of destroying all sins, as if turning himself over within it.

The meaning is that, for the sake of destroying all sins and for the purpose of purifying sin (*aghamarṣaṇa*), he performed a rotation within the water with his hand holding *kuśa* grass, like a whirlpool. || 19 ||
While moving within the water, his mind having forgotten meditation and mantras and the expansion of his consciousness being overturned, he beheld from the midst of the water: || 20 ||

Having submerged himself within the water, while engaged in the rite of *aghamarṣaṇa* characterized by the recollection of mantras beginning with the *praṇava*, he was one whose flow of consciousness was thus directed—overturned and intent upon grasping [the essence] in reverse. || 20 ||
He saw his own dead body, fallen in his own house and become an object of grief,
like a tree blown by the force of the wind into the interior of a mountain cave.
Like a tree fallen into the interior of a cave within a mountain pass. || 21 ||
With the flow of inhalation and exhalation ceased, it has reached the state of liberation;
the movement of its limbs has been completely stilled, like a lamp-flame in a windless place.
The explanation of "dead" is "inhalation and exhalation"; it is like a piece of plantain or similar fruit that has fallen in a windless place.
With a pale face, withered like a sapless leaf from a tree,
appearing as if turned to a corpse yet not decayed, he was like a lotus whose stalk has been severed.
"Become a corpse" (śavībhūtam); the particle *iva* refers to falsehood (*mithyātva*) and does not have the sense of a comparison. || 23 ||
In the morning, the sky appeared as if its vision were inverted;
the village seemed shrouded by a drought, and everything was grey with dust on all sides.
An *avagraha* is a withholding of rain; by it, [the world] is like a village submerged [by water]. 24.
It was surrounded by distressed kinsmen, their faces drenched in tears, uttering piteous cries of lamentation, like a tree surrounded by grieving ospreys.
With compassion, there was a wailing and weeping by the *kurara* birds—specific types of birds—who were performing that [act]. || 25 ||
He was attended at his feet by his wife, who resembled a lotus-pond whose lotuses have their faces carried away by the waters gushing from the breach of the dam.
By a lotus-pond whose face was as if being carried away by elephants emerging and flowing forth from the breaking of the embankment. || 26 ||
His chin, marked with fresh signs of food, was seized by his mother, who was greedy for his cries, lamentations, moans, and chatter.

With a loud, piercing cry, like humming bees with their *repha* sounds in their chatter—meaning in nonsensical, articulate speech and long-drawn-out lamentations—he was marked and distinguished by fresh whiskers; [she was] greedy for and attached to him.
He was surrounded by other wretched people standing at his side with faces streaming with tears,
clinging to him like dry leaves covered in falling frost cling to a tree.
"Resorted to" means surrounded. || 28 ||
It was covered by limbs that had extended far away as if out of fear of separation, as if intent on avoiding union, and as if they were no longer their own.

There is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) suggesting that they were as if intent on avoiding union out of fear of separation, a principle established by logic that "all unions end in separation. [They departed] with their limbs—hands, feet, and so forth—as if they were not their own, or as if they were non-relatives; this is a simile (*upamā*). || 29 ||
With his white teeth slightly visible between lips that do not touch one another,
he seemed to laugh at his own life as if it were devoid of passion, yet never withering.
With teeth that were slightly faded and somewhat soiled, he seemed to laugh at his own life as being in vain for all this time, appearing like a dispassionate man devoid of attachment. || 30 ||
He was as if entered into silent meditation, as if fashioned from mud,
as if fast asleep for the sake of non-awakening, and as if resting profoundly.
"Maunadhyāna" and so forth are the four poetic conceits (utprekṣās). || 31 ||
The cries arising from the tumultuous lamentation of his kinsmen seemed to listen with effort, as it were, for the sake of discerning the nature of his affection.
He was as if silently listening to their lamentations with an attentive mind and great effort, in order to discern whose affection for their kinsmen was greater and whose was less. || 32 ||

Then, by his own kinsmen, who were agitated by frantic gestures and incoherent outcries like those of a stormy wave at that moment, he was gradually expelled from the house—that is, driven outside—this is how it connects with the following verse. || 33 ||
Gradually, by his agitated kinsmen, who were making shrill cries like those of female ospreys,
that inauspicious being was driven out so as never to be seen again.
It was led to the cremation ground, defiled by a mire of flesh, entrails, and fat; drenched with both dried and fresh fluids, and crowded with hundreds of skeletons. (35)
The phrases beginning with "māṃsāntre" and ending with "jaratkhagam" are adjectives qualifying the cremation ground (śmaśāna). || 35 ||
The sun’s rays were shrouded by vultures like clouds, while the darkness was dispelled by the blazing of funeral pyres;
the earth was overspread with the spreading clusters of flames from the mouths of jackals and dogs.
The earth was as if covered in sprouts by the masses of flames issuing from the mouths of the inauspicious ones named Śiva. || 36 ||
It was bathed in flowing rivers of blood, where fierce herons and crows were submerged;
it was filled with aged birds ensnared in a web of spreading strings still wet with blood.

Wherein some herons have bathed and others are submerged in the flowing rivers of blood, along with fierce crows; wherein old birds are caught in nets and snares, characterized by the spreading of wet sinews moistened with blood.
There, in that blazing fire, his kinsmen reduced the corpse to ashes, just as the oceans reduce the submarine fire (vāḍava) with a flood of water.
Just as the oceans reduce their own flood of water to ashes in the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni), so did they [reduce him]. || 38 ||
With crackling sounds of *caṭa-caṭa* as it burst into flame, that funeral pyre quickly consumed the corpse,
its mass of matted flames swelling up like a great heap of dry fuel.
The funeral pyre, its mass of matted locks characterized by a network of flames swollen and increased by abundant dry fuel, quickly consumed that corpse with crackling sounds. || 39 ||
The fire, having filled the mass of clouds with the pervasive stench released by the loud *kaṭakaṭa* sounds of its blazing flames,
surrounded the heap of bones on all sides like a tusker surrounding a bamboo grove full of holes.
He caused the thick, sweet nectar vomited by the wicked to be shattered. || 40 ||

The fire, which had filled the masses of clouds with rising crackling sounds and released fragrances, vomited forth— that is, emitted from all sides— thick and accumulated fluids; such was the fire that crushed the heap of bones, which, being full of cavities, resembled a forest of hollow bamboos.
The meaning is that he split it open. || 40 ||

Thus ends the forty-fourth canto, titled "The Destruction of Gādhi," within the narrative of Gādhi in the Section on Tranquility (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the Means to Liberation (*mokṣopāya*) in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of the Sage (*ārṣa*). || 44 ||
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Destruction of Gādhi," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then Gādhi beheld with his own mind, which was heavy with its own affliction.
Remaining right there within the water, he [perceived] the inner self within the stainless self.
Herein is described his birth from the womb of a Pulkasī woman, his dwelling among the Kirātas, and the attainment of the kingdom by him whose kinsmen had died, in the city of Kīra. (1)

By means of her own mental sufferings—that is, by her intense (*pīvarayā*) or accumulated (*upacitayā*) [grief]—the connection with all the causal factors (*kārakas*) from this point onward follows in sequence until the word "saw" (*apaśyat*) in the twentieth verse. || 1 ||
He perceived himself, agitated, situated within the womb of a woman of the Śvapacas— a class of outcasts dwelling on the outskirts of villages at the edge of the Bhūta-maṇḍala.
The "limit" (paryanta) refers to the boundary of that specific region called the Bhūtamaṇḍala; it concerns those residing on the ground situated near the outskirts of the village therein. || 2 ||
Overwhelmed by the burden of the womb, his delicate limbs were oppressed;
he lay within the heart of a dog-cooker woman, as distressed as if in his own excrement.
By the term "dwelling in the womb," the sufferings existing therein are indicated; it is "overwhelmed by that burden.
The phrase "afflicted" and so forth is an elaboration of that very point. (3)
In due time, through gradual ripening, she gave birth to one of dark complexion, who was like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season— dark-hued and enveloped by impurities— born of a dog-cooker woman.
A dog-cooker (śvapaca) gives birth at the [wrong] time; [it portends] a cloud for a year. || 4 ||
In the house of a dog-cooker (cāṇḍāla), there was a child, beloved by the dog-cooker,
who was full of life and moving here and there like the overflowing waters of the Yamunā.
The Yamunā water, fallen into the current of the Yamunā, was like an uprooted lotus used as an ear-ornament. || 5 ||
He had reached the age of twelve, yet remained in the bloom of sixteen;
with broad shoulders and noble limbs, he was as full-bodied as a rain cloud.
Accompanied by a retinue of dogs, he roamed from forest to forest,
slaughtering hundreds of thousands of deer and adopting the lifestyle of a Paulinda hunter.
One whose retinue consists of dogs—specifically hunting dogs—for the purpose of the chase and other such activities; [he adopted] the state or livelihood of a Paulinda, that is, a Kirāta. (7)
Then he was approached by the wife of a dog-eater, who resembled a *tamāla* creeper, adorned with the clusters of her breasts and possessing hands like fresh sprouts.
Then [he was] resorted to by the daughter of a dog-cooker; that is to say, he had performed the marriage ceremony. || 8 ||
She was dark-complexioned, with a row of teeth as pure as a stainless rosary;
she possessed limbs gracefully curved with abundant charms, like a forest creeper with fresh sprouts. || 9 ||

By her whose row of teeth was stainless due to its natural whiteness, though appearing soiled from the absence of tooth-cleansing sticks; and by her whose limbs were bent with such playful movements that they seemed to follow after the forest shoots—the suffix *kvip* being applied to the root *yā-* with the word *vanapallava-* as an upapada. (9)
He was sporting at the edges of the forests with his new bride,
like a dark bee with a female bee amidst the abundance of flowers.
Or rather, by means of a sacrifice so that it may be ever-new and eternally fresh;
or else, by means of a sacrifice in the forest regions abounding with flowers and floral splendors. || 10 ||
Dwelling amidst the leaves of forest trees and creepers, he was afflicted by calamity,
appearing like the formidable Vindhya wilderness itself personified.
The figure of speech is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), imagining [the army] as if it were the Vindhya forest that has arrived in the form of a man and assumed a human shape. || 11 ||
It rested in forest thickets, slept in mountain caves,
hid among heaps of leaves, and made its home within shrubs.
Abounding with *kiṃkirāta* flowers as ear-ornaments, adorned with garlands of jasmine, beautiful with *ketaka* flowers as crest-jewels, and filled with garlands of mango blossoms. || 13 ||
By the words "kiṃkirāta" and so forth, their respective flower clusters are meant. || 13 ||
He had sported upon beds of flowers and wandered along mountain slopes;
he was an expert in the recesses of the forest and highly skilled in the killing of deer.
"In the treasuries of the forest" means in the objects of the senses; "one who knows that" means one who possesses extraordinary knowledge; "the much-knowing" means the wise man. || 14 ||
Then, upon the mountains, he brought forth sons who were the sprouts of his own lineage,
yet whose fortunes were exceedingly harsh, like thorns on a khadira tree.
Their reports and deeds were exceedingly difficult and impossible even to hear. || 15 ||
Though possessed of a wife and prosperous, he remained with his youth exhausted,
gradually falling into decrepitude like a dry land deprived of rain.
Then, having gone to that place of birth where he was possessed by the host of elemental spirits,
he stayed there like a lordly sage, having constructed a small hut at a distance from them using leaves.

A spirit-seizer known as Bhūtamaṇḍala, having reached the birthplace belonging to the village of that region, stayed there after constructing a small hut with leaves from palm trees and other plants at a distance. || 17 ||
It has reached a state of extreme decrepitude through old age; its own body is like that of its son, and it resembles a tamāla tree in a ravine whose sap is nearly exhausted.

He whose sons are equal in size to his own body, and whose vital juices are nearly exhausted—by such a person, [the world] is perceived as resembling a young *tāla* tree grown upon a crumbling mountain cliff. || 18 ||
He was leading a mature domestic life as a dog-cooker (śvapaca) with many kinsmen; his name, purpose, and speech were cruel, yet he had attained great prosperity.

"He saw his own [self] who had reached the highest prosperity of his family, whose names, designations, meanings, and verbal expressions were cruel"— all these preceding qualifiers are to be construed with the following [subject]. (19)
Then Gādhi saw that his wife was old and had become a remover of her own confusion by serving among the dog-cookers (outcastes).
This aged Gādhi was inferior even to other dog-cookers. Thereafter, for that householder who possessed a wife and followed after delusion itself— the delusion that dispels [all else]— his own family,
as far as his wife and household extended, was completely enveloped by death, leaving nothing remaining.

The connection of the two [verses] is "he saw that it had been carried away. The meaning is: just as a mass of dry leaves fallen in the forest is carried away by the flow of rainwater (*āsāra-salila*), so it was in this case. || 20 ||
That entire family was completely swept away by death,
just as a mass of forest leaves is quickly carried off by a torrential downpour.
Wasted by suffering in the forest, he laments all alone, like a deer separated from its herd—despairing and with eyes full of tears. (22)
Then that old man, all alone in the forest, laments and weeps.
Having spent a few days there with a mind overwhelmed by grief,
he abandoned his own country, just as a bird leaves a lake whose lotuses have withered.
The egg-born are the swans and so forth. || 23 ||
He wandered through many lands, free from attachment yet filled with anxiety,
as if impelled by another, like a cloud driven by the wind.
Driven by another, as if dependent on another. || 24 ||
Once, while wandering through the empty sky like a celestial being in a divine chariot, he reached the glorious city of Kīra-maṇḍala.
Dwelling and wandering in the empty sky over that region which was the dwelling place of the Kirātas and the people of the countryside.
Its paths were covered with dancing jewel-garments, its trees and creepers were like women, flowers were strewn as far as the ankles, and it was made beautiful by sandalwood and agallochum.

In that [city], the trees, creepers, and women standing along the road were covered with jewels and silken garments as they danced; such was the royal highway he entered—this is the syntactical connection with the following verse. || 26 ||
Surrounded on all sides by vassal lords, women,
and citizens, he reached the middle of the royal highway, which resembled the path to heaven.
It is densely packed without any intervals. || 27 ||
There he beheld an auspicious elephant in a pavilion made of precious gems, moving restlessly like the king of the immortals' mountain.
With its dwellings, its refuges, and its lattices fashioned from jewels and the finest gems;
with the abodes of the gods established upon the flank of the lord of mountains—[he beheld] Meru, the sovereign mountain of the immortals. || 28 ||
When the king had died, he wandered here and there for the sake of the kingdom,
like a connoisseur of jewels seeking gems, out of a desire to behold the wish-fulfilling gem.
Wandering and roaming here and there; a man who knows jewels, skilled in the examination of gems. || 29 ||
That outcaste gazed for a long time at the elephant, which was like a mountain possessed of movement, with eyes wide with curiosity.
He is a dog-cooker (outcaste). || 30 ||
Taking him who was looking on with his trunk, that elephant respectfully placed him upon its own shoulder, as Mount Meru places the sun upon its slope.
He placed [him] upon his own hip, that is, he set him there. || 31 ||
When he had ascended that chariot, the drums of the invincible [gods] resounded on all sides;
like the clouds at the end of an aeon, they rose into the sky as if they were great oceans.
The great ones are like oceans, like seas. || 32 ||
The king shone with his desires fulfilled, while the sound of the people crying "Victory!
arose like the chorus of birds awakened at dawn.
Āśās are the directions and mental desires. || 33 ||
Then there arose a dense clamor from the throngs of bards,
like the roar of oceans whose waters are tossed by the shore.
There, beautiful women surrounded him for the sake of adorning him,
like the waves rising from the Milk Ocean surrounding Mount Mandara.
They obstructed and surrounded him, bewildered by the path of the Ocean of Milk which had been churned into agitation.
The proud women filled him with various jewels strung upon threads of virtue,
just as the shores fill the mountain on the coast with the sun made manifest by various rays of light at dawn.

[The rays] are like garlands, as it were, strung together and woven through the threads of their qualities; they are such that the sun is made to shine by the various splendors reflected from the multicolored gems within them—rays that, like a mountain situated on its own shore, [illuminate] the immovable peak. 36.
They adorned him with necklaces whose touch was as cool as frost,
just as the dark rainy seasons adorn a lofty mountain peak with the floods of forest rivers.
The young women were dark-complexioned; like rain-showers from the clouds, they fell upon the cities of the forest rivers, appearing like mountain peaks submerged in their midst.
With their sprout-like hands trembling, the women surrounded him with flowers of various colors and fragrances, as if they were the very splendors of spring surrounding the god of love.
With ointments of various colors, tastes, and fragrances, they quickly anointed him with nets of light,
just as a mountain is covered by minerals and clouds.

The mountain is [described] by its minerals through their characteristic connection with the elements; and the sky is like a cloud, or rather like a mass of clouds, by means of networks of light. || 39 ||
Beautiful as a jewel and gold, he captivated the expansive mind,
just as Mount Meru occupies the sky filled with twilight clouds, stars, the moon, and rivers.
Adorned with ornaments of jewels and gold, that beloved king captivated their hearts; this is the implied sense.
(40) Adorned and surrounded by playful young women, he shone like a *kalpa* tree strewn with flowers of gems and silken garments. (41)
All the subjects, accompanied by their retinues, approached him who was like that, just as travelers approach a blossoming tree by the roadside.
There, they consecrated him in due order upon a lion-throne, just as the immortals consecrated Śakra upon the elephant Airāvata. || 43 ||

Having seated those subjects upon the lion-throne, they consecrated him in due order—that is, according to the sequence of the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. And having consecrated him, they followed after him, having seated him upon that aforementioned elephant; this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 43 ||
Thus that outcaste obtained the kingdom within Kīrapura,
just as a crow seizes a plump wild deer in the forest that has lost its life-breath.
His lotus-feet were rubbed by the lotus-palms of Kīrī,
and with saffron unguents applied to all his limbs, he shone like an evening cloud.
In the city of Kīra,
that king, accompanied by a multitude of women, shone like a lion joined by a pride of lionesses in a forest in full bloom.
His body adorned with clusters of pearls fallen from the temples of elephants slain by Hari, his anxiety and despondency stilled,
he took delight there in the lake in the company of the virtuous and in various enjoyments.
Like an elephant scorched by the heat of the sun's rays, [he was refreshed] by floods of water. || 47 ||

His body was adorned and embellished with clusters of pearls released from the frontal globes of elephants torn apart and slain by lions; being one whose former anxieties and dejections were thus stilled, he remained in that city together with virtuous ministers, citizens, and others.
He delighted and took pleasure in enjoyments, just as an elephant, scorched by the rays of the sun and by passion, delights in the abundance of water in a lake. || 47 ||
His royal majesty having spread abroad, his commands established in every direction, the administration of the conquered territories accomplished within a few days,
and the entire burden of the nobility fully supported by the subjects;
There, a king named Gavala reigned. || 48 ||

The king there in the land of Kīra was one whose royal power (*rāja-śakti*) had spread far and wide; for this very reason, his command was established in all directions. Within a few days, by his own will and effort alone, he had secured the administration of the kingdom; he was a Śvapaca named Gavala, renowned by that new name.
The meaning is that it came to be. || 48 ||

Thus ends the forty-fifth canto, titled "The Dog-Cook's Attainment of Kingship," within the *Gāthi-vṛttānta* of the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa*, in the section on the means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*) of the venerable *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage (*ārṣa*). 45.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Kingship by the Outcaste," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama*) within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Surrounded by playful women and honored by the circle of ministers, [the king...]
He was saluted by all the vassal lords and cherished with parasols and yak-tail fans. || 1 ||
Having heard from the outcaste about that [fire] among the people, when the outcaste entered the blazing fire, he too was consumed by it; then Gādhi awoke and was extolled.
The connection with the third [verse] is as follows: "surrounded by playful women" and so forth—through these qualifiers, he became one who had forgotten his own true nature. || 1 ||
He was beloved for his mastery of the teachings of the perfected ones; he understood the sequence of the qualities of sovereignty;
his wisdom was free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue; and he had attained the great ten-fold state. (2)
He whose unimpeded command and instruction are ever successful, and whose subjects are free from sorrow, fear, and exhaustion. (2)
Having forgotten his own true nature through constant hymns of praise and auspicious rites,
he was, as it were, completely intoxicated by the wine of a state of being filled with bliss.
Like one intoxicated when his wine has run out. || 3 ||
A Cāṇḍāla ruled over the parrots for eight years;
during that entire time, he maintained the conduct of an Ārya in its entirety.
Noble conduct consists of compassion, courtesy, purity, and so forth.
Then, once by chance, he stood there having cast off his ornaments,
like the sky when it is free from darkness and filled with the light of the stars, the moon, and the sun, as well as with clouds.
In which there exist no darkness, stars, moon, sun, light, or clouds; such as that, it is blue on all sides like the sky.
She did not value our necklaces, armlets, and bracelets;
for a mind swollen with lordship does not delight in things that are not naturally acquired.

He states the reason why he has cast off his ornaments with the word "much" (bahu). That which is augmented by power—that is, increased—is the artificial ornament and so forth; he does not delight in such things. || 6 ||
Wearing such a dress, he alone went out to the outer courtyard,
like the sun setting from the region of the sky after reaching its zenith.
From the courtyard, which was frequented by the principal people within, he went out to the outer area, a common place for low-born folk; just as the sun, about to set or having set,
departs from the central expanse of the sky toward the peripheral regions of the heavens.
It is the same as that. || 7 ||
There he saw a group of dark-skinned, stout outcaste dog-cookers (śvapacas),
singing softly like a flock of cuckoos at the onset of spring.
He sang softly and sweetly for a group of outcaste dog-cookers.
With the playful movement of his sprout-like hands, he was plucking the strings of the lute,
producing soft sounds like a tree whose bees hum softly while their rows of wings vibrate against it.

She was shaking the string—the wire—of the *vallakī* lute; she possessed a soft tone—a gentle sound—and was like a row of bees (*aliśreṇi*) whose wings were the humming *repha* sounds as she shook the tree. || 9 ||
Then one man arose from among them, aged and with blood-red eyes,
like a leader of dog-cookers (candālas) holding a horn filled with snow.
He stood like a mountain peak made of glass filled with snow—dark yet grey with dust. || 10 ||
"O Kaṭañjaya, speaking thus abruptly to King Kīra, he asked:
'Does the king here know the art of singing? (11)
Addressing him by his former name, "Kaṭañja," he spoke to awaken him.
Does he perhaps honor the red-throated cuckoo as if he were full of passion, or does he fill [his home] by bestowing garments and seats? (12)

Does he honor—that is, hold in high esteem—one who has a red throat and a sweet-toned voice? [He does so] because he possesses passion (*rāgavān*), knows musical notes (*svaravit*), or is full of affection for his beloved and others; and by means of the giving—that is, the presentation—of houses, garments, and seats. (12)
Like a mango tree with its branches laden with fruits and flowers, O honey-sweet one,
I have attained supreme bliss this day by the mere sight of you.
"Madhu" refers to spring. When the "ra" is elided, there is a lengthening of the vowel. "Nirvṛtiṃ" means happiness. || 13 ||
Just as the lotus [blooms] at sunrise and the medicinal herbs at the rising of the moon, so too does this [serve as the cause] for all joys and even for great acquisitions. (14)
"The meeting with a kinsman is the ultimate limit of infinite rest"—
even as the king spoke thus to the dog-cooker,
he showed his contempt by a gesture that was victorious at that very moment. (15)

*Sīmāntaḥ* means the ultimate limit. Since it is stated that *sīmantaḥ* refers to the arrangement of hair (*keśaveśa*), there is no application of the *pararūpa* sandhi rule. *Avadhīraṇam* means contempt; by way of this, it amounts to concealment. || 15 ||
Meanwhile, the beloved women who had gone to the windows likewise fell into a state of profound dejection upon realizing, "This is a dog-eater. (16)
"Extremely" means having reached a state of exhaustion and diminished joy. || 16 ||
The citizens did not shine, like lotus-pools during a downpour of frost, like villages beset by drought,
or like great mountains engulfed in forest fires.

"By that shower of frost" (*tuṣāraprāvṛṣṭyā*) means by that which fills (*prāvṛṣṭi*) with frost (*tuṣāra*). The word "like" (*iva*) is also connected here. From the root *prā* in the sense of "filling," with the suffix *kvip*, in the third case singular, the vowel *ā* is elided according to the rule *āto dhātoḥ*. "Possessing forest fires" (*sāvagrahā... dāvavantaḥ*) means those afflicted by drought (*anāvṛṣṭi*), as if they were possessed of the forest fire (*dāva*) that occurs in the wilderness (*dava*). || 17 ||
The king disregarded each of those conversations concerning the outcaste,
just as a lion ignores the yowling of a cat perched on the top of a tree.
He disregarded and rebuked her; [he abandoned] conversation and discourse. || 18 ||
He quickly entered the inner apartments, which were filled with dejected people,
just as a royal swan enters a lake whose lotuses have withered due to a lack of rain.
The lotus was sinking, while the mud-born flower was being purified.
With all his limbs utterly exhausted, he fell into a state of dejection,
like a withered tree whose great hollow between its knees is filled with fire.

[The body] is pervaded and rests within all its limbs. It has a "knee-stiffener" (*jānu-stambha*)—that is, the root portion which supports the knees—and within the great cavity or hollow situated between those [limbs], there is fire. A "bad tree" (*durdruma*) refers to the silk-cotton tree (*śālmali*) and others. || 20 ||
There he saw all the people with dejected faces,
like a net of saffron flowers whose base has been gnawed by a rat.

By the term *jālapada*, a shrub (*gulma*) that serves as the locus for a network of flowers is meant [the word *gulma* is not read in some versions]. By the mouse (*ākhu*), meaning a rat, is meant one whose roots have been eaten—that is, whose roots have been severed. || 21 ||
Consequently, the ministers, the citizens, and the women did not even look upon that lord of the earth as he stood there, as if he were a corpse in his very home.
Even while he was staying right there in his house, they did not touch him; that is, they did not come into physical contact with him. || 22 ||
Then his servants, receiving no hospitality, abandoned him from afar, just as children, though filled with grief and deep affection, leave behind a corpse.
With a face devoid of joy, a darkened body, and stripped of its luster,
they, though undisturbed, regarded him as if he were a scorched piece of ground.
The burnt ground was like a cremation ground. || 24 ||
As his body was smoking and he was in a state of intense suffering,
the people did not approach his side, just as they do not approach a fire on a mountain.
The multitude of people did not approach or draw near to his side, just as fire does not approach the side of a mountain consisting of earthen embankments and rocks. || 25 ||
Deprived of their assembly of courtiers, they became dispirited;
their commands found no footing, like drops of water upon ashes.
To the question of why he did not bring her under his control by means of his power of command (*ājñā-śakti*), he says: "She was of feeble energy.

Abandoned and neglected by the members of the assembly and by the hosts of warriors and others, her commands did not reach their destination—the person worthy of being commanded—nor did they find a subject upon which to operate. || 26 ||
Because he had the appearance of one who performs cruel deeds and brought misfortune upon those who associated with him,
people fled from him especially, as if from a *rākṣasa*.
"Fearing association with the impure, the wicked, and those who inflict death and other harms—as if from a *rākṣasa*," so says Śeṣa.
Though situated in the midst of people, he remained all alone,
like a traveler in a foreign land, being devoid of the qualities of wealth and the like.
"Artha" means wealth; by the word "etcetera," one's own kin, friends, and so forth are included. || 28 ||
Even though he spoke to them repeatedly, the citizens gave him no reply,
just as travelers do not respond to a hollow bamboo flute, even if it is adorned with a net of pearls.
To the *kīcaka* bamboo—a specific variety of bamboo that, being a source of pearls, resounds with a network of pearls when shaken by the wind—[he offered salutation]. || 29 ||
Now, having been defiled by the dog-cookers for a long time, we all cannot be purified by penances; we shall enter the fire. (30)
Having thus resolved, the citizens of the city and the ministers likewise set fires on all sides, fueled by dry wood.
They were nourished and increased by means of dry fuel. || 31 ||
Then, as those [fires] blazed on all sides like stars in the sky,
the entire city became filled with people whose sole concern was lamentation.

While the stars were blazing and shining—here the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) because the root is intransitive—the word "city" (*nagara*) indicates by metonymy (*lakṣaṇā*) the people residing therein. || 32 ||
It was crowded with cuckoos warbling cries of compassion and shedding tears,
while the people wept piteously at the edge of the blazing sacrificial pit.

He describes that very city with eight verses beginning with "karuṇā": "avaṣṭabdha" means supported or held up by the hands and other limbs; "where the subjects are sluggish, bewildered, and weeping in the vicinity of the blazing furnaces. (33)

With the servants weeping at the sight of the ministers who had entered the fire-pits, the place became like a forest made even more resonant with the cries of those wailing and lamenting by the winds.
"Rudat" means shedding tears; "krandat" means crying out—this is the distinction. "Mārutaiḥ" refers to winds accompanied by frost and gales. || 34 ||
The air was thick with the potent stench of the flesh of eminent Brahmins being consumed on the funeral pyres, while a portentous whirlwind arose, scattering the dust like falling frost.
By that wind, which possessed a thick and dense fragrance from the flesh of the foremost Brahmins who had been set ablaze upon the funeral pyres,
the place appeared as if shrouded in mist, with dust rising from the refuse-heaps and mounds of earth. || 35 ||
With its curved [rays], it became like the sky with the sun obscured by clouds.

The city became like a sky whose sun was obscured by clouds— clouds formed by the circles and swarms of powerful birds, such as *piśācas* and other creatures, who had been drawn from afar by the wind through the long-reaching, far-spreading odors of fat. || 36 ||
The circle of the sky blazed with funeral pyres fanned by the wind;
the horizons were filled with a rain of stars that were actually swarms of flying sparks of fire.
It was filled with the cries of intoxicated thieves and the screams of trembling children and youths;
the terrified citizens had abandoned all hope for their lives, and there was no stability whatsoever.
He further describes what that place was like at that time with the words "by the negligent":

it was a place where children, youths, and slightly mature ones were crying out, writhing, and trembling while ornaments and other belongings were being plundered by arrogant and reckless thieves; and where the terrified citizens had cast away and abandoned all hope for their lives.
Where there is no designation of one's own name and no established order, it is called "asaṃsthiti" (the state of non-abiding) or "nirmaryāda" (the absence of boundaries).
The city was such that its houses were unguarded, all its stores had been plundered by thieves, sons and wives had been abandoned, and the citizens were preoccupied with his death.
The citizens, agitated and hastening toward death, [arrived] where such a state had come to pass; this is how the sentence is to be connected. || 39 ||
While that painful reversal of fate was thus occurring, a state resembling the end of an entire eon for all living beings prevailed. || 40 ||
Gavala, whose intellect was purified by contact with the virtuous of the kingdom, reflected while his mind was agitated by grief. (41)
For my sake, this calamity has come to pass in this land—an untimely dissolution that destroys all leaders. (42)
This is a source of distress and misfortune. || 42 ||
What use have I for the suffering of life? Death is a great festival for me;
for a wretched creature condemned by the world, death is better than life. (43)
Having thus resolved, Gavala, in the blazing fire,
once more made his body an offering without hesitation, like a moth.
She offered her own body as an oblation into the blazing fire. || 44 ||
When that body named Balādgavalana had fallen into the mass of fire and reached a state of fragmentation of its limbs,
[he remained] in accordance with the throbbing of the burning fire that consumed his own members.
Gādhi suddenly attained awakening while submerged within the water.

When that body named Gavala fell into the mass of fire by the power of his world-weariness, Gādhi—performing the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite in accordance with the throbbings and stirrings of his own limbs, such as his hands and feet, during their burning—suddenly attained awakening while within the water; this is the meaning. || 45 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the performance of the evening rites.
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe;
and at the end of the night, it returned along with the rays of the sun.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Loss of the Kingdom," within the narrative of Gādhi, in the Section on Tranquility (Upaśama-prakaraṇa) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the Great Epic of Vasiṣṭha, composed by the Sage. 46.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Fall from Sovereignty," in the section on Tranquility within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The twelfth day.
The forty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after two muhūrtas, Gādhi, due to the delusion arising from mental anguish, [fell asleep].
The state of agitation subsided like a whirlpool on the shore of the ocean.

Having heard from his guest about that conduct of King Kīra—which he remembered as if it were a dream—Gādhi went there, saw it, and after questioning him repeatedly, became filled with wonder; this is now related. || 1 ||

It was calmed by the aforementioned delusion of worldly existence (*bhava-bhrama*) due to its superior form; *ākulībhāva* means that in which one becomes agitated (*ākulībhavati*), formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). It was like an eddy situated at the shore (*velā*). || 1 ||
Due to his delusion regarding mental creation, he desisted from it,
just as Brahmā desists at the time of the end of a kalpa from the creation of the world.
Having become tranquil, he gradually attained awakening to his own true nature, like one whose intellect is wide awake;
just as when intoxication has subsided, one whose disposition has reached maturity regains clarity.

He attained his own innate awakening, characterized by the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) that had been previously suppressed, like one whose intellect is wide awake and free from sleep. In a state of intoxication—such as the exhilaration from wine and the like—one whose disposition has matured possesses a clear mind. || 3 ||
He perceived: "This is I," "This is that which must be done," and "This is not [to be done]," just as the world perceives clearly when the night has passed and the veil of darkness has faded away.
"He who has descended into the water for bathing is this Gādhi, and I am he. The duties remaining from my bath, such as the libations (tarpaṇa) and so forth, must be performed by me.
This kingdom of the Caṇḍāla seen previously and other such matters are not to be done. It is just as the common people perceive it. || 4 ||
Then, having regained his memory, he drew up his foot from within the water,
just as Mādhava draws up a lotus whose face has blossomed at the end of winter.
He lifted up one foot after the other; at the end of the cold season, with the departure of the frost, his mouth began to open like a flower that has formed its buds; Mādhava is the spring. || 5 ||
Beholding this earth, with its gates, houses, and sky,
as if it were another world, he was filled with supreme wonder.

Alternatively, the analysis of the compound may be: "this [place] possesses those [features] which are water (vāri), the quarter (kakubh), and the sky (vyoman)," or "it possesses those very things—water and so forth—that are being perceived. || 6 ||
"Who am I? What do I see? What indeed have I done?"—reflecting thus, his mind remained for a moment with its eyebrows knit in a frown.
Thus he remained, reflecting within himself with a frown upon his brows.
"Exhausted, I perceived a state of agitation in that very instant";
realizing this, he rose from the water like the rising sun.

Therefore, due to the force of his exhaustion, in a mere instant he rose up from his great confusion—a vast delusion. [The form] "udasthāt" is derived from the root √sthā with the luṅ (aorist) suffix, where the *s* of *sic* is elided by the rule "gātisthā. He was like the sun rising there on Mount Udaya, or like Time itself. || 8 ||
And he reflected on the bank: "Where is that mother? Where is that beloved wife, since I have met my death in the midst of both my mother and my wife?"
He shows the very manner of her reflection with the words beginning "Where," etc. The form *mahele* for the word *mahilā* is a Vedic *guṇa* substitution. || 9 ||
It is said that both parents of me, a child of little understanding, have perished—
like a leaf carried away by the wind from a tree and creeper by the sword.

For one who lacks wisdom and whose state of mind is immature, the creeper and the tree—which stand in the place of mother and father for a leaf blown by the wind—have been destroyed by death, as if by a sword. 10.
I am unmarried and do not even know the true nature of women,
just as a twice-born man does not know the nature of wine, which is corrupting and agitating.
The twice-born Brahmin [perceived] the true nature of the wine, as if it were its very essence.
My own kinsmen have become exceedingly distant from my country; who indeed are they among whom I should give up my life? (12)
"Of my own country, my birthplace; my own kinsmen, my relatives—among whom I am casting off my life, having witnessed death—who indeed are they? This is the syntactical connection. || 12 ||
Therefore, what indeed have I seen arising from this—a world of various undertakings and activities, like a city of Gandharvas? (13)
What indeed has he seen—the various undertakings (ārambha), that is, the multitude of objects, as well as the agitation (saṃrambha), namely, the attachment to birth and so forth? || 13 ||
Let this matter rest; for such is the state of death even in the midst of kinsmen.
Not even the slightest bit of reality is perceived within this delusion of Māyā.
Having ascertained its falsity through sublation, as in the case of a dream, one remains indifferent, thinking, "Let it be so. This means: "Therefore, let this delusion remain as it is. || 14 ||
Thus, the mind of embodied beings perpetually wanders among infinite delusive perceptions, like a frenzied tiger roaming through forest thickets. (15)
Having resolved this matter in his mind,
Gādhi then took him to his own hermitage for some days.
He spent several days in his own hermitage.
Once, a certain dear guest arrived there unexpectedly;
weary from his journey, he took rest like Durvāsas resting before Brahmā.
Exhausted from his emaciation, that guest then rested in that hermitage; he took repose, which is to say, he stayed there for the evening. || 17 ||
That guest was brought to the highest satisfaction by Gādhi with offerings of fruits, flowers, and juices, just as a tree is nourished by the spring season.
Contentment and satisfaction. || 18 ||
Having mutually saluted at the twilight hour and both having performed their recitations,
they reached their beds in due order and lay upon soft sprouts.
Then there proceeded a peaceful conversation between those two ascetics, appropriate to their own duties, like the beauty of flowers on two trees that have reached the season of spring. (20)

A discourse appropriate—that is, consistent with—their respective activities of asceticism, meditation, and so forth, proceeded. [The word *ī* is a particle used in the sense of "indeed" (*khalu*). It was peaceful, meaning it was dominated by the aesthetic sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*).
[The term *ṛtutvamaḥ* refers to the Sun, who "measures" (*minoti*) and thus defines (*paricchinatti*) the nature of the seasons (*ṛtu*) through his own activity.]
In the union of hope and the northern direction, there was, as it were, the springtime glory of flowers appropriate for that season.
Gādhi questioned that guest with words that arose in the course of conversation:
"O Brahmin, why are you so emaciated in body? Why are you so overcome by fatigue? (21)
It fell into the course of their conversation. || 21 ||
The guest said:
"O Blessed One, hear the cause of my extreme emaciation and fatigue;
I shall tell it as it is, for we are not speakers of untruth. (22)
We: the plural form [is used] for the word *asmad* when two [are meant]. || 22 ||
On this surface of the earth, in a bower of the northern quarter, there is a great and glorious country, highly renowned by the name Kīra. (23)
There I dwelt for a month, being honored by the people in the city,
my soul greedy for the taste of various sensual pleasures and deluded by the vampire of the mind.

"Various self-delights" (*nānātmasvādāḥ*) refers to diverse kinds of food that are pleasing and agreeable to oneself; "greed for them" (*lobhas teṣu*) means attachment to those things. Being "of that nature" (*tadātmā*) means having that as one's primary characteristic. To the question, "How did you become like this?", he replies with the words beginning "cittena" (verse 24):
"Once, on a certain occasion, it was said by someone there in the course of a conversation."
"O twice-born one, it has been told to me that here there was a king who was a dog-cooker for eight years."
Then, when questioned by him, all the inhabitants of the villages said:
"A Śvapaca became the king here for eight years. (26)
Thus, having been fully understood at the end, he entered the fire with speed;
thereafter, hundreds of brahmins here likewise entered the sacrificial fire.
He is a dog-cooker (outcaste). "At the end" means at the end of the eighth year. || 27 ||
Having heard this from their mouths and having departed from that circle,
O twice-born one, I performed an expiation at Prayāga for the sake of purification.
For the sake of purification and for the pacification of the defects arising from residing in that region. || 28 ||
Having performed the breaking of my fast today at the end of the third Cāndrāyaṇa penance, I have come here; because of that, I am exhausted and exceedingly emaciated.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this, Gādhi then questioned that twice-born man once more, and he spoke exactly the same thing, not otherwise.
Then, filled with wonder, having spent that night there on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
the sun— the great lamp of the house of the world— arose.

Then, when the sun had risen and his guest had departed after taking leave, Gādhi—with a mind uplifted by wonder and with great gravity—reflected upon this which is about to be told; thus is the connection with the following verse. || 31 ||
When his guest had departed after performing the rites of morning ablution and taking leave, he reflected upon this with a mind overflowing with wonder: || 32 ||
"That which was seen by me in my agitation has been declared by the twice-born as being real; what indeed could this be, other than the method of Māyā-Śambhu? (33)

"That which was seen by me in my agitation, during a state of delusion, has been told to me as a reality by the twice-born guest. Could this be of such a nature that it is the method of creation belonging to the Asura Śambara, characterized by illusion (*māyā*)? [The suffix] *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). || 33 ||
"That death of myself which I saw in the midst of smoke was surely an illusion; there is no doubt about it. As for the rest, I see that very thing of his."

That illusion was entirely false; no correspondence can be found there. As for the remainder—that which remains—I see (the sense being "I shall see") that account of myself as a dog-cooker, which is the cause for that guest's performance of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. || 34 ||
Therefore, with an undaunted mind, I shall go quickly to the village on the edge of the circle of inhabited lands to see the account of that dog-cooker.
He says that very thing with the word "tad" (that): the *udanta*, or account, of that person in such a state, namely the *śvapaca* (outcaste).
Thinking thus, he rose with reverence to go to another mandala,
as if the sun were striving to see the side of Mount Meru.
Thinking thus, Gādhi rose up to observe another mandala; he was intent and prepared. || 36 ||
Even a kingdom of the mind is attained by the wise who are resolute;
Gādhi went and obtained, unimpaired, that which he had seen in a dream.
If it is asked how that can be seen, he says—“It is a kingdom of the mind”—to show that there is nothing unattainable through human effort. || 37 ||
Through resolute determination, even that which is difficult to attain is obtained;
Gādhi, beholding the world as an illusion, was intent on making it an object of knowledge. || 38 ||
To make it an object of cognition means to bring it within the range of the eye as a means of valid knowledge. || 38 ||
Having set out on his path with the speed of a monsoon torrent,
he traversed many lands like a horse driven by the wind.
On the path during the rainy season, he became as swift as a torrential flood of water; he was like a cloud whose vehicle is the wind itself. (39)
Having entered that circle of beings whose natural conduct was of such a kind, Karabha was alone like a thorn in a forest of *kārañja* trees. (40)
He first arrived at that Bhūta-maṇḍala, which possessed such a nature and whose own conduct was of the same kind as previously observed. || 40 ||
There, by means of that very same arrangement established in his consciousness,
he beheld a certain village, like a city of the Gandharvas.

While remaining in consciousness—that is, within his own awareness—he saw a certain Vāmaka situated there by means of a particular configuration, a specific arrangement that was being remembered. || 41 ||
At its edge, he beheld that very same abode of the dog-cookers,
like a multitude of hells in Pātāla beneath the world.
That supreme being, whose dwelling consisted of the vast expanse of his own mental constructs,
perceived himself as a Chandala, just like a Gandharva.

The meaning is that he again perceived through signs his own state as a dog-cooker (śvapaca), which was abundant with houses and other dwellings— such places where the expansion of his births and so forth had been previously seen and contemplated in his mind. || 43 ||
In that very same arrangement, he saw the dwelling place of a dog-cooker (outcaste) as seen before; this led his mind to an indescribable state of world-weariness.
That mind, which was the abode of a dog-cooker (outcaste), led him to, or brought him to, an indescribable state of detachment. || 44 ||
Swept by the downpours of the rainy season, with barley sprouts growing from its walls, its roof-covering half-tumbled and its bedsteads barely visible; (45)

He describes that very [state] with the verse beginning "The rainy season" (*prāvṛṭ*) and so forth. It is that in which some previously unseen object of recognition—a bed, a fragment of a couch, or the like—is perceived. || 45 ||
Poverty was as if solidified, misfortune as if it had become a wall,
wickedness as if its limbs had fallen away, and wretchedness as if it were shattered to pieces.
"Kuḍyamat" means having the form of a house reduced to mere walls; the change to "ava" occurs because it belongs to the *yavādi* group.
"Bhraṣṭāṅgam" means with its parts fallen away, like the wickedness of theft and such. "Dauḥsthityam" means a state of wretchedness. "Khaṇḍitam" means having one part cut off or broken. || 46 ||
Its banks were covered with white bones of cows, horses, and buffaloes, crushed by the tusks of elephants, which stood there as if to bear witness [to the slaughter]. (47)
"Gādhi gazed for a long time"—this is the connection with the third [verse]. || 47 ||
It was covered with those very skull-bowls in which he had formerly eaten and drunk,
filled as if with drink by the waters of motionless clouds.
By those [trees] which possessed waters from clouds that were motionless—meaning, waters from rain that had arrived by chance. || 48 ||
It was completely encircled on all sides by those very entrails, now withered like creepers, resembling long-reaching thirsts.

It was surrounded on all sides by "lattāvṛtaiḥ," meaning enclosures formed by creepers that wrap around pillars and other structures like creepers themselves. In the reading "āttatantrībhiḥ," the meaning is that it was enveloped by spreading tendrils which, as coverings for the creepers, had assumed the nature of strings (tantrīs). || 49 ||
Then, with speed, he gazed for a long time at his own former house,
as one possessed of self-control gazes upon a body that has become a dried-up corpse.
One who possesses self-mastery and knows reality regards [the world] as if it were his own body, which has become almost entirely like a withered corpse. 50.
Filled with great wonder, he arrived at the village, just as a traveler, having crossed a city of Mlecchas, reaches the land of the Aryas. || 51 ||
Having bypassed his own house, he went to a small village situated near it—a wretched village. || 51 ||
There he questioned the people: "O good sirs, do you perhaps remember the former history of this village—the succession of the outcaste dog-cookers at its edge?"
The conduct of the outcaste, the account of the outcaste. || 52 ||
"For it has been heard by me from virtuous people that all who possess wisdom clearly perceive even what occurred long ago as if it were held in their own hands. (53)
They see clearly; that is to say, they remember. || 53 ||
Do you not remember this excellent old outcaste living here in solitude, who is like a physical embodiment of sorrows? 54.
"O virtuous one, if you know, tell me that in truth;
O traveler, it is taught that the severing of another's doubt yields great merit. (55)
When asked again and again by the twice-born Gādhi, those villagers replied with no small measure of laughter and agitation, like physicians to one who is distressed.

"Not small" refers to pride, wonder, agitation, and the exertion for inquiry; these qualify the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) in which the deed consists. "By the afflicted" means by one suffering from disease. || 56 ||
The villagers said:
"O Brahmin, as you say, so it is; it cannot be otherwise.
There was once here a man named Kaṭaṃja, an outcaste (śvapaca) of terrible appearance. (57)
His retinue of sons, grandsons, friends, servants, kinsmen,
and relatives was exceedingly vast, like the mass of leaves upon a tree.
Death snatched away the entire family of that old man,
just as a forest fire consumes a mountain grove laden with flowers and fruit.
The word *bhava* is also [a synonym for] *dāva*. || 59 ||
Having abandoned that country, he went to the interior of Kīra’s city;
there he became king for eight years without any agitation.
He who, having fully understood the truth therein, is rejected from afar by people,
is like a heap of misfortune or like a poisonous tree in a village.
Then, as the people were entering the fire, he himself entered the consumer of oblations;
for through association with the noble, he had attained nobility and thus entered it.
"O Lord, why do you yourself inquire with such effort about the dog-eater?
Is he perhaps a relative of yours, or did you become so by your own nature? (63)
Did he become your kinsman, or did you yourself spontaneously become his kinsman? || 63 ||
As he spoke thus, Gādhi questioned him again and again;
he dwelt there for one month in all those border regions.
"In that village" means in all the outskirts, that is to say, in the various houses suitable for dwelling there. || 64 ||
Just as he had experienced it, so exactly was that story of the dog-cooker related by all those villagers to him without any omission. (65)
Then, having heard this unimpeded account from the mouths of all the beings and having thoroughly examined it according to his own experience,
Gādhi held it in his heart like the stainless moon.
With his form concealed, he was filled with the utmost wonder.
Having heard these words, which were unimpeded in their capacity to consume all beings and were not false in their meaning,

and having personally observed [the truth] through uncontradicted recognition exactly as it had been experienced, Gādhi— his appearance concealed by shame— perceived that supreme [sorrow], which had mounted upon his own heart like a spot on the moon, the lord of stars.
"He attained wonder" means he reached it. || 66 ||

Thus ends the forty-seventh canto, titled "Direct Perception," in the *Gādhi-vṛttānta* (The Story of Gādhi) within the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Chapter on Quiescence), in the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 47 ||
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Direct Observation," in the Section on Tranquility (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having rolled about in the house of the outcaste, he was filled with wonder once again.
For Gādhi’s mind found no satisfaction in beholding such wonders. || 1 ||
Gādhi went to the city of the Kīras and, having seen [the marvel], was filled with wonder;
Viṣṇu, gratified by his ascetic penance, said to him, "All this is Māyā."
*Luṭhitam* means turned over; that is to say, it has been clinging for a long time. || 1 ||
There he surveyed the sites and dwellings,
just as the Lotus-born Brahmā surveys the worlds overturned by the agitation at the end of an aeon.
A *kalpa* is a period of dissolution; during its agitation—that is, its upheaval—they were overturned and shattered. *Ambujodbhava* is Brahmā. || 2 ||
He spoke thus to himself in that forest where his dwelling lay in ruins,
amidst a garland of dry bones, like a tree inhabited by a piśāca.
In the ruined abode where the house was broken down, he spoke as if to himself at the tree in the cemetery. || 3 ||
These garlands made from the tusks of dead elephants, which were fashioned as enclosures,
remain even today for an eon, like the peaks of Mount Meru.
What he said, he expresses with the words "these are those," and so forth.

These are the rows of tusks of dead elephants, fixed like spikes in the enclosure wall; the meaning is that they are being recognized directly before one's eyes. With reference to the *kalpa*, the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*), [he speaks] of Meru...
The crests are like mountain peaks. || 4 ||
Here, that meat of a female monkey was formerly eaten along with tender bamboo shoots by those intoxicated by liquor, together with their outcaste kinsmen.
With ripe vaśā sprouts together with side-dishes of karīra shoots. || 5 ||
Having embraced the dark woman of the outcaste, O Kesarin, he slept here upon the armor,
having drunk the liquor mixed with the bitter ichor of elephants.

"On the skin of a maned horse"—by the statement that it was "bitter with elephant-ichor," it is understood that this *maireya* liquor was purchased from an elephant-driver; for it is well known that elephant-drivers mix even elephant-ichor into *maireya* to enhance its intoxicating power. (6)
The female dogs of the household, nourished on oil-cakes and bran,
were tied here with leather thongs to a wooden post for dead elephants.
The female dogs of the household were emaciated, having been nourished only on oil-cakes, offal, and meat;
they were bound with leather thongs and straps.
"Here you gave three pots of elephant-pearls,
bound with the fierce hide of a buffalo that shone like a cloud."

In this place, there was a vessel made of elephant tusks, measuring the size of three cooking pots (ukhā) and filled with three jars of pearls from elephants that had been shed by wild tuskers. || 8 ||
In these various places here, he rolled for a long time together with the children of the outcaste dog-cookers,
like cuckoos among a heap of mango leaves.
While these [women] are being seen—those previously seen—here, at the edge of this village; "rolled about" means engaged in playing in the dust. || 9 ||
Here, as if proceeding from flutes whistling with her sighs, she drank the blood of dogs; she was adorned with corpses and accomplished [her purpose]. (10)
By the sighs and breaths of the children, the flutes began to resonate;

likewise, the song proceeded in accordance with that resonance, following the movement of the musical scales and rhythms (*svaratāla*). From that which has the nature of adorning corpses—namely, the cemetery garlands, sandalwood, and so forth—it was thus accomplished.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "the adornment of all. || 10 ||
There, together with his family members at the wedding festivities,
the kinsman raised a great clamor, like the waves in the ocean.
In marriages other than those [already mentioned]. || 11 ||
Here, a bamboo cage has been constructed and secured for the sake of providing food to the crows, vultures, and birds that are eager to fly away elsewhere.

"Anyadā-aśanam-āśaḥ" means eating at another time, for the purpose of consuming [food] on another day. However, if the reading is "dāsārtham," then it is derived from the root *dasu* (meaning "to injure"); thus, the meaning is "for the purpose of harming on another day. || 12 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Recalling his former activities as a dog-eater in this manner,
Gādhi, his head trembling with amazement, reflected upon the supreme workings of the Creator.
He reflected, that is, he reasoned. || 13 ||
From that distant land, the knower of what must be done departed after a long time;
leaving behind the circle of living beings, he reached another country by degrees.
Having crossed the continuous succession of rivers, mountains, regions, and forests,
he reached that inhabited country— a settlement like a supreme jewel in the lap of the Snowy Mountains— which, as the meaning implies, was formerly the land of the Kirātas. || 15 ||
There he reached the city of Mahīpāla, which resembled a mountain,
just as Nārada, his soul weary from wandering through the worlds, reaches the realm of the gods.
Resembling a cloud, with palaces as lofty as mountains and enriched with jewels and other treasures. || 16 ||
Then, beholding in the city places that he had himself experienced, seen, and frequented, he respectfully questioned the people.
One has experienced one's own house, palaces, and so forth; one has seen the houses, palaces, and so forth of others; and one has frequented places such as groves, locations, and halls. || 17 ||
"O virtuous one, do you remember anything here regarding the outcaste lord?
If you know the truth, describe it to me quickly and according to the rules. (18)
"According to rule" means performing the ritual procedure without transgressing the prescribed injunction. || 18 ||
The citizens said:
"O twice-born one, for eight years now a Śvapaca has been the ruler here;
his name was bestowed by Maṅgalahastin. (19)
The word "nāma" is used in the sense of well-known or established fact. || 19 ||
And having been fully recognized before entering the fire,
O ascetic, twelve years have now passed today.
Whatever Gādhi asked people out of his curiosity,
he heard from their very mouths and even savored it.
The meaning is that he relishes and experiences a sense of wonder through the internal correspondence of his own self-recognition.
Then, in that city, he saw the king along with his army and vehicles—
the god Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus— emerging from the palace to the outside.
He states that, through the grace of the Blessed One, he beheld the Blessed One in the form of a king within that city: "He emerged from the palace, the royal residence, outside the temple. (22)
Seeing the sky covered by clouds of moving dust, and recollecting its former silver-like luster, he spoke with great amazement: || 23 ||

With the intention that his mind was deluded by the sight of external objects, so that even when the form of the Blessed One was seen, he had neither devotion nor reflection toward it, but rather his mind wandered only among the curiosities of recognition— namely, the women, parasols, chowries, and so forth experienced previously— the text says "he" (saḥ), [describing him as] with moving, uplifted...
The meaning is: having seen that army which had thus covered and obscured the sky with clouds characterized by dust. || 23 ||
These are those Kīra women, whose skin resembles the interior of a lotus,
who possess the hue of molten gold and eyes like trembling blue lotuses.
These are those very courtesans, the beloveds of King Kīra, now recognized. || 24 ||
These multitudes of yak-tail whisks, white as the massed rays of the moon,
resemble steady waterfalls or heaps of kāśa flowers.

The moonbeams are as white as a massed cluster— as if they were a solidified heap— and resemble mountain torrents, those cascades of water falling from mountains which have attained stability through their solidification into fixed forms. (25)
Fans with rows of young feathers are being waved by beautiful women;
these are like the splendors of forest creepers now coming into bloom. (26)
The supernatural powers are like the abundance of flowering clusters. || 26 ||
These are those herds of rutting elephants that fill the horizons; they are like the successions of peaks of Mount Meru, appearing as trees of the imagination.
"Herds" (ghaṭāḥ) refers to groups of rutting elephants; "those by which the edges of the quarters were pierced by the tips of their tusks.
This is an *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) based on poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*). [The mountains] are those in which there are trees that yield fruits according to one's mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
These kings, whose prowess is equal to that of Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera,
are like the world-protectors (Lokapālas) of Indra himself.

Like the world-protectors headed by Yama to Vāsava, these feudal lords and rulers of intermediate regions have come from the earth; these rows of houses stand like beautiful groves of *kalpa*-tree creepers, containing heaps of all things that grant every desire. (29)
In which all floods of things such as wealth, grain, and so forth [are contained]. // 29 //
This kingdom of the Kīra people, which was enjoyed by me in the past, has today become manifest as the very conduct of my own previous birth. (30)
The conduct of his previous lives, experienced in former births, became as if manifest before his eyes, like the life-story of another birth. || 30 ||
"Truly, this waking state has stood before me like a dream;
I do not know by what cause this illusion has arisen and expanded. (31)

This reality was certainly perceived like a dream in the past, yet it now stands as a waking state; by what means, through whom, or for what purpose was this arising or manifestation brought about? (31)
"Alas! Indeed, by this long and leaping delusion of the mind, I have been brought to a state of helplessness, like a small bird caught in a net. (32)
Helplessness is the state of lacking self-mastery. || 32 ||
Alas! Woe is me; my mind, struck down by latent impressions, perceives spreading webs of delusion like a child. (33)
Unawakened and not awakened. || 33 ||
"For this great illusion was indeed shown to me by that wielder of the discus; now I have rightly remembered it in its entirety. (34)
By that Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus, who had previously been propitiated.
Therefore, I shall now make such an effort in a mountain cave that I may understand both the origin and the nature of this false agitation. (35)
By the two words "birth" and "subsistence," its cause is indicated. || 35 ||
Having reflected thus, Gādhi departed from that city;
reaching a mountain cave, he stood there like a rested lion. (36)
There, for a year and a half, that one of great splendor performed penance, subsisting on a mere handful of milk, for the gratification of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The remainder of the sense is: "making his meal and drink from a cupped handful of milk. [This refers to] Viṣṇu, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
and by the rule *dhanuṣaś ca*, the suffix anaṅ is applied [to form *śārṅgadhanvan*]. || 37 ||
Then the lotus-eyed one approached him in a form of water,
dark as a blue lotus, like a great lake in autumn attaining clarity.
He whose form was by nature as serene as water— whose very essence, in the case of a lake, was water itself—
approached that cave of the king of mountains, the abode of the twice-born.
Then he dwelt in the sky with a complexion as clear and transparent as a water-bearing cloud.

The cave that served as the dwelling place of the twice-born Gādhi; its luster—its pure brilliance—was as clear and stainless as a cloud, or else it was as if it were residing in the sky like a cloud. 39.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Gādhi, have you seen my most powerful illusion? Have you seen the workings of the snare of the world, which is the very nature of fatalism?
He whose mind holds destiny alone—that is, fate—as the basis for conviction, and not the actual nature of things; || 40 ||
When this state has been attained and reached by your mind, you are blameless and practicing penance on the mountain slope; what else do you desire? (41)

The syntactical connection is as follows: "When this vision of my *māyā*, which was desired and reached by your mind, has been obtained, you—blameless and pure—are performing penance once again on the mountain slope; what else do you desire? (41)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Seeing Hari speaking thus, Gādhi, the best of the twice-born,
covered his feet with a profusion of flowers as an act of worship.
He performed worship at the feet of the image of the Blessed One, which was being constantly worshipped;
that is, he made it full with a flood of flowers—a stream of released blossoms—like a flood of water. By this, the arrival of the Blessed One at the time of worship is understood. 42.
Having offered the arghya water, scattered flowers, and quickly bowed with circumambulations,
the twice-born spoke these words to Viṣṇu, as a cātaka bird addresses a rain-cloud.
The *arghya* and the subsequent *arghya*; having performed circumambulations along with prostrations, one completes the worship ending with the final salutation. || 43 ||
Gādhi said:
O Lord, this illusion consisting of profound darkness which has been displayed by you—
may you make it manifest to me, just as the sun makes the earth visible at dawn.
O Lord, how is it that this delusion—which the mind perceives when garlanded by the impurity of latent impressions—is seen even during the waking state, just as in a dream? (45)
He states that portion which is to be understood therein: "delusion" (bhrama). Delusion is that which consists of a collection of false objects.
And how has this delusion of a dream within the water, perceived for but a moment, attained direct perception for me, O Abode of the Stainless State? (46)
He whose state—his abode and foundation—is pure, being free from the impurity of ignorance, and has long been within the range of the eyes and other senses, that is, directly perceptible. || 46 ||
Given the vast duration of this time, how could the births and deaths of this body not exist within me, through my delusions regarding outcastes? (47)

The meaning is: since my delusions regarding him being a dog-cooker (outcaste) occurred during this long duration of time, how could his births and deaths—the arising and perishing of that dog-cooker's body—not remain within my very mind? How could they not exist externally while I stand here? || 47 ||
The Blessed One said:
O Gādhi, this is the nature of the mind when it is shaken by its own mental afflictions; being one who has not perceived reality, it perceives manifold delusions. (48)

O Bhavānī, that which one perceives as a vast and great delusion of the world within the deep abyss is, in reality, the very nature of the Self— manifesting in this form to the mind that has fallen into the state of *citta* because it has not perceived the Truth, and is therefore seized by its own inherent mental afflictions and diseases. This is how it appears in substance.
The meaning is that it is neither internal nor external, neither small nor long. || 48 ||
Nothing exists at all externally—neither the sky, the mountains, the oceans, the earth, nor the directions;
all this exists within one's own mind, just as a mass of leaves exists within a sprout.

If you think that it exists, then [the author] says "it exists only within one's own mind," namely "externally. The meaning is that the world consists of space (kha), which is the sky; mountains (adrī); the earth (urvī); the directions (diśaḥ), and so forth. || 49 ||
Just as fruits and the like expand outward from a sprout, so too do [the elements] such as earth manifest externally from consciousness. (50)
It is true that earth and the other elements reside within the mind and are never external;
for the sprout contains the leaf, and from that [sprout] comes the glory of the fruit.
Because of which cause the splendors of the fruit are seen; "are seen" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 51 ||
The mind destroys and creates itself—consisting of form, light, mental attention, reality, time, and action—just as a potter fashions a jar. 52.

Regarding the present object, there is the manifestation of form through the eye and other senses; regarding the future, there is mental attention (*manaskāra*) due to the capacity of the mind; and regarding the past, when it is being remembered, there is "that-ness" (*tattā*). The threefold time is that which defines these [objects], and the activity of the sun and so forth is what manifests it—such is its nature. It destroys [the object] by withdrawing it into itself.
He acts and creates. || 52 ||
This is experienced by all men, even down to children, in their perceptions of dreams, delusions, the onset of intoxication, passion, disease, and so forth. (53)
And he says that this is established by the experience of everyone, beginning with the words "from childhood" (ābālam). || 53 ||
Within the mind, which has acquired latent impressions (vāsanā), millions of mental occurrences reside, just as fruits and flowers exist upon a tree rooted in the earth. (54)

This is for the purpose of illustrating that, like a tree by which the earth—the vast ground—is pervaded by its roots, the capacity to sustain the world arises from the power of a firm support that is the very seat of the mind. || 54 ||
Just as a tree that has abandoned the earth does not produce leaves again, so too for a soul that has been liberated from its dwelling place, there is no further birth or such.
