That is to say, of one who has been uprooted from the earth that was abandoned. || 55 ||
If even that splendor by which the infinite web of worlds is sustained manifests the state of a dog-cooker (outcaste), what cause for wonder is there in this?

And so, he says "where" [in verse 56] to show that this state of being an outcaste (*śvapaca*) is merely the manifestation of a single portion within the web of infinite latent impressions (*vāsanā*) residing in the mind.
You have realized that the state of being a dog-cooker was merely due to the power of appearance,
just like that which, with its great intensity, brings about various mental afflictions.

He states with the verse beginning "avabuddha" that even the entire array of phenomena, such as the arrival of guests, which you consider to be real, exists only within the mind, just like the state of being an outcaste (śvapaca). || 57 ||
In that very same way, you have seen the agitation caused by a twice-born guest who arrived, ate, slept, and told a story. (58)
Rising up in that very manner, I went on until I reached the realm of spirits;
you have seen this agitation regarding these spirits and these villages. (59)
"You have seen the agitation [expressed] as 'these are the villages'"; the word "iti" (thus) is to be supplied everywhere. || 59 ||
In this very way, this was the former, dilapidated house of Kaṭañja;
people said, "Have you seen the agitation of Kaṭañja? (60)
In that very manner, I arrived at the city of Kīra, and I was told by the Kīras: "You have witnessed, with great agitation, the sovereignty of the Śvapacas. (61)
Thus, O best of the twice-born, you have seen this entire web of delusion—both that which you perceive as truth and that which you understand to be untruth. (62)
What indeed does the mind, enveloped by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), not perceive within?
Even a purpose that requires years to accomplish is seen fulfilled in a dream. (63)
It was accomplished; it was perfected in an instant. || 63 ||
"O one of great intelligence, you have seen all this through delusion. (64)
O Brahmin, while traveling as a traveler to the land of the Bhūtas, you rested in a certain cave, like a deer in a forest. (65)
Furthermore, even now you have not gone to the realm of the spirits or to the city of Kīra; rather, having heard the words of a guest, you set out as a traveler toward the land of the spirits,
and on the way, you rested in a certain mountain cave, exhausted by the journey.

The meaning of these two [verses] is that, due to delusion and because the mind is under the sway of others, this circle of beings and that house of the outcaste are seen as if they were a dream; they are not so in ultimate reality. || 65 ||
In that very place, due to being deluded by fatigue,
one sees this circle of beings as "this is the house of a dog-cooker," but it is not so in reality.
In that very same way, you have seen the city of Kīra exactly as it is;
for whether at that time or at another, O twice-born one, you were indeed there for the purpose of a divine illusion.

The meaning is that you saw the city of the Kīras at that very time, in that cave during the period of exhaustion, or otherwise at the time of the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite; in either case, you perceived this object as being composed of illusion (*māyā*).

O Sage, though you have always dwelt in all things in their entirety, you have nevertheless perceived delusion with your mind, like one who is deranged, as you wandered through the quarters of the world.

Regarding the reading "cale jalakandare tadā" (or "kandare tadā"), there is no restriction of place or time for such delusion; rather, with the intention that one observes activities such as wandering about through delusion alone at all times until the realization of reality (*tattva*), he says: "at all times indeed. || 68 ||
Therefore, arise and remain performing your own duty with a tranquil mind;
for in this world, human beings do not attain prosperity without their own prescribed action.
One's own duties appropriate for the stage of studenthood (brahmacarya), such as the fire-rituals and the study of the Vedas. || 69 ||
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus spoke that Padmanābha,
who is worshipped by the multitudes of ascetics throughout the worlds.
Surrounded by hosts of gods and sages with purified hands,
he returned to his own abode, the ocean.

Being worshipped by throngs of ascetics from all three worlds who had come from every part of the universe, and being surrounded by hosts of gods and sages whose hands were purified by the service of touching the feet of the Blessed One, he— having spoken in the manner described as "Padmanābha"— went to his own abode, which was his home.
The meaning is that he went to the Ocean of Milk. || 70 ||

Thus ends the forty-eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Māyā" within the "Episode of Gādhi," in the "Section on Tranquility" of the "Means to Liberation" in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. || 48 ||
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Māyā," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Forty-Ninth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, after Viṣṇu had departed, Gādhi once again [performed] the rites for the elements and so forth in their proper sequence.
He himself wandered like a cloud in the sky for the sake of investigating delusion.
Gādhi returned once more to his country and, having questioned Hari again and again,
he gradually became liberated while living, having resolved that everything is mere illusion.

Rising up in that very same way, I departed and reached Bhūtamaṇḍalā. "These are the spirits, these are the villages; you have seen this confusion. There is no guest, no spirits, no parrots, and no city there."
However, Gadhi, failing to comprehend the meaning of these words of the Blessed One due to the firmness of his lack of conviction and contrary conceptions,
[perceived] the previously seen places and so forth even without the direct realization of the reality of the Self that is the substratum of the world.
Desiring to experience again whether there is obstruction or not, he wandered through regions such as the circle of spirits (*bhūtamaṇḍala*);

thus [the author] says, "Then" (*atha*). "The region of spirits and so forth" refers to places like the circle of spirits. Having perceived his own account of being a dog-cooker (*śvapaca*) and so on, exactly as it had been previously experienced—|| 1 ||
Having thus learned his own story from the people there,
he went once more to a mountain cave and propitiated Hari.
The meaning is that, having heard [the teachings] and having seen [the signs], he again propitiated Hari in order to understand the intended purport of the Blessed One's words. || 2 ||
Then, in a short time, Janārdana arrived;
for by a single act of propitiation, Mādhava becomes a kinsman.
The Blessed One, full of grace, spoke to Gādhi like a cloud to a peacock: "What more do you desire? Why do you seek further through austerity? (4)
Being full of serene faith, he was tranquil. || 4 ||
Gādhi said:
"O Lord, I have been wandering for six months through the land of the Bhūtakīras;
there, my very identity is disregarded even in conversation."
The meaning is that it does not deviate even from stories, public rumors, or even from corroboration through the recognition of gender and other such signs. || 5 ||
"O Lord, have you seen the world of beings through illusion?
For the words of the great are for the destruction of delusion, not for its increase. (6)

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he replies with the word "māyayā" (by illusion). The meaning is: objects perceived through illusion necessarily deviate at a later time, whereas these objects [of yours] are non-deviating; how then can they be determined to be "illusion"?
Thus, your statement has resulted only in the increase of delusion. || 6 ||
The Blessed One said:
By a chance occurrence, like the "crow and the palm fruit," the state of being a dog-cooker (outcaste) is reflected in the minds of all the bird-like beings,
just as it is in yours.
He provides the reasoning for why even that which is illusory (*māyika*) does not deviate from its narrative meaning, stating: "It is like the 'crow-and-palm' coincidence" (*kākatālīya*).

The meaning is that, just as in your own mind, the state of Kaṭhañjaka the outcaste appears as a direct perception through delusion in the minds of people born in the well-known land of Bhūta and those born in the land of Kīra. || 7 ||
Therefore, my dear, they relate your story exactly as it happened;
for an appearance that has once arisen does not again become non-appearance.

And thus, since they too speak in that manner solely due to their own delusion, the agreement with their words is sublated by the fact that it is merely a collection of meanings; it does not establish truth. He says this with the words "by that" (tena). Regarding the phrase "appearance" (pratibhāsa): the words "without contradiction" (vinā bādham) are to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 8 ||
A certain dog-cooker (outcaste) had built a house on the outskirts of the village; you saw it possessed by a spirit and reduced to fragments of brick.

Then, as for the status of the corroboration by recognition (*pratyabhijñā-saṃvāda*), he states it with the words "by someone" (*kenacit*). It is that which has been made the object of delusive insistence (*bhrānti-abhiniveśa*), [thinking] "this was previously composed by me. (9)
Sometimes a single intuition arises even for many people;
indeed, the movement of the mind is as diverse as the simultaneous perching of crows, palm trees, and date palms. (10)

Appearance is of the nature of an illusion; the manifestation is one and of a single form. It is like the perching or sitting of a *kākola*—a specific species of crow known as the *droṇakāka*—upon a ripe palm fruit or at the base of a palm tree.
For instance, many people may see the same dream.
Like one whose mind is sluggish from sleep, delusion, or intoxication by liquor.

Just as many people with sluggish minds, due to sleep or the intoxication of liquor, perceive the directions as if they were spinning even though they are all identical in form, so it is here. || 11 ||
Many children take delight in a single play,
just as deer do in a single dark forest thicket.

Many children delight in the playful illusion of houses, palaces, and fortresses imagined through conventions based on the arrangement of a single grain of sand; likewise, young deer frolic in a forest glade that is dark blue with lush green grass.
Young deer. || 12 ||
And many people, at the same time, strive for the ripening of their own fruits through the manifestation of karmas that appear in extremely vast forms. (13)
When the ripening of the fruits of one's own past actions (*prārabdha*) is obtained in a form that is manifold— consisting of various modes such as killing, binding, defeat, or flight—

many soldiers and other people strive in battle and the like out of greed, due to the delusive appearance of goals and activities that are identical in nature, such as the attainment of victory and the enjoyment [of spoils], even though they occur simultaneously.
The meaning is that it is well-known. || 13 ||
O Brahmin, that scriptural injunction which states "Time is the giver of prohibitions and permissions" is merely a mental construction; for Time itself resides within the Self.

If the world were merely a mental construction (*mānasakalpanā*), then there would be a contradiction with worldly consensus— namely, that winter and other seasons act as obstacles to the sprouting of rice and the like, while they permit the sprouting of barley and the like— because in the case of a mere mental construction, it would be impossible for external time to serve as its regulator. This is the objection.

Gādhi, avoiding [the objection], says: "Obstruction," etc. "Scripture" refers to the hearing of worldly report; the ellipsis is "that is not contradicted. For that time, which is the cause for both obstruction and permission, is merely a mental construction (*saṃkalpa-mātra*). Having perceived the movement of the sun as delimited by a specific direction, [one determines it] by the mind alone.
The sense is that [time] is conceived through distinctions such as months and seasons according to the scriptures. What, then, is the non-conceptualized (akalpita) time?

He states it: "Time. That which is the non-conceptualized, undivided time—the Supreme Self—abides in its own self alone; it neither grants obstruction nor permission to anything. This is the meaning. || 14 ||
The Blessed Time is formless; they know it to be Brahman itself, unborn.
It neither relinquishes nor acquires anything for anyone at any time. (15)
He clarifies this very point with the words beginning "amūrta" (formless), etc. || 15 ||
This worldly time, consisting of years, kalpas, and yugas,
is conceptualized by means of the multitude of objects, and yet the multitude of objects is conceptualized by means of it.

He establishes that the first [power] has the nature of volition (*saṃkalpa*) with the words "in the world" (*laukika*). Since everything produced is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of time, it is conceptualized (*saṃkalpyate*) by means of the multitude of objects such as the sun’s movements, the lunar orb, and so forth. And by means of that [volition], through both obstruction and permission, there is the regulation of the entire multitude of objects and the results of their actions.
The meaning is "it is conceptualized. The word *tu* has the sense of "and" (*ca*). || 16 ||
Those multitudes of living beings and birds, their minds deluded by the agitation arising from a similar appearance, perceived him in that very manner. (17)
Having resolved an incidental doubt, he takes up the subject at hand and says: "Equal," etc.
The multitudes of people—collections of persons—born in the land of Bhūta and born in the land of Kīra. || 17 ||
Devoted to your own duty, examine yourself with your intellect;
O virtuous one, remain right here once the delusion of the mind has departed, for I am going.

To the question "What, then, should be done by me?", he says: "Devoted to one's own duty" (svavyāpāra). This means being intent upon performing the conduct appropriate to one's own caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama). || 18 ||
Having spoken thus, the Lord Viṣṇu, the Sovereign, vanished;
Gādhi remained in the cave-cavern with a mind heavy with anxiety.
By means of a thought that is exceedingly robust and accumulated through reflection. || 19 ||
Then, after several months had passed on that mountain,
that twice-born man once again propitiated the one who holds the lotus in his hand.
And once, seeing her Lord arrived, she prostrated before him;
she honored him with her mind and speech, and spoke to the Lord.
He honored him with his mind, speech, and actions; and by means of the words spoken for the permission to ask questions, he both spoke and inquired.
Gādhi said:
O Blessed One, remembering this state of mine as a dog-cooker and this illusion of worldly existence, my mind is utterly bewildered.
And recollecting this illusion of saṃsāra, which abounds in misfortunes such as birth, death, and the like. || 22 ||
Having said that, speak according to the facts for the sake of dispelling great delusion;
enjoin me to a single, pure activity alone.

Therefore, for that reason, having stated the means for the cessation of great delusion, do not depart immediately; rather, remain until the destruction of doubt and delusion—this is the meaning. || 23 ||
The Blessed One said:
O Brahmin, this world is a grand display of the great illusion (māyā-śambara);
all manner of wonders arise here from forgetfulness (vismṛti).
"From forgetfulness" means from forgetting the reality of one's own self; that is to say, from ignorance caused by obscuration. || 24 ||
"In the city of Bhūtakīra, you saw that very thing out of delusion"—this is indeed possible, for such an illusion is seen by people. (25)
And since even a thousand things that are impossible within illusion can indeed occur, he says: "bhūta... (as a being).
That state of being a dog-cooker (*śvapaca*) and so forth was seen in such and such a manner; this occurs precisely through delusion, that is, through ignorance. For instance:
The meaning is that even a delusion, whose scope is not considered possible by people when they are overcome by sleep, is observed. || 25 ||

The bhūtas and the kīras, like you, likewise perceived that delusion as if it were real, even though it was in vain, because it arose simultaneously with [the perception of] time and other factors. (26)
"In vain" means "falsely. The meaning is that they perceived even that which has a false nature as having the appearance of reality.
This is because [the perception] arises from a corresponding mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth at the same time. || 26 ||
But hear this which I shall speak to you as it truly is and beyond reproach:
how your anxiety may come to attenuation, like a creeper in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.

"Yathābhūtam" means as it truly is; "yathāsthitam" means as it exists. "Aninditam" means that which prevents association with the reproach of being a dog-cooker (outcaste); this is the meaning. "Tanutām" means diminution or decay. || 27 ||
He who was formerly that outcaste named Kaṭañjaka in the realm of beings,
he became exactly like that again in his previous state.

The meaning is that he became endowed with that very same configuration—namely, the form of the body, the collection of senses, the house, the wife, and so forth—which was exactly like what you have seen. || 28 ||
The king of the Kīras then entered the fire. || 29 ||
The phrase "in the same way" is to be supplied everywhere. || 29 ||
At that time, the conduct of Kaṭaṃja appeared to you alone in your mind as if it were actually taking place within the water. (30)
If another such being existed, then how did it come within the range of my experience? To this he says:
"It merely appeared [to me] by the power of my own volition"—this is the meaning. || 30 ||
The mind sometimes completely forgets even an object that has been seen and experienced; yet at other times, it perceives even what has never been seen as if it were actually seen. (31)

To the question of how there can be a perception of that which has never been seen before, which is situated in another place, and which is past—as if it were present before one—the author says: "The Seer. The meaning is that just as one forgets even what has been experienced, so too does one see even what has not been seen. || 31 ||
Just as the delusions regarding the existence of dreams, mental kingdoms, and the elements are seen by the mind itself even while awake, so it is, my dear. (32)
The arrangement of the elements is their conjunction. || 32 ||
Just as that which exists in the future or the past appears as a clear intuition to those who perceive the three times,
so too does the life-story of Kaṭha appear clearly to Gādhi.

Just as an object, even one yet to come, becomes situated in the past when seen by a yogin who perceives the three periods of time through his vision among things being seen in subsequent times, so too, O Gādhi, even the past conduct of Kaṭhañja attains manifestation in the present; this is the meaning. || 33 ||
"One who possesses self-mastery does not sink into the thought, 'This is he, I am this, that is mine';
one who lacks self-mastery sinks into the thought, 'This is he, I am this, that is mine. (34)

If it is asked: "How can there be immersion [in the Self] when one identifies with what is non-self and non-belonging—such as a mat, a blade of grass, or one's own house and wife, thinking 'I am that very person,' 'that is mine alone,' 'it belongs to me,' or 'it is my property'?"—this objection is far too superficial.
For all those who do not know the Self, there occurs an identification even with the body, which is non-self, and with things belonging to the body, which are non-belonging.

With the intention that the conceit of "I" and "mine" is observed with respect to one's house, wife, and so forth, whereas for the knower of the Self alone there is an absence of immersion in them, he says: "This... (verse 34).
The knower of reality does not despair, thinking "I alone am all this";
he does not perceive the conceptualization of distinctions among objects as having any real purpose.

Even through the cultivation of the sense of "I" in its entirety, one who knows reality does not sink therein, because it is only the limited sense of "I" that causes such sinking; thus he says: "All indeed... (verse 35).
Therefore, even though he is immersed in the whirlpools of worldly existence which sport with pleasure and pain,
he does not sink, just like a gourd vessel in water.
Even though all sense of "I-ness" has vanished, because the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) still persists, he is as if submerged. || 36 ||
For your part, your mind is seized by the web of latent impressions and you are devoid of discernment;
like one suffering from a great illness with only a little remaining, you have not yet attained well-being. (37)
If one asks, "Then what am I like? he says that [the self] is intermediate: "Thou" (tvam). It has arrived at, or reached, the Self which is established in its own nature (*svarūpa*). || 37 ||
Because your knowledge is incomplete, you are unable to ward off the delusion of the mind, just as one who exerts great effort against the clouds [cannot stop them]. 38.
By the word "cloud," its effect—rain—is indicated;
[it is] like a man who is devoid of proper effort regarding such things as building a house or entering another's home. (38)
Whatever suddenly appears to your mind alone,
by that very thing you are instantly overcome, just as a tree is by a person of great height.
You are being trampled upon and humiliated by that very pride. || 39 ||
The mind, it is said, is the hub of this wheel of illusion here;
if one stands having taken hold of it, nothing can cause any affliction.

The navel is the center; the phrase "revolving in all directions" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Having seized that mind by dissolving it into oneself—that is, by suppressing it—that wheel of māyā does not bind at all. || 40 ||
Arise! Practice penance for ten years with an undaunted mind in a grove of this mountain; thereafter, you shall attain infinite knowledge.
Austerity is the practice of the restraint of the mind. || 41 ||
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one vanished on the spot,
like a wind-cloud, like a lamp, or like the swelling of the Yamunā, in an instant.
The "garland simile" (mālopamā) consists of [the comparison] with a cloud dispersed by the wind, a lamp extinguished, and a wave of the Yamunā. || 42 ||
Gādhi, having attained a state of dispassion born from the power of discernment,
became like a tree at the end of autumn that has turned sapless.
Vairasya is lack of moisture. || 43 ||
With a mind released from the weight of wandering delusion, he slowly censured his own wondrous conduct, which had reached such an improper state due to the mineral dust.
Being one whose mind has been released by a heavy burden of delusion,
he [perceives] the "divine" (daiva)— characterized by past karma— as "incongruous," meaning its diverse manifestations such as the state of being a dog-cooker (outcaste) are improper and unjust.
He did not reproach that action. || 44 ||
With his heart moistened by compassion, he went to Mount Ṛṣyamūka for the sake of supreme splendor through self-restraint and for the sake of rest, as a cloud goes toward a mountain.

For the sake of discipline— that is, for the practice of restraining the mind— he performed austerities at Ṛṣamūka, located in Mataṅga’s hermitage, which is immovable. Having cast aside all mental constructs, he practiced there for ten years, and by that means, he attained self-knowledge.
Austerity is well known as the one-pointed concentration of the mind and the senses; this is the supreme austerity. || 46 ||
Thereafter, having regained his own true nature, the Great-Souled One—
freed from fear and sorrow, tranquil, and possessing the form of one liberated while living— delighted continuously in the lands of the world of enjoyment.
Like the full moon, his heart was filled with intense longing. || 47 ||

Thereafter, immediately upon attaining self-knowledge, the great-souled Gādhi, having realized his own ultimate reality, became free from fear and grief; he was one whose nature was eternally joyful and liberated even while living, and consequently,
whose mind was reeling and overflowing with the intoxication of his own boundless bliss.
Being such as he was, complete and full of all digits like the moon, he took delight—that is, he sported—in the undivided space of Brahman; the meaning is that he attained rest. || 47 ||

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "Gādhi’s Attainment of Knowledge," within the narrative of Gādhi, in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the Means to Liberation (*mokṣopāya*), in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the Seer (*ārṣa*). || 49 ||
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "Gādhi’s Attainment of Knowledge," in the Section on Tranquility (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The narrative of Gādhi is complete.
The fiftieth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, O descendant of Raghu, this vast and difficult-to-comprehend illusion, consisting of great delusion and reaching to the very limit of the self, is treacherous.
The means for the mastery of the mind, the supreme majesty of knowledge, and the causes of the defect of mental rigidity are proclaimed here. (1)

He applies the narrative of Gādhi to the present context with the words "In this way," and so forth. [The powers] are difficult to know and inconceivable. "Pertaining to the Supreme Self" (pāramātmikī) means having as its object that which rests solely upon the Supreme Self. || 1 ||

On one hand, there is the appearance before the eyes of the world from the agitation of a dream lasting but two moments; on the other, the delusion of being a king among outcasts experienced for many years. (2)
He demonstrates this very difficulty of knowing in three ways with two verses beginning with "Where? (kva). || 2 ||
Where is there the state of being perceived through agitation, and where is direct perception? Where is unambiguous unreality, and where is the transformation of reality? (3)
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I say: this treacherous illusion daily entangles the heedless-minded person in calamity. (4)
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, how can they effect the blocking of this wheel of Māyā as it revolves with such force, causing the severing of all one's limbs?

"The mind, it is said, is the hub of this wheel of illusion (māyā-cakra) here; if one stands having taken hold of it, nothing can cause any affliction. Regarding that which was thus taught by the Blessed One at the end, Rāma, desiring to know the means [thereof], asks with the words "Thus" (*evam*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "the qualified practitioners (*adhikāriṇaḥ*) should perform [it]. [This refers to] the Self consisting of perfect bliss (*pūrṇānanda-ātman*).
The infliction of the pain of dismemberment itself constitutes "dismemberment" for the perpetrator, by virtue of its similarity to the act of cutting off a limb. (5)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, know that the mind is the great hub of this wheel of illusion that constitutes the form of this world, which, as it revolves, causes others to revolve as well.

He restates what was previously mentioned in order to first elaborate upon the method of supporting the wheel of māyā taught by the Blessed One, beginning with the words "of this" (asya) and so forth. || 6 ||
When that [subtle body] is swiftly restrained through the intellect and human effort,
the wheel of māyā is blocked by seizing the channel at the navel.

That whose hub is grasped by the wheel of illusion (māyācakra) is of such a nature that it is brought to a halt through being well-carried—that is, through its turning; it ceases, so to speak. || 7 ||
The wheel of delusion, when its hub—the mind—is firmly grasped, does not move;
just as a peg wrapped in a rope does not move when the rope is held fast.
Just as the toy wheel made of bronze or other metals by children— which has a central pivot wrapped with thread—
does not move or rotate when the string tied to its thumb-ring is pulled tight against the thread,
why do you, O sinless one, who are an expert in the single art of wheel-warfare, not understand it in that same way?
The wheel, when held fast by the hub, comes under control; not otherwise.

Furthermore, O Raghava, you are the foremost among those skilled in chariot warfare and are an expert in techniques such as immobilizing and circling; therefore, why do you not understand the aforementioned analogy? || 9 ||
Therefore, O Rāghava, by restraining the mind with effort, you must block the wheel of saṃsāra that carries away the self. 10.
Because it carries the self and brings about the succession of births, restrain it thoroughly by means of complete cessation. || 10 ||
Without this reasoning, one's own suffering is endless and immeasurable;
behold that in this view it reaches its end in an instant. (11)

Without this method, yoga, or means characterized by the restraint of the mind, you have encountered infinite suffering for yourself. Now, behold that very suffering as having reached its end—its destruction—once this vision has been attained. Having acted accordingly regarding the doubt concerning my words, you shall find it so.
The meaning is "behold. || 11 ||
But without the supreme medicine that consists merely in the conquest of the mind, the great disease of saṃsāra is not pacified even by effort. (12)
And he says that there is no other means: "By the mind," etc. (12).
Therefore, O Raghava, setting aside the practices of visiting sacred fords, giving gifts, and performing austerities,
bring the mind itself under control for the sake of the highest welfare.
Samsara exists only within the mind, just as the space within a jar exists within the jar;
when the mind is destroyed, there is no samsara, just as when the jar is destroyed, there is no space within the jar. 14.
Regarding that, he states the proof of its arising: "In another moment of consciousness" (cittāntare) || 14 ||
Having destroyed the hollow of the mind-pot—the cavity of space that is saṃsāra for a long time—enter the form whose nature is the incomparable space. 15.

Just as a mosquito or similar insect confined within a jar, having destroyed its own limited space of the sky-cavity— the sphere of its own suffering— by chance through the destruction of the jar, enters the nature of the incomparable and peerless great space and becomes happy, freed from bondage; so too you, by the dissolution of the mind, having destroyed the jar-like space of the mind, [attain liberation].
The meaning is: "Enter the incomparable space of Brahman. || 15 ||
By momentarily engaging with the present through an effortless external intellect, the mind,
having abandoned the past and the future, attains the state of non-mind.
If so, what is the means for the destruction of the mind? He says: "the present.
The meaning is that the mind is gradually extinguished precisely by abandoning the mental preoccupation with objects of the past and the future. || 16 ||
If you abandon the pursuit of even the fragments of volitional thought at every moment,
then you have indeed attained that purifying state of non-mind.
If you constantly and with vigilance practice the avoidance of conceptualizing future objects and the pursuit of things that are merely parts thereof, then— || 17 ||
As long as there is the mental construction of conceptualization, so long do the manifestations of the mind persist;
as long as the expanse of clouds remains, so long do drops of water exist in the sky.
The drops of the rain of the sky-water. || 18 ||
As long as there is a conscious mind, so long is there volition and the conceptualization of mental constructs;
as long as there is a world with its moonbeams, so long are there particles of frost.
Thus, he says "possessing a mind" (sacittam) to show that even such mental constructs are difficult to restrain when the mind exists; "cetanam" refers to the nature of the conscious self. || 19 ||
If volition is devoid of the mind and has been cultivated, know that the roots of one's own worldly existence have been burnt away from the very root, just like the roots of a perfected being.

"Empty of mind" (cittarikta) means separated from the mind—that is to say, rendered immutable (kūṭastha). Know that at that time the roots of your own worldly existence—desire, action, latent impressions, and so forth—have been burnt away from the root along with the primal ignorance (mūlājñāna); this is the meaning, expressed either as a statement of established fact or by way of equality with the Great Siddhas. || 20 ||
For consciousness devoid of the mind is called direct consciousness; it has the nature of being without the thinking faculty, and therein there is no stain of conceptualization.

One might object: "Granted that there is burning, nevertheless, why should the emergence of the mind and so forth not occur again in the conscious [Self] due to the influence of even a trace of conceptualization?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The conscious... (verse 21).

That is truth, that is auspiciousness (śivatā), that is the state of the supreme self. That which is the nature of consciousness devoid of the mind—that alone is the ultimate reality (paramārthasatyatā). Auspiciousness is the nature of unsurpassed bliss; it is that very state which constitutes the essence of the supreme self. It is omniscience.
The nature of consciousness is that which illuminates everything. Vision is the vision of ultimate reality (*paramārthadṛk*). "In which," meaning in whatever state;
"wounded" is an epithet used for the purpose of censure. || 22 ||
But wherever the mind is directed, there hope arises, and there too come both suffering and pleasure;
they always draw near like crows to a cremation ground. (23)
He shows the very seeds of blameworthiness: "The mind," etc. (23).
Through the realization of the true nature of reality, all things are established;
yet the seed of the creeping vine of worldly existence is produced by conceptual construction.
[Objection: Surely even the wise possess a mind; why then do desire and the like not arise in them as well? To this he replies:

"In the cycle of existence" (*saṃsṛti*). It is true that they have a mind, yet in their mental resolve there exists not even the seed, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), of the creeper of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-vallī*) which establishes all states such as desire and the rest.
The meaning is that [it] arises because it is sublated by the realization of the true nature of reality. || 24 ||
Through the continuous practice resulting from contact with the scriptures and virtuous people, the unsubstantiality of worldly phenomena is realized. (25)

He states the sublation (*bādha*), characterized by the realization of the non-substantiality (*avastutva*) of those things previously understood as substantial, by means of what method: "By scripture," etc. (25).
Having withdrawn the mind from its lack of discernment through efforts of resolve, it should be forcibly united [with the object] by means of the scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous. 26.

"Having brought near" means having turned toward [the goal]. "With exertion" means with human effort; that is, with firm resolutions such as, "I shall certainly accomplish knowledge in this very birth. || 26 ||
The Self alone is the primary cause for the vision of the Supreme Self;
a jewel fallen into the deep is perceived only by means of another jewel.

If it is asked what primary cause one must rely upon to seek the Self even through the scriptures and other means, [the answer is] the inner Self (pratyagātman) itself, whose nature is self-luminous. With the intention that this very Self is manifested by its own nature prior to all else, being distinct from any object of knowledge, he says: "The primary. By means of a shining jewel...
The meaning is: "by oneself alone. || 27 ||
One's own self alone desires to abandon the sufferings experienced by itself;
therefore, the self itself is remembered as the sole supreme cause for the realization of the Self.

He clarifies the aforementioned status as the primary cause with the word "sva" (by oneself). By that very reason—namely, the discernment (*viveka*) that the various objects of perception experienced by oneself are nothing but suffering—one desires to renounce them; for that same reason, in the contemplation of one's own Self, that [discernment] which has a nature opposed to those objects is itself the primary cause. For indeed...
The sense is that, since it would itself be by nature dull and devoid of pleasure, it would be adverse to that [pleasure]. || 28 ||
Whether speaking, releasing, grasping, opening, or closing your eyes,
remain intent solely upon infinite pure consciousness, free from all mental constructs.
Therefore, he says "pralapan" and so forth, [meaning]: "Be always intent on that alone for the sake of attaining it."
Whether being born, living, or dying, while engaged in action,
remain steadfast in that portion of consciousness which has attained purity within your own self.

The mention of birth and death is for the purpose of ensuring that one does not forget the inward orientation toward the Self even amidst other conditions of pleasure and pain similar to those [of worldly existence]. When the aspect of pure consciousness has attained stainlessness through purification, [it remains as such]. || 30 ||
Abandoning all latent impressions such as "this is mine," "that," "this is he," and "I am this," become intent solely upon the pure consciousness residing within through single-minded devotion.

Having completely abandoned the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that "this body standing before me is that same one which was far away," and "this is that very person being recognized as 'I am this body,'" [one should remain]. (31)
Regarding the present and future states of existence, be intent upon unifying them through self-awareness, and remain devoted to their synthesis and integration within a single cognition.
The present state of childhood and so forth, and the future state of youth, kingship, and so forth—the linking together of these two is *dhyāna*, *samādhāna*, and *samādhi*. || 32 ||
Whether in childhood, youth, or old age; in sorrows or in joys;
and whether in waking, dreaming, or deep sleep—remain centered in your own self-awareness.
He states clearly what has already been said: "bālya... (verse 33).
Having cast off the impurity of the object of perception and having liberated the mind from its bonds, cut through the foul snare of desire and become intent upon your own self-awareness.
The object of cognition is characterized by external objects. || 34 ||

Free from the cholera of attachment to your own conventions regarding the auspicious and the inauspicious, and with the vision of the desirable and undesirable destroyed, become intent upon the essence of pure consciousness.

He whose cholera-like affliction of desire for those two—characterized as auspicious and inauspicious, and whose conventions are established by one's own volitions—is completely stilled; for this very reason, he is one whose vision of extremes has perished.

Without touching the agent, the object, or the instrument, and immediately after the absence of contact with the self, become one who is free from conceptual construction, without support, and devoted solely to your own pure consciousness. 36.

The agent consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*); the objects are external; and the instruments are the sense organs along with their adjuncts. Since these do not touch the Self, they are "untouchable" (*svāsparśana*). Touching and manifesting such worlds of saṃsāra within the interior of the Self—just as a gem touches and displays the reflections contained within it—[is the nature of the Self]. || 36 ||
Indeed, while remaining awake, contemplate that state which is as if in deep sleep and perfectly stable;
thinking "I am all," become one whose body is the single essence of pure existence.
Deeply asleep, as if in a state of profound slumber, she was free from all conceptual construction.
Free from the ten states of diversity and non-diversity, and united with equanimity through liberation,
become one who is intent solely upon your own pure consciousness, the lamp that illumines all things.

He is liberated from the various states of waking and dreaming, as well as the non-variegated state of deep sleep—or from those two states of creation and dissolution. He is a lamp for the manifestation and perception of the entire field of the visible; like a lamp, he is the illuminator of all the diverse mental fluctuations of the collective intellect.
Having abandoned both selfhood and otherness, remaining undifferentiated within the state of the world, remain steadfast by taking hold of yourself like a diamond pillar. (39)
Having abandoned selfhood, otherness, alienness, and difference from those— || 39 ||
Abiding within, with a noble intellect whose sole characteristic is fortitude, cast off the mental fetters that take the form of desire, and attain the state beyond both dharma and adharma.
The state of being devoid of phenomena and their intrinsic nature, which is free from both dharma and adharma. || 40 ||
For one who relishes reality, which has self-awareness as its nature,
even the poison hālāhala will then become nectar.
The sense is that when everything has attained the state of immortality (*amṛtatva*), the immortality of even poison is established as a matter of course.
Then arises the great delusion (*mahāmoha*), the cause of the wandering in saṃsāra, when there is no recognition of consciousness (*saṃvitti*) which is stainless and partless. (41–42)
Ignorance is forgetfulness; that is to say, it is lack of knowledge. || 42 ||
Then delusion, the cause of the wandering in saṃsāra, is utterly destroyed when one is established in stainless and partless self-awareness. 43.
For you who have followed your true nature and crossed the great ocean of hope,
your consciousness will expand in every direction like the rays of the sun.

Regarding the word "tīrṇasya" (of the one who has crossed): the sense is that by the very attainment of his own true nature, he has crossed the great ocean of hope, in accordance with the Lord's statement: "Even his attachment ceases upon seeing the Supreme. || 44 ||
O Rāma, for one who beholds the intrinsic nature and abides in the non-dual state of bliss,
even a delicious elixir acts like a potent poison.
For one who is liberated, the possibility of desiring anything else is far removed;

on the contrary, even regarding the tasting of elixirs such as nectar, there arises the perception of them as things to be rejected—like poison—due to the apprehension that they would obstruct the savoring of the bliss of the Self. With this intention, he says: "one's own nature," which is adverse [to all else].
It behaves like poison; it acts as an antidote. || 45 ||
We associate with those men who have attained their true nature;
the rest, though bearing the name of "men," are merely long-armed donkeys. (46)
Those persons who have attained our own nature—the state of the inner self—and are liberated while living;

because they have made their human birth meaningful, accomplished the goals of human endeavor, and rendered their manly effort fruitful, we always maintain friendship with those preeminent men—this is the ellipsis. But others...

With the intention that those who lack the human effort necessary for attaining the goals of man (puruṣārtha) are "men" in name only and not even in the slightest degree in reality—and thus should be disregarded like donkeys, being unfit even for the vision [of truth] and so forth—he says: "The rest. (46)
Like elephants moving from mountain to mountain before a great peak,
[the stages] proceed toward the highest limit for one who has reached the pinnacle through the height of self-awareness.

"Surely there are other great yogis and devotees in the world as well; among them, who possesses such excellence that he alone is a knower of reality? To this, he says: "From the mountain... [and so on]. Because he stands at the highest point by virtue of his own self-realization, the knower of reality has reached the supreme limit—the pinnacle of excellence—and before him stand the yogis and others.

The meaning is that those great men, approaching various [teachers] for the sake of knowledge, appear as if they are moving from one mountain to another— from a mountain like Meru to a peripheral mountain— rather than standing firm and elevated like Meru itself. || 47 ||
Within the limit where the unseen meets the invisible, even all the lights beginning with the sun do not assist one who possesses the divine eye of self-awareness. 48.

He establishes the state of being elevated through self-awareness with the words "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*). For that knower of reality who possesses the divine eye characterized by self-awareness— whose boundaries or limits have never been seen by anyone before and are currently and in the future invisible, meaning impossible to perceive— the [state of elevation exists] within.
The meaning is that since all imagined lights, such as the sun and others, do not assist him, his exalted state is established by his own self-awareness alone. || 48 ||
For one who has realized the Self through knowledge, these great lights such as the sun and others become non-entities, like lamps at midday. (49)

He states that not only are they unable to help, but rather they appear as mere non-entities in his presence: "Before the rays of light, before powers, and even before those who are mighty and great, and before all who possess exaltation, the knower of reality remains supremely exalted. (50)

Therefore, he says "it is established" and explains: "In the rays of light," etc. This means: among all things—namely, the rays of light (the effects of fire) which are illuminations; the powers such as the perfection of yoga and mastery (*vaśitva*); those that are strong, possessing physical strength and so forth;
those that are great through sovereignty, long life, and so on; and others endowed with eminence such as eloquence. Among all these—
Supremely exalted; the sense is that all forms of loftiness are superimposed upon this [Brahman]. || 50 ||
Just as the sun, fire, moon, gems, and stars shine here with their light, so too do the best of men shine in this world, having known all that is to be known. 51.
The meaning is that they shine by the light of that Lord of the World, in a manner equal to it. || 51 ||
O Rāma, those men who do not know the ultimate reality are considered more insignificant than the insects in the crevices of the earth, than donkeys, and even than the animals.
They are more hollow and more deluded; the sense is that in the absence of knowledge of reality, it is difficult to avoid reaching even more inferior millions of wombs than those. || 52 ||
As long as one lacks self-knowledge, so long is that embodied being a vampire of delusion;
those who know the truth hold that only the knower of the Self is truly united with consciousness.

Because the Self, though existing, is rendered non-existent through ignorance, it is "without self" (anātmavat); for this very reason, it is "insentient. Therefore, those who know that [Self] say—this is the ellipsis—that only one who knows the Self is conjoined with sentience. || 53 ||
For one who does not know the Self, though writhing on the ground in this world of suffering, wanders about like a corpse; but he who knows the Self remains truly conscious. 54.
The word *tu* has the sense of "only" (*evārthe*), [referring to] one whose effort and exertion have the purpose of burning away suffering. || 54 ||
When the mind has become thick with ignorance, the knowledge of the Self recedes to a distance, just as the splendor of light vanishes when a great cloud rises on all sides. (55)
When the mind has attained fullness and grossness, self-knowledge, even if slightly accomplished, recedes to a great distance. || 55 ||
The mind should be gradually emaciated by disregarding both enjoyments and non-enjoyments;
that is to be understood as the withdrawal of its "flavors," like a leaf withering over time due to indigestion.
For this reason, the meaning is that the enjoyment— that is, the indulgence— in objects of sense-pleasure already attained,

as well as the deprivation of the savor— that is, the longing— for those not yet attained through repeated acts of rejection practiced over a long time, should lead to emaciation and decline, like a withered leaf, in the course of time. || 56 ||
By this false attribution of self to what is not-self, and by this reliance on the mere body,
along with children, wife, and family, the mind attains plumpness.
He states those causes of mental inflation by whose abandonment that emaciation would occur, beginning with the words "anātmani" and so forth. || 57 ||
Through the transformation of egoism, by the effortless stain of "mineness," and by the notion that "this is mine," the mind becomes swollen with attachment. (58)
"By transformation," that is, by expansion; "by play," meaning with ease or attachment, toward the impurity characterized by the sense of "mine-ness.
He states the root of all such "mine-ness": "this," meaning with the notion that "this body is mine, my self, or the locus of my enjoyment. || 58 ||
The mind grows fat with the suffering of old age and death, which brings about useless exaltation and serves as a treasury for the venomous serpents of the afflictions. 59.
He specifies that very state: "old age," etc. (verse 59).
Through the indulgence in mental and physical afflictions, through the consolation found in worldly existence,
and through the effort of accepting and rejecting, the mind grows fat.
Through the consolation of cyclic existence, there arises a sense of delight based on the false confidence that it is pleasant and long-lasting.
Through affection, greed for wealth, the acquisition of jewels and women, and that which is pleasant at first sight, the mind becomes swollen with attachment.
And by means of the practice of grasping, the serpent of the mind attains fullness.
By movement, that is, by wandering among various objects. || 62 ||
The mind grows fat with the terrifying expansion of enjoyments, which are transient by nature and indicative of the instability of poison.

By "the full extent of enjoyments" (*bhogānām ābhogena*), as previously explained, is meant that which consists of the coming and going of the body's nature—just as poison causes distress such as imbalance, burning, and fainting—as indicated by that [body]. This refers to that which culminates in such [suffering]. || 63 ||
The body is like a foul abyss where [suffering] has long grown deep; it possesses the high-stalked blossoms of a multitude of anxieties,
and it is bowed down by the heavy fruit-cluster of old age, death, and disease.
A flower that expands upon the flood of the enjoyment of sensual desires. || 64 ||

The syntactical connection with the following verse is as follows: "In this wicked abyss characterized by the body, where this poisonous tree of the mind has long since taken root, you must cut it down without hesitation using the saw of the essence of discernment.
In this tree, the clusters of blossoms are the high-reaching heaps of anxiety; the suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule *nady-ṛtaś-ca*. (64)
With the saw of the essence of investigation, [cut down] this tree of the mind, which is like a wondrous mountain,
with its great branches of hope, without hesitation.
Forcefully cut through the leaf of conceptual construction here.
That in which the conceptual constructions themselves are the petals. || 65 ||
With intoxicated eyes, seated on one bank, fierce and unable to endure the pleasures of rest,
longing for a sight of the lotus-feet of the virtuous—
And for Khaṇḍa, Caṇḍa was a boil of pleasure and pain. || 66 ||

Now, he describes that very mind as an elephant in two verses beginning with "mattekṣaṇam. O Rāghava, lion among kings, you—endowed with the aforementioned ten specific qualities—must tear apart this elephant of the mind with the extremely sharp row of claws of your intellect; this is the syntactical connection with the second verse. "Matte" means intoxicated by the negligence of one's own discernment.
He whose vision, characterized by scripture and inference, is reeling with intoxication;
he whose sitting is upon the mountain slope of transmigratory existence, which is characterized by outward-turned orientation;
for that very reason, incapable of the bliss of resting within; and fierce because of being terrifying due to hatred, envy, and the like.

The "steps of the virtuous" (*sujanakramāḥ*) are tranquility, self-restraint, forbearance, and so forth, by which the virtuous proceed. One who is "eager" (*utkaṃ*) to behold that lotus-pond (*abjakhaṇḍa*), a forest of lotuses characterized by those virtues, is full of longing; however, one who possesses a "fierce mind" (*caṇḍamatiḥ*)—meaning extremely wrathful—is unfit for its protection. [This concerns] pleasure and pain.
Thus, his cheeks were dripping with cold sweat, heat, tears, and intoxication.
Tear apart the elephant of the mind, which dwells in the forest of the body and possesses the long tusks of chronic distortions, with the row of sharp claws of wisdom.
O Rāghava, lion among kings, perform the ritual action! || 67 ||
He whose tusks are indeed the long-lasting transformations of desire and so forth; for this very reason, they perform the act of tearing asunder the ramparts of Dharma and the like. 67.
Always finding delight in improper places, nourished by devouring the flesh of the body,
with a harsh and formidable beak-staff for its wicked deeds—
With eyes like a blue lotus, well-nourished, and dark as a black antelope skin. || 68 ||
It has found delight and attachment in despicable places such as the female genitals and cemeteries;
it is nourished and increased by the swallowing—that is, the internalizing—of the flesh characterized by the body;
and its harsh beak-staff, which pierces the vital organs through wicked actions, is raised up therein.
That which has the function of lips similar to those; that which has vision—meaning sight—directed solely toward its own object.

It is black, meaning soiled, by means of the thick tamas-rays, that is, the functions of tamas. Regarding the "crow's wing" (the eyelashes), the four adjectives are clear: it is black like the thick tamas-rays, which are like portions of darkness.
The connection with the subsequent [verse] is: "Drive the crow of your own mind far away from the nest-cavity of the body. || 68 ||
Drive far away that which is a burden,
characterized by evil conduct and harsh clamoring;
[drive away] the Gandhodgata from the nest-like sheath of the body—
For the sake of pacifying the faults of one's own mind-crow.

It is a burden because it causes futile exertion for the bearer—the self—as well as for trees and other things; it has arisen from, appeared from, and set out toward "gandhas," that is, from evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*). 69.
Attended by the demoness of craving,
it has rested in the great pits of ignorance and wandered for a long time through the forest of hundreds of bodies.
In their own cycle of rebirth, among those devoid of consciousness. || 70 ||

He states that if one does not uproot that very mind which manifests in the form of a *piśāca* (demon), liberation cannot be achieved, in two verses beginning with "thirst" (*tṛṣṇā*). In great banyan trees or pits characterized by ignorance, or in hundreds of bodies—
in the forest consisting of infinite millions of bodies— this is a *vyastarūpaka* (partial metaphor) for the forest of one's own mind.
In this cycle of existence, among those devoid of consciousness— that is, among insentient things— this demon of the mind is directly perceived.

As long as one does not expel such a demon from the heart, which is the abode of one's own conscious self, liberation— which is the perfection consisting of the very nature of the Self— will not be attained.
"Why?"—this [question] applies to both cases. (70)
One should not drive away this demon of the mind from the house of one's own conscious self by means of discrimination, dispassion, the efforts of a guru, or independent mantras.
As long as that [object] exists, so long is there the establishment of a self here. || 71 ||
It has a face of both auspicious and inauspicious, it destroys the flood of pride, it possesses the poison of anxiety and the cloak of bodily frailty,
and it is constantly fed by the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
And it bestows the destruction of all various fears. || 72 ||
Now, describing [the Lord] as having a mind that is not beneficial, he causes [the listener] to abandon [such a view] with two verses beginning with "śubha-".
That which exists in the mouth is "āsya" (oral), according to the rule *śarīrāvayavād yat*. He who has a pair of fangs;
he whose food is the breath—the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*)—which is clear (*accha*), meaning untouched by defects such as fatigue.
Because he subsists on air; and because he bestows various kinds of fear, destruction, and death, he is called *Nānābhayanāśada*. || 72 ||
O Rāma, having brought the great serpent of the mind to rest by means of the unfailing power of the mantra of the movement of consciousness residing within the dur-śālmalika tree of the heart-lotus;

Having utterly cast off fear, one whose self is fearless toward existence— [the reading "whose self is non-existent" (abhavātma) also occurs]— should bring to rest such a characteristic of the mind through the power of those mantras that awaken the bird of consciousness (*citkhaga*)— the *garuḍa* whose sole essence is consciousness— by means of [mantras] such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. It brings peace by means of the force of those [mantras].

Having brought about the total eradication along with primordial ignorance (mūlājñāna), and having completely cast off and abandoned fear, the Self becomes non-existence or fearless; this is the meaning. || 73 ||
Bearing an inauspicious appearance due to his constant attendance upon a succession of corpses,
he was exhausted by the fatigue of wandering through the various quarters of the world.
He frequents cremation grounds, his body wounded. || 74 ||
That very mind manifests itself as a vulture through two verses beginning with "amaṅgala.
This occurs by means of the constant attendance upon, the contemplation of, and the devouring of rows of corpses characterized by bodily marks;
and by means of a body wounded by the beak-strikes of crows and herons, and by insults, loss, grief, fear, and so forth.
In deep sleep, one who possesses that disposition resorts to the tree of the cremation ground and to a sleeping body resembling it. || 74 ||
The vulture of the mind, with neck outstretched and its greed increased by the steady presence of sensual enjoyments, flies off and departs as it runs toward the directions for the bait of pleasures.
From that tree of the body, may your victory be skillful. 75.

If such a "vulture of the mind"—characterized by lack of fortitude, excessive growth, greed, and longing—were to fly away from the tree of your body, then indeed you would be thoroughly and completely victorious; this is the meaning. || 75 ||
Wandering through forest edges and distant quarters in search of fruit— with restless and agitated limbs—
he has gone from the land of his birth to the land of his birth.
He laughs at the people bound by the cycle of existence. || 76 ||

That very mind now depicts itself as a monkey with two verses, beginning with "Bhrāntam" (Wandering): It has wandered from one birthplace to another birthplace; it laughs at the multitude—the mass of people—and mocks their worldly bondage through its own antics. (76)
Upon the tree whose trunk is the eye and nose, whose flowers are the [facial] blossoms, whose branches are the arms and so forth, and whose leaves are the clusters of trembling fingers—
[I see him] shining brilliantly, destroying the enemies...
O dear one, for the sake of accomplishing the great monkey of the mind. || 77 ||

In this tree of the body—wherein the eyes and nose together form the "eyes-and-nose" (akṣināsa), which is itself surrounded by flowers; wherein the arms, hands, and so forth are the branches; and wherein the network of trembling fingers are the leaves—the great monkey of the mind leaps about, obstructing it on all sides.
There is also a reading "by cessation" (nirodhena), which means "kill. || 7 ||
Risen up for the destruction of the fruits of merit, flashing with the light of lightning clinging to its radiant face,
raining down a torrent of a multitude of misfortunes—
Or it is shaken within by the wind of latent impressions. || 78 ||
Now, he characterizes that very mind as being like a cloud with two verses beginning with "arisen" (*abhyutthita*).

It has appeared at an improper time for the destruction of the good fruit—that is, the ultimate happiness—and the ripened harvest of grain. It is attached to the "mouth," meaning at the tip of the outward-turned mental modification which resembles a mouth, by means of reflection.

That whose light of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is attached like a flash of lightning; which rains down a torrent in the form of a multitude of misfortunes; and which is agitated—that is, tossed about—within by the whirlwind characterized by latent impressions (vāsanā).
By the power of the formidable mantra that abandons all volitional constructions, energetically dispel the cloud of the mind situated within the sky of the heart.
Having attained Bṛhatphala, he became the foremost of the Bhavas. || 79 ||

Drive away with vigor this cloud-like mind situated within the garment of the heart— this mind which consists of the various conceptualizations and repeated justifications of volitions— by means of the power of the formidable mantra consisting of their total abandonment;
and by that, having attained the fruit of great liberation while living, become one whose primordial nature is that of a perfected being (*pūrvasiddha*).
The meaning is that the eternally liberated self alone is sufficient for perfect existence. || 79 ||
Knotted by its own self-created actions, unbreakable by mantras and unburnt by fires,
it inflicts supreme suffering upon the self.
A long chain of all the various classes of existence.
Now, he characterizes that very mind as a snare with two verses beginning with "granthīkṛtam" (knotted):

from the creation of the self— that is, taking the cosmic manifestation at the beginning of the kalpa as its limit— up until the present time, [the mind] is continuously [bound] by the good and evil deeds performed, which have the self as their material cause.

It has been knotted by the gift of knots and made firm; for this very reason, it remains like a long rope for the gradual binding of all the various classes of beings, that is, the different births within the manifold wombs. || 80 ||

O Rāghava, having yourself severed the snare of the mind— by forcibly using the weapons of mere non-conceptualization to cut through the countless series of bodies that have been spread out— [you shall attain liberation].
Dwell as you please, free from fear. || 81 ||
For this very reason, he is one in whom countless successions of bodies have been completely dissolved; being free from doubt, he is devoid of any apprehension regarding rebirth.
A venomous serpent that has scorched all travelers with its hiss,
whose awakening by others is extremely difficult to achieve,
and which has withered the very regions of the world.
His staff-like body was raised up by his gaping mouth as he seized the prey. || 82 ||

Now, describing that resolve as the form of a python, he states the means for its destruction with two verses beginning with *phūtkāra*: "By whose hissing"—meaning by whose venomous breath in the form of anger and the like—all travelers on the path, the living beings moving along the southern and northern routes, were scorched; [he is] a venomous serpent (*āśīviṣa*), a bearer of poison. For this very reason, they have been withered away.
By him the regions of the world and the divisions of the universe were scorched;
by him the fourfold staff of the body was raised and shaken for the sake of the bait of sense-objects, through the gaping mouth characterized by craving. 82.
With the speed of the great fire of desirelessness, [one should quickly consume] that sluggish, terrible python of volition hidden within the caves of the body.
Having burned [them] with your power, become one who possesses worldly prosperity. || 83 ||

The meaning is: having burned and reduced to ashes with the great fire of its own name—that terrible python of conceptualization (saṃkalpa), which is sluggish and slow-moving due to its indolence regarding the exertion for liberation—by means of dispassion (vairāgya) that is free from desire, may you become one whose own glory is full bliss. || 83 ||

O virtuous one, having swiftly brought the mind to tranquility by means of a pure mind— just as one neutralizes a terrible weapon through the skillful application of another weapon— abandon your fickleness forever.
Like a tree from which the monkeys have departed, its splendor remains unimpaired. || 84 ||

He says "by the mind" to show that when detachment leads to the conquest of mental constructs and the purification of the mind, the conquest of the mind itself is likewise accomplished through the sequence of awakening and samādhi. He says "for a long time" so that one does not prematurely cease effort with the thought of having already achieved the goal. He states the result of this: "abandon. (84)

Regarding it as stainless, with a mind free from doubt and inwardly pacified, look upon everything from the very body onwards as light as a blade of grass, effortlessly regarding it with the vision of what is to be abandoned.
Drink, dwell, and rejoice, having reached the further shore of saṃsāra.

With the intention that the ultimate pacification of the mind— the bliss of dwelling in liberation while living— is accomplished through the complete attainment of abandoning the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, he concludes with the word "amalam" (stainless). Thus, by the aforementioned method, and by the realization of reality previously taught— as indicated by the word "ca" (and)— within...

Having made the mind pure by pacifying it within the inner self (pratyagātman) and having removed the impurities such as passion (rāga), one should, with such a mind, view through the lens of renunciation (heyadṛṣṭi) everything that is perceptible— extending from the gross, subtle, and causal bodies until the very end of the physical frame— as lighter than even a blade of grass, most insignificant.
Seeing that [the body] is indeed non-existent and utterly unworthy of concern—just like a dream-body—you have reached the further shore of saṃsāra;

therefore, for the sake of experiencing the remainder of your *prārabdha* karma, drink the soma and so forth as a sport, delighting in the Self and performing actions with the "play" (*līlā*) shown by the Śruti: "He who plays with the Self, rejoices in the Self, and performs action—he is the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman. For the welfare of the world, drink the soma and so forth.

Perform the ritual acts in sacrifices through the officiating priests and others, and also delight in worldly activities that are not contrary to the scriptures; the meaning is that by doing so, there is no further possibility of bondage for you. || 85 ||

Thus ends the fiftieth sarga, titled "The Application of Rāghava’s Intent," in the section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Application of Rāghava’s Intent," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
Fifty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Do not abide within the fluctuations of the mind, which are like the edge of a razor.
As the sage Uddālaka sought repose in the state of peace, his mind, while practicing yoga, was distracted in many ways by mental defects. (1)

Even when the reality of the Self has been ascertained through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), the bliss of undistracted liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*) cannot be attained without the mind’s complete rest; therefore, for that purpose, it is necessary to increase one's realization through diligent practice of *samādhi*. This is taught by means of the narrative of Uddālaka.

Regarding the phrase "in those that are exceedingly long": because of attachment to objects situated far away in this world and the next, they are "exceedingly long"; because of the abundance of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they are "slender"; because they cause injury by suddenly severing the bliss of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for one who is negligent, they are "extremely sharp."

The meaning is: "Do not remain trusting, out of negligence, in the activities or conducts of the mind—which, because they possess the purity characterized by the capacity to reflect one's own image, are white and for that very reason comparable to the edge of a razor. || 1 ||
O you who are skilled in statesmanship, this creeper of intelligence has grown in this field over a long period; lead it to growth by watering it with discernment.

The meaning is this: upon the creeper of the body born from the field of a noble family, this vine of intelligence—characterized by the acquaintance with the Supreme Self—has arisen for you through the means of hearing about the purification of the mind and so forth; now, cause it to grow by means of the nectar of discrimination, which is characterized by the turning away from external objects of perception. || 2 ||
As long as this creeper-like body does not wither under the sun of time, lift it up while it has not yet fallen to the ground and preserve it. (3)

And that creeper of the body, having been watered since childhood, grows; yet, due to the withering caused by old age and the like, there is the danger of its falling, and even its rescue from that is impossible—let alone the cultivation of its blossoms—with this intention he says:
"As long as... [he waters] this creeper of the body before it has fallen to the ground, through service to the guru, listening to the teachings, and so forth.
The meaning is: "Having uprooted the creeper of the intellect, protect it. || 3 ||
O knower of the single reality that is the meaning of my words, through the contemplation of that single meaning of my words,
you shall attain happiness, just as the enemy of serpents [Garuda] did through the contemplation of the sound of clouds.

And the "sprinkling of discernment" (*vivekaseka*) consists in hearing and ascertaining the meaning of my very words—which take the form of the narrative to be described—and then contemplating that same meaning again and again, since all methods of reflection and reasoning reside therein. With this intention, he says:
"my words. Just as the peacock, the enemy of snakes, [is not moved] by the sound of clouds, i.e., the thundering of the sky; [so too is the wise man unaffected by worldly noise].
The meaning is that one attains happiness from cultivation in the same way. || 4 ||
Having repeatedly torn apart and scattered the five elements like the roots of the *uddālaka* plant,
reflect upon them within yourself with a steady and resolute intellect.
Having introduced that very narrative, he states the necessity of investigating its meaning: "Like Uddālaka.

With an intellect intent on purifying the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*, [one should realize] that the five elements—which constitute the body and so forth, as well as the external phenomenal world—are such that, as it is said: "O dear one, seek the root, water, by means of the shoot, food."

Having cut down the sprout of the effect—which is distinct from its cause—by means of the reasoning shown in the scriptures, and having shattered it through the dissolution of root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), you should investigate within with a steady intellect, even more steady than that of the wise, in order to seek out the pure Being (*sanmātra*) which is its substratum; this is the meaning. || 5 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, by what sequence did the sage Uddālaka,
having cut through that pentad of elements, investigate them within?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O Rāma, how in former times Uddālaka attained the supreme, unimpaired vision through the investigation of the multitude of beings.
In a certain corner of this world, which is like a dilapidated house,
situated in the region of the earth known as Vāyavya (the northwest), and filled with mountains that serve as vessels.
"Because it was crowded with mountains themselves serving as overturned vessels," is the qualifying phrase that establishes the similarity to the corner of a house. || 8 ||
It is said that on the mountain-king named Gandhamādana there is a certain plateau,
strewn with flowers and the camphor-like filaments of trees.
In that [city], the trees were like camphor because they were covered on all sides with blossoms and filaments whose pollen resembled camphor; thus it was called Karpūrakesarā.
It was filled with birds of variegated colors, graced by various creeping vines,
its banks occupied by forest-dwellers, and radiant with the filaments of flowers.

In some places it abounded with great jewels; in others, it was filled with swaying lotuses and water-lilies; in some places it had a mass of mist for its braid of hair, and in others, it was like a mirror for the lake.
In which [city] the lakes and great ponds were like mirrors.
There, on a certain rising ridge covered with *sarala* trees, where flowers were strewn as far as the ankles and which possessed great trees of glossy shade; (12)
On the ridge, in the region of the plateau. || 12 ||
A sage named Uddālaka, who was silent, dignified, and highly intelligent,
lived formerly as a fierce ascetic even before he had reached his youth.

"Proud" means one who possesses the conceit, "I shall certainly accomplish the goals of human endeavor through my efforts," and who is skilled in the pride derived from scripture, inference, and so forth. "Of great intelligence" means one whose mind is not small-minded. (13)
At first, however, he was one of little wisdom yet possessed of reflection; his mind rested in no [attained] state, and though unawakened, he possessed a virtuous disposition. (14)
One whose disposition is virtuous and whose inner being is filled with merit conducive to awakening. || 14 ||
Then, through the gradual practice of austerity, the study of scriptural meanings, and disciplined observances,
discernment came to him just as autumn comes to the earth.
By stages means by the sequence of the maturation of practice. "The new season" refers to the first season, spring. || 15 ||
Then, dwelling in solitude with a tranquil mind, he whose intellect was fearful of the disease of saṃsāra reflected upon this at one time. (16)
He reflected in the manner about to be described; his mind was lovely, his heart auspicious.
In the reading *klāntamānasaḥ*, the meaning is clear. || 16 ||
What could that primary goal to be attained be, upon reaching which one no longer grieves, and having reached which, no further connection with birth arises? (17)
Among the human goals (puruṣārtha) to be attained, what might that primary goal called liberation (mokṣa) be? || 17 ||
When shall I find long-lasting rest in that supremely pure state where all mental activity has ceased, like a cloud upon the peak of Mount Meru? (18)
In which all forms of mental deliberation and the activities of the mind have been abandoned. || 18 ||
When will these perceptions of internal enjoyments come to rest within me, like the waves of the ocean with their sounds of restless surging? 19.
Those who possess the consciousness of enjoyment have a thirst for enjoyment. || 19 ||
"When shall I laugh within myself with an intellect resting in the ultimate state, [free from] the conceptualization that 'having done this, that other thing must also be done'? (20)
When will the web of conceptual construction no longer cling to my mind, remaining detached like water upon a lotus leaf? (21)
Though it remains as a mere appearance, it is free from attachment because it is being treated with equanimity.
When shall I, by means of the supreme vessel of wisdom, have completely crossed over this intoxicated river of craving with its many surging waves? (22)
Intoxication increased by lack of discernment. || 22 ||
I shall mock this action, which is being performed by beings born of the earth and composed of unreality, as if it were the confused play of a child. (23)
Action refers to external activity; "disturbed" means having a distracted mind. || 23 ||
When will my mind, which is overturned by conceptual construction and tossed about like a swing, attain tranquility—like a whirlwind subsiding when the force of the wind has been stilled? (24)

"Overturned by conceptual constructions" means distracted. "Like a swing" refers to that which has a swinging motion; thus, it is restless. For one whose power of wind has been stilled—that is, for one whose disease of the deranged wind (unmāda-vāta-roga) has been pacified—there is no more delusion, which is like a state of distraction. || 24 ||
With the splendor of my form thus illuminated, laughing at the comings and goings of the world,
I shall attain inner contentment, like the Virāṭ self whose intellect is full.
With his form arisen and his true nature manifested, by means of his own luminous radiance,
he is like the Self within the body of the Virāṭ-Brahmāṇḍa, possessing a mind full of wisdom.
With an inner form of perfect equanimity, gentle and free from desire for all objects, when shall I attain tranquility like the ocean of nectar released from churning? (26)

He whose form is equal to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), equal in essence (*ekarasa*), and equal to Viṣṇu who is equanimous and endowed with Śrī; he who is free from longing for all objects— whether they be *dharma*, *artha*, and *kāma*, or the nectar, the Kaustubha gem, and so forth— and who is like the ocean of milk, the sea of nectar, which was released from churning (*manthan*) and agitation.
Beholding the entire splendor of the visible world— immovable as a mountain yet consisting of hundreds of desires— as if in deep sleep, I shall become inwardly expanded. (27)
Seeing [all] as the self consisting of pure existence, like one in deep sleep. || 27 ||
When shall I perceive everything—both internal and external—as pure consciousness alone, through an intellect in which all conceptualization has been stilled? (28)
