I shall cultivate that through its cultivation; I shall become firm. || 28 ||
When my mind and self have become tranquil and I have attained supreme consciousness,
I shall reach the highest light, as if from the disappearance of one born blind.
The supreme consciousness is that which has the single flavor of pure awareness (*cidekarasa*). "The Supreme" refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the other person standing before one.
The term "born blind" (*jātyandha*) is an expression emphasizing the state of being;
the intended meaning is that it results from the removal of primordial ignorance (*anādimūlājñāna*), which is like being born blind. || 29 ||
When shall I behold from afar this slender digit of Time with the beautiful light of consciousness, attained through long practice? (30)

The meaning is: "Because it consists of a thin, obstructed, and continuous form, I shall behold from afar—even from a great distance—that minute, insignificant fraction of time characterized as the remainder of my life. || 30 ||
Free from desires and aversions, devoid of that which is to be rejected or accepted, when shall I attain inner contentment, established in the state of self-luminous consciousness? (31)
When will this night of my faults—strewn with the owls of desire and whose heart-lotus is withered by dullness—come to its end, O Kṛṣṇa? (32)

The night is characterized by the defect of ignorance (avidyā), which is darkness; it is that night by which the lotus of the heart has been withered and decayed through dullness, folly, and frost. || 32 ||
With my mind pacified, in a mountain cave,
I shall attain equality with a stone through non-conceptual meditative absorption.
Through non-conceptual samādhi, his mental activity is stilled, and the fluctuations of the mind have dissolved into the state of oneness with consciousness. || 33 ||
When will my elephant of pride, intoxicated by the great rut of self-conceit, meet its destruction, slain by the deer of the awakening of courage? (34)

The elephant is characterized by pride and egoism; its great streams of rut are nothing other than the functions of self-conceit (abhimāna), which constitute its own constituent parts. That elephant is destroyed by Hari—the lion whose characteristic is the awakening of that [elephant's] true nature as pure, ultimate reality alone. || 34 ||
When will the forest birds build a nest of grass upon my head, as I remain silent, resting in partless meditation? (35)
For me—who am mute, observing a vow of silence, and who finds rest in a partless and thought-free meditation—there is a nest made of grass upon my head; *ghūrṇikās* are a species of birds. 35.
When will birds, their minds steady in meditation, rest without fear upon my chest, which remains as motionless as a mountain pillar? (36)
One whose intellect is steadfast and firm in meditation; that is to say, on his chest, in a nest constructed from the tips of his matted locks hanging down from his breast. || 36 ||
When shall I depart, having abandoned this lake in the forest of saṃsāra, which is overgrown with the thorny brambles of craving and infested with the shrubs of birth? (37)

It was dense with *karañja* trees growing on its banks, characterized by craving; within it were thickets of thorns representing the very cycles of birth, worn down by the roaming of the deer of desire and other passions.
Thus, the twice-born Uddālaka, overcome by anxiety in the forest,
sat down again and again and practiced meditation.
He did not obtain that state of meditative composure which bestows joy. || 39 ||
Once, immediately after abandoning external contacts,
the monkey of his mind experienced agitation while abiding in the state of pure being (sattva).
Immediately after abandoning contact with external objects through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*),

while he was intent on abiding in a meditative concentration (*samādhi*) dominated by the quality of goodness (*sattva*), his mind— being agitated by the quality of passion (*rajas*)— fell into a state of agitation characterized by fear, discontent, and lethargy. Or rather, [this occurred] while he was established in goodness.

He experienced agitation—a movement of his mind through longings—regarding objects fit for enjoyment by sattvic deities and the like, or regarding the savoring of the pleasure of sattvic mental states. (40)
At times, having abandoned internal sensations, the monkey of the mind, due to its fickleness, wanders toward external objects as if scorched by poison. (41)

Regarding the internal touches of the bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi*): just as one who has been consumed by poison and died departs for another world, so it is in that case; the "internal touches" refer to the sensations associated with the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), namely the warmth of the body. (41)
O lotus-eyed one, once, upon seeing within his mind a splendor resembling the rising sun, it became directed toward sense objects.
Having seen the light, resembling the rising sun, within the inner Brahman of the heart; for thus says the Śruti:
"Frost, smoke, the sun, fire, wind, fireflies, lightning, crystal, and the moon—these forms appear as precursors in yoga that bring about the manifestation of Brahman. (42)
Having abandoned internal blindness and darkness, the mind of one who is greedy for sense objects sometimes flies away like a frightened bird. (43)

The meaning is: having brought about the abandonment—that is, the slight pacification—of the inner blinding darkness of the gloom of ignorance through a partial manifestation of Brahman, he immediately thereafter became greedy for that [manifestation] due to the arousal of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding sense objects. || 43 ||
Having abandoned external and internal objects of touch as well as sleep,
that mind occasionally attained a perpetual state in the proximity of darkness and light.

The external and internal touches have been explained. Having dissolved into the junction between darkness (ignorance) and light (the self-luminous soul), he attained a state of perpetual sleep—a condition that persists for a long time. || 44 ||
Thus, with his inner being agitated, he indeed remained amidst the states of meditation like a tree submerged in the wind within fierce mountain caves day after day. (45)

With his mind deeply absorbed in meditation within the caves— [the reading *manasaḥ paryākulasya* (of a distracted mind) is also found]— he remained in a state of peril, his body tossed by the waves of the shore characterized by craving; like a tree submerged and sinking again and again in water brought near by the wind, he stood amidst that difficulty.
There is a concomitance with another. || 45 ||
With his mind deeply rooted in meditation, he remained as if in a narrow strait,
his body swaying like a wave on the shore of trivial craving.
Then, with a troubled mind, the sage wandered upon the mountain,
like the lord of the day alone upon Mount Mahāmeru every day.

"Vijahāra" means he moved about. Because the sun's rays are always seen to be connected with Mahāmeru, there is a figurative description based on the conceptualization of the sun "dwelling" there. || 47 ||
Once, the sage reached a cave that was difficult for all beings to attain,
where all movement had completely ceased, resembling the state of liberation.

Difficult for all beings to reach, and for that very reason with all movement completely stilled— these are the qualifying attributes common to the state of liberation. From the beginning of creation until its end, the cave is thus qualified as being undisturbed by winds and unvisited by beasts or birds.
Unseen by gods or gandharvas, it was supremely beautiful like the sky. || 49 ||
Shining like Brahmā himself, she was the supreme ether. || 49 ||
It was covered with a profusion of flowers and as tender as soft green grass,
appearing as if it were fashioned from emeralds set within crystals of jyotīrasa stone.
The moon is the essence of light; it is as if fashioned from emeralds joined together with moonstones (candrakānta) that have been thoroughly infused with its rays. || 50 ||
It possessed a very pleasant and cool shade, made manifest by jewel-lamps,
and was as well-guarded as the inner apartments of a forest goddess.
At the gate, [he saw] a very pleasant and cool shade.
She was the light for her family, neither too hot nor too cold,
like the golden-white radiance of the autumnal sun when it has just risen.
They are called *kulambanāḥ* because they hang down and spread out at the level of the doorways.
It is a place where there are lights capable of warding off only the cold; therefore, it is neither too hot nor too cold. It is as yellow as gold, fair like the rising young sun. 52.
She was like a young *mālāvatī* creeper, withered by the light of the sun, possessing soft sounds and breezes, and entwined with clusters of blossoms.
Faded and withered by the light of the sun; by this it is understood that the cave faces the east.

In which there is a soft, gentle, and noiseless breeze; by this it is understood that there are windows even on the western side. Endowed with trees thick with clusters of blossoms; by this its fragrance is understood. Prepared for a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage).
The meaning is that she was like a young princess, such as Mālāvatī. || 53 ||
Resembling the very path to tranquility, a fitting form for the repose of the Lotus-born One,
and delightful with its softness like a mass of flowers—
Soft all around like the interior of a lotus. || 54 ||

The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: he reached a cave that was soft like the interior of a lotus, and for that very reason, possessed a form suitable for the repose of the Creator born from the lotus; it was lovely and soft on all sides due to heaps of flowers, and perfectly suited to always serve as a refuge, like the path of tranquility. || 54 ||

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Aspiration of Uddālaka," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Tranquility) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 51 ||
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Wish of Uddālaka," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Fifty-second canto:
That righteous-souled one entered that cave of Gandhamādana,
which he had reached by wandering through various paths, like a bee entering a lotus-bower.
Seated in a cave and desiring to enter into meditative absorption (samādhi), the means for awakening the mind were contemplated and described here. (1)

By means of various and manifold wanderings and searches, it is understood from the phrase "as if into a lotus-pavilion" that for one who has entered there, there will be a state of rest through drinking the essence of unsurpassed bliss. || 1 ||
Intent upon attaining meditative absorption, he shone as he entered [his state], like the lotus-born Brahmā entering his own city when his activity of creation has ceased. || 2 ||
Either in his own city situated in Satyaloka called Aparājita, or in that characterized by the lotus-navel of the Blessed One. || 2 ||
There he fashioned a seat from unfading leaves, with clusters of blossoms within,
like a soft cloud-formation creating a mass of rain-clouds.
An *āsana* (seat) such that one's own body shines within it like a cluster (*guccha*), or one in which one's own flower-clusters attached to various petals shine at its extremities;
[it was] like a mass of clouds (*kadambita*) or a cloud-cluster (*ambhoda*), [the latter being] Indra— the "cloud-ordainer" (*meghavidhi*)— who brings forth the clouds.
In that context, it should be construed as: "that in which lightnings are spread among the extremities like their own clusters. || 3 ||
He spread out upon his back that beautiful deer-skin,
which was like Mount Meru on the slope of a sapphire, with the sky— filled with its essence of stars— as its covering.

On the back of that seat, or above it, was his own deerskin (mṛgājina) resting in its armpit; for in it the stars themselves were the "essence" (sāra)—the highly precious gems. By this, it is understood that it was a spotted deer skin (pṛṣatājina) [the reading *puruṣatājina* is also found]. || 4 ||
There he sat down, bringing about a thinning of the mental fluctuations,
like a cloud on the peak of a mountain whose interior is pure, yet which is as silent as a bull.

The movement of the mind attains thinness and lightness by abandoning its dull objects; just as a cloud, having abandoned its own dullness through rain, sits upon a mountain peak with a pure body, a bright form, mute and without thundering—so it is here. In the word *vṛṣya*, the suffix *lyap* is used despite the absence of a compound, which is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. [It refers to the mountain] Ṛṣyamūka.
In the place called Ṛṣyamūka, on a peak of the Sahya mountain. || 5 ||
Firmly assuming the lotus posture like a Buddha and facing north,
he pressed his heels against his testicles and formed the Brahma-añjali.

"Like the Buddha," meaning like Kapila and others who were fully awakened. The mention of the "lotus posture" (padmāsana) is an elliptical expression for the "perfected posture" (siddhāsana), because that [latter] is appropriate given the instruction to "hold the testicles with both heels. "The Brahma-añjali" refers to the añjali gesture used for prostrating before the lineage of gurus beginning with Brahmā. (6)
Having withdrawn the agitated deer of the mind from its latent impressions (vāsanās),
he undertook this investigation for the sake of non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi).
"Upa" means "nearby," and "plutam" means "rushed" or "run toward" the objects of the senses. || 7 ||
O foolish mind, what purpose do you have in the activities of worldly existence?
The wise do not pursue actions that result in suffering in the end.
"O," used here as a term of endearment. || 8 ||
He who pursues enjoyments after abandoning the elixir of tranquility goes to a poisonous jungle after having forsaken the Mandāra grove.
Mandāras are a species of celestial trees; [it is] their forest.
Even if you go to the cavity of the earth or to the world of Brahmā,
you will not attain nirvāṇa without the nectar of peace.
Mahīrandhra is the netherworld (pātāla). Nirvāṇa is repose in unsurpassed bliss. || 10 ||
Since even a hundred hopes remain unfulfilled, you must abandon that which bestows all suffering and proceed instead toward the supreme good, which is supremely and exclusively beautiful.
As long as you remain unfilled by hundreds of desires for enjoyments, you will continue to be, in the manner previously described, the giver of all suffering.

Therefore, having abandoned—having cast off—desires for enjoyments, go toward the supreme good, which is Nirvāṇa; it is uniquely beautiful because its nature consists of freedom from suffering and unsurpassed bliss. (The form *tyaktvā* is Vedic.)
These various mental constructions, consisting of existence and non-existence,
lead only to your own fierce suffering and never to happiness.

The manifestation of what is desired is existence (bhāva), and the warding off of what is undesired is non-existence (abhāva); the various mental constructions abounding in these constitute the objects of experience. || 12 ||
O fool, what is the use of these things such as sound, which have destroyed your true nature?
You wander about incessantly and in vain, like a female frog in a rain cloud. 13.
The word *hata* has the sense of "censured. The meaning is: just as a female frog wanders about amidst clouds with futile activities such as croaking and so forth, so too [is this]. || 13 ||
O mind-frog, what have you finally attained by wandering aimlessly through the world for so long in blindness? (14)
He states that very point clearly: "The mind," etc. "Bhuvana" means the world, as well as water. || 14 ||
O fool, why do you not fix your mind upon that tranquility from which you obtain everything and in which you find peace? 15.

O mind, why do you not attain— that is, reach— the state of resolve toward that tranquility characterized by the cessation of all mental fluctuations, wherein you bear— that is, obtain— the bliss of disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya), which is somewhat beyond the reach of speech and mind, as well as the bliss of repose in the liberation while living (jīvanmukti)?
You do not bind [them]. || 15 ||
O fool, having come within the range of hearing, do not go to your destruction like a deer, following after sounds with a mind nourished by futile exertions. 16.
He elaborates with individual examples and illustrations that which was stated— that "conditioning leads only to suffering"—

beginning with the words "Having come," and so forth. Having attained the state of being the sense of hearing (*śrotratva*), which consists in the identification with the auditory organ and is augmented and accumulated by a futile outward-turning arising;
Having attained [the body], it becomes called "breath" while breathing, "speech" while speaking, "sight" while seeing, and "hearing" while hearing;

thus, from this indicative mark, the Self assumes the state of the ear and other organs at the time of hearing and so forth, just as the Veda describes the existence [of the elements] in their respective functions—like a deer deluded by the sound of a hunter's song or a bell. 16.
O fool, having come into contact with the skin, do not become bound by a mind intent on touch for the sake of pleasure, like a great elephant lusting after a female elephant.

*Tvaktaḥ* means having the nature of the sense of touch (*tvagindriyatām*). *Gajī* refers to a female elephant (*kareṇu*); [the phrase] "like a lordly elephant greedy for her touch" refers to the well-known fact that mahouts capture a wild lordly elephant by luring him with a well-trained female elephant, drawing him near and then binding him through such means as causing him to fall into a pit. || 17 ||
O you who are blinded by greed for the state of the tongue, do not meet your destruction like a fish greedy for a baited hook. 18.
He [is the cause] of those who are blind and of those with poor vision, and of those with bad food, through greed and longing. || 18 ||
Relying on the visual function that tends toward the accumulation of light-forms, O simpleton, do not go to your own destruction like a moth lusting after radiance. (19)

The visual function is the state of being the eye; it is directed toward—that is, inclined toward—the accumulation of forms, which consists of various distinctions of color and luster, such as radiance and beauty. || 19 ||
Resorting to the path of the nose within the hollow of the lotus of the body,
do not take refuge in bondage by being intent upon fragrance, like a bee.
Like a bee sitting within the heart of a lotus crushed by an elephant. || 20 ||
The deer, the bee, the moth, the elephant, and the fish are each destroyed by a single [danger];
O ignorant one, how can there be happiness for one who is beset by all these misfortunes combined? (21)

He says—starting with "kuraṅga"—that even if attachment to each [object] individually leads to such misfortune, for you who are attached to all of them, unsurpassed suffering is indeed unavoidable: "O ignorant one!"—this is an address to the mind (*citta*). [The mind is] joined with, or possessed of, the objects of sound and so forth, which are the means to misfortune, when they are combined. (21)
This web of mental impressions (vāsanā) of the mind leads to bondage and is harmful to one's own self;
it is innate to the self, like foam, and is therefore like a foul worm. || 22 ||

Just as the innate, natural saliva-foam produced by a loathsome silkworm (*kośakārakīṭa*) is spread out in the form of a cocoon for its own bondage, so too the web of latent impressions (*vāsanājāla*), fashioned by false reasoning, is imagined for the bondage of one's own self. Or, [the reading] may be *bhavato 'hitam iti vā chittvā tatam*, meaning "having cut through that which is harmful to you, it has been spread."
It should be applied by changing the gender. || 22 ||
If you are pacified root and branch, then your victory will be infinite.
How, then, is there victory over this bondage created by negligence? To that he says: "śaradabhra" (like an autumn cloud).

First, having attained purity through ritual action, meditation, and so forth—becoming like an autumn cloud—and then, through the arising of knowledge resulting from the ripening of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means, if you are pacified root and branch, then that is infinite victory.
This is the meaning. || 23 ||
Even though you know that the creation of the world is a nurse of its own destruction and rise, causing torment at its very end, you will not abandon it; you shall perish.
Summarizing everything that ought to be said, he speaks in a single statement: "Kṣaya... etc. "Kṣaya" and "udaya" refer to birth and death;

"daśā" refers to the stages of childhood and so forth, as well as poverty and so forth. She is the nurse (*dhātrī*) of these states. Even at the end, after death, she is characterized by the torment of the various destinies such as hell and the state of stationary beings. She is the creation of the world, the worldly activity (*jāgatī pravṛtti*). || 24 ||
"Or for what purpose do I perform this service of yours?
For, O sinless one, a man who possesses discernment does not have such a mind [as you describe]. (25)

Alternatively, with the intention that one should not merely provide instruction for a harmful mind, but rather forcibly restrain it and effect its eradication through inquiry, he says: "I shall do so. "Instruction" (anuśāsana) means beneficial advice. || 25 ||
As long as there is density of ignorance, so long is there density of mind;
as long as there is the state of rain-clouds, so long is there an abundance of mist.

Alternatively, one need not exert a separate effort for the cessation of the mind, because since that [mind] follows the presence and absence of its root, ignorance (*ajñāna*), its cessation is accomplished by the very cessation of that [ignorance].
With this intention, he says "as long as" in three verses. || 26 ||
As long as there is a thinning of ignorance, so long is there a thinning of the mind;
as long as the rainy season comes to an end, so long does the mist disappear.
The two particles *uttarau* and *yāvat* signify "as much as," having the sense of "whatever [amount] there is, that much. || 27 ||
To the extent that the pure mind has reached its full development through investigation,
to that same extent I consider it to have been utterly destroyed, like an autumnal cloud.
Tenuity is subtlety resulting from the destruction of latent impressions. || 28 ||
This instruction which is given to one who is non-existent or perishing is like striking the sky, water, or the wind.

The mind of one who lacks discernment is indeed unfit for instruction; however, for one who possesses discernment, it is even more so when that mind is in a state of perishing or has already perished—with this intention, he says: "Instruction... It is as futile as striking the sky, water, or the wind. || 29 ||
Therefore, because it is wasting away, I abandon you, who are composed of unreality;
for they say that the highest form of folly is the instruction of one who is to be abandoned.
He concludes by restating what has already been said: "Therefore," etc. (30).
I am the non-conceptual lamp of consciousness, free from the latent impressions of egoism;
I am not bound by you, the seed of egoism, for I am composed of unreality.
With the intention that the very perception of the self's lack of connection with that [object] is its relinquishment, he says: "Nirvikalpa" (verse 31).
"This false view—'This is I'—has been grasped by you in vain; it is a cholera-like poison of doubt for the destruction of the deluded. (verse 32)

If it is asked, "What is my offense that you abandon me for destruction?", he says, "This [is it]," meaning that it is precisely the reliance on the false vision of egoism (*ahaṃtā*) regarding the body and so forth. And that false vision, though having a false cause, acts like cholera induced by the poison of doubt among the deluded.
The meaning is that it results only in destruction; thus, it is a transgression. || 32 ||
The notion that the infinite reality of the Self is "minute" cannot abide in the mind, just as it is impossible for an elephant to reside within a wood-apple fruit. (33)

If it is asked, "Whence this falsity? [the author] says: "Because it is untenable," namely, because of the word *anantasya* (of the infinite). In such a limited mind (*manasi*), a limited state (*paricchinnā sthitiḥ*)—that is, a state consisting of the ego-identification with the body and so forth—is not possible; it does not logically follow. Just as the state of being inside a wood-apple fruit (*bilva*) is impossible for both a female elephant (*vāsitā*) and a tusker (*dantī*).
The meaning is "so it is. || 33 ||
"Alas, this mind of yours is as deep as a great abyss, rooted in latent tendencies and a bringer of suffering; therefore, I shall not follow after it. (34)

He states another reason for the mind’s necessity of being abandoned: "mahāśvabhri" and so forth. O mind, by you has been created a great abyss—a deep, unseen-bottomed pit like an old well—which is painful because it is the abode of serpents, scorpions, and piśācas such as desire, anger, greed, and the like; that abyss is indeed evil latent impression (durvāsanā).
"She has resorted to being a cooking pot"—the word "vatā" expresses lamentation. The meaning is: "But as for me, I do not follow her; therefore, I abandon you who are following her. || 34 ||
What indeed is this vain delusion, like that of a thoughtless child?
This error of "this is I" is merely imagined through the notion of egoism. (35)

Furthermore, this body and that notion "I am the self" which you have imagined as egoism is merely the delusion of an undiscerning child; what indeed could it be for me, who am discerning? The meaning is that it is nothing at all—it does not exist.
From the big toe up to the head, it has been analyzed into its constituent atoms.
That which is called "I" has not been found; who then could exist as "I"? Thus it stands.
Having reflected upon that very non-existence, he clarifies it with the words "from the big toe" and so forth; the phrase "having analyzed bit by bit" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 36 ||
That which fills every corner of the directions, which alone exists throughout the three worlds, is consciousness—unperceivable by itself, yet omnipresent and devoid of a separate self-nature. (37)
If the referent of the word "I" does not exist at all, then who are you? To this he replies with two verses beginning with *bharita*.
[The Self] fills all the quarters and corners (*dikkuñja*), being devoid of the limitation imposed by space. It is one, being devoid of that which is produced by things.
It is unperceivable, being free from the limitation imposed by time, characterized by the three states perceivable in succession. Therefore...
Thus, in all respects and in every manner, that whose nature is devoid of any other entity—such a consciousness itself would be "I"; this is the meaning. || 37 ||
Its measure is not perceived, nor indeed is it a conceptual construction;
it has neither oneness nor otherness here, neither greatness nor minuteness. (38)

Limitation (*iyattā*) is delimited form. Oneness (*ekatā*) is the number one. Otherness (*anyatā*) is the number other than one. Greatness and minuteness (*mahattā-aṇute*) are dimensions (*parimāṇe*). || 38 ||
I know you, who are self-evident and pervasive, to be the cause of suffering;
by means of the awakening born of discernment, this very [ignorance] of yours shall be destroyed by me. (39)

Since I am of the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvedanātman*), therefore, by means of my own self acting as the witness, I know—that is, I perceive—you, the mind. Consequently, because it is the very cause of suffering, you are struck down by taking up this discernment (*viveka*) which is about to be described: "This is flesh, this is blood, these are the bones, O little body!"
These are your breath-winds; who is this that stands [within them] thinking, "Who am I? (40)
He demonstrates the very manner of discernment with the words beginning "this" (idam), etc. || 40 ||
For the vibration of the powers of the wind is the awakening of the Great Consciousness;
old age and death in this body are merely that which stands [in the mind] as "Who am I? (41).

Every aspect of vibration belongs to the vital breaths, which are powers of wind; however, the aspect of pure awareness belongs to the Great Consciousness, the Supreme Self. Aging and death pertain only to the millions of bodies. (41)
O mind, the flesh is one thing, the blood another, and the bones yet others; consciousness is one thing and the throbbing another—what, then, remains as "I"? (42)
"Other" means distinct from the referent of the word "I. || 42 ||
"This is the nose, this is the tongue, this is the skin, these are the ears;
this is the eye, this is touch—what is this that stands as 'I'? (43)
In its state of being as it truly is, I am not the mind, nor you, nor even latent impressions;
this pure manifestation of consciousness alone, the Self, unfolds. 44.

When investigated according to reality and from the perspective of the ultimate truth, the mind is not "I"; you are not "I," nor is the intellect, nor even the latent impressions (*vāsanā*). He says "the Self" (*ātman*) to indicate that the Self is in every way untouched by the notion of "I-ness.
"I alone am everywhere here, or else I am nothing at all here."
Thus, there exists only this vision consisting of Being; no other sequence is found.

If there is the view of superimposition (*adhyāropa*) upon that Self, then "I alone am the substratum everywhere," and thus everything is indeed "I. If, however, there is the view of negation (*apavāda*), then "I am nothing at all";
the meaning is that no other sequence of egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) exists, characterized by an "I-sense" limited merely to a single body.
For a long time I have been crushed by the "I-am-ness" (ahaṃtā), which is a rogue of ignorance, like a young animal caught in the forest by a proud wolf. (46)

I have been long tormented and afflicted by the rogue, that gambler whose characteristic is ignorance, through the deception of egoism (*ahaṃtā*). [The suffix] *kta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), meaning "by means of delusion" (*vipralambhena*). The phrase "like a young deer" is to be understood as the ellipsis. The reading *labdhveva* is correct; *potaka* means a calf or a young one. || 46 ||
By good fortune, I have now recognized this thief of ignorance;
I shall never again take refuge in it, for it robs one of the true nature of one's own self.
It is the thief of one's own ultimate nature, which is the true characteristic of reality and wealth. || 47 ||
Free from suffering, I am not that which is subject to suffering, nor is this [suffering] mine;
it is as a cloud is to a mountain, even while remaining upon it.
With the intention that there is no connection even between two things of mutually contradictory natures, let alone their identity, he says:
"He is free from suffering. Just as a cloud can never become a mountain, so it is in this case. (48)
Having become this [body], I speak, I know, I remain, and I go;
yet, through the vision of the Self, I have attained a state free from egoism.
If you do not possess egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and the like in any way whatsoever, then how do you engage in worldly activity through speech and so forth?

To this he replies with the word "having become" (*bhūtvā*): "Like an actor, having assumed that state for the time being through a mental construction, I speak these words of instruction to you and so forth, and I perceive them through the eyes and other senses. (49)
"Surely I alone consider these—the senses such as sight and the rest—to be my kinsmen;
whether they depart from or remain in the body, they are nothing to me. (50)

I consider this to be certain and beyond doubt: these [faculties] such as sight and the rest are, in reality, myself alone. If they were distinct from me, then—being ignorant and insentient—let them stay in the body or let them depart; they are nothing whatsoever to me.
Alas! What is this so-called "I," and how, by whom, was it fashioned?
He is a Vetāla for the children of the world, possessing a form that is exceedingly tall and incomparable. || 51 ||
His form is taller than even a palm tree, long, and incomparable. || 51 ||
For so long a time, I have rolled in vain within this pit, like a deer upon a rugged mountain from which the grass has been cleared away. (52)
Now he laments his former state of non-investigation: "For so long," etc. (verse 52).
If the eye has turned its face toward looking for one’s own self-interest, then who indeed could this "I" be that is not deluded by this suffering? (53)
Now, he searches for the locus of the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) in relation to each sense-object through the verse beginning with "svārtham" (verse 53).
If the skin has become oriented toward its own true essence for the sake of touching it, then what is this so-called "I" that has arisen like a wretched ghost? (54)
In its own essence, regarding its object. || 54 ||
While this gustatory faculty is intent upon its own sequence of tastes, from where does this contemptible delusion arise: "I am an eater of delicacies"? (55)
In its own sequence, within its own domain; the singular number is used for the universal (sāmānya), because it relies on the position of word-formation (padasaṃskāra). || 55 ||

When the wretched sense of hearing has reached the power of sound and is oppressed by its own object, what source can there be for the suffering of ego-identification, which is now devoid of its seed? (56)

The power of sound refers to the domain of the definition of words. One's own interest is the thirst for hearing; when one is afflicted—that is, brought under control—by that, there occurs the traditional scripture (*āgama*), which is the relevant context (*prasaṅga*). || 56 ||
When one's own scent reaches one's own nose, which is intent on supporting itself, I do not recognize that thief who thinks, "I am the smeller. (57)
"By self-centeredness" means by the state of filling one's own belly—that is, by greed; "mother" here refers to the ego-sense (abhimantṛ). || 57 ||
Following the sequence of a mirage, this cultivation is a vain imagining;
the notion that there is a real entity within that which is unreal is merely a delusion. (58)
This aforementioned mental cultivation (bhāvanā) is the conceptualization of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā), which is well-known in the contexts already mentioned.

When that cultivation is absent—that is, when it has become objectless—the notion that "this body is I" is nothing but a delusion or error. Therefore, the meaning is that the latent impression (vāsanā) of identifying with the body as the self must be abandoned by all means. || 58 ||

Even though this [consciousness] is devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā), it proceeds by itself through the sense organs such as the eyes toward its own external objects; latent impressions are not the cause here. (59)

[Objection: "But surely, if there were an absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there would be a cessation of all external activities, and thus life itself would not exist for a person. To this, he says: "Even though devoid of latent impressions. This body continues to function toward its own purpose—that is, toward the karma that is the cause of life—even while being devoid of latent impressions, as in the case of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
The meaning is: [this is said] because it precedes the description of the commencement of the battle and so forth. || 59 ||
O mind, surely action is performed free from latent impressions;
only the perceptions of pleasure and pain that appear before it are not experienced. (60)

If it proceeds, then the suffering caused by it will surely also arise; what benefit, then, is there in abandoning latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? To this he says: "Latent impression" (*vāsanā*). There is no conceit such as "I am suffering" regarding the mere appearance of momentary enjoyment;
however, future perceptions of pleasure and pain have not yet been experienced, and thus they are [not yet] caused by that.
The intended meaning is that the very pacification of all torments—such as grief, delusion, fear, despondency, anxiety, and agitation—is its quality.
Therefore, having abandoned the foolish senses and your own internal latent impressions, perform all actions; you shall not encounter suffering. 61.
Now, having awakened the senses, he teaches this matter by analyzing it, beginning with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt) and so forth:

"It was in vain that you, like children, were perfumed by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for the sake of suffering; you have become distressed as if by the destruction of a plaything made of mud. (61–62)

The meaning is that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) for enjoyment— which first resembles children’s play with mud and later causes distress through its destruction— has been instilled in the non-Self by you solely for the sake of suffering, both in the acquisition of sense-objects and in their loss. || 62 ||

All perceptions, beginning with latent impressions (vāsanā), are not distinct from the Self, just as waves and the like are not distinct from water; this is so for the knower alone, O sinless one, and not for anyone else.

For this very reason, he says "impressions and so forth" (vāsanādyāḥ) to show that for the wise, once ignorance has been sublated, they have become the pure Self itself along with their own effects, and thus do not exist separately. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), their effects—such as attachment and activity—are included. These do not exist for the knower alone.
The meaning is that it does not belong to anyone else who is ignorant. || 63 ||
O childish senses, you have been ruined by craving alone, in vain, just as silkworms are destroyed by the thread produced from themselves. 64.
For this very reason, he says "by craving alone" to show that the ignorant have destroyed their senses through craving itself—craving that has arisen spontaneously from within. 64.
It is through craving alone that you wallow here in the peril of old age and death,
like travelers on a mountain path whose vision is wandering amidst chasms.

Here you roll upon the ground of the lower cycle of existence, which is like a stony thicket; just as travelers on a mountain peak, while descending, might wander due to a vision blurred by bile and fall from the summit to tumble among the uneven terrain below, so it is with you. 65.
In this world, latent impression alone is the cause of your bondage to one thing,
just as a string threaded through an empty space serves as the support for pearls that have been strung.
Just as a long rope or thread, when strung through and stretched across an empty, pierced cavity or womb, serves as the cause for binding pearls, so it is in this case. || 66 ||
For this [world] is truly constructed by mere conceptualization and does not exist in reality;
it is severed by the mere absence of conceptualization, as if by a sickle.
This latent impression (*vāsanā*) is produced and brought about solely by that delusion arising from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Indeed, this leads only to your own confusion and destruction, like a gust of wind to lamps, even as their flames flicker with light. (67–68)
For you, the mind and the senses increase for the sake of delusion, for the sake of exhaustion, and for the suffering of death and so forth;
[this is true] even for the throbbing splendors of meteors, lightning, and the like. 68.
O Mind, treasury of all the senses, having surely attained oneness with all the senses,
behold the Self whose nature is non-existent in the sky [of the intellect].
Abide in nirvāṇa itself, which is stainless awakening.

Therefore, for the reason stated, O Mind, you who are the support of all the senses like a sheath, having attained oneness and harmony with all the senses, must certainly and with certainty perceive yourself as being of an unreal nature— that is, as false— and remaining in reality become that which is merely self-witnessing, extinguished, and pure consciousness. Stay thus.
The meaning is: "Do not again assume the form of the mind. || 69 ||
Having skillfully cast off the endless cholera of the poison of sense-objects— the latent impressions of worldly existence— by means of the application of mantras that abandon all that is desired.
The Blessed One is both existence and non-existence, and he is not the ground of fear.

Those who consider themselves knowers of the truth of all scriptures [employ] the method of mantra characterized by the abandonment of desired objects— which is itself characterized by the removal of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of duality—
to [overcome] the state of "I-ness" (*ahaṃkāra*), which consists of the latent impressions of that [ego], and which endures as infinite and innumerable suffering.

Having skillfully cast off cholera induced by ignorance, which is like virulent poison, may the Blessed One—who is free from worldly existence (*visaṃsāra*), who is not a ground for all fears such as death, and who is the very self of perfect bliss—become my refuge. This is the meaning. || 70 ||
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Reflections of Uddālaka," in the Section on Quiescence (*Upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 52.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Reflection of Uddālaka," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The fifty-third canto. Uddālaka said:
"His body is both boundless and infinite, yet he is as minute as an atom."
When consciousness is thus unobjectified, latent impressions and the like have no power to overcome it. || 1 ||

In this [work], it is established that the self is unstained by latent impressions (vāsanās) and free from egoism (ahaṃkāra), and that there is enmity between the body and the mind, and so forth. || 1 ||

Sesame seeds and the like, being delimited, are perfumed by flowers and such; likewise, the gross elements—earth, water, fire, and air—are [perfumed] by musk and other substances. That which has a limit, a boundary, an extremity, and limits on its eastern and western sides is of such a nature. Similarly, the gross elements—earth, water, fire, and air—are [perfumed] by musk and so forth.
The meaning is that the mind is perfumed by the *paramāṇu* (atomic constituent), which is subtler than unquintuplicated space (*apañcīkṛtākāśa*) and unmanifest space (*avyākṛtākāśa*).
Therefore, even in the slightest contact during its occupation [of the body], the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth are not capable [of being deposited]; this is the sense.
Even though there is no direct capacity for contact with that [mind], [the senses are affected] through the medium of contact with its objects (*taccetya*).
To ward off the suspicion that there might be a connection with that [object], he specifies: "unperceivable" (acetya). || 1 ||
Through the mind, intellect, ego, and the reflections of the dull senses, they are spread with latent impressions, yet empty, intent upon terrifying others like ghosts. (2)

[Objection: But surely, since no arising of latent impressions (vāsanā) is observed regarding objects not manifested by you, how can it be that they are spread out [by others] while remaining untouched by you? To this he says: "The mind" (manaḥ). It is not by me that they are spread out;
rather, they are [spread] within the intellect (buddhi) and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), which constitute the faculty of cognition for objects acquired by the dull senses.

By means of the causes that are reflections of consciousness, [the mind] experiences the *manas* which, being of the nature of those subtle states, is therefore empty or even non-existent in form; yet, like malevolent spirits (*vetāla*), it is intent on causing terror, having been expanded and spread out by the proliferation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This is the syntactical connection with the following verse. || 2 ||
Even from the numerous investigations performed by that [intellect] and from those experiences, I—the stainless consciousness—indeed experience [them] again within myself. (3)

Due to the numerous investigations into sense-objects performed during the waking state and the objects experienced therein, that mind experiences, once again in the dream state, objects consisting solely of latent impressions (vāsanā) within the hollows of the internal channels. And yet, there is no taint for me from what is produced by the intellect (buddhi) or the ego (ahaṃkāra), nor from what is experienced by the mind. For...
Because I am indeed untainted—meaning that I am not the self consisting of the aggregate of the mind and so forth. And thus says the Śruti:
"Let the body, constructed from its own impure dispositions, assume or even abandon its state within saṃsāra; for I am consciousness, untainted. (4)

Thus, he says "by one's own evil thoughts" (*svadurbhāva*) to show that there is no taint even by what is done with the gross body: "constructed by evil thoughts," meaning by wicked actions (*duśceṣṭā*). || 4 ||
Since consciousness is indeed omnipresent, there is neither birth nor death for it;
what being, then, dies, or by whom could anyone be killed? (5)

For this very reason, he says "of the consciousness" (citeḥ) to show that even birth and death do not belong to oneself. The particle *kila* is used to indicate that the two qualifiers—"because of being all-pervasive" (*sarvagatatvāt*) and "because of being consciousness" (*cittvāt*)—contain the underlying reasons. Upon seeing the indestructible, non-dual Self, the notion of the victim and the slayer becomes entirely devoid of an objective basis.
With the intention that this constitutes the attainment of absolute fearlessness, he says: "What indeed... (verse 5).
There is no purpose in life for one whose soul is destroyed; all life belongs to the soul.
What will this wretched soul gain by striving for life at any time? (6)

For one who has need of life, there would be fear of death; however, Consciousness (cit) is not such [a thing]. Thus he says: "Consciousness" (cit). Since Consciousness alone, as the Self of all, is the life of all things, if its own essential nature—Consciousness itself—is the life that is pervasive and extended across all places, times, and objects, then at what time could there be fear for that life?
What else remains unattained that he would seek to attain for which purpose he has this desire? This is the meaning. || 6 ||
The notions "one lives" and "one dies," which are defiled by false conceptualizations, belong only to the minds; they do not pertain to the stainless self.
He says— “One lives” (verse 7)— to show that since death and life are merely mental constructs, there is no possibility of attachment to aversion for the former or desire for the latter.
For he who has attained the state of egoism is grasped by existents and non-existents;
but for the Self there is no egoism—whence could existents and non-existents belong to it?
For he who has attained the state of identifying with the body is grasped by births and deaths, which consist of the appearance and disappearance of that bodily state. || 8 ||
The sense of "I" is a vain delusion, and the mind is a mirage;
the entire collection of material objects is inert—of what, then, can there be a conception of egoism?

Is this notion of "I" (dehāhaṃbhāvanā) a property of the ego (ahaṃkāra), or of the mind (manas), or of the category of objects (padārthavarga)? Among these, the first two are not established by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and are therefore unreal in nature. Furthermore, objects are utterly insentient and thus incapable of conceit; consequently, that notion is without an object and without a substratum. Thus he says: "The notion of 'I'. Here, "the notion of 'I'" (ahaṃbhāva) refers to the ego (ahaṃkāra). || 9 ||
The body consists of blood and flesh; the mind has perished through inquiry.
Since the intellect and all else are inert, whence can there be the cultivation of the sense of "I"? (10)
He explains the same point at length through a different approach, beginning with the words "attached" (*rakta*) and so forth. || 10 ||
Since the senses have always been fully established in their self-sustaining nature, and objects remain as mere objects, whence can there be any cultivation of the sense of "I"? (11)

The meaning is: by being self-sustaining—characterized by being occupied solely with one's own respective objects—and thus by merely filling one's own belly, rather than by benefiting others, which is characterized by nourishing the ego; "in the state of being an object" means within the nature of an object.
(11) The qualities function for the sake of the qualities; Nature is established in Nature.
When [the mind] has come to rest within that very Reality, whence can there be the cultivation of the sense of "I"?
The *guṇas*, such as *sattva* and the others, [rest] in their own functions characterized by illumination, activity, and delusion, which serve the purpose of the *guṇas*.
In *prakṛti*—that is, in the essential nature (*svabhāva*) characterized by the state of equilibrium of the *guṇas*—[they rest]. *Prakṛti* is called *pradhāna*; it is *māyā*.
It rests only in that which is real, in Brahman, in that which is existent, in its own self-nature, in the very essence of Being. (12)
All-pervading, residing in all bodies, consisting of all time, and great—
the absolute Supreme Self alone exists here as the conscious self.

In this body, that which is the conscious self (cidātman) also remains having identified itself as "I" with the Supreme Self alone, characterized by omnipresence and other such attributes; the meaning is that even that [conscious self] is not the locus of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). || 13 ||
Thus, what is my form, who am I, what is my instruction, and by whom was I made? What is my nature, what am I composed of, who am I, what do I grasp, and what do I abandon? (14)
This being so, what is the form of this "I" which identifies with the mere body; what is its lineage, or what is its configuration?

In reality, who is it, or what is its designation; by what cause was it created, or what is its color, and of what is it a modification? By identifying with that [body], what do I grasp, or by not identifying with it?
Or what shall I abandon? || 14 ||
Therefore, there is no such thing as "I" here that could arise as either an existent or a non-existent;
for one whose nature is free from egoism, how and with what could there be a connection? (15)
Therefore, because it is incapable of being defined, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is indeed false; thus, there is no connection between the Self and it.
He says this with the words "by that" (tena): [the ego-sense] possesses a logical basis whether it be a positive entity (bhāvatva) or a negative one (abhāvatva). || 15 ||
When the ego-sense, which is unreal, has ceased to exist, whose relation with what could there be, and of what kind?
Once the non-existence of all relations is established, the conceptualization of duality dissolves.
The conception of duality is the conception of the twofold nature as "you" and "I. || 16 ||
Thus, whatever exists in this world has Brahman as its self; I am that very reality, I am that very reality—why then do I grieve in vain? (17)

Thus, even when searching for the referent of the word "this" as something distinct from real existence, it ultimately results in its being merely illusory; therefore, the sovereignty of the non-duality of the Real Brahman is firmly established, and there is no room for sorrow.
Thus he says: "In this way... (verse 17).
When the one stainless state, which is omnipresent, is established, how could there even be the name of the stain of egoism, and from where could it arise? (18)
With the intention that the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) can also be refuted by the power of the established proof of non-dual reality (sadadvaita), he says: "In one... (verse 18).
Indeed, the splendor of objective entities does not exist at all; here, only the Self exists as the omnipresent.
And when the splendor of objective entities is present, there is no connection whatsoever for anyone.

Or, even if the nature of categories (padārtha) were to exist, their relationship remains difficult to express; thus, since it cannot be established through the operation of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the like that would prove them, he says—displaying his boldness—"In the nature of categories" (padārthalakṣmyām). || 19 ||

When the senses play with the senses and the limbs, and the mind plays within the mind, how can there be a connection for the consciousness whose body is untainted? To what does it belong, what is it, and how could it be so?

He demonstrates this very lack of connection with the words "by the senses" (*indriyaiḥ*). By means of the senses—which are conceived as its own limbs—the mind (*manas*) leaps about within the mind itself, like in a dream;
it is not capable of touching external objects. But the *citta* [is capable] by means of both the senses and external objects.

Her body is unstained and her nature is non-attachment; thus, what connection could there be for whom, with what, or how, and by what means could anything be established? This is the meaning. || 20 ||
Just as there is no mutual connection between pebbles and sticks,
so too there is no such connection among the body, the senses, the mind, and consciousness, even when they are observed together in one place.
He states an example regarding the lack of connection: "Like a pebble," etc. (21).

In this world, which has arisen from the non-existent and is a great delusion of futile egoism, this entire universe is perverted by thoughts such as "this is mine," "this is I," and "this belongs to him."
If so, from where does the worldly convention such as "this wealth is mine" arise? To this he says: "unreal. It is perverted, that is, erroneous. || 22 ||
This wondrous manifestation of egoism, which arises when the light of reality has not yet dawned, dissolves upon the vision of reality, just as a streak of frost vanishes under the heat. 23.
Apart from the Self, nothing at all exists;
"All is Brahman"—this is my truth, and this I meditate upon. (24)
Thus, this is my conviction, or rather, that reality which is established by direct experience. || 24 ||
I consider the non-recollection of this arisen delusion of egoism—which is like the color of the sky—to be truly better than its remembrance; indeed, forgetting it is preferable. (25)
Now he states the means for cleansing the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)—namely, "the ego-sense" (*ahaṃkāra*). This has been explained previously. || 25 ||
Having completely abandoned for a long time the delusion of egoism along with its very root,
I abide as one whose self is tranquil within the Self, like the autumnal sky in the autumnal firmament.
It was like the autumnal sky, or as the sky appears in autumn when it is stainless, as if it were its own true nature.
The ego-sense, when pursued, bestows a multitude of misfortunes, expands one's evil deeds, and spreads intense suffering. (27)
If that [objection] exists, what harm is there? He states that [harm] with the words beginning "He gives," etc. (verse 27).
In the watery sky of the heart, dense with the throbbing ego,
the cluster of faults blossoms everywhere within the tree of the body.
Within the nature of water, which contains within its womb the waters of evil latent impressions.
Death is at the end of life, and life ends in death;
existence is cut off by non-existence—how bitter is this painful sensation! (29)

Death is the suffering pertaining to the world beyond, beginning with death itself. Life, moreover, is rebirth; it is delimited by that [death] and has that as its boundary. Thus, life is the suffering of this world, ending in death and having death as its limit.
Existence (*bhāva*)—the category of objects of enjoyment—is severed and broken by non-existence (*abhāva*), that is, by destruction. || 29 ||
"This has been gained; this I shall obtain"—such is the distress of the foolish that causes burning;
it does not subside, like the fire of sun-gems in the summer heat. (30)
Like fire from sun-gems—sūryakānta-maṇis—in the summer season, it does not subside;
the meaning is that it constantly arises. || 30 ||
The thought "this does not exist" or "this exists" runs toward the ego-sense,
just as a dull-witted person, with a dull mind, pursues a mass of clouds as if it were a range of mountains.

With a dull disposition, resting upon that which is dull, and taking refuge in water, she runs and follows after [the mountain range]. In the case of the range of mountains (*śailāvalī*), it means "dull" (*jaḍāṃ*) because it is exceedingly heavy (*gurutarām*). || 31 ||
When the sense of "I" is completely exhausted, the tree of saṃsāra withers;
being sapless, it never again produces a sprout, just like a stone.
It does not bestow, nor does it produce; because it is tasteless—lacking the power to generate the "limb" characterized by passion—it is therefore equal to a stone. || 32 ||
The black female serpents of one’s own craving, which have made their dwelling in the tree of the body, flee somewhere when the son of Vinatā—the discerning self—has arrived. (33)
In the nature of reflection, in the form of reflection; in Vinatā’s son, Garuḍa. || 33 ||
When the entire universe has arisen from the unreal, consisting of the delusion born thereof, and its activity is composed of the unreal—then what sequence can there be for "I" and "you"? (34)

Since [the world] has arisen from ignorance—which is non-existent and illusory—and precisely because of this delusion, that is, from superimposition (*adhyāsa*) alone, even though the universe is unreal, the empirical activity (*vyavahāra*) prompted by it might be considered real; therefore, he says: "in the vibration consisting of the unreal. However, if the mere empirical activity of differentiation were unreal, then the sequence of "you" and "I" [would not exist].
What, moreover, is the conventional usage of difference? || 34 ||
This world arises at the beginning from a causeless source;
how can that which has arisen without a cause—[even if there is a reading "that which has arisen as a cause" (kāraṇamucchūnam)—be called real? (35)
For this very reason, it arises from ignorance—which is itself causeless and devoid of any purpose—precisely because it is unworthy of being a cause.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That which... (verse 35).
Just as a form like a jar arises in clay at some boundless time in the past, so too this body has come into being now, and it shall exist likewise in the future. (36)

Thus, it is established that the state of the body and so forth prior to its arising is exactly the same as it is at all times; this he states with the words "aparyanta" (without end). It is like the form or configuration of a jar existing within the clay. The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "api" (also).
Just as water, having abandoned its initial and final states of calmness, becomes for some time merely a mixture of moving and unmoving waves; || 37 ||

He provides an illustration for the stated point with the verse beginning "madhya" (in the middle). Just as water is merely water—unchanged—in its prior and subsequent states, yet for a certain time in the middle it becomes moving and unsteady, [and] having abandoned its well-known placidity at the beginning and end—the prior and subsequent times—it exists in the form of waves; [so too is the nature of the mind].

Just as water remains as water and not as something else, so too the body and other such things are, throughout the three periods of time, Brahman alone and not something else; this is the meaning. || 37 ||
Those of wicked intellect who fix their attachment upon this body—which is subject to the flickering of moments and is prone to dissolution—and upon the wave of existence, are truly ruined. 38.

The meaning is that those of evil intellect who fix their attachment upon this body—which is subject to momentary vibration and is as prone to dissolution as a wave—are destroyed by that very destruction. || 38 ||
All things exist neither before nor after; they have no essence from the very beginning.
What reliance can there be on their manifest appearance in the middle, which is but a form destroyed by its own nature? (39)
He says "prāk" (before) because it is also improper to have attachment toward objects such as the body due to their being limited by space.
In the middle, there is clarity—that is, being perceived as existing—within a limited space measured by one's own span (*vitasti*) or similar units;
yet even that, when investigated through the alternatives of being either the whole or a part, is simply impossible to define.
Even there, since it lacks any objective basis, what kind of reliance could there be? The sense is that it would be entirely improper. || 39 ||
The mind was previously and will be hereafter the locus of consciousness, even as it is called "peaceful";
whether existent or non-existent, it is withdrawn into itself—what has arisen for you in this interim? (40)
Having stated this principle regarding the Self, he shows it to apply to the *liṅga* (the subtle body) as well, stating its similar nature: "The mind," etc.

The "mind" refers to the *liṅga* characterized by the mind; prior to its own arising—that is, in the preceding time—and in the space before it, it is the "body of consciousness" (*ciddeha*), whose essential nature is pure consciousness as its own witness. Likewise, in subsequent time and in other places, it is "quiescent."

"It is lost"—by this very [phrase, "by this very," etc., the portion to be investigated], even though it is delimited by space, it is as if dissolved in the sky, utterly hidden, and difficult to describe as either existent or non-existent. What has been said regarding such a mind being "presently in the middle" or "in this place"? The meaning is: nothing at all. || 40 ||
Just as in the transformations of a dream, just as in perceptions during a state of agitation, just as in the playfulness of intoxication, or just as in the dizziness caused by traveling on a boat.

If the gross and subtle bodies and so forth are indeed non-existent, then what is the nature of their appearance? To this he replies with the words beginning "just as" (yathā). Just as in the case of those who perceive [an illusion], there arises everywhere a suspicion of tigers and the like—even though the tigers and such do not exist—due to the delusion of fear caused by tigers, thieves, and so on; so it is here. || 41 ||
Just as in cases of bodily humors being disturbed, as in the impairment of the senses, as in states of extreme agitation or joy, and in conditions of possession by malevolent spirits; || 42 ||

In the transformations of the bodily elements (dhātu), such as the derangement of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and their combination (sannipāta); in the impairment of the sense organs, such as cataracts (timira) affecting the eye; in the error of perceiving two moons and the like due to a defect; in the joy caused by the attainment of something exceedingly dear, which serves as a cause for extreme agitation;
and in the states of those afflicted by passion and the like—just as the form of existence and non-existence, or being and non-being, appears [in these conditions].

The connection [of the words] is as follows: something unstable, such as the form of a beloved woman, which exists only for the duration of its perception, is seen and then immediately perishes due to sublation; in that very way, this is an illusion. || 42 ||
Form is seen and indeed perishes, being unstable in both its existence and non-existence;
in this very same way, there is here this fluctuation of deficiency and excess in the course of time. (43)

He states that distinction with the words "But here... (iha tu). The meaning is that the distinction lies solely in the difference of duration: dreams and the like last for a short time, whereas the delusion of the world lasts until liberation; thus, there is a disparity in their temporal extent. || 43 ||
And that [thought] has been constantly produced by you, O mind, at the arising of both suffering and pleasure;
just as thoughts of separation destroy one who is full of passion. (44)

O mind, that deficiency or excess which you have constantly created through the delusion of reality regarding conventional objects— acting as the cause for the arising of suffering and pleasure through their separation and union—
now kills and afflicts you, just as it would even if there were no actual death of a wife, son, or others.
The meaning is that, in the same way, the notions of death arising from the words of a deceiver and the nights of separation imagined by them destroy one who is full of passion. || 44 ||
Due to the habitual practice of the unreal here, you perceive me as if I were real, though I am false—like a mirage; therefore, this which was done by you would be as if done by me.

Alternatively, this is not your fault; rather, it is my own fault as one habituated to the sense of "I" in relation to you, by which you are perceived as if real, though you are actually unreal. The meaning is that everything performed by you has become as if performed by me. || 45 ||
Whatever is experienced as an object of perception, all that is the circle of the visible;
having determined that it is insubstantial, the mind reaches the state beyond the mind.

For this very reason, he says "yad idam" (this which... [verse 46], meaning that your peace regarding my offense—which is of the nature of your own lack of discernment—comes from that very discerning knowledge of yours alone.
When the mental certainty that "this world is unreal" has taken root within the expansive mind, the latent desires for enjoyment wither away like blossoms in winter. (47)
He says that for this very reason, even the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of experiences caused by you are destroyed; thus he states: "Non-existent," etc. (47).
Surely, by means of the mind— which is conscious, has perceived the Self, is truly free from passion, and is devoid of mental vigor— one becomes established in one's own natural state.

Alternatively, with the intention that "by the mind—which, through the grasping of the reflection of consciousness, possesses consciousness; which, for that very reason, is free from passion and has abandoned the addiction to mental deliberation; and which, having seen the Self through the final state of direct realization, is itself established in its own nature and rests in liberation—I remain as such, because I am eternally of one form," he says:
[This is] by means of [the reason] "because of being conscious," and so forth. || 48 ||
Cast into the fire of the Supreme Self, the mind itself, having consumed its own impurities by means of the veil of phenomenal existence, attains eternal purity. (49)

The meaning is that the mind, having itself turned outward, conceals its own constituent parts such as the senses; then, being impelled by the fire of the Supreme Self through the awakening to reality, it burns away the self which is the very nature of the mind and attains an absolute, eternal, and perpetual state of purity. || 49 ||
Having perceived the body as distinct [from the self], having abandoned the latent impressions of sense objects, and having accepted its perishability, one conquers the mind like a hero. (50)

The meaning is that just as a heroic man in battle— perceiving his own body as something other than himself destined for heaven, and having abandoned the latent desires (vāsanā) regarding objects such as the house, field, and wealth associated with that body— accepts even death and conquers the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), so too does the mind. || 50 ||
The mind is the enemy of the body, and the body is the enemy of the mind; through the absence of one, both perish, like the relationship between a container and its contents. (51)

Now, [the author] explains in detail the opposition between the body and the mind by way of their mutual scorching and being scorched; their mutual dependence through mutual growth based on the conceit of mutual identity; and the destruction of both through the destruction of the conceit of either one.
He begins to demonstrate this with the words "the mind" (*manaḥ*). The words *śatru* (enemy) and *ripu* (foe) refer to that which causes affliction.

By the absence of one—that is, by the eradication of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of either one—just as the conjunction resulting from the relationship between a container and its contents, such as water and a jar, perishes through the destruction of either one, so it is here. || 51 ||
For those possessed of passion and hatred, which are eternally and utterly opposed to one another, the destruction of these two by uprooting them is the supreme happiness. (52)
And thus, because they subsist upon one another, like two passionate lovers; and because they cause mutual affliction, like two hating tigers;
while these two exist, there is no happiness for the living being, just as there is none for a forest deer.
Rather, the meaning is that supreme happiness consists only in their destruction through the uprooting of their very foundation—the destruction of primal ignorance (mūlājñāna). || 52 ||
The talk that death occurs when these two are in one place is equal to the talk that the earth is enjoyed by another woman in the sky.

Now, one might ask: "Is it not the case that through death alone, by the destruction of the body which is the locus of experience, there would be the avoidance of all suffering? To this he says: "Of these two" (*etayoḥ*). Even upon the destruction of the body, because the mental construction of a body cannot be prevented as long as the single mind persists, the talk of "death" is like the earth being consumed by a woman traveling through the sky.

"Grasped" (grastā) means equal to a story; that is to say, one whose subject matter is impossible. From the root *aya* with the suffix *kvip*, followed by the elision of *y*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, and the lengthening of the vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*), we have *ayā*. In the reading *ayaḥstriyā*, however, the meaning is: "the earth was consumed in the sky by a female image made of iron"—that is, by a statue of iron. For it is possible for an iron statue to move through the sky.
The sense is that just as eating the earth is utterly impossible, so too is death while the mind still exists. || 53 ||
Wherever both [opposites] are joined together in a state of natural contradiction, there the successions of misfortunes fall like torrents of rain. (54)

Regarding what harm could there be when those two exist, he says: "unartificial" (akṛtrima). It is like the edge of a sword or an arrow [piercing] the body of one standing between two combatants. || 54 ||
For that base person who finds delight in the association of mutually contradictory things must be abandoned, like fire in a house plastered over with straw.

In this context, "contradictory conjunction" (*viruddhasaṃsarga*) refers to the union of the body and mind, which are mutually opposed; it is the enjoyment of sensual pleasure. That person who fixes his delight upon such a base thing falls like water into a mass of fire—the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*)—in which the waters of the ocean fall, being uncoated and uncovered.
It must be abandoned; the meaning is that even there, he will find delight. || 55 ||
Having nourished the mind with its own volitions like a child-demon nourishing its body,
it offers its own sufferings as food for that very life-force.

Regarding what was stated—that [the mind] possesses passion and hatred—the text shows how these portions of passion and hatred reside in the mind within the body with the words "by means of volition" (*saṃkalpena*).

The mind, by its own volition, constructs the body like a child imagining a spirit; having constructed food for it—meaning for as long as the duration of life lasts—it nourishes it, thereby producing the causes for its own obsessive attachment (*abhiniveśa*).
The meaning is that it bestows all sufferings. || 56 ||
The body, tormented by the sufferings of old age, then desires to destroy the mind;
even a son kills his father when he has become an assailant. (57)
He shows that the body also possesses a portion of aversion toward the mind by means of its cause, using the word "by them" (taih).

The meaning is that, through the service of those [objects], it desires to afflict the mind by generating attachment, aversion, sorrow, delusion, sin, and so forth in the mind. Now, since the body is produced from the mind, it is like a son, while the mind stands in the place of a father.

Regarding how he intends to kill him, he says: "A son... and so forth. "One should know these seven as *ātatayin* (assassins): one with a raised sword, one with poison or fire, one with a hand raised to cast a curse, one who kills by means of the *Atharva-veda*, a slanderer among kings, and one who violates his wife. Thus it is said.
The meaning is that he reached the state of those designated as *ātatāyins* by Viṣṇu and Kātyāyana—that is, he arrived at the point of intending to cause harm even to himself. || 57 ||
There is no enemy by nature, nor is there ever a friend;
one who bestows happiness is called a friend, while those who cause suffering are known as enemies. (58)
He establishes its enmity according to a principle well-known in the world: "It does not exist," [verse 58].
Experiencing sufferings, the body desires to destroy its own mind;
in an instant, the mind makes the body a vessel for its own sorrows. (59)
"Saṃketa" means a dwelling; that is to say, a place for enjoyment. || 59 ||
Thus, when suffering and pleasure are intertwined with one another, how can there be the arrival of happiness for these two—the body and the mind—which are by their very nature utterly opposed? (60)
Having restated the contradiction that has been established, he concludes by stating the rarity of happiness therein:
"Thus, when the mind alone is utterly exhausted, the body is no longer a vessel for suffering;
yet, out of an intense longing for its own destruction, the body constantly runs about. (61)

He says "in the mind" (manasi) to show that when the mind is destroyed, there is no further attachment to the suffering of the body. Therefore, upon its destruction, one runs with intensity and longing toward the means for knowledge and its instruments; that is to say, one exerts oneself. || 61 ||
The body, whether lost or not lost, is for one's misfortune and is the very seat of calamities;
it is produced from a mind that has failed to attain self-discrimination.
In that case, why does the mind not strive for the destruction of the body as well? To this he says: "Destroyed... (verse 62).

By the mind that has not attained discrimination of the Self, whether the body is destroyed or not destroyed, it becomes a locus of calamities and leads only to misfortune; thus, the desired goal is not accomplished by its destruction. This is the meaning. || 62 ||
For these two—the mind and the body—have indeed grown fat together, being insentient in nature like a cloud and a lake joined by their forms. (63)

The phrase "through mutual favor" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Even in the case of a lake, it might occasionally be a benefactor by means of providing water for the accomplishment of *havis*-sacrifices and the like; thus, the justification for the simile is established. || 63 ||
Though they have arisen for mutual suffering, are of one nature, and exist as two, they remain engaged in worldly affairs together like water and fire. (64)

If it is asked why there is a coexistence of these two, which are mutually contradictory, the intention is that it is for the sake of the person's worldly activity regarding the means to enjoyment and liberation—just as water and fire exist together for the purpose of cooking; with this in mind, he says "mutually" (*mithaḥ*).
Although these two stand in a dual state due to their mutual contradiction, when they become of a single form through the superimposition of mutual identity, [they lead] to suffering.

The meaning is that they have become fully accomplished in the means for the worldly transaction of both enjoyment and liberation, [and thus] in experiencing sufferings and avoiding them together. || 64 ||
When the mind is diminished and completely exhausted, the body indeed becomes uprooted;
but when it increases, it proceeds like a tree with a hundred branches.
He states the result of the teaching that the body is dependent upon the mind: "In the mind" (verse 65).
When the mind is exhausted, the body—its latent impressions (vāsanās) having been destroyed—is likewise exhausted;
yet the mind is not exhausted when the body is exhausted. Therefore, one should exhaust the mind.
Having cut down the forest of the mind— the tree of volition and the creeper of craving—
and having reached the vast expanse of the earth, I dwell in happiness as I please.
Therefore, he says "by volition" (saṃkalpa) [in verse 67], meaning "I shall destroy the mind itself."
This very mind, no longer remaining within the mind, is indeed wasting away;
the web of its latent impressions is subsiding like a cloud at the end of the rainy season. (68)

And when conceptualization ceases, the mind, abiding within the mind by its very nature as the mind, will—its web of latent impressions having been pacified—perish like a cloud at the end of the rainy season; this is the meaning. || 68 ||
This arrangement of the elements, known as the body, is my enemy;
may it remain only while the mind is wasting away and dissolving. (69)

The meaning is this: this body, which consists of the arrangement of the constituents (dhātus) known as skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen, suffers no loss whatsoever—whether it dissolves or remains—when the mind has perished. || 69 ||
That for whose sake the glory of enjoyments indeed desires its own body—neither that belongs to me, nor do I belong to it; what purpose, then, could there be for me in a mere fragment of pleasure?

If it is asked, "While the body remains, why should suffering not also exist?", the author says, "For the sake of which," with the intention that since the mind—the cause of that connection—has been destroyed, the connection itself no longer exists; far less, therefore, can there be any attachment to suffering.
Listen now to the reasoning in this sequence regarding the thought "I am not the body":
if all the limbs are indeed present, why does a corpse not move? (71)

In the context of the realization "I am not the body," the word *krama* refers to the sequence of understanding; the meaning of *avaśyajñātavya* is that which must necessarily be known. In that regard, *yukti* means logical justification. One "moves" (*valgati*) by engaging in worldly activity through seeing, hearing, and so forth. || 71 ||
