Therefore, I am beyond this body, eternal, with a radiance that never sets;
having attained union with the luminous one, I perceive the sun in the sky.

Therefore, because no perception [of the sun] occurs prior to the awakening of the corpse (śava), he who—by virtue of his omnipresence (vibhutva)—exists even within the solar orb, having attained union with the luminous one, knows the Sun in the sky as "I am that very one whose nature is consciousness" (cidrūpa); this is the meaning. || 72 ||
"I am not ignorant, nor do I have suffering, nor misfortune, nor am I afflicted; let the body exist or let it not exist—I remain free from all feverish distress. (73)
Where the Self resides, there is neither mind, nor senses, nor latent impressions;
common folk do not remain in the vicinity of a mountain.

But since there is no possibility at all for the mind and the other [senses] to exist in the Infinite (bhūman), he says: "Where... He cites a worldly convention regarding the inability of the lowly to remain in the presence of the superior: "The common folk... [referring to] "the mountain-possessor," that is, the king. || 74 ||
I follow that very path; I am alone, I am victorious.
I am extinguished, I am partless—I am without activity, I am without desire. (In some versions, "I am without activity" and "I am without desire" are read in reverse order. || 75 ||
Having followed that path, I have attained it. || 75 ||
Now I am disconnected from the mind, body, senses, and so forth,
like sesame oil separated from the sesame seeds by its trickling away.
Furthermore, for me who have sportively moved away from this supreme state of my own, and whose mind has become detached, this auspicious retinue indeed remains.

Furthermore, while moving from the supreme state which is his own essential nature—through the play of experiencing the remainder of his *prārabdha* karma—the meaning is that, due to former latent impressions (*vāsanā*), his intellect becomes differentiated, and he thinks: "This body, senses, and so forth are my retinue, like attendants for the sake of diversion. || 77 ||
Transparency, vigor, existence, loveliness, truthfulness, and wisdom;
bliss, tranquility, and always speaking with gentleness. || 78 ||

In that *līlā*, he characterizes the abundance of qualities such as purity as being the beloved women dear to his own heart through three verses beginning with "purity" (*svacchatā*). *Ūrjitatā* is the state of having all desires fulfilled; *jñatā* is the state of knowing the Self.
It is fullness, magnanimity, truth, splendor, and one-pointedness; it is the oneness of all, fearlessness, and the state in which the conceptualization of duality has perished.
Magnanimity is the absence of greed; truthfulness is the nature of being uncontradicted. || 79 ||
Ever-arisen, equanimous, self-abiding, beautiful, and dawning with auspicious fortune,
they are my beloveds, dear to my heart, as I am one with their very self.
These beloved ones of mine are eternally joyful and endowed with prosperity. || 80 ||
Therefore, since everything is possible for everyone, everywhere, and at all times,
my desire and lack of desire, as well as pleasure and pain, have ceased with respect to everything.

The phrase "it occurs through conceptual construction" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Therefore, desire and aversion toward the entire range of objects are passion and hatred; pleasure and pain are their respective fruits. || 81 ||
Free from delusion, free from mental distress, and with a mind devoid of conceptual construction, I clearly bring rest to myself within this cooling state.
Like a mass of clouds in the sky during autumn. || 82 ||

Therefore, in autumn, like a fragment of a cloud in the expanse of the sky, I shall rest within my own self—which is cool and free from heat—having abandoned the state of being an object of perception; this is the meaning. || 82 ||

Thus ends the fifty-third canto, titled "The Playful Deliberation of Uddālaka," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. || 53 ||
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Playful Deliberation of Uddālaka," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Fifty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus resolved with that expanded and pure intellect, the sage—
He stood with his eyes half-closed, seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana). || 1 ||

Having meditated upon his own Vaiṣṇava body through [the visualization of] burning, flooding, and so forth, and having shaken off all conceptual constructions, he who rests in samādhi is described as such. || 1 ||
Having determined it in the manner described—by means of an intellect that is white (pure), purified, expanded, and not narrow. || 1 ||
Having thus determined that "Om" is the Supreme Brahman, that sage then declared:
"By whomsoever the syllable Om is uttered, by him the supreme state is attained. (2)

That sage Uddālaka—by him who has uttered the syllable *Oṃ*—the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*) has indeed been attained. The elision of the letter *ya* [in the compound] and the sandhi are archaic (Vedic). Since this syllable *Oṃ* is the designation of the Supreme Brahman and its symbol, it is determined to be the Supreme Brahman itself; thus, the *Tāra* is a high pitch.
The construction with the subsequent clause is as follows: he made—that is, uttered—the *oṃ* syllable, which was of such a kind that its sound ascended upwards. || 2 ||
He uttered the syllable *oṃ* with a piercing sound whose resonance traveled upward,
like the ringing of a bell struck firmly upon its handle.
In that [battle], the bell’s cavity—the space within its mouth—was like a roar, containing iron in the form of a hanging tongue that had been struck correctly. || 3 ||
As he utters "Oṃ," while his consciousness is directed toward that [reality],
it extends up to the peak of the syllable Oṃ, abiding in the expansive and stainless Self.
Regarding how long he uttered the syllable *oṃ* there, it says: "Oṃ.
As Uddālaka was repeatedly pronouncing the *oṃkāra*, [the light] reached the top of that well-known *oṃkāra* which extends from his *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*.
When the cessation of the half-mora has occurred and [the mind] is manifested in the expanded,
stainless Self— that is, in Brahman— the consciousness conditioned by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of the syllable *Oṃ*,

as well as the reality that is the immutable consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*), [remain] directed toward that [Brahman], being oriented toward the undivided consciousness of Brahman.
The connection with what precedes is that he uttered the syllable *oṃ* for such a length of time. || 4 ||
In the first third of that which consists of three and a half measures, there is the clear resonance of the *praṇava*, while the body vibrates with the intensely agitated vital breath.

Therein, for the sake of accomplishing the fitness for abiding in non-conceptual samādhi, one must first— by means of that very *praṇava*— perform the drying out, burning, casting off of the wicked portions of the ash, and bathing of the gross body, as well as the creation of another divine body.

He states that it first occurred through the cultivation of that [state] with the words beginning "sārdhatryaṃśa": in the first part— the acute (*udātta*) portion consisting of the letter *a*— of the *praṇava* which has as its own parts (*ātmamātrāḥ*) the letters *a*, *u*, and *m* known as the three-and-a-half portions, namely, the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) together with [the other two].

When the *sphuṭārava*— the state of being clearly manifested through a loud sound— occurs, and consequently, when the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), being thoroughly agitated and intent on exiting, cause the body to resonate from the *mūlādhāra* up to the lips, the process of the exit of the vital breaths known as *recaka* [purifies] everything.
The meaning of the two [terms] is that he made the body empty by means of exhaling, that is, he dried it up. || 5 ||
The process known as *recaka*, by which the vital breath exits the body,
emptied his entire frame just as Agastya emptied the ocean after drinking its waters.
Having abandoned the body, like a bird that has left its nest, he remained in the sky filled with the essence of consciousness, his vital breath suspended in the atmosphere.

Regarding where his exhaled vital breath (prāṇapavana) remained, he says: "It remained" (atiṣṭhat). It remained in the "void" (ambare), that is, in the external space, which was filled with the essence of consciousness—the nectar of the heart manifested through the contemplation of Brahman. || 7 ||
The fire of his heart, with its blazing flames, consumed his entire body,
like a forest fire driven by a tempestuous wind consumes a dry tree.

He now describes what occurred at that time through his meditative visualization (bhāvanā): "The fire of the heart" and so forth. Due to the friction caused by the departure of the vital breaths (prāṇas), a fire was kindled in the heart by means of visualization. A "dāva" fire is a forest fire, one that occurs in the woods (araṇya). || 8 ||
To this extent, this state [of the breath] occurs through the initial stage of the *praṇava*;
it does not happen by force alone, for *haṭhayoga* indeed causes suffering.

This entire process occurs through meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*) within the first part of the first sequence previously described regarding the *praṇava*, and not by force (*haṭha*) alone. To the question "Why is that?", he says: "Haṭhayoga. The sense is that if the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) were expelled by force, there would be the risk of fainting, death, and so forth. || 9 ||
Then, at the moment when the other two parts [of the breath] were in equilibrium within the *praṇava*, there occurred a stage of the vital breaths known as the "unwavering *kumbhaka*. (10)

The other portion is the part consisting of the syllable *u*; because at the time of its low-pitched (*anudātta*) and soft (*mandra*) pronunciation, it remains motionless and full like water in a jar, this stage is called *kumbhaka*. 10.
Neither outside nor inside, neither below nor above, nor in the intermediate directions—
there your vital breaths did not undergo agitation, as if they were completely solidified.
He clarifies what was stated regarding the name "kumbhaka" with the words: "not outside. || 11 ||
The fire that had consumed the body was instantly extinguished like a thunderbolt;
only the white bodily ash, pale as snow, remained visible.
Like a thunderbolt, like the fire of lightning. || 12 ||
Where the motionless and white bones of the body appear as if they were comfortably sleeping upon a bed of camphor. (13)
In which state, by the vision of meditative cultivation, the bones of the body appear as if they were lying upon a bed fashioned from camphor powder. || 13 ||
The wind brought that ash along with the bones and joined them to its own body,
which was greatly wasted away, as if it were observing the vow of the Three-Eyed One.

The wind, carrying upward with its currents that ash along with the bones— bones having been brought up by the gusts— the fierce wind, possessing a flow directed upwards, applied it to his own body, which was now indistinguishable, as if he were one who had observed the vow of the three-eyed Rudra, the wearing of bone-ash; thus, he thoroughly covered himself, appearing emaciated by asceticism.
...up to verse 14.
And that [ash], stirred up by a fierce wind, having covered the sky in an instant like autumnal mist or clouds,
vanished somewhere into the liquor.
That bone-bearing ash went away somewhere. || 15 ||
Thus, in this other sequence of the Praṇava, this state came about;
for Haṭhayoga does not arise through force alone, as it is indeed a source of suffering.

In this sequence known as *kumbhaka*, which is to be accomplished through the middle portion of the *praṇava*, even this state came about solely through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and not by force (*haṭhāt*). || 16 ||
Then, on the third occasion, there arose the process known as *pūraka*, which brings peace to the *praṇava* through its filling. || 17 ||

"At the third occasion" means at the time of the utterance of the third part. Although it is well known that the entire *praṇava* serves as the means for *recaka*, *pūraka*, and *kumbhaka*, nevertheless, in *recaka* only the initial part is extended, in *kumbhaka* only the middle part, and in *pūraka* only the final part.
Because the portion corresponding to the vowel *a* is manifested by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as it exits from the throat,

the portion corresponding to the vowel *u* is manifested by the constricted lips, and the portion corresponding to the consonant *m* is manifested when the lips are closed; thus, even when the vital breath re-enters, only the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that [final *m*] persists.
It should be understood that this is a statement regarding the division of the respective portions and their appropriate occasions. || 17 ||
At this moment, the vital breaths, moving within the nectar of consciousness,
attained a coolness in the sky as beautiful as the touch of snow.
Volition is the living consciousness; that which is cultivated within it is the immortal nectar, situated in the midst of which. "In the sky" means in the external space.
Gradually, situated in the midst of the sky, the smokes attained the form of lunar discs, like cool clouds resting within the expanse of the heavens. (19)
The smoky fogs situated in the treasury of the sky, like portions of mist, attained the state of cool clouds. || 19 ||
In that lunar disc, which was complete with its full array of digits,
like a mass of merit or a great ocean of elixir, [he entered].
In that lunar orb— a mass of merit and a great ocean of elixir, completely filled with clusters of nectar-like digits,
and thus overflowing with bliss like the meditative absorption known as the Cloud of Dharma— those vital breaths consist of that very elixir.
The connection with what follows is: "the streams of rays became composed of nectar. || 20 ||
The vital breaths have become streams consisting of elixir;
they take the form of jeweled pillars, like the rays of the moon within a lattice.
A jeweled staff is one with a crystal handle; those [other staves] have the same form as that. || 21 ||
That stream fell from the sky onto the ash of Śiva’s body,
like the celestial river Gaṅgā, the source of elixirs, falling upon the head of Hara.
In the remainder, which is what is left after being shaken by the wind, there is the *pravahaṇī*, the carrier of the essences. 22.
A four-armed body, radiant like the orb of the moon, emerged from her,
like the Pārijāta tree rising from the ocean after the churning of Mount Mandara.
By that stream; from such an ocean as that, in which Mount Mandara was shimmering due to the churning, [he emerged] like the Pārijāta tree. || 23 ||
That body of Uddālaka, having arisen as Nārāyaṇa,
shone with its lotus-like eyes and face in full bloom, beautiful with radiance.
By virtue of being Nārāyaṇa, by virtue of having the body of Nārāyaṇa. || 24 ||
The vital breaths, consisting of elixir, filled his body,
just as floods of water fill a lake or sweet juices fill a tree.
In the springtime of Madhu, the earthy essences that cause the emergence of new shoots [serve as the cause for the arising of passion]; thus, there is a supreme simile: [the lover] is like a tree.
The vital breaths, filled with reverence, filled the internal Kuṇḍalinī,
which had spread out following the path of the wheels, just as waters fill a great river.
The Ganges, the best of rivers, flowing forth with whirlpools that turn in the shape of circles;
[if the reading is "saritpati," then it should be read as "prasṛta" (flowing forth)]. 26.
The body of that twice-born man returned to its natural state,
like the surface of the earth washed clean when the rainy season has ended.

He states the purpose of describing the origin [of the world] from the body of Viṣṇu through burning, flooding, and so forth, with the words "prakṛtastham" (situated in primordial nature). Just as the surface of the earth, having been washed by the final rains of autumn and immediately dried, is distinct from the mud, moss, and other impurities characteristic of the rainy season;
Just as the body, upon the departure of its own [ordinary] form, becomes clear and stainless and fit for the worldly activities such as the journey of the virtuous, so too this [yogi’s] body,
cleansed by the meditative cultivation of burning, flooding, and so forth, being free from impurity, remains established in the activity of the present samādhi.
The meaning is that it came into being. || 27 ||
Then, seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), having established a firm stability within the body,
he bound the five senses as one ties an elephant to its tethering post.
Having assumed a steady posture by binding the lotus position (padmāsana) within the body, one should restrain the five sense organs. || 28 ||
He undertook the resolve for the sake of non-conceptual samādhi, in order to lead his own nature to clarity, like the stainless autumn season. (29)
One's own nature, one's own self, or one's own mind. || 29 ||
With her anxiety, she drew his heart from afar toward herself, like a rope pulling a stake, as he moved through the quarters of the sky like a deer whose breath has been stilled.

He qualifies the very nature [of the mind] itself as "tranquil" (*praśānta*). Through the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the deer-like vital winds such as *prāṇa* and the rest have become stilled within it. By means of the well-known group of terms—such as *āśā* (hope), *tṛṣṇā* (thirst), *lobha* (greed), *utkalikā* (longing), and *pratīkṣā* (expectation)—the nature [of the mind], which is habitually inclined toward outward movement, [is restrained].

"Having made the deer [of his mind] free from the wind [of agitation], he undertook the effort to lead it to clarity"—this is the connection with what precedes. He describes what happened to him as he did so, beginning with "by thoughts":
his heart—that is, his mind—was led away by thoughts of the house, fields, sons, friends, and so forth, previously experienced. Just as:
Just as a stake for tethering horses and the like, if it is not firmly driven in, is uprooted and removed by pulling on the rope attached to it, so it is in this case. || 30 ||
He forcibly restrained the mind—which was running downward, intoxicated, pure yet agitated—just as a dam holds back a swift torrent of water. (31)

He then describes what he did: "running" (dhāvamānam). The meaning is that, by means of the power of discernment (*viveka*), he made the running mind pure and restrained it—just as a dam or embankment (*setu* or *āli*) restrains water that is rushing forward or about to flow. Alternatively, "drutam" may mean "quickly. || 31 ||
She closed her eyes, which were beautiful with their thick lashes and motionless pupils,
like a lotus at twilight.

Then, as to what he did, it is said: *nimimīla* (he half-closed). He half-closed his two eyes, which were beautiful with pupils that were motionless, and which on all sides—on both parts—were as if possessed of eyelashes due to the interlacing of their tips. He closed them halfway.
In the case of the lotus, they are motionless like two pupils; in the case of the bees, they are "sweet" because they drink honey. || 32 ||
The silent sage brought about gentleness— the state free from agitation, imbalance,
and the like— into the movement of the prāṇa and apāna breaths at his mouth,
just as an auspicious time brings prosperity to a favorable place.

First, he describes the restraint of speech, prāṇa, and apāna that is conducive to *rājayoga*, beginning with the words "saumyatām" (toward gentleness). Just as for universal monarchs (*cakravartins*), there is an auspicious time that serves as the cause for their birth and so forth, which, for the welfare of the world and to indicate good fortune, brings about a wind (*śvasana*) characterized by qualities such as coolness and mildness; [so too does the yogin bring about this state].
In the same way, it carries [the breath] evenly and steadily to the place of its birth. Thus it has been said by the Blessed One:
"Having made the prāṇa and apāna equal, moving within the nostrils... (33)
He diligently separated the senses from the objects of the senses, just as one extracts oil from sesame seeds, or as a tortoise withdraws its limbs for protection.
He states the sequence for its withdrawal with the words beginning "from the sesame seeds" (tilebhyaḥ).
The word "the senses" (indriyāṇi) is also to be connected here with the word "absorbing" (ropayan). || 34 ||
That man of steady intellect completely cast aside all external objects of touch from afar,
just as a gem covered by a cloth is suddenly abandoned when its distant luster is no longer perceived.
Regarding the word "bāhya" (external): a jewel covered—that is, closed—by a *kuṇḍaka*, a small vessel, [does not emit] its rays, which have spread far. || 35 ||
He caused the internal sensations to melt away by abandoning his visual perceptions,
just as a tree in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa causes the sap within its buds to dissolve.
He drew in and dissolved within the wheel the internal objects of touch, which consist of mental impressions, by means of attraction into the reality that is the substratum. || 36 ||
Then, by contracting the anus, he obstructed the winds of the nine gates;
like a jar with its mouth covered, he blocked them as one would block the apertures of a hollow vessel.
By pressing the perineum with his heel and contracting the anus, he restrained the winds of the nine gates within his heart through the support of the *mūlādhāra*.
Just as a full jar turned upside down, its mouth firmly sealed and covered,
cannot leak water from its other openings due to the absence of air entering within, so [did he restrain] the others.
In the same way, it blocks the apertures of the sheath. || 37 ||
The steadfast one bore his neck, which was richly illuminated by the jewel of his own self, clearly adorned with a flower, just as Mount Meru bears the peak of its summit.
Rich with the light of its own self as a jewel and the lights of the jewels of its own self;
clear because it is unobscured by *rajas* and *tamas*; marked by the lotus-flower of a serene face and by the flowers of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*); just like Mount Meru, such was she.
In the same way, he wears a topknot characterized by his own horn. || 38 ||
He bore within the space of his heart the mind that had attained self-restraint, like a mad elephant brought under control by skillful means in the Vindhya ravine. (39)
He describes *dhāraṇā* (concentration): "babhāra" and so forth. *Dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* upon a single object constitute *saṃyama*;
[the mind] was directed toward that, being oriented toward it. It was brought under control by means of reasoning, that is, by the methods of *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).
Having attained an extreme serenity as stainless as the autumnal sky, [it remained].
It bore the unshakable splendor of a full ocean that is free from wind.
Through retention (*dhāraṇā*), due to the clarity of the mind, he describes the rest in the meditation of the perfected self with the words:
"like the autumnal sky" (verse 40).
He shook off the floods of excessive conceptual constructions that had come into appearance before him like shimmering forms, just as the wind disperses gnats.

He washed away—that is, he cast off—the floods of conceptual constructions arising from contrary mental impressions, which appeared intermittently in the midst of the stream of his few mental fluctuations that were directed toward the nature of Brahman. || 41 ||
As the mental images appeared again and again according to his will,
the hero cut them away with his mind, just as one cuts down enemies in battle with a sword.
When the flood of conceptual constructions had been completely severed, he beheld within the sky of his heart that [ego],
which was like the darkening of flickering collyrium, obscuring the sun of discernment.
Tamas is the darkness produced by the predominance of the quality of tamas. || 43 ||
He too he completely wiped away with the sun of his own inner mind,
which had arisen through perfect knowledge, just as soot is quickly removed by a breeze.
By his own mind, which was like a sun risen with perfect knowledge ignited by the manifestation of the qualities of sentient beings—that very form of the sun—he [illuminated] it. || 44 ||
When the darkness had ceased, he beheld that lovely mass of splendor,
like a lotus at the morning twilight when the nocturnal gloom has subsided.
To one who was intent on manifesting the virtues of sentient beings, there arose a delusion of a mass of splendor corresponding to that; thus it is said:
Like a young elephant, he tore up the forest of land-lotuses;
and like a vetāla, he drank the flood of blood with speed. (46)
Is it then that he devoured [the enemy] through the emergence of the quality of *rajas* and so forth, which is opposed to that [knowledge]? No; thus he says, "he drank" (*apibat*).
The meaning is that he consumed [the enemy] by subverting him through the vision of the reality of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-tattva*). "A flood of blood" (*asṛkpūram*) refers to a stream of blood.
Because fire is red in color, there is a comparison with blood. || 46 ||
When his vital heat had subsided, the mind of that sage,
reeling like a night-lotus, fell into sleep as if it were unsteady or intoxicated.

He describes the sinking into sleep resulting from the dissolution of the mind—which had been set in motion by passion (rajas)—due to its failure to find an object: "Or like one intoxicated by wine. (47)
Like a serpent to a garland of clouds, like the sun to a night-blooming blue lotus pond, or like the hot-rayed sun to the night, he swiftly tore that [bow] as well.
By the word *vyāla*, which is a synonym for a serpent or an elephant, a libertine or an elephant is indicated;
the sense is that he destroyed [it] through the awakening of discernment (*viveka*). || 48 ||
When his sleep had passed away, his mind contemplated those [clouds],
just as a creature with eyes as dark as the sky beholds the crests of peacocks in the firmament.
"One who perceives the sky as dark" (vyomaśyāmaladṛk) refers to a person who, when extending their gaze toward the sky in the direction of the sun's glare,
perceives [illusory objects] such as hair-tufts, water-bubbles, or the crests of peacocks; in that same manner, one should understand the mind.
The meaning is that he meditated upon the sky as having a form imagined through various latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 49 ||
Just as a rain cloud [cleanses] the *tāpiccha* tree, as the wind [dispels] the mist, and as a lamp [removes] darkness, he quickly wiped away that [impurity] from his pure self. (50)
The *tāpiccha* tree, that is, the *tamāla* flower, indeed withers by the rain and loses its dark hue;
yet even that sky, whose nature is pure and transparent, was cleansed by it. 50.
When consciousness in the void had perished— [there is also a reading "when consciousness was destroyed"]— his mind became deluded,
as if intoxicated by liquor once sleep had dissolved away.
"Deluded" means overcome by dejection. || 51 ||
This noble-minded man wiped away that delusion of his mind, just as the sun dispels the dullness produced by the night from the world. (52)
He wiped it, having cleansed and removed [the dust]. || 52 ||
Then, freed from radiance, darkness, sleep, delusion, and the like, the mind attained an indescribable state and rested for a moment. (53)

He rested—that is, he attained repose—in an indescribable state of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*) that transcends the range of words, for a moment, that is, for a brief duration. || 53 ||
Having quickly rested, O dear one, he attained consciousness of his universal form,
like the water of a lake dammed by a bridge returning to its own source against the current.

He says "having rested" because one does not attain stability therein due to the intensity of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of mental distraction (*vikṣepa*). "Aṅga" is a term of address. "Viśvarūpiṇīm" means having the same form as the external phenomenal world; "papāta" means she attained it—that is, the consciousness of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti-saṃvit*). [This refers to] that which was previously withdrawn from the external form and restrained within the Full Self.

Having turned back, he provides a corresponding illustration regarding the re-occurrence of external forms, beginning with the word "setu" (dam): Just as water from a lake, having entered a field through the opening of a canal and filled that field, is then blocked by a dam and turns back through the opening of the canal— flowing in reverse, against the current— it returns once more to its own source, the lake.
The meaning is that he enters in exactly that same manner. || 54 ||
Through the power of long-continued inquiry and from the tasting of his own consciousness,
he then attained the state of pure spirit, just as gold attains the form of an anklet.

He describes the attainment of conceptual meditative absorption (*savikalpaka-samādhi*) in the interval for one who, having turned away from external consciousness, is being led back toward self-consciousness— using the word "long" (*cira*) as follows: due to the cause of long-term continuous contemplation through prior meditation and so forth, and because of the tasting and experience of bliss within that meditative absorption (*samādhi*), by means of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, as the mind was being drawn back from that state, it attained a state of pure consciousness (*cinmayatā*)—the nature of a non-conceptual meditative absorption (*samādhi*) abounding in consciousness—in the interval. The meaning is that it is just as gold attains the form of an anklet corresponding to its suitability for a foot-bracelet. || 55 ||

Then, having completely abandoned its state as mind, the mind attained the nature of the true essence of consciousness (cittattva) and quickly became something entirely different, just like mud situated within a jar.

Thus, by means of conceptual meditation (*savikalpaka-samādhi*), [the mind], gradually wasting away like a fire without fuel or like milk mixed with water, attained a state of oneness with consciousness (*cidaikarasya*); so he says: "The state of the mind" (*cittatvam*).

Having completely abandoned its own state of being the mind (*cittatva*), it became something entirely different from its previous condition, having reached that reality which is pure consciousness itself.
The meaning is that it is just as when the mud from muddy water contained in a jar, upon the evaporation of the water, coats the jar and assumes the very nature of the jar itself. || 56 ||
Having completely abandoned the object of consciousness, the pure consciousness attained the state of universal consciousness,
just as the ocean, having abandoned distinctions such as waves and the like, becomes a single mass of water.

He says— “the object of thought” (cetyam)— that when the mind’s state as mind has departed, the consciousness that was its reflection attains oneness with the universal consciousness of the original image (bimba). Having completely abandoned the object of thought, which is its own manifestation in the form of a mental modification (vṛtti), it becomes pure as the reflected consciousness.

The meaning is that she attained the state of the universal witness-consciousness (sākṣicit-sāmānya-bhāva), which is common to all mental modifications; thus, "she whose single intellect" (ekadhīḥ) has become of one flavor (ekarasi-bhūtā), meaning her own limiting adjunct, the intellect, has reached such a state. || 57 ||
Having abandoned the mental conception of the multitude of elements, he then became the great sustainer of the universe;
thereafter, having attained awakening, he became the pure space of consciousness.

Thus, it demonstrates the direct realization of reality resulting from the maturation of Uddālaka’s establishment in non-conceptual samādhi, as well as the state of becoming Brahman shown in the scripture, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," by means of the verse beginning with "Having abandoned": thereafter, immediately following that, Uddālaka—of such a nature as that— [The rest of the passage continues: ...having abandoned all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding the internal and external, having abandoned all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and having abandoned all mental activity (*cittavṛtti*), he remained like a log of wood. Then, at that time, the sun set. Having thus become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the sun rose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the moon set. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the moon rose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the wind ceased. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the wind began to blow. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the fire was extinguished. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the fire blazed up. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the water dried up. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the water flowed. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the earth collapsed. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the earth became firm. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the body fell away. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the body arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the senses were withdrawn. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the senses emerged. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) ceased. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the vital breaths began to function. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the self (*ātman*) was dissolved. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the self arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the supreme Self (*paramātman*) was dissolved. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the supreme Self arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the universe occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the creation of the universe occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the night passed. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the day arrived. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the year passed. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the year arrived. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the world occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the creation of the world occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, death occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, birth occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, old age occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, youth occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, disease occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, health occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, pleasure occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, pain occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, happiness occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, sorrow occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, virtue occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, vice occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, knowledge occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, ignorance occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, liberation occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, bondage occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of all things occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the creation of all things occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the body occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the body arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the elements occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the elements arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the qualities (*guṇa*) occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the qualities arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the *māyā* occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the *māyā* arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the *avidyā* occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the *avidyā* arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the *tamas* occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the *tamas* arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the *rajas* occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the *rajas* arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the *sattva* occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the *sattva* arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the *prakṛti* occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the *prakṛti* arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the *puruṣa* occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the *puruṣa* arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the *liṅga* occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the *liṅga* arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the *avyakta* occurred. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the *avyakta* arose. Having become one whose mind was dissolved, he attained the supreme state. Then, at that time, the dissolution of the

Having attained the awakening of samādhi— the direct realization of reality— he became the pure, great space of consciousness (cidākāśa), which sustains the universe, is the substratum of the entire world, has abandoned all mental conceptions of the multitude of elements, and is devoid of the appearance of duality. || 58 ||
There he attained bliss, free from both the seen and the seeing, infinite and of supreme savor, like an ocean of elixir. (59)
He shows that the attainment of unsurpassed bliss occurs precisely through that state: "In that regard" (tatra).

It is called "the supreme relish" (uttamāsvāda) because it is tasted by the highest beings, such as Brahmā and others. It stands like an ocean, a receptacle or support for all "flavors" (rasa), which are the minute particles of happiness derived from all sense objects. || 59 ||
Having descended from his body to a certain spot on the earth,
he, whose nature is the universal form of pure existence (sattāsāmānya), became an ocean of bliss.
He describes that very state with the words beginning "from the body" (śarīrāt): having completely cast off from the body, he has emerged as it were; that is to say, he is purified. || 60 ||
This swan of the consciousness of the twice-born, dwelling in the lake of bliss,
remained in the sky as clear as autumn, like the moon full of its digits.
Uḍupa means the moon. || 61 ||
He became like a lamp sheltered from the wind, resembling a figure depicted in a painting;
he was like an ocean devoid of waves, with a stillness like that of a rain-stilled and silent cloud.
Its condition is like that of a cloud which rained previously, but later in autumn becomes mute and devoid of water.
Then, while staying in that great world for a long time, Uddālaka beheld many sky-faring Siddhas and even gods.

This shows that one who has ascended to that state does not look even with a sidelong glance, much less by lowering his feet, at the hosts of perfected beings (siddhas) who pray for his favor as far as the world of Brahmā; this is indicated by the words beginning with "atha. || 63 ||
Various nets of supernatural powers arrived from all sides,
bestowing the status of Indra and the Sun, and were densely crowded with throngs of celestial nymphs.
That twice-born man, profound in intellect and unperturbed, paid no heed to those multitudes of supernatural powers, just as one disregards the playful antics of childhood.
Disregarding the caravan of supernatural powers (siddhis), he then remained for six months in that temple of bliss, like the sun upon the northern horizon.

In that temple of bliss, within such a state of meditative absorption (samādhi), he remained for six months like the sun on the northern horizon, the quarter based upon the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa). || 66 ||
O twice-born one, as long as he had not yet attained that state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta),
the Siddhas, Suras, Sādhyas, and the gods beginning with Brahmā and Hara remained there.
Each subsequent stage is more excellent than the preceding, culminating in the establishment on the seventh bhūmi. "Suras" refers to the gods; "siddhas" are a specific class of divine beings;

"sādhyas" are the deities of the Gaṇas. Their separate mention from the general category of "surās" follows the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (where the specific is distinguished from the general). 67.
Having transformed [the mind] into bliss, he reached the state beyond bliss;
neither in bliss nor in the absence of bliss did that consciousness then manifest.

And because that bliss (*ānanda*) is empty of the transformation of the mind characterized by the tasting of flavor, he has reached— that is, attained— the state of *anānanda*, a term analyzed as "one for whom this bliss does not exist. Therefore, for that reason, his consciousness— the sentience of the Self— did not shine like the trivial bliss of sense-objects, nor did it shine in the pain of the blissless state.
Rather, the meaning is that he remained established in the fullness of the single essence of self-luminosity. || 68 ||
Having found a stable state there for either a moment or a thousand years, the mind finds no pleasure in a flood of enjoyments, just as one who has seen heaven finds no delight in the earth.

He says "for a moment" to show that once that [state] is attained, there is no further arising of desire for petty pleasures: "A man who has seen heaven"—that is, one who has experienced the splendor of the celestial realm—[has no longing] for the earth, meaning for the happiness of the world of mortals. (69)
That is the state, that is the peaceful goal; that is the supreme good, eternal and auspicious.
For one who has attained rest therein, delusion no longer afflicts them again. (70)
He describes that very [state] as the most excellent with the words beginning "That" (tad) and so forth. || 70 ||
Having attained that state, the virtuous do not return again to this perception of the visible world, just as those who have reached the Caitraratha grove do not return to a garden of khadira trees.
Having attained that state of great bliss from their own minds, embodied beings no longer value the visible world, just as kings disregard wretchedness.

Having attained—that is, having reached through direct perception—from the mind refined by hearing (śravaṇa), reflection (manana), and meditative concentration (samādhi); or, according to the reading "from knowledge" (vittāt), from the scripture that has been investigated. || 72 ||
O sinless one, when the mind rests in that state, having realized the nature of the visible world,
it either attains a realization free from affliction, or rather, it does not attain [any such realization] at all.
The awakened mind, having been subjected to hardship during the states of perception and the states of meditative absorption and emergence,
attains awakening for others through great effort on the sixth stage; however, it does not attain it at all on the seventh stage.
Having dwelt there for six months, Uddālaka cast far away the realm of supernatural powers; he emerged like the sun from the womb of the clouds at the onset of spring.
From the interior of the clouds, from the mass of mist; in the spring month of Caitra. || 74 ||
With his soul fully awakened, he again beheld those beings of supreme splendor, who were eager to offer salutations, affectionate, and possessed bodies like the orb of the moon. (75)
The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: "She saw again the very same beautiful women and the successions of celestial chariots that she had seen before."
There were successions of celestial chariots, delightful with fly-whisks made of bees and the pollen of white mandāra flowers,
and adorned with fluttering clusters of banners.

"Those [trees] which are covered with the pollen of white mandāra flowers, those upon which bees and chowries shimmer, and those upon which clusters of banners flutter"—these are common epithets. (76)
[He saw] sages such as ourselves, whose lotus-hands were marked by the sacred grass *darbha*,
as well as lords of the Vidyādharas surrounded by Vidyādharī women.
"He also saw the lords of the Vidyādharas"—this is drawn forward [from the previous verse]. || 77 ||
They spoke thus to that high-souled sage Uddālaka:
"O Blessed One, look upon us with favor through your grace."
Those celestial beings and sages said to Uddalaka: "O Blessed One, look upon us with favor through your grace, with a compassionate gaze. || 78 ||
"Ascend this celestial chariot and come to the city of the Thirty-three;
for heaven alone is the ultimate limit of all worldly enjoyments and prosperity. (79)
"Come, come!"—they state the reason for not disregarding heaven: "In heaven itself... (79).
O Lord, enjoy for an entire kalpa the desired pleasures that are appropriate for you;
indeed, all ritual acts of austerity are solely for the sake of enjoying the fruits such as heaven.

"Until the end of the kalpa," meaning until the time of destruction at the conclusion of two parārdhas. By this very [attainment], they say that the austerity, hardship, and so forth of all [practitioners] have become meaningful—referring to "heaven and so forth. (80)
Behold these excellent women of the Vidyādharas, bearing necklaces and chowries, as they attend upon you like female elephants attending a male elephant.
Desire is the essence of both dharma and artha; women of excellent character have desire as their essence, and they become like the very heaven itself, just as blossoms are to the spring.
Because dharma and artha are the fruits [of the Vedas], they constitute the essence. || 82 ||
Having thus addressed all his guests, the sage honored them according to tradition and remained composed, free from agitation.
He remained in such a state that all agitation had vanished and his curiosity was gone due to his certain conviction regarding false views and the like.
That man of steady intellect neither rejoiced in nor abandoned that prosperity;
saying, "O Siddhas, depart," he became intent upon his own duties.
His own activity was meditative concentration; he became intent upon that. || 84 ||
Then, after attending upon him—who was devoted to his own duty and had attained a lack of interest in worldly enjoyments—the Siddhas themselves departed within a few days. (85)
Having worshipped him by means of prostrations, praises, and other honors, one should serve him after waiting for a long time. || 85 ||
And that sage, liberated while living, wandered at his pleasure as long as he desired through the forest regions and the hermitages of the sages.
On the peaks of Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Himavat, and Vindhya;
on the islands, groves, cardinal directions, thickets, jungles, and forest lands. (87)
From that time forward, the twice-born Uddālaka, having attained his goal,
dwelt in the caves within the recesses of mountains, living like a firefly.

He dwelt in such a way that he had attained the state [of liberation]. By the phrase "with the play of meditation," it is indicated that even meditation was merely his play; there was nothing further for him to accomplish through it. || 88 ||
Sometimes after a day, sometimes after a month, sometimes after a year,
and sometimes after a multitude of years, he, absorbed in meditation, awoke.
Attached to meditation, he has ascended into samādhi. || 89 ||
From that time forward, although Uddālaka was engaged in worldly affairs,
he remained perfectly composed, having attained oneness with the essence of consciousness.
The meaning is that even at the time of legal proceedings, he remains perfectly composed and is not distracted like one who is ignorant. || 90 ||
Through the intense practice of the singular essence of consciousness, he attained the state of the Great Mind (mahācitta) and became,
everywhere and in all things, like the solar radiance upon the earth.

The essence of consciousness (*cittattva*) is the pure consciousness that witnesses the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and its modifications; it is that very [consciousness] which, through the practice of ascending samādhi characterized by a continuous stream of discerning vision, becomes the Great Consciousness (*mahācitta*), which is undivided. It is "equal" (*sama*) because of the abandonment of attachment and aversion, due to compassion, and because of perceiving the state of Brahman as uniform. By this, its...
It has been stated that, in due order, there is the attainment of the sixth stage from the fifth stage. || 91 ||
Through long practice of the universal consciousness, having attained the universal existence,
he neither sets nor rises in this visible world, like the sun in a painting.

Next, he shows his rest in the seventh stage: "Citsāmānya... (Universal Consciousness). When the visible world and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are completely eradicated, even the conventional usage of "mind" (*citta*), which is characterized by the manifestation of those [objects], ceases; thus, there remains only self-luminous, supreme bliss.

The meaning is this: one should not undergo rising and setting, characterized by manifestation and disappearance, as shown in such scriptural passages as, "Having arisen from these visible elements, it perishes after them;
there is no consciousness after death," because of the absolute eradication of the seeds of that [ignorance], namely ignorance, desire, action, and latent impressions (vāsanā). || 92 ||
With a mind thoroughly stilled through the attainment of the supreme state of peace,
the bonds of birth dissolved (or, according to another reading, destroyed), and the oscillation of doubt exhausted,
he is like the autumnal sky— tranquil, vast, and radiant.
He clearly assumed that stainless, mindless body.

Expanding upon this very state, he concludes with the word *śameti*: "He whose mind is perfectly stilled and dissolved through the cessation of all distractions and the attainment of the supreme state consisting of unsurpassed bliss; and for this very reason, because the seeds of all karma have perished, his bond of rebirth has been dissolved."

Having become one for whom the states of the swing of doubt—[the reading "saṃdeha-dolā" is also found]—have been exhausted, he is like the autumnal sky: tranquil, with the tumultuous clouds of ignorance completely stilled;
vast and therefore undivided.

Because it was unrestrained and vast, because it possessed the excellence of unsurpassed existence, manifestation, and bliss, and because it was free from all veils, that body—having attained the nature of Brahman—became "mindless" (acetasaḥ) due to the complete forgetting of its former state; thus it assumed its true form, not the same exuberant body it had previously as Uddālaka. This is the meaning. || 93 ||

Thus ends the fifty-fourth canto, titled "The Resting of Uddālaka," in the Section on Tranquility (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) within the Means to Liberation (*mokṣopāya*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the lineage of the Seers (*ārṣa*). 54.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Resting of Uddālaka," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-fifth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
O sole sun for the day of self-knowledge, O forest fire for the grass of my doubts!
O Lord, is the moon that cools the fire of ignorance the universal existence (sattāsāmānya)? || 1 ||
The process of abandoning the body through reasoning, characterized by the universal mark of existence,
as well as the fashioning of ornaments for Khiṅkhiṇī by one who has cast off the body, is described here.
Having propitiated the Guru with hymns of praise, Rāma, desiring to know the nature of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) expressed in the final verse, asks— "O Knower of the Self"— and so forth.
[He addresses him as] the "cool-rayed one" (śītāṃśuḥ) for the burning and torment characterized by the threefold affliction caused by ignorance.

The intended meaning of the three epithets is this: you alone are capable of destroying the darkness of ignorance, destroying the doubt and error induced by that [ignorance], and destroying all suffering induced by that [ignorance].
The expression "O Lord" (Īśa) is used to indicate that one must always maintain the vision of the Guru as the Lord, and not regard him with an ordinary perception.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the mind is completely dissolved through the contemplation of absolute non-existence, then there arises the state of universal existence belonging to that which is the nature of universal consciousness.

On the sixth stage, having polished away the internal distinctions of consciousness (*cit*) through the intense cultivation of the absence of objects of cognition— which constitutes the very nature of universal consciousness— when the mind is utterly exhausted upon the absolute destruction of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of objects, that which remains is established by itself through its own mere existence.
The meaning is that the very existence (sattā) which inheres in both consciousness (cit) and the unconscious (acit) is the universal existence (sattāsāmānya). || 2 ||
When consciousness, devoid of the "this-ness" aspect, dissolves into itself,
it then becomes the utterly transparent generality of existence (sattāsāmānyatā), appearing as if it were non-existent.

When consciousness (cit), which is reflected in all mental modifications (vṛtti), remains free from the objective portions—the modifications and their objects—upon the sublation of all that is perceivable, it merges into its own self, the original image-consciousness (bimba-caitanya). At that time, its existence should be understood as the "sattāsāmānyatā" (the state of pure being-in-general), which is as utterly transparent as space (ākāśa) because it possesses a nature devoid of unreality (asadrūpa) within that original image. This is the meaning. || 3 ||
When the mind dwells having negated all this— whatever exists, including the internal and external aspects— then it abides in the state of pure universal existence.
The mind (cetas) is the undivided consciousness manifested through the modifications of the intellect (citta-vṛtti). || 4 ||
When all objects of perception are experienced as the universal existence (sattāsāmānya),
appearing as their own nature through their own nature, that is the state of universal existence.

When all beings, by their own ultimate nature, become pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)— that is, the residual awareness whose very essence is the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*), whose manifestation is its own form, and which has no other appearance— then,
like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs, the objects of perception dissolve into the Self by means of the Self.
When they are indeed not cultivated, that is the state of their commonality as mere existence. || 6 ||
The meaning is that they are "uncultivated," which is to say, they are perceived as innate even without the effort of cultivation. || 6 ||
For this supreme vision, resembling the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), is indeed possible at all times for both those with bodies and those without bodies who are liberated.

Since this vision of one who has ascended to the seventh stage is comparable to the state beyond the fourth [dhyāna], the meaning is that there is no difference in the abiding nature between those with a body and those liberated from the body. || 7 ||
O sinless one, this [state] occurs for both the one who has emerged from meditation and the one established in samādhi;
it belongs solely to the wise man and does not belong to the ignorant one, for it is born of awakening.

This vision belongs to one established in meditative absorption even on the fifth and subsequent stages, but it belongs to one who has ascended to the seventh stage even when emerged from meditation. The meaning is simply that it does not belong to the ignorant at all.
All those of great soul who abide in this vision are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
They were like perfected elixirs upon the earth, or like the winds in the path of the sky.

The meaning is that all those who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta), remaining established in this vision, stand upon this earth like perfected alchemical elixirs such as mercury and the like, or like winds in the celestial path, untouched by the dust of craving for worldly and otherworldly enjoyments. || 9 ||
O Raghava, all of us beginning with myself, as well as Narada and others,
and Brahma, Vishnu, Ishvara, and the rest, have been seen established within this state.

He cites those very examples: "beginning with us" (*asmatprabhṛtayaḥ*). This means that on earth there are Nārada and others; in the path of the sky, Brahmā and others; and in the worlds above that, [others]. || 10 ||
Having taken recourse to this path that destroys all fear,
Uddālaka dwelt in the house of the world for as long as he desired.
As long as one desires, until the exhaustion of prārabdha karma. || 11 ||
Then, after a long time, a firm resolve arose in him:
"I shall remain liberated from the body (videhamukta) once I have cast off this physical frame. || 12 ||
"Immovable" means firm. || 12 ||
Having thought thus, he remained upon a seat of young leaves within a mountain cave,
seated in the lotus posture with his eyes half-closed.
He reflected, possessing a firm resolve regarding the object of his thought.
Restraining the nine gates of the mind by the suppression of the anus, and investigating the contacts of the sense-objects, he whose wealth of consciousness is cultivated within his own limbs; (14)

Discerning the contacts of the senses— the functions directed toward objects such as sound and touch— and withdrawing them one by one like jujube fruits, he places them within his heart; and having placed them there, he— whose nature is consciousness, who has become dense with the cultivated form of ultimate reality— unifies them with his own self as if they were his own limbs.
By whom [the world] is of a single flavor, like a mass of rock salt. || 14 ||
With the vital breaths restrained, the neck held in a balanced posture, the root of the tongue pressed against the base of the palate, and the face radiant. || 15 ||

His neck is symmetrical in its proportions; his face shines with an appearance of being uplifted by the root of the tongue, which is fixed like a door-panel within the cavity of the throat and attached to the base of the palate. 15.
With the mind and gaze focused neither externally nor internally, neither below nor above, neither on an object nor in emptiness, he remains without touching his teeth with his teeth. (16)
Regarding the object, which is the domain of form and so forth; he by whom the mind and views have not been joined [to it]. 16.
O dear one, he whose facial complexion is as clear as the cessation of the flow of vital breath, and whose body is characterized by the awakening of consciousness and the bristling of his hair; 17.

By the restraint of the flows of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, he is devoid of the restlessness of body, mind, and senses produced by all activities; his facial complexion is clear and his countenance is serene. "O dear one" (*aṅga*) is used as a term of address. Through consciousness (*cit-saṃvit*), that is, by the experience of the bliss of Brahman which is of the nature of consciousness.
His body was bristling, with its hair standing erect and upright like thorns. || 17 ||
Through the practice of the consciousness of the limbs, he attained the universal consciousness;
from that practice, he reached the supreme vibration of inner bliss.
Regarding the manifestation of bliss in that [state], he states the previously mentioned sequence itself, beginning with "aṅge" (in the limbs):

consciousness (*cit*), reflected in the various modifications (*vṛtti-bheda*) of the internal organ which constitute its parts, is limited by those very modifications that serve as its own adjuncts (*upādhi*). And by that consciousness...
Through the practice of dissolution, he took hold of and entered the universal consciousness (citsāmānya) which serves as the archetype (bimba).

And through the practice of contemplating that pure consciousness which serves as the archetype, he attained—that is, experienced—the supreme, most excellent vibration of bliss (ānandaspanda) within his heart. || 18 ||

Then, through the relishing of that [bliss], the universal sustainer, whose nature is infinite, attained the state of the commonality of existence—the sequence of the general condition of the withdrawn mind. (19)
Regarding this, he describes the entry into the generality of existence (*sattāsāmānya*) as before: "by means of relishing that" (*tadāsvādanataḥ*).

As long as there is no relishing of unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*), the mind continues to function outwardly due to its inability to endure the affliction of cessation (*nirodhakleśa*). However, once bliss has been relished, by the analogy of the ant and the jaggery (*guḍapipīlikanyāya*), the mind becomes attached to that very [bliss] and [loses interest in] its own true nature (*svarūpa*).

Having forgotten its own inherent universal consciousness (*citsāmānya*), it leads [the individual] to the state of the universal existence (*sattāsāmānyabhāva*) which is unsurpassed self-luminosity; this is the meaning: that very dissolution of the sequence of the state of universal consciousness is its attainment of universal existence. || 19 ||

He remained with his physical form perfectly balanced, having attained supreme repose; the radiance of his face was utterly charming, filled with a bliss equal to that which is beyond all worldly joy.

In that very context, he describes his state as one from which there is no return, saying "He stood" (*tasthau*). His *ābhoga*—his essential nature—is equal even toward equals, being devoid of the inequality of ultimate distraction.
Furthermore, because his bliss is such that no other joys are equal to it, and because of its supreme clarity, he stands even above those who are charming and beautiful.
Being one whose splendor of the face is charming (mugdhā). || 20 ||

With the horripilation of perfectly tranquil bliss, having attained the stainless state, he has gone where the delusion of worldly existence—consisting of thought-constructs and the like—has been utterly exhausted over a long period of time. (21)
He describes the gradual cessation even of the signs such as the manifestation of bliss and horripilation with the words "completely stilled" (saṃśānta):
having attained the state while still living, and having become stainless through the destruction of the remainder of impurities that cause the experience of *prārabdha* karma.
That Great Being became like a figure fixed in a painting;
he was equal to the spotless autumnal moon when it is one digit short of fullness.
By means of the digits [of the moon] that are full. || 22 ||
In a few days, he gradually became tranquil in his own stainless self,
like the sap of a tree at the end of autumn in a pure state.
In the solar heat, one transcends the period of birth. || 23 ||

In accordance with the scriptural statement, "His vital breaths do not depart; they are merged right here," he says "they subsided" (upaśaśāma), intending that his vital breaths were gradually extinguished right there, like the heat of hot water. At the end of autumn, in winter, the sap of the trees [subsides] in their own pure state, as does the power of the sun's rays.
It was pacified. || 23 ||
With all conceptual constructions gone, changeless and delightful, his form liberated from the limiting adjuncts of every manifestation of impurity—
he attained that primordial bliss in which all pleasure has dissolved.
The fortune of Indra is carried away like a blade of grass in a mass of water. || 24 ||
He describes the nature of that which remains when the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth have subsided, beginning with the words "gone" (*gata*),

etc. That which is primordial, beyond the reach of speech, and from which the pleasures of objects ending with those of Hiranyagarbha have fallen away— that is, have been emitted like sparks from a fire— [is that which remains].
He attained that bliss in which even the splendor of Śakra is carried away like a blade of grass in the ocean—
[the phrase "ādye sa uhyate" is to be parsed as "ādye saḥ uhyate"]— meaning it is swept away or considered by those who perceive it.

Immeasurable, pervading the interior of space and pervading all directions, full, possessing the nature of sustaining the worlds, served by many fortunate beings, beyond description and qualities, the primordial truth and bliss—
That brahmin became one who possesses infinite and supreme bliss.

This Brahmin Uddālaka has the nature of pervading not only the countless and infinite spaces that exist within his own belly—spaces which differ in every universe—but also those very quarters of space; by this, the limitation imposed by spatial boundaries is rejected. He is ever-full in all things at all times.
His nature is the supporting, sustaining, and nourishing of all things, substrata, and worlds.
By this statement of being the substrate of all, the distinction based on substantial entities is refuted.
He is to be served by many fortunate and excellent persons, and he possesses the quality of discourse.

The meaning is that he became the supreme bliss called the Infinite (bhūman), characterized by bliss because it gladdens—that is, it renders everything one with the essence of happiness—and which transcends those dharmas that are the causes for the activity of speech; which is infinite and beginningless; which is devoid of limitations imposed by time; and for that very reason, possesses characteristics such as truth. || 25 ||
Once his mind had attained its primordial state of purity,
the body of the twice-born remained seated for six months;
scorched by the rays of the sun and made resonant with the whistling of the wind, it became beautiful.
Her slender arms became the strings, and the mountain itself became the lute. || 26 ||
Then, when that [soul] had attained the primordial state— the pure nature and stainless essence—

within the living being (jīva), the body of that twice-born man, while remaining seated right there, became parched after being scorched for six months by the rays of the sun; it became beautiful with the tinkling sounds produced by the friction of the blowing winds against its exceedingly slender limbs.

With her veins acting as strings suitable for playing upon her arms, which were characterized by the marks of tender trees, she became the cause of delight like a lute belonging to the mountain—this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 26 ||
Then, after a considerable time, the Mothers, accompanied by the daughters of the mountain, descended from the sky to that ground of the mountain; indeed,
they all arrived together for the sake of attaining their desired fruits.
Like rows of flames, they have tawny hair. || 27 ||

Then, after a much longer time— specifically six months— the following occurred: from the surface of the sky, all the Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, remained ever united and joined together, accompanied by their consorts, due to the necessity of their mutual association.
For the sake of accomplishing the desired fruit for a certain devotee, rows of crests—flames—descended upon that ground of Mount Tāma like fire itself. || 27 ||
The skeleton of the Brahmin, dried by the rays of the sun,
was suddenly placed upon the tip of her crown between the sword and the skull-topped staff;
she is the goddess Khiṃkhinī, worshipped by all the gods.
At night, having assumed a fresh form, she took on the splendor of her beloved.

Among those Mothers, she who at night possesses ever-new dances such as the *lāsya* characterized by the variety of ever-fresh ornaments; she who is to be saluted by all the gods beginning with Brahmā;
the goddess of even the gods, worthy of worship; *Khiṅkhiṇī*, that is, Cāmuṇḍā; [she who is] dried by the rays of the sun.

The meaning is that he instantly made the skeleton of the Brahmin Uddālaka— an ornament of lovely luster— his own crest-ornament on the tip of his crown, positioned in the space between his raised sword and skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga). || 28 ||
Thus, upon the body of Uddālaka, which is adorned with clusters of shimmering peacock feathers,
tossed by the waves of the ocean, and entwined with fresh garlands of Mandāra flowers,
the great goddess Khiṅkhiṇikā lies, the very ornament of playful grace upon the creeper.
Like a bee in a net, it subsequently enters into the midst of the mass of flowers. || 29 ||

Since even the gross body, composed of impurities, flesh, and so forth—which is imagined by those of deluded vision—has attained supreme excellence as an ornament upon the head of the Goddess who is worshipped by the three worlds, what more need be said about the attainment of the most exalted state [by one who possesses true knowledge]? Thus, demonstrating the excellence of the majesty of knowledge, he says: "Thus" (iti). Thus.
In the manner described, Uddālaka’s wretched body (*dehaka*) shines forth beautifully (*suvilasati*),
amidst a mass of peacock feathers (*māyūrabarhavrajāḥ*) that is characterized by shimmering, trembling fragments of clouds (*vyālolābdalavāḥ*),
and is encircled (*vivalite*) by clusters of fresh (*navaiḥ*) garlands of *mandāra* flowers.

On the crest-ornament garland—the beautiful head-adornment of the great Goddess known as Khiṅkhinikā—for the sake of her play, there are clusters of flowers at its ends, that is, at the front portions; upon the network of creepers that follows behind, as if in the guise of a braid, he rests, enjoying a state of peaceful repose, like a bee—such is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 29 ||
This creeper of the mental fluctuations of Uddālaka has spread through the forest of his heart, its blossoms radiant with the expansion of the innate bliss flashing forth from discernment.
He upon whom [the tree] has once taken root, even while wandering, does not suffer separation from its beautiful shade; rather, he attains a most exalted union with it that is truly fruitful.

Concluding the narrative of Uddālaka, he demonstrates that for those devoted to its constant study, there is the cessation of the heat of saṃsāra and the attainment of the fruit of the supreme human goal, by saying: "This...
That very self-bliss which shines forth in the discernment of all objects of perception is itself the blossoming flowers that illuminate.

Such is this training— characterized by diligence and continuity— which was demonstrated in the manner described for Uddālaka’s mental state (*cittavṛtti*), whose entire life culminated in the attainment of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*). [The reading "uddālake cittavṛtteḥ" is also found.]

That person in whose heart-forest the wish-fulfilling creeper has taken root and, having manifested, has spread forth by way of ascending through ever-higher stages— even while wandering and moving about in the forest of worldly activity, which is crowded with the suns of the three-fold suffering— remains [cool] by means of that creeper, fragrant and cool with virtues such as truthfulness, peace, and self-restraint.

By means of the shadow characterized by innate contentment—the particle *eva* being used in the sense of "even"—it never at any time undergoes separation; that is, it certainly does not attain such separation. Furthermore, it attains union with the fruit of liberation, which is the highest of all and free from rebirth, through its own essential nature; therefore, that creeper must necessarily exist.
The meaning is that it should be planted in the heart and then expanded. || 30 ||

Thus ends the fifty-fifth canto, titled "The Liberation of Uddālaka," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki and spoken by the Divine Messenger. 55.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Uddālaka," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The fifty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Wandering in this manner and investigating the self by means of the self, [one attains liberation].
O lotus-eyed one, find rest in the expansive state.
Having rubbed away the darkness of illusion, awakened, and destroyed all latent tendencies, one is said to be established in samādhi even while engaged in worldly activity. (1)
Dwelling by means of this aforementioned method, through the sequence of practice consisting of discernment, dispassion, and meditative concentration. || 1 ||
One should investigate with the mind, guided by the scriptures and their meaning,
for as long as it takes to attain that state through the practice of dissolving all objects of perception.

The essential meaning is that, through hearing the scriptures, investigating the reality of the meaning, trusting the words of the guru, and purifying one's own mind, one must necessarily engage in inquiry until reaching the ultimate repose in the supreme state, which culminates in the sublation of all perceived objects. || 2 ||
Through the stages consisting of dispassion, practice, the meaning of the scriptures, wisdom, and the guru—
[the reading "guru-yama-krama" is also found; in that case, by the word *yama*, the restraint of the mind is to be understood].
Or rather, the meritorious state is attained through wisdom alone. || 3 ||
An intellect that is fully awakened, sharp,
and free from blemish attains the eternal state, even if it lacks all other favorable conditions.
He states the essential nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) as "possessing perfect awakening. It attains [the goal] and causes [others] to attain it. || 4 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, is there anyone who, having attained samādhi, remains as if awakened and at rest even while engaged in worldly activity? (5)
The grammatical construction is as follows: a certain awakened person, even while engaged in worldly activity, is at rest as if one who has attained meditative absorption (samādhi). || 5 ||
Someone else, having resorted to solitude, remains fixed in meditative concentration.
O Blessed One, tell me which of these two is superior.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For one who perceives this collection of qualities as not being the self,
that inner coolness which arises is called samādhi.

The meaning is that inner coolness and the fulfillment of all desires are the fruit established in knowledge; upon its attainment, because there is no possibility of distraction, that very state is designated as *samādhi*. The meaning is that one must resolve: "While the mind exists, there may be a connection with objects of perception that causes distraction, but for me, that [mind] does not exist. || 7 ||
Having determined that the connection with visible objects resides in the mind,
