one person remains engaged in worldly affairs, while another is established in meditation.
The reading "dṛśyair manana-sambandhaḥ" (the connection of the mind with the objects of perception) is indeed quite clear. || 8 ||
O Rāma, these two are happy within if they are cool at heart (or, according to another reading, "if they have attained perfection").
That which is inner coolness is the fruit of infinite austerity.
If the mind of one established in the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is still flickering with mental activity,
then that concentration of his is equal to the frantic dancing of a madman.
If the mind of one engaged in the frantic dance of madness has its latent impressions (vāsanā) exhausted,
then that madman’s conduct is equal to the meditative absorption (samādhi) of a Buddha.
The one who is awakened while engaged in worldly affairs and the one who is awakened while dwelling in the forest—these two are truly equal; they have undoubtedly attained the same state.
The meaning is that they have reached the supreme state which undoubtedly cuts through all doubts and are firmly established therein.
(12) Even while acting, this mind has its latent impressions attenuated and acts as a non-doer, just as a person whose mind is far away does not truly engage when listening to a story. (13)

To the question, "Could there not be bondage for the worldly agent caused by that very agency?", he says: "The non-agent" (akartr). This refers to one whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have become thin or who is free from impressions (*nirvāsana*). Just as when listening to stories of a beloved woman or the like, even while engaged in other activities, because no modification such as passion arises, one is not bound by the defects associated with those [emotions].
The meaning is "in that same way. || 13 ||
Even while not acting, the mind acts as if it were doing so when its latent impressions (vāsanā) are intense,
just as one whose limbs are motionless in a dream feels as if they are standing on the edge of a precipice.
Even though his limbs—the parts of the body—are motionless, the mind of one who is thus asleep acts just as it does when falling into a pit or remaining there. || 14 ||
That which is the non-agency of the mind is the supreme concentration;
know that to be the state of absolute liberation, that auspicious and highest nirvana. || 15 ||
Nirvṛti is the rest of happiness. || 15 ||
The mind's state of being restless or steady is considered the supreme cause; therefore, by means of meditation and non-meditation, make that very mind free from the sprout of desire.

In the meditations and non-meditations, there are concentrations and non-concentrations regarding those two views; "without sprout" means, that is to say, empty of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the seeds of sprouts. || 16 ||
That very mental meditation (manodhyāna) is said to be unwavering and steady;
it is indeed the state of absolute liberation (kevalībhāva) and that which is eternal peace itself. 17.
It is said that the mind with subtle latent impressions (vāsanā) strives for the highest state; therefore, by making the mind free from latent impressions, the state of the agent is attained. 18.

"Thinly perfumed" refers to the state where latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are being attenuated in the fourth and subsequent stages; "unperfumed" refers to the state where impressions have been exhausted, which is the station established in the seventh stage. (18)
This mind, dense with latent impressions (vāsanā), is the vessel for agency and the source of all suffering; therefore, one should bring those impressions to attenuation.
That by which the self becomes established in its own nature—remaining within the world yet tranquil, with sorrow, fear, and desire removed—is known as *samādhi*. (20)
He for whom attachment, egoism, possessiveness, and dogmatic clinging toward the visible world of the body and so forth have been stilled;
by what means does he become established in his own true nature? || 20 ||
Having completely renounced with your mind the notion of selfhood regarding all things,
remain as you are— whether on a mountain or in a house.
In all things, one should cultivate the realization of the Self, free from the superimposition of "I" and "mine," whether remaining concentrated on a mountain or engaged in worldly activity at home.
For those householders whose minds are well-composed and whose faults of egoism have been stilled, the home itself is like the solitary forest lands.
For you whose minds and vision are composed, the forest dwelling is equal [to any other],
just as it is for great beings among all living creatures here.

Here, in this inner self (pratyagātman) which is eternally immediate, [there is the dissolution] of the great elements that abide within it, just as [all things dissolve] into the ether and other elements. || 23 ||
O Prince, even though the great cloud of his peaceful mind was present, the cities— though ablaze with the fires of the people— and even the forests became desolate.
The meaning is: of one whose great cloud-like mind is peaceful, resembling the autumnal sky. || 24 ||

O slayer of enemy heroes, even forests devoid of people seem crowded to one whose mind is intoxicated by worldly existence, while cities filled with great multitudes appear empty to one who has attained right conduct.
Of one intoxicated by the mind which possesses the activity of passion and so forth. || 25 ||
The mind that has emerged from its state reaches the end of delusion and attains deep sleep;
it then enters nirvāṇa—nirvāṇa indeed! Do as you wish.

The mind that has emerged from samādhi and is distracted by passion and the like enters a state of deep sleep (suṣuptatā), which serves as the seed for thousands of future emergences through the internal dissolution of its various fluctuations regarding diverse objects. However, the mind whose latent impressions of passion and the like have been extinguished attains nirvāṇa, which is liberation. || 26 ||
He who always perceives the Self as transcending all states of existence and yet as being the essence of all states of existence is said to be composed in meditative absorption (samāhita). || 27 ||

If so, how is it that the same state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) was previously said to belong equally to both the one who engages in worldly activity and the one who does not, provided they are knowers of reality?
To this he replies with the word "all": In the meditative absorption of the knower of reality, he perceives that which transcends all states of being;

yet in worldly activity, he perceives that which consists of all states of being. Because there is no sense of ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) even with a single lump [of matter], there is no passion or the like in him.
The meaning is that there is no possibility of distraction. || 27 ||
He for whom the desirable and the undesirable have perished, whose internal form is expanded, and to whom all states of being are equal— he is called one who is composed in meditation (samāhita).
He states the same point in terms of its result: "In what is desired... etc. Desires and aversions are [respectively] toward what is sought and what is not sought. (28)
O Lord of Men, the mind perceives this world as being truly existent through its own nature of existence;
it is exactly as it is in a dream, so too in this waking state.

He demonstrates how all things are equal by saying, "as being of the nature of existence" (sadātmanā). Just as his mind perceives this visible world as truly existent (sat) through its own nature of existence even in the waking state, just as it does in a dream; the meaning is that he does not perceive the world as having a form distinct from existence. || 29 ||

Just as those who live in the light of a marketplace are equal to those in a state of non-existence due to their lack of connection [to reality], so too, for the wise man, even a village is like a forest because of its lack of connection [to worldly concerns]. 30.
He establishes what was stated—that even cities are empty—with the words "Just as... (yathā).

Although many people are gathered there in the marketplaces (vipaṇikā), which are rows of stalls for goods, they are, despite being occupied with their respective affairs, as good as non-existent because they are indifferent and offer no assistance; it is just like that. || 30 ||
With his mind always turned inward, the awakened one, even while walking, remains as if asleep;
he beholds the city, the countryside, and the village as if they were a forest.
Everything becomes like space due to its constant inward orientation;
this world, agitated by the elements, is entirely useless in every respect.
Even though it is crowded with elemental beings such as the earth and so forth, it attains the state of space—that is, emptiness—because it is not obstructed by them. || 32 ||
But once inner coolness has been attained, the world becomes cool for those who are free from fever, lasting as long as life endures. (33)
As long as life lasts; for as long as one lives. || 33 ||
For all living beings tormented by internal thirst, this world becomes like a forest fire; for that which exists within is situated without.
The meaning is that because the mind is internally heated or cooled in whatever manner, it exists externally in the form of the world. || 34 ||
Day, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions are like external portions of the reality of the internal organ. (35)
He says that very thing: "The sky," etc. (35).
Just as the seed of a banyan tree contains within it the future banyan tree, so that which exists eternally within the Self manifests externally in radiant expansion, like the fragrance of a flower.
Nothing exists anywhere that is external, nor anything that is internal (though some read "na vāntastham");
whatever appears in whatever manner, that very thing arises as reality because of the nature of consciousness.

Having spoken from the perspective of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), he speaks from the perspective of negation (*apavāda*)—saying "not external. To the question, "How then does the appearance of the world-form manifest there?", he replies with the word "yat" (which). The meaning is: that reality which was previously manifested by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arises in that very form as the ultimate reality itself. || 37 ||
The inner reality of the Self appears as the external world;
like camphor appearing as fragrance, it expands even within its own contraction.

That internal reality which is the very nature of the Self shines forth externally as the world; even while undergoing contraction according to various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it remains expansive. The meaning is that it shines and exists just as camphor situated within a casket manifests in the form of fragrance. || 38 ||
The Self alone vibrates extensively as the world, as the ego, and as both the external and the internal; yet that all-pervading Lord is neither non-existent nor existent.

It is not non-existent, in the form of the ego-sense and so forth which are invisible to the eyes and other senses; nor is it existent, in the form of the external gross objects visible to them. Rather, the meaning is that it is all-pervasive, consisting of pure existence alone that threads through both.
By that which is external, the internal is perceived as external; by that which resides within, that which is situated within is perceived.
Just as this self is known, so does it perceive its own mind. || 40 ||
Therefore, this very Self perceives its own internal mind as it has been known— following the sequence of successive prior cognitions—
as the external form of the world through the outward-turned eyes and other senses;
and through the internal impressions of waking and so forth, it perceives that which resides within the inner heart.
The meaning is that one perceives such things as a kingdom in a dream. || 40 ||
The entire world, including its exterior and interior, is peaceful and non-different from the Self;
yet, when duality such as "I-ness" and so forth persists, that [world] becomes fearful with its many fluctuations.
He demonstrates through reasoning what was stated—that it is neither external nor internal—with the words "sabāhya" (along with the external).

The meaning is that the world, in its two-fold form as both external and internal, when separated and distinguished from the Reality-Self (sadātman) which is woven through both, becomes merely existent-and-non-existent; that is to say, it is extinguished, as if dead.

But in the absence of their separation, since the distinction between the external and internal remains by their very existence, there arises from the superimposition of "I" and "mine" upon them a fear of manifold ruin should they be destroyed; such is the meaning. || 41 ||
For one whose mind is struck by mental anguish, heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions— all are set ablaze as if at the beginning of a cosmic age.

He produces the fear of manifold calamities with the verse beginning "dyauḥ" (the sky). The meaning is that for those whose souls are struck by various afflictions (*ādhi*), every object—beginning with the celestial realm—is ablaze with the flames of the threefold suffering (*tāpatraya*); thus, even at times such as the beginning of a *kalpa*, it is always as if it were the very moment of universal dissolution (*pralaya*). || 42 ||
But he who, finding delight only within himself, performs actions with the organs of action,
and is not subject to joy or sorrow— he is said to be composed.
However, in the vision of the Self as pure Being (*sanmātra*), even while engaged in worldly activity through the organs of action, there is an absence of egoistic conceit (*abhimāna*);

thus, not even a trace of distraction such as joy or sorrow can arise. With the intention that this results in a state equivalent to being perpetually established in samādhi, he says: "But he who... and so forth. (43)
He who, perceiving the self as omnipresent, possesses a thoroughly tranquil intellect, neither grieves nor broods; he is said to be composed in meditation.
He who, observing the course of the world from its prior to its subsequent limit, laughs at these views, is said to be composed. (45)

"Having its beginning in the past is 'origination' (utpatti), and its end in the future is 'destruction' (nāśa); [I am established] amidst these views of 'I' and 'mine' which are well-known among deluded people. (45)
Likewise, there is no sense of "I" in others, nor is there the birth of the world in me;
just as heated fruits do not exist in the sky, though they appear within clusters of waves.

If it is asked, "For what reason does he laugh? [the author] says, "In the same," because of the falsity of the ego and the world—the locus of which is unestablished—characterized as the conceit (*abhimāna*) and the object of conceit (*abhimantavya*) within the range of the views of "I" and "mine. For those two are of a nature directly perceived and established by the experience of all.

[The two] might reside either in me, or in Brahman whose nature is established by scripture. First, they cannot reside in me, because it is impossible for the seer to have the seen as its locus; nor can they reside in the supreme Brahman, because in that [Brahman], which is of the nature of the unattached, non-dual, and immutable, and is equanimous, it is impossible for it to be the substratum of such diversities as the sense of "I" or the birth of the world. Just as:

In the clusters of waves visible from afar, which are dispersed by the autumnal heat, there appears a shimmering mass of luster that seems like molten, refined silver; yet this luster does not exist within the waves themselves, for it vanishes upon approaching them or searching for it after immersing oneself in them. Nor is it...

Because within that [Self], in the space that is both internal and external, which is unattached and immutable, there is no perception of the fourfold categories of action, result, instrument, and locus; and because, by the non-perception of these, the status of being a substratum for results produced by successive actions is utterly cast aside—therefore, the meaning is that this egoity and the world are indeed false, like a mere luster, since they lack any substratum. || 46 ||

He within whom the state of "I-ness" does not reside, who has neither differentiation nor mind, and for whom there is neither consciousness nor unconsciousness—he alone exists; all other people do not.
Having discarded the distinction between the ego and the world, he discards the distinction between the observer and that [world] with the words "of whom" (yasya).
For that wise one (*jña*) in whom the internal ego-sense (*ahantva*)— which exists as the nature of the innermost Self (*pratyagātman*)— no longer persists,
and for whom there is no mind nor the division of the visible world and so forth, [there can be no conceptualization] dependent upon those.

Neither consciousness nor unconsciousness exists [independently]. Therefore, He alone is the Self of all; other than that, there is no other conscious element. This is the meaning of such scriptural passages as, "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23). || 47 ||

He who, pure as the sky, conducts himself here in this world with perfect detachment from external desires, remaining as calm as a piece of wood or a clod of earth amidst the transformations of joy and anger, is one who has attained tranquility.
He states its characteristics with two verses beginning with "vyoma": "samyak" means in accordance with the scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous; "śamaḥ" is the nature of tranquility. || 48 ||
He who, by his very nature and not out of fear, regards all beings as himself and the property of others as a clod of earth—he truly sees. 49.
An object, whether large or small, is not perceived as having the nature of non-existence;
nor is it experienced by the ignorant as having the nature of existence, nor indeed by the wise as being that [non-existent] in its true state. (50)

He states the reasoning for why only the knower of reality possesses equal vision: "The object," etc. By the ignorant and deluded person, an object (*artha*)—whether it be a vast body as great as Hiraṇyagarbha’s sovereignty, or a small body such as a mere *kākiṇī* coin, or gold, women, and so forth—is not perceived, that is, not seen, as being unreal in nature, i.e., as false.

Furthermore, since that which has that [universe] as its substrate—the form of pure Being—is not experienced [as an object], it is not cognized even as having the nature of mere existence (*asanmātra*).
Because it is seen in such a way only by the knower who knows reality (*tattvavid*), it follows that he alone possesses equal vision (*samadarśitva*) in both respects;
this is the meaning. || 50 ||
Endowed with such an intention and having attained the state of a Mahāsattva, let him remain, arise, depart, or meet his death; he does not abide in that [worldly state].

He says, beginning with "īdṛśa" (of such a kind), that he in whose heart the vision of equality is firmly established is not tainted by joy, sorrow, or the like, in any place or in any state whatsoever. Let him remain destitute; let him rise—may he attain prosperity such as sovereignty—or face death, such as the passing away of sons, kinsmen, and so forth.
May he not attain that state, the state of worldly prosperity. || 51 ||
One may dwell either in one's own home, which is rich with the highest enjoyments and crowded with people,
or else in a vast forest, devoid of all enjoyments and free from worldly activity.
Let him dance, intent on drinking and with unrestrained passion;
or let him come to the mountain, having renounced all attachments and attained equanimity.
"Uddāmamanmatham" (with unrestrained passion) is an adverbial modifier. "Samam" means without change or transformation. || 53 ||
Let him anoint his body with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor;
or let him fall instead into a fire spreading with masses of tangled flames. (54)
Whether he commits great and abundant evil or even merit, whether he meets death this very day or at the end of a multitude of kalpas; || 55 ||
There is nothing that he does not do, yet nothing is done by that Great-Souled One;
he incurs no stain, just as gold remains untainted even when situated in mud.
He is the one who views all with equanimity. He is not the locus of the ego (ahaṃtā), which is the basis for the body, mind, and so forth that undergo transformations such as the suffering of death.
Therefore, nothing has been done by him. 56.

He is stained by the meanings of the words "consciousness" (saṃvit) and "person" (puruṣa), which are themselves tainted and take the form of the latent impressions of "I-ness" and "you-ness," resembling the silver perceived in a mother-of-pearl shell. (57)

If that is so, then whose fault is it among the ignorant? He shows this with the word "consciousness" (*saṃvit*): by means of tainted sensory consciousnesses—which are defiled by the practice of what is not permitted by the scriptures and exist in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—and by the person (*puruṣa*), who is the locus of those [impressions] in the form of the body, as well as by the objects of experience in the form of words and their meanings.
The self of the subtle body (liṅga-ātman) has "I-ness" and egoism as its primary characteristics. || 57 ||
Through the complete cessation of all things by means of right knowledge, one abides in the state as it truly is;
thus, the internal stain of one's own nature is pacified by its very non-existence.

He states the means by which the internal stain is pacified: "entirely," and so forth. The implication is that the stain of the mind's own nature—which consists of affliction—is inherently pacified through its non-existence. || 58 ||

From the consciousness-self (saṃvidātman), which gives rise to the misfortune of the latent impressions of "I-ness," there arise for the person (puruṣa) the various pleasures and pains throughout birth. (59)
Then, what is the cause for the attainment of the suffering of saṃsāra? To this he says: "Because of the superimposition of 'I-ness' (ahaṃtva).
The meaning is that due to the superimposition of "I-ness," misfortunes characterized by latent impressions (vāsanā) arise; because of their awakening, they exist for the person at birth. || 59 ||
Just as when the delusion of a snake in a rope has subsided, there is the peace of the thought "the snake is not there," so too,
when the sense of "I-ness" has completely subsided, internal equanimity is attained.

For this very reason, he says—starting with "In the rope"—that the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra occurs through the pacification of the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃtva). Equanimity (samatā) is the state of being devoid of the inequalities of all suffering. || 60 ||
Whatever one does, whatever one eats, whatever one gives, or whatever one offers in sacrifice—that does not belong to the knower, nor does the knower exist therein; let him not act, or let him act.
Since even the fruit of good deeds does not exist for the knower, just like the fruit of evil deeds, he undergoes the abandonment of all duties;
thus [the author] says, beginning with "That which... (yad...). 61.
For him there is no purpose served by action, nor is there any purpose served by inaction;
through the realization of his own true nature, he remains established in the Self alone. (62)
By non-action, that is, by the renunciation of action. || 62 ||
From that [Self], desires arise—not like sprouts from a stone;
and all those that do arise are that very Self, like waves in the water. (63)
For activity toward the means [to a goal] occurs through the desire for the fruit; yet, because that very [desire] has ceased for him due to his perfection, it does not arise—thus he says:

"Desires. Even if desires should occasionally arise from the habituation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they are, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛśā*), truly one with his own self—thus he says: "And those which... (63).
All this and that— the entire world in its totality— is without any division here;
for he is the singular, purifying form of the Supreme Person.
That which is "existent" (sat) is indeed that very existent; it is not something else.

Strengthening the fact that He is the self of all and that all have Him as their self, [the author] shows that, in ultimate reality, the fruit is simply the non-dual, pure consciousness (*niṣprapañca-cinmātra*) of both:

"There is no such thing as 'other'. Thus, when the various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of cause and effect—which create differentiation—are themselves seen to be nothing but the pure consciousness that is the witness (*sākṣī*) of each, [that state is realized].

The knower of reality [realizes] that there is only pure Being (*sanmātra*), the substratum of the entire universe; for that Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the Puruṣa because of His perfection, and He is like the wind (*pavana*) because He is untouched by any defect. In this manner, being of that singular form, He is eternally liberated, with only the nature of Being remaining, entirely freed from the bondage of all duality and nothing else.
The meaning is "endowed. || 64 ||

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Investigation of Meditation," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation of the Holy Vālmīki’s Great Rāmāyaṇa of Vasiṣṭha, belonging to the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Investigation of Meditation," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as there is within the pepper of the self a sensation of sharpness due to its consciousness, so too is it with this world.
Therefore, [it is free] from such things as the ego-sense (ahaṃtā), distinctions (bheda), and space and time (deśakāla). || 1 ||

When consciousness, its own nature being unknown, assumes the nature of the object due to its capacity for seeing, it is described as being that very consciousness itself; it is not anything other than consciousness. || 1 ||

Thus, when it is established that the entire world is non-different from consciousness in the ultimate sense, it follows that even in conventional reality, the diversity of the world is nothing but the manifestation of the nature of consciousness in its various forms. He states this with the words beginning with "yat": "The Self alone is the sharpness of self-luminosity; because it is consciousness, its experience is the manifestation of that very sharpness."

That which corresponds to it—the world—is precisely the nature of the unknown Brahman, appearing in the forms of "I-ness" and "thou-ness," as well as the distinctions of pots, walls, and so forth, and the forms of the space and time that serve as its substratum.
Therefore, the meaning is that this is established as the result of proving non-difference from Consciousness. || 1 ||
Since the saltiness within the atom of the Self is experienced due to its consciousness,
so too do egoity, duality, space, time, and the rest abide within Me.
From itself, for the inner self who beholds within, there arises through its consciousness the experience of sweetness;
from that, the ego, the distinctions, the world, the principles, and so forth, have unfolded.
It has blossomed forth—that is, it has become manifest—through the various distinctions of its respective forms, beginning with the [five] principles (tattva). || 3 ||
When the stone of the self perceives its own hardness by virtue of its consciousness, that [perception] assumes the forms of egoity, duality, space, time, and so forth.

When the mountain of the Self, by virtue of its inherent consciousness, experiences its own insentience, that [experience] manifests as the ego (ahaṃtā), the various distinctions (bhedādi), the worlds (bhuvanādī), and so forth. || 5 ||
Dullness is heaviness. || 5 ||
When there is the state of being composed of consciousness, fluidity, and so forth, by its own nature and as its very self,
then there arises, as it were, the manifestation of forms such as whirlpools and the like, or the distinctions of "I-ness" and so forth.
It is understood that they remain as if possessing those respective forms. || 6 ||
When there is the perception of the branches and so forth belonging to the tree that is one's own self,
then the ego-sense and its various distinctions manifest as the world and such, while being truly real.
The existent is thus manifesting and appearing in the present. || 7 ||
When there is the realization of emptiness within the sky of the self due to its consciousness,
that is the contemplation of the ego, the various distinctions, the worlds, and so forth.
Cultivation is conceptualization. || 8 ||
When there is the perception of hollowness within the sky of the self due to its being consciousness,
then egoism, duality, the body, and so forth are illuminated.
The distinction is that emptiness (*śūnyatva*) is the absence of substance externally, whereas porosity (*sauṣirya*) is the state of having cavities within a material substance. || 9 ||
When there is a state of non-interruption for the self and the wall by their own nature, that [state] stands as if external to the mind through the distinctions of "I-ness" and so forth. (10)
"Uninterruptedness" means density. The meaning is that, because it is perceived externally, it appears as if distinct from consciousness. || 10 ||

When, by virtue of its own nature as consciousness, there is the singular awareness of its own existence, that state—consisting of "I-ness" and so forth, as well as differentiation and the like—is established as being "sentient," just like the term *cetana*. (11)
The conscious ones are the manifestations of consciousness. || 11 ||

That which is the self-manifestation of the inner self’s own light—consisting of "I-ness" and so forth, as well as consciousness and so forth—he knows that very thing as the individual soul (jīva). 12.

The intellect (citta), which is the universal commonality persisting through the various manifestations of consciousness divided by their different modes of functioning, conceives itself as the individual soul (jīva).
When that which is the essence of consciousness—the elixir of consciousness—exists within the moon of the Self, it is tasted by itself; thus, egoity (ahaṃtā) and the like are aroused.
The elixir is the nectar of immortality. It is tasted by itself, experienced through its own self-luminosity.
It has arisen, meaning it has become manifest. || 13 ||

That which consists of the arising of the sweetness of consciousness within the sugar-candy of the Supreme Self is alone tasted by him; therefore, egoity and the like do not exist within him of their own accord.
Internally, within one's very own self. || 14 ||
Because the Supreme Self, which is like a jewel, possesses consciousness, it manifests spontaneously within itself;
and within that state of conscious selfhood, it perceives "I" and so forth.
In the state of the self, which is the nature of volition and intrinsic form. || 15 ||
And he knows nothing within, because of the impossibility of an internal object here;
nor does he taste any flavor, because of the impossibility of anything to be tasted. (16)
In order to establish that the experience of the world’s illusory forms is nothing but the self-luminous experience of one's own Self,

[the author] states "na ca" (and not), meaning that the designation of the relationship between object and agent— as in "he sees," "he knows," "he tastes," or "it is tasted"— is not intended to prove a difference between them. || 16 ||
And because there is nothing to be perceived within, it does not perceive anything; and because there is no object of knowledge existing, it does not know anything at all.
It accumulates and transforms by means of its inner conscious self; [this refers to] that which is to be known and attained. || 17 ||
The Self, appearing as non-existent, is infinite and full in form;
it remains forever as a single solid mass within itself, like a great mountain.
It is "of such a nature" because it is that in which the world-appearance—that is, the appearance of the world-form—manifests as if it were a seat. 18.
O descendant of Raghu, by this turn of phrase, I have demonstrated to you that there is no distinction such as "I-ness" (ahantā) or "the world-ness" (jagattā), and so forth.
Then, what is the intended meaning of the statement beginning with "of the mirage of the self," etc.? He states that: "By this... (verse 19).
There is no mind, no cognizer, and no delusion such as the state of the world;
like the silence of a rain-cloud, it is merely the peaceful subsiding of that which was already stilled.

The meaning is that, like a cloud which first rained and later, in autumn, becomes silent and mute, the world— which was previously perceived as real— is sublated by its reduction to the pure, white, and stainless substratum of pure existence alone, and thus it simply subsides into peace. || 20 ||
Just as water attains the state of whirlpools and the like due to its fluidity within water,
so too does the Knower, through consciousness, attain the state of egoism and the like within the conscious Self.

The Knower, the Illusionist, the All-Knowing One, within his own Self—which is veiled by his own illusion and whose nature is pure consciousness—assumes the form of egoism and so forth, that is to say, the state of being the individual soul (jīva) and the world (jagat). || 21 ||
Just as liquidity exists in water and motion in the wind,
so do the notions of "I," space, time, and so forth, exist within the Knower, who is pure consciousness alone.
In the wind that always moves; in the Knower who, in the ultimate sense, is of the nature of mere cognition; in the Lord who is omniscient. || 22 ||
O Śiva, the Knower knows knowledge through the expansion of knowledge for the sake of knowing;
that "I" is known by the Knower through the vital functions such as living beings and so forth. (23)

If the living being (*jīva*) and the world are not other than consciousness (*jñapti*), then what is the distinction between the states of being a living being and being the Lord (*īśvara*) within that consciousness? To this he says: "The Knower" (*jña*). The Lord is the Knower; in the state of being the Lord, which is the state of knowing, there is *śiva*, which is the innate knowledge (*svarūpajñāna*) consisting of unsurpassed bliss. [By the expansion of innate knowledge...]

[The reading in the printed manuscript: Through the nourishment of knowledge—characterized by being unobstructed and undifferentiated—that is, through the increase of knowledge, he knows always. However, in the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) consisting of egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) and the gross body, even though it is conscious and knowing, [it acts] through the means of living (*abhijīvana*), which are the causes of life.

The meaning of the distinction is this: through the associations with the vital breaths, the organs, and their objects, the self is known as being merely of the nature of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, but not in its true reality. || 23 ||
Just as [the Self] arises, and whatever kind of satisfaction the ignorant man derives from knowledge,
once he has realized non-duality as being otherness, he expands in that very manner.

For this very reason, he says "as" (yathā) to show that the Lord manifests (*vivartate*) in exactly the same manner as the delusion of the individual soul (*jīva*). By whatever latent impressions of desire and action (*kāma-karma-vāsanā*), by whatever kind of knowledge of objects, and by whatever manner of diversity in vision, attainment, and enjoyment for the ignorant one— such [is the manifestation].

Various kinds of satisfaction, such as pleasure, joy, and so forth, arise as enjoyment within His non-dual essential nature; yet, through the diversity of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the act of enjoying, or through the appearance of otherness, that Supreme Lord— perceived by the wise—
is manifested in various ways according to those respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of His own desires and the like, and thus He expands Himself, bending His own limbs.
It evolves; that is to say, it assumes manifold variety. || 24 ||
Life is consciousness, the knower is life, and life is the very life of the living being;
there is absolutely no difference between the knower and the living being in their nature as consciousness. 25.

But when, through instruction on the true scriptures and the true form [of reality], he realizes that the very manifestation of the world of objects— which is essentially nothing but the existence of the substrate— is itself life, the essence, and the ultimate state;
and when he understands that the life of all living beings depends upon that [existence], then life is indeed of the nature of bliss.

When the essence of the enjoyer is known, and when both—the object of enjoyment and the substratum of the enjoyer—remain as being of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), then there is absolutely no difference between the knower and the individual soul, or between the individual soul and the Lord; the meaning is that [the distinction] ceases entirely in every respect. || 25 ||

Just as there is no such thing as a difference between the knower and the individual soul, know that there is likewise no difference between the knower and Śiva—He who is peaceful and indivisible. 26.

When the ignorance that differentiates the individual soul (jīva) from the Lord (īśvara) has perished, even the distinction between the state of deep sleep (prājña) and the fourth state (turīya) ceases;
thus, the sovereignty of the non-dual, full, blissful, single-flavored pure consciousness is established. He says this with the words "Just as" (yathā).
"All is stilled, unborn, one, without beginning or middle..."
The Ābhāsvara realm is merely self-experience, devoid of any objectifiable mark;
"all is utterly tranquil"— such a view consisting of words exists only for the sake of awakening, for this "Om" is indeed in vain.

Having restated the extracted meaning, he concludes with the words "all this": "All this world is, on all sides, luminous—meaning its nature is full self-luminosity—and consists solely of self-enjoyment, having the single flavor of bliss, devoid of cognizable objects, devoid of signs (i.e., distinguishing marks), and tranquil; it is Brahman."

The thought that "all this is utterly tranquil" is merely a superimposed perception of non-difference, consisting of words for the time being and directed toward the relation between the denoted meaning and the word;
it is indeed in vain because it lacks immediate utility, for [it arises] when there is a conscious awareness of contradiction.

This is solely for the sake of the indivisible cognition (*akhaṇḍabodha*) of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), by means of relying on the characteristic of the abandonment of [the literal] parts as taught by Bhagavat Āgastya.

Indeed, the cognition arising from that sentence consists of an indivisible meaning; having unified the world, Brahman, and the syllable *oṃ*—namely, the Virāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, Avyākṛta, and Turīya aspects—one [realizes this].
Having divided the syllables *a*, *kā*, *se*, and *kāra* into four parts consisting of half-measures (*ardhamātrā*), one dissolves each preceding part into the subsequent ones;

that which is then indicated by the half-measure—non-dual, of the single flavor of perfect bliss, and of the nature of eternal, immediate, direct pure consciousness—is this very [reality]. It is not... [the rest of the sentence is omitted in the source].
The meaning is that its form is intermingled. || 27 ||

Thus ends the fifty-seventh canto, titled "The Dispelling of Duality," in the section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Refutation of Duality," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The fifty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this very context, they cite this ancient history.
The account of the Lord of the Kirātas, who is as fierce as a god, which is a source of wonder.
In this [chapter], the despondency of Suraghu, the lord of Kirāra, is described,
as well as the instruction given by Māṇḍavya regarding the means beginning with the renunciation of everything.
In this context, regarding the stated meaning, it is said that the view consisting of words is solely for the purpose of awakening. || 1 ||
It was like the fat of the northern quarter, a mass of camphor from the earth,
the laughter of Śiva come to life, or the white radiance of the moon.

He describes a peak of the Himalayas situated near that region of Suraghu’s abode, beginning with the words "of the north" (*uttarasyāḥ*). "Essence of fat" (*medaḥ-sāra*) means, in effect, camphor. It refers to a mass or heap of camphor produced from—that is, emerged from—the earth. Or else, it refers to the laughter of Śiva or the moonlight.

This is a single, qualified *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on various optional causes established through poetic imagination: namely, that the moonlight is either the fat of the quarters of the sky or the camphor-powder produced upon the earth after reaching it. || 2 ||
On this Himālaya mountain there is a peak, a mountain named Kailāsa,
which is like the leader of a herd of mountain-elephants that has shed its tusks.

By the qualification "the peak of the Himālaya," it is understood that this [peak] is distinct from the well-known silver and other such substances situated on Mount Meru. The meaning is that it stands like the central gem of a pearl necklace, which consists of a series of pearls (the peaks) released and held by the "mountain-elephant," namely the Himavat, the best of mountains.
Or rather, it is like a heap, the leader and gatherer, of a string of pearls fallen from elephants standing on a mountain. || 3 ||
His home was like the ocean of milk to Viṣṇu, like heaven to the Lord of the Gods, and like the navel-lotus to the Lotus-born One; it was also like [the abode] of the Moon-crested Lord.
The "navel-lotus" refers to the lotus from Viṣṇu’s navel; it is understood by implication that this is his dwelling, provided by his father-in-law. || 4 ||
He shines with swings made of rudrākṣa trees and celestial nymphs,
like the ocean with its waves of shimmering jeweled rods.
With dangling *dilā* fruits from the *rudrākṣa* trees, which are like swinging cradles, and with their flickering jeweled rods—this is an epithet for the waves as well. (5)
There, the playful Aśoka trees shine like actual Aśoka blossoms, struck incessantly by the feet of intoxicated women from the courtesans' quarters.
Of the women of the Gaṇas, that is, the wives of the Pramathas. || 6 ||
Wandering through the quarters among the Bhrigus, Śaṅkara [resided] there, where waterfalls flow forth and recede incessantly, like the liquid from moonstones.
In whichever directions he wanders, there [the waters] flow among the Bhṛgus at the precipices, while in other directions they turn back. || 7 ||
It was as if covered by a multitude of creepers, trees, shrubs, ponds, lakes, rivers, and streams, along with deer, herds of wild animals, and living beings, like the cosmic egg itself.

Regarding the phrase "as if like the cosmic egg" (*brahmāṇḍavadiva*): the usage of words whose meaning has already been expressed is observed, as seen in the statement of the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Bring two cakes. Since even multiple indicators can be used together—as in "the fire ascends after the rising sun"—it is possible for them to be employed simultaneously, even when the sense is already conveyed by the suffix *-vat*.

The word "iva" (like) is used in the sense of similarity; or else, it should be construed as ending in the possessive suffix -mat, meaning "Brahman itself is characterized by the form of Virāj, like an egg. || 8 ||
On that land dwell the Kirātas known as Hemajaṭas,
like ants gathered within the hollow at the root of a banyan tree.
Of that Himavat peak; on the dry land, at its base. || 9 ||
In the forests at the foot of Kailāsa, those base beings who live by proximity dwell like owls among the rudrākṣa trees and shrubs.
He describes their means of livelihood: "Kailāsa," etc. The foothills (*pāda*) of the peak named Kailāsa are its surrounding mountains;
those who live nearby subsist on the *rudrākṣa* berries and other trees, shrubs, fruits, flowers, wood, roots, and so forth belonging to the forests situated there. || 10 ||
Among them there was a noble-souled king, a conqueror of enemy cities, who was like the right arm of the Goddess of Victory and a protector of his subjects. (11)

Like the arm of Jayalakṣmī, the king was victorious over the cities of his enemies and skilled in protecting his subjects; furthermore, because he is seen to possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman through the qualifiers to be mentioned later, it is understood that he was a Kṣatriya.
Named Suraghu, he was powerful, the destroyer of the pride of his formidable enemies; he was like Arka in valor, as if the Wind-god were incarnate.
The construction is: "In prowess, like the sun. || 12 ||
The leader of the Guhyakas was indeed surpassed by him in royal power and wealth;
the teacher of Indra was surpassed in wisdom; and the preceptor of the Asuras was surpassed in poetic compositions. (13)
By means of his royal splendors and wealth, he has even surpassed the Lord of Wealth, the King of Kings and leader of the Guhyakas; this is the implied meaning.
By means of his poetic compositions—treatises characterized by aesthetic flavors (rasa) and figures of speech (alaṃkāra)—he has surpassed Śukra, the preceptor of the Asuras. (13)
He performed his royal duties through the sequence of punishment and favor,
according to what presented itself, with an untiring body, just as the sun does throughout the days.
Then he was overwhelmed by the pleasure and pain born from that [union],
like a bird whose limbs are entangled in the snares of its own flight-path.
"Why do I afflict this distressed one with my power, as if crushing sesame seeds in a machine?
For all living beings alike, suffering arises just as it does for me. (16)
He shows that [suffering] arises from the power of pain, such as anxiety, grief, and so forth—by asking, "What is this affliction?"—referring to these people. || 16 ||
"I shall bestow wealth upon him; through wealth, every person becomes full of joy, just as I am. Therefore, enough of my excessive restraints. (17)

When there is doubt as to what ought to be done, he shows the first alternative: "Wealth. For that reason, I shall bestow wealth upon this distressed person; enough with excessive restraints—the meaning is that there is no purpose [for them]. || 17 ||
"Or rather, I shall bring about the subjugation of this [demon] without whom this progeny cannot exist, just as a river cannot flow without water. (18)

He shows the second [alternative] with the words "or else" (athavā). By this restraint, the subjects simply cannot exist—[the phrase] "within their respective bounds" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 18 ||

"Alas, what misery! Alas, what misery indeed! This one who ought to be punished by me is instead always worthy of my favor. By fate, today I am possessed of happiness; alas, today I am possessed of sorrow. (19)
One who is to be suppressed is to be punished by means of execution, imprisonment, and so forth. || 19 ||
Thus the king’s mind, oscillating— [the reading "lolāyitam" is also found]— found no rest,
wandering like one long-thirsting within a single great whirlpool of water.
It found no rest in any one place; rather, like the mind of one who is thirsty and exhausted from long thirsting, it wandered within a great whirlpool of water. (20)
Then once, the sage Māṇḍavya arrived at his house,
having wandered through every corner of the quarters of the earth, like Nārada to the abode of Vāsava.
By whom all the groves of the quarters and the circles of the directions were made to wander in confusion. || 21 ||
Tamasī worshipped that great sage,
who was an axe to the trunk of the evil tree of doubt and was proficient in all things, and questioned him.
Suraghu said:
"O Sage, by your arrival I have attained supreme bliss,
like one who has reached the surface of the earth during the month of Mādhava."
Supreme peace and happiness; [this occurs] in the spring season (mādhava), or in Viṣṇu. || 23 ||
O Lord, today by virtue of dharma I stand at the forefront of the blessed, since I have been beheld by you as a lotus is by the radiant sun. (24)
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you have long been at rest;
therefore, sever this doubt of mine, as the sun dispels the darkness.
If you have come to rest and are free from fatigue, then—alternatively, because you have long rested in the supreme state—for that reason. (25)
By association with the great, whose suffering indeed does not perish? Yet those who understand suffering say that doubt is the supreme affliction. (26)
Arising from the restraint and favor [of others], these anxieties, residing within the bodies of my servants, torment me excessively, like the claws of a lion upon an elephant. (27)

The mention of "servants" (bhṛtya) is an elliptical indication for all [relatives] such as enemies, friends, and so forth. Being situated within the body—that is, firmly rooted in the object—they "scratch," meaning they cause pain. || 27 ||
Just as the sun’s rays always rise with impartiality, O Sage, let there be no other thought in my mind; act accordingly through your compassion. (28)
Equanimity is even vision; it is that by which other uneven visions do not arise. || 28 ||
Māṇḍavya said:
O King, by one's own effort, established in oneself, and through one's own means, this mind’s frailty dissolves like snow upon the Himalayas. (29)

By one's own effort in the form of dispassion, renunciation, and so forth—namely, through the means of its manifestation such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*)—and by that which is established in itself, culminating in the awakening to one’s own Self; "fragility" means softness, that is to say, the state of being susceptible to being pierced by thousands of thorns in the form of occasions for joy and sorrow. || 29 ||
By one's own investigation alone, the fever of the inner mind is quickly pacified, just as a great mist vanishes at the mere arrival of autumn. (30)
With his own mind, he should inwardly investigate his own sense organs located within his body: what they are like and what they are.

The meaning is: reflect upon your own sons, friends, and so forth, as well as the senses residing within your own body and other things, according to reality—what they truly are and what their nature is by way of reasoning. || 31 ||
"Who am I? How did this come to be? Or what is it, and how do birth and death occur?"—by reflecting thus within yourself, you will attain greatness. (32)
[It attains] greatness through the removal of the limitedness superimposed by non-investigation. || 32 ||
For you, whose true nature has been fully understood through investigation,
states of joy and resentment shall not cause your mind to waver, for it remains immovable.

The minds of those who have heard [the truth] will not weigh you—who have become the ultimate reality—unsteadily; that is to say, they will not cause you to be unstable in your position through rising and falling, as if on a scale. || 33 ||
Having cast off its own nature, the mind will attain peace, free from fever;
it will become as it was before, like a wave returning to the water.

Your mind, having cast off its own form as a mental construct and having become its former body—the primordial nature of Brahman already established—will attain peace, that is, a state free from distraction. || 34 ||
O sinless one, even while remaining alive, he will cast off his human form,
like the moon sheds its blemished body at the end of a manvantara.
If so, will the very existence of the mind perish? No; he says: "While remaining.

Just as at the end of a previous Manvantara, upon reaching the Kali age, the world—rendered destitute by stains of sins—is freed from those stains when the next Manvantara arrives, even while remaining [in its state], so too is the mind.
The meaning is that while remaining capable of worldly activity as one liberated in this life (*jīvanmukta*), he abandons his former mental form.
"All those wealthy ones shall become objects of compassion for him,
who has seen the truth and is content, just as people on earth are for a father" (36).

The fruit of knowledge is not merely the cessation of suffering, but also the sovereignty of unsurpassed bliss, wherein even Brahmā and the other gods are objects of compassion; thus he says: "anukalpyāḥ" (they are to be pitied). || 36 ||
O King, having perceived the Self through the lamp of discrimination, you shall place even Meru, the oceans, and the sky beneath you, thereby attaining a greatness that bestows the supreme goal.
(37) For when even the vastness of space and the other elements is dependent upon its existence, then its own greatness is unsurpassed.
With the intention of stating what is to be said, he says: "By means of the lamp of knowledge born of discrimination" (viveka), by whom the Self has been seen. || 37 ||
O virtuous one, when your mind has attained greatness, it does not sink into the currents of saṃsāra, just as an elephant does not sink into puddles the size of a cow's hoofprint.
But the wretched mind, O King, sinks even into a trivial matter, just as an old-bodied gnat sinks into the water of a cow's footprint. (39)
Miserable and defiled by the wretchedness of desire, he sinks and becomes deluded even in a task that is trivial and insignificant. || 39 ||
Through that wretchedness of your own, which clings to mere appearances, you wallow in the mire like a worm because of the mental impressions of the mind. (40)
By that which is well-known. || 40 ||
O mighty-armed one, to that same extent everything is abandoned by oneself, until only the Supreme Self remains as the supreme vision. (41)

If it is asked, "In how many objects and for how long should dispassion (vairāgya) be practiced? he says in response: "Until then" (tāvat). This means until the experience of the Self alone remains as self-luminous. || 41 ||
The ore is washed away until only the gold remains;
likewise, everything is scrutinized until only the Self is attained. 42.
He states that even the thorough investigation of various scriptures and treatises culminates only in the vision of the Self, using the word "tāvat" (only so long).
"Dhātuḥ" refers to the ore from a gold mine; "sarvam adhyātma-śāstram" means the entire body of spiritual science. || 42 ||
Having completely renounced everything, in every way, everywhere, and at all times, by means of a universal intellect, one perceives the Self through the self. (43)

The meaning is that by means of an all-encompassing intellect (*sārvikī buddhi*) which constitutes all things, having at all times and in every place renounced every object of perception in every way, the entire, perfect Self (*sarvaḥ pūrṇātmā*) is realized through one's own self alone; it is not [realized] merely by the abandonment of a few objects, nor at any particular time, nor in any particular place, nor in any particular manner. || 43 ||
As long as everything has not been relinquished, the Self is not attained;
when all states have been abandoned, that which remains is called the Self.
He confirms the very point already stated by means of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as well, beginning with "yāvat" (as long as). He asks, "Why is that?
and answers with "sarva" (all). || 44 ||
O virtuous one, as long as something else has not been relinquished, the object remains merely a generality; what need is there to mention the attainment of one's own true self? (45)
The common [wealth] is that which is shared in worldly transactions, such as cattle and property. The particle *eva* is used in the sense of "also.
As long as other things that are opposed to it have not been abandoned, that [common wealth] is not attained. || 45 ||
O King, that alone—and nothing else—is truly attained where one, having abandoned all other activities, strives by oneself with one's whole being for the sake of the Self. (46)
In which [place], that is, in whatever object; that [place], namely that object. || 46 ||
Therefore, for the sake of beholding one's own Self, one should renounce everything;
having renounced all things whatsoever, that which is seen is the supreme state. (47)
The meaning is that having abandoned everything visible—whatever is seen that cannot be abandoned in any way—that alone is the supreme state. || 47 ||

Having thoroughly cast aside from your mind the manifestation of all things existing within the world— which consists of the entire succession of causes and effects— therefore, [focus on] your own body.
Having completely dissolved [everything], that which goes forth is indeed that very same thing. || 48 ||

In this world, which consists of a succession of causes and effects, the mind— pervading like a thread through jewels— is manifested by its own conceptualization as the mere Reality (sanmātra). Having completely cast away every form that appears distinct from that Reality,
and immediately thereafter, having dissolved even its own mental form along with its body through sublation upon the destruction of root-ignorance (mūlājñāna);
The meaning is that whatever reality, whose sole essence is pure existence-consciousness (saccinmātra), one attains—that alone is the nature of Brahman. || 48 ||

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction of Māṇḍavya," within the narrative of Suraghu, in the Section on Tranquility (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the Means to Liberation (*mokṣopāya*), in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition. || 58 ||
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction of Māṇḍavya," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
Fifty-ninth Sarga.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O descendant of Raghu, having spoken thus to Suraghu, the Blessed One—
Māṇḍavya went back to his own beautiful circle of silence. || 1 ||
For the king who, in solitude, completely abandons both the external and internal objects of perception through inquiry, the attainment of his own Self is proclaimed here. (1)
When the supreme sage had departed, the king went to a secluded and blameless place and reflected within himself with his intellect: "Who indeed am I? (2)
Having spoken and instructed [him], he went to his own circle of silence, the region that is the dwelling place of the sages. || 1 ||
I am not Mount Meru, nor is Meru mine; I am not the world, nor is the world mine.
I am not the mountains, nor are the mountains mine; I am not the earth, nor is the earth mine.

Therein, first, having investigated and discarded the notions of "self" and "belonging to self" regarding external objects of perception, he refutes them with six verses beginning with "I am not... The term *jagat* (the world) here refers to the worlds above and below. || 3 ||
This Kirāta territory is not mine, nor am I the territory;
by mere convention alone, it is simply a region belonging to me.
One's own convention is the notion "I am the king" arising from the consensus of all people through such acts as the ceremonial enthronement; it exists by that alone. || 4 ||
"This agreement has been abandoned by me; this [territory] is not deficient for me.
Now the city alone remains; this indeed is the certainty in this matter. (5)
In this very city as well, by abandoning conventional designations, this is the certain conclusion. || 5 ||
Abounding with rows of banners and groves, crowded with servants' gardens, and filled with elephants, horses, and vassal lords— this city is not mine, nor is it my city.
He states that very same certainty clearly: "The banner," etc. (verse 6).
The multitude of enjoyments and the wife have their connection to convention rendered useless when that convention perishes; neither am I, nor is all this mine. (7)
It is called "connection" because it is connected with a convention that has no [corresponding] object. || 7 ||
Thus, including my servants, my army, my vehicles, and my city—neither do I possess this kingdom, nor does the kingdom belong to me; for this agreement is indeed fraught with confusion.
It is confused, meaning that it is established through a blind tradition, like the relationship between a *kākiṇī* and a *kārsāpaṇa*.
"I consider myself to be nothing more than the body, joined with hands, feet, and so forth;
therefore, I shall now look closely at the interior of this very thing. (9)

Having rejected the connection with external objects by means of abandoning [the view that they are] mere conventions, he now begins to reject that [connection] even with the body, senses, and so forth, using the reason of their insentience, starting with the verse beginning "The body alone," etc. (9).
Therefore, in this matter, I am not this flesh and bone, which are insentient;
nor do they enter into union with me, just as water does not with a lotus.
It does not even enter into conjunction or connection; the meaning is that this is because of its non-attachment (*asaṅgatvāt*). || 10 ||
Flesh is inert; I am not that, nor am I even the blood.
The bones are inert; I am not them, nor do they ever belong to me. (11)
I am not the organs of action, nor do the organs of action belong to me;
for that which is indeed inert within this body, I am not, being pure consciousness.
I am not the enjoyments, nor are the enjoyments mine; nor are my faculties of perception.
These faculties of perception are inert and devoid of reality, and I am not the faculties of perception.
The faculties of perception are the organs of knowledge. || 13 ||
The mind is the root of the defects of saṃsāra, for it is not the "I," which is indeed insentient.
Furthermore, the view that "I am the intellect" or "I am the ego" is merely mental in nature.

Furthermore, that vision which perceives "intellect" (buddhi) as "I" (ahaṃkāra) is also followed by the realization: "It is not I, nor is it mine. For that is a state of the internal organ consisting of mind (manomayī); that is to say, it is of the nature of duality. 14.
The sheath of the elements, consisting of the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth, has a fluctuating form.
I do not perceive the body and so forth as being thus [the self] in the manner taught by the learned.

The sheath of the elements (bhūtakośa), consisting of the body, mind, intellect, senses, and so forth—the aggregate of gross and subtle elements—is not "I" according to the manner described above. I observe that which remains; that is to say, having seen it, I investigate it. || 15 ||

But the remaining conscious being is the individual soul (jīva); if that [soul] perceives by means of an object of perception, then, being awakened by another, it would not possess the nature of the reality of the Self. || 16 ||

The conscious knower perceives together with the object of perception, which is the perceived. Thus, being made aware by the witness of the threefold division (tripuṭī) in the form "I perceive this," that knower cannot be conceived as having the true nature of the Self as its real form; this is the meaning. || 16 ||

Thus I renounce all that is to be experienced and all that is thought; for indeed, I am not that. I remain as the residual, free from conceptual construction, established as pure consciousness. || 17 ||
Thus, by this very reasoning, I abandon the means of knowledge (*pramiti*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which are perceivable by a witness (*sākṣisaṃvedya*).

For it is well known that "I am indeed not the object of thought" (*cetya*); I remain as the pure consciousness, the pure witness, the Self (*ātman*). This means that one is established in this certainty. || 17 ||
"Behold, I am he who has attained his own nature; born in due time, I am now possessed of purpose.
I am that very one, the infinite Self; there is nothing beyond this Supreme Self. (18)

By the mere sight of that, he shows how its attainment is a matter of wonder, like finding gold around one’s neck—this is expressed by the word "wonderful" (citram). The meaning is: even though I have been striving since beginningless time, today I have become one who has accomplished his task, possessing the fruit of the supreme human goal. || 18 ||
In Brahmā, Indra, Yama, Vāyu, and likewise in the hosts of all beings, this very Blessed One, the Self, exists like a thread within pearls. (19)
He corroborates this with scriptural passages such as "This is Brahman, this is Indra," by means of direct experience, stating: "In Brahman."
This very power of consciousness is stainless and free from the disease of the objectified world;
filling every corner of the quarters, she assumes the form of Bhairava.
Because she is the cause of fear for the ignorant, she assumes a terrifying form.
Pervading all states of being, subtle, and free from existence and non-existence;
she dwells within the entire universe up to the realm of Brahmā, containing the treasury of all powers.
It has entered into all states and mental fluctuations, for the Śruti says: "That which is known through awakening is considered [the truth]. (21)
She is the most beautiful and auspicious of all, the lamp illuminating everything;
she is the thread in the form of a web for all those liberated from saṃsāra.
All beauty is unsurpassed bliss; by that she is fortunate, being full [of it]. Of the pearls characterized by saṃsāra, she is the one who has attained liberation. 22.
Rich with all forms and transformations, yet devoid of all forms;
she has become the flood of all beings and has always attained the state of being everything. || 23 ||
These fourteen kinds of beings exist within the interior of the world;
this worldly manifestation, consisting of them, is essentially of the nature of perception.
The ellipsis is that he sustains the fourteen kinds of beings according to the number of worlds. || 24 ||
The course of states of pleasure and pain is merely a false appearance;
all that appears in various forms is only the Supreme Consciousness, which is the Self alone. 25.
This very self of mine is all-pervading, and this is that awakening;
this [awakening], having assumed a form with limbs, produces the illusion of a king. || 26 ||
Pervasive and following along with the world, it is the awakening that witnesses my own intellect.

This very consciousness (citt), assuming a body not distinguished by the difference between the seer and the seen, creates the delusion "I am the king"—the meaning is that it has acted as if it were a prior creator. || 26 ||
By the grace of this very [mind], the mind, situated upon the chariot of the body, goes, gallops, and dances amidst the playful activities of the web of saṃsāra. (27)
This mind, body, and so forth do not exist as anything at all in reality;
when this fragile [body] perishes, nothing whatsoever is destroyed.
This dance, consisting of the web of the world, is performed by the actors that are the minds;
it is perceived by this single thread of intellect, like a streak of light from a lamp.
By her who has been thus described, who is the very form of direct witness. || 29 ||
Alas, my concern regarding the state of restraint and favor was entirely in vain;
it was centered on the body, yet there is no such thing as a body at all.
"Aha! I have awakened; my evil vision has vanished.
Everything that was to be seen has been seen, and this which was to be attained has been attained by me. (31)
Whatever is seen here as this entire visible world, it is nothing other than a mere portion of the vibration of consciousness; there is no eternal thing whatsoever apart from that.
That which is the conscious, motionless [Self] is [the ground]; the delusion of the state of being a living soul (jīva) through illusion (māyā) is a portion of that;

the delusion of the seventeen-fold mark (liṅga) is a portion of that; the delusions of the distinctions between the external and internal organs are portions of that; the delusion of the objects seen in waking and dreaming is a portion of that. Other than that, there is nothing else that is eternal and uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time.
The meaning is that the visible object does not exist. || 32 ||
Where are those two, of what nature are they, what is their basis, and what is their essence?
Likewise, [tell me] regarding the processes of restraint and favor, as well as joy and resentment, in this world.

Thus, since the world is illusory, the processes of punishment and favor, as well as the sequences of joy and resentment that motivate them, become supportless, devoid of modality, objectless, and lacking any essential nature; thus he says: "Where? (kveti).
What is pleasure, and what indeed is pain? All this is the expansive Brahman.
"I existed"—this was my vain delusion; by good fortune, I have now realized that I was but a fool. (34)

He says "What? to show that once one's own delusion has departed, there is no longer any attachment to pleasure, pain, and so forth; the meaning is: "Now, being undeluded, I am established in my true nature. || 34 ||
In such light as this, why is there lamentation? Why is there delusion? Why is it gazed upon? Why is anything done, or why does one stand still, or why does one depart? (35)
Thus, Ānanda, it is perceived and experienced by its nature as being filled with a single flavor; therefore, there is "light" (āloka) in that state.
The interrogative particles [kiṃ] imply a negation; the meaning is that even the possibility of grief and the like does not exist. || 35 ||
Something like this, known as the space of consciousness, shines forth;
salutations, salutations to you, O reality-less one! By good fortune, O beautiful one, you have been seen.
Something of extraordinary wonder; this is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 36 ||
"Aha! I have truly awakened; I have fully understood.
Homage to myself, the infinite, and to the arising of perfect knowledge! (37)

To him whose arising—that is, manifestation—is in right knowledge (samyagjñāna); the word "ca" (and) serves to include those who were to be saluted in the preceding verse, or alternatively, it means "and for the sake of prosperity characterized by right knowledge. || 37 ||
Free from passion and abiding in the state beyond sense objects, having transcended the delusion of worldly existence and abandoned all that colors it,
he then attains the stage of stable, profound sleep.
I dwell as the equal of the equal within the self. || 38 ||

Precisely because it is free from passion (*rañjana*), its state of abiding in the three objects [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep] has been wiped away; this is the indication of the purified meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (thou). Precisely because the delusion of worldly existence (*bhava-bhrama*) has departed, it is devoid of being stained by the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of space and so forth; this is the indication of the purified meaning of the term *tat* (that). The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of a state (*bhāve*).

Through the steady state of deep sleep (*suṣupti-kalā*), by means of the method of absorption (*svāpyaya-yukti*) as if through the removal of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi-vigama*), I have attained oneness; thus there is the designation of undivided unity. Therefore, from that [state], I abide in the inner Self (*pratyag-brahman*) with absolute equality, characterized by ultimate non-difference; never indeed do I [depart from it].
"The recurrence of inequality" is the description of the state of the fruit. || 38 ||

Thus ends the fifty-ninth canto, named "The Resting of Suraghu," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Chapter on Tranquility) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Resting of Suraghu," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Sixtieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus did Hemajaṭādhīśa attain the unsurpassed state.
Just as Gādhi’s son [Viśvāmitra] attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa through resolute discernment. || 1 ||
Until the fall of the body, the conduct of that one who is liberated while living is said to be like that of a god; then, upon the cessation of the body, he abides in the void.
Gādhi’s son was Viśvāmitra. || 1 ||
He did not grow weary in his efforts toward tasks that were purposeless, fruitless, or harmful,
even as he applied himself again and again over the course of many days, like a sovereign lord.

When the efforts employed as means for attaining dharma and artha have been applied again and again, repeatedly performed, yet— due to fate— their results are such that their activities take on the form of misfortune, become fruitless, or culminate in suffering.
He was not weary; Īśvara is the Lord of the Day, the Sun. || 2 ||
From that time forward, he remained forever free from distress,
steadfast in his own duty like a mountain at the forefront of a flood of water.
In his own royal duties, consisting of both favor and punishment, he remained as unshakable as a mountain situated in the middle of a river. || 3 ||
Free from both joy and anger, performing his duties every day,
he, with a noble and profound form, surpassed the splendor of the ocean.
"Kārya" refers to income, expenditure, and so forth; "āharan" means performing. || 4 ||
He shone with a mental state possessing the quality of deep sleep—
a state that was unwavering and luminous— just as a lamp shines by its own flame.
That is to say, make it motionless, as if in deep sleep. || 5 ||
He was neither merciless nor compassionate, neither dualistic nor envious;
he was neither wise nor unwise, neither a seeker of gain nor a seeker of loss. || 6 ||
In the reading *amatsarī*, it means one who, like one entirely free from envy, is indifferent toward the faults of others. (6)
With a constant vision of equanimity, a steady and unflappable conduct,
and an inner coolness, he shone like the full moon over the ocean.
The division of the compound is *acāpala-dhīra-ya*. It is like the ocean and the moon, both of which are full.
Perceiving the entire world as a mere conceptualization of the nature of consciousness, his mind shone forth in fullness, with the glory of pleasure and pain completely stilled.
The connection with the subsequent clause is that he became established in perfect meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The reason for this is that his intellect had become fully perfected. (8)
Whether rejoicing, expanding, full, standing, walking, entering, or sleeping,
remaining in a samādhi that is equal to the unmanifest, he is awakened and has attained dissolution into consciousness.
Exulting with his body, blossoming with his mind. || 9 ||
Then, while ruling the kingdom free from attachment, that lotus-eyed one remained for many hundreds of years, his form unimpaired.
Thereafter, he himself abandoned this arrangement called a body,
overcome by his own splendor, just as a speck of frost melts away.
Overpowered and withered. Form is the shape of a physical body. || 11 ||
He entered the Supreme Cause, the Lord of Causes, who is without beginning or end,
just as the water of rivers enters the ocean filled to the brim by its wisdom.

The meaning is that he entered, by means of the mental modification consisting of direct realization through wisdom, the Supreme Brahman— the Lord and controller of all internal organs such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others, and the cause of the creation and dissolution of all worlds at their beginning and end—
just as one enters the ocean, which is the seed-cause of birth and so forth. || 12 ||
Having attained the stainless splendor of the singular form and having reached a state free from people, with his sorrow stilled,
he was fully capable of perceiving the supreme nature.
The Great-Souled One was like a jar joined with the sky. || 13 ||

Having entered that, he describes what he was like at that time with the words beginning "adhigata": Suraghu, being one by whom the stainless, uniform light— whose sole essence is bliss and whose nature is self-luminous— had been attained through wisdom as his own self (*svātmatayā*), [remained] in a state devoid of people, meaning free from the transformations such as birth and so forth.

Having reached the final stage and with all sorrow stilled, upon the breaking of the pot, he became as if one with the supreme nature, united with the space within the pot by means of the great space [of the universe]. This is the meaning of his *nirvāṇa*. || 13 ||

Thus ends the sixtieth sarga, titled "The Liberation of Suraghu," within the narrative of Suraghu, in the section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) concerning the means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*), in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition. || 60 ||
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Gods," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*. 60.
The sixty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"Thus, O lotus-petal-eyed one, regarding the removal of Rāghava’s affliction..."
May you attain the pair of feet; be free from sorrow for the sake of prosperity. || 1 ||
In order to demonstrate the practice characterized by the single, innate meditative absorption, the dialogue with Parigha is here described by Suraghu. (1)

That very Rāghava, like a celestial hero (suraghuvat), [remains] when there is the reversal—that is, the uprooted destruction—of sin (agha) caused by joy, sorrow, and so forth, through the awakening to reality (tattvabodha). || 1 ||
By clinging to this view, the mind does not suffer, like a child who has found a lamp while submerged in a terrible darkness. (2)
The mind, like a child or an infant submerged in the terrible darkness of ignorance, does not suffer once it has grasped this view and obtained a lamp, having attained illumination. || 2 ||
Through the state of discernment, the mind attains such peace as if it were falling into a chasm while clutching a firm bundle of grass. (3)

As his mind was falling into the abyss of the blind well of delusion, he experienced a sense of relief and the bliss of rest, as if by grasping at a support— a thicket of dense grass— provided by that very state of discernment described in the *Suraghu*. || 3 ||
Now, having cultivated this purifying vision and proclaiming it,
remain constantly absorbed in one-pointed concentration, thereby adorning the surface of the earth.
Having cultivated it again and again, having made it firm for oneself through repeated practice, one should also proclaim and teach it to others. || 4 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord of Sages, how is single-pointed concentration achieved, and of what nature is it?
For the mind is as restless as the feathers on the body of a peacock struck by the wind. (5)
