How and by what means can the mind—which is as flickering and unsteady as a peacock’s feather struck by the winds—be brought into single-pointed concentration? || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O royal sage, to what happened then to that very Suraghu, who was awakened,
and to Parṇāda (this is another name for Parigha).
This wonderful dialogue.
I shall relate to you this mutual conversation between the two of them, whose minds were awakened and united through their singular concentration on Rāghava.
He, whose self was awakened and concentrated in a single-pointed absorption, went to Rāghava. || 7 ||
There was a king of the Pārasīkas, a slayer of enemy heroes,
renowned by the name Parigha, who was like an iron bar upon his chariot.
The Pārasīkas are a specific region. The pārthiva is a king. In the syandana, or chariot, the parigha serves as the supporting axle-shaft. || 8 ||
O descendant of Raghu, Suraghu became his supreme friend,
just as Mādhava is to Madana when he resides in the Nandana grove.
Mādhava is the spring season. || 9 ||
Once, there occurred a great drought over the entire realm of Parigha,
like that at the end of an eon in this world, born from the fault of the people's evil deeds.
"Avarṣam" means drought. To the question "Is this due to the king's fault?", he replies with the word "prajā" (the subjects). || 10 ||
There, many people perished, their lives emaciated by hunger, like successions of living beings in a blazing forest fire. (11)
Seeing that suffering, Parigha fell into incomparable despair;
he abandoned his entire kingdom instantly, just as a traveler leaves behind a burnt village.
Incapable of remedying the destruction of his subjects and possessing a dispassionate mind,
he went to the forest to perform austerities like a great sage clad in deerskin.
The lords of sages have the deerskin as their primary [attribute]; thus, they are "deerskin lords of sages. || 13 ||
In a certain distant forest unknown even to the inhabitants of the city,
he dwelt with a detached soul, as if in another world.
Others [saw it] in the second world-interval, as if it were the next world; this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 14 ||
Practicing austerities with a tranquil mind and self-controlled, he dwelt in a mountain cave and there subsisted on withered, fallen leaves.
Because of his extreme detachment, he did not even possess a leaf-hut or similar shelter; this is indicated by the phrase "in a cave-dwelling. || 15 ||
Then, for a long time consuming only withered leaves like a fire,
he acquired the name Parṇāda among the ascetics.
That is the iron bar. || 16 ||
From that time forward, this best of royal sages became known as Parṇāda in Jambūdvīpa, renowned throughout the abodes of the sages.
Then, after a thousand years of asceticism performed with a resolute mind,
he attained through the power of practice that knowledge born of self-purification.
Self-composure, purity of mind, and the grace of the Lord—through these, he attained, that is, reached, the knowledge of reality born therefrom. || 18 ||
He became free from dualities, devoid of expectations, with a tranquil mind;
passionless, without worldly attachment, liberated while living, and possessed of awakened intellect. (19)
O virtuous one, he dwelt at will in this monastery of the three worlds together with the Siddhas and Sādhyas, like a swarm of bees among a bed of lotuses.

Sometimes surrounded by Siddhas who have already ascended [to heaven] and Sādhakas who desire to ascend, he, together with Haṃsas, was like a bee (*alir bhramaraḥ*) amidst a lotus pond (*abjinī*) accompanied by swans (*sahaṃsaḥ*). || 20 ||
Once, he reached the palace of King Hemacūḍa, which was constructed of jewels and resembled another peak of Mount Meru.
Hemacūḍa, known as Svarṇajaṭā, was the country of that king Suraghu.
There, those two former friends paid honor to one another;
they were now fulfilled, having understood all that is to be known, and had emerged from the womb of ignorance.
Samsara has ignorance as its essence; therefore, the meaning is that those who have emerged from it are liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 22 ||
"Ah! Indeed, my auspicious and purifying deeds have now borne fruit, since I have obtained you!"—thus they spoke to one another. (23)
"By auspicious good deeds"—the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). || 23 ||
With their bodies embraced and their forms gladdened by one another,
the two sat upon a single seat like the moon and the sun upon a mountain.
Parigha said:
My mind has attained supreme bliss through the sight of you;
like the orb of the moon emerging from the water, my heart has become cool.

The separate mention of "cetas" and "manas" is intended to highlight the distinction that the manifestation of bliss occurs when the power of consciousness (citiśakti) predominates, whereas the subsiding of suffering occurs when the power of reflection (mananaśakti) predominates. || 25 ||
Natural love, when separated from its object, spreads into a hundred branches, like a tree with unbroken roots on the bank of a pond. (26)
It should be understood as being like a tree whose roots are uncut but whose branches are severed. || 26 ||
O virtuous one, remembering those confidential conversations, those playful gestures, and that former conduct, I rejoice again and again.
Confident and filled with trust; those former conversations concerning the stories of pleasure and pain. || 27 ||
O sinless one, this knowledge, born from the grace of the Supreme Self, has been obtained by me through the favor of Māṇḍavya, just as it was known by you.

Just as this knowledge was obtained by you through the grace of Māṇḍavya, so too have I attained this knowledge through the grace of the Supreme Self, the Lord, who was propitiated by my ascetic penance. || 28 ||
Are you free from suffering today? Are you at rest, like the sovereign of the earth upon Mount Meru, the supreme cause? (29)
Have you perhaps found rest in Brahman—the supreme cause, characterized as the material source of the world’s manifestation—through the ripening of the successive stages [of spiritual practice]? (29)
O most virtuous one, does clarity arise in your mind through delighting in the self, like the water of a lake in autumn? (30)
Purity (prasāda) is the state of being unobstructed by rajas and tamas. || 30 ||
O fortunate lord of men, do you perform all necessary duties with a gaze that is both very gracious and profound? (31)
You perform those very duties and actions which must necessarily be done because they are for the welfare of all people. || 31 ||
Are the wise people in your lands free from mental and physical ailments, well-provided with rice, and dwelling without the fever of distress? (32)
The people are the multitudes of subjects. || 32 ||
I hope that your earth, like the *phalinī* creeper bent down with its abundant fruit, sustains your subjects exceedingly through the fullness of its harvests. (33)

Does the earth— the broad ground, abounding in fruit such as excellent crops, and bent down by its harvests like a wish-fulfilling creeper— support, sustain, and nourish your subjects exceedingly well with an abundance of fruits at the proper times, fulfilling their various desired objects?
I trust that your purifying fame has spread to the ends of the earth like the lattice of rays of the moon, appearing as if it were a mass of frost. (34)
Like the cage of rays, that is, the network of beams, of the moon. || 34 ||

I hope that these quarters have been made free of gaps by you through your multitude of virtues, just as the lands surrounding a lotus pond are filled with its waters so that no space remains for lotus stalks to grow.

Have the quarters of the sky been made free of gaps—that is, filled—by you with your multitude of virtues and glories, like the beds of lotus stalks (*bisas*) submerged within a pond are filled by the water of the lake? (35)
I hope that in every village, your young maidens, rejoicing in the corners of the fields during the harvest season, sing of your gladdening fame. (36)
The corners of the rice fields—the junctions of the four sides—are the locations of the couches situated therein.
"Hṛṣyantiḥ" and "hṛṣyantyaḥ" [are used]; this is a Vedic variation of case endings. || 36 ||
Is all well with your grain, your wealth, and your possessions; and with your servants, your wives, your sons, and your cities? (37)
Is this vine of your body free from mental and physical ailments?
May it bear the fruit known as merit, which is proclaimed to be attained both in this world and the next. (38)

In this context, rites such as the Kārīrī are enjoined as having results in this life (aihika), while rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma are enjoined as having results in the hereafter (pāralaukika). || 38 ||
Is your mind free from attachment toward those serpents of sense-objects, which are pleasant at first sight but are in fact eternal enemies? (39)
Does your mind abide with detachment toward the serpents of the sense-objects? Does it so abide? (39)
"Alas! For a very long time we have been separated;
by the power of time, we have now been reunited once more, like the spring season and the mountain slope. (40)
O friend, those states of happiness and suffering born of union and separation, which are not seen by living beings, do not exist in this world. (41)
The states of pleasure and pain arising from union with desired persons and from separation from them. || 41 ||
In this same way, having reached a state of difference throughout these exceedingly long stages of life, we have once again become united; for the operation of destiny is indeed manifold.

They have come to, that is, attained, a state of separation from one another. The ordinance—that is, the wondrous and marvelous play—of destiny (niyati), which follows the karma of living beings and is the will of the Lord (īśvara), is extraordinary. || 42 ||
Suraghu said: "O Blessed One, who indeed can understand the course of this destiny, which is as profound and wondrous as the path of a serpent?"
Rejoicing in the meaning expressed by Parigha, Suraghū also spoke to him in the same way, beginning with the words "O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*).
[The phrase] *daivikyāḥ* means of that which is divine, namely, of the nature of the will of the Lord (*īśvara*). || 43 ||
Having cast aside the distance and all far-off conditions, you and I have once again been united today; oh, what is impossible for Fate? 44.
"Having thus removed and separated [them] as being distant in terms of space and distant in terms of time, in such states. || 44 ||
"O Great Being, today we stand exceedingly well;
through the merit of your arrival, we have attained supreme purity. (45)
Behold how, for us whose sins have been destroyed by your arrival, the trees of merit have borne fruit in such a way that we are no longer distressed. (46)

Thus, through the nature of such concentration of mind, it has borne fruit in such a way that we are no longer agitated; being liberated from all agitation, we have become those who have accomplished what was to be done. || 46 ||
"O royal sage, all our prosperities were already established in the city;
by your arrival today, they have branched out into a hundredfold. (47)
"Having a hundred branches" means, in other words, being ready to bear fruit in every respect. || 47 ||
O one of great majesty, your sweet speech and your holy glance scatter a bounty on all sides, like a heap of elixirs.
For association with the virtuous is indeed equal to the supreme state. || 48 ||

O magnanimous one, your virtuous speech, your glance, and your very sight scatter and, as it were, rain down a multitude of elixirs and nectars. For the company and meeting with the holy is equal to the supreme state; that is to say, it is equivalent to the attainment of the bliss of liberation. || 48 ||

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Encounter between Suraghu and Parigha," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Meeting of Suraghu and Parigha," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The sixty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, with such confidential conversation as this, they remained there for a long time.
Standing there, he who was named Ayudha spoke with words imbued with ancient affection.

When the veil of ignorance is destroyed and one abides in the eternal refuge of Consciousness, the constant and singular state of meditative absorption (samādhi) of the wise is described here. || 1 ||
The name of which is "Abhidhā" [the smiter]; that iron club is called "Āyudhābhidha," meaning it has the name "Smiter of Weapons. || 1 ||
Parigha said:
"O sinless protector of the earth, whatever action is performed within this web of worldly existence leads to happiness for one whose mind is concentrated, but not for another."

To examine whether one who knows reality will describe the gradations of happiness in both worldly activity and meditative absorption, or not, [the author] first reveals his own experience with the words "Whatever... Is there perhaps for another— an ignorant person— a supreme state of rest free from all volitional construction?
You practice the concentration that is the highest tranquility and the supreme good. || 3 ||
Having thus disclosed his own experience, and desiring to know whether the experience of others is likewise corroborated or not,

he asks— "Kaccit"— thereby demonstrating, as it were, an increase in his repose within *samādhi*. [He asks] regarding the supreme pacification of the sufferings of distraction and the superiority [of this state] over worldly pleasures.
It is more praiseworthy; or, due to a grammatical anomaly, there is neuter gender in the sense of a general category.
Suraghu said:
O Blessed One, tell me this: what is that supreme peace, free from all mental constructs, which is the highest good? For what indeed is called "samādhi"? || 4 ||

For one who perceives that all action is bliss for a concentrated mind, it is entirely untenable to observe a superiority in resting within meditative absorption or to raise an objection based on the acceptance of a distinction between conventional and meditative states; thus, my own experience is indeed in agreement with this experience.

With this intention, Suraghu— accepting for the time being that "the highest tranquility free from conceptual construction is the supreme good" because such a portion of what was stated is possible even within the nature of the self (*ātman*)—
practiced meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which is the locus of rest; [this is said] regarding the mind, which is the cause of non-rest for that which is to be pacified through absorption.
Thinking that [the former view] is impossible precisely because it has been refuted, he objects with the words "this" (etad).

"Tell me this: that the highest good is the supreme tranquility devoid of all mental constructs; for that is logical. The meaning is: for what purpose do you say that meditative absorption (samādhi) must be practiced? || 4 ||
O Great-souled One, for one who knows, whether constantly standing still or engaged in worldly activity, when indeed could he ever be of uncollected mind, and who indeed could such a person be? (5)

Who indeed is that knower of reality, even while engaged in worldly activity, and of what nature is he? Since his very essence is the eternally unobscured non-dual consciousness, when could he ever be of an unconcentrated mind? The meaning is: never at all. || 5 ||
But those whose minds are eternally awakened, even while performing worldly activities,
remain ever established in the single reality of the Self and are always in a state of perfect meditative absorption.

If, however, you consider that samādhi is simply the state of abiding in the nature of the immovable Self, then since that exists always, there would be nothing at all to be practiced; thus he says: "Eternally" (nityam). || 6 ||
Even for one who has assumed the lotus posture and joined his palms in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, what is *samādhi* and how can it exist for one whose very nature is restless? (7)

If you consider me ignorant, even then the instruction on *samādhi* is untenable; with this intention, he says "bound" (*baddha*). How? By what means? The meaning is: because there is no familiarity with that very object upon which the mind is to be concentrated. || 7 ||
O Blessed One, the realization of reality, which is a fire that burns away the grass of all desires,
is what is designated by the term "samādhi," and not merely remaining in silence.

The meaning is that "realization of reality" (tattvāvabodha) refers to the establishment of the self in its ultimate nature through the complete subversion of all objects of desire along with their roots; this is because of the etymological derivation [of the term] as "samādhi. || 8 ||
O virtuous one, that which is concentrated, eternally satisfied, and perceives the meaning of things as they truly are, is called supreme wisdom by the wise under the term "samādhi. (9)
Supreme wisdom is of the nature of the vision of the Self, which is uncontradicted. || 9 ||
Unperturbed, free from egoism, and not following after dualities—that which possesses a form even more stable than Mount Meru is designated by the term "samādhi. (10)
He describes that very [state] in terms of its fruit with two verses beginning with "akṣubdhā": || 10 ||
Free from anxiety, having attained the desired, and devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted—the complete movement of the mind is designated by the term "samādhi. (11)
From the moment his mind became endowed with ultimate awakening,
from that time forth, the concentration of that Great-Souled One remained uninterrupted.
But with the intention that "she has already been accomplished by me, so she need not be practiced," he says, beginning with "yataḥ" (since), etc. || 12 ||
For once the mind has become awakened, meditative absorption (samādhi) is not severed again, just as a lotus fiber drawn out by a child cannot be pulled back from afar.
"Just as a lotus fiber, when pulled too far, snaps from the hand of a playing child—this is the example by way of contrast. || 13 ||
Just as the inexhaustible sun ceases from its shining at the end of a full day,
so too our wisdom does not cease from the contemplation of reality until the end of life.

[Objection: "But surely, when the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of Brahman is interrupted, there would be an interruption of samādhi due to the emergence from it (*vyutthāna*). To this, he says: [the word] "ceases" is to be connected [to the previous statement]. Likewise, wisdom (*prajñā*), which is the mental modification in the form of Brahman, does not cease until the end of life—that is, until the attainment of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*)—because it is the illumination of reality (*tattvāloka*).
The meaning is that it indeed continues to follow due to the force of firm latent impressions (saṃskāra). || 14 ||
Just as a river is not obstructed by its constant flow of water, so too, through the awakening of the vision of wisdom, it is not obstructed for even a single moment. (15)

With the intention that there is no possibility of the destruction of samādhi—characterized by the cessation of one's own nature—due to the total destruction of ignorance (ajñāna), which veils that very nature, by means of a mental modification (vṛtti) that has arisen once and for all, and because of the subsequent absence of any further veiler, he says: "unceasingly" (ajasram). It is not [the case that it ceases].
It is obstructed by a veil, yet it is not impeded. || 15 ||
Just as time never ceases to forget the movement of its own moments,
so too the intellect of the wise never ceases to forget its own self.

Or, with the intention that because it is the object of supreme love, there is no possibility of forgetting that which has been obtained even once, he says "he does not forget" in two verses. || 16 ||
Just as the wind, moving everywhere, does not forget its course, so too, O wise one, the intellect does not forget that which is to be determined: pure consciousness alone.

Just as the movement of the divisions of time remains constant while accumulating [moments], so too does consciousness— devoid of the object of thought— remain while accumulating various states of being.

With the intention that the very Self, its veils shattered, remains throughout one's life generating a continuous succession of its own modalities (*svākāravṛtti*), he says: "The course" (*gatim*). The "parts" (*kalā*) of time are its forms (*mūrti*), such as the sun and so forth.

And "consciousness" (*cit*) is the manifestation of sentience (*caitanya-sphūrti*); this is a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), like the expression "the head of Rāhu. "Courses" (*gatayaḥ*) refer to the modalities of its own form.
This is a Vedic variation of case endings. || 18 ||
Just as a category of existence devoid of being is not perceived, so too time devoid of the knowledge of the Self is not found by the knower. 19.
Or, with the intention that there is no possibility of interruption because that [consciousness] is the very nature of the living state of awakening, he says:
"Just as... (verse 19).
Just as one who possesses qualities cannot exist in saṃsāra without those qualities, so too one who possesses the Self cannot exist devoid of self-awareness. || 20 ||
With the intention that there is no possibility of interruption because it is of the very nature of that [consciousness], just as heat is the nature of fire, he says: "It is not possible. (20)
I am always fully awakened; I am always stainless;
I am always peaceful in nature; I am always composed in meditation.
By what means is a distinction produced in my samādhi, or how could it be?
Since it is non-different from the Self, its nature as the eternal Self is forever constant.
"Differentiation" (bheda) means separation. The meaning is: by reason of its non-distinction from my own nature, which is samādhi.
"The state of being the existent Self" (sadātmatā) means that existence (sattā) is established. || 22 ||
Therefore, at no time has my mind been devoid of meditative absorption,
nor has it ever been merely concentrated, because it arises solely from the reality of the Self.

If you think that the mind exists, then it must always be in a state of meditative absorption; if, however, it does not exist, then let there be no absorption either, since the cause of distraction would never even arise—with this intention, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). || 23 ||
The Self is all-pervading, eternal, and indeed everything in every way; for what could possibly be non-concentration, and what is traditionally known as concentration? (24)
The great ones, whose intellects are eternally concentrated and who are perfectly equanimous, abide free from the distinctions of the transformation of effects;
therefore, by means of the dissolution of the distinction between the unconcentrated and the concentrated—
Where indeed is that eternally risen proliferation of supreme speech? || 25 ||

By those whose intellect is fixed through the correct refutation of [the notion of] distinctness, for that reason, your elaborate discourse—which proceeds by means of breaking down the distinction between the non-concentrated and the concentrated—where indeed, in what object, could it possibly find its final resting place? Therefore, the meaning is that it has been uttered in vain. || 25 ||

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Ascertainment of Samādhi," in the Section on Quiescence (*Upaśama-prakaraṇa*) within the *Deva-mokṣopāya* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 62.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Ascertainment of Samādhi," in the section on Quiescence (*upaśama*) within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The sixty-third canto.
Parigha said:
"O King, you have surely awakened; you have attained that supreme state."
With an inner heart that is perfectly cooled, you shine like the full moon.
Having examined this matter with the iron club (of logic), that sage, being thus praised,
described at length his own innate state of existence right here.
Surely, by your very certainty, you are an awakened knower of reality; or rather, through my own investigation, I have realized that you are awakened,
for you are filled with the honey of bliss and embraced by supreme splendor (or, according to another reading, "by the splendor filled with the honey of bliss").
Cool, smooth, and sweet, you shine like a lotus.
Filled with honey—the nectar characterized by bliss—you shine like a *rājīva*, a lotus.
Stainless, expansive, full, profound, and with your intentions made manifest,
you shine like the ocean when it is released from the play of the coastal winds.
Because of his very purity, his inner disposition, internal region, and mind were manifest and clearly visible. || 3 ||
Transparent, filled with bliss, with the cloud of egoism destroyed,
you shine clearly, vast and profound, like the autumnal sky.
Everywhere you appear composed; everywhere you are fully contented;
everywhere you are free from passion, O King; everywhere you shine resplendently.
In all cases, regarding objects that are desired or undesired. || 5 ||
Having reached the further shore of discerning the essential from the non-essential through your great intelligence,
you know all this exactly as it exists, without exception.
Delimitation is the investigation and determination; one who has gone to the further shore of that [realizes] the nature of Brahman, which is undivided and unlimited. || 6 ||

Your body remains established as one who knows the reality of the discernment between existence and non-existence, whose disposition is gladdened, and who is free from the agitation of the states of coming and going.

The term ending with "tattvajña" is an address (vocative). Alternatively, there is a word-break as "uditāśayam. It is free from the coming and going—that is, the ascending and descending—of that state which causes them, namely the condition of attachment to enjoyment, and from the restlessness induced by it.
[Verse 7: Like the ocean [is separated] from the shore by a substance as if by a non-substance, as if by an internal island.
O handsome one, you are satisfied for the sake of never again falling into decay.

Since no object exists that is an ultimate reality, you are satisfied in your own station, in your own majesty—like an ocean with its own nectar—by means of such an entity as yourself, abiding within your own self. || 8 ||
Suraghu said:
"O Sage, there is no object whatsoever in which there is anything for us to accept;
whatever is seen here, all that is nothing at all."

Confirming and approving all that had been said through logical arguments, Suraghu spoke, beginning with the words "Not that," and so forth: "There is nothing whatsoever"—meaning, there is nothing false. || 9 ||
And since there is nothing to be accepted, what indeed could there be that is to be rejected?
Without a counter-correlate—that which is to be excluded—how can something be called "rejection"? (10)

For "abandonment" (*hāna*) is the relinquishing of what has been appropriated (*upātta*); its counterpart (*pratiyogin*) is that which is opposed to abandonment, namely appropriation (*upādāna*), which is to be excluded by abandonment and is perishable.

What can be said [of that which is] not to be abandoned through such relinquishing? The meaning is: nothing at all, because all entities are insubstantial (*tuccha*) and because [abandonment] is non-substantial in terms of time.
For a long time, my mental states have been utterly exhausted and trivial.

[Objection: "Surely that which is insubstantial (tuccha) is to be abandoned; why should that which is substantial (atuccha) not be accepted? To this he says: "Because of its insubstantiality" (tucchatvāt).
As they have said: "A king who was once bound is satisfied with merely a village; yet the same man, when previously complete [in power], does not highly value his kingdom. (11)
In this world, it is solely by virtue of place and time that the empty becomes non-empty, while the non-empty becomes empty; therefore, the wise should avoid both censure and praise. (12)

The phrase "it is thought here" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Therefore, he says "in what is to be avoided," meaning that nothing at all is to be censured or praised by one who possesses a mind that perceives neither the trivial nor the non-trivial. || 12 ||
In this world, praise and blame arise from passion; passion, in turn, is directed toward that which is desired.
And by one of noble intellect, even toward a highly exalted object of desire, [passion is not stirred]. (13)
In the three worlds, women, mountains, oceans, and rows of forests—all these beings are empty of substance; in reality, there is no essence here at all.
The word *vastu* emphasizes the state of being (*bhāva*); the meaning is that they are empty of reality. || 14 ||
In this dilapidated world composed of flesh, bone, wood, earth, and jewels—devoid of anything desirable and utterly empty—what indeed is there to be desired? || 15 ||
Internally, it consists of flesh and bone; externally, it consists of wood, clay, jewels, and so forth. Here, the word "jewel" (ratna) refers to stone. || 15 ||
When desire has ceased, there is the destruction of hatred and passion,
just as light and heat vanish when the splendor of day has departed.
Enough with these excessively extensive elaborations of speech; here, for the sake of happiness, this one view alone is appropriate:
a mind that is equanimous and whose passions have been stilled.
If that [joy] is joyful, it is the unsurpassed foundation. || 17 ||

If everything is indeed essence-less, then what is it that ought to be cultivated as the essence? To this he says: "Enough," and so forth. If the mind has its flavor stilled, is entirely free from disease, is even—devoid of the unevenness of distraction—and rejoices within itself in the Self alone, then that indeed is the supreme foundation.
The meaning is that this very vision of rest alone is always fit to be cultivated for the sake of happiness. || 17 ||

Thus ends the sixty-third canto, titled "The Resolve of Suraghu and Parigha," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki and spoken by the Divine Messenger (*devadūta*).
Thus [ends] the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa* (The Illumination of the Essential Meaning of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa), in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa*.
The sixty-third canto, titled "Suraghu’s Resolve Regarding the Iron Bar."
The sixty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus reflected upon this delusion of the world, Suraghu and Parigha—
Having honored one another, they were both satisfied and departed, each intent upon their own respective duties.
Those means by which one skilled in means is not afflicted by mental defects, and by which the self is extracted from suffering—those means are here proclaimed. (1)
Having reflected in the manner thus described. || 1 ||
O Raghava, having heard that very [teaching] which is the supreme cause of awakening, become clearly established through this very awakening. (2)

Having heard that cause of awakening, which consists of the aforementioned dialogue, the first *eva* (only) is used to indicate that merely hearing this much was sufficient for his realization. The second [instance of *eva*] is intended to illuminate that this very realization, once firmly established, is sufficient for the attainment of the supreme state. || 2 ||
When the dark cloud of egoism dissolves in the sky of the heart through supreme wisdom, sharpened by the steady investigation of the wise, [the self shines forth]. (3)

When, through deliberation with wise and learned men, and by means of one's own steady and unwavering inquiry, the dark cloud characterized by egoism—which has become sharp and attained a state of keen intensity within the firmament of the heart—begins to dissolve; || 3 ||
When the autumn season has arrived—agreeable to all the world, fruitful, gladdening, pure, and expansive—the mind [is likewise]. (4)
The qualifiers beginning with "samasta" (all) should also be applied to the autumn season. || 4 ||
One abides in the Supreme Self, the space of consciousness, which is the object of meditation, the refuge, the easy path, and the perfection of all bliss, and which is perfectly serene.
She is the refuge because she turns back all misfortunes. || 5 ||
He who is always absorbed in the inner self, always inward-turned and happy,
and constantly contemplating consciousness, is not afflicted by the sorrows of the mind.

One whose nature is introverted is abundant in the singular inquiry into the Self; he is inward-turned and devoid of attachment to the external; his continuous reflection consists of the repeated and respectful savoring of consciousness alone. (6)
Even while being intensely devoted to worldly affairs and filled with passion and aversion,
he does not incur internal blemish, just as a lotus situated in water remains unstained.
Though it is imagined by the deluded to consist of passion and hatred, as if abounding in passion and hatred, [it is not so]. || 7 ||
The sage who possesses right knowledge, who is pure and whose mind is inwardly tranquil,
is not troubled by the mind, just as the king of beasts is not harassed by an elephant.

The mind of the wise person never takes refuge solely in enjoyments nor becomes dejected; for the mind of the wise is like a great tree in the Nandana grove, which does not falter even amidst ill-fated trees.
The "evil tree" is a tree of poisonous thorns; for indeed, because the mind of the wise man is a great body—meaning it is free from desire even for a mere fragment of petty pleasure. (9)
Just as a person who is detached from birth and death does not suffer,
so too the mind that has fully understood all ignorance is not afflicted by suffering.

Just as a dispassionate man is not pained by the birth and death of his wife even though he might otherwise be lustful, so too, having investigated thoroughly, the mind of the wise person—who has realized that all objects of perception, such as the senses, the body, and so forth, are merely ignorance and false delusion—does not become afflicted; this is the meaning. || 10 ||

O virtuous one, one who has fully understood the delusion of the mind through its manifestation as the arising of worldly existence is not touched by sin, just as the surface of the sky is not touched by dust.

He states that he has no connection even with the sin that is the cause of future suffering, saying: "by thorough knowledge," etc. In the world, which is the sphere of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), there arises from the notion of being an agent (*kartṛtva-abhimāna*) that which is born of worldly existence;
by means of that, through the self, [he is free] from *enas*, i.e., sin. || 11 ||
This very [knowledge] is the great medicine thoroughly understood through the comprehension of ignorance;
it is like a lamp for the darkness of the disease spread by ignorance. (12)

The meaning is that for this widespread disease characterized by the world-form of ignorance, the great medicine is precisely the knowledge born of inquiry which correctly realizes that the world is nothing but ignorance. || 12 ||
For as soon as ignorance is thoroughly understood, it is utterly destroyed; indeed, it vanishes like a realm of enjoyment experienced in a dream. 13.
Just as the ground for experiencing that dream is exhausted by the dream itself once it is fully recognized as "this is a dream," so it is here. || 13 ||
Even while intent on worldly affairs, the virtuous person whose mind is inwardly attached and whose intellect is unified is not touched by sin, just as water does not touch the eye of a fish.

The vision—the eye—of fish is not touched by water; the meaning is that if it were so touched, those whose eyes are thus covered would have no such functional activity as seeing while in the water. || 14 ||
When the light of consciousness has dawned, the night of ignorance is utterly destroyed;
the intellect of the wise man, having attained supreme bliss, shines forth. 15.
Śemuṣī is wisdom (prajñā). || 15 ||
When the sleep of ignorance has been stilled, a person awakened by the sun of knowledge attains that enlightenment by which he is never again deluded.
"Jñāna" is that by which something is known; it is the scripture. Awakened by the sun in the form of that [scripture], he attained such an awakening. || 16 ||
Those days are lived joyfully, and those sequences of ritual actions are truly blessed,
in which the moonlight of consciousness arises within the sky of the heart from the risen moon of the Self.

Now he praises the Vidyā with the verse beginning "dināni" (days). In the word "jīvyate," the suffix *la* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). In "dināni," the accusative case is used according to the rule for expressing the complete connection of time or distance (*kāladhvanor atyantasaṃyoge*), and not in the sense of an object (*karmaṇi*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "in those days, the moonlight of consciousness (*cijjyotsnā*) gladdens—that is, shines brilliantly—in the sky of the heart. || 17 ||
The person who has crossed over delusion through constant contemplation on his own self attains inner coolness, just as the moon does by means of its own nectar.
Those friends, those scriptures, and those very days—through them, the splendor of dispassion arises, and from them, the awakening of the self-mind clearly emerges. (19)

The remainder [of the meaning] is that from those causes such as friends and so forth, the emergence of the mind—characterized by a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of the Self and accompanied by the radiance of dispassion—is clearly accomplished. || 19 ||
Those wretched ones, who have not rid themselves of sin and who are indifferent toward the vision of the Self, grieve for a long time as miserable creepers in the jungle of birth.
*Helā* means disregard; that is to say, indifference. [This refers to] those whose sin (*enaḥ*) has not departed—that is, whose evil has not been exhausted. || 20 ||
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope, greedily longing for the bait of enjoyments, its form worn out by old age, and distressed by sighs of grief. (21)

From this point onward, all the words ending in the accusative case are to be connected with the phrase in the ninth verse, "the bull Jīva should cause [them] to cross. *Ulapas* are a specific kind of grass. || 21 ||
[He saw] one who bore the heavy burden of accumulated suffering, whose life was like a forest of births, who was smeared with the mud of evil deeds, and who lay in the pond of delusion. (22)
By whom the great burden of suffering has been specifically carried. || 22 ||

Bitten by the swarm of the stinging insect of passion, dragged by the excellent rope of craving, dwelling in the abode of the merchant of the mind, and rendered motionless by the bonds of kinship. (23)
With the leather thong of the triple-folded nose-rope, he stands in the dwelling of the merchant characterized by the mind—
that is, in the abode and convention characterized by his commands— and rendered motionless and unable to move by the bonds characterized by kinsmen;
he is submerged and emerging from the foul mud of the decrepit old age of sons and wives.
Exhausted, deprived of rest, and broken down upon the long path. || 24 ||
In the foul mire of cow dung. || 24 ||
Exhausted by coming and going, wandering through the forest of saṃsāra, he has not found the cool shade and is tormented by intense heat. (25)
Resplendent in form yet wretched, his senses assailed by external objects;
overcome by the ringing of the bell of karma, he is struck by the blows of his own misdeeds. (26)
Shining outwardly in mere form, but wretched within;

overcome and mounted upon by the external senses, such as the eyes and so forth; by the term "karma," the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that incite one toward optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) are indicated; it is overcome by the sound of bells characterized by those [rites].
It has been whirled around. || 26 ||
Bearing the yoke of the revolving cycle of manifestation and concealment,
it wallows in the vast forest of ignorance with its limbs utterly exhausted.
The yoke is the burden of the wheel-turning; for it is that which revolves along with the wheels of the cart while bearing them.
[He saw him] perpetually submerged in his own misfortune, sinking down, destitute, with limbs exhausted by the burden of karma, and uttering piteous cries. || 28 ||
He was crying out piteously, as if in deep distress. || 28 ||
O Rāma, exerting the utmost effort, one should by force rescue this bull of a living being from the pond of saṃsāra for a long time. (29)
The meaning is that, having applied supreme effort for a long time, one should cause [others] to cross over by means of the power of knowledge. || 29 ||
When the mind has been extinguished through the observation of reality, the individual soul (jīva) is never born again;
at that time, it has crossed over the ocean of existence.
He prevents the suspicion that one who has been rescued might sink back into the mud by saying "the reality" (tattva). || 30 ||
O Rāma, through association with those of great power, a clear method for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra is obtained, just as a boat is obtained from a navigator.
With the intention that the attainment of the knowledge of the means for crossing over is accomplished by approaching a true guru, he says: "O you of great majesty" (mahānubhāva). || 31 ||
In that desert-like land where there is no tree of a virtuous person— neither bearing fruit nor providing cool shade— a wise man should not dwell.
The region is like a desert; he dwells in that desert-like region. || 32 ||
O Rāma, one rests deeply for a moment under the campaka tree of the virtuous man, which possesses the cool shade of affectionate speech and the blossoms of a smile.
Regarding the *campaka* tree, which possesses the characteristics of a virtuous person (*sujana*), the adjectives should be applied as common to both. || 33 ||
In the absence of that [discernment], which bestows the attainment of the heat of great delusion,
a wise person should not sleep here with only a slight degree of discernment born.
In the absence of that—that is, in the absence of resting in the attainment of one's own true nature—one should not sleep here in this cycle of existence. || 34 ||
For the self alone is the friend of the self; thus, one should uplift the self by means of the self.
One should not cast oneself into the mirey ocean of rebirth through arrogance. (35)
Thus, by this means, one should uplift oneself; this is the meaning. [One should not do so] through arrogance—that is, through the pride of identifying with the body.
(35) "What is this? How has it come to be? What is its root? What is its destruction? Thus should the wise diligently investigate bodily suffering. (36)

Why is there destruction, and what is it that is destroyed? One must observe that suffering is dependent upon the body; it should be scrutinized by one's own intellect and investigated with the aid of the scriptures and virtuous people. The two words "iti" (thus) are intended to indicate the multiplicity of the methods for investigating and the objects to be investigated. || 36 ||
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor scriptures, nor kinsmen can assist men when they are submerged and seek to lift themselves up from that state. (37)
The treatises are those that are not treatises on the self. || 37 ||
Having reflected upon something together with the mind alone—his constant companion and friend—the self becomes fully uplifted. (38)
What, then, does it assist? To this he says: "by the mind alone," meaning by a friend who is completely pure.
By means of the boat of the vision of reality, which is born from self-reflection through the efforts of dispassion and practice, one crosses the ocean of worldly existence. (39)
Though constantly pitied by people and burned by evil desires, one should not despise oneself; rather, one should uplift it with diligence.
One should neither despise nor neglect [them]. || 40 ||
One should rescue the elephant of the living being, which is sunk in the mire of birth, from its great tethering post of egoism, with the rope of craving and the intoxication of the mind.
An *ālāna* is a pillar for tying an elephant; [the world] is submerged in the mire of the *jambāla*. || 41 ||
O Raghava, by this much alone is the self saved:
that delusion is cast aside and the ego is wiped away. (42)
Delusion is ignorance of one's own self. || 42 ||
By this alone, the true path clearly attains its manifestation:
that the ego-sense is severed once the web of the mind has been cast aside. (43)

The path is the search for the True Supreme Self; it is the investigation culminating in awakening. Within that [path], there is the manifestation—that is, clear perception—of the web of mental constructions born from attachment to external and internal objects. (43)
By this alone, O Lord of Gods, the Supreme Self is understood:
when the body is regarded as being equal to wood or a clod of earth. (44)
With the intention that even there, the primary task is the abandonment of the egoistic conceit regarding the body—which is so difficult to relinquish—he says: "By this much alone.
When the cloud of egoism has perished, the sun of consciousness is seen;
thereafter, through its transformation, that supreme state is attained. (45)
Through the transformation of that vision— that is, through the ripening of the stages or by attaining the state of the sun of consciousness—
just as there is the spontaneous perception of light upon the total destruction of darkness,
so too is there the spontaneous perception of the Self upon the cessation of the ego-sense.
The word "is accomplished" is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. || 46 ||
When the ego-sense has completely perished, that state born of bliss and joy is a state of fullness; it should be cultivated with diligent effort. (47)
Blissful joy is the repose in unsurpassed bliss; arising from that, it is the non-conceptual state manifested as having that very nature.
Resembling the full ocean, it does not come within the range of our perception; it admits no comparison and does not pursue worldly passion. (48)
He describes that very [state] with the words beginning "ever-full" (paripūrṇa) and so forth. "Coloring" (rañjana) refers to the superimposition of the visible object. || 48 ||
If the fourth state (turyā) is attained—that which is merely the spark of the light of consciousness having reached stability—then it is compared to that [vision]. || 49 ||
The meaning is that it is compared to itself alone; there is no other simile for it. || 49 ||
That state, whose similarity [to deep sleep] is not yet fully reached, is characterized as being like deep sleep;
it is full in form and expansive like the splendor of the sky.

By what illustration, then, might there be a possibility of that? He says: "not far" (*adūra*). This means: because of a similarity based on proximity in the aspect of being free from distraction (*nirvikṣepatva*). It is perceived in close vicinity (*upa*). The meaning is: by this method, if it were [merely] the veil of ignorance (*ajñānāvaraṇa*), then it would not be so; rather, it would be the fourth state itself (*turyāvasthā*)—thus is the sense. || 50 ||
When the ego of the mind dissolves, that supreme bliss which arises, abiding within all states of being, is the body of the Supreme Lord. 51.

He states that just as when a jar is destroyed, the space within it becomes the great space (mahākāśa), so too, upon the dissolution of the limiting adjuncts of the mind and ego, the true nature of the Self—which is the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃpada)—is established as being identical with the referent of the term "that" (tatpada): "The mind... (verse 51).
She is herself perfected through yoga, occurring not far from deep sleep;
she is not accessible by words, O Rāma, but is experienced here within the heart alone.
The meaning is that it is experienced as if right within the heart, not far from deep sleep and indeed close at hand; there is no means of defining it other than one's own direct experience. || 52 ||
Without experience, the reality of sugar and the like is not experienced;
without experience, the form of the self is not experienced either. (53)

Just as there is no means of knowledge other than direct experience for the cognition of the specific nature of a cow or the like—such as its broken-hoofedness and so forth—so it is with the Self as well; thus he says: "direct experience" (anubhūtim). The "form of the Self" (ātmano rūpam) refers to its ultimate reality (paramārthasvarūpam).
The particle "ca" (and) has the sense of "also" (api). || 53 ||
When the mind remains firm within, this entire infinite reality of the Self is established inside;
when external [perceptions] have been stilled, one becomes the very soul of all that moves and is stationary.
The God of gods is indeed experienced by oneself.
If all this is indeed the reality of the Self alone, then how is it experienced? To this he says: "Firmly...

When the mind has been stilled regarding external objects and remains motionless, firmly transformed into a state of uniformity (aikarasya) with the inner inward-facing Self—like milk and water mixed together—the Self of all moving and non-moving beings becomes manifest as the inward-facing one.

The meaning is that the God of the gods—the eye and other senses—is Himself the illuminator as the witness; He is indeed directly experienced, so one should not entertain any doubt in this matter. || 54 ||
Following that, there is the destruction of the latent impressions of sense objects; following that, the supreme, auspicious, and manifest light;
and following that, by virtue of equanimity, [one abides] in one's own true nature.
The transformation of the great ones is of an inconceivable nature. || 55 ||
Thus, when there is self-experience on the fourth stage,

following that, upon the fifth stage, there occurs the absolute destruction of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding sense objects; thereafter, on the sixth stage, the auspicious supreme goal of human life manifests for one's own self without any effort.
The manifest light, which is the experience of the state of eternal fullness, is accomplished; thereafter,
on the seventh stage, due to the equality of samādhi and non-samādhi, there occurs the cessation of absolute disparity.
The transformation into a single flavor of bliss, like a mass of sea salt dissolved within the ocean, is accomplished;

yet that [state] is of an inconceivable nature even for the great ones such as Brahmā and others, because of its lack of measurable limit. This is the meaning according to the Śruti: "From which words turn back, not having attained it, along with the mind. || 55 ||

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction," in the Section on Tranquility (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) within the Means to Liberation (*mokṣopāya*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the "Instruction" in the Section on Tranquility of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The sixty-fourth canto, titled "Nāma."
The sixty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
If the Self is not beheld after cutting through the mind with the mind itself, [then it remains unperceived].
Having abandoned the notions of "mine" and "I," O lotus-eyed one! (1)
There, on the mountain named Sahya, the hermitage of Atri is described;
therein is told the sequence of the birth, deeds, and the arising of grief for Vilāsa and Bhāsa. (1)

Intending to introduce the narrative titled *Bhāsavilāsa* on the meaning that the succession of sufferings such as grief and delusion is difficult to ward off when one neglects the means for seeing the Self, he says: "By the mind alone... The connection with what follows is: if [the Self] is not beheld, then this worldly suffering does not set, just as the sun depicted in a painting does not set.
The suffering of the world does not set, like the sun depicted in a painting;
calamity arrives with endlessness, as vast as the great ocean.
The state of being infinite in calamity results in its being immeasurable. || 2 ||
Again and again it approaches, caused by the waves of worldly existence; the monsoon of saṃsāra is agitated and dark as a cloud or deepest gloom.
Darkened by clouds and deepest darkness, the rainy season—the time of the rains—is characterized by the cycle of worldly existence. || 3 ||
In this very context, they cite this ancient history: the dialogue between two friends, Bhāsa and Vilāsa, on the ridge of the Sahya mountain.
Of two friends or two enemies, and of two with pure minds. || 4 ||
There is a mountain that has conquered the sky with its height, the surface of the earth with its pedestal, and the netherworld with its base; it is a conqueror of the three worlds.
By "pīṭha" is meant the foothill region; by "tala," the portion of the base that has entered into the interior of the earth. The word "jita" means one who has overcome or surpassed others. || 5 ||
Filled with countless flowers, possessing countless pure waterfalls,
containing treasures guarded by Guhyakas, it is named Sahya and possesses unbearable brilliance.
That in which the luster of jewels and other such things exists, which is unbearable and obstructs the range of vision.
With its golden slopes filled with clusters of pearls and walls radiant as the sun, it was as brilliant as the temples of a celestial elephant.

With walls radiant with the rays of sun-gems and other jewels, and with shining embankments; this remains the same even if the reading is "pāṭalabhittibhiḥ" (with pale-red walls). With golden slopes, ridges, flanks, and cheeks—the plural number is used here because it denotes a class. || 7 ||

In some places there was a downpour of flower-clusters; in others, it was spread with the finest minerals; in some places there was the essence of blossoming lakes; and in others, it consisted of rocks abounding in jewels.
It was spread with the finest minerals, such as yellow orpiment, realgar, red ochre, and others.
Thus it resounded with the roar of waterfalls here,
with the whistling of hollow bamboos there, with the howling of mountain winds here, and with the humming of bees there.
"Here, here" is an expression indicating a specific location. || 9 ||
On the mountain peak, the songs of the throngs of apsarases were heard; in the forest, there was the sound of deer and birds;
on the plateau, there were intoxicated clouds; and in the skies, the cries of birds.
On the ridge—that is, on the plateau—wherein the clouds roar as if intoxicated. 10.
Guha is inhabited by Vidyādharas; it is a lotus-pool with bees for its song;
it has the Kirātas for its surrounding shores; and its forest trees have birds for their song. || 11 ||
Enveloped by the gods in its upper parts, enveloped by men at its base,
and enveloped by the nāgas in the underworld, it was like another house for the world.

By the word "jagat" (the world), the inhabitants of the three worlds are indicated. It stands, as it were, like their home, or like the cosmic egg-house characterized by the three worlds; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 12 ||
It was inhabited by perfected beings (siddhas) in its caves, by treasure-hoards within its interior,
by elephants among its sandalwood trees, and by lions upon the peaks of its summits.
By means of treasures buried as hidden wealth. || 13 ||

His body was enveloped by clouds of flowers; he was made dusty by the clouds of floral pollen; he wandered with a heart captivated by the whirlwind of blossoms; and he was as white as the trees laden with flowers.

The flowers fallen below, the pollen of flowers that have just fallen while still in the air, the falling flowers, and the flowers remaining on the trees are successively described as being like clouds. || 14 ||
Tawny like a cloud of mineral dust, he was fully attended by the throngs of city women standing upon the surfaces of jeweled stones, as if they were celestial *mandāra* flowers. || 15 ||
It was like a Mandara mountain, a portion of the Kalpa tree, with those [beings] as if mounted upon its branches.
There, the rocks— clothed in garments as blue as clouds, adorned with ornaments of precious gems, and beautiful as gold— are like women going to meet their lovers upon the mountain peaks.
The rocks themselves are imagined as women going to meet their lovers (*abhisārikās*): "They are like clouds" (*abhra*).
Because jewels set in tinkling anklets and such are obstacles to a secret tryst, they are adorned with silent gems.
Because they embrace [the sky] with their peaks as if they were women going to meet their lovers, they are called "peak-women-going-to-meet-lovers" (*śṛṅgābhisārikāḥ*). || 16 ||
There, on the northern slope where the fruit-bearing trees were bending low, and where the waters of cascading waterfalls flowed into a network of jewel-encrusted lotus-pools; || 17 ||
The connection with the fourth [verse] is that "there, on the northern bank, there is the hermitage of Atri. || 17 ||
In a place bristling with clusters of blossoms shed from mango trees and creepers, and where the edges of the quarters were filled with full-blown *aṅkola*, *punnāga*, and blue lotuses; || 18 ||
The mango trees were jagged with clusters of flowers spread upward by their branches and creepers, standing like protruding teeth; [there were] blue lotuses, that is, *nīlotpala*s. || 18 ||
Where the sun was shielded by the canopy of creeping vines, where it shone with the splendor of the rays of jewels,
where it was infused with the flowing juice of the jambu fruit, and which brought delight to its own world.
It was as delightful as Svarloka, the abode of heaven.
Equal to the world of Brahmā, as delightful as heaven, and comparable to the city of Śiva,
there is the glorious and great hermitage of Atri, which removes the fatigue of the perfected ones (siddhas).
In that great hermitage, there were two ascetics who were as learned as Śukra and Bṛhaspati in the path of the sky. (21)
In that great and vast [assembly], there were two who were learned and wise; indeed, Śukra and Bṛhaspati are the mention of their names as well.
(21) Then, from those two who shared a single abode, there were born two sons there, like two blossoming sprouts with pure bodies from the lotuses in a lake. (22)
Like two buds, the very essence of flowers, upon two lotuses—that is, two lotus-bushes—just as they are about to bloom. || 22 ||
Named Vilāsa and Bhāsa, the two grew up in due course, like two long sprouts upon the creepers and trees of their parents. (23)
They grew like two sprouts on a creeper and a tree. || 23 ||
Let them remain as two dear friends, mutually affectionate toward one another;
let them stay embraced like sesame seeds and their oil, and like a flower and its fragrance.
Though they were not joined by a son, the couple remained as if deeply enamored; their minds were equal, as if they had attained a unity within duality.
Neither joined nor separated, they were like a husband and wife, united for the sake of a son and deeply attached to one another.
Thus, those two of most enchanting form, delighted with one another, remained in silence in their own hermitage like a pair of bees upon a lotus. (26)
In silence, with [the lips] sealed, and joined with the practice of a sage. || 26 ||
Having cast off childhood, those two new lovers attained youth in a very short time, like the rising of the moon and the sun. (27)
Then those two parents,
afflicted by old age, abandoned their bodies and ascended to heaven, like two birds flying up from a nest.
When their parents had passed away, the two of them became dejected of face;
with their limbs scorched and their vigor gone, they were like two lotuses plucked from the water. (29)
When both had reached the state of the five elements, that is, death. || 29 ||
Having performed the funeral rites there, they both lamented;
for the way of the world is indeed insurmountable, O giver of honor, even for the great.
The term *aurdhvadaihika* involves a vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both parts of the compound because it belongs to the *anuśatikādi* group. *Paridevanam* means lamentation.
Having performed the funeral rites, they were then overwhelmed by the agony arising from grief; lamenting with piteous voices of compassion,
they stood as if depicted in a painting, all their physical movements stilled.
The two of them remained there, their hearts not empty, having revealed [the truth] with ease.

If it is asked, "If all movement has been cast out, are they then dead? he says, "with hearts not empty. Thus, the meaning is that they became unconscious (mūrcchitau) and yet remained wide awake (vivṛtau). || 31 ||

Thus ends the sixty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Sahya Mountain," within the narrative of Bhāsa’s *Vilāsa*, in the section on Quiescence (*Upaśama-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, concerning the means to liberation (*Mokṣopāya*).
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sahya Mountain," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The sixty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Overwhelmed by extreme grief, the two ascetics remained steadfast.
With all their limbs withered by ascetic heat, they were like two forest trees.
The wandering of one with unawakened intellect within this ocean of suffering is here elucidated in detail through the words of Bhāsa. (1)
In the case of the forest trees, their entire bodies were completely withered by the heat associated with the sun—namely, the summer heat and the forest fire. || 1 ||
Free from passion, the two twice-born ones spent their time in the forest,
having reached a state of supreme detachment like two deer separated from their herd.
Disregard for, and non-attachment to, house, field, wealth, and so forth. || 2 ||
Then days, months, and years passed for the two of them;
gradually, both reached old age like two trees growing from the edge of a chasm.
Once, those two ascetics—who had long been worn out and had not yet attained pure knowledge—met together and spoke thus to one another. (4)
Having been joined together for some time, they were separated by fate and then met once again.
Vilāsa said:
O fruit of the foremost tree of life, O ocean of nectar dwelling within the heart, O great kinsman in this world, O Bhāsa, welcome to you! (5)

"Life is the foremost and best; that living is the fruit of the tree characterized by such [qualities], and he whose abode is in the heart is thus an ocean of nectar"—this is a qualifying epithet for the kindling of the excellence of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). (5)
"O virtuous one, tell me, where have you spent all these days and nights while separated from me? Has your asceticism been fruitful?"
Is your intellect free from fever? Are you born with self-mastery? Have your studies borne fruit? And are you well? (7)
He is self-possessed, having attained the Self through awakening, and for that very reason, his knowledge has borne fruit.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: To him who had spoken thus, being so utterly distressed by the cycle of existence and having not yet attained great wisdom, his friend spoke with affection to that friend.
He spoke clearly enough. || 8 ||
Bhāsa said:
"O virtuous one, welcome! By good fortune you have been seen today, O giver of honor.
But how can there be well-being for us who remain here in this cycle of worldly existence?"

As long as the object of knowledge has not been realized, as long as the realm of the mind has not been exhausted, and as long as cyclic existence has not been transcended, how can there be any virtue for me? (10)
That which arises in the mind is "mind-born" (cittabhū), such as desire, volition, and so forth. || 10 ||
As long as the hopes born of the mind have not been cut down entirely, like creepers by a sickle, how can there be well-being for us? (11)
"Vīrudhaḥ" refers to creepers and climbing vines; "with a small sickle" means with a pointed tool or similar implement. || 11 ||
As long as wisdom has not been attained, as long as equanimity has not arisen, and as long as enlightenment has not dawned, how can there be any virtue for us? (12)
Knowledge is the purified reality, while the knowledge of the meaning of words is *bodha* (awakening), which is the indivisible meaning of the sentence; such is the distinction.
O holy one, without the attainment of the Self and without the great medicine of knowledge, this cholera-like plague of miserable worldly existence arises once again.
The wicked tree of saṃsāra approaches again: sprouting in childhood, its foliage flourishing in fresh youth, and blossoming in old age. (14)

The characteristic of childhood is the budding [of youth]; "having surpassed that blossoming" (ujjṛmbham atītya) employs either the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) with the elision of a *lyap* suffix or in the sense of a causal reason (*hetau*). || 14 ||
From this body, which is like a withered tree, there arises once more the cluster of blossoms that is death—a cluster whose flowers are old age, while its bees are the wailing of kinsmen. (15)

In which [forest], the lamentations of kinsmen are the bees—metaphorically, because they possess the humming sound of those [bees]—and it has blossomed with old age, meaning flowers have come forth. || 15 ||
The series of years, whose seasonal flavors have been consumed and which is woven from days long past, is led away until it is almost entirely devoid of essence. (16)

After death, by chance, when one attains birth as an inhabitant of hell, an immobile being, or an animal, one experiences the fruits of evil deeds in such states crowded with cold, heat, wind, rain, gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like; and during the seasons such as spring,
due to a lack of authority over the accumulation of merit and the exhaustion of previously accumulated merit, there arise [afflictions] such as joy, resentment, envy, and desire.

Moreover, due to the great abundance [of people], because of the impossibility of tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth, and because even knowledge is difficult to attain; and because, being solely addicted to enjoyment, they have experienced such things many times before according to the Purāṇas, there is an absence of novel objects, and thus [they pass their time] by means of days that are almost like those of old.
The meaning is that the year, having been spun out and filled—therefore becoming for the most part sapless—is spent once again in vain. || 16 ||
He wallows again in the great caves of the mountain of the body, which are bristling with the thorns of craving,
and in ritual actions that are like venomous serpents.

Thinking that even if one should by chance attain human birth—and therein a body such as that of a Brahmin, which is most difficult to obtain—one would still find it hard to resist wandering about with a craving for enjoyments just as in this present body, he says:
"In great caves," etc. In these caves, the fruits characterized by the enjoyment of sense-objects are themselves the serpents.

He does not wallow in worldly and Vedic rites— which are means for attaining enjoyments in this life and the next— nor in the attachments of the senses, which are like the openings of most terrifying caves within the mountain of the body's characteristics, where thorns have grown from thousands of cravings for those very objects.
The meaning is that even there, the possibility of discriminating from the self exists. || 17 ||
Nights come and go, their arrivals and departures never-ending, consisting of long-lasting and fleeting states of suffering and pleasure, both auspicious and inauspicious. (18)

In these [worlds], the cycles of coming and going are inexhaustible and incomplete because they consist of long and short sufferings due to being experienced for either long or short periods of time. The mention of "night" is an illustration for any period of time. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "they go [there] in all births. (18)

Life is wasted by base actions that fail to achieve their intended purpose—actions which are but sprouts of obsession with wicked desires—and by those actions that strike down one's own life-force. (19)

He states that very cause by way of its effects: "ayathārtha... etc. [The meaning is: Life is exhausted by those beings whose actions have been struck down—that is, rendered false—by means of such karmas as have their results initiated through activities that are "ayathārtha," meaning they are illusory (mithyābhūta).
It is destroyed. || 19 ||
The intoxicated elephant of the mind, its tethering post of the physical basis uprooted and awakened by the female elephant of craving, runs far astray. (20)

He elaborates upon the strength that opposes discernment (*viveka*) and the weakness of its auxiliaries in birth after birth—[strength] which has been uprooted by him. By the word "thirst" (*tṛṣṇā*), its object is indicated;
because he possesses desire for the female elephant characterized by that [thirst], he is "wide awake," meaning free from sleep. || 20 ||
Clinging to the flickering tongue within the great abode of the tree of the body,
the aged vulture of greed grows stronger as the wish-fulfilling gem falls away.

Since the wish-fulfilling gem—characterized by life-span and characterized by discernment—is useless when it falls [from its place], yet is beneficial for the supreme human goal; therefore, the vulture is that very greed, which is the longing for sweet food and the like, residing in the great nest characterized by the heart, which itself rests upon the tree characterized by the body. || 21 ||
Lacking moisture, devoid of joy, and light, with limbs as fragile as falling petals, this succession of days wastes away like the color of a withered leaf. (22)
In that [state], the limbs—tender and rendered incapable of action by fatigue, weakness, illness, and so forth—fall away;
by the term "series of days," the creeper-like body delimited by them is understood. 22.
Defiled by the dust of humiliation and with the beauty of its form set, the face turns ashen, like a lotus struck by frost. (23)

One whose bodily splendor has set—being thus destroyed by the insults of sons and servants in old age as well as by the impurities of passion; [the form] *klībe* is used with the elision of the case-ending (*aluk*), which is Vedic (*chāndasa*). 23.
From the lake of the body that is drying up, as the water of youth flows away, the royal swan of life—once gone, never to return—flees in an instant. (24)
The phrase "like a royal swan" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the simile]. || 24 ||
From the tree of life, shattered and shaken by the force of the wind of time, the flowers of enjoyments and the leaves of days fall downward. (25)
The flowers characterized by enjoyments and the leaves in the form of days fall downward; that is to say, they depart.
One sinks into the floods within the dark wells of mental delusion, which are inhabited by those who indulge in enjoyments and harbor the croaking frogs of internal suffering. (26)

Even when enjoyments have ceased, the longing for them, the suffering born of that incapacity, and the mental distress, grief, delusion, and anxiety caused by them continue to increase; with this intention, he says "bhoge" and so forth.
Untouched by various forms of attachment, craving—tremulous and fragile—ascends far aloft like a banner atop a shrine. (27)
A *caitya* is a sanctuary for deities and the like; it is raised high for a great distance, as if a banner were fastened at its summit.
The rat named Death gnaws away the thread consisting of the hope for life within this great cave of the machinery of saṃsāra. (28)
The thread of life, which is abundant with the hope for survival, is the warp of the continuum characterized by saṃsāra. || 28 ||
The turbulent river of life flows on, with the surging waves of youth, foaming with flickering swords, and possessing great whirlpools of recurring reversals. (29)

It is foamy with anger, hatred, fear, and the like, which resemble the swaying waves of a river; it possesses great whirlpools in the form of the revolutions of greed, thirst, and other such passions. || 29 ||
The river of action flows on boundlessly, agitated by the surging waves of the world’s manifold activities arising from the assembly of arts (kalās), its hollows filled with turmoil. (30)

The meaning is that the river characterized by such activity— agitated and crowded with waves consisting of the arts of sculpture, logic, and political science, along with the multitude of skills and the various worldly affairs and functions— flows in this very manner at every birth. || 30 ||
Endless rivers of kinsmen fall incessantly into the vast ocean of time, which has a deep hollow.
O Father, this jewel-case of the body is lost within the belly of the ocean of the mire of destruction;
it is not known where it has gone from birth to birth.
The body itself is a "jewel-pin" (ratnaśalākā), because it is the means for accomplishing the supreme human goal. 32.
Bound for a long time to the wheel of thought and restless in its pursuit of wicked conduct,
the mind wanders like a blade of grass in the whirlpools of the ocean's depths.
In a whirlpool in a pit, that is, in a whirlpool containing a hole. || 33 ||
Carried away by the infinite great waves of mental activity, the mind—its inner disposition dancing with anxiety—does not find rest for even a moment. (34)
"This has been done, I am doing this, I shall do that"—the bird of the intellect is thus ensnared by the web of conceptualization and rendered unconscious. (35)
Enveloped in the snare of time, she was bound, rendered unconscious, and deluded. || 35 ||
This great elephant of duality, which perceives "this one is a friend" and "that one is an enemy," cuts through my vital organs just as it would blue lotuses.
Just as one cuts down blue lotuses, so too does it cut my vital organs. || 36 ||
In the great whirlpool of the river of anxiety, amidst a mass of waves, the fish of the mind for a moment swells with pride, and in a moment it loses its way. (37)
"Ucchūnatām" means expansion or increase. "Kṣaṇādgatiḥ" means one whose movements proceed in moments; the sense is that he is fickle in his course. || 37 ||
Sufferings are not one's own; they are empty in this way.
Yet, by investigating them with the notion of a self, a person falls into a state of wretchedness. (38)

These things are not one's own, do not touch the self, and are not the signs of a self-body and so forth; yet, through the notion of a self with respect to the body and so on, they are [perceived as such].
Falling into various kinds of pleasure and pain,
shattered by the pervasive winds of old age and death,
these people are rolling upon the mountain within the belly of the world.
Thus, like a leaf whose sap has departed, it reaches a state of decay. || 39 ||

Demonstrating the infinity of states of suffering throughout all births, he concludes with the words "of many kinds": like a sapless leaf, this person— broken by the fierce wind of the torrent characterized by old age and death, and repeatedly crushed— tumbles upon the mountain of rising [existence] which is the world.
Like a dry leaf. || 39 ||

Thus ends the sixty-sixth canto, titled "The Exposition of Impermanence," within the narrative of Bhāsa’s Delusion, in the Section on Quiescence of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Impermanence," in the section on Tranquility within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The sixty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus did those two exchange inquiries regarding each other's welfare.
Having attained pure knowledge in due time, they subsequently reached liberation. || 1 ||
The lack of connection between the body and the self is now established;
bondage is caused by internal attachment, and by abandoning that, one is liberated. (1)
Thus, there is the exertion of wholesome effort, abundant with reflection on the worthlessness of cyclic existence in the manner described above. (1)
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I shall speak how there is no way other than knowledge for crossing over the cycle of existence, for the mind that is bound by its fetters. (2)
The term *pāśa* refers to bonds that are the causes of bondage; the *saṃsāra* is the wandering of such a mind, and the *taraṇa* of that [wandering] is the way, the means [to cross over it]. || 2 ||
For one of noble intellect, even this infinite suffering is but a trifle; for a base bird, however, the ocean that cannot be crossed becomes like a mere cow’s footprint.

This suffering of the kind described is fragile and tender to a discerning person of noble intellect—that is to say, it is easily destroyed by happiness. Otherwise, it is difficult to cross, like the ocean for Garuḍa, the enemy of serpents. || 3 ||
The great-souled ones, having transcended the body, abide in their own self which is pure consciousness;
they observe the body from afar, just as a spectator observes a crowd.
With the intention that the very abandonment of the conceit of the two bodies is the means for their destruction, he says: "Those who have transcended the body," and so forth. (4)
When the body is violently agitated by suffering, what loss has befallen us? What injury is there to the charioteer when the chariot is overturned and broken? (5)
In the reading "duḥsthitiḥ," the meaning is that "duḥsthitiḥ" signifies injury (kṣati). || 5 ||
When agitation arises in the mind, what has come to the nature of consciousness? Is there any change in the ocean when there is a succession of waves and water? (6)
The reversal of the Self, which is consciousness and whose nature is pure awareness, is the falling away from its own essential state of plenitude.
What were the swans of the waters? And what were the stones of the waters? What indeed were the rocks of the woods? And what are the enjoyments of the Supreme Self? (7)

With the intention that when egoism (*ahaṃtā*) is abandoned, there is no possibility whatsoever of attachment to "mine-ness" (*mamatā*) for anyone anywhere, he says, beginning with "Who were [they]? and so forth. For it is understood that neither insentient things nor the unattached Consciousness possess any possibility of attachment to "mine-ness."

O Illustrious One, what kind of connection could there be between a mountain and the distant ocean? And what connection could there be between the mind and the reality of consciousness amidst the crowded mass of mountains? (8)

"In the midst" means within. "Even though crowded by mountains" means even in a state of being filled with them. "The nature of consciousness" (cittattva) is the Supreme Self; "bondage" is transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). What connection can there be between these two? The sense is that space is not bound by fetters. || 8 ||
