Even lotuses being carried along in the currents of rivers are merely what they are; how much more so are the bodies of the self in this world? (9)
Even the lotuses, though being carried and supported as if in her lap or on her bosom, [did not fall]. || 9 ||
Just as from the friction of wood and water there arise high sparks and the like,
so too do these mental fluctuations arise from the conjunction of the body and the self.
From collision—that is, from impact—and from conjunction—that is, from the superimposition of mutual identity—arise the mental fluctuations of pleasure, pain, and so forth. || 10 ||
Just as reflections of wood appear in water due to the connection between the wood and the water, so too do bodies appear within the Self.

He provides an illustration for the fact that the connection with the body is illusory (adhyāsika) by saying, "From the connection" (saṃbandhāt). This means from the connection, which is the cause consisting of mere proximity. || 11 ||
Just as reflections in a mirror, a ripple of water, and so forth, are neither unreal nor real in an ultimate sense, so too are the bodies of the Self.
Just as one is never distressed by the striking together or apart of wood,
water, or stone, so too there is no injury when the five [aggregates] are joined or separated.

In the five elements, which have transformed into the forms of the body and so forth, when they are joined with whips, sandalwood paste, and the like, or separated from wife, children, and so on, there occurs injury, the onset of suffering, and the rest. (13)
Just as trembling, sound, and other phenomena arise from water when it is enclosed within wood,
so too do they arise from this body when it is awakened by consciousness.
Having presided over [it] by his mere proximity to the funeral pyre, he awakened [the king] on all sides.
These cognitions do not belong to the pure or the inert, nor to consciousness and its body;
for these belong only to ignorance, and when that is destroyed, for us there remains only consciousness.
If it is asked, "To whom then do these manifest cognitions of pleasure, pain, and so forth belong?", he says, "Not [to anyone]"—meaning they belong to no one at all.
Just as there is no experience of anyone [as a single entity] in the joining of water and wood,
so too there is no experience of anyone [as a single entity] in the union of the body and the embodied self.
Experiences are the perceptions of pleasure and pain occurring in the union of the body and the embodied one—that is, between the physical frame and the one who identifies with it.
(16) Just as this world appears to the ignorant man as having attained reality, so too does this world not appear as having attained reality to the wise man who perceives it as it truly is. (17)
In that case, one might ask: "Why should there not be no distinction between the knower and the ignorant? To this he replies: "Of the ignorant... (verse 17).
Just as moisture in a stone is devoid of internal cohesion, so too are the experiences of external enjoyments for one whose mental state is free from attachment. 18.
He then states what the experiences of the enjoyment of *prārabdha* karma are like for the knower: "Internally... etc.

"Internal attachment" (*antar-saṅga*) means egoism (*abhimāna*) and internal penetration (*anupraveśa*). "Affections" (*snehāḥ*) means relationships. [The compound refers to] the collection of stones and waters. || 18 ||
Just as there is no internal attachment between water and wood, even though they are joined together, so too is the internal attachment between the body and the embodied soul. 19.
He is unattached, being empty of attachment even to the ultimate truth. || 19 ||
The connection between water and wood is devoid of internal attachment;
such is the relationship between the body and the embodied soul, as well as between a reflection and the water [in which it appears]. (20)

The phrase "just as in the case of water and wood" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. That is the relationship. The word *ca* has the sense of *api* (also). There is no tautology, because the previous mention of water and wood was for the sake of an illustration regarding the absence of conjunction (*saṃsargābhāva*), whereas here it is for the sake of an illustration regarding the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*). || 20 ||
Pure consciousness, devoid of any object of cognition, abides everywhere;
however, that which is marked by duality is another, a distorted consciousness, which does not truly exist. (21)
One might object: "If the cognition of pleasure, pain, and so forth is negated, then since no other cognition is established, there would be emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Anticipating this, he says: "It remains" (*sthitā*). The meaning is that it does not exist [as a separate entity], because its object cannot be defined. || 21 ||
That which is not suffering clearly becomes suffering through internal perception;
a Vetāla becomes expansive when it is conceived as a Vetāla. (22)
He states that even for that which is non-existent, its appearance as "existent" through ignorance and delusion is well known: "aduḥkham" (verse 22).
Even a non-connection becomes a connection through internal determination, like sexual union with a woman in a dream, or like an association with a post or a ghost. (23)

The connection is the relation of superimposition (*ādhyāsika-yoga*). The first is an illustration for the superimposition of relation (*saṃsargādhyāsa*), and the second is an illustration for the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*). || 23 ||
For a connection that is essentially non-existent is like that between water and wood;
in the very same way, the false connection between the body and the Supreme Self is likewise unreal.
Without internal attachment, water is not seized by the falling of logs;
the Self, free from attachment to the limbs, is not burned by the sufferings of the body. (25)
"Without internal attachment" means because of the absence of the superimposition of egoism (*ahaṃkāra-adhyāsa*). "Is not seized" means it is not afflicted;
that is the meaning. "Free from attachment to limbs" means devoid of the superimposition of the body (*dehādhyāsa*). || 25 ||
By the very cultivation of the body, the self remains under the sway of bodily suffering;
therefore, the wise know that by abandoning it, one becomes liberated. (26)
O dear one, because they lack internal attachment, these things do not possess suffering, even though leaves, water, dirt, and wood are joined together with one another. (27)
Those ending in "dāru" [are feminine] by implication, like those fallen into a pond. || 27 ||

Those who are free from internal attachment attain supreme freedom from suffering; likewise, they remain entirely detached even though the self, body, senses, and mind are closely joined together. 28.

*Rahitā* means *rahitāni*. The substitution of *ḍā* for *śas* is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*), as in the expression *tā tā piṇḍānāṃ prajuhomi* ("those very [portions] of the rice-balls I offer"). || 28 ||
For internal attachment, O Rāma, is the seed-cause of all embodied beings in this cycle of existence— of the trees that are old age, death, and delusion. (29)
A living being who possesses internal attachment is submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra;
but one who is liberated from internal attachment has crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra. (30)
The mind that possesses internal attachment is said to have a hundred branches;
the mind devoid of internal attachment is said to be dissolved. || 31 ||
It has a hundred branches and infinite branches, because the modes of desire are infinite. || 31 ||
Know my mind to be unattached and resembling an unbroken crystal; know that the attached mind is impure, like a broken crystal. (32)
Just as a crystal linga or similar object that is broken or split within is impure and unfit for worship and other rites, so it is in this case.

The mind that is unattached and stainless is clearly liberated even while wandering in saṃsāra; but the attached mind is like one in extreme bondage, even if it is engaged in long-term ascetic penance.
The mind bound by internal attachment is liberated when freed from that attachment;
indeed, internal attachment alone is the sole cause of bondage and liberation. (34)
For one who is free from internal attachment, there is no sense of agency even while acting,
just as a boat carrying timber moves upon water without being affected by its virtues or defects.
Just as a boat, by which logs or loads of wood are carried and brought ashore,

is itself made of wood and thus possesses the qualities and defects inherent in wood— such as being subject to cutting, splitting, and burning, or being affected by the movement, turning, turbidity, and mud of the water— so too is it with the self.
The meaning is that, due to qualities such as oiliness and so forth, it does not possess those [qualities] in the same way. || 35 ||
Due to internal attachment, a living being experiences agency even though it is not the actual agent, just as one experiences a state of agitation in a dream involving pleasure and pain. (36)
Agitation and the state of being intent upon flight from fear of tigers and the like refers to the turmoil of fleeing out of dread of tigers and so forth. || 36 ||
When the mind is the agent, agency exists even for that which is bodiless;
it is like the perception of agitated pleasure and pain in dreams and the like. (37)

Even for one who is bodiless and devoid of bodily movement, yet perceives the death of his son, battle, and so forth—as if in a dream even while awake—the state of agency exists. The meaning is that because he experiences agitated pleasure and pain, that [agency] is indeed equivalent to that of a primary agent. || 37 ||
In the non-agent mind, internal agency becomes manifest;
for a person whose mind is empty does not perceive even while acting. (38)
"He neither wills nor conceives; the knower of reality, being disciplined, should think, 'I do nothing at all,'" according to the words of the Blessed One. || 38 ||
You attain what is done by the mind, but not what is not done by the mind;
the body is never the cause, nor does agency belong to the mind. (39)

"Nor [is it the case that...]"—the word "ca" (and) is used here in the sense of a reason. The meaning is: it is not that the mind lacks the capacity for agency such that the body would have to be postulated as the agent. || 39 ||
The wise know that the mind, though acting, is as if non-acting because it is unattached;
being unattached, it does not become an enjoyer of the fruits of action.
The second particle *eva* is used in the sense of "also" (*api*).
One who is not attached to both the killing of a Brahmin and the horse-sacrifice is not tainted by them,
just as one whose mind is absorbed in a beloved woman standing at a distance is not affected by the duties that lie before him.

The meaning is that this is well known through the effects such as the experience of cold and heat by those who have gone before him and preceded him; and it was previously elaborated upon in the narrative of Indra and Ahalyā concerning Purūravas, who was attached to Urvaśī. || 41 ||
The individual soul, liberated from internal attachment and possessing a sweet disposition,
is never truly an agent or an enjoyer, whether it is externally active or inactive.
One who possesses a sweet disposition has the happiness of being free from distraction. || 42 ||
That mind which is free from internal attachment becomes a non-agent;
it is liberated, tranquil, engaged [in its true nature], and untainted.
With the intention that all the qualities of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) are perfected within the mind merely by abandoning attachment, he says: "Internally... (verse 43).
Therefore, one should certainly abandon the cruel internal attachment that causes all suffering, even toward all objects that appear interconnected externally. 44.

He concludes: "Therefore. This alone is determined to be the primary means for the removal of all objects—which constitute bondage—consisting of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) that are externally attached to the innermost Self, as well as the entire category of enjoyables.
That one should abandon the internal attachment which produces all suffering; this is the meaning of "abandoning. || 44 ||
The mind, freed from the internal defect of attachment and having attained primordial tranquility with a radiance as stainless as the sky,
attains oneness with the Self, which is liberated from all impurities.
Resembling a steady gem, it is like water in the midst of water, blue as the depths of the ocean.

Internal attachment is clinging; one should be completely free from that defect. If the inner reality (pratyaktattva) attains oneness and homogeneity with the Supreme Self, it reaches a state of unity. Just as a steady crystal gem [reflects its surroundings], so too does water appear like that [crystal]. Those which possess sharp edges are "ariṇaḥ," such as swords and the like.
The meaning is that just as [the waters of] the Yamunā and other rivers, when meeting the dark water, attain oneness, so it is in this case. || 45 ||

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Reflection on Internal Attachment," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "An Inquiry into Internal Attachment," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-eighth canto.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, what is association like, and how does it lead to bondage for men?"
And what is said to lead to liberation, and how indeed is it treated? || 1 ||

In this [chapter], the distinction between those who are worthy of veneration and those who are not, along with the means for treating both the attachment to and the detachment from marks, and the resulting fruit, are described.
In what way, by what manner, and of what kind is bondage; and who, and of what nature, is liberation; and how, by what means, is it treated? || 1 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the contemplation that completely abandons the distinction between the body and the embodied soul, there arises a conviction in the body alone; such attachment is said to be worthy of bondage.

The body, which is the field (*kṣetra*), and the embodied one, who is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), possess a distinction characterized by the natures of insentience and consciousness respectively;

this is a state of contradictory natures. By the total abandonment of one [of these], through a complete lack of reflection, and by means of the cultivation of a mutual identity and exchange of attributes, [the notion of] the body [arises].
The very confidence in the selfhood of the Mother is what is subject to bondage; the meaning is that attachment is the cause of bondage. || 2 ||
When there is a determination that the infinite reality of the Self has limits, whatever longing for happiness arises therein is called attachment, which is fit for bondage. (3)
He states other characteristics with the words beginning "of the infinite" (*anantasya*). "Having a limit" (*saparyantatva*) means being accompanied by the three kinds of delimitation;
the meaning is that when such [limitation] is ascertained, there arises a desire for pleasure from external objects due to the forgetting of one's own nature, which is unconditioned bliss.
"All this is the Self alone; what do I desire, or what shall I abandon?"—know this state of non-attachment to be the condition of one whose body remains while liberated in life (jīvanmukta). || 4 ||
He characterizes the state of non-attachment, which is opposed to that [bondage], with the words "all" (sarvam) || 4 ||
"I am not, nor does another exist; let things be or let them not be"—the man who, being thus internally unattached to pleasures, speaks in this way, is said to be a possessor of liberation. || 5 ||

I am not delimited by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), nor is there anyone other than me. Therefore, whether false objects such as the body experience the pleasures of sense-objects or not, I remain unattached through the firm conviction that my very nature is one of non-attachment to the body and so forth. || 5 ||
He who does not rejoice in inaction nor clings to actions,
who is perfectly equanimous and renounces the fruits of action— he is remembered as one who is unattached.

*Naiṣkarmya* is the renunciation of all actions. He "clings" or becomes attached by aiming for the fruit. The phrase "equally disposed toward success and failure" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 6 ||
He whose mind, being solely established in the reality of the Self, does not fall under the sway of joy or anger,
and who is unattached— he is called one liberated while living.
He who skillfully renounces all fruits of action and the like through the mind alone, and not by means of physical action, is known as one who is unattached.
The phrase "not by action" is used to indicate the necessity of the welfare of the world. || 8 ||
All various activities that have manifested here, when practiced without attachment, become a form of healing and bring about the highest good.

Having resolved the three questions, he resolves the fourth question with the words "by non-attachment": "Activities" refers to improper activities manifested by various cravings for fruits; however, activities such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, when free from obstacles, bring about the highest good. || 9 ||
Due to the power of attachment, all these vast heaps of suffering branch out into hundreds of directions, like a thorny tree in a ravine.
Now he elaborates upon the fruits of attachment, beginning with the words "by the power of attachment" (saṃsaktivaśataḥ) and so forth. || 10 ||
That a donkey, its nose pulled tight by a rope, carries a burden along the road with a terrified soul—that is the manifestation of attachment to that [burden]. (11)
Even for donkeys, the nose-rope is well known in different regions;
this is merely an illustration of being born as a domestic animal. The same applies hereafter. "The unfolding of attachment" refers to the expansion of its fruit. || 11 ||
That the tree supports with its body the suffering of cold, wind, and heat while remaining seated in one place—that is the manifestation of attachment. 12.
With her body seated in one place, she moves by means of her stationary form; that is to say, she experiences [the journey]. || 12 ||
That a worm, submerged in a fissure of the earth with its body tormented, passes its time in distress, is the manifestation of attachment to that [world]. (13)
With a belly emaciated by hunger, fearing obstacles, he passes his life perched on the tip of a tree—this is the manifestation of attachment to that [world]. (14)
"Vyāghātaḥ" refers to the impact of arrows, stones, lumps of clay, and so forth; therefore, "bhīrurdhīḥ" means one whose intellect is fearful [of such impacts] at every moment. || 14 ||

That a deer gives up its body due to the affliction of a hunter’s arrow, even while subsisting on a diet of durvā grass sprouts and blades, is the manifestation of attachment to worldly existence. || 15 ||
These people, being born again and again, become worms and insects; that they have thus grown old is the manifestation of attachment to worldly existence.
The people are the multitude of individuals who are the agents of merit and demerit. || 16 ||
Arising again and again, they dissolve like waves in a river;
that the infinite elements manifest is the unfolding of attachment to them. (17)
O wavy one, O possessed of waves, like a body of water possessing waves. || 17 ||
That men, having lost their mobility, repeatedly reach the state of creepers and grass and die again and again—that is the manifestation of attachment to that [world]. (18)
A creeper is a climbing plant. || 18 ||
When grass, shrubs, creepers, and the like produce a certain form through their union with the essence of the netherworld (rasātala-rasa), that is the manifestation of attachment (saṃsakti). || 19 ||

The connection is as follows: "that which they produce" [is the result] from the application—that is, the consumption—of the *rasa* (essence) or water that has fallen into the subterranean region of the earth, by means of their roots. || 19 ||
That the river of saṃsāra is intoxicated and crowded with hundreds of objects appearing as if they were not distinct from one's own self is the manifestation of attachment to that [saṃsāra]. (20)

It is crowded with hundreds of external and internal objects— objects that are not distinct from itself, which are non-entities because they are not distinct from non-entity, and which constitute a succession of misfortunes— serving as the causes for thousands of distractions such as the delusion of continuity and the fall [into lower realms].
Matta means increased. || 20 ||
Attachment is said to be of two kinds, O Raghava: the venerable and the barren.
The barren kind belongs everywhere to the deluded; the venerable kind is innate to those who know reality.
"Vandyā" means praiseworthy; "vandhyā" means barren, being devoid of the fruit of human goals (puruṣārtha). || 21 ||
That firm attachment to the cycle of worldly existence, which arises from objects such as the body and is devoid of the realization of the true nature of the Self, is called "barren. (22)
That attachment to cyclic existence which is firm is barren.
Indeed, attachment born from the discernment of reality through the awakening to the true nature of the self is said to be venerable, for it is further devoid of worldly existence. (23)
The Lord, whose hands hold the conch, discus, and mace, protects the three worlds through various means, out of his attachment to those who offer him praise. || 24 ||
He elaborates upon how the association with those worthy of veneration sustains the excellence of all activities, including the conduct of one liberated while living:
"By virtue of his association with those worthy of veneration, the sun daily performs the role of a traveler on the path through the sky, which is incessant and without support. (25)
"Unceasingly" means continuously. "The sun makes for the state of a traveler" means, in other words, that it moves along. || 25 ||
Through the power of attachment to that which is worthy of worship, the Brahmanic body indeed manifests, having been conceived for a long time through the concentration of a great aeon.
A *mahākalpa* is a natural dissolution (*prākṛtapralaya*); therein lies the absorption, the repose in disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*).

For that purpose, the conceptualizations of creation and so forth have been fashioned for a long duration of two *parārdhas*. The body of Brahmā, belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha, vibrates and functions [within it]. 26.
The body of Śaṅkara stood there, adorned with ashes, playfully clinging to the fire of women, and rendered venerable by its attachment [to that state]. 27.
Lalanā is Gaurī; in that characteristic, [the elephant] is effortlessly bound and attached to the *ālāna*, the tethering post. || 27 ||
The lords of consciousness, the perfected ones, the world-protectors, and others likewise, remain upon the courtyard of the world through the power of their attachment to the venerable one. (28)
Those whose progress toward the realization of the reality of Brahman within consciousness is firmly established. || 28 ||
Another series of worlds maintains a multitude of bodily machines, which—by virtue of their connection with the venerable one—is devoid of old age and death. (29)

She is other than the three worlds. By the term "succession of worlds" (*bhuvanasaṃtati*), those who know reality residing in the worlds of Mahar, Jana, Tapa, Satya, and so forth, are indicated through figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*). || 29 ||
The mind falls upon sense-objects like a vulture upon scraps of meat, due to its attachment to things worthy of reverence and its futile suspicion that they are delightful. (30)
He establishes the barrenness of that which has a barren connection with the words: "The mind... (verse 30).
By the power of attachment, the wind blows within the hollow of the universe;
the five elements abide therein, and this is the sustaining order of the world.

Explaining that worldly transaction, common to both the liberated and the unliberated, is carried out through attachment alone, he demonstrates this with the verse beginning "by the power of attachment" (saṃsaktivaśataḥ) and so forth. || 31 ||
In heaven are the gods, on earth are men, and in the netherworld are the serpents and asuras;
they all exist within the fig-like fruit of the cosmic egg like shimmering gnats. || 32 ||
Infinite beings are born and die, they fall and they rise, just like the waves upon a river. (33)
Arising again and again, beings dissolve away; this is the manifestation of attachment to them, becoming repeatedly devoid of flavor, like droplets from a mountain waterfall. (34)
In such a way that it becomes tasteless, arising again and again.
With their limbs swallowed by one another, the people, shattered by dullness, wander about in confusion, O dear one, like withered leaves in the sky. (35)
By the law of the fishes, their limbs are swallowed by one another.
The circle of constellations in the sky, like a swarm of gnats on a tree, vibrates with the very motion of whirlpools, just as a flood of water does in the netherworld, O dear one. (36)
The phrase "like the continuity of mosquitoes" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "Aṅga" is used as a term of address. || 36 ||
Even today, the moon does not abandon its turbid body of water, which is like a ball for the child of Time— subject to rising and falling, passing through various states, and becoming stale.

Because of its constant rising and falling, its appearing and disappearing, its waxing and waning, and its perpetual sinking and leaping—because it is worn out and loosened by that very condition; because it is like a ball for the child who is Time itself;

because it is water, which is inert (*jaḍa*) due to the non-difference between *laḍa* and *jala*; and because it is soiled, stained, and withered—it is fit to be cast away on account of its many defects.
Even though her body is now fit [for liberation], she does not yet abandon it due to the power of attachment. || 37 ||
The assembly of suffering gods does not cut the fragment of their hearts, though it is harsh with the sight of the manifold sufferings of the cycles of the ages.

By beholding and repeatedly experiencing the various and boundless sufferings of the cycles of the ages, his mind— characterized as a hard and cruel fragment that requires the treatment of excision— becomes a particular kind of wound; and though he is perpetually suffering on account of that [wound],...
The host of gods, the circle of Gīrvāṇas led by Indra, does not cut [the bonds] by means of severance, nor does it treat them, solely due to the power of attachment. || 38 ||
"O Rāghava, behold this wonderful and variegated painting created by someone else in the supreme ether, solely through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā). (39)

To show that attachment can be severed by the knowledge arising from mere discernment (*viveka*), he states that the world, which is its object, is constructed solely from latent impressions (*vāsanā*): "Latent impression... (verse 39).
This painting of the world, composed within the void of space which is the sole stage for the attachment of the mind—that is never real. (40)
Attachment of the mind means its clinging; by that alone, characterized as a single dye—a coloring substance—it [is dyed]. || 40 ||
For those engaged in worldly affairs whose minds are attached to this cycle of existence, craving devours their bodies just as a flame of fire consumes blades of grass. (41)
Craving devours and consumes bodies. 41.
Who is able to enumerate the bodies of the Lord of Waters, which cling to his mind like grains of sand, any more than one can count the multitude of motes of light in a sunbeam? 42.

He states the infinity of bodies obtained through the fault of attachment and devoured by craving with the verse beginning "parisakta": for a living being whose mind is attached on all sides to sense-objects, it is impossible to count—that is, to enumerate—the sands of the lord of waters, the ocean. || 42 ||
From the foot to the summit of Mount Meru, the waves of the Gaṅgā—like strings of pearls—are counted; yet the bodies of those whose minds are attached [to worldly things] are not even reckoned.

The meaning is this: from the foot to the summit of Mount Meru, the waves—which are like pearls—of the Gaṅgā may perhaps be counted by those with a focused mind, as she is imagined to be a hanging pearl necklace; but the bodies of those whose minds are attached [to worldly things] can never be counted. || 43 ||
For those whose minds are deeply attached, these rows of beautiful inner apartments are fashioned as the Raurava,
Vīci, Kālasūtra, and other hells.

Because they are ablaze with fire, weapons, and so forth, the heroines called "torments" (yātanā) have been fashioned by the artisans of karma as rows of inner apartments, since they serve as places for sexual union. This is the meaning. || 44 ||
Know that a person whose mind is attached is a heap of dry fuel for the blazing fires of hell; by means of that [attachment], those fires burn. (45)
Whatever this so-called web of suffering exists within the world, all of that is imagined for the sake of those with attached minds. (46)
All successions of suffering come upon one whose mind is attached, like great rivers surging with waves of water flow into the ocean. (47)
They approach one whose mind is attached. || 47 ||
Everything is pervaded by ignorance, which consists of mental association, which is a burden in the form of the body, and which seeks the states of decline and rise.

Association (*saṃsarga*) means attachment; its object is precisely this body, which—like a load of stone or the like taken up upon one's own head—is a burden that must necessarily be carried. Since ignorance (*avidyā*) persists as if it were actually praying for the miserable condition of both decay (*kṣaya*, death) and arising (*udaya*, birth) for the living being, everything [is thus affected].
The meaning is that the net of suffering is spread out. || 48 ||
O Rāma, through non-attachment to enjoyments, all prosperities reach their highest expansion,
like great rivers during the rainy season.
He says that the renunciation of attachment brings all happiness, beginning with the words "by non-attachment," etc. (verse 49).
Know, O Raghava, that internal attachment to the limbs of the body is like charcoal;
know, O Rama, that the absence of such attachment to the limbs is an elixir.
The infinite is free from attachment; it is the relinquishing of internal attachment. || 50 ||
Nature itself is consumed by the internal attachment that arises from its own creative power, just as a medicinal plant is burnt by the fire produced from within itself. 51.

*Erā* refers to specific types of grass; one who desires them for support is *erakāṅkṣī*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied here according to Pāṇini’s rule on the object of desire (*karmaṇyaṇ*). Just as a medicinal herb or creeper, by mingling with or mixing with certain grasses, is consumed by the fire arising from them, so too the individual soul (*jīva*), though itself primordial (*prakṛtibhūta*), is consumed through its attachment to the body and other effects of *prakṛti*.
The meaning is that it is being burned. || 51 ||
Unattached everywhere, profoundly peaceful, abiding as if infinite, appearing as real though unreal—such a mind leads only to happiness.
(52) A mind unattached to everything leads only to happiness; it abides like the infinite sky. (52)
By one who has attained the arising of the vision of knowledge,
who has reached the state of the destruction of ignorance,
and who is entirely free from attachment everywhere.
He who abides in his own consciousness is liberated. || 53 ||

Explaining the state of being an unreal construction (*asatkalpatā*) and the appearance of reality (*sadābhāsatā*) through the distinction of objects, he concludes with the verse beginning "vidyādṛśī":
"the preeminent arising," which is a manifestation like that of the sun and other luminaries. (53)

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Discerning Attachment," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Discerning Attachment," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The sixty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
By that which always abides in all things and exists together with everything...
Even while engaged in all activities, the mind should be kept alert by one who possesses discernment.
The mind becomes firmly established as pure consciousness alone through the renunciation of attachment to all objects;
the process by which consciousness alone remains is here described. (1)
By one who is discerning and always abiding by all worldly and scriptural conventions appropriate for each specific occasion,
remaining with everyone— including beloved friends, servants, sons, wives, and others suitable for those various dealings—
even while engaged in all worldly and scriptural activities that are not prohibited, the mind [should possess] the characteristics to be described hereafter.

The meaning is "that which is to be done. Alternatively, in order to prevent limited attachment— which results in being occupied with only a few activities through the assistance of individual times, places, friends, servants, and so forth— one should first,
by means of the possession of all requisites across all places and times, [act] as one who is engaged in the activities of worldly affairs throughout the entire universe.
The meaning is that, having become [thus], one should subsequently perform the mental activity in the manner that will be described. || 1 ||
He was not attached here to activities, nor to thoughts, nor to objects;
neither to the sky, nor below, nor above, nor to the directions, nor to the creepers.

The connection is that the mind should not be attached to activities and so forth, up to the calculation of time. This refers to activities directed toward goals to be accomplished, reflections on past objects, and present things; [not attached] to the front or the middle, nor to the creepers—that is, the intermediate directions consisting mostly of diagonal branches. || 2 ||
It is not in the external world of vast extension, nor in the functions of the senses;
it is not within, nor in the vital breath, nor in the head, nor in the palate.

"Externally" refers to the physical world. "In the expansive" means in the sphere of enjoyments such as wife, servants, and so forth—specifically, in the functions of the senses characterized by the enjoyment thereof. "Internally" refers to the spiritual self; it also includes those locations for concentration (*dhāraṇā*) mentioned in the Yoga scriptures, such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the head, and others, which are conducive to the attainment of various desired powers. || 3 ||
It is not between the eyebrows, nor at the tip of the nose, nor in the mouth, nor in the pupil;
it is not in darkness, nor in light, nor in this space of the heart.
In the *tāraka*, that is, in the pupil of the right eye. || 4 ||
It is not in the waking state, nor in the dream, nor in deep sleep, nor in the stainless;
it is not in the black, nor in the yellow, red, and so forth, nor in the variegated.

In the stainless quality of pure being (*śuddhasattva*); in darkness (*tamas*) which is black; in passion (*rajas*) such as yellow and red; in the variegated aggregate of the qualities (*guṇasamāhāra*);
in that which is neither moving nor stable, neither at the beginning nor in the middle nor elsewhere;
neither far nor near, neither in front nor in an object nor in the self. || 6 ||
In the moving category of effects; in the stable, unmanifest cause; in their respective times of creation and so forth—beginning, middle, and end;
in the delimitations of space such as "far" and so on; in the object, which is a composite of name and form; and in the self, that is, the individual soul (jīva). || 6 ||
Neither in sound, touch, or form; nor in states of delusion or bliss;
nor in the activities of coming and going, nor in the calculations of time.
The mention of "form" (rūpa) is an elliptical expression that includes taste and smell as well. "Delusion" (moha) is the state of being under the sway of longing for sense objects.

[This applies] even to the fruits of enjoying sense objects, which consist of states of bliss; to the activities of going and coming, such as the supernatural powers of moving through the air (khecaratva) and so forth; and to the calculations of time, such as the powers of knowing the past and future and living for long periods. || 7 ||
Having come to rest in pure consciousness alone, let the mind— though still slightly leaning upon objects of thought— abide everywhere as if devoid of flavor, finding its only essence in the Self.

Whatever is an object of thought, the intellect remains unmoving while resting upon it; yet, in its witness—the Self—it finds its own essence, being inclined toward the bliss of the Infinite (bhūmānanda), and for that very reason, it is devoid of flavor (nīrasa) regarding everything else. This is because of the Lord’s statement: "Even his taste for objects ceases upon seeing the Supreme. The word "as if" (iva) indicates that even such a state of the mind [is merely figurative].
The purpose is to illuminate falsity. || 8 ||
Established therein, free from attachment, the soul has attained the state of the non-soul;
let it perform all this worldly activity, or let it not perform it.
The state of being lifeless is the state of Brahman. || 9 ||
Even while performing actions, the living being who delights in its own self does not incur a connection with the fruits of those actions, just as the sky is unaffected by clouds.
Delighting in his own self, having his own self as his sole beloved. || 10 ||
Or else, having abandoned even that objective aspect, let the living being remain as the peaceful mass of consciousness,
utterly tranquil within itself like a glowing gem.
And this aforementioned state of being the witness of the intellect is the nature of the Self. || 11 ||
O Rāmabhadra, though the living soul (jīva) constantly abides in the Self that has attained Nirvāṇa and remains ever-arisen,
it does not incur attachment while engaged in worldly activity, due to its state of being free from attachment toward the fruits of action.
And by the arising of karma, he indeed bears the burden of the body.

The living being (*jīva*), devoid of desire for the fruits of worldly activity, because it is free from attachment—due to the cause of being empty of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of ignorance, desire, and karma which are the grounds of attachment—does not enter into attachment with the results born of karma; rather, until the exhaustion of its *prārabdha* karma, it merely bears the burden of the body as if it were still engaged in action. Of that [being]:
The meaning is that this is according to the scriptural passage beginning with, "Only so long is the delay as I am not liberated. || 12 ||

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Yoga Attained through Peace," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Rishis. || 69 ||
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Yoga Attained through Peace," in the *Upaśamaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Seventieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
By those whose selves are expansive and established in the practice of the happiness of non-attachment, [the world is perceived as follows...]
Even those engaged in worldly affairs remained with their inner grief and fear dispelled. || 1 ||
One who rests in the bliss of non-attachment is not afflicted by the defects arising from worldly conventions; this is established through reasoning as follows.
The practice of the bliss of non-attachment is its uninterrupted savoring by those who remain and rest therein. || 1 ||
In one whose body is neither agitated nor unagitated, because of the non-contradiction of consciousness,
splendor is perceived in the face of one who is full within, like that of the moon.

By what sign is their state as such known? To this he says: "Agitated," etc. For, although consciousness—the mental modification—is observed to have its body agitated by causes of agitation such as the loss of sons, wealth, imprisonment, or insult, it is in reality devoid of them.

By reason of non-deception and non-delusion regarding ultimate bliss, he is "one whose interior is full. In the case of the moon, because his body remains steady in its own seat despite being agitated by the movement of the chariot of the circle of luminaries (the stars), he is "one whose body is unagitated.
He causes [reality] to be fully known, thus he is *saṃvit* (consciousness); by reason of the non-deception of that *saṃvit*-sun...
On the full moon day, because of the extreme directness [of the gaze], the reflection—which is like a face—is filled with internal spaces that are not uneven. || 2 ||

The mind of one who is free from the fever of passion, having abandoned the objects of thought and taking consciousness as its sole support— by him the world is purified, just as water is by the clearing-nut (*katakaphala*).

With the intention of showing that if even others are liberated from agitation and impurity through his grace, what need is there to mention his own state of being free from agitation, he says: "cetya... (verse 3).
Constantly absorbed in the vision of the Self, the knower remains established in his own nature even while being restless;
though he appears agitated, it is as false as the reflection of the sun in water.
The great-souled ones, delighting in the Self, are awakened and possessed of supreme excellence;
they are as flickering as the tips of peacock feathers on the outside, yet as immovable as Mount Meru within.
The mind, having attained the nature of a self, becomes colored by pleasure and pain; yet it does not truly undergo that change, just as a smooth crystal, though joined with colors, remains as it is.

He provides an illustration for the absence of that [disturbance] even when a disturbance is perceived—namely, "the mind. *Raṅga* is a coloring adjunct such as a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*) and the like. *Masṛṇa* means smooth or glossy. || 6 ||
For one who has understood the higher and lower states of the world, the vision of saṃsāra that has arisen does not defile the true mind, just as a streak of water does not stain a lotus.
He has arisen, having attained the emergence of unsurpassed bliss; he by whom the supreme reality of the Lord and the lower reality of the individual soul have been known.
One who is absorbed in meditation on the Self, awakened to the Supreme Self,
and freed from the impurity of conceptualization, is said to be "self-attached" (svasakta).

With the intention that as long as this [mind] is not unattached within itself, so long is non-attachment toward external objects difficult to attain, he states the characteristic of internal attachment: "The Self," etc. When this [mind], having attained awakening to the Supreme Self and being liberated from the impurities that cause conceptualization, remains in a state of unsurpassed bliss even during meditation—

The meaning is that because of its self-radiance, as if always immersed in non-conceptual samādhi, he remains as if absorbed in the bliss of meditation upon the Self; at that time, he is said to be "attached to himself. || 8 ||
Through delighting in the Self, the living being attains non-attachment in this world;
through knowledge of the Self, attachment becomes attenuated, and not otherwise.

He says that attachment is destroyed through the sequence of increasing self-attachment resulting from the excellence of the maturation of knowledge—namely, by "delighting in the Self" (ātmārāmatayā). || 9 ||
O Rāghava, while remaining awake, the living being becomes situated in deep sleep;
having gone in this direction, it is free from duality and eternally beyond setting or rising.
In this aforementioned vision of one's own attachment, he has gone—that is, he has reached transformation—being free from duality, devoid of the pleasant and the unpleasant. || 10 ||
Having attained maturity here, he reaches the state of the purifying sun,
just as the moon, by the power of its transformation, reaches the state of the sun on the new-moon day.
"Prāuḍhim" means the state of having fully developed through repeated practice. "Pariṇāmaḥ" refers to the gradual accumulation of parts;

by virtue of that, just as the moon—which consists of the reflection of the sun within the water-element—attains the state of being the sun itself (its own original form) during the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), so it is here. This is the meaning. || 11 ||
That state of those whose minds have been attenuated, wherein the mind is devoid of its various conditions, is called the cessation of mental construction;
it is a state of deep sleep even while awake.
He clarifies what was stated—that one remains in deep sleep even while awake—with the verse beginning "In the mind" (citte). || 12 ||
Having attained that state of deep sleep while living and conducting worldly affairs,
a person is never dragged by the thongs of pleasure and pain.
He who, while remaining awake, stays as if in deep sleep and performs the activities of the world,
does not become a witness to pleasure and pain, being like a mechanical puppet.
Due to the equality of being devoid of the sense of "I," it is like a mechanical puppet or a dancer's statue, possessing a body similar to that.
The power that obstructs the mind and brings about the affliction of existence and non-existence—once the mind has attained the state of the Self, what can obstruct it, and how? (15)

The power characterized by the sense of "I" (ahaṃkāra) is indeed an affliction that causes distress to the mind; for it brings about suffering through the arrival and departure—the presence and absence—of both undesirable and desirable things. (15)

One whose intellect is as if in deep sleep, performing actions with utter indifference from the very outset, is not bound; such a living being remains established in the state of liberation while alive (jīvanmukta).
From the very beginning of the stage of practice, one should act with nonchalance by abandoning all dogmatic attachment. || 16 ||
O sinless one, resorting to the state of deep sleep, whether you perform action or not,
let that which is born of nature remain as it is, arrived through the power of its own ripening.

"Nature" (prakṛti) refers to the inherent character of one's caste and stage of life; "born from that" means appropriate to it; "arrived through the ripening of past actions" means obtained by the force of the fruition of prārabdha-karma; and "established in worldly and scriptural tradition" means conforming to the conventions of the world and the treatises. || 17 ||
Neither the undertaking nor the abandonment of action is pleasing to one who lacks knowledge;
those who have realized the Self remain as they are, following whatever comes to them. 18.
To those who believe that even the action appropriate to one’s stage of life (āśrama) must be abandoned, he says: "Not non-giving."
Even while acting, you are not an agent through a mind established solely in deep sleep;
and even as a non-agent, you are an agent—act however you wish.
Whether he knows reality or does not know reality—this is the completion of the preceding and following sentences. || 19 ||
Just as an infant does not move on its cradle while perceiving nothing at all,
so too, O Rāghava, perform your actions without perceiving their fruits.
Perceiving no purpose whatsoever and forming no mental constructs, he vibrates solely through the play of innate bliss.
Established in the state of the non-objective consciousness (acetyacitpada)—[the reading "svaccha" is also found]—one possesses the intellect of deep sleep even while awake;
whatever such a person, having attained their true self, performs, there is no sense of agency in him regarding that act.
That word [“tac”] should be understood as being used distributively (vīpsita). || 21 ||
Having reached the state of deep sleep within his own mind and being free from latent impressions,
the knower attains inner coolness, just as the moon does through its nectar.
Abiding in deep sleep, he is of great splendor, full like the orb of the full moon;
he remains the same in all states, like a mountain through the seasons.
Just as a mountain remains unchanged throughout all six seasons, the meaning is that he remains the same in all circumstances, whether they be calamities or prosperities. || 23 ||
The wise-souled one, though established in deep sleep, comes out to the restlessness of external activity;
yet there is no trembling in his actions, like a mountain that has begun to quiver.

The meaning is: one whose self is steadfast (dhīrātmā) appears thus to possess outward restlessness in worldly and Vedic activities, yet there is no internal trembling within him; he is like a mountain, which is immovable though shaken externally by the wind among trees and grass. || 24 ||
Having become established in the state of deep sleep, with the body free from all taint,
either cast it down at once or hold it for a long time like a mountain.
With the intention that his state of changelessness regarding death and life is equal to that regarding actions, he says: "In deep sleep... and so forth.
O Rāma, this very state of deep sleep, when it becomes mature through the yoga of practice,
is called the "Fourth" (turya) by those who are experts in the principles of reality.
Anticipating the doubt that the state of the fourth (turya) is always appropriate for the wise, whereas it is not so in deep sleep, he says: "This very [state]... (verse 26).
The knower of the Great Awakening, whose every affliction has been extinguished within and who consists of bliss alone, becomes one whose mind has utterly set [into quiescence]. (27)

Regarding the statement "then it is the state of deep sleep," what is the intended meaning? He explains it with the words "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*). The meaning is that because the quality of bliss (*sattva*) exists in deep sleep—characterized by the absence of suffering and the abundance of unsurpassed happiness—it is described as such with that intention. || 27 ||
Abiding therein, the wise one is delighted and reeling with supreme bliss;
he always perceives this creation as if it were a mere play.
He explains what the vision of the world is like for one established therein: "Therein" (verse 28).
Free from sorrow, fear, and exertion, with the agitation of saṃsāra gone, the self-possessed one who has ascended to the fourth state (turya) does not fall again. 29.
One might ask: "Would he not fall there again while beholding that divine play? To this, he says: "vīta... (verse 29).
Having attained his own holy state, he—possessing a steady intellect—looks upon this world as it revolves, laughing at it like one standing on a mountain peak looking down at those below. (30)

To explain why he does not fall [into that state], he says: "Having attained... The meaning is that he looks upon it with laughter through the perception of its defects, rather than through the notion that it is a human goal (puruṣārtha). || 30 ||
But having attained an imperishable state in this fourth stage (turya-avasthā), because of being completely absorbed in absolute bliss, he has reached the state beyond bliss.
Indeed, because he has transcended even the stages of non-bliss and great bliss, the yogi who has reached the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is called "liberated. || 32 ||

Having thus described his state of *turya* (the fourth) for as long as he lives, the text now describes the state of *turyātīta* (beyond the fourth) for one who is *videha* (bodiless), beginning with the verse "anānanda" and so forth. In comparison to the three states (*avasthātraya*), the state of *turya* is considered "great bliss" (*mahānanda*);

this is always the case for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). However, in the state of liberation after death (*videhamukti*), since there is no possibility of recollecting the absence of bliss (*anānanda*)—as that state has transcended all reference points—it is [described] in relation to that.
The meaning is that, because of the impossibility of attributing magnitude to it, one who has transcended even that is said to have reached the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
With all the bonds of birth completely dissolved and all conceit consisting of darkness entirely melted away,
one attains an existence composed of the supreme essence.
The Great-Souled One is like a fragment of rock salt dissolved in water. || 33 ||
Describing that very state, he concludes with the words "parigalita" and so forth: because all egoistic identifications (*abhimāna*) consisting of darkness have dissolved within him,
this Great Soul (*mahātman*) has consequently cast off the noose of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and action, which are the causes of all births.

The meaning is that, like a lump of rock salt dissolved in water, once the state of being a solid fragment has vanished, it becomes the supreme *rasa*—that is, bliss—and as the aspect cognizable solely through tasting, it attains an existence consisting of that [bliss], which is the ultimate state of reality. || 33 ||

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Non-attachment and Conceptualization," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Tranquility) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "Instruction on Non-attachment with Mental Constructs," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: As long as there is the reflective awareness of the fourth state (turya), so long is there the state of absolute oneness (kevalatā).
O descendant of Raghu, this is the subject of the words of one who is liberated while living.
Because the other [states] are not subject to conventional usage, the fourth state is described here;
just as the sequence of births arises from delusion through the negation of the body and so forth. (1)
To demonstrate that the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta-pada*) is not an object of linguistic or other conventional discourse, he prepares the following introductory framework:

As long as there is even the slightest conceptual reflection (*parāmarśa*) regarding the fourth state— which is characterized by the remaining of pure consciousness alone— that much constitutes the state of absolute isolation for the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), as well as the purport of the words of the Vedas and other scriptures.
The object [of the cognition]. The sense is that the non-dual (akhaṇḍa) mental modification (vṛtti) produced by the sentence terminates precisely there. || 1 ||
Beyond this, O mighty-armed one, there is no object for the speech of those who are bodiless and liberated, just as the sky is not the domain of ordinary men.
Beyond that, even the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which is attainable by the liberated ones who are bodiless,

is not the domain of those Vedic words, because the mind— the cause for establishing anything as an object— has ceased to exist. Just as the atmosphere, the space traversed by the wind, is not the domain of men, that is, of human beings.
The meaning is "in that same way. || 2 ||
For that state of rest is more distant even than the farthest distance;
it is accessible only to those liberated while in the body-less state (videhamukta), like the path of the wind to those without bodies.
"Accessible" means reachable. "Khalekhā" refers to the path of the sky. It is like [the path] of the winds (nabhasvats). || 3 ||
Having enjoyed the maintenance of the world for some time through the state of deep sleep,
he thereafter attains the fourth state (turya), reeling with supreme bliss.

Therefore, he states that for those liberated while still embodied, their abiding occurs only within the stages ending with the seventh, following the sequence of the fifth stage, in the verse beginning with "suṣupta" (deep sleep). || 4 ||
O scion of Raghu’s lineage, just as those who know that [reality] and are skilled in the Self reach the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), so too do you attain that state free from dualities.

However, you must achieve firmness in knowledge that culminates in resting in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), rather than merely concluding at the intermediate stages; thus he says: "Beyond the fourth... (verse 5).
O Rāma, subduer of enemies, engage in worldly affairs with the state of deep sleep; like the moon of a painting, you shall have neither waning nor agitation.

In this regard, with the intention that the first [state] alone, belonging to the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), must be practiced for the sake of carrying out the technical conventions of the treatise, he says: "by means of the state of deep sleep" (*suṣuptāvasthayā*).
"Decay" (*kṣaya*) refers to death and the diminution of the *kalās*. "Agitation" (*udvega*) refers to fear and the eclipse by Rāhu. (6)
Whether the configuration of the body perishes or consciousness remains stable, do not grasp at this delusion which expands, thinking, "This is the body. (7)
[Objection: "But surely, since the destruction of consciousness (saṃvit) is unavoidable when the body perishes, how is it that there is no decay for me whose self is consciousness?
To this he replies with the verse beginning "śarīra..."—the ellipsis being "the destruction and the stability of consciousness. (7)
What purpose do you have in the destruction of the body, and what purpose do you have in its preservation? Engage yourself in the activities of nature; let this [body] remain as it is.

If there is the delusion that "this is the body," then let that very delusion perish; regarding this, he says: "deha" (the body). Become one whose effort—the exertion—is directed toward the stability of the realization of your own Self in this context; such is this body. || 8 ||
You have known that truth; you have awakened to that state;
you have attained your own true nature. Be free from sorrow for the welfare of all beings.

He removes doubt regarding the realization of one's own Self with the words, "You have known it. "Truth" (satyam) is the reality that is the substratum of the world. "The state" (padam) is the substratum of the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]. "Your own form" (svaṃ rūpam) is the nature of the meaning of the indivisible sentence. || 9 ||

Having abandoned both the desired and the undesired, you shine like the sky freed from darkness and clouds by the beauty of its cool light— [if the reading "śobhase" were used, it would be more appropriate]. 10.
"Kha" means, by implication, the autumnal sky. || 10 ||
One who is endowed with mental praise and self-perfection does not run downward,
just as a person perfected through yoga, mantra, and austerity does not fall from the sky to the earth.

"Below" refers to the pleasures of the objects of the senses belonging to the lower realm. "Accomplished" means one who has attained the power of moving through the sky; just as one who has left the sky does not run back toward the earth, so it is in this case. (11)
Here, there exists only pure consciousness, devoid of near and far;
let there be no delusion in you regarding "this," "I," "that," or "mine. (12)
"On this shore and on the further shore" means on the near bank and the distant bank; that is to say, within the limits of spatial division. || 12 ||
The designation "Self" is imagined for the sake of conventional usage regarding the All-pervasive One;
however, distinctions such as name and form have long since departed from Him. (13)
If pure consciousness alone exists, then it is the Self; how then can there be any designation other than that? To this he says:
"The Self. (13)
Just as the ocean is nothing but water and not distinct from its waves and so forth, so too all this is only the Self and not distinct from the elements such as earth and water. 14.
Just as nothing other than water can be found within the entirety of the ocean, even so, nothing other than the Self can be found within the vast expanse of the world. 15.
From the entire, full water; from the expansive world, which has spread out through its own nature as the world-soul. || 15 ||
O wise one, where do you establish the notion "this is I"?
What is that reality, and what would belong to you; what is that reality, and what would not belong to you? (16)

Regarding the entities such as the body and so forth: what is that which you are, and what is that which belongs to you? Or, where you are not, what is that which does not belong to you? Since, from the perspective of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), it is impossible for anything to possess your nature or to be conjoined with you, [you are] everywhere indeed from the perspective of the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
And the sense is that it arises from that. || 16 ||
There is no duality, nor are there bodies, nor does any connection with them exist; nor can any stain be conceived [in it], just as darkness cannot affect the sun. (17)

But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even duality does not exist; therefore, the possibility of a body, its relation [to a self], its material cause, or any such defilements is cast far away. Thus he says: "No."
Even granting, O Slayer of Enemies, that duality exists, I declare that there can be no connection between the All-pervading One and the body and so forth, even though they exist. (18)

Even if duality and the reality of the body and so forth were accepted, contact between the conscious self (cidātman) and those [phenomena] is simply not possible; demonstrating this bold assertion, he says, beginning with "dvitvam" (duality), etc. (verse 18).
Just as no connection is possible between the spreading of shadow and sunlight, or between light and darkness, so indeed it is with the body and the embodied soul.

In the first case, characterized by the spreading into a single spatial point (pradeśa), the illustration [is given] for conjunction (saṃsarga); in the second case, it is for identity (tādātmya). || 19 ||
Just as there can never be a connection between cold and heat, which are eternally opposed to one another, O Rāma, so it is with the body and the self.
But how can the relationship between these two—the insentient and the sentient, the body and the embodied—which is characterized by inseparable concomitance, be experienced? (21)
"Let there be neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor identity (*tādātmya*); why then should there not be inherence (*samavāya*)? To this he replies:
"Of two things that are inseparable (*avinābhāvin*). This means "of two things that are not established separately (*ayutasiddha*). || 21 ||
This discourse concerning the connection of the Self, which is pure consciousness alone, with the body—
its meaning is as difficult to comprehend as the ocean [being contained] within a forest fire.
The meaning is that this statement is difficult to comprehend because: if the body were the locus of consciousness, it could not be an object, which would result in its non-manifestation;
if it were an object, it could not be the locus, as inherence (samavāya) and other relations would be unestablished;
and since the relation of being an object is common to both real and unreal things, it cannot be established as real. It is like saying "an ocean in fire."
"He speaks"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 22 ||
By the contemplation of truth, this false view perishes, just as the ocean evaporates under the heat of the sun through such contemplation. (23)
If it is argued that the relationship is merely superimposed there as well, he replies with the word "real" (satya).

The meaning is that if the superimposition of the relationship between the body and the self were based upon the Self as its substratum, then that superimposition would be sublated by the mere perception of the Self. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the similarity [of the two cases] consists in the fact that the difference superimposed [upon the Self] undergoes sublation. || 23 ||
The conscious self is stainless, eternal, self-luminous, and free from affliction;
the body, however, is impermanent and impure—how then can it be bound by that [consciousness]? 24.

He states that the Self does not touch the impure body and so forth because of the contradiction with its innate purity, established by such scriptural passages as "pure, untouched by evil," etc.—thus: "The conscious Self" (cidātman). || 24 ||
The body vibrates due to the wind or is made corpulent by the elements;
therefore, there is not even the slightest connection between it and the Self.

If it is asked, "In the absence of a connection with a self, how can there be movement and so forth in the body, since such things are not observed in a dead body? he says in response: "Movement... [The body] is made robust—that is, nourished and increased—by the wind, namely the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), and by the elements, such as food and so forth, which are the causes for the support of the vital breath; that is to say, its strength is infused. Thus, regarding movement:
The meaning is that either vital breath (*prāṇa*) or strength (*bala*) is the cause, not the self (*ātman*). The particle *eva* is used in the sense of "also. There is no connection with the body.
Even if duality were established for the body, a connection [between it and the self] would not be possible;
but if duality itself is not established, O wise one, how could such a conceptualization even arise? (26)

Thus, when there is no connection even when the reality of duality is accepted, what need be said when it is not accepted? Concluding this bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), he says: "When [it] is established" (*siddhe*)—that is, when [duality] is real.
Therefore, while that [reality] exists, establish your inner abiding right there.
There is neither bondage nor liberation for anyone, at any time, or anywhere. (27)

Now, one might ask: "But why is duality itself not established? Anticipating this objection, the author extends the previously demonstrated arguments—which were intended to refute the relationship—to that case as well, saying "iti" (thus). If anyone should suspect the existence—that is, the reality—of that duality, then this very collection of arguments mentioned earlier must be presented.

For if a second consciousness were established, there would have to be duality; yet if that second consciousness exists, there is no factor to differentiate it from the first. If it were insentient, then—due to the contradiction between sentience and insentience, like light and shadow—it could not be established as opposed to the previously established consciousness.

Furthermore, the claim that consciousness establishes an insentient object with which it is not connected is a discourse whose meaning is difficult to comprehend. [If it is argued that it is] superimposed...

The sense is this: if [impurity] were to perish merely by the observation of consciousness (*cit*), then how could that which is impure and insentient—which is contrary to the nature of the Self consisting of stainless non-attachment—be established by means of that non-attachment? Such logical arguments apply equally here as well.
Therefore, abandoning the delusion of duality, remain steadfast in that very non-dual pure consciousness (*advitīyacinmātra*). And therein:
The meaning is that there is not even the slightest doubt regarding bondage, liberation, and so forth. || 27 ||
"O Rāma, bring to firmness everywhere, both internally and externally, this clear conviction that 'everything is composed of the Self and is peaceful. (28)
He states what that state is like which must be maintained by me: "All," etc. (Verse 28).
"I am happy," "I am miserable," "I am deluded"—these are known as false views (durdṛṣṭi).
If you regard these as real objects, then you shall long experience suffering.

With the intention that the view of a self in all things becomes firm only through the rejection of contradictory and false views, and not otherwise, he says: "Happy," etc. That, then, [is the case]. 29.
The same sequence that applies to a mountain and a blade of grass, or likewise to silk and a stone, is said to apply to the Supreme Self and the body.
Now, an objection may be raised: "Are not the body, suffering, and so forth also presented by perception and other means of knowledge? And is not the Self also presented by scripture and reasoning?

Since these two are thus equal, what is the distinction on account of which it is said that one should rely upon the vision of the Self and discard the vision of the body and so forth? To this, he says: "He who... The word *krama* (sequence) refers to the distinction. As follows:
With the eye, from a distance between a mountain and a blade of grass, perception of the mountain is easy because of its largeness and stability;

perception of the blade of grass is difficult because of its movement and fragility. Or, just as with the skin, the touch of silk is to be accepted because of its softness and pleasantness to the touch.

Because it is harsh and because it causes suffering, the perception of the touch of a stone is to be abandoned; likewise, because it is undivided, eternally self-luminous, and of the nature of bliss, the vision of the Supreme Self is easy to achieve and is to be accepted.
However, the perception of the body and so forth as the Self is [to be abandoned] because they are insubstantial, unstable, and dependent upon the mind and other such factors.
The meaning is that there is no equality between the two, because there is a great difference: [the former] is difficult to abandon, whereas [the latter] is easy to abandon. || 30 ||
Just as there is no connection nor any equality between light and darkness,
O Rāma, so it is with the absolute difference between the Self and the body.
With the intention that similarity, like their relationship, can also be refuted because of their mutual contradiction, he says:
"Just as the unity of cold and heat is not seen even in mere discourse, so too there is no union between the insentient and light; likewise, there is no [union] between the self and the body. (32)
With the intention that, precisely because of this contradiction, there is no possibility of even suspecting identity, he says "yathā" (just as).
The intention is that since even conjunction (*śleṣa*), which is contact, is impossible, unity is all the more remote. || 32 ||
The body moves by means of that very wind; by it one comes and goes.
It produces sound through the wind that sports within the channels of the body. (33)

Previously, it was stated that bodily movements and the like are accounted for by the wind even in the absence of a prior relationship with a self; here, however, it is stated that this occurs even in the absence of identity with a self, so there is no tautology. || 33 ||
Just as sound consisting primarily of the letters ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and pa vibrates within through the internal winds,
so indeed does it arise from the body's cavities, just as [sound arises] from a bamboo flute.

The meaning is that it is established by direct perception that sound—such as the *ka*-group, *ca*-group, and *ṭa*-group—manifests when the breath-wind (*prāṇasamīraṇa*) emerging from the cavity of the throat strikes the tongue and other organs at locations such as the throat and palate, and is then expelled. [This occurs] from a bamboo, specifically a hollow *kīcaka* reed. || 34 ||
The throbbing of the pupil is the throbbing of the eye caused by the vital air (māruta);
that very same [throbbing] is merely the vibration of the sense organ, which is the consciousness of the Self alone. 35.

In this way, even the movement of all the sense organs, such as the eyes, arises solely from the vital air (vāyu). He states that for the Self, however, consciousness alone is its function and nothing else, by saying "the pupil" (*kanīnikā*). Even the movement of the pupil, which serves as the cause for the movement of the eye toward the location of the object, arises from the vital air alone. Thus...
The meaning is that she, who arises from the radiance of all the senses and is characterized by that radiance, is consciousness alone, nothing other than the Self. || 35 ||
The state of the Self resides everywhere—in space, stones, walls, and so forth;
it is perceived here within the mind alone, like a reflection in a mirror. (36)
Although that consciousness is all-pervading and eternal, it is nevertheless manifested only within the mind and its modifications, and not elsewhere; thus he says: "Like space," etc. (36).
Having abandoned the abode of the body, wherever the bird of the mind goes by the power of its own latent impressions, there alone the Self is experienced.

For this very reason, he states—in the verse beginning with "śarīra"—that the conventional usage of the self's "going to the next world" and so forth also arises solely from the movement of that [body]. || 37 ||
Just as where there is a flower, there the perception of fragrance is established,
so too where there is the mind, there the perception of a self is established.
Just as space, which is omnipresent, is reflected in a mirror, so too the Self, though omnipresent, is perceived within the mind. 39.
Just as the place where water settles is its locus upon the earth,
so too is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) the locus for the self's cognitions.
"Downcast" means low-lying. "Of those who possess self-awareness" refers to the reflections of consciousness. || 40 ||
The consciousness of the Self, reflected within the internal organ, expands this form of the world— both real and unreal— just as the radiance of the sun produces light.
The real is the empirical; the unreal is the apparent. The sense is that this is according to the Śruti: "Entering with this living self, let me manifest names and forms. || 41 ||
Therefore, it is the internal organ alone that is the cause in the cycle of existence for beings;
but because the Self transcends all, though it is the Reality, it is not a cause.

The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of those organs; although he is the cause by means of reflection, he is not a cause in his own right. || 42 ||
The great-minded say that lack of inquiry is ignorance and folly;
it is the essence of wandering in saṃsāra and the cause of the internal organ. (43)
What, then, is the cause of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)? He states it: "non-investigation" (*avicāraṇa*).
The employment of three synonyms is for the purpose of highlighting its well-known nature. || 43 ||
Due to improper observation and delusion, the mind grasps at the existence of a self;
thus, the seed-particle of total confusion appears like darkness before the sun. (44)

Due to improper observation, through the force of habitual tendencies (*saṃskāra*) from grasping things otherwise, and because of delusion (*moha*), there arises the existence of the mind— the transformation into the forms of consciousness— which serves as the sowing of the seeds for various confusions and errors. From this delusion, just as darkness arises from the sun, there emerges the succession of misfortunes such as birth, old age, and death, which would otherwise be utterly impossible.

The meaning is that it is perceived. Alternatively, ignorance is perceived by everyone directly within their own self as "I am ignorant," just as Rāhu is seen when he emerges from the sun; such is the meaning. || 44 ||

O Rāghava, by the thorough knowledge of the single reality of the self as it truly is, the mind completely reaches a state of non-existence in an instant, just as darkness does by means of a lamp. (45)
By what, then, is there the destruction of the mind? To this he says: "Just as... (verse 45).

One should personally investigate from this [text] the cause of saṃsāra, which is the mind (cetas), known by such names as the individual soul (jīva), the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), consciousness (citta), and the intellect (manas). (46)

He states by what means the thorough knowledge of the reality of the Self is attained: "saṃsāra... (beginning with the word *saṃsāra*). For this reason—that ignorance is the cause of transmigratory existence—the qualified seeker, whether having arrived at this point or acting of his own accord, should investigate that [Self];
He describes that [Self] as "jīva... (beginning with the word *jīva*). That is, [the Self] whose names are *jīva* and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādipada), there is also an inclusion of other names mentioned in the section on origination (utpatti-prakaraṇa). || 46 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord, O Brāhmaṇa, how have these designations become established in the mind? Tell me this, O giver of honor, for the sake of my spiritual perfection.

"Rūḍhi" means conventional usage; "yogarūḍhi" means conventional usage based on etymological derivation. How? By what derivation? For the sake of accomplishment—that is, for the sake of accomplishing the investigation as it has been stated. || 47 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
All these phenomena are eternally of the single nature of the reality of the Self,
just as the multitude of waves are nothing but water.

Therein, at the outset, Vasiṣṭha constructs an introductory framework (pīṭhikā) to etymologically define the name "Jīva" through both its conventional (rūḍhi) and derivative (yoga) senses, beginning with the words "All entities" (sarve bhāvāḥ). This is a reminder of what was previously stated: that all entities (bhāvāḥ), meaning objects, arise from the collective mind (samaṣṭicitta) as being of a single form due to the superimposition of identity with the reality of the Self (ātmatattva). || 48 ||
The Self, whose nature is solely vibration, resides here and there within them, just as the water of the ocean exists within its restless waves. (49)
He states the cause for the differentiation of the stability of those [states] that have arisen, beginning with the words "the self" (ātman) and so forth. || 49 ||
In some places, Maheśvara remains among them as one whose nature is motionless,
like the state of water in waters that have not yet attained the condition of waves.
In that regard, entities such as stones and the like are motionless and abide in their own nature;
however, beings such as humans are restless, possessing movement like the foam of wine. (51)
