Within those bodies, that [Supreme Self], whose nature is all-powerful, has assumed the conceptualization of ignorance; therefore, it remains as ignorance.

The conceptualization of ignorance—which is itself imagined and constructed—is well known. For that reason, having become that very ignorance which it itself imagined, it remains in the states of dissolution and deep sleep. (52)
That ignorance, adorned by the infinite Self, is called the *jīva*;
it is an elephant trapped within the cage of the great delusion of *māyā* in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). || 53 ||

It shines as if adorned by the infinite Self that has entered into the state of a reflection; that very [Self], through its aspect of manifestation (*rūḍhyaṃśa*), is called the individual soul (*jīva*). 53.
It is called *jīva* because of its vitalizing function; through the state of "I-ness," it becomes the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
By virtue of its determinative nature, it is the intellect (*buddhi*), and through the formation of volitions, it is the mind (*manas*). (54)

In that regard, he states the aspect of yoga: "from sustaining life" (*jīvanāt*). This means from the maintenance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). He explains the etymology of the name "I" (*aham*): "from the sense of 'I'" (*ahaṃbhāvāt*). According to the Vedic scripture: "He first uttered 'I am' (*so'ham*); therefore, he came to have the name 'I'.
He also mentions other names with the words beginning with "intellect" (*buddhi*). || 54 ||
The primordial nature (prakṛti) exists as the primordial nature, and the body exists as that which is smeared [with it];
the insentient exists by way of its state as primordial nature, while the sentient exists by its own self-existence. (55)
By being smeared, that is, by being accumulated; by its natural state, that is, by the predominance of the factor of ignorance;
and by its own existence, that is, by the predominance of consciousness. || 55 ||
That supreme self-nature which lies between the inert and the conscious—that very same reality is spread out as manifoldness under various designations. (56)

The meaning is this: that which lies in the intermediate space between the insentient and the sentient—the ignorant mind and its witness—is the mind accompanied by the appearance of light (sābhāsa-manas).

It is this very thing that, having attained multiplicity, is spread out under various designations such as the individual soul (jīva), intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), consciousness (citta), and ego (ahaṃkāra). || 56 ||
O sinless one, the true nature of the individual soul has indeed been proclaimed in many ways and in numerous places within the Vedāntas, such as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and others. (57)

He cites scriptural authority (*śruti*) for the fact that the Supreme Self alone, through its entry into limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), acquires various designations based on those adjuncts: "Thus," etc. Beginning with the words, "This very [Self] has entered here, even to the tips of the fingernails," it is said:
"Breathing, it becomes breath (*prāṇa*); speaking, it becomes speech (*vāk*); seeing, it becomes sight (*cakṣus*); hearing, it becomes hearing (*śrotra*)."

"Thinking 'I am the mind,' these are merely its names derived from its functions. Likewise: "Being the same [in both states], it moves through both worlds; it meditates, as it were, and it stirs, as it were. Becoming thought (dhī), and becoming dream, it transcends this world and the forms of death. And likewise in another Śruti passage: "By the quality of the intellect (buddhi) and by the quality of the Self..."

"Indeed, it is seen to be even as small as the tip of an awl; the individual soul (jīva) should be known as a part of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold, and yet it is capable of infinity. "Having created that, he entered into it; having entered it, it became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat). In the Taittirīyaka, he [the Lord] this...

Having split open the boundary, he entered through this door; therefore, he is named *Indra*. As it is said in the *Aitareya Upaniṣad*: "That which is this heart and mind—this is consciousness (*saṃjñāna*), discernment (*ājñāna*), understanding (*vijñāna*), wisdom (*prajñāna*)," and so forth.
"You alone are one, having entered into many. One God, though manifoldly distributed; being one, you are distributed in many ways."
The meaning is that this has been declared in many ways in hundreds of such scriptural passages. || 57 ||
But regarding these designations, false conceptualizations have been fruitlessly established by ignorant and deluded sophists solely for the purpose of deceiving the foolish. (58)

For this very reason, with the intention that the various and inconsistent conceptions of the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) held by non-Vedic sophists (*kutārkika*) are not to be respected, he says: "By the ignorant," etc. *Āsthāḥ* means attachments or dogmatic convictions. (58)
Thus, O mighty-armed one, this individual soul is the cause of saṃsāra;
what has been done here by this mute and most wretched body? (59)

And thus it is established that neither the pure Self nor the body possesses transmigratory existence (saṃsāritā), but rather it belongs only to the intermediate *jīva*; with this intention, he says "evam" (thus). [The text continues: "by the mute one," meaning by one devoid of speech and so forth; that is to say, by the insentient (*jaḍa*).
When either the support or the supported perishes, the other is not destroyed.
In whatever way the body and so forth may perish, there is no destruction of the self.

For this very reason, he states that even upon the destruction of the body, there is no destruction of the living self (jīva), using the words "ādhāra" etc. The word division is: "nāśe na" (not at destruction).
Just as when the sap of a single leaf has been exhausted, the essence does not undergo further decay, yet the leaf-sap enters into the network of the sun’s rays; || 61 ||
Upon the dissolution of the body, the embodied soul does not undergo destruction for anyone;
if it is free from latent impressions (vāsana), it likewise abides in the state of the Self within the ether.

If one possesses latent impressions (*savāsana*), then upon the dissolution of the body, one remains within those impressions; if one is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), the meaning is that one abides in the void, which is the very nature of the space of Brahman (*brahmākāśa*). || 62 ||
I consider that for one whose ignorance is such that they harbor the delusion, "I am destroyed when the body is destroyed," a vampire has arisen from the slope of his mother’s breast. (63)
For that fool who [perceives] the destruction of the body— which is the cause of fearlessness according to the Śruti, "Indeed, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless"—
as being a cause of fear due to his perverted vision,
even survival through suckling at the mother's breast becomes difficult to achieve, as he suspects the emergence of a Vetāla from it.
This is the intended meaning. || 63 ||
For that whose destruction is absolute is declared to have arisen;
indeed, the destruction of the mind would be destruction, and that is called liberation. (64)

If it is argued that since the body is distinct from the living soul (jīva), fear arises for the mother upon its destruction; whereas since the mind is of the nature of the living soul, it is indeed appropriate for the soul itself to have fear upon its destruction—to this he replies with the words "yasya" (of whom):
if there were the absolute destruction of that limiting adjunct (upādhi), which acts as a bond like an adamantine shackle, then that [entity] would be the living soul.

Being one who has remembered and recognized his true nature as Brahman, he becomes "risen," having attained the exaltation characterized by unsurpassed bliss; for such a dissolution of the mind would indeed be the destruction of the individual soul (*jīva*), and that is considered his liberation (*mokṣa*), which is described in the scriptures as the supreme goal of man (*paramapuruṣārtha*).
Therefore, the apprehension of fear even from that [source] is utterly improper; this is the meaning. || 64 ||
It is said that one who has died is "lost," yet I consider that to be false and unreal;
for having become separated by space and time, he is experienced again and again.
That is the living soul (jīva). Furthermore, it is experienced and seen again upon the assumption of another body. || 65 ||
Thus they are perceived by people as if by blades of grass within waves, under the designation of "death," while hidden by space and time. (66)

In this saṃsāra, within the rivers designated as death, by people who are like blades of grass tossed amidst the waves— by living beings whose essential natures are concealed by space and time— the states described in this manner, such as "dead," "lost," "born," "grown," "happy," or "miserable," are inferred; that is to say, they are conceptualized through delusion.
The individual soul, abiding in its latent impressions (vāsanā), departs after casting off the body, just as a monkey, having left one forest tree, takes its stand upon another. || 67 ||
Likewise, with the intention that the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is the cause for the diversity of mental construction (*ūhana*), he says: "Latent impression" (verse 67).
Again, O Rāghava, having abandoned even that, it goes elsewhere in an instant— to another vast region and at another time.
Driven here and there by their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), living beings are led for a long time by that which sustains them, just as children are led by a cunning nursemaid.

Having concealed those living beings—that is, having set them aside—she whose nature it was to live by such means was "tadapījīvinī"; by such a disposition, that is, by a deceitful nurse (dhātrī), who is so called because she is attached to a rogue (dhūrta)—the suffix *ṅīṣ* being applied here due to connection with a masculine noun (*puṃyoga*). || 69 ||
Ensnared by the rope of latent impressions and worn out within the mountain caves, those who live by the lives of living beings waste away their own lives with extreme suffering. (70)

Bound and entwined by the ropes of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), those very living beings (*jīva*) whose livelihood (*jīvikā*)—the means of subsistence—is mutual utility, having perished in the past, now cause others to decay. (70)
The women, burdened by the weight of suffering brought on by advanced old age, their lives shattered by the decrepitude of decline,
yet following the persistence of impressions born in their hearts—
People fall for a long time into the burden of hell. || 71 ||
The people— living beings who, due to the influence of latent impressions formed in the heart as a cause, are more decrepit than even the aged; being worn out,

they have taken upon themselves the heavy burden of sufferings such as poverty, disease, and separation— and are, by the process of transformation through the various miserable conditions of diverse births, shattered as if made frail by fragments of misery.

The meaning is this: alas, for those whose very life consists of such [actions], they fall and dwell for a long time amidst the burdens of hell; thus, the misfortune brought about by the defect of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is endless. || 71 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the sage had spoken thus, the day passed away, and the sun went to its setting for the performance of the evening rites.
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe;
and at the end of night, it returned along with the rays of the sun.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "Instruction on Saṃsāra," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki;
and thus concludes the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-first canto, titled "Instruction on Saṃsāra."
The thirteenth day.
The seventy-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"When the body is born, you are not born; when the body is destroyed, you are not destroyed."
You are the stainless self within yourself; this body is nothing at all to you.
Because the body is composed of material elements, it is incapable of sorrow, delusion, and the like;
the Witness, being pure, is described as distinct from the relationship between the seen and the seer. (1)
The meaning of the second half [of the verse] is the reason for the meaning of the first half. || 1 ||
The analogy of the jujube fruit in a bowl, or the situation of the space within a jar—when one of these two is damaged or diminished, the notion that "both are" is a futile conceptualization. (2)

[Objection: But surely, because of the experience of identity with the body in the form "I am fair" or "I am fat," how can the Self remain when the body is destroyed? To this he says: "He [is... (*yaḥ*). Here, "abiding" (*saṃsthiti*) should be understood as the *maryādā* (boundary or limit), not as identity (*tādātmya*). This being the case, when one—either the basin or the jar—is broken or destroyed, both are likewise destroyed.
The meaning is that this is a futile conceptualization of the deluded. || 2 ||
When this perishable body has been destroyed and has returned to its own state, fie upon that blind-minded person who grieves, thinking, "I am perishing. (3)
In that which is perishable, having a nature subject to destruction. || 3 ||
Just as the relationship between two chariots and their reins is devoid of affection or agitation,
so too is the connection of consciousness with the body, mind, and senses.

If there is no identity between the self and the body and so forth, then how is it that this [self] transmigrates through the activity of those [body etc.], just as a tree does through the trembling of its branches?
To this, he says: "Of such a kind... It is devoid of affection, which is the capacity for attachment, and agitation, which is the capacity for aversion. || 4 ||
O Rāghava, just as the relationship between the mud and the turbid water of a lake exists through mutual dependence, so too is the connection between the body, the senses, and the self.
Mutual dependence is reciprocal attachment. || 5 ||
Just as the path of those who have traveled the road is free from expectation and lamentation,
so too is the union and separation of the body and the embodied soul.

The meaning is that for those travelers who have already gone their way, there is no basis for the conceit of "I" and "mine," nor for lamentation—the wailing born of separation from them; he is unworthy of both.
Just as those terrified by the transformations of an imagined vetāla are themselves falsely imagined, so too are affection, happiness, and the like.

To explain why that is so, he says: "Just as... The transformations of an imagined vetāla—such as its gaping mouth and bared fangs—arise from the initial fear produced by it; yet, conversely, the people fashioned from the aggregate of the five elements do not [fear] it.
Separately... [the verse continues: "The multitudes of people, constructed from the massed collection of the five elements..."
Like various little figurines [carved] from a single piece of wood. || 8 ||
In a load of wood, nothing other than wood is seen;
in this body, which is a mere mass of elements, nothing other than that is seen.
O people, when the five elements are agitated, destroyed, or produced, why have you fallen under the sway of joy, resentment, and despair? (10)
What excellence indeed is there in men toward that fragile aggregate of elements called "woman," which bears another name [for its opposite] and is like a sudden calamity befalling people? (11)

Having established the unsuitability of affection and the like toward one's own body, he demonstrates that same [unsuitability] even toward the physical forms of women and others with the verse beginning "Who" (ka).

The meaning is: what indeed could that degree of excellence be, by which the activity of people—who, like moths, are driven by delusion and passion—appears as if they were being cast into the fire of sense-objects?
The diversity of arrangements and parts is for the satisfaction of the ignorant alone;
but for those who know that [reality], there is the vision of the five elements exactly as they are.
That excellence is seen precisely in the particular arrangement of the delicate and beautiful limbs; regarding this, he says:
"arrangement" (saṃniveśa). || 12 ||
Just as there is no passion between two stone statues, even though they are joined together like two figures carved from a single rock, so too there is no passion between the mind and the body. 13.

He restrains attachment toward brothers and others with the word "mutually" (*mithaḥ*). [This refers to] two sons of the same stone, born from the same stone; "embraced" means closely joined. || 13 ||
May your union of intellect, senses, self, and mind be such as the mutual disposition of clay figures would be when they meet. 14.

This statement is made by imagining the disposition—that is, the state of being—of clay-made human figures, such that even when they are brought together, their intention would be devoid of possessiveness and the like. (14)
O sons of stone, you do not possess the capacity for mutual affection; so who here should lament over the body, the senses, the self, and the vital breaths? 15.
Just as waves thoroughly entangle masses of grass blown hither and thither, so does the perception of a body entangle the elements.
And furthermore, there are networks of grass grown in different locations here and there. || 16 ||
Just as blades of grass in the waters of the ocean are joined together and then separated,
so indeed do the elements within the body unite and disperse within the Self once internal conceptualization has ceased.

The meaning is that, with internal mental constructions ceased and free from passion and egoism, living beings— whether they be children, cattle, and other creatures, or the elements such as earth and so forth— are joined with and separated from their own commenced body, their own locus, and the Self, in whatever manner may be. || 17 ||
The Self, existing as consciousness, remains embracing the elements that constitute the body,
like the ocean surging with the turbulent movement of its waves that encompass the blades of grass.

Just as the ocean, having assumed the form of whirlpools through its revolving movements, becomes swollen and agitated by that mental construction and remains embracing blades of grass, pieces of wood, and so forth; in the same way, the Self also, by becoming the mind, assumes the guise of the mind—this is the meaning. || 18 ||
Through awakening, having abandoned the state of being an object of thought, the Self spontaneously attains its own true nature,
just as water, by the power of its own movement, abandons its turbidity and attains clarity.
By what means, then, is the self liberated from the state of the mind caused by attachment to the elements?

He explains this with the words beginning "through awakening" (prabodhāt). Having abandoned both clarity and lack of clarity—[this is explained as follows]: in a negative *tatpuruṣa* compound, the letter *n* is elided;
the long vowel [in *anacchatvam*] arises from the rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), and the absence of the augment *nuṭ* is a Vedic anomaly. || 19 ||
Then, with the multitude of elements separated, the living being situated within the mass of air perceives its body as one perceives the circle of the earth.

At this time of awakening, the celestial beings and others, having entered the mass of air and being freed from the attachment to the elements produced by the mind, have their multitudes of elements disintegrated. || 20 ||
Having seen the collection of elements as separate, the unborn one transcends the body and attains supreme radiance,
like the brilliance of the sun during the day.
He states the result of that: "separately," etc. (verse 21).
Then he knows himself by himself, freed from the maladies of the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge,
like one who has recovered from intoxication, inwardly recollecting his own consciousness.
By being freed from intoxication, that is, by being released from the madness of liquor. || 22 ||
The Self alone vibrates as the entire universe, appearing as if arisen through a multitude of objects, just as the infinite waters of the ocean appear as waves, droplets, and surges. (23)
Having attained such great enlightenment, free from passion and devoid of sin, those who have reached the state of great beings wander here as liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 24 ||
Just as great waves move by means of various jewels and gems, so do the supreme ones, free from latent tendencies, move through the conventional activities of the mind.
Even when bound with various excellent jewels, because they are unattached to them, they move about and conduct themselves as if those jewels were mere fragments of stone. || 25 ||
The ocean is not filled by the wood scraped from its shores, nor the sky by dust;
likewise, the self-possessed person here does not wither through his own worldly activities.
The words "just as" and "so too" are to be supplied here [in the verse]. || 26 ||

For one who has realized the Self, there is neither attachment nor aversion toward the ocean of worldly enjoyments— whether they have come or departed, whether they are pure or turbid, fickle or dull.
Passion does not arise from clear [states], nor does hatred from those that are turbid; these qualifiers are to be applied to both cases.
This refers to one who has realized the self, the knower of reality. 27.

Whatever mental reflection exists in its entirety within the world, the wise know that to be the radiant play of the principle of consciousness (cittattva) as it inclines toward the object of thought (cetya). 28.
He asks from where there is no passion there, and says: "That which... The meaning is that since they know all mental ideation to be nothing but the play of consciousness (*cidvilāsa*). || 28 ||
That which is myself and that which is the primordial being (bhūtādi), as well as whatever exists throughout the three periods of time—
that all expands through the extensions of the relationship between the seen and the seeing.

The meaning is that whatever appears as the entire expansion of the relationship between the seer and the seen, beginning with "I," that is merely the mind itself manifesting, and nothing else. || 29 ||

Whatever is perceived, whether it be non-existent or existent, rests upon a single vision; yet another [vision] is free from such attachment. Therefore, whence can there be the states of joy and sorrow? (30)
In this context, between the two—the seer and the seen—that which is the seen depends upon one of them, the seer;
its very establishment is contingent upon that [seer]. Because it is undetermined as to whether it is real or unreal, the seen is unfit for joy or sorrow.
The other, however, is the seer whose nature is self-established; it is untainted and unattached, even by those things that have arisen.
"He is not joined with joy or sorrow"—the meaning is that there is no possibility whatsoever of these two occurring in either case.
"Untruth is indeed untruth; truth is indeed always truth. Know that the 'truth-untruth' is non-existence (asat); for what purpose, then, do you become deluded? (31)

Furthermore, he states that joy and sorrow are not appropriate in any of the three cases—whether regarding an unreal object, a real one, or one that is both real and unreal—with the words "only unreal" (*asatyam eva*). It is simply unreal; in that case, the lack of an objective basis for joy and sorrow is quite evident. As for the real...
Since it is eternally existent, it is clearly unfit for the joy associated with the acquisition [of gain] or the sorrow associated with its loss.

As for that third possibility—being both real and unreal—that too is non-existent because of the impossibility of a contradictory unity; thus, it falls into the very first category. And so, since nothing at all in this world is fit for such [joy or sorrow], the delusion regarding it is indeed improper. This is the meaning.
Abandoning false vision, see correctly, O one with beautiful eyes;
the mature person who possesses right vision is never deluded in this world.
It expands through the elaborations of the relationship between the seen and the seeing;
that which is the supreme spiritual bliss within the relationship of the seen and the seeing— // 33 //
Furthermore, for the sake of the happiness of enjoyment, a connection between all objects and sense organs—the seen and the seeing—is desired;
therein, that which is manifested is indeed the supreme Self itself. Because it is self-luminous, it is non-different from experience.
By dispelling distinctions such as degrees of difference caused by the limiting adjuncts of mental modifications (*vṛtti*), it is Brahman alone in its undivided unity. Thus he says:
Therefore, Brahman is said to consist of pure experience;
it is the unsurpassed consciousness of bliss within the relationship between the seen and the seer. (34)
To the ignorant, it grants the cycle of worldly existence; to the wise, it grants ever-rising liberation.
The knower knows the bliss of the relationship between the seen and the seer as the very body of the Self.
When tasted through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) bearing the form of an object, it bestows *saṃsāra* by generating defects such as passion (*rāga*) toward that object;
however, when grasped through its discrimination as the undivided, singular Self, it results in liberation—this is the meaning. || 35 ||
Enveloped by the visible is bondage; freed from it, it is called liberation.
[This occurs] through the healthy consciousness of the blissful experience of the relationship between the seer and the seen. 36.

If that liberation is said by the wise to be free from decay and excellence, then what is that experience within its own domain which occurs during the relationship between the seen and the seeing? (37)

If [the cognition] is freed from those two—diminution and excess—which are brought about by the destruction of activity and the excellence of clarity resulting from the gradations of merit, then it consists of the manifestation of indivisible, perfect bliss within its own objective domain. (37)
Free from both the seen and the seeing, by taking hold of that [state], one experiences existence and non-existence;
for this is the state of deep sleep, and thus it shines forth.
When the object of focus is of such a nature as has been described, the vision that obscures one's true nature during deep sleep departs;
this vision of one's true nature then shines forth clearly. || 38 ||
In this way, it attains the state of the Fourth (turya), and thus it is known as liberation, when the perception of the visible has ceased through being joined with the supreme intellect. (39)
But in this consciousness of the relationship between the seen and the seeing, O Rāghava,
the Self is neither gross nor subtle, neither perceptible nor otherwise.
The consciousness of the relationship between the seen and the seeing—thus it attains the state of the Fourth (turyatva); this is the connection with what precedes.
He shows what kind of Self remains when liberation, characterized by the state of the Fourth, is attained, beginning with the words "But in this... (asyāṃ tu). || 40 ||
I am neither conscious nor inert, neither non-existent nor composed of existence;
I am not the self, nor another, neither one nor many, nor possessed of multiplicity.

He is conscious (*cetana*) and possesses sentience (*caitanyavān*). He consists of existence (*sanmaya*), being abundant in the second modification of being known as "existence" (*astitva*). He is one (*eka*), the substratum of the quality of the number one. || 41 ||
It is neither situated nearby nor far away; it neither exists nor does it not exist.
It is neither attainable nor unattainable, neither all nor all-pervading. || 42 ||
One who stands nearby, in close proximity, is called "standing near" (*abhyāśastha*). It is that which is the substratum of existence (*sattāśraya*). 42.
It is neither a thing nor a non-thing, neither fivefold nor five;
that which has come into the state of being visible is the locus of the mind and the six senses. (43)

It is not a positive entity (*padārtha*), because it cannot be the object of verbal expression; nor is it a non-entity (*apadārtha*), because it is indicated by words such as "the Fourth" (*turya*). It is not the self of the five elements, nor does it possess the nature of the five elements—this is the meaning. He states the logical justification for this point: "That which is this... (43).
That state which is beyond that is, in this world, as if nothing at all,
for one who knows it as it truly is and perceives the world correctly. (44)
For one who perceives correctly, according to reality, as it truly exists, and in its essential nature. || 44 ||
The entire universe consists of the Self; nowhere does anything exist that does not consist of the Self, [manifesting] through solidity, fluidity, motion, space, and vision.

How, then, is the state of being earth and so forth perceived there? To this he says: "By hardness," etc. It is the Self alone that, through its own perceptions of hardness, fluidity, vibration (spanda), the great void called space (kha), and light, stands like an actor within the worldly phenomena such as earth, water, and the rest, in their respective order.
This is the meaning. || 45 ||
The Self alone is everything within all beings—earth, water, air, ether, and fire. There is no existence of objects whatsoever apart from consciousness, O Rāma;
know that to say "I am separate from that" is the prattle of a madman.

To the question, "How is it certain that the Self alone exists in this way? he replies: "Being itself" (sattaiva). The meaning is: because whatever being there is of objects does not exist apart from consciousness, which is the nature of its manifestation. || 46 ||
He alone is all the worlds, passing through the succession of all times and the cycles of cosmic dissolution;
he is the Self alone, and there is no other fabrication of parts whatsoever.
O Great-souled One, let your mind be fixed on what is seen; do not go beyond it.

He summarizes everything that has been said by bringing it together in the word "one" (*eka*). Throughout all time, within the infinite succession of cosmic cycles (*kalpa*), and amidst the worlds situated therein, as well as all the movements of coming and going—the transmigrations of living beings—it is the Self alone that is one. There is no other arrangement of parts whatsoever. O Great-Souled One!
The meaning is: "With such an understanding as this, through that very understanding, may you transcend saṃsāra. || 47 ||

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "Instruction on the Nature of Liberation," in the Section on Tranquility (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) within the Means to Liberation (*mokṣopāya*), as spoken by the Divine Messenger in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "Instruction on the Nature of Liberation," in the Section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The seventy-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, by means of such a vision of inquiry and through the abandonment of duality, [the mind becomes tranquil].
Its true nature is attained by those who know it, just as the wish-fulfilling gem is obtained by those who know it. || 1 ||
Two conceptions of "I" are to be grasped, while the other conception of "I" is to be abandoned.
When the threefold conception of "I" has ceased, the absence of desire for liberation is proclaimed. (1)

Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is liberation characterized by abiding in one's own true form; it is [known] by those who know that—that is, by those who know the Self—and by the gods who know the reality of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). || 1 ||
Now hear this other view, O Rāma;
by means of this, you shall behold the immovable Self within the visible world and become one possessed of divine vision.
He begins to demonstrate the view of the "I-am-ness" (ahaṃbhāva) in its entirety with the words: "Now... (atha). || 2 ||
I am the earth, I am the sun, I am the quarters, and I am also below;
I am the Daityas, I am the gods, I am the worlds, and I am the Great Radiance.
The great splendor of the moon and other luminaries. || 3 ||
I am darkness, I am the clouds, and I am the earth, the oceans, and so forth;
I am dust, wind, and fire—indeed, I am this entire universe.
Rajas means dust. || 4 ||
I am indeed the Self alone who abides everywhere throughout the three worlds;
who am I, and what is this body and so forth? How can there be duality for that which is one?

Who am I, distinct from all and yet limited? What is this body and so forth that is other than me? For me, who am one and the soul of all beings, what kind of duality could there be in the form of internal difference? (5)
Thus, possessing this certainty that the world is contained within oneself as one's own self,
you shall see it and will not be helplessly overcome by joy or sorrow.
Having thus reflected and become firm in his resolve, thereafter, behold [the world] as being contained within yourself, for it is your very self.
O sinless one, since this entire world is established as being composed of that [Brahman], tell me, O lotus-eyed one: what could be one's own and what could be another? (7)
"In *tanmaye* means 'in one's own time' (*ātmasamaye*); the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of the word itself. (7)
Apart from that Knower, what exists that, having arrived, could cause joy or dejection? For the Knower, who is identical with the universe, there is no dejection. (8)

The phrase "if [it] has come" is the ellipsis. But if dejection is observed, he is indeed ignorant; for the meaning is that he consists of the world (*jaganmaya*) and not of consciousness (*cinmaya*). || 8 ||
These two views of the ego are of the nature of sattva and are exceedingly pure;
arising from the knowledge of reality, they are ultimate and bestow liberation.
These [terms] will be explained [later]. The sandhi is archaic (ārṣa). || 9 ||
"O scion of Raghu, the first form of egoism is 'I am the supreme atom, whose nature transcends all things'; the other is said to be 'I am everything. (10)
The subtle [Self] has a nature that is not gross, like space; it transcends everything that is perceivable in the three states. || 10 ||
But there exists a third view regarding the ego, O sinless one;
know that "I am the body" leads only to suffering and not to peace. (11)
It exists by way of intrinsic nature, not through the authority of scripture. || 11 ||
Now, having abandoned even these three for the sake of attaining all perfections,
remain firmly established, relying upon that which remains as your sole objective.
That which remains, being taught, is the state devoid of ego, the fullness of pure consciousness alone. || 12 ||
Although its nature transcends all things and it surpasses the existence of everything,
the Self, which fills the world with non-existence, truly exists as the illuminator.
Through purification, he has attained a nature that transcends all; through sublation (*bādhana*), however, he has reached the non-existence of all things.

To ward off the doubt that if everything were sublated, the Self would be left behind, he says: "non-existence" (*asattā*). By means of this very non-existence, which is the method for sublating the world, the world is filled by him with his own self. || 13 ||
Behold quickly through your own direct experience that you are indeed that which is eternally arisen;
O best among the knowers of reality, abandon the knot of the heart along with all doubt.

With the intention that logical arguments, scriptures, and the words of the teacher serve merely as a pointer, while their actual mastery occurs through one's own experience alone, he says: "by one's own experience" (svānubhūtyā).

"Aśaya" refers to the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the body and so forth; together with these, it denotes the "knot of the heart," which is the superimposition (adhyāsa) of identity with the ego (ahaṃkāra). || 14 ||
O Rāma, the self does not exist through inference, nor through the words of authoritative persons and the like;
rather, it is always, in every way, and in its entirety directly perceived through experience. 15.

[Objection: "But surely, from the Śruti text, 'I ask you about that person taught in the Upaniṣads,' it is known that the self exists as something non-empirical, based solely on faith in the Śruti and the reasoning shown therein—just like dharma, adharma, and so forth.
How then can it be known through one's own experience? To this, he says: "No. It is not [so].

The meaning is that the scriptures and other authorities do not proceed to establish the existence of the Self— which is entirely beyond perception like dharma and so forth— but rather to discern the Self whose existence is established by universal experience.
That which is touching, that which is movement, and even whatever is consciousness and so forth—all that is the Lord, the Self, devoid of the seen and the seeing. || 16 ||
He explains what was stated—that this [Self] is perceptible to all—with the words "yad idam" (that which is this).

That perception which is well-known as immediate (*aparokṣa*), consisting in the direct manifestation of objects, and which vibrates due to the movement of the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) with respect to external and internal objects; and that which...

Whatever is well known—be it even some form of inferential, analogical, or verbal cognition—all that [remains] as the Lord, the self-luminous Self alone, which is eternally immediate and established by universal experience, upon the exclusion of the visible object, the act of seeing, and the limiting adjunct of the modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti); this is the meaning. And so says the Śruti:
"That which is known through awakening is considered [the truth], for through it one indeed finds immortality. || 16 ||
That deity is neither existent nor non-existent; he is neither an atom nor is he large.
He is not the middle between these two states of perception, yet he alone is all this everywhere.

By stating its distinctness from both the manifest and the unmanifest—whether known through direct perception or indirect inference—he establishes its freedom from the seen and the seer: "neither existent nor non-existent. He further establishes this by demonstrating that the world is sublated within it: "that alone" (sa eva). || 17 ||
He speaks in this manner, yet it is not fitting for him to speak;
O dear one, see that this is not something other than the stainless Self.

Thus, having recognized that which is beyond the reach of speech and other means of expression as the cause for the activity of the organs of action such as speech, and by means of the sublation of speech and its objects therein, he concludes that "it is that very one" alone remains; with this intention, he says: "sa eva" (it is that very one).
This refers to speech and so forth, as well as their objects of expression. || 18 ||
"This is not the Self, nor is this [other] the Self; it is merely a difference in designation"—thus [the distinction] is imagined within its own self by that very all-pervading power. (19)

With the intention that the distinction between self and non-self, as well as name and form, is imagined by that very power of one's own ignorance (svājñāna-śakti), and thus its sublation is logically established, he says: "No" (na). || 19 ||
For that sun is established everywhere throughout the three times;
yet, because of its subtlety and its extreme greatness, it is not perceived at all. (20)

The meaning is that although its nature is eternally immediate, self-luminous, and full, it cannot be perceived by those whose intellects are attached to gross objects because of its subtlety. || 20 ||
While the infinite categories of existence exist,
the Self naturally reflects as the individual soul (jīva) upon the mirror of the *puryaṣṭaka* by its own inherent nature.

With the intention that, due to delusion regarding gross attachment, the cause for the soul's attainment of the state of a *jīva* is its reflection within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), he says: "When [they] exist. This means when the various objects such as the objects of enjoyment and the bodies of enjoyment have arisen through the process of creation. || 21 ||
Only through the emergence of the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka) is the Self experienced by itself,
always abiding within all things, like the wind in the sky which is not perceived due to the lack of movement of the clouds.
It is experienced as having its own nature manifested as "I," being made manifest by means of a dense, material object such as a fan and so forth, through vibration and impulsion. || 22 ||
The conscious self is all-pervading and omnipresent; it is not established anywhere in particular.
Just as existence (sattā) belongs to all objects, so too is the Great Lord.
The word "nāma" is used in the sense of restriction; the meaning is that he is not situated in any particular body alone. || 23 ||
When that subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) exists, the individual soul (jīva) vibrates, but not in a stone;
just as dust moves when there is wind, or sight functions when there is a lamp. 24.
But he states that the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) is the cause for the manifestation of a delimited egoity, saying: "When [it] exists," etc. (verse 24).

This desire within the city of eight exists by its own will when one is established in the Self alone; it manifests when that [Self] has arisen, just as the longing of people appears when the sun has risen.

This well-known "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) manifests as the desire for one's own will and the desire for diverse enjoyments when one is established in the Self—the object of supreme love and unsurpassed bliss. Just as when the sun is situated in the sky, the longing for the fruits of various actions flashes forth in all people, so it is here; for "it is for the sake of the desires of the Self that everything [exists]."

The meaning of the scriptural statement "it becomes dear" is that the Self alone, although remote from all empirical transactions, is the sustainer of all transactions such as the pleasant and the unpleasant. || 25 ||
If, while the sun remains in the sky, this worldly activity perishes due to such an unsuitable state, then what has happened to the sun? (26)
Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "yadi" (if). One whose state is appropriate—that is, conformable—to such fruits of those respective desires. || 26 ||

If, while the Divine remains established in the self, the body— which has attained its existence through that very presence— should meet its destruction, then what is lost here for the self? (The reading is *tat kiṃ naṣṭam ihātmani*).
This Self of everyone is at all times neither born nor dying, neither taking [anything] nor desiring; it is neither liberated nor bound. 28.
In that case, what is the nature of the self in itself? To this he says: "No" (na). || 28 ||
Arising from the lack of awakening to the Self, it takes on the nature of a self within that which is not-self;
like the delusion of a snake in a rope, this error leads only to suffering. (29)
For this very reason, he states that from the ignorance of that [Self] alone arises the delusion of misfortune: "The Self," etc. (29).
Because it is beginningless, this Self is not born; because it is unborn, it does not perish.
Furthermore, it does not desire anything distinct from itself, for such a thing is impossible.
Then, as for what it is like upon awakening, he says: "Because of its unoriginated nature. (30)
Because it is never delimited by space, time, and so forth, this [Self] is never bound;
since there is no bondage, where could there be liberation? Therefore, it remains in a state of non-liberation (amokṣa). || 31 ||
O Raghava, this Self is distinguished by such qualities as these for everyone;
yet, due to the power of lack of inquiry, this deluded world weeps piteously.
"Endowed with such qualities" means having such an intrinsic nature. || 32 ||
O wise one, you who have correctly perceived the entire sequence of the world’s past and future, do not fall into grief like those people overcome by folly. (33)
Those people in the world who have fallen into such a state through folly are just like that. || 33 ||
Just as one should abandon the two mental constructions consisting of liberation and bondage, so should the wise man conduct himself, remaining silent within himself like a machine.

Just as when a water-mill is set in motion on a mountain slope, the person remains by its mere proximity as if he were the one performing the action, yet he himself remains silent, devoid of activities such as desire; in the same way, the wise man should conduct himself through the body and other instruments—this is the meaning. || 34 ||
Liberation is not on the back of the sky, nor in the netherworld, nor upon the surface of the earth;
for liberation is indeed the stainless mind awakened by perfect knowledge. (35)
Awakened by right knowledge, it is led to the state of being pure consciousness alone. || 35 ||
The spontaneous dissolution of the mind through non-attachment to all objects of desire is what has been called "liberation" by the knowers of reality who perceive the Self. (36)
Through non-attachment to hopes and the objects of hope, there is destruction [of the karmas] by means of the activity of one's own awareness of their transformation. (36)
O Rāma, as long as the stainless awakening has not arisen, so long is liberation desired through devotion, out of ignorance and dejection. (37)
"By wretchedness" means by miserliness; "by devotion" means by imagining that something not yet attained has been attained, even though it is eternally present. || 37 ||

Having attained supreme awakening and when the mind has become the very nature of consciousness (cittattva), even the ten types of liberation are not desired, much less a single liberation alone. || 38 ||

The meaning is as follows: if even those ten types of liberation—which are distinct from one's own self—were merely the state of consciousness, which is the ultimate reality of the nature of mind (cittattva), they would not be desired; how much less so a single, small, or limited liberation? || 38 ||
"This is liberation and this is bondage"—having abandoned such fragile conceptualization, you are that very one who is the great renouncer, O Bhava and Abhava! (39)
He was non-existence; you alone are that liberation. || 39 ||
Having reached a state where conceptualization has completely dissolved, he beheld the circle of the earth, marked by a girdle dug by the multitude of Sagara’s sons,
with all internal attachment vanished.
May you protect [us] for a long time, with glory ever-risen.

In that state where conceptualization has completely dissolved, you have reached such a condition; therefore, protect for a long time the ocean—which was dug by the sons of Sagara—as your girdle, and the circle of the earth marked by it.
Since you are free from internal attachment, the protection of your kingdom and so forth does not constitute a fault; this is the meaning. || 40 ||

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "Inquiry into One's Own Self," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "Inquiry into One's Own Nature," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The seventy-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through play, one perceives a body; in the course of time, it arises within the self.
It was like the perception of ugliness in the heart of one who beholds a beautiful face without seeing its curve. || 1 ||

The delusion of wandering in saṃsāra due to negligence, the state of eternal fullness through awakening, and the cluster of qualities of one liberated while living—all this is described here in detail. (1)
He first elaborates upon what was stated— that "this deluded world cries out due to the power of non-investigation"—

with the verse beginning with "līlayā" (by way of sport), etc. Because [the state] is veiled by ignorance during dissolution and deep sleep, it is the object of supreme love, being of the nature of unsurpassed bliss.

Not perceiving its own true nature within itself, through the power of *līlā*—that is, by the mere play of consciousness—the body, consisting of the subtle and gross levels of both the collective and individual (*samaṣṭi-vyaṣṭi*) aggregates, is born. This occurs during the time of creation, waking, and so forth, which is attained through the sequential ripening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and action; as for example, in the case of a beautiful [dream].

The meaning is as follows: just as in the heart of a man separated from his beloved, son, and so forth—who does not behold them—there arises incessantly a state of mental dejection (*daurmanasya*) that produces deformities such as pallor and emaciation;
it is by the power of that [dejection] that this great [shadow] has arrived, with its thick belly.
Illusion is the great power of intoxication, as it were, arising from even a mere drop of the taste of wine.

Due to the influence of those two bodies, through the superimposition of the sense of "I" upon them, one falls under their control; thus, this illusion—which is of the nature of unsurpassed misfortune—manifests as the great power of intoxication consisting of passion, greed, delusion, and so forth. || 2 ||
By this very [nature], which is subject to change and consists of both that and its opposite,
all this has come to be, just as water [appears] in a desert due to heat.
By this power of passion and so forth—
which possesses a succession of evils such as worldly activity, enjoyment, merit, demerit, and latent impressions—
and which has attained its existence through that non-existence or transformation (atadbhāva) of that Supreme Self. || 3 ||
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the latent impressions, and even the senses— thus,
through these marked by various names, the ocean of the Self surges with its waters.
Thus, by means of those very waters of their own nature, which possess names, numbers, and forms so designated,
there is a duality of mind (citta) and ego (ahaṃkāra) in speech, but not in reality;
for that which is the mind is indeed the ego, and that which is the ego is the mind.
Having explained the manner in which misfortune arises, he now states the means for its eradication:

first, the mind (*citta*) arises from the volition toward objects; from the reflection upon that, the intellect (*manas*); from the determination thereof, the intellect (*buddhi*); and from the identification with that, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).

He states in two verses beginning with "citta" that the single internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) remains spread out in every direction like a tree, through the sequence of growth from sprout, stalk, root, shoots, and branches. || 5 ||
Just as whiteness is conceived as being distinct from snow,
so too is the difference between the mind and the ego falsely imagined.
When one of the two internal factors— mind and ego— is destroyed,
both are indeed destroyed, just as when a cloth is destroyed, its whiteness is also destroyed.
He states the fruit of the declaration of unity: "The mind," etc. (verse 7).
Having abandoned the hollow notion of liberation, as well as the perception of bondage and worldly desire,
one should solely exhaust the mind through one's own dispassion and discernment.
Now he states the means for its eradication: "Tucchām" (verse 8).
If the thought "May liberation be mine" arises within, the mind has become active;
when the mind is intensely intent on such thinking, it leads only to physical defects.

To the question "Whence arises the desire for liberation? he replies: "Liberation... When the mind is intent on contemplation, it assumes that very form, which is the shape of the body; and that [body], by causing outward-facing orientation, leads to defect—this is the meaning. || 9 ||
Whether the Self is transcendent beyond everything, or rather all-pervading within every being—what is bondage, and what is liberation? Render such thinking rootless.

With the intention that the fault lies only in the state of having a limited form, and not in the state of being the pure Self or the Self of the universe, he says: "In the Self. Therefore, the meaning is: uproot the very notion of limitation. || 10 ||
Since wind is characterized by movement, when it moves within the body,
then the series of sprout-like fingers, limbs, and the tongue quivers.

He demonstrates the self’s distinction from the body and other things whose movement and such qualities depend on the vital airs (prāṇa) and so forth, by means of the passage beginning with "vāyu" [the wind]. It "sphurati," meaning it moves. || 11 ||
Just as the wind causes a row of sprouts on a tree to tremble,
even so the vital air (vāyu) thoroughly moves the series of limbs within the body.
Consciousness is all-pervading, subtle, unmoving, and indeed cannot be moved;
it does not undergo vibration of its own accord, just as a mountain remains unshaken by the winds.
Devācala is Meru. || 13 ||
Reflecting all objects while abiding solely within itself, it illuminates these worlds through its consciousness, like a lamp. (14)

[Objection: "Granted that this may be so for the pure self-nature (*ātmabhāva*), but in the case of the self-nature as a whole, movement of the self is unavoidable—just as a tree moves because its branches move. To this, he says:
"reflected" (*pratibimbita*). Thus, just as a crystal slab, even when it has assumed the nature of many moving reflections, [remains unmoved].
The meaning is that the Self, likewise, is immutable (kūṭastha). || 14 ||

In this regard, what is this vain delusion of yours that causes such extreme suffering? It is the notion of "this is I," "these are my limbs," and "this is mine," which belongs only to those of perverted intellect. (15)

In this context, such being the case of absolute dissimilarity, there arises the delusion that "this body is that well-known 'I'," and "this external world, consisting of wife, sons, and so forth, is mine. The phrase "of you" is spoken in reference to people other than Rāma. Those whose intellects are thus poorly situated—according to the rule that prefixes (pra, etc. receive the designations of *gati* and *upasarga* only when joined with a verbal action [the following applies].

One meditates upon the meaning [of the word *dūra*] because of its being difficult to access; since it is stated that a *yaṇ* [substitution] is not desired for a preceding member other than *go* or *eka*, there is no *yaṇ*. 15.
Thus, through a vision that is both eternal and transient, and which is struck by waves,
the activities of knowing, acting, and experiencing are perceived.

Thus, even though there is absolute dissimilarity between the body and the self, attributes such as "knowership" in the body and "agency" in the self are contradictory properties; they appear due to the superimposition of identity and association with the body and so forth, caused by the non-eternal affliction of ignorance, the surges of passion, and other such defilements.
The meaning is that they are perceived solely by a deluded vision. || 16 ||

In that regard, this latent impression (vāsanā)—arising from the heat of ignorance and being utterly futile like a mirage—manifests as the notions: "I am there," "I am the enjoyer," and "I am the agent. (17)
He says "therein" [to explain] that even the latent impression (*vāsanā*), which serves as the seed for subsequent delusions, arises precisely in accordance with perception:
"The heat arising from that" refers to the heat produced by the wind and sunshine, which is unknown—that is, obscured by the *tūla* (cotton-wool-like) ignorance (*ajñāna*). || 17 ||
This ignorance, though unreal, yet appearing as if real, drags away the intoxicated deer of the mind that thirsts for sense-objects, just like a mirage. (18)
O limb whose form is truth, once recognized, one meets destruction or flees,
just as a Cāṇḍāla girl, once discovered, flees from the midst of Brahmins.
When ignorance is fully understood, it no longer drags this deer of the mind;
when the mirage is fully understood, it does not draw in the thirsty one. (20)
O Rāma, through the realization of the ultimate truth, latent impressions fall away along with their very roots,
just as the mass of darkness vanishes when light arrives like a lamp.
Light is the manifestation of the undivided self; it comes forth, it becomes manifest. 21.
When the certainty that "ignorance does not exist" has arisen through the scriptures and reasoning,
ignorance dissolves like a drop of frost under the heat.
With the firm conviction that "What is the use of enjoyments for the sake of this inert body?",
the knower shatters the cage of desire, just as a lion tears apart its enclosure.

The term *itiniścaya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The "knower" (*jñātā*) is one who knows reality (*tattvajña*). He shatters the impurity of ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the instigator of desire (*āśā*). || 23 ||
O Rāma, when the surrounding fence of hope has indeed been removed from the heart,
a person attains a beauty that has arrived and experiences joy like the moon.
In the "accessory of hope," which constitutes its retinue, such as the identification with the body and so forth. || 24 ||
He attains supreme coolness like a mountain washed by rain;
he experiences the highest bliss like a lowly man who has obtained a kingdom. (25)
The lowest is the poor man. || 25 ||
He shines with supreme splendor like the vault of heaven in autumn;
yet he cannot be contained within himself, being as vast as the ocean at the end of a kalpa.
It does not fit; it is not commensurate; that is to say, it cannot be delimited. || 26 ||
Free from agitation, he becomes like a rain-stilled cloud;
the knower abides within himself, as tranquil as the ocean.
Free from agitation and having abandoned stubborn attachments, he is like the rain in the monsoon season, and like the silence in autumn, devoid of thundering and the like. (27)
He assumes supreme fortitude and remains as steady as the immovable Mount Meru;
he shines with a pure splendor like a fire whose fuel has been extinguished. || 28 ||
Fortitude is the state of being unassailable by sense objects; steadfastness is the state of being unshakable by causes of fear. || 28 ||
He becomes extinguished within himself like a lamp that has been stilled;
the man attains supreme satisfaction, just as one who has drunk the nectar of immortality. (29)
Like a lamp within a jar, like a fire with its flame in the center,
or like a gem with its radiant luster, it attains internal illumination.
He beholds his own self as the soul of all, omnipresent, the lord of all, the leader of all, possessing all forms yet devoid of form.
In conventional reality it possesses all forms; in ultimate reality it is formless. || 31 ||
Enough of laughing at those fragile successions of days that have already passed—days upon which my mind, as fickle as a volley of Cupid’s arrows, once took its stand. (32)
Having emerged from the arena of worldly conflict, with the fever of his pride and mind stilled,
he sat delighting in the inner self, full and pure in heart.
He has emerged from association with worldly people and from attachment to sense objects. || 33 ||
Having wiped away the stains of the mire of desire, having severed his own bonds of delusion, liberated from the fear of the defects of dualities, he has crossed the ocean of saṃsāra. || 34 ||
Cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and so forth, are the defects of dualities.
Having attained supreme rest, having reached the unsurpassed state that is no longer to be attained,
he has arrived at the station from which there is no return, through mind, deed, and speech.
The state of sovereignty is empty of both non-returning and returning; this connects with the subsequent portion beginning with "by the mind."
He who undertakes all desired activities desires nothing at all;
he whose joy is approved by all rejoices in nothing at all. 36.
He whose undertaking is desired by all people as something to be adopted is one whose conduct is such;
bliss is the fruit of that conduct. || 36 ||
He neither gives nor takes, neither praises nor blames;
he neither sets nor rises, and neither rejoices nor grieves. (37)

The meaning is that it neither sets—meaning it does not undergo the concealment of its own nature—nor does it rise; nor does it undergo rising again, which is the manifestation of its own nature, because it is once and for all manifest (sakṛdvibhātatvāt). || 37 ||
One who has renounced all undertakings, who is free from all limiting adjuncts, and who has completely abandoned all desires is known as one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 38 ||
Having abandoned all desires, become silent in mind, just as the ocean becomes still after completely casting off its flow of waves. 39.
He instructs Rāma regarding those characteristics with the words beginning "all desires" (sarvaiṣaṇā):
the meaning is that he should become like a cloud that has completely, without remainder, cast off its streams of water. || 39 ||
O dear one, a woman of excellent complexion clinging to the body does not bring such happiness as the hopelessness that is cool as the moon brings to the heart. (40)
He praises the very abandonment of seeking with the words beginning "not so," etc. (40).
O Raghava, even the moon pressed against one's neck does not bring such happiness as the complete coolness of hopelessness brings within.
Because the entire world is cooled by it, it is called Sakalaśītala.
Spring does not shine so brightly with its fresh creepers full of flowers as does one of noble mind who is silent and whose heart is equanimous through freedom from desire. (42)

Neither from the Himalayas, nor from pearls, nor from plantain trees, nor from sandalwood, nor even from the moon is such coolness obtained as that which is attained through the absence of desire. 43.
Even more than sovereignty, even more than heaven, even more than the moon, even more than Mādhava,
and even more than union with a beloved, freedom from desire is the supreme happiness.
O virtuous one, where the splendors of the three worlds do not benefit one even as much as a blade of grass, that supreme bliss is attained through the absence of desire.
Take hold of hopelessness—the axe for the *karaja* tree of calamities, the state of supreme bliss, and the cluster of blossoms from the tree of tranquility. (46)
To one whose form is adorned with hopelessness, O Rāma, the earth is but a cow’s footprint, Meru a mere post, the quarters of space small caskets, and the three worlds a blade of grass. (47)
A *sthāṇu* is a tree remaining after being cut down; *āśā*s are the directions; *samudrikā*s are small caskets.
(47) In this world, actions such as giving, taking, gathering, wandering, and the display of wealth are ridiculed by the best of men who are free from desire (*nirāśa*). (48)

Giving (*dāna*) is both worldly and scriptural. Taking (*ādāna*) is the appropriation of wealth and so forth. Accumulation (*samāhāra*) is the gathering together of stores, treasuries, and so on. Enjoyment (*vihāra*) is the diversion of children through the expenditure of wealth. Prosperity (*vibhava*) refers to the abundance of resources such as clothing, ornaments, food, drink, and the like; these and others are laughed at.
The sense is that it is worthy of laughter because it is regarded otherwise by the deluded, being the seed of misfortune with much exertion and trifling results. || 48 ||
By whom can he be compared, who has rendered the three worlds as mere straw and whose heart is never bound by any mental construction? (49)
The expectation is the longing. || 49 ||
How can people weigh that Lord of the Self, in whose heart there is no attachment such as "let this be mine" or "let this not be mine"? (50)
One whose mind is under his own control, being the master of his own self; or [one who is] himself the Lord, the Sovereign of all.
Relying upon hopelessness, which brings an end to all distress, is free from danger, and is perfectly blissful—the supreme good fortune of the intellect. (51)
The limit is the further shore; it is the supreme fortune and the meaningfulness of the intellect. || 51 ||

Know that the state of being a thief of hope is the very nature of hopes; know the world to be a false delusion, arisen like the apparent revolution of the quarters of the sky for one standing on a moving chariot. (52)
O Rāma, those desires do not belong to you, nor are you related to desires. Therefore,

because you possess the primary qualification through the perfection of the means such as dispassion (*vairāgya*), and through the perfection of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the world moves and runs like the delusion of directions on both sides of a person standing in a chariot.
The meaning is that one should understand [the world] to be merely a false delusion, like the circular whirling of young shrubs and the like.

Alternatively, let no hope be relied upon; for the thievery of hopes consists precisely in their causing the loss of the bliss of the Self by stealing away discriminative knowledge. Indeed, worldly happiness—
The world is desired by the deluded through thousands of hopes; yet it carries a false delusion like two wheels mounted on a chariot,

where the revolution of the upper and lower directions causes misfortune— such as falling and being crushed— for the ants and other creatures clinging to the rim, just so for those who cling to [the world].
The meaning is that you should know [this world] has arisen solely for the sake of misfortunes such as birth and death. Alternatively,
since one observes the sublation of the desire for inferior pleasure by the hope for superior pleasure, another desire arises for the purpose of subverting each preceding desire.

"No. Do not think that I spoke of hopelessness with the intention that those who possess superior hopes would become thieves of the inferior. For such [a state] causes delusion by generating a succession of hopes for nothing but the false objects of the world; since even the "inferiority" that serves as the correlate to "superiority" is unestablished. Because...

The meaning is that it has arisen like the confusion of directions experienced by one standing on a moving chariot—either due to the successive revolution and circling within the circles of the quarters caused by the speed of the moving chariot, or due to a disorientation regarding the directions. Alternatively, there is a word-break as *na āśāstena tvam āśānām*. *Vit* means one who knows the Self; he does not desire or long for even the slightest thing, for (*hi*)...

Since the world is a false delusion, there exists nothing in the world that can be desired in the form of a human goal; therefore, the meaning is that you should not be one who possesses desires. The rest is as before. || 52 ||
Why do you remain deluded, O mighty-armed one, like a fool even though you have been enlightened,
with a mind wandering in the thoughts, "This is mine," "This is that," and "I am this"?

Observing Rāma as if bewildered because he could not find the means for absolute freedom from hope after searching for it, [the Lord] spoke with insistence to remind him that the previously mentioned abandonment of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth is indeed that very means:
"What is this 'I' which is well-known in past and future times and is perceived as 'this very I' in the present time?"
The meaning is that you are deluded. || 53 ||
This entire world is indeed the Self; no diversity exists here.
Having realized that the world is of one single form, the wise are not distressed by its name. 54.
Let it be so; nevertheless, how is there the cessation of the torment of hope? To this he says: "The Self alone... (verse 54).
O Raghava, through the very vision of the flood of objects as they truly are,
the intellect attains supreme consolation in the form of desirelessness.
Because of the vision of the multitude of categories of things as they truly are, that is, as having their own real nature. || 55 ||
Relying upon that nature which is free from contradiction regarding existence and non-existence and remains constant at the beginning and the end, establish the stability of all things.
What, then, is the true nature of all things? To this he says: "bhāva... etc.
"Visaṃvāda" means conceptual construction (vikalpa). || 56 ||
This illusion, which utterly deludes the mind of one who is heroic through dispassion, flees away like a doe from a lion when the worldly man [approaches]. (57)
From him whose mind is heroic by virtue of the great dispassion characterized by the complete abandonment of all conceptual constructions. || 57 ||
A man of steady intellect regards his beloved—though she possesses intense passion and is as fickle as a forest creeper—as being equal to a crumbling stone doll. || 58 ||

With the intention that even defects such as desire flee away in this manner, he says "the beloved" (kāntām): [she is] equal to a crumbling stone statue (upalapāñcālī), that is, a stone image. || 58 ||
Enjoyments do not gladden the heart within, nor do calamities distress it;
O dear one, the splendors of the visible world carry it away, just as winds blow down a low-lying mountain.
"They carry away" means they cause one to fall from steadfastness. "Aṅga" is used as a term of address. 59.
Even for a sage of noble intellect who has conquered passion, the arrows of Love— though aimed at his red-blooded young wife— are reduced to dust, fragment by fragment, within his mind.
Even for one such as he, toward whom young women are red with passion and deeply attached. || 60 ||
One who knows his own true nature is not helplessly dragged away by passion and hatred; even their mere vibration does not affect him, so how much less could there be an actual assault? (61)
The true nature is the reality of the Self; one who knows that is a knower. || 61 ||
With the swaying creepers appearing like women before his eyes, he, whose form is like a mountain rock,
does not delight in sensual pleasures, just as a traveler finds no joy in desert lands.
By whom the creeper and the fickle woman are seen as equal and of identical form— therefore,
with a mind unattached through effortless ease,
the wise man enjoys the abundance of enjoyments as the eye perceives light. (63)

To the question of whether, in that state, even food and other necessities are abandoned, he says: "Without effort," etc. "Everything" refers to food, drink, and so forth, provided they are not prohibited.
"By play" means by activity conducive merely to the maintenance of the body. The analogy of the eye is given for the state of being unattached in mind.
(Verse 63) The series of enjoyments, such as women and the like, is obtained by chance, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence.
Even when experienced, my friend, it leads neither to suffering nor to satisfaction for the steadfast man. (64)

He says—beginning with the word "kāka"—that for a householder who knows reality, there is no extraordinary delusion of passion, even while experiencing the enjoyment of his own wife and other pleasures, as there is for one who is still subject to desire. || 64 ||
For one who knows that path and has correctly seen it, even the slightest notions of pleasure and pain are unable to cause agitation,
just as two waves cannot shake the king of mountains.
He by whom the path of the inward vision has been correctly seen and cultivated—that lord of mountains, Mandara;
[the form "śailendram" is derived from "śailendra," where the suffix *ap* is elided according to the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathām*].
Beholding worldly enjoyments with detachment, gentle, self-controlled, and free from feverish anxiety, he takes refuge in his own true state, which abides within all beings. (66)
"With ease" means with disregard; that is to say, with the thought that it is untrue. "Looking on"—the ellipsis is that he remains there, taking refuge in his own self alone. || 66 ||
Though he remains free from agitation even while surrounded by the agitated, he stays established in wisdom;
like Brahmā himself, devoted solely to the Self, he continues to bring forth the worlds.

Even when accompanied by a body, senses, and so forth that are occupied with various activities appropriate to the time, the wise one who knows reality remains entirely free from agitation and undistracted, like Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha.
When pleasure and pain arrive according to their time, place, and sequence, the great king does not experience agitation, just as the earth remains unmoved through the changing seasons.
*Bhūbhṛt* means a mountain; *ṛtuṣu* refers to the seasons, such as spring and the rest. || 68 ||
O Rāma, even if one who possesses great knowledge should sink due to the delusions of the organs of action,
he whose mind is eternally unattached does not sink at all.
Even though the organs of action, such as speech and the rest, are immersed in sense objects through their delusive activities; || 69 ||
Gold is said to be stained by a stain, and not otherwise;
likewise, a living being is said to be attached through attachment to worldly objects, and not otherwise. (70)
Regarding the fact that it is internal attachment alone that is corrupting, and not external attachment, he provides an illustration with the word "kalaṅkī" (stained):
gold is called "stained" only by an internal blemish; otherwise, even if smeared externally with mud or the like, it is not so called. Such is the meaning. || 70 ||
For the discerning person who perceives the knower as distinct from the body, nothing at all is cut away even when the limbs are being severed. (71)
He states that when internal attachment is abandoned, there is no longer even the occurrence of bodily suffering and the like—thus: "From the body... (verse 71).
Once that stainless state has dawned and been known, it remains known forever;
for a kinsman who has been recognized does not again fall into a state of being unknown.

To the objection that suffering might arise again if one forgets the Self as distinct from the body, he replies with the word "once" (sakṛt). The meaning is that there is no possibility of such forgetting. || 72 ||

Just as when the delusion of a snake has ceased, the perception of a snake no longer returns to the rope—unlike a mountain torrent that, having fallen from a ridge, flows again during the rainy season; 73.
To show that forgetfulness does not occur, he states the reason along with an illustrative example and its logical justification, beginning with the words "sarpa" (serpent) and so forth:
"Gold whose form has been purified by heating does not again acquire natural impurity; even when submerged in mud, it does not take on filth once more. (74)
The nature [of gold] has not at all ceased; it has merely reached the state of being pure gold. || 74 ||
When the knot of one's own heart is destroyed, there is no further bondage by the qualities (guṇas);
for even with effort, by whom can a fruit that has fallen from its stalk be bound again? || 75 ||
A fruit fallen from its stalk on a tree cannot be fastened back to the stalk as before by anyone, even by one who is capable and exerts great effort; that is to say, by no one at all. || 75 ||
Who has the power to join together again a stone and a gem that have both been reduced to fragments on all sides by the processes of cutting and analysis? (76)

Just as a jewel within a stone, once separated from it by cutting away the stone and through the discernment of the jewel's true nature—having been removed from all non-jewel fragments—is it possible for anyone, however unfortunate, to reunite that former stone with the jewel again? This is the meaning. || 76 ||
Once ignorance has been fully understood, who would sink back into it?
Having thoroughly comprehended the way of life of outcaste dog-cookers, what twice-born man would look upon it with favor? (77)
A journey, going to a festival or a social gathering. || 77 ||
Just as the perception of milk in pure water ceases through investigation, so too the latent impression of saṃsāra ceases through the investigation of the intellect. (78)
The delusion regarding milk is the notion that it is milk; [this ceases] through the investigation of the intellect and through the perception of the Self abiding within the intellect. || 78 ||
It is drunk by the best of brahmins under the suspicion that it is honey-water, as long as it has not been fully recognized; once it is fully recognized, it is abandoned. (79)
"Madhu" means liquor; "with the suspicion of water" means through the delusion that it was water. || 78 ||
Though endowed with beauty and charm, a passionate woman is viewed by those who know reality as being like a painted beauty, consisting merely of material substance. (80)
She is like a beloved woman depicted in a painting. || 80 ||
Just as soot, saffron, and the like [are used] on a woman's painting, even so are her hair and lips while she is still alive; what attachment, indeed, can there be for her? (81)

Just as in a painting, the various colors such as ink and saffron of a woman consist of nothing but the five elements, so too do the hair, lips, and other features of a living woman; thus, in reality, the object such as a woman exists quite differently from the form in which it is perceived. The same applies to the experience of one's own self.

If it is asked, "Could it not be otherwise than the nature of bliss, which is renowned as the object of supreme love? he says in response: "It is experienced. Just as the sweet taste of molasses is experienced, so too [the Self] is experienced through the instruments of experience such as the tongue, or by the experiencer such as Devadatta.

The meaning is this: even by hundreds of efforts such as burning or cutting, that experience of sweetness cannot be altered into an experience of bitterness and so forth; likewise, the experience of the soul's ultimate bliss remains exactly the same.
Even when molasses, though sweet, is experienced through burning and cutting— [it does not lose its nature]. (Verse 82)
The light of reality within the self cannot be made otherwise.

When something has been experienced even once, it cannot be made otherwise; therefore, when it is experienced constantly due to a singular addiction to it, that is all the more so—this is the intention with which he says, beginning with "addicted to another" (paravyasaninī) and so forth. || 83 ||
A woman devoted to another man, even while busily engaged in household chores, relishes within herself that very elixir of union with another. (83)
Thus, when the wise one has attained rest in the supreme, pure reality,
he cannot be shaken even by the gods together with Indra.
