By what powerful husband was a woman devoted to another made to forget the great festival of union with the lover of her own imagination? (85)
By whom can the intellect of that great-souled knower of reality be made to forget its reliance upon the light of consciousness, which is the bliss of the world’s essential equality? 86.

By the word "jagat" (the world), all the various forms of worldly sensory pleasures are indicated. When all these become of one flavor (*samarasa*), like the juices of various flowers in the state of honey, by what means does the intellect of the knower of reality (*tattvajña*) attain such a support of the light of consciousness— the bliss of one's own Self— which is a continuous stream of tasting?
The meaning is that it can be made to be forgotten. Thus it has been said in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Once the nectar-essence of knowledge has been tasted by someone, leaving behind all other activities, the mind runs toward that alone. (86)
Engaged in uninterrupted worldly affairs fraught with all manner of pleasure and pain, he remained dependent on his kinsmen, while being wearied by his husband and father-in-law.

The connection with the following verse is as follows: "Even though she always performed her domestic duties and worldly affairs without fail, and was vexed and oppressed by her husband and her parents-in-law, women are [naturally] possessed of concern for the misfortunes of others. (87)
Just as the world of brides, when slowed by the bliss of union with their beloveds of their own imagination, is not afflicted by the multitudes of sufferings arising from calamities. (88)
Likewise, one whose ignorance has dissolved, though fully engaged in worldly activity, being possessed of right vision and virtuous conduct, attains joy within his inner self. (89)
He is not cut, even when his limbs are severed; he does not weep, though tears are falling from him; he is not burned, even when being consumed by fire; and he does not perish, even when destroyed.
Regarding that, he speaks of the excellence of stability for one who has ascended to the seventh stage: "It is cut asunder.
Even though the body is destroyed—that is, even when the body has perished—[the mind remains]. || 90 ||
Free from the encounter of pleasure and pain, and undisturbed even amidst calamities that thwart one's plans,
may he sport either in his home or in the supreme city.
On a vast mountain, in a forest, or in a grove for asceticism. || 91 ||

The foremost of men, who is beyond the mind and established in the stage where the mind has been destroyed, remains— by virtue of the law of past *prārabdha* karma— in adversity, in poverty and the like devoid of enjoyment, or in calamities such as being impaled on a stake like Māṇḍavya, or in a magnificent palace, or upon a vast mountain.

Whether he dwells in a forest or in a grove for asceticism, nevertheless, he always remains entirely free from the onset of pleasure and pain; the meaning is that he is not touched in the slightest by worldly joys or sorrows. || 91 ||

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Instruction on Dispassion," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Instruction on Dispassion," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The seventy-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Janaka remained established in his kingdom, even while being intent upon worldly affairs.
Always free from fever, with an inner mind that is never agitated. || 1 ||
Even in great positions of authority, those who remain unattached to joy, sorrow, and the like—many such gods, asuras, humans, and others mentioned here—have been liberated. (1)
Janaka of Videha. || 1 ||

His grandfather Dilīpa, though fully intent upon all worldly undertakings, for a long time experienced within himself the piercing [pleasures of sovereignty] solely through his state of detachment. || 2 ||
Being stainless, the Buddha protected the people for a long time;
Manu, eternally possessing the form of one liberated while living, governed the kingdom. (3)
By virtue of being stainless—that is, being free from the impurities of passion and so forth—he is the Buddha, the fully awakened Manu. || 3 ||
Engaged in various battles of strength and in numerous legal affairs,
Māndhātṛ remained for a very long time and indeed attained the supreme state.
In such battles as those, which possessed various forces, armies, and the strength of arms. || 4 ||
Bali, residing on the seat of Pātāla, maintained his existence as if it were eternal;
ever-renouncing and ever-unattached, he remained established as one liberated while living.

"Sat" means the established order of things as they truly are, or conventional usage. In the reading "divasasthitim," it refers to the maintenance or protection of the days that had been ordained by Hari for their residence in the netherworld (pātāla). || 5 ||
Namuci, the lord of the Dānavas, was always intent on conflict with the gods;
amidst various conducts and deliberations, he was never inwardly tormented [or, according to another reading, "never internally stained"].
In battle against the gods, whether in a formal duel or in the transgression of boundaries, he was solely devoted to his adversary. Of many kinds...
In the investigations and deliberations concerning the conduct of gods and asuras.
In the battle with Vāsava, Vṛtra— renouncing his body,
expansive in mind, inwardly tranquil, and full of honor— engaged in combat with the gods.
Saṃgara means battle. || 7 ||
Performing the duties of a Dānava as the protector of the netherworld,
Prahlāda attained a joy that was free from misfortune and devoid of reproach.
It is free from reproach, beyond the range of speech, a joy, and a bliss. || 8 ||
O Rāma, although Śambara was solely intent on the art of illusion, he emerged from within as one with the ultimate Reality; thus Śambara abandoned this illusory world of saṃsāra.
Śambara is illusion (māyā); though intent solely upon that, he has become manifest—arisen through oneness with that internal Śambara, which is the space of consciousness within the heart. || 9 ||
Engaging in battle with the Dānavas with an unattached intellect,
Hari attained supreme consciousness and, being skillful, abandoned this world.
He alone, or another named Kuśala, was a Dānava. || 10 ||
The fire-god, the mouth of all the immortals, though indeed intent upon the web of ritual actions,
enjoys the prosperity of sacrifice for a long time and remains here as one truly liberated.
Being drunk by all the gods, the Soma, whose essence is equanimity,
does not at any time undergo attachment, just as the sky is not overcome by contact.

Within whom the equal Brahman itself is the essence, the elixir, and the nectar of resurrection; [who has cast off] attachment, which is the contact with pleasure, pain, and so forth; and who has traversed the sky, the ether, by means of his two feet—that is, through his strides. || 12 ||
Even Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, though already liberated, resorted to a wondrous stratagem in heaven for the sake of a wife, even while contending with Candra. || 13 ||
For the sake of a wife, he engaged in various endeavors and activities pertaining to his office as the domestic priest of the gods.
Śukra, illuminating the expanse of the sky, and Budha, the protector of all interests—the preceptor of the Asuras—spends his time with a mind free from perturbation. (14)
The wise one is the learned man; by the composition of treatises on ethics, he is the protector of all desired objects for everyone.
Even though it has long been causing the limbs of the multitudes of beings in the world to move,
the wind is always moving through everything and is indeed liberated.
The worlds are the upper realms, and the bodies are the multitudes of beings, the collections of living creatures. || 15 ||
O Rāma, though he knows the agitation caused by the constant coming and going of the worlds, Brahmā remains undaunted in mind and, with an equanimous heart, passes his vast lifespan.

The cycles of coming and going for living beings in the worlds—consisting of movements upward, downward, and across—and the agitations caused thereby, even though he knows them; [and this world] is spread out, extensive over a period of two *parārdhas*.
Even though he is liberated, the Blessed Lord Hari wanders here for a long time, as if in the playful sport of the dualistic conflicts of kingship, death, war, and the like. (17)
He is liberated, though eternally liberated. || 17 ||
Even by the liberated Three-eyed One, Gaurī— like a cluster of blossoms on the tree of beauty— is borne upon half his body, as if he were a lover carrying his beloved.
By the use of the particle "iva," it is suggested that he is not a lustful man nor she a passionate woman, but rather that they are both Brahman and the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā). || 18 ||
Even though Muktā was bound around the neck of Gaurī, the three-eyed Lord appeared as white as Gaurī herself,
like a necklace of perfectly pure pearls adorned with a spotless digit of the moon.
Guha, the hero of profound intellect and the sole ocean of the jewels of knowledge, though already liberated, performed all the martial deeds against Tāraka and the others.
One of profound intellect, whose mind is diverse and difficult to fathom. || 20 ||
O Rāma, with a mind that was resolute, purified by meditation, and liberated, Bhṛṅgīśa offered his own blood and flesh to his mother.

Bhṛṅgīśa, here, is Bhṛṅgiriṭi, a specific attendant (*gaṇa*) of Śiva. For he, disregarding the Goddess and being intent solely on the worship of Śiva, was cursed by the enraged Goddess to have a body composed of the flesh and bones of his own mother and father; [of this body], the portion belonging to his mother—
It is well known in the Purāṇas that, having been entreated by his own mother after she had turned back [from her purpose], he cut off his own blood and flesh and gave them to her. || 21 ||
Although the sage Nārada is by nature liberated, he wandered through this forested tract of the world with a cool disposition for the sake of his purposeful activity. (22)
She, by her very nature, was intent on instigating quarrels and amorous intrigues.
This lord Viśvāmitra, whose mind is liberated while living, is worthy of honor;
he presides over the performance of the sacrifice as prescribed in the Vedas.
Śeṣa supports the earth, the sun creates the succession of days,
and Yama performs his duty as the Restrainer— all indeed by virtue of their state of liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā).
The state of Yama consists of inflicting punishment. || 24 ||
Moreover, hundreds of others— yakṣas, asuras, humans, and gods— in this triple world have attained liberation and yet remain within the cycle of existence.
Established in worldly affairs among those who maintain various modes of conduct,
some are cool within, while others are as dull as stones.

Some are liberated, remaining inwardly cool even while engaged in worldly affairs such as kingship, which involve the accumulation of sons, wives, wealth, and power, and entail practices such as war, slaughter, and imprisonment— all of which lead to manifold misfortunes like grief and delusion.
Having attained supreme awakening, some have come to the forest, such as Bhṛgu, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Śuka, and others. || 27 ||
However, some have resorted to the forest for the sake of turning back mental distraction; he cites them with the words "as follows," and so on. || 27 ||
Some remain in kingdoms protected by royal umbrellas and chowries, such as Janaka, Śaryāti, Māndhātṛ, Sagara, and others. || 28 ||
Some abide in the sky, situated within the circle of celestial spheres,
such as Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Candra, Sūrya, and the lords of sages.
The stellar sphere (*jyotiścakra*) is the abode and support for the planets, constellations, and so forth; within it reside the lords of sages, the Seven Seers (*saptarṣi*). || 29 ||
Some have gone to the station of the gods, seated in rows of celestial chariots,
such as Agni, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Yama, Tumburu, and Nārada.
Some, liberated while living, reside in the depths of Pātāla,
such as Bali, Suhotra, Andha, Prahlāda, Āhlāda, and others.
Even among those born as animals, there are always those of refined intellect;
even among those born as gods, there are the wise who possess foolish minds. (32)
Among the animal births [are] Garuḍa, Hanumān, Jāmbavat, and others. || 32 ||
For indeed, everything arises from everything, everywhere, in every way, and at all times, within the Self of all, which exists as the most pervasive form.

If it is asked, "How can fools exist among the divine classes of beings, who by their very nature possess manifest knowledge and sovereignty due to being preeminently composed of *sattva*?"— the answer is that because the Lord (or, according to another reading, "the state of being the Lord") is omnipotent,
He exists at all times, in every way, everywhere, and in every manner within the Self, which is the Self of all.
He says "all" [in verse 33] to show that since even a thousand things that are impossible [to occur] are seen in dreams and so forth, one should not entertain any doubt regarding anything whatsoever.
The destiny of fate is manifold and its operation is slow due to its infinite undertakings;
because of the diversity of its arrangements and parts, everything is seen everywhere. (34)
He states clearly the meaning already expressed: "Of the injunction," etc. (34).
"Ordinance (vidhi), destiny (daiva), the Ordainer (dhātṛ), the Lord of All (sarveśa), Śiva, and Īśvara—by these names our inner conscious Self is called. (35)

He states what that "method" (vidhi) is with the word "vidhi. There is no tautology, for the first term "vidhi" refers to the name of the Supreme Self through the medium of Viriñci (Brahmā), while the second refers to it through the medium of Viṣṇu. He is the "Self" (ātmā) of all of us.
In the reading "antaḥ," however, he resides within the five sheaths (kośa-pañcaka). He is "conscious" (cetana) because of being intermingled with the power of consciousness (cicchakti). || 35 ||
There is a real thing within an unreal thing, like gold in sands;
there is an unreal thing within a real thing, like impurity in grains of gold.

With the intention that "where even two things that are absolutely impossible [independently] are conceived as existing within one another, what else could possibly be impossible?", he says, beginning with "it exists" (asti), etc. (verse 36).
When examined through reasoning, the propriety of what is improper becomes apparent;
for it is out of fear of sin, O Rāma, that people engage in dharma. (37)

The meaning is that even in the case of an utterly improper sin, when examined through reasoning, a great merit characterized by the capacity to impel a person toward dharma is seen, due to its terrifying nature in terms of its result. || 37 ||
O virtuous one, eternal truth is perceived within the unreal;
the eternal state is attained through the practice of meditation on emptiness. (38)

The meaning is that, as a result, there is truthfulness; for in the meditation on universal emptiness, because the self-luminous self who witnesses that meditation is impossible to deny, it follows by implication that only that which is real remains. || 38 ||
That which does not exist arises quickly through the play of place and time;
indeed, even rabbits are seen possessing horns when Śambara is present.
In the state of Śambara, there is the manifestation of a magician's creation. || 39 ||
Those things which appear to be as firm as the essence of a diamond have gone to destruction;
just as at the end of a kalpa, the moon, the sun, the earth, the oceans, the gods, and so forth [perish]. (40)
The meaning is that even those whose essence is as firm as a diamond, for whom decay was never before conceivable, [are subject to it]. || 40 ||
Seeing thus, O mighty-armed one, the sequence of existence arising from being and non-being,
abandon joy, indignation, and dejection, and attain equanimity.
Concluding by showing that even this incidental demonstration of the possibility of the improbable has the very same result as the primary subject, he says: "Thus" (iti). || 41 ||
In this world, the non-existent appears as existent, and even the existent is seen as non-existent; therefore, having abandoned both reliance and non-reliance, quickly attain equanimity.

O Rāghava, in this world, the attainment of liberation is not at all possible for one who lacks discernment; indeed, millions of people remain submerged in worldly existence because they have not applied such discernment. (43)
If this were so, it might be suspected that even in the state of disembodied liberation (videhamukti), there could be a recurrence of transmigratory existence; to this he replies:
[it occurs] during the state of ignorance, when true knowledge has not yet arisen, characterized by the delusion of imagining millions of calamities that are absolutely impossible [in reality].
They are not liberated; the meaning is that the ignorance which causes their immersion has been destroyed. || 43 ||
O Rāghava, in this world, liberation is indeed always attainable through the practice of discernment; for by means of such discernment, the millions of beings have been liberated.

He says—“In liberation” (muktau)—that there is no fear of the loss of liberation even because its nature is eternally attained; for it is acquired through mere discernment, like a golden necklace forgotten around one's neck. || 44 ||
Liberation becomes easy to attain through solitude and difficult to obtain through lack of solitude; since it is reached by the dissolution of the mind, therefore, kindle your discernment.
Liberation, though easily obtained through solitude, becomes unattainable through a lack of discernment. || 45 ||
One who desires prosperity should exert effort in the contemplation of the self;
through the illumination of the self, the severing of the head of all suffering occurs. (46)
By one desiring prosperity and liberation. || 46 ||
Free from passion and free from attachment, those of great intelligence who are liberated while living appear frequently in this world, such as Suhotra and Janaka.

He dispels the doubt that while liberation while living (jīvanmukti) was possible for those of former times, it is not possible for those of the present day—by stating, "free from passion" (nīrāgāḥ). This means they are free from attachment (nirupāsaṅga) and free from dogmatic insistence (nirabhiniveśa), even at this present time. || 47 ||
Therefore, you too, with an intellect made steady by the wisdom arising from dispassion and discernment,
wander as one liberated while living, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
Two kinds of liberation exist in this world for those who possess a body: one is with the body (sadeha), and the other is without the body (videha). Hear now this distinction between the two.

Now he begins to state the cause for the distinction between liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), starting with the words "of two kinds," etc. (verse 49).
Through non-attachment to objects, there is peace of mind and liberation;
O sinless one, this occurs even while the body still exists.
Therein, first he shows the meaning of the word "liberation" (mukti) as common to both [the individual soul and Brahman]: "Because of non-attachment," etc. (50).
O dear one, the wise know that the supreme state of liberation (kaivalya) is indeed the exhaustion of all attachment (sneha).
That [liberation] occurs both when the body exists and when it is absent. (51)
He states the reason for arising there: "Affection," etc. Affection is the love [felt] due to the delusion that [others] are one's own self; [the verse speaks of] its destruction. (51)
He who lives free from attachment is called one liberated while living;
he who lives with attachment is bound, while the third is truly liberated.
Effort should be made with diligence and according to proper method for the sake of alms;
for one devoid of effort and method, even a cow’s footprint becomes difficult to cross.

Among the four means of realization (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), once each preceding one has been established with effort, effort must also be applied toward the attainment of each subsequent one. The reasonings (*yukti*) are those logical arguments conducive to the ascertainment of the truth regarding the purport of the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and their objects (*prameya*); they are preceded by that [ascertainment]. (53)
But one should not, out of mere delusion, allow oneself to fall under the power of another for the sake of suffering that is vast and boundless, which results from a lack of firm resolve. 54.

An effort based on reasoning must be carried out until the final ascertainment of the true nature of the self; one should not act impulsively. For if there is no ascertainment, due to despondency in the interim, one might cease the effort and thus place the self under the power of misfortune. To this he says: "But not...
The meaning is that when there is no ascertainment, there is a lack of regard for the effort. [The genitive case] is used in the sense of "in the absence of."
And in the sense of disregard, the genitive case is used to denote a characteristic action. || 54 ||
Relying upon great fortitude with a resolute mind,
investigate the self by means of the self for the sake of your own long-term perfection;
for one whose determination is vast, the world becomes like the footprint of a cow.

He states the aforementioned point clearly with the words "sumahat" (very great): by one who is resolute—that is, one possessing firm determination and not ceasing effort until the attainment of the result—and for the sake of success that may take a long time; the meaning is: aiming for perfection even if there be obstacles or it takes many births. || 55 ||
That supreme state which the Sugata attained,
from which no king has ever departed,
and that highest station which the great ones have reached.
That is the great fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree of diligent effort. || 56 ||
That state known as the "remainder of the self alone," which is self-luminous— the Sugata (the Well-Gone) being one who has attained excellent discernment, and Kapila having departed because,
despite much deliberation, he was unable to ascertain it— [is that state] from which [Kapila] withdrew due to the perceived impermanence of the self.

He has accepted the nature of a momentary stream of consciousness as the self, and the *pradhāna*— characterized by the state of equilibrium of the three *guṇas*— as the ultimate ground and reality. Likewise, a certain king named Arhat, a Kṣatriya who was otherwise unacceptable [to the Buddhist community] due to his disparagement of the Vedas, even though he had departed [from his former path], accepted the self (*ātman*) as having the nature of consciousness (*cit-svabhāva*).

Because they accept that [the self] is of the same size as the body, they fall into the most inferior and false position, for when entering the bodies of elephants or mosquitoes, it would follow that its parts undergo increase or decrease, thereby falling into instability. However, the great ones who are proficient in the secrets of the Vedas have reached the supreme state characterized by truth and other such qualities.

The meaning is that just as those [ancients] truly attained that great state which was declared in the Vedic path as the great fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree characterized by diligent effort, so too should another person strive in the same manner. || 56 ||

Thus ends the seventy-fifth canto, titled "The Inquiry into the Liberated and the Unliberated," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Inquiry into the Liberated and the Unliberated," in the Section on Tranquility (*Upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The seventy-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, these worlds emerge from Brahman.
They attain stability through lack of discernment, but they are indeed pacified by discernment.
Here, the ocean of saṃsāra is described as having women for its waves;
therefore, the means to cross it is taught, so that once crossed, one may sport at ease.
From the uncomprehended Brahman they come forth, they manifest; through lack of discrimination they reach a state of stability.
By this, the cause for the arising and persistence of misfortune has been shown. He states the means for its cessation:
"they become tranquil. || 1 ||
Who is able to count the revolutions of the whirlpools of the world-net within the ocean of Brahman, or the motes of dust in the rays of light? || 2 ||
And the motes of dust belonging to the web of rays of the sun are impossible to count. || 2 ||
Know that incorrect perception is the cause for the persistence of the world;
O beloved, correct perception is the cause for the cessation of saṃsāra. (3)
"O beloved" is an address to Rāma. || 3 ||
For this terrible ocean of saṃsāra is difficult for others to cross; O Rāma, it cannot be crossed without the application of skillful means and effort.
Whose further shore is exceedingly difficult to reach. || 4 ||
This ocean of his is filled to the brim with the waters of delusion, its depths unfathomable, and its hollows agitated by waves and whirlpools of worldly existence.
He describes that very ocean of *saṃsāra* with the words beginning "of which" (*yasya*).

This ocean characterized as *saṃsāra*, distinguished by the various qualifiers to be mentioned, is filled and made full by the mass of the waters of delusion (*moha*); if it is not crossed because one is submerged therein by that very [delusion], then—
The connection is with the seventh [verse]. Its hollow interior is agitated by unfathomable whirlpools characterized by death and by billows, that is, great waves. || 5 ||
It has the foam of wandering merit, the blazing submarine fire of hell, waves tossing with craving, and the elephant of the mind’s waters. (6)
His merits alone were the foam and froth; the submarine fire was the Vāḍava; and the aquatic creature resembling an elephant was the Jalodbhava. || 6 ||
It is a casket for the jewels of the enjoyments of the river of life that has been swallowed up;
it is filled with the agitated serpents of disease and resounds with the gurgling of the crocodiles of the senses.
There, the rivers of life have become still on all sides and are utterly exhausted; yet the seizing organs of sense produce a gurgling sound, creating a tumultuous noise.
Behold, O Rāma, these beautiful and flickering waves spreading forth;
they are known as the charming women capable of drawing one toward their peaks. (8)
In that regard, he describes women as being like waves with the words beginning "Behold" (paśya):
"They are capable of attracting even the steadfast, like mountain peaks. (8)
Rich with the lotus-gems of their lips, filled with the blue-lotuses of their eyes,
strewn with the flowers and fruits of their teeth, and adorned with the foam of their smiles.
Their lips were like ruby-studded lotuses, rich with the splendor of their teeth, and were strewn with flowers, fruits, and buds. || 9 ||
With their hair like circles of sapphire, rippling with the playfulness of their eyebrows, expansive with the sandy banks of their hips, and adorned with conch-like necks; || 10 ||
They were adorned with conch shells possessing the characteristics of [auspicious] necks. || 10 ||
They are adorned with the jeweled plaques of foreheads, teeming with the crocodiles of playful gestures,
possessing the deep pools of flickering side-glances, and having the golden sands of their complexions.

They are enriched with jeweled slabs—the marks upon their foreheads—and with surfaces of precious gems; they are deep and difficult to fathom due to the flickering of their side-long glances; and their very bodily radiance constitutes the golden sands of those rivers.
If one who is submerged in this ocean of saṃsāra, so terrifying with its restless waves,
can cross over it, that would indeed be the supreme human effort.
When the great ship of wisdom exists and the navigator of discernment is present, fie upon him who has not crossed over this ocean of saṃsāra! (13)
He who, having traversed from the near shore to the far shore and having measured it on all sides, plunges into the ocean of saṃsāra—he alone is known as a true person (puruṣa). || 14 ||

Having ascended by means of the vision of reality and having sublated [the world], it therefore makes that [world] consist of nothing but Brahman as the object of knowledge; it plunges into and enters the inner self (pratyak), meaning that it leads even the inner self to that very state. || 14 ||
O Rāma, after the noble ones have reflected upon and surveyed this ocean of saṃsāra with their intellect, only then does play appear beautiful therein; not otherwise.
Thereafter, following the realization of reality; in this world which has attained the state of Brahman. || 15 ||
O virtuous one, you are capable here; therefore, with an intellect intent on inquiry, this very cycle of existence is now being investigated by you. (16)
You are fortunate and blessed, since by virtue of that auspiciousness, you have now [attained this] even at such a young age. || 16 ||
He who, having first reflected like you, plunges into the world with a most transcendent understanding, does not sink here.
"He plunges" means he enters; "Brahman" is the understood object. "The world" refers to the people who possess the qualification [for this practice]. || 17 ||

O Rāma, having first examined these enjoyments with the intellect, one should consume them only at the very end, like Garuḍa consuming serpents, for they bring about the fear of the serpent of rebirth.

The remainder of the meaning is that enjoyments should first be disregarded. Just as Garuḍa disregarded the serpents before bringing back the nectar, but afterwards consumed them fearlessly after being released from his mother’s curse, so it is here. || 18 ||
Those prosperities which are pursued after reflecting on reality and perceiving it, result in a favorable outcome for a living being; all others lead only to suffering. (19)
He says "having deliberated" because this principle is well known in the world regarding the enjoyment of royal splendor:
"the truth," meaning the secret [knowledge] such as the favor and grace of the king. || 19 ||
The strength, intellect, and splendor of one who has perceived reality increase, just as the beauty and other qualities of a tree flourish in the springtime. (20)
He shows that the attainment of the specific qualities which bring about the wearing away of experience occurs only after the awakening to reality, and not before, by stating: "Power," etc. (20).
With a constant splendor that is pure, equanimous, perfectly cool, and filled with the essence of profound nectar,
you shine forth intensely like the moon, the one of cool rays.
O descendant of Raghu, you have known that which is to be known; [therefore] happiness [is yours].
To dispel the doubt that Rāma might lack the capacity for the digestion of worldly enjoyments, [the text] demonstrates his attainment of the realization of reality—
beginning with the word "dense" (*ghana*). O descendant of Raghu, because you have known all that is to be known,
you are now possessed of a splendor (*śrī*) that is dense with the nectar of bliss, full, most cooling, and which has dispelled the threefold suffering.
You shine exceedingly like the full moon with its cool rays; on the bright fortnight, you appear perfectly circular on all sides due to your complete orb.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Similarity between Saṃsāra and the Ocean," in the section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage. 76.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Similarity to the Ocean of Saṃsāra," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The seventy-seventh canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, once again [explain] in brief the wonder of perceiving the reality that has been seen.
Tell me this noble account: who can ever be satiated with your words?
Like a garland of Mandāra flowers, this string of qualities of those liberated while living is woven here by Vasiṣṭha; it should be borne upon the head or upon the chest by the wise.
"In brief" means by way of a summary of what has been stated here and there in various places. "Noble account" refers to his life story;
that is to say, the qualities that constitute his defining characteristics. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed one, the characteristics of one liberated while living have been described by me in many ways; listen now once more to this which is being told.
This is the form of inclusion. || 2 ||
Free from all desires, the self-possessed one constantly perceives this entire world as if in deep sleep—unattached and as if non-existent in every respect. (3)

From the perspective of conventional discourse, it is mere darkness like deep sleep; but from the perspective of ultimate reality, because it is merely a persistence of what has been sublated, it is as if non-existent in nature.
Having attained the vision of the Self, he remains as if having reached isolation (kaivalya), as if his mind were in deep sleep, and as if reeling with bliss. || 4 ||
With a mind that is inward-turned, noble in form, and equanimous, he does not take up even what is not given, nor does he grasp with his hand even what has been taken.

Although wealth, clothing, ornaments, and so forth were first "taken" (ādatta) by the eyes and other senses, and subsequently "appropriated" (upātta) by the hand, one does not appropriate them through the intellect. The suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here in the sense of the initial action; for this very reason, there is no substitution of *ta* for *t*. (5)
Beholding this succession of people as the movement of mechanical puppets with an inwardly withdrawn gaze, he of tranquil intellect laughs.

He perceives that the sequence of worldly activity is like the movement of a wooden statue or similar object, because it proceeds solely through the mere proximity of a Self that is unattached and indifferent. || 6 ||
He does not depend on the future, he does not abide in the present,
he does not recall the past, and yet he performs everything.
He does not remain, nor does he form a basis for attachment. || 7 ||
Though asleep, he becomes awakened; and though awakened, he remains as if asleep.
He performs all actions within, yet does nothing at all.

Even though one is as if asleep regarding worldly affairs (*vyavahāra*), one remains awake within one's own self (*svātman*). As the Blessed One has said: "That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled one is awake. The meaning is that even if one is most skillful and awake in worldly affairs, one remains as if asleep; one does not become attached to the fruits of that skill. 8
Having renounced everything within, and being eternally free from inner seeking,
he remains in a state of equanimity even while performing external activities.
For this very reason, he says that its state is always equal: "internally," etc. (9).

Externally, he continues with all worldly activities as they were before, intent on performing actions as they arise, and devoted to following the duties toward his kinsmen as they come according to the sequence of his own karma.

He remained devoted solely to his own duty— specifically the duties appropriate to his particular body, caste, and stage of life (varṇāśrama), as well as the royal affairs inherited through the lineage of his father and grandfather, including the duties toward kinsmen such as giving gifts and showing honor.
His very self being the enjoyment of complete happiness, as if established within all hopes,
he performs all actions while having abandoned the delusion of agency.

All enjoyments of happiness are the Self alone for him; or rather, he himself is the Self of all enjoyments of happiness. For this very reason, from the perspective of the ignorant, at the time of enjoyment, he appears as if established in and possessed of longing for all objects, yet unlike the ignorant, he does not appear so through the conceit of being an enjoyer—this is the meaning. || 11 ||
Remaining as if indifferent toward the natural sequence of actions, he neither desires nor hates, neither grieves nor rejoices. (12)
In actions, the desired result is obtained; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 12 ||
While living beings were intent on their worldly attachments, he remained with a mind unattached;
among the devoted he behaved like one devoted, yet among the deceitful he stood as if he were deceitful himself. (13)
"Anubandha" refers to the practice of acting with either favorability or unfavorability toward those intent upon that [goal]. (13)
Among the foolish he is a fool; among the aged he is aged; among the steadfast he is steadfast;
among those in the prime of youth he shares their youthful conduct; and among the suffering, he is sorrowful. (14)

His speech was engaged in meritorious discourse; his worldly intent had vanished due to humility; he was wise, filled with joy at having wept [in devotion], graceful, and one whose fame was rooted in merit. || 15 ||

He states the distinction between this and the previously mentioned equal conduct of children and others with the words "pravṛtta" (engaged). Being one whose speech is engaged (*pravṛttavāk*), he tells meritorious stories; the meaning is that, unlike children and others, he is not a speaker of idle chatter. In the same way, other points should also be inferred. Meritorious *kīrtanas* are descriptions of [saintly] characters in the world.
Of whomsoever. || 15 ||
Wise, serene, and sweet, he is full upon the dawning of his own creative intuition;
having cast off weariness and misfortune, he is an affectionate kinsman to all.
In all people. || 16 ||
His form was that of noble conduct; he was equanimous, a gentle ocean of happiness, exceedingly affectionate, and cool to the touch, like the risen full moon. || 17 ||
His touch is cool, removing all afflictions, and he is free from attachment. || 17 ||
He has no need for his good deeds, nor for enjoyments, nor for ritual acts;
he has no need for his misdeeds, nor for the renunciation of enjoyments, nor for his kinsmen. (18)
"Not by evil deeds" is for the purpose of avoiding the performance of prohibited actions; therefore, [this applies] to enjoyments that are not prohibited. || 18 ||
Neither by the commencement of cause and effect, nor by purification, nor likewise by bondage or liberation, nor by the netherworld, nor by heaven. (19)
By means of the undertakings of necessary actions—those deeds which are the causes of results pertaining to this world and the next;
the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of completion (*niṣkṛtatayā*), or alternatively, the reading is *niṣkriyatayā* (by way of being free from activity). "By day" means by heaven. || 19 ||
When the world is seen as it truly is— as a single, uniform essence—
then the mind never feels distressed by bondage or liberation.

The meaning is that, amidst the bondages of worldly pleasures and the liberations consisting of the cessation of all suffering and its causes, the mind occasionally becomes "miserly," that is to say, possessed by a sense of wretchedness. || 20 ||
For one whose webs of doubt have been consumed by the fire of right knowledge, the bird of the mind has flown away for good, free from all hesitation. (21)

The "nets" (jālikāḥ) are characterized by doubt and are like cages. Thus, while such a state might give rise to the possibility of wretchedness in the mind, that very thing does not exist for him; this is the meaning. || 21 ||
He whose mind is free from delusion and abides in equanimity neither sets nor rises; like the sky, it remains so amidst all perceptions.
It has become the Brahman of equal flavor. || 22 ||
Just as a child seated within a chest moves about, so too is he whose bodily movements are devoid of any sequential coordination of his limbs. (23)
To the question of how bodily movement and so forth can occur in the absence of the mind, he says: "In a chest" (*mañjūṣāyām*).
This means on a comfortable bed on a swing. For his movement of the limbs arises solely from the splendor of the manifestation of his own bliss;
just as, for example, a great king, a great Brahmin, or a great prince [might move] due to an intense state of bliss.
"Having gone, one should lie down"—this is well-known from the Śruti and other sources, like the dancing of the Lord. 23.
Reeling like one intoxicated with joy, his rebirth having been brought to an end,
he no longer remembers what was done or left undone, owing to his realization that nothing is worth grasping.

The meaning is that because there is an absence of the cognition that the result of the action is to be accepted—due to the rule of recollecting what has been done and what has not been done with the thought that [the action] is not to be undertaken. || 24 ||
He grasps everything in every way, and he likewise abandons it; having no purpose for any object that is not to be taken up, he acts like a child. (25)
The passage beginning with "all" (sarvam) and so forth should also be applied to the position of the ignorant (bālapakṣa). || 25 ||
Even while engaged in activities according to the sequence of place, time, and action,
he is not affected in the slightest by the pleasure or pain arising from those activities.
[The soul is not affected] by pleasure and pain resulting from actions performed [in a previous life]. || 26 ||
Although externally engaged with all objects, he nevertheless, through inner desirelessness, does not attribute reality to objects nor does he pursue their fruits.
In the object—that is, in the external object—he places his reliance through the notion of its reality; for this very reason, he pursues the fruits [of action].
He disregards the state of suffering and does not depend on the hope for pleasure;
he feels no joy at the success of an undertaking, nor does he grieve at its failure. (28)
He does not perceive even the state of suffering that is present and close at hand. || 28 ||
Even if the sun were to become cool-rayed, even if the lunar orb were to become intensely hot,
and even if fire were to spread downwards— [the reading is *pratapati*]— no wonder would arise in him,
even if the sun were to become cool-rayed, even if the lunar orb were to become intensely hot, and even if fire were to face downwards.
It spreads forth and even blazes; yet, no sense of wonder or astonishment arises in him. (29)
"Such are these powers that manifest here from the conscious self"—for one who thinks thus, no curiosity arises regarding these webs of wonders. (30)
To the question "Why is it not born there?", he says: "Of the conscious self (cidātman). The powers (śaktayaḥ) are the māyās. || 30 ||
It does not adopt the wretchedness of compassion, nor does it pursue cruelty;
it does not maintain a sense of shame, nor does it fall into shamelessness. (31)
Modesty [is present] in such things as enduring insults and living by begging; it does not fail to manifest as a lack of shame regarding improper acts. (31)
Never dejected in spirit, never elated in spirit;
never heedless, never weary in spirit; never agitated, and never filled with joy. (32)
In his mind, which is vast and as stainless as the autumnal sky, anger and other such passions do not arise, just as new sprouts do not grow in the open air.
In this world, where the stability of living beings is subject to incessant arising and passing away, how, indeed, and in what manner could anyone be truly happy or unhappy? (34)
In this [world], living beings—creatures that have been born and produced—fall and die incessantly and without interruption.
Furthermore, the sense is that even if you consider this [Self] to be "constantly born" or "constantly dead," according to the principle shown by the Blessed One;
for what is there to be said regarding these three states in terms of place, time, mode, and essential nature?
For the sake of attaining the state of being inconceivable. || 34 ||

Just as the movement of foam occurs in water through the rapid succession of elements, where indeed is this [self], from where does it come, and what connection is there from this to pleasure and pain? (35)

He supports this with an illustration: "Like foam," and so forth. Where or from what could there be stability in the constant coming and going—that is, the tossing about—of foam driven by waves? Therefore, what occasion is there for pleasure or pain? || 35 ||
Those men who are capable of creating through their vision do not perish nor do they arise, despite the endless and incessant births of living beings through existence and non-existence.
They do not disintegrate, they do not perish, nor do they grow weary; they do not rise, they are not born, nor do they rejoice.
For them, the very perception of the phenomenal world is its creation; thus, seeing that "I alone create the illusory world within myself," they are liberated while living (jīvanmukta). 36.
Just as other visions seen in dreams during the night perish in a single moment, so too do these worldly perceptions vanish in an instant. (37)

Furthermore, according to the principle that "all entities indeed undergo transformation at every moment," the eternal Self (*sadātman*), which persists through the phenomena of the world that are changing at every instant, perceives— just as in a dream— only within itself, as if it were the object of perception, imagining and witnessing the six modifications of being (*ṣaḍbhāvavikāra*) at every moment.

With the intention of showing how there could be any attachment to joy and the like once they have attained certainty, he says "nimeṣam" and so forth. The word *prati* is a *karmapravacanīya* used here to indicate repetition (*vīpsā*). Since the formation of either a reduplication or an *avyayībhāva* compound would necessarily follow from this, its absence is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). 37.
In this world, which is eternally arising and eternally perishing, what sequence can there be here between compassion and bliss for one who is consumed by saṃsāra? (38)
Kramaṇa means stepping; it is a sequence or a logical consequence. || 38 ||

When the presence of the pleasant and unpleasant has ceased and one has reached a state devoid of pleasure, what are those perceptions of suffering like, how have they arrived, or where do they reside? (39)

Furthermore, while the fruits of auspicious actions (*śubhakarma*) are well-established, things opposed to them—such as the suffering of separation from one's son—would find no footing [in the case of the liberated]. Since for those liberated in this life (*jīvanmukta*) there is an absence of the auspicious itself, neither [of these opposites] applies; thus he says: "Due to the absence of the auspicious" (*śubhābhāvāt*). "Dissimilar" (*vilakṣaṇāḥ*) means dissimilar to the fruits of the auspicious. What kind of occurrences? [They are the occurrences of suffering.]
As before. || 39 ||
How can this state of suffering, which arises from the end of the experience of pleasure and expands its own seed, be peaceful while that pleasure has already vanished? (40)

That state of suffering which, having acquired its existence through the non-existence of the perception of pleasure or the experience of happiness, expands its own seed— its effects such as grief, delusion, and so forth— that very state of suffering, being itself stilled within peaceful happiness due to the absence of virtuous karma, is without cause; how could it [arise]?
"It may arise" is a clarification of the very meaning previously stated. || 40 ||

When pleasure and pain have been exhausted, and with their exhaustion, what remains of that which is to be rejected and that which is to be accepted? Furthermore, when the auspicious and the inauspicious have dissolved, where can the desired and the undesired exist? (41)

When the desire for enjoyments has vanished due to the destruction of both pleasant and unpleasant sights, and when a constant, mature state of hopelessness has arisen, the mind melts away like snow upon the Himalayas.
He states what follows from that: "ramya" (delightful). When [the hope] has gone away, having departed; when despair has become mature, having become firmly established.
When the mind has been destroyed from its very root, what talk can there be of volition? Where is the possibility of oil when the sesame seeds have been completely burnt? (43)
Let there be the destruction of the mind; what follows from that? To this he says: "From the very root," etc. (Verse 43).
Through the cultivation of the dense non-existence of all phenomena, the Great-Souled One remains like space, free from all mental construction;
rejoicing within his own mind, he is pervasive and of a single form.
He knows, he stays, he sleeps, he lives, eternally satisfied. || 44 ||

Through the intense contemplation of non-existence (*abhāvaghanabhāvanā*)— by means of the firm conviction that nothing exists apart from oneself— one remains like the sky, with the nature of pure being (*sanmātrasvabhāva*), while all entities and visible objects are free from mental synthesis, such that there is no conceptualization or discursive thought (*niḥsaṃkalpavikalpa*).
Due to the absence of any cause for delimitation, the Great Self— being all-pervasive, uniform in form, knowing, eternally satisfied,

and blissful by its own nature as unsurpassed bliss— is joyful; it abides in the mind during waking and dreaming, which consists merely in the observation of objects as they arise, and [abides] in that dissolution [of the mind].
The meaning is that he sleeps in deep sleep (suṣupti) and lives until the exhaustion of his prārabdha karma. || 44 ||

Thus ends the seventy-seventh canto, titled "Description of the Nature of the Jivanmukta," in the Section on Tranquility (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) within the Means to Liberation (*mokṣopāya*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Sages (*ārṣa*). 77.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of the Jivanmukta," in the section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as a circle of fire is perceived from the whirling of a firebrand, so too does this world appear.
Just as that which is non-existent appears as existent, so too does the world arise from the vibration of the mind.
The delusion of the world arises from the vibration of the mind, and the nature of that mental vibration is such that yoga, for the purpose of its cessation, is correctly explained herein. (1)
The meaning is: just as at night, due to the movement—that is, the whirling—of a burning brand or firebrand, a circle of fire is seen through delusion, so it is here. || 1 ||
Just as a circular whirlpool appears to be distinct from the water due to the movement of the water,
so too does the world appear [distinct] due to the movement of the mind.
The whirlpool has the shape of a circular navel. || 2 ||
Just as a circle of peacock feathers or pearls is seen as if real, though unreal, in the sky due to the flickering of the eye,
so too is the world perceived due to the flickering of the mind.
Due to the movement of the eyes toward the sunlight, they appear like a mass of peacock feathers; due to movement in another direction, they appear like a circle of pearls. || 3 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, tell me that by which the mind vibrates and that by which it likewise does not vibrate; for I shall indeed treat it with that very thing.
By which intrinsic nature it vibrates, and by which means it does not vibrate. || 4 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, just as whiteness is in snow, as sesame oil is in sesame seeds, as fragrance is in flowers, and as heat is in fire; || 5 ||

Since the nature of vibration (*spanda*) cannot be described as being separate from the mind, he demonstrates it through examples beginning with "just as" (*yathā*): "Just as the sesame seed and the drop of oil—those two—[are inseparable], so too, O Rāghava, are the mind and its vibration joined together. The word "just as" (*yathā*) is used in the sense of conjunction. 5. Thus, O Rāghava, the mind and its vibration are indeed joined in that very same way.
These two are non-different; their distinction is merely a false mental construction.

Here too, the first word *tathā* is used for conjunction (*samuccaya*), while the second is intended to connect the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the subject. In all cases—such as between a quality (*guṇa*) and its possessor (*guṇin*)—because no investigation is made, the connection is simply non-difference (*abheda*) that tolerates difference. In that regard, he shows through investigation that the aspect of difference (*bhedāṃśa*) is false (*mithyā*), whereas the aspect of non-difference (*abhedāṃśa*) is real (*vāstava*): "They are non-different" (verse 6).

When one of the two sides— the mind or the movement of the mind— is destroyed, both perish without a doubt, having remained as the quality and the possessor of the quality (or, as is logical, the quality and the qualified). || 7 ||

Anticipating the objection, "Why might it not be that the aspect of non-difference itself is merely imagined? he provides the answer to the part of the question, "How is it that one does not move," by saying "citta" (the mind). That which is itself the causal self, conceptualized as both a quality (*guṇa*) and a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), remains in its own nature; thus, both conceptualizations of quality and possessor of quality perish and do not [persist].

The meaning is "without continuity. Thus, since the destruction of the distinction between quality and the possessor of quality is observed precisely while remaining as a single causal essence, it follows that only the aspect of difference (*bheda*) is imagined, not the aspect of non-difference (*abheda*).
And because both [aspects] cease absolutely depending on the destruction of either one of the two—the mental faculty (*manas*) and its vibration (*spanda*)—the mind (*citta*) [is liberated].
The meaning is that while the mind vibrates, it does not yet live; and it is established that this vibration of the mind cannot be prevented.
O Rāghava, there are two methods for the destruction of the mind: yoga and knowledge.
Yoga is indeed the restraint of its fluctuations, while knowledge is right discernment. (8)

For this very reason, the sequence of knowledge (*jñānakrama*) has been shown in the scripture for the purpose of destroying both [the subject and object] through the cessation of vibration (*spandanirodha*); thus he says:
"There are two sequences" (verse 8).

Śrī Rāma said: At what time, in what manner, and by what method— namely, through the practice called yoga consisting of the binding of the prāṇa and apāna breaths— does the mind attain peace that bestows infinite bliss?
Thereupon, Rāma, desiring to know the first sequence, asks: "When? (*kadā*).

The term *prāṇāpānanibandhā* means the binding of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths. The suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule *bhāve gurośca halaḥ*. The meaning is: by means of that which is characterized by the restraint of *prāṇa* and *apāna*. || 9 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
That wind which vibrates everywhere within the bodily channels of this body—
like water upon the ripples of the earth— is celebrated as "prāṇa."

Intending to describe the answer to this very question until the end of the creation, [the author] first states the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in order to explain that the vibration of the mind is dependent upon the vibration of the vital breath,
beginning with the words "In this body" (*dehe 'smin*), etc. Within the channels of the body, there are seventy-two thousand branches for each division.

The meaning is that there are thousands of channels (nāḍīs), through which the vyāna breath moves, according to the Vedic scripture; just as water, having pervaded everywhere, vibrates within the cavities that serve as the paths of vibration for the earth.
Due to its vibration, as it attains a variety of internal activities,
names such as *apāna* and others have been devised by those of perfected self.
Now, one might object: "Does not the prāṇa go only outside [the body], while other winds such as apāna and so forth circulate within the body?
To this he says: "Of that" (tasya). The meaning is that these are merely different modifications (vṛttibheda) of the prāṇa itself, and not distinct entities. || 11 ||
Just as fragrance is inseparable from a flower, and whiteness from a conch shell, so too is the flavor inseparable from its support; it has attained non-difference from the mind.

The qualification "taste" (rasa) is for the purpose of establishing the analogy with water. The meaning is that the vital breath (prāṇa) consists of water, and because of the Vedic scripture stating, "They consider this very [breath] to be Aṅgirasa; for the vital breath is indeed the essence (rasa) of the limbs," it is so designated.
The support [of the mind] has, as it were, attained non-difference through its complete adhesion on all sides, like a sheath.

For the mind, my dear, is bound by the vital breath (prāṇa); the sense is that [the self] follows the form of the person because of such scriptural passages as, "It is of the form of a person, following the person-like form of that [mind]," and so forth. || 12 ||
O Rāghava, know that this consciousness which arises from the internal vibration of the vital breath and is oriented toward the formation of volitional constructs—that is the mind. (13)

For this very reason, he states that the vibration of the mind is the cause of the vibration of that [breath], beginning with the words "internally" (antar). The mention of "volition" (saṃkalpa) is an illustration for all mental modifications (vṛtti) whatsoever. || 13 ||

From the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) comes the vibration of consciousness (cit); from that very vibration arise the various states of cognition, just as waves, which create the turning of whirlpools, arise from the vibration of water.

The vibration of consciousness is the differentiation of its modes pervaded by the manifestation of consciousness; these are the appearances of consciousness in the form of various respective objects.
Those adorned with the scriptures declare that the mind is the vibration of the vital breath;
when that [breath] is restrained, the mind will surely become tranquil. (15)

The movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is a movement dependent upon the vital breath. Those adorned with the sacred scriptures—knowers of the secret of the Upanishads who declare, "For, my dear, the mind is bound to the vital breath; indeed, this [mind] rises from the vital breath and sets in the vital breath; then speech merges into the vital breath, the eye into the vital breath, and the ear into the vital breath"—[affirm this]. 15.
Through the subsiding of the vibration of the mind, this saṃsāra dissolves,
just as worldly activity ceases when the movement of the sun's light comes to rest.
Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "The mind," etc. (verse 16).
Śrī Rāma said: How can the movement of the vital airs— prāṇa and the rest— which travel through the sky within the body-temple and move incessantly, be restrained?

[This refers to] those who move incessantly within the body—characterized by its own abodes such as the heart and other locations, and within the seventy-two thousand divisions of the channels (nāḍīs)—as well as those whose nature is to travel through the apertures of the mouth, nose, and so forth, in the spaces [of the breath], and in the external ether. || 17 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Through the study of the scriptures, association with the virtuous, detachment, and the practice of yoga,
one develops a lack of reliance on and a firm reliance upon the former states of worldly existence.

He begins to explain the means of Rājayoga—such as being without an object of support (*nirālambana*) or with an object of support (*sālambana*)—for the purpose of arresting the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*):

"When there is absolute detachment, established in the heart, through the ultimate renunciation [of worldly things] and through the practice of [the eight limbs] such as *yama*, *niyama*, *śama*, and *dama*, which are contrary to [worldly attachment], [then the state of non-duality arises]. (18)
From meditating for a long time with one-pointedness upon whatever is desired, and from the intensive practice of a single reality, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained. (19)

He says that one should practice restraint (*nirodha*) precisely where this mind finds delight—whether on a large mountain peak, the orb of the moon, or the form of a deity made of jewels—and so forth; thus he says, "according to one's desire. This means: having arisen as a single state, that is, through one-pointedness; the meaning is, having attained a transformation characterized by one-pointedness. Immediately after that:
He states what that task is: "The single principle," etc. (verse 19).

Through firm practice of breath control such as *pūraka* and the rest, until perspiration arises, and through union with solitary meditation, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained. (20)

He states that the suppression of the fluctuations of the mind—which is difficult to subdue—must be accomplished through the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of the sequence of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*): "By *pūraka*, etc. [This means] by the extension (*āyāma*) of one's own vital breath through *pūraka* and the other stages. (20)

Through the experience of the reality of sound at the conclusion of the utterance of the syllable *oṃ*, when consciousness becomes as in deep sleep, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained. (21)

Or, when consciousness has reached a state of absolute cessation of the perception of external objects due to the yoga of taking as its support the four measures (*mātrā*) of the *praṇava* pronounced slowly and long, [the state of deep sleep arises]. || 21 ||
When exhalation has indeed been practiced and the vital breath, becoming expansive, has entered the void,
the vibration of the breath no longer touches the apertures of the body and is thus restrained.

Now, he says— in two verses beginning with "In exhalation"— that the cessation of breath occurs not only through the practice of meditation accompanied by an increase in the duration of time, but also through the relaxation of each individual inhalation and exhalation during *recaka* (exhalation) and *pūraka* (inhalation). When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has expanded and become vast, it gradually becomes the void (*kha*), the state of emptiness, like a scattered cloud.
Or when external space has entered, it does not touch the cavities of the limbs or the openings of the nostrils. || 22 ||

When inhalation (pūraka) has certainly been practiced until the breath is firmly established like a mountain cloud and its movement has become completely stilled, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa-spanda) is restrained.
When [the mountain] stands motionless, gradually increasing until its fullness—like clouds on a mountain from the filling of one flood by another—until it reaches its limit. || 23 ||
In the practice of *kumbhaka*, one remains for an infinite time like a water jar;
when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is rendered motionless through fearlessness, the vibration of the breath is restrained. (24)

After filling [the lungs], when the breath is held for an infinite duration like a full jar during *kumbhaka* and remains stationary, the sequence of the three types of *prāṇāyāma* mentioned has been elaborated upon in the Pātañjala Śāstra:
"In that state, the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation is *prāṇāyāma*. Regarding that which was previously stated:
When mastery of posture has been achieved, the drawing in of the external air is inhalation (*śvāsa*), and the expulsion of the abdominal air is exhalation (*praśvāsa*).
The suspension of their movement, characterized by the absence of both, is *prāṇāyāma*; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, that [prāṇāyāma] consists of external, internal, and stationary modes, and is regulated by space, time, and number.
It is long and subtle. That wherein there is a cessation of movement preceded by exhalation is the external [breath].

That wherein there is an absence of movement preceded by inhalation is the internal [breath]. The third is the state of suspension (*stambhavṛtti*), wherein both are absent simultaneously through a single effort, as when [the breath] is held during the heating of the body.
Water placed upon a stone contracts from all sides; likewise, there is an absence of simultaneous movement in two [objects].

These three are also observed through space: by means of the movement of a tuft of cotton outside and the movement of the navel and so forth within, [it is understood that] "space" is the locus of such [dimensions]. They are observed through time by determining the measure of moments (*kṣaṇa*).

It is observed by means of numbers: "The first, second, and third [breaths] have been awakened for this many counts of inhalation and exhalation. Likewise, it is [observed as] mild, moderate, or intense. Indeed, breath control (prāṇāyāma) practiced in this manner—

The meaning is that through the vital breaths (prāṇas) having attained length and subtlety—like a mass of cotton being fully expanded, or like a lotus fiber being gently drawn out—the [breath] becomes long and subtle. Furthermore, by the phrase "when the prāṇa is stilled through practice," even the fourth method, which is attainable through its maturation, is indicated; that too has been shown by Patañjali.

"The fourth [type] casts off both external and internal objects. This means that the fourth *prāṇāyāma* is the steady cessation of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), preceded by the casting off [of objects], resulting from the previously mentioned mastery over both [external and internal]. Patañjali has also stated the fruit of being established in *prāṇāyāma*: "From that, the veil over the light is destroyed."

"And the fitness of the mind for the concentrations (dhāraṇās). But even that is not the highest [result], because from breath control (prāṇāyāma) follows the purification of impurities and the radiance of knowledge; such is the commentary. 24.

Having diligently pressed the uvula with the tongue so that it reaches the root of the palate, when the vital breath (prāṇa) has entered the upper aperture, the vibration of the breath is restrained. (25)

The uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*) is seen hanging from the root of the tongue like a breast in the mouth of one with an open jaw; for the Śruti states: "That which hangs down between the two palates like a breast is the source of Indra. One should [meditate] upon that with a turned-back [tongue].

The meaning is: when the breath has entered and is held in the upper aperture—the *brahmarandhra*—having been drawn upward by the tongue which, through the effort of practice such as *vardhana*, is made to enter the path of the internal movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and having pressed down upon it, subdued it, and forced it upward; by this, [the practice] is combined with the *lambikā-yoga*.

The concentration on the sky (nabhodhāraṇā) has been shown. Its method was stated by the Blessed Lord Skanda: "By placing the tongue in the cavity of the palate and drinking the nectar with the face turned upward, one will attain immortality within six months; of this there is no doubt.
He who, becoming steady with the tongue turned upward, performs the drinking of the soma, [attains it] in half a month; of this there is no doubt."

The knower of yoga conquers death. One should dissolve the vital breath for five *ghaṭikās* and hold it, joined with the mind, in that which is like the sky or a mirage of water, situated at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), accompanied by the Lord Sadāśiva, peaceful, and consisting of the syllable *Ha*. This is [the practice].
"The concentration on space (nabhodhāraṇā) is said to be skillful in splitting open the door-panel of liberation. Thus [ends verse 25].
When consciousness has dissolved through meditation into that subtle space called "nothingness," which is free from all temporal divisions, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained.

All mental constructions and modifications are therefore absent in that which is liberated from them—namely, in the subtle space of the heart (hārdākāśa), which is consciousness itself; for when the mere activity of internal and external perception has dissolved through non-conceptual absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi), nothing remains. || 26 ||
At the tip of the nose, at a distance of twelve finger-breadths in the stainless ether,
when the vision of consciousness becomes tranquil, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained.

He says "twelve" [in verse 27] to indicate that the cessation of the eyes and the mind occurs either by means of the external space measured at twelve finger-breadths, characterized by the tip of the nose, or by the cessation of that [space].

Through practice, when the vital breath has ascended by way of the upper aperture above the palate to the limit of twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśānta) and its movement has dissolved, the vibration of the breath is restrained.

He states that the accomplishment of its cessation occurs either through the practice of the *lambikā-yoga* or from the previously mentioned concentration on space (*ākāśa-dhāraṇā*) practiced by means of another method—
by saying "through practice. When the vital breath has almost dissolved into the *dvādaśānta*, which is the location of the *brahmarandhra*:
When it has come about. || 28 ||

When the light of the star [of consciousness] has reached its cessation between the eyebrows, and when the conscious mind has become awakened as the abode of awareness, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained. (29)

Thus, he states that the khecarīmudrā is also a cause for the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇaspanda), beginning with the words "between the eyebrows. This refers to the two stars—the pupils of the eyes—which are the locus of light, meaning the radiance of the visual faculty.

When, through long-term restraint, these have become stilled—that is, have come to rest—and likewise when [the senses] are directed toward the tip of the tongue and the vital breath according to the method previously described;

The meaning is: when the banner (the vital breath) has reached its end at the *dvādaśānta* by entering the cavity of the skull—that is, having reached the *bhrūmadhya*, the *avimukta* location—and when one has realized as the Self the Supreme Lord, whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), who is established as the imperishable and infinite Consciousness according to the *Jābāla-śruti* and other sources; [this] is also the *khecarīmudrā*.

As stated by Skandanātha: "The tongue enters the hollow of the skull and moves in reverse; the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows—this is the Khecarī Mudrā. He who knows this Khecarī Mudrā is not afflicted by disease, nor is he tainted by karma, nor is he constrained by time. (29)
When that knowledge which has arisen instantaneously is firmly relied upon,
the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is arrested within that state where no portion of conceptual thought remains attached.

He says "jhaṭityeva" (immediately) to indicate that when knowledge arises instantaneously—either through the grace of the Guru or the Lord, or by way of the "crow-and-palm-fruit" maxim—the cessation of that [mind] occurs immediately due to the subsiding of mental fluctuations. || 30 ||
O Sage, when for a long time the perception of the beloved void has been withdrawn,
the vibration of the vital breath is restrained through mental meditation free from latent impressions.

Now, he says "for a long time" (*ciram*) to indicate that its realization is achieved through the long-term settling of the mind upon the "small space" (*daharākāśa*)—as famously established in such scriptural passages as, "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is the small space"—by means of the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) thereof. Thus it has been stated in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga-sūtra]:
And: "From saṃyama upon the consciousness of the mind within the heart, there is knowledge of the Puruṣa. (YS 3.34)
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, what is that which is called the heart of all beings in the world,
in which this entire universe is reflected as if in a great mirror?

The question arises from the doubt of one who observes the word *hṛdaya* being used for a specific type of lotus-shaped flesh, for the mind (*manas*), and for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). It "shines forth" (pratibimbati), meaning it appears like a reflection in a mirror. || 32 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O virtuous one, it is traditionally held that the heart of living beings in this world is of two kinds—the acceptable and the rejectable. Listen now to this distinction between the two.
In this context, since the flesh and the mind are limited in extent, their identity must be assumed, and then the division into two should be understood:
"Know that which is the interior of the chest within the body—limited by its specific dimensions—is the heart; it is situated on one side of that [chest]. (34)
But pure consciousness alone is established as the heart to be accepted; it is remembered as being neither within nor without, yet neither without nor within. (35)
Raising the objection, "Could the word 'heart' (hṛdaya) with respect to the Self not be figurative, since it resides only in the physical heart? he says: "And within that... (35).
That indeed is the primary heart; therein this [knowledge] is fully established. It is the mirror of all objects and the treasury of all prosperity. (36)
The meaning is that this is because of the Vedic scripture stating, "In him, heaven and earth are contained as if within. || 36 ||
For all living beings whatsoever, consciousness is said to be the heart;
it is not a mere portion of a bodily limb, like an inert, worn-out stone. (37)
Therefore, when the mind is forcibly fixed in the pure heart consisting of consciousness, the vibration of the vital breath is obstructed by one whose latent impressions have been removed. (38)
By these methods, as well as others devised through various intentions and residing in the mouths of various teachers, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is restrained. (39)
Through practice, these various methods of yoga become effortless;
for one who is capable, they serve as the means for shattering worldly existence.

He says "by practice" (abhyāsena) in order to prevent one from engaging in haṭhayoga impulsively; the sense is that if restraint is attempted through force (haṭhāt), afflictions such as diseases will certainly arise. || 40 ||
When it has attained firmness through practice and is marked by dispassion, the restraint of the vital breaths according to one's latent impressions is considered fruitful. (41)

The meaning is that whenever and whichever latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arise according to their respective tendencies, [the practice] serves to suppress each of them. Alternatively, the meaning is that when the latent impression for liberation arises, it is fruitful by means of the fruit of liberation;
but when the latent impression for enjoyment arises, it is fruitful by means of the various fruits consisting in the accomplishment of those respective enjoyments. || 41 ||
Through practice, the vital breath becomes stilled within the twelve finger-breadths located at the eyebrows, the nose, and the palate, like a mountain river far away.

For this very reason, with the intention that various types of *dhāraṇā* (concentrations) are shown in the *Pātañjala-śāstra* according to the distinction of specific locations such as the space between the eyebrows for the sake of attaining various fruits of accomplishment (*siddhi*), he says:
"between the eyebrows," "the nose," and "situated in the palate. "Situated in the palate" refers to the location starting from the tip of the throat.

The "twelve-end" (*dvādaśānta*) refers to the boundary at a distance of twelve finger-breadths. The plural number is used due to the distinction between different types of persons. As Patañjali has said: "Knowledge of the bodily arrangement [is attained] at the navel-center; the cessation of hunger and thirst at the pit of the throat; and stability at the tortoise-channel, which is below the pit of the throat."

The *kūrmanāḍī* is well known as the elevated region resembling the back of a tortoise; [it is said that] "the vision of the perfected ones occurs in the light of the head," and so forth. The "light of the head" (*mūrdhajyotis*) is the radiant light within the aperture of the skull. It is like a mountain river or a waterfall:
just as it flows far away and then dissolves right there, so it is. (42)
Through repeated and long-term practice, the uvula is touched with the tip of the tongue at the palate, whereby the vital breath flows upward with great force.
Regarding what was previously stated—"having reached the uvula with the tongue"—he explains the means for that with the word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*).
It is touched; that is, it is reached. || 43 ||

Although these meditative absorptions abound in conceptual construction due to one's own habitual practice, they quickly lead to the state of non-conceptuality for the sake of supreme tranquility. (44)

Although these various types of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) involve a great deal of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) regarding their respective fruits of accomplishment (*siddhi*), for one who is free from desire, the fruit of supreme tranquility (*paramopaśama*) consists in the very absence of conceptualization for all of them; thus he says: "Conceptualization... (verse 44).
The person who delights in the Self becomes free from sorrow and possesses inner happiness; this arises from practice alone and from nothing else. Therefore, be devoted to practice. 45.
When the vibration of the vital breaths has come to an end through practice, the mind attains tranquility, and only nirvāṇa remains. || 46 ||
The mind, enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā), takes on birth; free from latent impressions, O Rāma, it attains liberation. It also sustains the vital breath (prāṇa); do as you wish.

The mind, enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā), grasps the body of birth and the vital breath (prāṇa) therein through ego-identification; however, when free from latent impressions, it attains liberation.
