The vibration of the vital breath is the form of the mind; from that arises the delusion of saṃsāra.
When that very [vibration] comes to rest, the fever of saṃsāra is extinguished. (48)
In this manner, according to the method of practice described, it is given—that is, it is broken down; that is to say, it is treated. || 48 ||
Through the exhaustion of the portions of conceptual construction, that state remains for the living being, from which all words, along with every form of mental fabrication, turn back. (49)

That wherein all is, from whence all comes, that which is all, and from which all proceeds; wherein this world is not, from whence this world is not, that which is not this, and which is not like this world. (50)

The meaning is that this visible world is not similar to Brahman in any respect whatsoever, because its relationship with the *saccidātman* (the Being-Consciousness-Self) is negated: it is negated as a substratum (*yatra na*), as something to be acquired (*yataḥ na*), and as being identical with it (*yan na*). Thus, there is no aspect in which the world resembles Brahman.
Because it is subject to destruction, because it is conceptual, and because it possesses qualities, no example whatsoever has been seen that is similar to the Self, which is devoid of qualities. (51)

For this very reason, since the world possesses attributes such as perishability, there is no illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) whatsoever for Brahman; thus he says: "Because of perishability," etc. (Verse 51).
She is the relisher of all rice-grains, the illuminator of all splendors,
the fashioner of all desires, and the moonlight of consciousness arisen within.
If there is no illustrative example, then how can there be acquaintance with that? To this he says: "By tasting" (*svādanī*).

The meaning is that it is to be known through that [tasting], because it illumines both the triads of external functions—whose objects are taste, form, and so forth—and the triads of internal functions, such as desire and the rest. || 52 ||
For from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), many rows of fruits of worldly existence arise and fall incessantly, possessing manifold flavors.

He says "because of which" (yasmāt) to indicate that it is to be understood as such by means of the principle "the fruit [arises] from this because of its logical possibility," since it is the cause for the emergence and exhaustion of the fruits of various karmas. || 53 ||

That person of great intelligence who, having taken hold of that state which is the ultimate limit of all things, remains steady-minded and knows it—that one is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 54 ||
Showing that the accomplishment of the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha) depends upon familiarity with that [knowledge], he concludes with two verses beginning with "That" (tat). || 54 ||
Free from all longing and curiosity, with the conceptualization of benefit and harm completely stilled,
he remains poised within the sphere of all worldly conventions.
The Supreme Person becomes one whose mind is liberated. || 55 ||

One from whom all longings and curiosities have departed, and whose yearning for sensual enjoyments has vanished; therefore, one whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding benefit and harm are completely stilled toward both favorable and unfavorable circumstances; therefore, one whose disposition is equanimous toward all worldly dealings and devoid of joy or sorrow—such a person is one whose mind is liberated.
He becomes the best of men; the meaning is that he even becomes the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu. || 55 ||

Thus ends the seventy-eighth sarga, titled "Description of Yoga," in the section on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) within the Means to Liberation (*mokṣopāya*) spoken by the Divine Messenger (*devadūta*) in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* of Valmiki, a work of the Sage (*ārṣa*).
This concludes the "Description of Yoga" in the section on Quiescence of the *Tātparyaprakāśa* commentary on the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*.
The seventy-eighth canto, titled "Nāma."
The seventy-ninth canto.
Śrī Rāma said: "The pacification of the mind engaged in yoga has indeed been described."
O Lord, out of your grace, please now explain to me right knowledge.
The two sequences of yoga and knowledge have indeed been indicated for the destruction of the mind;
once the first of these has been fully understood, the second is now being described here.

"O Rāghava, there are two methods for the destruction of the mind: yoga and knowledge. The meaning is that, between these two methods thus indicated, you have already described the first—the cessation of the mind—as a mode of its destruction. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"The Supreme Self exists here as the essence of manifestation, without beginning or end—this expansive, singular certainty is what the wise know as perfect knowledge. (2)

Desiring to elaborate upon perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) by means of its characteristics, essential nature, proofs, and so forth, [the author] first states its definition—characterized by the sublation of the world through the thorough acquaintance with the Self—in the verse beginning with "without beginning or end" (*anādyanta*). It is "one," meaning unique; "expansive" (*sphāra*), meaning of unlimited form. || 2 ||
These hundreds of rows of objects, appearing in the forms of jars, cloths, and so forth, are indeed the Self alone; there is nothing else—this certainty is right vision. (3)
Thus, because the world is sublated, he states that its characteristic is either the nature of self-cognition or the nature of the Self itself—“these,” etc. (verse 3).
Birth arises from incorrect perception; liberation comes from correct observation.
Due to incorrect perception a rope is [mistaken for] a snake, not due to correct observation. (4)

He demonstrates that right knowledge has the power to bring about liberation with the words "not [seeing] correctly": "By seeing correctly, there is no snake. This means that liberation results from the cessation of the state of being a snake. || 4 ||

Consciousness that is entirely free from the components of volitional construction and devoid of any object of cognition is designated as "pure awareness" (saṃvitti); this alone exists here in the state of liberation, and nothing else.
Then, what remains in liberation? To this he says: "by conceptualization," etc.
By consciousness itself, whose very nature is self-luminous, it is thoroughly and perfectly proclaimed as manifesting here in liberation. || 5 ||
When that pure form is fully realized, it is called the Supreme Self (paramātman);
when it is pure yet possesses an internal impure form, it is called ignorance (avidyā) by the wise.
The word "tu" (but) is used in the sense of "also."
Consciousness alone is the object of consciousness; there is no conceptualization of duality between these two.
O Rāma, the Self alone gathers itself; indeed, nothing else exists.

Thus, he states that the distinction between consciousness (*saṃvitti*) and the object of consciousness (*saṃvedya*) is produced solely by ignorance and is not real: "Consciousness itself... The meaning is that through ignorance one accumulates [the sense of duality], whereas through knowledge one discerns [its true nature]. || 7 ||
The vision of the self as it truly is in these three worlds consists of this much:
having ascertained that the entire world is indeed the self, there is fullness. (8)
He states the nature of right knowledge as it has been extracted: "yathābhūta... (verse 8).
Everything is indeed the Self; where in the world are existence and non-existence ordained, and where do the notions of bondage and liberation reside? O Rāma, what else is there to be grieved for?
"Diṣṭau nirdiṣṭau" means they have been extracted and defined; the sense is: "What else is there for which the foolish grieve?"—this is the ellipsis. || 9 ||
There is no object of thought other than the mind, nor is there any mind other than this; it is Brahman alone that expands as all this.
Everything is the one supreme void; what is liberation, and for whom could there be bondage?
This Brahman, whose form is expanded, vast and established in greatness, has its duality extinguished through knowledge; you yourself, O Self, have become that very Self by means of the Self. 11.
Even from the Great One, the Great Brahman, this visible world has become established through Māyā within its own self, assuming an expanded form like an actor on a stage. || 11 ||
When form is correctly observed, there is not even the slightest difference between wood, stone, and cloth; where then are you, intent on conceptual construction? (12)

When [reality] is perceived solely as the true nature of perfect empowerment (*samyag-adhiṣṭhāna*), where are you? The meaning is that neither conceptualization (*saṃkalpana*) nor discursive thought (*vikalpana*) regarding what is to be abandoned or accepted is possible within that single, uniform reality. || 12 ||
That which is peaceful in the beginning and at the end, the indestructible essential nature of both the object and the self— be absorbed in that, O Rāghava.
That which is indestructible in its essential nature is alone the reality; "nāma" is used here for the sake of common designation.
Since the essential nature of the Self is of this kind, the meaning is: "Become absorbed in that. || 13 ||
Beyond this entire sky is this world of the moving and the unmoving;
where is the sequence of pleasure and pain? Be free from feverish anxiety, O Rāghava.
Brahman is the supreme, unsurpassed form of bliss. || 14 ||
Through the delusions of old age and death arising from duality and non-duality,
the Self alone manifests by means of its own diverse forms, just as water appears as various waves.
"It flashes forth for the ignorant"—this is the ellipsis. || 15 ||
For one who stands embracing the pure Self with an intellect that is eternally situated within, what worldly enjoyments here are capable of binding that Self? (16)
To that knower of reality: what are enjoyments? 16.
For one who has cultivated expansive discernment, the enemies such as mental enjoyments and the like cannot pierce him even slightly, just as gentle breezes cannot shatter a mountain.
Mental enjoyment is desire; these and others are the six enemies. || 17 ||
In this world, those who lack discernment, are ignorant, deluded, and devoted to hope, swallow up their sorrows just as herons swallow fish that have no water.
It is without water, emerged from water, or situated in a small amount of water. || 18 ||
"The entire world is indeed the Self; ignorance does not exist anywhere. Having firmly grasped this vision, remain steady in your true nature. (19)
There is no diversity in mental constructions, nor is there any difference in reality within the various kinds of lakes and their waters;
thus, the person who consists of this single certainty is liberated.
Thus he is called "One who has clearly perceived the correct meaning. || 20 ||
The phrase "water and so forth" implies that waves, foam, bubbles, and the like are not other than the water; this is the sense of the word "just as" (yathā), which is understood from the context.

Having thus analyzed and perceived the true meaning, the person whose primary focus is the singular certainty of that [truth] is said to be liberated through the ultimate dissolution of the mind. This is the meaning of verse 20.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of Perfect Knowledge," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of Perfect Knowledge," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Eightieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For the discerning person who contemplates this mind with regard to enjoyments, [it is as follows].
O dear one, even when [objects] are standing right before one, longing never arises for them.
That firm discernment, in which even a longing for divine enjoyments does not arise—even when they stand before one—is described here. (1)
This is the presentation of the reflection that is about to be explained; the grammatical connection is that even toward enjoyments standing before one, no longing whatsoever arises. (1)
The eye exists merely for the purpose of seeing; likewise, the living being exists for the sake of pleasure and pain.
Just as a bullock is for the burden, the enjoyer is the master of material objects. (2)

In that regard, first, when desirable and undesirable forms are perceived by the eye, pleasure and pain are seen by the living being (*jīva*) due to the attachment to "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) regarding the eye. To show that in this context his ownership of the eye alone exists and not his "I-ness," and thus there is no resulting attachment to suffering and so forth, he says: "The eye... [It is] like a bullock [suffering] for the sake of the pain of carrying a burden.
Nor is he the leader of that herd of cattle; for "he" does not mean a bull. || 2 ||
When the eyes are immersed in forms, what agitation can there be for the embodied being?
When a donkey has sunk into a puddle, what loss is there for the army commander? (3)
Its ownership, moreover, does not reside in the eye alone,

but rather in the infinite variety of effects, instruments, aggregates, desires, karmic impressions, and their resulting fruits. Among these, it belongs somehow— through the succession of ego, intellect, mind, and vital breath— to that single entity which has entered into the sphere of "mineness."

Thinking that when the eye is sometimes in contact with an undesirable form, what need is there even to mention it, and from where could its attachment to suffering arise? With this intention, he says: "In the eyes. [O] you base one, who relishes this mire of forms in the eyes of the donkey—the donkey belonging to the washerman within the army!
This perishes in the twinkling of an eye; indeed, it harms even you.
With the intention that it is indeed possible to ward this off by virtue of one's own mastery, he says: "Rūpa... etc.

This refers to beauty characterized by [the attractiveness of] wife, children, and so forth. It "hiṃsati" (destroys) or causes destruction; here there is a Vedic substitution of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa-vyatyaya*). O lowest one, O most foolish one! || 4 ||
By the very means by which one calculates and by the very means by which one pursues horses,
so too is the wise man quickly bound by his own cruel deeds.

Then, what is the wise man like? To the question of where he is bound, he says: "By which. The cruel one has a sharpened intellect, but the wise man is he by whom—through the internal Self of consciousness alone (*cidātman*)—perfect knowledge (*saṃkhyāna*), that is, illumination, is produced through the attainment of external and internal objects; by whom alone [is known] this series of sheaths (*kośaparamparā*) which are non-self (*asva*).

It is followed by means of the superimposition of identity with the self; it is bound—through repeated practice—to its own activities and conduct, which consist in the illumination of objects as they are encountered and are characterized by indifference, and not, like a fool, to activities such as tasting the mire of forms. And so it is said:
The meaning is: you too should manifest the nature of existence as being indifferent, but do not relish it. || 5 ||
O eye, do not rely upon form—which arises and perishes, which is charming only for a moment, and which is composed of unreality—for the sake of that which is subject to destruction. (6)

The qualifiers "perishing as soon as it arises" and "pleasing only at first sight" serve to establish that [the world] is composed of unreality. For that which is indestructible and irresistible leads to destruction, which is to say, entry into the mouth of death. || 6 ||
The eye remains as a witness; form resides within the self.
Why do you alone suffer from heat due to the power of time?

Furthermore, O eye, while the Supreme Self— though always independent and capable of illuminating all objects regarding the domain of form— remains indifferent, why do you alone suffer, illuminating [objects] only occasionally by obtaining the light of lamps and such due to the power of time? Therefore, you too are situated like a witness.
The meaning is: "Behold that which has the nature of reality. || 7 ||
O mind, like a ripple in water or a tuft of down rising from the sky, your vision flickers with well-formed knots; what has come upon you?
Now, it is said—beginning with the word "salile"—that even when a form is perceived by the eye through delusion, there is no cause for the mind’s attachment to it:

"O Mind, this vision of various forms is manifold and unstable, like the various and fixed fluctuations in the water of rivers and the like; it is observed in the sky by eyes with tears, directed toward the light of the sun."

Like a peacock’s feather, false as it is, the eye flickers with various conceptual constructions—whether of good or bad species—such as "this is a white horse" or "this is a female form. What has come upon you there, by which you become attached and suffer? This is the meaning. || 8 ||
Just as a minnow quivers in the waters of a cosmic aeon, so does the egoism characterized by self-manifestation quiver within the mind; from where else could this "you" have arisen? (9)

Or, even if there were a mental activity (*vṛtti*) in the mind consisting of the form of an object seen by the eye, nevertheless, because there is no cause for the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) which is the basis of attachment, he says: "It is imagined" (*kalpa*). If a form such as color (*rūpa*) manifests of its own accord in the mind, let it manifest; but from where has this ego-sense arisen? (9)
Since light and form are eternally insentient yet manifest in mutual dependence as support and supported, your agitation regarding consciousness is futile. (10)

Furthermore, the form characterized by the female body and so forth manifests depending on the light of the sun and other sources, while the sunlight itself depends upon the body; thus, in their mutual conjunction, the agitation of the mind caused by desire and the like due to the delusion of beauty is well known.
However, that [agitation] is rendered futile because there is no actual connection between those two [the body and the light] and the mind. This is the meaning. || 10 ||
Form, light, and mental attention are mutually unattached, yet they appear as if they have come together, like the reflection of a face in a mirror. (11)

He clarifies this very lack of connection by means of an illustration with the word "rūpa" (form). The sense is that the perception of external form by the eye and the mental activities such as volitions within by the mind are [unconnected] precisely because they occupy different locations;
thus, they appear as if they were joined together or contiguous. || 11 ||
For these have become closely joined together by the ignorant creature;
when ignorance is swallowed by knowledge, they remain separate, consisting of unreality.
He states that ignorance alone is the cause for the delusion of being attached to that [substratum]—thus, "through ignorance.
However, when they are perceived as separate and detached, being unreal and sublated, they remain only as the residual substratum. || 12 ||
For these—form, light, and mental attention—are bound together by the conceptualization of the mind, just as wood is joined by lac. (13)
Dāruṇī is on wood; with *jatunā* means with lac. || 13 ||
The thread of one's own mental conceptualization is severed through diligent practice of the mind by means of inquiry; once severed, the cultivation of ignorance is destroyed.
One's own mental conceptions alone constitute the thread that binds one like the cocoon of a silkworm;

and for those of dull or middling capacity, this is severed through diligent inquiry by means of mental practice involving dispassion, self-control, tranquility, restraint, and so forth. However, for the person of primary capacity, once that [bond] is severed by means of knowledge suddenly arisen, [it does not recur].
The meaning is that when [the self] exists, the cultivation of ignorance, being severed by its very nature, simply does not arise at all. || 14 ||
When the mind has been exhausted through the destruction of ignorance, none of these—form, light, and mental attention—ever again collide with one another. (15)
Regarding that, he states that for the second [type of person], there is no effort: "Through ignorance," etc. (15).
The mind alone is the awakener of all the internal senses; therefore, it must be eradicated from within, just as a demon is driven out from a house. 16.
But he says that by the first effort the mind must be severed: "Of all [beings]," etc. (16).
O mind, you leap about in vain; the end of you has been seen by me.
You are utterly insignificant at the beginning and the end, and you perish even in the present. 17.
Now, he awakens the mind itself by means of the words beginning with "citta": "The end" refers to the means of sublation.

Since [the mind] is utterly void at both the beginning and the end, it follows that even in the present moment you are perishing; you are non-existent. For the meaning is this: a son of a barren woman, who is void in the prior and subsequent times, cannot possibly exist in the present time. || 17 ||
Why do you dance about within in vain through these five forms?
You dance only for him who knows you as his own self. 18.

[The meaning is: You appear as objects such as sound, presented by the five sense-faculties. However, you sport about as an instrument only for that conceited cognizer who knows you as "his own" or "mine," and not for me, whose sole essence is unattached, indifferent, and pure consciousness. || 18 ||
Your leaping about does not bring even the slightest satisfaction to my mind; like the flickering of a deceptive mind, you burn in vain amidst the fluctuations of worldly activity. 19.

The mention of "satisfaction" (tuṣṭi) is also an elliptical indication of "despair" (viṣāda), just as in the case of the mind's vibration in the form of perceiving various objects when employed by the illusions of a magician. || 19 ||
Stay or go, O mind; you do not belong to me, nor do you live.
By nature you are eternally dead, and through inquiry you are known to be perfectly dead.

By its very nature—that is, by its own false essence—you are dead and devoid of self; yet, through investigation, being thus remembered, you are "well-dead," meaning you are absolutely non-existent. || 20 ||
O you who possess the form of eternal death, you are devoid of reality, inert, deluded, and ever-deceitful;
only a fool, not one possessed of discernment, is to be oppressed by you, for you are ignorant.
Out of folly, we did not recognize you; you have quickly become as one dead.
Today you are dead like a crow, just as darkness is to lamps. 22.
For all this time, we did not know—that is, we were unaware—that you existed as the selfless (nairātmya), as if dead; [only] today, at the time of seeing the reality of the self. || 22 ||
By you, who are deceitful, my body-house has for a long time been entirely obstructed and deprived of contact with the virtuous. (23)
The virtuous possess tranquility, self-restraint, discernment, awakening, and so forth; [it is] devoid of association with them. || 23 ||
Now that you, dull-witted, ghost-like in appearance, and treacherous in mind, have departed, this house of my body is fit to be inhabited by all virtuous people. (24)
Only those who possess tranquility and the like are truly virtuous people. || 24 ||
"You existed previously, yet you do not exist now; the world is indeed deceitful. O Vetāla, are you not ashamed that you do not exist even at this moment? (25)

O rogue, you who are a world-forming mind-demon (cittavetāla), you did not exist previously, you do not exist now, and you shall not exist in the future. Even though you are thus denied by me throughout the three periods of time, are you not ashamed to remain here now? Oh, how shameless you are! This is the meaning. || 25 ||
Depart, O mind-vampire, from the dwelling of my body, together with the female demons of craving and the guhyakas of anger and the rest! 26.
"If you have a sense of shame, then depart," he said; thus [the author] says "together" (saha). || 26 ||
By good fortune, through mere discernment, the intoxicated vampire of the mind has emerged from the temple of the body, like a wicked wolf from its cave.
Oh, how truly strange and immense is this: by this dull, momentary, and deceitful mind, all these people have been rendered helpless! (28)
He pities those people deceived by their own minds, exclaiming: "Alas! (28)
What is your prowess? What is your strength? What is your refuge?
If you leap about alone, you are merely harassing dead men. (29)

Among people, you strike down as dead one who is already dead by his own nature through the perception of the body as the self—which is subject to death; what prowess is this of yours? If you can advance against me, who am the one and non-dual Self, then indeed that would be your prowess—this is the implied meaning. || 29 ||
O you of base mind, you are by no means being killed by me;
O fool, you have merely understood today that you are dead. (30)

O ignorant one of feeble mind, you are not being killed by me today because I have already realized that you were dead in every respect from the very beginning; this itself is what constitutes "killing. || 30 ||
For so long a time, knowing you, I have remained alive;
I have clung to you for a long duration throughout the nights of worldly existence, which abound with attachments.

Having known him to be "possessing the state of being alive"—that is, one whose essential existence (*svarūpasattā*) is like that of one who is actually living—he has become united with you through identity (*tādātmya*). || 31 ||
"Indeed, I have realized today that this mind is dead and does not exist;
therefore, having abandoned hope for you, I abide solely in the Self. (32)
"By good fortune, I have today personally realized that the mind is dead;
my entire life must not be spent together with a rogue. (33)

He says—“Not by the deceitful”—that for those liberated while living (jīvanmuktas), it is appropriate that after awakening, they spend the remainder of their life in a state of mindlessness (niścitta). || 33 ||
Having expelled the deceitful mind— the "I-maker"— from the dwelling of the body in an instant,
I remain established within myself as one who is self-abiding and entirely free from the Vetāla.
Having driven out from the abode of the body the mind—which serves as a festival for the wicked ones such as desire, anger, greed, and so forth—[one should remain]. || 34 ||
Having long ago acquired the vampire of the mind, I myself have produced various transformations; remembering this now, I laugh. (35)

The meaning is: "Now that I have myself become the Self of ultimate reality (paramārthātman), I laugh upon recollecting those transformations, by means of this self of mine which was once possessed and deceived by the vampire (vetāla) of the mind and had become identified with it. || 35 ||

By good fortune, the vampire of the mind— towering as tall as a palmyra tree— has finally been struck down after a long time, having been thoroughly tormented by the sword of discernment from its dwelling within the heart.
Having been struck down, he was indeed cast down and killed. || 36 ||
Now that the vampire of the mind has been stilled and has reached the pure state, by good fortune I abide alone in happiness within the city of the body. (37)
When he has gone to—that is, reached—the pure state of the path of the doors of the senses, due to the absence of impurities such as desire; || 37 ||
The mind is dead, thought is dead, and the demon of egoism is dead; by means of the mantra of inquiry, I remain established in my own nature as pure consciousness alone. (38)
Being equal, he is one from whom all inequality has been cast out. || 38 ||
"What is my mind? What is my hope? And what could my ego be?
By good fortune, this futile web of mine has been destroyed without remainder. (39)
The wife and the group of dependents. || 39 ||
Salutations again and again to me alone, who am the one whose purpose is fulfilled, the eternal, the pure-souled, and known as non-conceptual consciousness.
Now, with the verse beginning "To the One," he pays supreme homage to the Self, which is the remainder [of all things] and whose sole essence is unsurpassed bliss. || 40 ||
There is no sorrow, there is no delusion, nor indeed am I myself;
neither am I not, nor am I another—I bow again and again to me alone. (41)
I am certainly not that dull portion consisting primarily of the conceit "I am I," nor am I "not-I";
for the Self is the direct consciousness that transcends egoism, and it is not the case that it is "not. (41)
I have no desire, no actions, no cyclic existence, and no agency;
I have no state of being an enjoyer and no body—salutations again and again unto Me alone.
I am not the self, nor is there anyone else; I am not this, nor am I the other.
I am indeed everything; salutations, salutations unto myself alone.

The Self is not the object of the word or the notion "Self. Thus, it is stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya* and its *Vārttika* regarding the passage "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self'" (*ātmeti evopāsīta*) that the word "iti" is intended to exclude the status of being the object of the word or the notion "Self.
Nor is there any other non-Self that could be the "I"; for who else could possibly be conceived by one who perceives reality such that they might be the "I"?

Thus, that which is the object of the notion of the word "I" and its opposite is not "I. And since nothing other than itself is established, it is "all by itself"; the meaning is that everything indeed is "I. (43)
I am the beginning, I am the sustainer; I am consciousness, I am the worlds.
There is no separation from me; salutations, salutations unto me alone.
He is the beginning of the worlds and their cause; He is the Ordainer (Dhātṛ), the Sustainer; and "delimitation" refers to the threefold circumscription.
Salutations again and again to me alone—the great Self who is changeless, eternal, partless, all-encompassing, and present at all times. || 45 ||
To the one who exists at all times, the eternal one. || 45 ||
Salutations again and again to me alone— the formless, the ineffable, the luminous, the Great Self, who abides solely as the self by itself.
I have attained that Being which is equal, all-pervading, subtle, and the sole illuminator of the universe; salutations, salutations unto myself alone! 47.
This very one is the mountains, the oceans, the earth, and the rivers; it is not I alone, nor am I alone.
To me alone belongs this entire world, rich with all its objects; salutations, salutations unto me! || 48 ||

The mountains, the oceans, the earth, and the rivers—this visible beauty that exists now, accompanied by these, is not I. In this same way, it should be applied that even the entire world, rich with past and future objects, is not I; rather, I am indeed the Self alone. || 48 ||
Free from mental construction, delightful in its equanimity,
it has manifested the universe yet is not the universe, and is infinite [the reading "formless" (arūpam) is also found];
it is itself unborn and undecaying, transcending all qualities.
I bow to Acyuta, the Lord, whose body is [the universe]. || 49 ||

I bow to that form, the essential nature (*svarūpa*), which is called *Īśvara* because it is capable of ruling—that is, of being empowered to dispel ignorance and its effects—by virtue of being unswerving from its own arisen nature; it is delightful through equanimity, manifest as the universe, infinite, and imperishable, since all mental conceptions and mental constructs have departed from it. Why? Because it does not fall away from its own arisen nature. I bow to that essential nature.
The meaning is: "I have taken refuge with supreme excellence. || 49 ||

Thus ends the eightieth sarga, titled "The Relation Between the Perceived and the Perceiver," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 80.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Relationship Between the Perceived and the Perceiver," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus reflected and understood within, one reflects further in this manner.
O mighty-armed one, the Self must be known by the great-souled ones who possess knowledge of reality.

The vampire of the mind, which was previously expelled from the house of the body through strenuous efforts, is here rendered non-existent by means of both direct experience and logical reasoning. (1)

The Self must necessarily be known; thus, by those who know the reality of inquiry, it is further investigated in the manner about to be described—[the object of] this investigation being, as the context implies, the mind. || 1 ||
The truth that "this world is indeed the Self alone" has been cleansed by the mind; yet from where could the mind have arisen? Oh, how the mind is itself a non-entity!

From where could that mind have arisen by which the world was cleansed through the realization "this is indeed the Self," yet which, by falling within the sphere of the world, is itself non-existent? "Aho!"—an expression of wonder. || 2 ||
Because it is characterized by ignorance, because it is insentient, and because it is like an illusion, the mind is indeed non-existent;
or rather, it certainly does not exist at all as anything other than a delusion, like a tree in the sky.
It establishes its very lack of substantiality by stating "because it is ignorance.

Because it is insentient, because it is devoid of any other mind, and because it is an effect of *māyā*, the mind certainly—meaning with certainty—does not exist at all; thus it is non-existent. Alternatively, like a tree in the sky, it appears as something else due to delusion alone, but in reality, it is pure.
The meaning is that it is indeed the self of the sky-goer (the sun). || 3 ||
Just as the movement of a post appears to a child in a boat,
so the mind— which is composed of the non-existent— appears to the unawakened, but not to the awakened.

Just as the movement of a post perceived by a child or an infant who has not yet attained a single-pointed state is established merely through delusion, so too the mind, though established for one who is unawakened, is not established for a Buddha who knows the Self; rather, the meaning is that it is composed of unreality alone. || 4 ||
When the delusion of ignorance and confusion has subsided, we no longer perceive the mind,
just as one no longer perceives the shaking of a mountain once the whirling of a wheel has ceased.
The meaning is: at the end of the rotation induced by mounting the wheel of a machine for pressing oil, sugarcane, and so forth, that is, after descending from it.
(5) For in this way, the mind does not exist at all; only Brahman exists, whose nature is such.
Since the mental conceptions of objects arise from the mind, they are unreal and have been abandoned by me. (6)
Since the mental constructions of external and internal objects have issued forth from the unreal mind, for that reason they are unreal; thus, they have been abandoned and relinquished by me. (6)
I am born with my doubts stilled; I stand free from the fever of anxiety.
Thus I remain, thus I abide, entirely devoid of longing.
The meaning is that just as I abide by way of that ultimate nature, so too do I now abide through my own direct experience, and not otherwise. || 7 ||
In the absence of the mind, qualities such as childish craving are utterly exhausted, just as the various designations of colors vanish when light ceases. (8)
Childhood and the fickleness of a child's actions describe and manifest the various colors and distinctions of forms,
just like visual perceptions of that same kind.
The mind has died, craving has departed, and the cage of delusion is destroyed;
selflessness has arisen, and while awake, he has become enlightened.
The meaning is: while this Self was awake—being free from the sleep of ignorance—I became awakened to my own natural essential nature. || 9 ||
The entire world is indeed one and peaceful; even this diversity is not real.
What else could I contemplate within? Enough with this talk! 10.
The world is peaceful, eternally one, and is indeed Brahman alone. Enough with this discourse concerning the non-existent; the meaning is that there is no purpose [in it]. || 10 ||
I am the Self, eternal, established as subtle, all-pervading, and gentle; I have attained that pure state which is free from appearances and without beginning or end. || 11 ||
The manifestation has emerged, wherein the state of being a living soul is characterized by the manifestation of consciousness.
Whatever exists here and whatever does not exist— mind, self, and so forth, as well as non-entities—
that is more transparent than the sky, peaceful, infinite, ungraspable, and all-pervading.

Whatever is well-known in the world through the perspective of worldly convention (*vyavahāra-dṛṣṭi*) and the perspective of scriptural terminology (*śruti-dṛṣṭi*)— such as the mind and so forth, or the Self, Brahman, and Consciousness (*caitanya*) as existing— and whatever is well-known as non-existent, such as a rope-snake or the son of a barren woman, both the real and the unreal—
all that is clearer and purer than even the sky (*kha* or *ākāśa*), ungraspable, and self-luminous.
The meaning is that Brahman alone is spread out there, due to the superimposition of conceptual constructions regarding the forms of existence and non-existence. || 12 ||
Whether the mind exists or not, whether it dies within or remains stable—what use have I for deliberation, since my self has long since arisen in equanimity? (13)
Out of ignorance, I was a limited being characterized by the mode of discursive thought;
through inquiry, I have become infinite in form—where indeed am I, that "inquirer"? (14)

The meaning is this: for so long a time, due to ignorance, I was a non-investigator and a non-doer, remaining limited and possessing the nature of a circumscribed body and so forth; now, through investigation, having become one of immeasurable form, it is impossible to determine where that former "I" has gone. || 14 ||
Even though the mind has died, this splendor of my conceptual constructions is useless;
for what purpose does it arise, serving only the function of the mind-demon? (15)

Once the mind has died, even the splendor of the conceptualization as to whether a deliberator exists or not is meaningless; for what purpose would it arise again to sustain the activity of the mental demon and to provide it with life? Therefore, "I shall abandon this"—this is the connection with the subsequent verse. || 15 ||
"I shall abandon this internal fabrication of conceptualization"— having thus resolved "so be it," I remain with a tranquil soul, like one observing silence, established within the Self.
"Oṃ" refers to the fourth state (turīya), the Self which is the objective of the syllable Oṃ; "as in silence" is the illustrative example for the act of remaining [in that state]. || 16 ||
O Raghava, one who knows that [reality] should daily investigate with wisdom and the mind everywhere—whether eating, walking, sleeping, or standing. (17)
Having concluded the discussion, he states that this inquiry must always be practiced: "While eating," and so forth.
As they say: "Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping—he whose mind is not intent upon inquiry is said to be dead. (17)
Having investigated with their own minds, which are established in themselves and self-abiding,
the virtuous remain free from agitation amidst their ordinary duties.
In their respective duties, that is, in the conduct appropriate to their own caste and stage of life. || 18 ||
Free from pride and intoxication, with joyful intentions and a radiance equal to the autumnal moon,
they moved about engaged in their ordinary worldly activities.
But here, those of great intelligence dwell in happiness. || 19 ||
The radiance of their serene facial beauty was equal to the moon brought near by autumn.

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Non-existence of the Mind," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Non-existence of the Mind," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this manner, such an inquiry was formerly made by the learned Saṃvarta."
It was told to me on the Vindhya mountain by that very one who knows the Self.
In this world, Vītahavya awakens his senses and mind from causes such as futile exertion for the sake of achieving one-pointed concentration on the Self.
He demonstrates the traditional authority of the inquiry performed [in this work] with the words: "The inquiry... [It was performed] by Saṃvarta, the brother of Bṛhaspati. || 1 ||
Firmly grasping this view, with an intellect intent on discernment,
cross over this ocean of saṃsāra by means of gradual stages.
Through the gradual ascent of the stages (bhūmis), which is joined with the ripening of the excellence of resting the mind further and further by degrees,
O Rāma, now hear this other view that bestows the [highest] state—
the one by which the sage Vītahavya remained free from doubt. (3)

The other [view] consists of the awakening of the senses and the mind; by means of that vision, the sage Vītahavya ascended to—the meaning is that he attained—the fearless state without hesitation. In the reading "yathā," it means "in whatever manner. || 3 ||
In ancient times, the highly effulgent Vītahavya wandered through the forests,
traversing the long caves of the Vindhya mountains like the sun moving through the caverns of Mount Meru.
Searching for caves in the Vindhya mountains suitable for meditation, he wandered about.
From this terrible sequence of actions, which causes the wandering of saṃsāra and takes the form of mental and physical afflictions, he eventually came to feel revulsion in the course of time.
From where did his desire for meditative concentration arise? To this he says: "From this," [verse 5].
Through his noble desire for others, attainable through a portion of non-conceptual meditative absorption,
he withdrew the succession of worldly activities that had grown old.
"Jahāra" means he withdrew; that is to say, he renounced [them]. || 6 ||
He entered his own leaf-hut fashioned by Rambhā,
which was brightened by her presence and fragrant, like a blue lotus that has become white.
It was fashioned by Rambhā, constructed from plantain leaves; it was made white and yellow with camphor and powders, and for that very reason, it possessed a most fragrant scent. || 7 ||
There, upon that level and pure seat covered with a well-spread deer skin,
he rested— immovable and tranquil, like a cloud whose rain has ceased.
In a place that is peaceful and free from distress, at the edge or on the slopes of the Himavat, the mountain of the Immovable One. || 8 ||
He stood in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), with his fingers placed over his heels;
he remained with his neck held straight and his movement stilled like that of a mountain peak.

Being one whose fingers of the hands were positioned above the heels— that is, above the roots of the soles of the feet (an irregular compound used in the Vedic style)— he [stood] with his neck clearly extended, that is, with his neck held upright. || 9 ||
Slowly withdrawing his mind from the light scattered across the quarters,
he entered the cave of Mount Meru at evening, just as the sun withdraws its mass of rays.

From the objects appearing to the senses in all directions, he withdrew his mind which had become scattered; by the means of its restraint, he gathered it within the heart. The meaning is that he did so gradually, as he was about to proceed with the awakening to be described hereafter. || 10 ||
Gradually abandoning both external and internal objects of touch, he,
whose mind was free from sin, reflected upon this with his intellect.

While abandoning—without casting them off—the external, non-sensory contacts with objects and the internal, mental ones, he reflected upon and deliberated this which is about to be described; [the absence of the *num* augment] is due to the rule "not after *abhyasta*. || 11 ||
Alas! This mind is indeed so fickle that even when withdrawn, it does not attain stability for even a moment, like the broad leaves of a tree tossed by the waves.
"Like a leaf carried away by mature waves" means similar to a leaf moved by strong waves. || 12 ||
With its agitation aroused by the unrestrained forms of the eyes and other senses,
it leaps up incessantly like a ball struck by the palm of the hand.
Agitated by the various forms of objects through the eyes and other senses, it leaps up and dances as if bound or like a ball. 13.
He abandons the gods and clings to the functions of the senses that have been strengthened;
though he is restrained from them, he runs toward them like one who is mad.
Abandoning each preceding state of existence along with its corresponding tendencies, one indeed assumes each subsequent state of existence following them. || 14 ||
From a pot it goes to a cloth, from a cloth to a formidable cart;
the mind wanders among objects like a monkey among trees. (15)
These five gates of the mind, beginning with the eye, are fully designated as the "burnt senses"; for now, I shall examine them. (16)
Having thus reflected upon the defects of the mind, he considered the gateways through which they exit; this is what he states with the word "five.
The word *dagdha* (burnt) is used here in the sense of censure. Because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*), the compound *kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ* was not employed.
Ha! Ha! You hosts of unruly senses, why do you not assist me here toward enlightenment?
You are as fickle as the waves of oceans whose waters are tossed by the wind. (17)

Now, having rebuked the very senses, he awakens them with the words "O, O!"— O restless ones, you host of ruined senses, is there not even a moment, an opportunity, for your long-standing awakening through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) so that I may behold the Self? 17.
O you of fickle minds, do not act with rashness to your own detriment;
remember the vast webs of suffering that occurred in the past. (18)
O forms, you are indeed merely inert and base;
for vanity in that which is inert is as futile as a shimmering mirage. (19)

You are merely conceptualized forms of the mind itself through various distinctions of its gateways. In the inert state, due to the non-distinction between the letters *ra* and *la*, the quality of being "elevated" (*utsiktatā*)—like the swelling of waves upon water—flutters in vain. 19.
This arrogance of the blind, which is always devoid of light and whose nature is essentially substanceless,
serves only to make themselves visible.
For you, whose nature is essenceless and false, this emergence— which is devoid of light (meaning,
according to the root text and the commentary, "devoid of self-knowledge")— is a movement onto the wrong path due to ill-discipline; it belongs to those who are blind.

It arises solely for the sake of similarity, for the purpose of comparison; the meaning is that it serves as a comparison for the fall into a well of those who are blind and running on a wrong path. || 20 ||
"I, the Lord whose nature is consciousness, act as the witness for this body.
You, whose hosts of senses have been destroyed, why are you agitated in vain? (21)
If we are insentient, then who performs all worldly transactions such as seeing and so forth? To this, he says:
"The conscious Self" (cidātman). || 21 ||
My formless eyes and other senses whirl about in vain; they are like a circle of fire from a whirling torch, comparable to the delusion of a snake in a rope. (22)
Formless, they are empty of the nature of reality. || 22 ||
Therefore, the eyes and other [senses] have been thoroughly understood by that omniscient Self;
there is not even the slightest connection between them, just as there is none between heaven, the surface of the earth, and the mountains.

The meaning is as follows: there is not even the slightest connection between that witness—who is all-knowing and illuminates everything—and these [senses] such as the eyes, just as there is no connection between the sky and the surface of the underworld, or between the underworld and the mountains, or between the sky and the surface of the underworld and the mountains. || 23 ||
Like a traveler afraid of snakes or a twice-born man afraid of outcasts,
pure consciousness— untainted and free from disease— remains far removed from the senses.
Pure consciousness alone, whose sole essence is consciousness, the inner self (pratyagātman), stands far removed from the external senses;
for the meaning of the Vedic scripture is: "The Self-existent pierced the openings [of the senses] directed outward" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.1.1). || 24 ||
"Merely by the existence of consciousness, enough of your mutual agitation;
remain at ease, like those engaged in their daily tasks while the sun stands still. (25)
If that is so, how is it established that the self is the instrumental cause (nimitta) in the operation of the sense organs? To this he says: "The existence of consciousness" (citsattā).
Just as those who perform rites for the ancestors (śrāddha), agriculture, and so forth [are the causes] of their respective effects during the day... // 25 //
O mind, you who wander like a Cārvāka, a mendicant for the sake of filling your belly in the four directions—do not roam thus in vain for your own ruin, O world! 26.

Now, having awakened the mind, he causes it to awaken by means of the words beginning with "O Mind" (*citta*). It is called *cāraṇa* because it is the cause for the outward-turning movement of the senses; it is called *cārvāka* because of its identification with the body as the self; and it is called *bhikṣuka* because it wanders in the four directions for the sake of filling its belly. (26)
"Your notion that 'I am consciousness' is futile and unreal;
O rogue, there can be no identity between consciousness and the mind, for they are absolutely distinct. (27)
The notion that "that which possesses consciousness is conscious" is an error of latent impression (*vāsanā*). || 27 ||
"This wicked notion of 'I' of yours, that 'I indeed live,' has arisen in vain for the sake of suffering; it is not true, being devoid of reality. (28)

"It is not truth," [he says]. For life dependent on the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is not true; for even when that [ego] is absent, as seen in deep sleep, life is observed. Furthermore, that [life] is merely false because it is devoid of the True One, the Supreme Self. "No mortal lives by means of the out-breath (*prāṇa*) or the in-breath (*apāna*); rather, they live by something else upon which these two depend. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.18)
This is the meaning of the scriptural statement. || 28 ||
Upon the arising of the ego, abandon this agitation of thinking "I am that";
O fool, you are not anything at all—why do you flutter about in vain? (29)

When the rise of egoism—known as the transformation called *abhimāna* (self-conceit)—occurs, it is that state of agitation consisting of the thought "I am this aggregate of cause and effect" which is called *abhimāna*. || 29 ||
Consciousness is the mind, without beginning or end; nothing other than consciousness exists. O great fool, what else could that which is called "mind" be within this body? (30)
With the intention that your very own nature is difficult to attain, and that protecting others through egoism is utterly cast aside by you, he says: "Consciousness" (saṃvit) || 30 ||
O mind, this state of being an enjoyer and a doer has arisen like an elixir that results in poison; alas, it is indeed in vain! 31.
In its final transformation, it results in poison; at the time of enjoyment, it arises like an elixir.
Do not become an object of ridicule by relying on the collection of foolish senses;
you are neither the doer nor the enjoyer, for you are inert and are made conscious by another.
"Taking as a refuge" means making the collection of sense-faculties the support; "by another" refers to a witness. || 32 ||
Who are you among the objects of enjoyment, or what enjoyments do you possess?
For one who is inert, even a self does not exist for you; how then can there be kinsmen, friends, and the like? (33)
He says, "Who are you? (verse 33), meaning that your hope for enjoyment is in vain, since you are inert, false, and devoid of the power to experience enjoyments.
Whatever is insentient does not exist at all, even while appearing to exist, because it is devoid of existence;
for in it, consciousness, agency, enjoyership, and other such qualities are impossible. (34)

He establishes that "the self itself does not exist for you" with the words beginning "yad" (that which). That which appears as existing by virtue of the existence of another—just as redness [appears] in a crystal—is inherently endowed with non-existence. And "manya" is the essence [of the mind], which conceives of knowing, agency, and experiencing, and which synthesizes the preceding and the succeeding.
And because those [qualities] are impossible without consciousness. || 34 ||
If you are of the nature of immediate consciousness, then your very self is your body;
what kind of existence of the mind, consisting of being and non-being, could possibly cause you suffering? (35)

If it is asked, "In that case, why should I not be the very nature of the inward consciousness (pratyak-caitanya)? [the author] replies with the verse beginning "pratyak": "Then it is fitting for you to be eternally established in the state of being free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), and not in a state consisting of the conceptual constructions of agency, enjoyership, existence, or non-existence, which brings about suffering. The implication is that once all conceptual constructions have been abandoned, there is no longer any state of "mind" (cittatā) remaining for you. || 35 ||
Just as you have understood agency and enjoyership to be entirely false, so shall I wipe them away for you; listen to how this is done gradually through reasoning. (36)
But since, if [the self] were insentient, agency and so forth could be dispelled with ease, he says: "Just as..."
You yourself are indeed insentient; there is no doubt about this.
What kind of agency can belong to that which is insentient? How could stones dance here? (37)
The stones are the stone-images (statues). || 37 ||
Therefore, subsist for a long time upon that pure, divine portion;
you live, you desire, you kill, you wander in vain, and you prance about.

If you say that a wooden statue is seen dancing by depending upon the activity of consciousness, then you too must depend upon that portion of the Lord which is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). And just as the enjoyer of the fruit of the statue’s dancing is the conscious being itself and not the statue, so too the enjoyer of the fruits of life and other experiences produced by you is the conscious Self alone; therefore, you [are not the agent].
The meaning is: "You run about in vain for the sake of livelihood and such. || 38 ||
Whatever is done by means of a certain power, that is considered to have been done by that [power] itself. A sickle cuts by means of a man's power, yet it is the man who is called the cutter. (39)
A sickle and a wedge. || 39 ||
He who is slain by the power of another is indeed slain by that very [power];
a sword kills by the power of a man, yet it is the man who is called the slayer. (40)
The grammatical connection is that "the male alone is called the slayer. || 40 ||
Whatever is drunk according to one's capacity, that becomes truly drunk by him alone;
for it is the vessel that drinks the drink, while the man is merely called the drinker. (41)
But that man alone is called the protector (pātā), not the recipient (pātra). || 41 ||
By your very nature you are utterly dull-witted; you are awakened by one who knows all.
Therefore, it is as if the Self itself, by means of the Self, gathers this [knowledge] for us. 42.
It accumulates [the world] by way of the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, the instruments, and the accessories, just as in a dream;
for the word *bhavat*, being a pronoun used in the neuter, takes the form *bhavat*. || 42 ||
The Supreme Lord, your very Self, awakens you incessantly;
yet fools must indeed be awakened by the wise through hundreds of repetitions.
It awakens by means of the pervasion of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*); it makes manifest. And this is logical, as he says: "those who are to be awakened."
For here it is the very existence of the Self, whose sole nature is consciousness, that shines forth;
and by means of that alone, you have remained having accepted the referents of the word "mind. 44.
For this very reason, he says "the Self" to show that your acquisition of individuality through name and form is dependent upon the existence of consciousness.
Thus, O mind, you have come under the power of the self through ignorance;
but in the presence of knowledge, you have dissolved like snow in the intense heat of the sun. (45)

Thus, he says "evam" (in this way) to show that the Self itself, through its own ignorance, becomes like you, and through its own knowledge, is liberated from the state of being like you—the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). || 45 ||
Therefore, you are dead, you are a fool; in the ultimate sense, you do not exist.
"That very thing is I"—this is vain; let it not lead to your unhappiness.
Let there be no superimposition of identity, thinking "I am that very Self"; [otherwise] there would be birth and other sufferings leading to unhappiness. || 46 ||
The mental construction of unreality is like a creeper of Indra’s net;
here, it is only consciousness that has manifested as the limb of Brahman. (47)
The Brahmic limb is its own essential nature. || 47 ||
The power of Brahmā arises fully in the forms of the world of men and gods;
it surges like a shore against the mass of waves from the ocean's spray.
Power (śakti) is Māyā conjoined with the power of consciousness; for this very reason, it is like a shore (velā). 48.
O fool, if you are composed of consciousness, then you are eternally non-different from that supreme state; why do you grieve otherwise? (The reading *vyatiriktas tvam* is more appropriate). 49.

O fool, if you were to become composed of consciousness through the awakening to your own selfhood, then, because there is no cause for the differentiation of consciousness, you would be eternally non-different from the supreme state. 49.
For that state is all-pervading, abiding in all beings, and indeed possessing all forms;
O ignorant one, upon attaining it, everything is eternally attained.
With the intention that, since there is then an absence of any object not yet attained, remorse would be impossible as it would lack an object, he says:
"all-pervading" (*sarvagam*). This means it abides even within all past and future states;
in other words, it is devoid of any limitation imposed by time. (50)
There is no "you," there is no body; here, only the Great Brahman vibrates.
When the notions of "I" and "you" flash within that which is motionless, for whom indeed is there suffering? To whom does it belong? 51.

At that time, you do not exist as a separate entity. This is a Vedic archaism involving a transposition of persons (puruṣavyatyaya). The appearance of "I" and "you" flashes forth within the motionless Self; therefore, who could have what affliction? || 51 ||
If you are the Self, then the all-pervading Self alone exists here and nothing else;
if that which is other than the Self is insentience, then that [Self] does not exist, yet its very form does exist.
Furthermore, he states clearly the two aforementioned alternatives with the words: "The self," etc. (52).
The self alone is the entirety of the three worlds; there is nothing else whatsoever. If you are that reality, then you are the self; if you are other than that, then you are nothing at all.
Therefore, if you are anything other than the Self, then there is no reality whatsoever in the form of the ultimate truth; such is the meaning. || 53 ||
"Why do you strive in vain with thoughts such as 'this is I' or 'that is mine'?
Does an unreal body manifest, or who has ever been killed by a rabbit's horn? (54)

"I am this body of a child; I am that body of an old man. "The toys and such belonging to that body of a child, and the sons, grandsons, and so forth belonging to that body of an old man—they are mine. Why do you strive for this in vain? For the state of being a body does not truly belong to the Self; thus, the meaning is: why does this unreal form manifest itself? || 54 ||
O rogue, there is no third mode of being other than the conscious and the insentient;
it is like a third coloring between shade and sunlight. 55.
"In that case, why could I not be a third essential nature (svarūpa) distinct from both consciousness (cit) and unconsciousness (acit)? To this he replies:
"A third," etc. The meaning is that just as in the world there is no third category whatsoever among all things that is not colored by either shadow or light, so it is here. || 55 ||
When the dullness of mind and vision has perished due to the arising of the observation of truth, that which is produced is merely self-cognizing awareness born from that [observation]. (56)

If it is asked, "What then is its true nature?"— it is precisely that self-luminous, full nature of the Self which manifests through the final direct realization upon the destruction of your own insentience along with ignorance, as well as the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) residing within you.
He says "you" with the word "satya"; that which is born from it has manifested from that vision of truth. || 56 ||
Therefore, O deluded one, there is neither agency nor enjoyment for you either;
you are indeed that Supreme Brahman itself. Abandon your ignorance and become established in the Self.

It is only for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of instruction regarding the object of pure knowledge that it is said, "the Self acts by means of you [the intellect] acting as an instrument. (58)

If I am indeed the Self, then how is it stated in such scriptural passages as "It is to be seen by the mind alone," "This is to be attained by the mind alone," and "There is no diversity whatsoever here," that I am an instrument for the Self? To this, he says:
"By you, who are conceived as an instrument for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the teachings such as 'That thou art'..."
The final direct realization makes its own object the pure, absolute reality of consciousness (*jñatva*).
The sense is that it is just as one who desires to see the true nature of one's own face sees the face by means of one's own face reflected in the medium of a mirror; such is the meaning. || 58 ||
An instrument that is non-existent in its own nature, insentient, without support, and motionless cannot move without being impelled by an agent. (59)
If you consider yourself to be of the very nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*), then even in your movement there is no inherent capacity; thus, your conceit of agency is entirely in vain.
This is demonstrated by the verse beginning with "asatsvarūpam" (having a non-existent nature). "Niḥspandanam" means devoid of the power of movement by itself.
And the address to the agent is produced by consciousness for the purpose of illuminating the object to be accomplished. || 59 ||
No power whatsoever exists in this instrument which is itself a non-agent;
for what capacity does a sickle have to perform its function in the absence of a reaper? (50)
It is impossible for that which is not presided over by an agent to act.
O mind, the capacity for the act of severing by a sword-strike resides in the person, not in the utterly inert sword; nor does that capacity reside even in all the limbs [of the body].
"O friend, since you possess all limbs from head to foot, all members, and all necessary organs, do not act as a mere agent for yourself; do not undergo suffering in vain.
O fool, being afflicted for the sake of others does not become one who is base. (62)
In worldly matters, which are like those of common folk, it is indeed fitting for the self. || 62 ||
A lord such as this is not to be pitied by one who would be like you;
for he has no concern here with what is done, nor any with what is left undone.

If you argue: "Surely it is the Lord himself who, through delusion, has assumed the state of individual souls (jīvas) and is afflicted by hunger and other such needs; how can I neglect him? Therefore, striving with every effort, I shall purify him"—to that, he says: "The Lord. Only one who is like you may be grieved for by you; but the Lord—
The meaning is that it is not like this. || 63 ||
Out of pride, thinking "I am helping him," the person of small intellect merely exhausts himself;
for those who dwell [in this world], no real purpose whatsoever is served. 64.

Out of pride—that is, from the conceit of identifying with this aggregate of causes and effects—you, through the delusion that "I am benefiting this self," cause this limited and circumscribed intellect (*dhī*) to suffer and be afflicted. Since all the components dwelling within this aggregate—the five vital breaths, the mind, the intellect, and the ten senses—are insentient, they have no need for enjoyments; therefore, [your effort is in vain].
The meaning is that something is of use to someone. || 64 ||
If you thus comply with the purpose of the Creator, the Lord of Enjoyment,
then he has no desire whatsoever here, for he is forever satisfied.
Therefore, by process of elimination, your activity must be said to be for the sake of the Lord; however, he states that the answer to that has already been given:
"By the one, all-pervading Self of Consciousness, which shines forth as uncreated, this entire world is filled; there is no other conceptualization. (66)
If it is asked, "Why does he not desire [anything]?", it is said in reply: "Because of his perfection and non-duality"—namely, "akṛtrima" (uncreated/artificial). || 66 ||
By means of the manifestation of the one and the many, as a whole and as that very essence, what is desired is brought within the inner self, right within the self itself? (67)

He says "one" (ekā) because there is no lack of attainment for that [world] within itself, since the entire world is imagined by that very [Self]; thus, it has no desire for it. By the Self, through its own ignorance, that form of the world is created as a manifestation of both one and many; therein, what is there that is unobtainable which might be desired? || 67 ||
But for one such as you, agitation arises in vain merely by sight,
just as it does for a youth upon seeing a queen full of passion.
If everything belongs to God, then how can there be my will in that regard? To this he replies: "of one such as you.
This means: of a fool. || 68 ||
O handsome one, you are the agent whose mind is bound together with the self;
however, you are not its essential constituent, just as a fruit is not that of a flower.
"In that case, I shall obtain enjoyments through the grace of that very Lord by becoming connected with Him. To this, he says:

"By the Self" (ātmanā). Because the desire for connection with the Self is delightful, He calls it "beautiful" (sundara). You are not related to this Self, nor are you fit for such a relationship; just as a fruit, though produced from a flower, [is not the flower itself].
Because it is turned away from the flower, it is not fit for connection with the enjoyment of its fragrance and so forth;
the meaning is that upon its further growth, the flower itself vanishes, and thus [the fragrance] likewise ceases to exist. || 69 ||
That which is this oneness with the second is called the state of relation; previously there was duality, and now there is oneness. (70)
In order to establish the fitness for relation, he states the definition of the primary relation: "by means of a second.

Through the meeting of one with a second—either by the action of one or by the action of both—that former [element] comes into being; its inclusion within the other results in their oneness. That is the way of relation, the nature of relation.
The meaning is that it is the definition by way of its result. He states that very point in brief: "Previously," etc. (verse 70).
With its manifold arrangements and intent upon various forms of activity, worldly existence is remembered as being of many kinds, serving as the causeless source of states of pleasure and pain. (71)

And in such a well-known relationship, you are not the cause; for it is universally remembered—that is to say, well-established—that your own various states of pleasure and pain, arising from diverse causes and consisting of manifold arrangements, are oriented toward various kinds of prescribed and prohibited actions. || 71 ||

A relationship is observed between two equal things, as well as between two things that are half-equal; but when that [equality] is absent, there is no other [relationship] between two dissimilar things in the three worlds. (72)
In the case of two equal [quantities] of milk; in the case of two unequal [quantities], such as milk and water;

or in the case of two things that are utterly opposed, like water and fire—since it is observed that when there is such a collision of opposites, one of the two must necessarily perish, and no state of coexistence is possible; this is the meaning. || 72 ||
Many substances indeed depend upon the qualities of other substances;
the falling away from consciousness is suffering—do not fall away from consciousness. (73)

[Objection: But surely, just as there is a connection between the subtle elements—which possess mutually contradictory qualities such as sound, touch, form, and so forth—through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), why should there not be a similar connection for me with the Self? To this, he says:
"In another substance" (*dravyāntare*). In that case, there is no mutual contradiction because even the qualities of different substances [coexist] when they are blended together.

They rest upon the fivefold-composed substances (pañcīkṛtadravya). Thus they say: "Space has sound as its sole quality; wind has the qualities of sound and touch; fire is said to have the three qualities of sound, touch, and form;
water has four qualities through the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste; [earth has all five] through sound, touch, form, taste, and smell."

"The earth has five qualities. However, in this case, since consciousness (*saṃvit*) and insentience (*jaḍatva*) are contradictory, if there were a falling away of consciousness from you who are insentient, then because of the absence of a means of proof (*sādhaka*), the insentient portion would simply not be established;
thus, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga-duḥkha*) of your own non-establishment. If, on the other hand, there were a falling away of you from consciousness...

The connection with the self would have to be sought only for the sake of its own destruction; therefore, the meaning is that you, while depending on such a connection with the self, must not fall away from consciousness in either case. || 73 ||
By this alone, through one-pointed meditation, one becomes constantly absorbed in meditation or a seer of the Self;
for, by inward vision, there is the absence of the object of perception which bestows suffering. (74)
Alternatively, when the visible world— the object that bestows suffering such as yourself— is absent through the internal vision of pure consciousness (*saṃvit*),
meaning it has been destroyed, there remains only the Self, which is free from suffering and consists of unsurpassed bliss. If you are satisfied with this much, then,
being one-pointed through meditation, you shall become eternally meditative, possessing uninterrupted *samādhi* for a long time.
The meaning is: "Become one who perceives the self, one who sees the self. || 74 ||
Know that the tendency toward conceptualization is a fall from pure consciousness, which brings about suffering,
occurring within the insentient objects perceived as stones, such as the mind, body, senses, and so forth.

Your happiness lies in samādhi alone, and not in being oriented toward volitional thoughts (saṃkalpa). For, through volitional thoughts, consciousness—having fallen away from the body and so forth—is fragmented in many ways as it passes through the doors of the senses, like water from a waterfall falling upon rocks; thus, that very state is suffering. This is what he expresses with the verse beginning "saṃkalpa... (verse 75).

O mind, what kind of agency can there be? How could a flower exist in the sky, which is devoid of all mental constructs and whose nature is the destruction of thought within the mire [of worldly existence]? (76)
If it is argued, "But I do not will; rather, the Self itself wills because its very nature is that of agency," he says "this is not so" with the verse beginning "Of what kind... (verse 76).
Moreover, agency is not possible in the Self, just as it is not in the ether;
this Self alone appears as manifold within itself through its various forms.
The meaning is that, through the manifold diversity imagined by you, the Self merely manifests itself; it does not engage in imagining. || 77 ||
Just as the ocean vibrates with its waters through foam, bubbles, and waves, so does this Self of Consciousness (cidātman) vibrate within all that appears as mere manifestation. 78.
There is no second conceptualization, just as there is none for a glowing coal in the ocean;
for the Lord is devoid of conceptualization, whether in the body or in the insentient mind. (79)

Just as there is no heated ember in the ocean, so it is when the divine Self, which is devoid of conceptualization, exists, while the body and mind remain inert. Through the vision of discernment (*viveka-dṛś*), such false imaginings as "this is one thing and that is another," "this is impure and this is not," or "this is pure"—all of which arise from the presence of a conceptualizer—cease to exist due to the absence of that very conceptualizer. Thus, that which remains is consciousness itself, devoid of any object of cognition.
The connection with what follows is: "it is established that it is not the other. || 79 ||
Freed from both consciousness and the object of consciousness, O beautiful one, that alone is the essence and nothing else;
there is neither "this" nor "that," neither auspicious nor even inauspicious. (80)
Thus, this false conceptualization does not exist, just as a forest does not exist in the sky.
This expanse is merely consciousness alone, devoid of anything to be perceived; how then can there be the false fabrication of "this is I" or "this is another"? (81)
He states that very point clearly: "by means of direct experience" (saṃvedya) || 81 ||
In that which is beginningless, formless, all-pervading, and the expansive Self—who could superimpose the conceptualization of the Ṛgveda? Who could draw [lines] in the sky? (82)
The mention of the *Ṛgveda* is an illustration intended to include all [Vedic] texts in written form.
When the Self— ever-arisen, the essence of all things and categories, established as pure consciousness, filling and overflowing the vast quarters of space—
has properly entered into a state that is, due to its stainlessness, as if unreal;
The fragments of pleasure and pain have indeed perished; that delusion of mine is truly gone.

O Mind, when you have properly— without doubt and through direct perception— realized and understood the Self, which, by virtue of its stainlessness and intrinsic purity, abides as the essence within all things and objects well-known as substantial entities, and which exists as the very nature of pure consciousness; and when you have realized it as being full, overflowing, and pervasive in every direction, then for me, the fragments of pleasure and pain [no longer exist].

Since [the world] is like something unreal—like the water of a mirage, a rope-snake, or silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—that former perception of pleasure and pain is, by the certainty (*vai*) of this realization, merely a delusion and an error; it is not according to reality.
Thus it is said in the *Ārṣa* Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki. (De.)
In the section on tranquility within the means to liberation, the eighty-second canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Training the Senses," is concluded. || 82 ||
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Controlling the Senses," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Once again, the wise and excellent sage, with his intellect purified by a clear understanding, spoke.
Having protected his own group of senses, he awakened them well with this [instruction]. || 1 ||
When the collection of mind and senses exists, there is the attainment of all defects and misfortunes;
when they are absent, the attainment of all virtues and happiness is proclaimed here. (1)
By such an intellect—one that is white, pure, and characterized by meditative retention (*dhāraṇā*)—he is protected while remaining in solitude.
1 Listen as I shall explain clearly to you the true object of that group of senses;
having heard it and attained the contemplation thereof, proceed to the supreme state beyond suffering. 2
I shall clearly tell you that secret instruction which was given by him for the sake of the group of senses. || 2 ||
This existence of yours, which brings only suffering and ends in death, you should abandon by relinquishing the notion of a self’s existence. (3)

These groups, beginning with the sense organs, are established for you through this unexamined vision; their own existence and presence lead only to manifold misfortune and suffering during life, and after that, they bestow an end—granting repeated death, hell, and so forth. Therefore, by means of the aforementioned inquiry, [abandon] that [notion] of the self.
Let them abandon existence when it is non-existent. || 3 ||
"I clearly believe that through my instruction this very existence of yours has already come to an end, for you are born of ignorance. (4)

By my instruction on the true nature of the Self as previously given—indeed, because you are born of ignorance—the meaning is that once ignorance is destroyed by this instruction, you shall no longer have existence. || 4 ||
O mind, your own existence becomes manifest for your own suffering,
