just as the glow of molten gold leads only to the burning of its own sides.

Now, he speaks similarly regarding the mind as well—referring to it as "one's own being" (*svasattā*). It is called *taptakāñcanarut* because it roars or sounds like glowing molten gold; in that fire, the play (*lāsa*) of children or birds serves only to burn their sides. || 5 ||
Behold: while you exist, the multitudes of the rivers of worldly existence, agitated by the waves of delusive waters, enter the ocean of Time.
He demonstrates the succession of misfortunes joined with the existence of the group of mental faculties by means of the words "Behold," and so forth.
Because there is no distinction between the *la* and *ḍa* sounds, [the phrase refers to] those who are dull-witted and foolish, who are agitated by the waves of passion, hatred, and the like. (6)
Multitudes of sorrows fell from somewhere, like torrents of rain, driven by a competitive "I-first, you-later" impulse and mutually agitated.
Those [streams] in which there are deliberations such as mutual killing, defeat, and oppression, produced by "I-first, I-first" attitudes— that is, mutual egoisms. || 7 ||
The cruel cholera of existence and non-existence throbs boundlessly, intent on uprooting the heart and causing lamentation.
Existence and non-existence, prosperity and adversity.
Upon this withered tree of the body, where coughs and labored breaths act as humming bees,
the blossom-cluster of old age and death unfolds with its stainless radiance.
In the sky of the dense mist of the body, which is coiled by the serpents of turbulent waves and riddled with the chasms of its cavities,
the restless monkey of anxiety dwells within the heart.

In the hollow of the body-cave, which is coiled with the fierce waves of mental desires, there is a heart whose apertures—the openings of the sense-faculties—are like dense mists of thick inertia; therein, a restless female monkey characterized by anxiety, intent on weaving a web, wanders about—meaning she is like a spider. 10.
Crying out with the dance of greed, this bird uses its sharp beak of duality to sever the fragments of virtue from this withered tree of the body. (11)

With its own playful movements characterized by greed, crying out and warbling, the bird— with its sharp beak characterized by the duality of pleasure and pain— tears apart the cluster of qualities, which consists of the fruits and flowers of peace, self-restraint, virtue, and so forth. || 11 ||
The harsh, impure, and ill-behaved cock of desire scatters the refuse of the heart here and there. (12)

The cock, characterized by lust, repeatedly makes a heap—meaning he scatters with his two feet—the refuse which is the heart, that is, the mind, filled with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion and the like. || 12 ||
In the great night of delusion, the fierce owl of ignorance flutters about the tree of the heart like a Vetāla in a cremation ground.
Ignorance is erroneous cognition; Kauśika, the owl, is characterized by that. || 13 ||
When the collection of senses exists, these and many other misfortunes run rampant like female spirits in the night. (14)
But if you were not present, O virtuous one, all auspicious glories would shine forth brilliantly with light, like lotus ponds at dawn. (15)
Now, he demonstrates the perfection of all virtues in the absence of the mind and the senses with the verse beginning "In you" (*tvayi*).

The address "O virtuous one" (*sādhu*) is used because [virtue] exists even in the state of non-existence. "The splendor of auspiciousness" (*śubhaśriyaḥ*) refers to the splendor of the virtues to be described; "with light" (*sālokam*) means accompanied by the light of discernment (*viveka*). This should be applied accordingly even in the case of the literal dawn.
The same applies to what follows as well. || 15 ||
The sky of the heart shines, its mist of delusion having been stilled; it is encompassed by stainless light, its inner space rendered utterly free from passion.

The "garment of the heart" is the Brahman within the heart, which is exceedingly free from passion (nīrajaskatara), having completely transcended the quality of rajas, and wherein the internal mind [is absorbed]. || 16 ||
Like a turbulent flood falling unexpectedly from the expanse of the sky, the surges of conceptual construction do not fall for long, causing such disarray. (17)
Without hesitation and indeed free from fear, the floods of torrential rain that fall or emerge from the expanse of the sky, agitated by the wind and other elements, do not descend;
likewise, the surging waves of conceptual construction (vikalpa), which cause impairment and serve as causes for distraction, do not fall upon [the yogi]. || 17 ||
Gladdening for all, peaceful, supremely purifying, and dear to the heart, loving-kindness (maitrī) arises from the heart like a cluster of blossoms from a fine tree. (18)
Inwardly riddled with flaws, itself possessed of qualities both fit and unfit, anxiety undergoes withering like a lotus plant scorched by frost. (19)

"Antaśchidra" means having an internal flaw or incompleteness. It refers to that [woman] in whom qualities such as learning and skill are applied—that is, employed—only among those who are dull-witted and foolish. In the case of the lotus plant (*padminī*), the meaning is clear. || 19 ||
When ignorance is destroyed, light attains clarity within,
just as the orb of the sun shines in the sky when the clouds have subsided in autumn.
Internal light is the radiance of one's own knowledge; it attains clarity, that is, manifestation. || 20 ||
Clear, vast and deep, unagitated and unassailable, the heart attains equanimity like an ocean when the wind has subsided. (21)
The heart, that is, the mind, is indeed unassailed and remains undefeated by the causes of imbalance. || 21 ||
Filled with a flood of nectar and consisting of eternal bliss,
he dwells within as a person, like the cool moon.
Upon the destruction of ignorance, consciousness attains clarity within;
the entire world, including the moving and the unmoving, finds its sole rest in that consciousness.
The mental modifications (*vṛtti*) of consciousness take on clarity, which is an expansion that brings about fullness.
Consequently, the entire world, including all moving and non-moving beings, being sublated, comes to rest solely within a single portion of consciousness; this is the implied meaning. || 23 ||
One meditates upon a form full and slow with bliss; it does not belong to those attached to the vital breaths who create the snares of desire. 24.

The meaning is that the *vapuḥ*—the essential nature of the Self, whose form is full and complete—is contemplated and experienced; it does not, however, belong to the side of the body and so forth, which are bound to the vital breath (*asu*), tied by the snares of desire, and attached to life. Alternatively, *vapuḥ* refers to the body, which is slow to manifest bliss.

The meaning is that one’s form is conceived as being filled, as if by the consumption of the eternal nectar (amṛta), and not on the side of those who are attached to the breaths and the like— the evils of attachment which produce the snares of hope for food, drink, and so forth. || 24 ||
Just as sap returns to burnt leaves, so too does [the essence] return to men who have exhausted the great path of worldly existence, old age, and birth. 25.

Just as there is a reappearance of leaves on trees through the emergence of new sprouts during the rainy season after they have been burnt by a forest fire, so too, for those men whose long journey—characterized by the old age and birth of saṃsāra—has been consumed by the fire of knowledge, there occurs a reappearance of the "flavors" (rasas), which are the qualities such as health, contentment, nourishment, and luster. This is the meaning. || 25 ||
One rests for a long time upon the tree of the Self so as not to wander again;
such and other perfections of virtue arise in this manner. (26)
With the intention that rest alone in the Self of unsurpassed bliss— which is free from rebirth— is the ultimate limit of all qualities,
while other attendant qualities are infinite and impossible to describe, he concludes with the verse beginning "apunar-" (verse 26).

But when you, O All-Consumer, who bring about the destruction and exhaustion of all desires, are absent, [the distinction between] these two sides—the existence and non-existence of the nature of the mind—[persists]. || 27 ||
Between these two positions: [the first being] that they exist as an absolute self-nature, and [the second being] the acceptance of absolute selflessness. || 27 ||
Accept for a moment that very path by which you perceive the highest good;
O best among men, I consider your own true nature to be happiness.
Regarding this, he states that the first position is superior: "One's own self," etc. (28).
Meditate upon that very non-existence, for the abandonment of happiness is indeed folly;
if, however, it were real, then the internalized consciousness would truly exist. (29)
"Non-existence" means empty of any other existence. Now, for what reason do you not desire my life in the form of a previously established mind that contains consciousness within it?
Or for what reason do you desire my absolute non-existence? To this, he says, beginning with "If," etc.: O Mind!

If that form which is well-known to you, wherein consciousness is internalized, were real, then who would desire your non-existence while you live in that form? But you do not exist in that form; you are unreal.
I say this having investigated through truth—by means of scripture, sacred tradition, and personal experience—and not by superficial observation; such is the meaning.
Who would desire the absolute non-existence of one who is living?
But you do not exist; I tell you this in truth, O handsome one. (30)
Therefore, do not be happy with the thought "I live," for that is entirely false;
you were non-existent from the very beginning, and your existence is merely due to delusion.

He says "by that" (tena) to show that this abiding in the ultimate nature of the self is beneficial for you as well: "For as long as you were previously [only] belonging to the first eon (prāthamakalpika). || 31 ||
That very same [nature] has now reached utter decay through investigation;
O virtuous one, your form is nothing other than this lack of investigation. (32)
That itself is the delusion. || 32 ||
When investigation is correctly performed, it remains equal and uniform;
yet that which arises from non-investigation is like darkness arising from the absence of light. (33)
It remains uniform, consisting of pure existence alone, equal, and devoid of the inequality of distraction;
it is so because of the absence of light, that is, due to the lack of manifestation. || 33 ||
"O friend, just as darkness is pacified by light, you have been pacified by discernment; for all this time, your lack of discrimination was slight. (34)
This swelling of yours has become the sole cause of your suffering;
through mere deluded imagination, it has come to be like a child’s phantom. (35)
By this reason of having little discrimination; [the author] says "moha... [in response to the question]: "But how could there be fatness for that which is non-existent? || 35 ||
The duality that existed as a decaying state, perishing through the conceptualization of beginning and end, has now arisen as eternal once its own prior form had reached dissolution. (36)

The connection with the preceding clause is that "fatness" and the dualities such as pleasure and pain, which were caused by it, came into being. Since [these] were exhausted at the very moment of the Creator's initial and final volition (*saṃkalpa*), the word "perishable" (*kṣayī*) is an adjective qualifying the dualities. By the grace of that discernment (*viveka*), at this present time of the arising of knowledge, [the dualities] are non-avidyic (*āvidyaka*).

When one's own prior form has passed away, the eternal, beginningless, and endless nature of the Self arises; "salutations again and again to that discrimination"—this is the connection with the following verse. || 36 ||
Through the grace of discernment, salutations again and again to discernment!
Though you are awakened in many ways, you have been further enlightened even by the mind.
O mind, you have already awakened to many things by yourself, and you have been further enlightened by the scripture. || 37 ||
When the state of being a mind has perished, you remain as the Supreme Lord; your manifestation in your primordial nature has come to abide for the sake of ultimate welfare. || 38 ||

Even previously you existed as the Supreme Lord; even now, through your awakening, the play of your own nature has attained its manifestation—thus, "you are indeed Maheśvara," is the connection with what follows. || 38 ||
Now you are the Great Lord (Maheśvara), liberated from all latent impressions (vāsanā);
for he whose birth arises from lack of discernment perishes through discernment. 39.
As he proceeded toward the end with light, a darkness devoid of vision arose;
O virtuous one, even though you did not desire it, this state of inquiry has come to pass. (40)
This destruction has come from every direction for the sake of accomplishing happiness;
therefore, by means of established principles and reasonings, it is determined that you do not exist. (41)
O Lord of the mind and senses, may it be well with you; you have reached your end—you who were eternally non-existent in the past, and now possess no form. 42.

In the reading *vittvā*, [the meaning is]: O Lord of the senses, having known—meaning having attained your true nature—by means of established conclusions and reasoning, become one who has reached the end, the further shore of saṃsāra. May it be well with you (*svasti astu*). He states the non-existence of the mind even in the three periods of time with the word "eternal" (*nityam*). || 42 ||
And there shall be no future for me; may it be well with your own mind. I am attaining final nirvana; I am at peace; by good fortune, I am free from the fever of passion. (43)
He demonstrates the attainment of the supreme human goal through the very non-existence of the mind, beginning with the words "I enter final nirvana," and so forth. || 43 ||
Established in the state of the fourth form (turya), I abide in my own self alone;
therefore, there is truly no such thing as an unstable mind within saṃsāra.
The Self indeed both exists and does not exist, because it is found elsewhere;
this Self is I myself, that [Self] is I, and there is nothing else anywhere apart from me. (45)
I am always present everywhere as the very consciousness that vibrates, whose nature is awakening;
I do not entertain the notion "this is the self" within my stainless interior.

With the intention that where even the conceptualization "this Self consists of the single essence of pure consciousness" is difficult to find, other conceptualizations are all the more remote, he says: "This... (verse 46).
How can there be the conceptualization of a single entity as being distinct from its counter-correlate?
Without uttering such a conceptualization as "I am this Self," I remain silent within my own self, like a wave in water. (47)
For this very reason, he says that it is not the object of words for that [Self], namely: "I. This means not citing an example and not expressing it in speech. || 47 ||

Having attained that portion of perfect consciousness which is free from the object of perception, in which the seat of thought is utterly stilled, in which the aspect of volition is not dependent, in which there is no movement of the vital breaths, and in which the defect of partiality has set;
I am becoming tranquil; I myself am silent and devoid of internal desire.

Within my own heart, I am that which is devoid of the inert portion perceivable [by the mind], whose latent impressions have been pacified due to the sublation of even the ignorance that causes it, and whose conscious element is non-dependent because the reflection of consciousness does not exist separately from it.

Due to the cessation of the power of action dependent upon that [breath], there is no movement of the vital breaths. Precisely because of the absence of any differentiating factor, it is one whose distinctions of parts have set; it is even, of a single flavor, the aspect of consciousness characterized as pure consciousness alone, the remaining portion after the sublation of the world. Having attained this, one enters silence—devoid of effort, devoid of mental activity, and free from exertion.
And I become quiescent, devoid of the activity of speech; the meaning is that I am at rest. || 48 ||

Thus ends the eighty-third canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating the Non-existence of the Mind," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating the Non-existence of the Mind," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus reached this conclusion, that sage Vītahavya was freed from all mental impressions.
He remained motionless in meditative absorption within a cave in the depths of the Vindhya mountains.
The meditative absorption of Vītahavya consists in his abiding within a cavity in the earth;
it is described as the attainment of sovereignty over the Vidyādharas, the status of a Gaṇa, and so forth, [all] residing within the heart. || 1 ||
Having thus determined and ascertained in the manner described. || 1 ||
Beautiful with the bliss of consciousness in which all movement has ceased,
his mind having set, he shone like the ocean when it is perfectly still.
He who is motionless, complete in his entirety, full, and whose nature is self-luminous consciousness-bliss—being of that very form, he is beautiful. || 2 ||
Within him, the continuity of his vital breaths gradually subsided, like a fire whose mass of flames has ceased its flickering once its fuel is consumed. (3)
When the external object has reached the state of non-existence and no longer persists,
and the remainder remains established within, his eyelashes do not even blink.

He describes her eyes being half-open with two verses beginning with "anantara": they have not reached the state of being completely closed within, nor have they gone to the extreme of being fully open; rather, they remain in the remaining portion beyond that which is opened. (4)
With their eyes fixed on the slight glances reaching toward the tip of the nose,
they attained an equal beauty with lotuses that were half-bud-shaped.

The "tip of the nose" (ghrāṇaprānta) refers to the end of the nose; "gone there" means extended to that point. The two eyes (īkṣaṇe) are perceived as if they possess a light (āloka)—that is, a radiance—which is very slight, even on both sides, and equal. || 5 ||
With his body, head, and neck held perfectly erect, that one of great intelligence sat as if carved from stone or as if depicted in a painting.
As he remained thus for three hundred years,
within a hollow of the Vindhya marshes, it passed for him like half a muhūrta.
Of Kaccha, a region situated near a mountain torrent. || 7 ||
It is said that for all this time, that self-possessed man did not perceive [the passage of time];
being liberated while living and absorbed in meditation, he did not abandon that body.
For that duration, that fortunate one, a knower of yoga, did not wake up,
despite the noble roars of clouds rumbling with the weight of heavy downpours.
Even by the gurgling sounds of the falling torrents of rain and mountain streams, which were heavy with their mass of water.
[He was accompanied] by the deep roars of the lords of the surrounding regions as they hunted,
by the cries of birds and monkeys, and by the sounds of the slapping of elephants' trunks. (10)

By the trumpeting and roaring of the elephants belonging to the lords of the circles, the vassals, and the frontier-dwellers who had arrived or were coming for the hunts— [the word *āgata* (arrived) occurs in both readings]— the word "even" (*api*) should be supplied everywhere. 10.
With the roaring of lions in their fury, the hissing sounds of waterfalls, the falling of fierce thunderbolts, and the dense clamor of people; || 11 ||
By the furious roars and wrathful bellows of the lions. || 11 ||
By the trumpeting of intoxicated śarabhas, by the crashing of mountain slopes during earthquakes, by the roaring sounds of forest fires, and by the leaping of water-borne currents; || 12 ||

By the crumbling of riverbanks and mountain embankments due to earthquakes; by collisions and impacts; by the blasts of forest fires and their contact with fire, as well as by the sounds produced thereby; and also by the strikes, splashes, leaping, and flowing of the masses of water—by these means as well. (12)
By the blows from the slopes of great boulders, by the earth, mud, and water on the surface of the ground, by the surges of water-floods that have arrived, and by heats as harsh as fire; || 13 ||

He did not wake even from the heat of the summer season, which was as harsh as fire and consisted of muddy waters flowing from the surface of the earth; this should be applied everywhere [in the verse]. 13.
It flows freely at its own will when the causal conditions have dissolved, just as waves in water do when the rains have passed. (14)

The connection between the two [verses] is as follows: when the cause for its falling away has ceased and it remains useless while the rainy season flows on, that [elephant] is made to enter—meaning he is driven—into a cavity of the earth, a subterranean hollow within the surface of the ground, by the mud pushed forth from above during the torrential downpour of the monsoon, in a very short time. 14.
For in that mountain cave, in a very short time,
he was turned into mud on the surface of the earth by the floodwaters of the rainy season.
There he dwelt upon the ground within a narrow-wombed hollow,
his shoulders pressed down by the mud like boulders upon mountains.
The meaning is: one whose shoulder is pressed or embraced. For there is no pain for him who is immersed in the bliss of meditative concentration (samādhi). || 16 ||
Then, when three hundred years had passed, that self-effulgent Lord,
whose nature is the Self, awoke while still confined within the hollow of the earth.
Consciousness itself seized that body which was being crushed by the earth;
for the body is merely the vibration of the vital breath, existing without the movement of the life-force.

To explain how his life was sustained while he was in such a state of peril, he says: "Consciousness alone... Consciousness itself, reflected in the subtle body (liṅgadeha) as a result of the unseen merit of living (jīvanādṛṣṭa), took hold of that body and protected it. However, the vibration consisting of breath—that is, the activity of the vital force (prāṇavṛtti)—did not take hold, because the body [was otherwise].
It is subtle; the meaning is that there is an absence of the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 18 ||
Having attained full maturity upon arising, that mental construction, taking the form of his own mind, was experienced by him right within his heart. (19)

He describes what happened to him after three hundred years with the words beginning "utpatti" (arising). Now, his *kalanā*— the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvasaṃvit*)— for the sake of experiencing the remainder of its *prārabdha* karma, having attained maturity and grossness through the process of unfolding (*unmeṣa*) by way of arising within the heart, and having assumed the form of its own mental constructs, [perceives] everything to be described through imagination.
She experienced it as if within her very heart; the meaning is that she felt it as though she had actually perceived it. || 19 ||
In the lovely forest of Kailāsa, at the foot of a Kadamba tree,
he attained the state of a sage for a hundred years— a stainless self liberated while living.
He describes exactly what he experienced with the verse beginning "Kailāsa," and so forth. || 20 ||
For a hundred years, he shall possess the state of a Vidyādhara, free from all mental afflictions; for five yugas, he shall hold the sovereignty of Indra, saluted by gods and celestial musicians.
Indra-hood is the state of being the king of the gods. || 21 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, regarding these manifestations of his as Indra and others,
how can there be both regularity and irregularity in the constraints of space and time?

The meaning of the question is as follows: how can the restriction of direction—beginning with "in the forest of Kailāsa"—the restriction of time—beginning with "simultaneously for five [ages]"; and the lack of restriction due to experiencing that [vision] in a very short time and in the region of the heart alone, be logically justified? For it is impossible to otherwise alter the restrictions of space and time. || 22 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This power of consciousness, which is the self of all, whatever manner it arises in and wherever it does so, it immediately becomes that very thing, owing to its nature as the one Self.

He offers a rebuttal with the following intention: when consciousness (citi) is known as being non-universal (asārvātmyena), there indeed occurs a contradiction with the principle of necessity (niyati), because even for two small [units] of space and time, there would be the capacity to imagine other extensive spaces and times; however, this is not the case when that which is universal in nature (sarvātmikā) and endowed with all powers (sarvaśaktisaṃpannā) is fully known.

Just as a restriction exists within the intellect regarding where, when, and what [something] is, so too the sequence of restrictions concerning space, time, and so forth, consists of that very [intellect]. (24)
Restriction and non-restriction regarding contraction and expansion belong only to space and time as they are experienced by one's own intellect;
these two are contradictory [only] when applied to what is experienced together with what is not being experienced.
[This applies] in the case of very small channels and short durations.

With the intention of showing that dreams are experienced as occurring over vast spaces and durations, he says "yathā" (as). The meaning is that wherever and whenever there is an experience in the intellect (*buddhi*), at that time and place, such a restriction is established. "Being composed of that" (*tanmayātmatā*) means being superimposed upon the self which consists of the intellect; this is the sense of the phrase. In the reading *tanmayātmanām*, the term contains the reason [for the following].
The qualification. || 24 ||
Thus, free from latent impressions and with his mind purified, Vītahavya beheld various other worlds within the space of consciousness in his heart.
By those two aforementioned reasons. || 25 ||
For those possessing perfect awakening, this very latent impression (vāsanā) is no longer a latent impression;
for one whose seed has been burnt by the fire of knowledge, what seed-nature can remain? || 26 ||

Because that which has been burnt is perceived through the destruction of the power of its seed, whereas that which is not burnt is not; that is to say, it refers to that which has been parched. || 26 ||
For one kalpa, he served as an attendant to the Moon-crested Lord;
he was skilled in all branches of knowledge and possessed stainless vision of the three periods of time.
Having resolved this doubt, he describes the subject at hand with the verse beginning "kalpam" and so forth. "Gaṇatvam" means the state of being a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatyam). || 27 ||
Whatever kind of firm impression one possesses, one perceives things accordingly;
Vītahavya experienced this very state through his liberation while living. (28)

Even for one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), it is said that only the firm latent impression (saṃskāra) awakened by the *prārabdha* karma that impels experience is the cause for the appearance of the diversity of bodily enjoyments and so forth; thus he says: "He who... (verse 28).
Śrī Rāma said:
"O best of sages, this being the case, even for one whose mind is liberated while living,
there remain perceptions of bondage and liberation, just as they did in the case of Vītahavya."
Rāma’s apprehension is evident. || 29 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This universe, as it exists, is peaceful and as pure as the sky; it is Brahman alone. For those liberated while living, how could there be any perception of bondage or liberation?

With the intention that, according to the analogy of the burnt cloth, the appearance of the non-existent due to the remainder of *prārabdha* karma is merely the persistence of what has been sublated and is not bondage, he provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "as it stands" (*yathāsthitam*). || 30 ||
Wherever and in whatever manner this expanse of consciousness shines,
there and in that very manner it attains its pervasive extension to that same extent.
They find it, as it were, they obtain it. || 31 ||
O Rāghava, by that [Brahman] which exists as the self of all, many worlds have been experienced and are indeed being experienced in the form of Brahman.
With the intention that the Lord’s manifestation of that [world] occurs without bondage, just like our own manifestation of the world, he says: "By him" (tena). || 32 ||
In those countless, formless, and great-souled worlds, the conscious selves of the Vītahavyas were submerged within the cavities of the earth.

With the intention of stating that it is equally well-said that the experience of the world by all living beings belongs to that very consciousness which is characterized by the heart of Vītahavya, since it is the self of all beings including ourselves, he says "Dharā" and so forth: "He who [resides] in the formless,
essence-less, and vast worlds (bhuvanas) which appear as great souls..."

He who was Śakra has today become [a king] among the wretched in various regions (*deśaviśeṣa*). The term *janapada* is used here in the sense of "an abode of days" (i.e., a country). Regarding the formation of this word, when the *taddhita* suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "born in," the suffix is elided by the rule *janapade lupa*. Because of the elision, the rule *yuktavadbhāvaḥ* applies, whereby the plural number is used. || 33 ||
He who was Śakra, unaware of his true self, has today become a king among the wretched;
even at this very moment, he is engaged in hunting in the forest.
He who was the swan, his self unawakened, born from the lotus of Brahmā,
is that very same one now dwelling as the lord of fishermen in a forest grove on Mount Kailāsa.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in the *Paitāmaha-Padma* Kalpa, during the time when Vītahavya held the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (*gāṇapatya*), he who was the royal swan (*krīḍāhaṃsa*) in a grove of the Kailāsa forest is now present, having become the lord of the fishermen (*dāśendra*), the king of the Niṣādas. The same applies to what follows. || 35 ||
That king who, unaware of his own self, [ruled] over the region of Saurāṣṭra on this earth—
he is he who stands today in a village of the Andhras, abounding in trees.
Śrī Rāma said:
This was indeed the mental creation of Vītahavya; those embodied beings therein were merely objects of delusion (or, according to another reading, "mere delusion").
How can that which has the form of the body be consciousness? 37.

Rāma asks—"Mānasa?"—intending to instruct those people who do not understand the teacher's intention regarding the universal nature [of all things], by means of the teacher’s own words which resolve that doubt. The meaning is: how is it that those possessing consciousness take on the forms of bodies, such as the bodies of Śakra, the swan, and so forth? || 37 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, if that world of Vītahavya consisted solely of a single delusion, then why does this one of yours appear so much more real?"

Since it has been stated many times that the entire world is a product of the mind and is merely an illusion, the meaning is: given their equality, how and why does this world, which is well-known to you, appear as something endowed with consciousness to sentient beings? || 38 ||
This too, my dear, is pure consciousness alone, resembling a delusion consisting of the mind;
even that space is pure consciousness alone, resembling a delusion consisting of the mind. (39)
He shows the very equality of the two with the words "this" (idam) || 39 ||
In reality, O Rāma, that world does not exist, nor does anything else;
even for you, there is no existence of the world—this is Brahman alone that shines.
Thus, this world is not similar [to itself], nor is it different from itself;
for the meaning is that similarity and difference are impossible without the establishment of a counter-correlate (pratiyogi). || 40 ||
Whatever has been, whatever is, and whatever will be—just as this is, so too is everything else;
this entire visible world is composed of mind and consists of pure consciousness alone. (41)
That mind which remains as pure consciousness alone is itself composed of that [consciousness]. || 41 ||
As long as this form, which is such as this, has not been fully understood, so long is it known as the firm essence of the vajra; but when understood, it is the supreme sky.
Through ignorance, this very mind unfolds in such a manner by means of its surges and playful manifestations, like water in the ocean.
"Pratyullāsa" means origination, and "vilāsa" means transformation such as growth and so forth; [the compound refers to] by means of those two. || 43 ||
By the very expanse of the sky of consciousness as it truly is, one's own mind itself attains the designation "manas";
by that [mind], the world is made vast and becomes the object of perception.
Thus, it is neither extended nor is anything at all unextended.

He states the aforementioned point in brief: "As it truly is. By its very nature as the unmodified space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), the mind (*citta*)—as if perceiving something slightly through *māyā* and imagining itself—attains the designation "mind" (*manas*) due to its repeated thinking (*manana*). Through that [mind], the expansive universe comes into being. Thus...
The visible world is spread out; however, in the ultimate sense, the meaning is that nothing at all is spread out. || 44 ||

Thus ends the eighty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the World of Vītahavya’s Mind," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means to Liberation, in the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, a work of the Seers. 84.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the World of Vītahavya’s Mind," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-fifth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Then what did Vītahavya do while remaining within that cavity of the earth?
How did he cast off his body, and how and what did he become?
Having entered into the sage Piṅgala, the extraction of his body is described here;
furthermore, the state of one liberated while living and the final samādhi are described. (1)

The inquiry is made in sequence by means of four interrogative particles (*kiṃvṛtta*) regarding: (1) the extraction (*samuddhāra*), (2) its specific mode (*tatprakāra*), (3) the subsequent conduct (*taduttaracaryā*), and (4) the remaining state of the one liberated while in the incorporeal body (*videhamukta-pāriśeṣya-tadrūpa*). || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Immediately thereafter, the mind named Vītahavya, whose nature is infinite, realized that it was nothing other than its own self-manifesting wonder.
He fully realized the form of the infinite Self, the undivided Brahman; this is the meaning of "in samādhi. || 2 ||
Once, there arose within this attendant of Śarva a spontaneous desire to remember his former birth,
directed toward beholding all his previous lives.
The primordial light is the conscious self; it is remembered during the time of meditation upon it. || 3 ||
Then he beheld all his own bodies, both those that had perished and those that had not; from among those that had not perished, he saw each one situated within its respective hollow.

The meaning is that he perceived the body of Vītahavya as existing through his own imagination alone— according to the principle to be explained in the story of Jīvaṭa— where some parts were lost and others not lost, some destroyed and others not destroyed, all situated within the hollow of the heart of those respective undestroyed bodies. || 4 ||
By mere chance, the thought occurred to him to lift up that body;
he saw it there, lying like an insect in the mud.
The body known as Vītahavya was crushed within the hollow of the earth; it was like a mass of mud carried on the back of a mountain by the torrential rains of the monsoon.

By the phrase "carried by the flood of the rainy season," it is understood that [the object] was brought some distance away by the current; and by the expression "standing on the back," it is also implied that it was cast down face-first. (6)

Having seen that earth, which was covered with a network of grass and whose surface and back were like skin, and which was constrained within the cavity of the earth by that one of great splendor; || 7 ||
[He is one] whose skin and the surface of his body are strewn—that is, bound—by a network of grasses such as *kāśa* and the like;
by the word "body" (*deha*), its constituent parts are indicated. // 7 //
Once again, he reflected with his intellect of supreme awakening:
"Because all my limbs are so oppressed, my body is deprived of its vital breaths."
By the vital airs; that is to say, by their movements. || 8 ||
Once liberated, he is not able to move or act even in the slightest degree;
knowing this, I shall quickly enter the body of the Sun.

"To perform even a little" means to act; since the action has not been explicitly stated, there is no tautology in saying that its power has not been explicitly stated. Therefore, having known the means for its extraction, his Piṅgala will then extract my body by means of this method of entering another's body (parakāyapraveśayoga).
Or rather, what need have I for this? I shall attain peace without obstacle.

His attendant, a Gaṇa named Piṅgala, shall deliver him by his command. He states another thought of his: "Or else" (athavā); the meaning is: "I shall find peace through this very body, that is, by means of liberation while in the body (videhamukti). || 10 ||
"I shall enter nirvāṇa; I go to my own state. What purpose do I have for this physical body?"—having reflected thus in his mind, O high-minded one, Vītahavya [attained liberation]. (11)
Having remained silent for a moment, he further reflected upon the ground:
"Indeed, for my body, neither abandonment nor reliance is to be adopted. (12)
Whether there is renunciation or reliance, neither is to be adopted nor is either to be disregarded, because there is no distinction between them. || 12 ||
As is the abandonment of the body, so is the taking up of a body;
therefore, as long as this body exists and has not yet reached the state of subtlety (atomization), [one must act]. 13.
He says that very thing: "of such a kind," etc. [It refers to] the state of minuteness, the condition of being dust. || 13 ||
Therefore, having ascended this, I shall dwell here for a while in order to uplift my own body, Piṅgala, by means of an ascetic form. (14)
By means of Piṅgala, through the gateway of Piṅgala, I enter the solar body for the purpose of extraction. || 14 ||
"I shall enter the sun, situated in the sky, like a reflection in a mirror"—
thinking thus, that sage, assuming the form of the wind, entered the sun.
"Assuming the form of air" means, that is to say, having become subtle. || 15 ||
Having assumed a body consisting of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), like fire emerging from the opening of a bellows,
the Blessed One, the Sage, likewise beheld that leader of sages situated within his heart.

The "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*), previously explained, is that body which is the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). It is like the space within a bellows or the interior of a hide. Having seen that leader of sages—the venerable Sun who is the very nature of contemplation—entered into the heart, [the Lord perceives] his task and its sequence.

The syntactical connection with the remote [verb] is: "Having seen [him], he beheld the body of the sage, which had entered the interior of the Vindhya mountain, was unconscious, and was nearly dead. (16)
Having seen it, that noble-minded one, reflecting on the sequence of past and future events,
beheld the body of a sage within the interior of the Vindhya mountain’s rocky womb.
Standing in the midst of the sky, Bāṇu saw [the sage] covered with grass and stones and deprived of consciousness;
having understood what the Ṛṣi intended to do, he [intervened]. 18.
Then, as for what Ravi did next, he says: "Of the sage... (verse 18).
To rescue the sage from the earth, she commanded her foremost host;
that consciousness of Vītahavya-muni took the form of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka).
The sage is one whose body is that of a sage; the *gaṇa* is named Piṅgala. He states what the consciousness (*saṃvit*) of the sage did when it entered the heart of the Sun: "Vītahavya... (verse 19).
Having quickly honored the venerable Ravi with her mind, she bowed down; and being permitted by Bhānu with due respect, she went before him.
Having been granted leave with great respect by the Sun as if into his own heart, that sage entered the body of Piṅgala, which was setting out for its own purpose.
That Piṅgala, having left the sky, entered the cave-dwelling of the Vindhya mountains,
which was tawny-hued and as beautiful as a forest elephant.
It was beautiful with bowers, vine-cottages, and elephants.
He reached the Vindhya forest, which shone like a garment of clouds intoxicated by the rainy season;
there, with the surface of the earth torn up by his claws, he tore it from the womb of the earth.

In the rainy season, the sky is like that [cloudy one] where the clouds are intoxicated; in that sense, it should be construed as beautiful with its thickets (kuñja) as if with elephants (kuñjara). Piṅgala is one by whom the surface of the earth has been torn up or dug out with his claws. || 22 ||
Then, like a crane extracting a lotus stalk from the mud, he withdrew his own subtle body— the silent city of eight constituents— from the sage’s physical frame.
The sage’s silence, along with his subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), entered his own physical frame from the body of Piṅgala.
Like a bird wandering through the expanse of the sky, it found its support;
then the embodied Vītahavya and the sky-dweller bowed to one another.
Ālaya, his own nest; Mūrta, who had attained a physical form; Vītahavya; and Nabhaścara-Piṅgala—these all bowed down to one another.
Those two treasuries of splendor became solely intent upon their respective duties;
Piṅgala went into the sky, and the sage went to the pure lake.
The lake is for the purpose of bathing. || 25 ||
Vītahavya quickly sank into the lake, which was like a night-lotus with stars for its form and whose appearance was like the rays of the sun, amidst its blossoming lotuses.
He whose form was as if adorned with yellow and red garments by the sun, like a woman wearing a silk scarf; that is to say, his waters were colored by the glow of the rising sun. || 26 ||
Like a young elephant in a forest at the edge of a muddy pond,
having bathed there, performed his recitation, and worshipped the Sun,
he shone once again with a body adorned by his mind, just as before. (27)
At the end, that is, at the conclusion, of her play in the small ponds covered with mud; [she was] adorned by the mind, meaning possessed of mental activities such as reflection. || 27 ||

Endowed with that loving-kindness, supreme equanimity, and profound peace, as well as true wisdom, sympathetic joy, compassion, and glory— the Sage, whose mind is liberated from all attachment, [is thus perfected].
Having gone to the bank of a river in the Vindhya mountains, he enjoyed himself for the entire day.
He enjoyed [her] for only a single day, not for long; the meaning is that he remained there after having fallen from his meditative absorption (samādhi). || 28 ||

Thus ends the eighty-fifth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Samādhi for Vītahavya," in the Section on Tranquility (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) within the Means to Liberation (*mokṣopāya*), in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the Sage Vālmīki. 85.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Samādhi for Vītahavya," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: At the end of the day, that sage once again sought to compose his mind in meditative absorption.
He entered a certain vast and well-known cave of the Vindhya mountains.
Furthermore, through samādhi, one remains liberated while living for six nights, and for a long time thereafter;
samādhi is described as the salutation offered to liberation against passion and other afflictions. || 1 ||
Known from before, previously familiar. || 1 ||
Without abandoning that very contemplation of the Self, he who had perceived the higher and lower worlds brought about the welfare [of others] with his mind, remaining equanimous toward the senses.
By whom the supreme essence and the inferior lack of essence have been seen in the world.
Long ago, the collection of my senses was clearly abandoned by me;
now there is no purpose for me in further reflection or expansion of thought. (3)
He states what he then conceived by means of the words beginning with "pūrvam" (formerly), etc. || 3 ||
Having severed the conceptualization of "it exists" and "it does not exist," like a tender creeper,
I remain as the Residue alone, fixed in its form like the peak of an immovable mountain.

The two-fold conceptualization of the visible as "it exists" or "it does not exist"—having taken hold of that which remains, which is the pure consciousness witnessing both—is the remainder [of the process]. With the body, head, and neck held straight, one should remain in a firm posture. (4)
Like one who has risen and yet gone to his setting, like one who has attained well-being and yet arisen;
equal, appearing as the very essence of equanimity, I remain, having attained transparency. (5)
To the vision of the ignorant, he has risen though living, yet he has set as if dead; but to the vision of reality, it is the opposite:
he is the manifestation of the flavor of equanimity, whose nature is pure consciousness of a single essence. (5)
Though awakened, I remain as if in deep sleep; though in deep sleep, I am like one who is awake. Taking hold of the Fourth State (turya), I abide within the body with a motionless stability.

Even while awake, one who is awakened remains as if in deep sleep, not perceiving the web of duality; likewise, even while in deep sleep, one is like the awakened due to the clear experience of one's own true nature. This is the fourth state (turya), the plane free from the gross, subtle, and causal bodies.
Standing like a pillar in solitude, with my inner self established in all things,
I abide free from affliction in the state of equanimity toward the commonality of all beings.

At the end of one's own mind, which has become the further shore, free from mental construction, abiding everywhere, full, characterized by the universal nature of existence, and in supreme equanimity. || 7 ||
Having reflected thus, he remained again in meditation for six days;
then he attained awakening, like a traveler who has slept for a moment.
Then that blessed Vītahavya, a great ascetic who had attained perfection,
lived for a long time thereafter as one liberated while living.
The perfected one maintains a state of meditative absorption even while in the state of emergence.
He did not rejoice in what was favorable, nor did he ever reproach what was unfavorable;
likewise, he experienced neither agitation nor joy.
He did not rejoice through the perception of virtues, nor did he revile through the perception of faults.
Whether walking or standing still, this thought arose in his heart:
"For the diversion of my distracted mind, let there be a discourse with myself. (11)
The discourse, characterized by the investigation to be described hereafter, [proceeds] together with one's own mind in which sublated [notions] still persist. (11)
O Lord of the group of unchanging senses, behold what kind of pervasive blissful happiness has been attained by you, who possess such tranquility of mind! 12.

O Mind, Lord and Master of the group of senses—which is imperishable, being devoid of the exhaustion of its capacity caused by the enjoyment of sense-objects—[grant] that bliss which is called "Ānanda" because it gladdens and delights the entire world;
such a happiness, which is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss, or that beautiful space (sukha-kha) which is like the ether. 12.
Therefore, O best among the fickle, you must constantly maintain this very state of passionlessness and abandon all restlessness.
Even in the future, you must maintain this very same state of passionlessness;
the two words "only" (eva) and "just" (eva) are used for the sake of emphasizing the firmness of the restriction. 13.
O you thieves of the senses! O you of ruined hopes and ruined names!
This self does not belong to you, nor do you belong to the self. 14.
"O you who are hopeless"—this is an individual address to the hopes. "This Self being experienced by me does not exist for you. (14)
As you depart, your share of destruction approaches; your hopes have been rendered fruitless.
You, whose very foundations are fragile, are not capable of overcoming me. 15.

Thus, because of the perpetual absence of a connection with a self, may your own nature remain, while that part subject to destruction passes over to the side of non-existence; [may it] fall upon me—this is the remainder of the sense. || 15 ||
This latent impression of yours that "I am the self" has indeed arisen from the forgetting of reality, like the perception of a snake in a rope that has been seen.
If it is asked, "How did we previously possess the capacity to be overcome by you?", he says, "We... (verse 16), meaning that it was due to the power of the superimposition of identity with the Self.
This notion of self in what is not-self, this notion of reality in what is unreal, has arisen through lack of investigation and perishes through investigation. (17)

"You are one, we are another, and Brahman is something else; agency belongs to another, while the enjoyer is yet another who receives [the fruit]. What fault is there, and for whom, and of what kind? (18)

Thus, he states that even the connection with the faults attributed by you does not exist for anyone who possesses the vision of discernment—beginning with the words "You" (bhavantaḥ). You are the instruments; we are the ego-apprehenders (*abhimantāraḥ*). Brahman is non-dual.
Agency (*kartṛtā*) is the state of being the cause of actions instigated by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The enjoyer is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). [The ego] takes up the mind. (18)
Wood is produced from forests; ropes come from bamboo and hide; the adze has an iron blade; and the carpenter is intent on obtaining his meal. (19)

If this is so, how can the accomplishment of worldly affairs occur? To the question of this, he says "from the forests," and so forth, using the analogy of the house, [explaining that it occurs] by way of the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit (*kākatālīyanyāya*).
Binding a load of wood with bamboo bark; an adze is well known; by the word "and" (*ca*), axes, chisels, and so forth are included; [the material is] iron.
The fruits are the purposes, meaning they are directed toward filling the belly of the world-creator; thus, the carpenter is intent on his own sustenance, not for the sake of building a house. 19.
Thus, just as in this world, through a combination of factors whose constituent parts possess their own inherent capacities,
a firm and excellent house-structure is produced by chance.

And thus, the form of a house being produced from its constituent parts—actions and factors of action—which have distinct purposes, arises solely by way of the "crow-and-palm-fruit" maxim; such is the meaning. || 20 ||

Those who have attained perfection through a chance occurrence, their senses being restrained by their own power—likewise, in this age of strife (kali), whose fickle fortunes can be thwarted, and by whom? 21.
Likewise, here too, within this aggregate of causes and effects (the body),

the organs of knowledge and action— each restricted by their own specific capacities which result in the fruits of seeing, hearing, speaking, grasping, and so forth— are such that these sprouts of activity for various worldly dealings arise merely by chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit" (kākatālīya).
They have become as fickle and unstable as they were before. In that state, who has what impairment or injury? The meaning is: no one has any at all. || 21 ||

Forgetfulness has been forgotten far away; mindfulness has been clearly recollected. What was real has become real, and what was unreal has become unreal; the wounded is healed, and the stable remains stable.
Forgetfulness is ignorance; mindfulness is the knowledge of the Self. He states its fruit: "It is Being" (sad). || 22 ||
In this manner, that tiger among sages, a great ascetic, remained here for many groups of years engaged in such contemplation.
Wherein thought has reached its end for the sake of non-rebirth alone,
and where delusion remains far removed— there he dwelt forever.
It has reached its end, its destruction; there, in that state of self-luminous full bliss. || 24 ||
Relying on the mere consolation of meditation— which is useless since it arises from seeing the flood of phenomena as they truly are— he dwelt always in a state of bliss.

The meaning is that, in order to ward off that lack of confidence— which arises at times from seeing a multitude of diverse objects through delusion regarding the state of reality as it actually exists, and which is thus attached, useless, and futile— one must repeatedly rely on the confidence born of meditative concentration. || 25 ||
When the perception of what is to be abandoned and what is to be acquired, and of attachment and aversion, had ceased,
the mind of the sage Vītahavya transcended both desire and non-desire.

He describes what his mind was like when the remainder of his *prārabdha* karma was exhausted: "In the cessation of the views of rejection and acceptance," even when there occurred an attachment to objects that were either fit for rejection or fit for acceptance. (26)
At the boundary of birth and karma, in the state of disembodied liberation (videha-kevalībhāva),
there arises a desire for the drinking of the nectar of the total renunciation of attachment to worldly existence.

Even while remaining as a mere appearance, having completely abandoned attachment to the cycle of existence such as the body and so forth, he entered—by his own will and with intense longing—into that which remains, the nectar-essence of Brahman; this is the connection with the subsequent verse.
In the reading "vāñchām āpātiśāyinīm" (desire reaching its highest limit) regarding the abandonment, however, the meaning is clear. || 27 ||
At the end, having perceived the web of the world as something from which there is no returning, he quickly entered a golden cave on the Sahya mountain with her alone.
By that desire. || 28 ||
Remaining there in the bound lotus posture, he spoke within himself:
"O passion, go to passionlessness; O hatred, proceed to freedom from hatred. (29)

Cultivating freedom from hatred and maintaining loving-kindness even toward his innate enemies—namely, passion, aversion, and the like—he offers them a salutary instruction as if wishing to depart, and after bowing to them, he addresses them with the words beginning "Passion," etc. (29).
For a very long time, I have sported here with you both;
let there be salutations to your enjoyments, and may I [attain them] for hundreds of millions of births. (30)
Just as a child is cherished in the world by those who fondle him,
so too have I been cherished by you in this supreme and meritorious path to Nirvāṇa.
Salutations again and again to that by whom I have been made to forget;
O Suffering, you were diligently sought by me through my own burning with passion for you. 32.
For the sake of happiness—that is, for the sake of a mere fragment of sensual pleasure—you were heated, meaning you caused me to suffer. || 32 ||
Therefore, this path taught by you is mine; salutations be to you!
By your grace, I have attained this cool state.
Therefore, this path of discernment has been taught to you by you alone, who are like a guru. || 33 ||
Obeisance to you, the reality of suffering, whose very name is "suffering," yet whose nature is the giver of happiness!
May there be well-being for you, O friend, whose life is the essence of this worthless saṃsāra. (34)

O Self, who are the reality of suffering yet the bestower of happiness, he now addresses the body— which is currently helpful for the generation of knowledge— with the words beginning "Kalyāṇam" (Verse 34).
"This is the state of our bodies; we shall go to our own abode.
Alas, how strange is the course of destiny for living beings who have their purposes unfulfilled! (35)

This separation of our two bodies is of the nature of beginningless destiny (*niyati-svabhāva*); the sense is that, according to the maxim that "unions end in separation," this is the course and the uneven way of the purposes and self-interests belonging to living beings (*jantu*). It is for the sake of these pursuits that one abandons even one's most intimate friends and kinsmen.
The meaning is that "the men are running. || 35 ||
Even after undergoing hundreds of births, I shall be separated from this body as well;
for you, my friend, who have been a long-standing kinsman, are being abandoned by me. (36)
He says, "Even with the body," [meaning] that very same thing has presented itself to him as well. || 36 ||
That very destruction which you brought upon yourself through the power of self-knowledge has now resulted in the annihilation of the self once you had attained that realization of the self. (37)
As if lamenting, "This is not my fault; you have rendered me this assistance solely for the sake of your own destruction," he says: "By you alone... (37).
Your body was not broken by another; you yourself have brought this upon yourself, while I was peaceful, by you—miserable and alone—even as you withered away.
This very thing was practiced and performed by you alone. Now she requests silence—[the reading "tṛṣṇīṃ" appears in the printed edition]—with the words "ekākinyā" (being alone). || 38 ||
"O Mother Tṛṣṇā, you must not cause me grief; I am departing.
O Lord Kāma, you must forgive those offenses born of my perversity. (39)
For the sake of your victory, my faults—which arise from offenses such as practicing a detachment contrary to yours—[must be removed]. (39)
"O Mother Tṛṣṇā, you have at last, after a long time, commanded us to go toward the absolute tranquility of the quarters; may this be auspicious for us forever. (40)

"Exclusive tranquility" means absolute cessation. "Command" means instruct. By repeating [the word], he says "after a long time" (*cirāt*) in order to ward off the possibility of becoming attached again to the gateway of craving; that is to say, for a long duration. The ellipsis is "from now on. (40)
This separation, caused by the fault of yoga, is my final salutation;
let there be obeisance to you, the god of virtuous deeds, who were formerly served by me. (41)
May that well-performed merit be for the sake of the God who possesses those characteristics. || 41 ||
Having been delivered from the hells, I was appointed to heaven for him who has taken root in the field of evil deeds and carries the trunk of hell upon his shoulders. (42)

To one who has taken root in a field characterized by evil deeds—that is, the performance of forbidden actions—and who possesses the nature of bearing the massive branches of the aggregates (skandhas) that characterize hell. || 42 ||

Homage to the one who bears the weight of the flowers of the Teaching and whose branches are the suppression of evil deeds—he with whom the various common births were long ago consumed like fuel. (43)
Whose very burden of flowers consists of punishments and tortures. || 43 ||
From this day forward, salutations to Him who is invisible, whose nature is delusion,
whose speech is as sweet as a sounding flute, and who is clothed in leaves.
To that ascetic woman characterized by a cave, whose garments were merely withered leaves, and who possessed sweet-sounding bamboo flutes (kīcaka) that resounded— (44).
Salutations to you, Huātapasvinī, my companion in meditative absorptions;
for me, who am weary on the path of saṃsāra, you are the cause of consolation. (45)
The term "cause of consolation" (*āśvāsakāraṇam*) is a qualifier of the cave (*guhā*), retaining its original gender. || 45 ||
My dear friend was exceedingly affectionate and the remover of all greed;
yet, distressed by every calamity, I fled from her due to my own faults. (46)

You were a most affectionate companion, exceedingly full of love; by bestowing the repose of the perfect Self, you removed all greed and [protected us] from faults that obstruct meditative absorption. 46.
You alone are my supreme friend, resorted to for the sake of destroying my grief,
you who grant a supporting hand within the thickets and pits of calamity.

Now, describing the qualities of the wooden staff (*daṇḍakāṣṭha*), he pays homage to it with the verse beginning "In distress" (*saṃkaṭe*): "In distress"—that is, in dangers such as from hissing snakes and in uneven terrains; likewise, in pits and thickets, it provides support for the hand. (47)
Salutations to you, the staff of wood, the sole friend in old age;
[salutations] likewise to my own skeleton, with its threads of blood and entrails. 48.
Now he offers his entire bodily portion to the Body, saying: "The bones," etc. (48).
O body, depart, taking with you only this much essence;
let there be salutations even to your baths, which consist of such methods of agitating the water.

Taking only this much— the essence, the reality— of that which is such, namely your own unique portion, go to your own constituent elements. O body, whatever disturbances arise from the corruption of water by your own impurities, foul odors, perspiration, and so forth— [let them be].
Salutations also to those ablutions, which consist of various types of offenses against Him, yet serve as the means for achieving purity. || 49 ||
Homage be to worldly conventions; homage be to you, the cycles of transmigration.
These, O sirs, are my innate and ancient friends. (50)

Likewise, salutations be to those worldly activities such as eating, sleeping, anointing, and adorning, and to those cycles of rebirth characterized by running hither and thither to procure their necessary requisites! O vital breaths, my innate friends, today, through this sequence of saluting my friends, these—
You, sirs, have also been made exalted and preeminent; that is to say, you have been honored. || 50 ||
In due course, my vital breaths have been drawn out; may it be well with you, for I am departing.
Together with you, I shall dwell through many diverse wombs.
He describes his former friendship [with them] itself: "By you... (verse 51).
He rested in mountain bowers, wandered through other worlds,
sported within city courtyards, and dwelt upon the mountains.
Within the ancient seats and the fields of the perfected ones.
Whether engaged in the play of worldly affairs or set out upon various paths,
there is nothing within the treasury of the world with which I have not already associated with you.
Nothing was done, nothing taken, nothing departed, nothing given, and nothing supported.
Now, O dear ones, you may go to your own directions; I am going. 54.

Nothing was done, nothing taken, and nothing given by my two hands; I did not walk with my feet, nor did I even rely upon my mind. O sirs, go to your own direction, which is your true nature. I, as Brahman, depart. O dear ones! 54.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall;
all unions end in separation—this is the nature of everything on the path of saṃsāra.

"For what purpose do you dissolve us into the primary elements? Remaining as the very self of the aggregate of causes and effects (the body), why shall we not obtain the collection of objects of enjoyment as before? To this, he says: "All," etc. O all you—Prāṇa and the others! (55)
May this visual light enter the solar orb;
may the forest flowers enter the consciousness of the bliss of fragrance. (56)

Now, he analyzes and demonstrates the respective natures of the sense organs and so forth that are to be attained, beginning with the words "This... and so on. By the term "the consciousness of fragrance and bliss," the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇendriya*), which is the instrument for that [perception], is indicated.
And by the term "forest flowers," the earth, whose essence consists solely of fragrance, is indicated. (56)
Let the vital breath today enter the wind that stirs;
let the powers of hearing sound enter the hollow of space. (57)
May the powers of the essence of taste enter the orb of the moon,
like the ocean without Mount Mandara, or like the day when the sun has departed.
Thus, by the phrase "the lunar orb," it is understood that water is to be grasped; in this sequence, the fifteen digits (kalās) have departed.
According to the direction shown by the sacred scripture (śruti), the meaning is that all [elements] should return to their respective primordial natures (prakṛti).
Thus, when you, who serve as the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), have departed...

"I too, having become the individual soul (*jīva*) whose nature is the reflection of consciousness mirrored in you, shall find rest within the Self that is Brahman— the source of my own reflection, which is indicated by the half-measure of the *praṇava*," he says with the verse beginning "nirmandara" (without Mount Mandara) and so forth. || 58 ||

Like an autumn cloud, like the creation at the end of an aeon, I have arrived here of my own accord; at the conclusion of the syllable Om, I cause my own mental activity to subside within the Self by means of the Self—like a flaming fire whose fuel is consumed, or like a lamp devoid of oil. (59)

It moves by itself and generates itself, thus it is "svaira" (self-moving); its own material cause, having reached dissolution like a cloud at the end of an aeon during the time of universal destruction, [appears] like the creation, like the phenomenal world. "Svamanana" means that there is a complete absence of mental activity, such that there is absolute peace of the mind. || 59 ||
With the entire succession of activities vanished, his state transcends all conditions of the visible world;
his intellect is stilled by following the peace of the *praṇava*.
I stand here, free from the stain of delusion. || 60 ||

One whose intellect (*dhī*) has become tranquil by following the peace within the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*) through the long-uttered *praṇava*, and has ceased [from worldly activity] by attaining the state of being solely of the nature of Brahman; and who, for that very reason, is free from the stains of the remaining fragments of ignorance obstructed by [past] *prārabdha* karma. 60.

Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Rejection of the Group of Senses," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Dispelling of the Group of Senses," in the section on Tranquility within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus he reflected within himself, his thoughts stilled and his desires extinguished.
Uttering the Praṇava slowly and clearly, he has attained the [spiritual] stage.
The sequence by which one who is free from worldly desire attains the state of bodilessness (videhatā),
having taken hold of that which culminates in the *praṇava*, is here described.

Thus, by means of the sequence to be described, pronouncing the *praṇava*— the *tāra*— first with a very loud voice and then slowly through prolonged resonance, having attained the sixth and seventh stages (*bhūmi*) through the process of calming the desire for mental objects (*manana*), he realized and attained Brahman within his own heart.

The ascetic, recollecting the *praṇava* through the division of its syllables beginning with the vowel *mā*, [perceives] his own pure and immutable nature by means of the negation of superimposition and denial. (2)
The ascetic renunciant Vītahavya [says]: "This entire universe is this syllable Om;

its further explanation is that all that has been, is, and will be is indeed the syllable Om, and whatever else transcends the three periods of time—that too is indeed the syllable Om," according to the sequence shown in the Māṇḍūkya Śruti.

While recollecting the *praṇava*— which is conceptualized through the vowels known as *a*, *u*, and *m*, along with the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*), and divided into quarters characterized as gross, subtle, unmanifest, and the fourth (*turya*)— one should [merge it] into the fourth [quarter], which transcends the quarters characterized as Virāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, and the Unmanifest, as described in the *Pañcīkaraṇa*.

In accordance with the direction stated in such scriptural passages as "First, [the Self] has the waking state as its locus and is conscious of external objects," one should, through superimposition (*adhyāropa*), [realize the Self], and then, through negation (*apavāda*) such as "neither conscious of the internal, nor conscious of the external, nor conscious of both, neither consciousness, nor unconsciousness,
nor a mass of consciousness," [realize the Self] even in its forms of gross, subtle, and causal.

Having abandoned all internal and external parts, and having perceived one's own pure and immutable nature—which is the cessation of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), auspicious, peaceful, and non-dual—they consider that to be the Fourth (*turīya*). As it is stated in the Śruti: "That is the Self; that is to be known. Abiding in that Fourth Self, [one reaches] up to the limit of the Praṇava.
The connection with the sixth verse is as follows: "He abandoned the web of the senses and the subtle elements (tanmātra) along with its long-extended thread.

[Verse 6] "Having abandoned all internal and external portions—both gross and even more subtle—that arise within the three worlds and are fashioned by the imagination and non-imagination [of the mind]. [Verse 7]
Standing with an unshaken appearance within himself like a wish-fulfilling gem,
he was like the full moon or like Mount Mandara at rest.
He was like one confined upon the potter’s wheel due to whirling;
he was like the ocean, full, still, vast, and pure.
When his agitation was stilled by the cessation of wandering, he became like the wheel in a potter’s house when its spinning has stopped—possessing an unperturbed appearance.
His mass of light and darkness was extinguished; it was like the autumnal sky, infinite, clear of smoke, clouds, and dust, and devoid of sun, moon, and stars.
Because the simultaneous subsiding of light and darkness is not established, this is an *abhūtopamā* (an impossible simile).
Together with a long, resonant thread of sound culminating in the syllable *praṇava*,
he cast off the web of the senses and their subtle elements, just as the wind sheds fragrance.

The "end" (paryanta) of the *praṇava* is its foremost part; by means of that characteristic, which is a long-sounding thread (*dīrghaniḥsvanatantu*), [the text] says "he abandons," and so forth—all this is an elaboration of the very statement "having abandoned even all things other than the gross and the subtle. || 7 ||
Then he abandoned that mere darkness which had appeared like a flash in the sky,
just as a wise man casts off a trace of anger as it arises with a flickering form.
Then, by means of the witness-consciousness, that which is pure darkness arose with a throbbing form.
Then, having reflected for half a moment upon that manifested splendor, he abandoned it;
and at that time, there was neither darkness nor light.
Having reached that state, he destroyed with his mind that mind— which was as fragile as a blade of grass—
even as it quivered slightly, within half a moment.
Having attained that state which is devoid of both darkness and light, he destroyed—that is, cut away—the "grass" of the mind, which is the cause of that conceptualization. || 10 ||
Then, O dear one, consciousness becomes established in its own state, having attained the nature of manifestation, pure and equal in character to the cognition of a newborn infant. (11)

The word "aṅga" is used as a term of address. Having relied upon the clarity of manifestation—which is like a lamp in a windless place—he abandoned even that mental construction (kalana) in a period of time less than half of a half-moment, before its further growth.
This is the meaning: he alone [attained] the state of consciousness having abandoned the state of being an object of consciousness (cetyadaśā). || 11 ||
In a period of time equal to half of half a moment, the Lord abandoned the state of being an object of consciousness for his own consciousness,
just as the wind abandons its power of vibration.
Then, having reached the state of *paśyantī*, which consists of pure existence, he took hold of the state of deep sleep and remained as immovable as a mountain. || 13 ||

In this manner, having reached the state of *paśyantī*—which is characterized by the fact that only the witness (*sākṣin*) remains—one should take hold of the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*), which is characterized by abiding in that [witness], the causal reality consisting of pure existence alone that remains after the sublation of ether and the other elements. This is the meaning. || 13 ||
Then, having remained for a short while in the state of deep sleep again and again,
the Lord attained stability within that deep sleep and reached the form of the Fourth State (turya).

These very two [states] exist on the sixth and seventh stages while still embodied. Thereafter, when there is complete identity with the Witness, because of the manifestation of unsurpassed, indivisible bliss, he shows the attainment of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*) through the absolute cessation of appearance along with the remainder of *prārabdha* karma, by the words "the form of the Fourth" (*turyarūpam*). || 14 ||
Though joyless, he was full of joy; there he was both being and non-being.
He was neither something nor nothing, like the light of that [state] which is like darkness.
He provides the answer to the fourth question, "What happened then?", with the words beginning "devoid of bliss" (nirānanda).
Although devoid of the bliss derived from sense objects, he is blissful by his very nature. Although devoid of existence apart from himself, he is of the nature of Being (sadrūpa).
This same logic should be applied to everything. Just as at night, for the eyes, darkness itself is the light, so it is here. || 15 ||
That which is said to be "not this, not this"— neither consisting of consciousness nor consisting of consciousness— from that indeed did He arise, who is beyond even the reach of words.
Due to the absence of anything to be perceived (cetya), it is composed of consciousness; by its own nature, consciousness itself is composed of consciousness.
Then he attained that state which is perfectly even, expansive, supremely purifying,
situated within all states of being, yet devoid of everything.
That which is the Void for the proponents of emptiness, O best of those who know Brahman;
that which is mere consciousness for the knowers of consciousness—that stainless state. || 18 ||

He states with the words beginning "That which... (yad... that even though it has been conceptualized by all disputants through various mental constructions as their own respective tenets, it is indeed that very same [reality]. || 18 ||

To those with the Sāṃkhya view, he is the Puruṣa; to the proponents of Yoga, he is Īśvara; to those who mark him with the crescent moon, he is Śiva; and to those who maintain that Time alone is the sole principle, he is Kāla.
This refers to the Śaivas who bear the mark of the crescent moon; even if the reading is "those established in the doctrine of Śiva," the meaning remains the same. || 19 ||

For those who know the self, there is the self; for those whose view of the self is such [as non-existent], there is selflessness; and for the Madhyamikas, whose minds are perfectly equanimous toward all things, there is the Middle Way. 20.

That is the self for those who know the self. The genitive case in the phrase "na loka" is Vedic and functions as an object of negation. Nairātmya (selflessness) is the continuum of momentary consciousness; for that [continuum], which appears to be permanent, does not exist at all—this is selflessness. This refers to such selves held by the Sautrāntikas and Vaibhāṣikas. As for the Mādhyamikas:

For those who maintain that reality is merely the void situated between consciousness and the unconscious, and for those whose minds are perfectly equanimous and liberated while living, everything is entirely full. Beginning with the proponents of the Void (Śūnyavādins) and concluding with all other proponents of philosophical views, the doctrine of the finite and the infinite constitutes the ultimate limit between these two.
However, it should be understood that this is intended to illustrate that for other intermediate views, there arises a mixture of both [extremes] through a variety of gradations. || 20 ||
That which is the established conclusion of all scriptures, that which conforms to the heart of all,
that which is everything, omnipresent, and universal— he remains as that very reality, both being and non-being.
The reality of everything is universal; such is that which exists, meaning that it remains as that very reality after having become it. || 21 ||
That which is the unsurpassed, motionless radiance even of all luminous energies,
which consists solely of one's own direct experience— that reality alone remains as both existence and non-existence.

That which is unsurpassed, motionless, and absolutely inactive—even more so than space, because in space there still exists the activity of birth and so forth; therefore, it is "immovable" (kūṭastha). The phrase "even of lights" implies "by way of being their illuminator. That which is established solely through its own self-experience—that well-known Reality—is "this," as explained previously. || 22 ||
