That which is both one and many, both with taint and without taint,
that which is both all and not-all— that reality, He remains as that very being.
Then he remained established in that stainless state— which is unborn, undecaying, beginningless, manifold yet one, both with parts and without parts— and whose nature is like the sky.
Furthermore, the Lord, whose state is stainless, [attains it] in an instant. || 24 ||
He, known as Vītahavya, having become established in a state of purity even beyond the nature of the sky through the aforementioned sequence of liberated vision,
remained as the unborn, undecaying, beginningless, one, stainless, and partless (niṣkala) state; however, by means of bound vision,
he remained in an instant as the Lord (Īśvara), becoming manifold and with parts (sakala) through the distinctions of his own effects— this is the meaning.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Liberation of Vītahavya," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation of the Holy Vasiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage. 87.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Liberation of Vītahavya," in the Section on Quiescence within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reached the very limit of worldly existence, he has arrived at the further shore of the ocean of suffering.
Thus the sage Vītahavya became tranquil through the state of non-recurrence of mental activity. || 1 ||

When Vītahavya was liberated, the dissolution of his vital breaths within the heart is described—the withering of the body and the absorption of the constituent parts (kalās) into their cause. || 1 ||
In this manner, when there is no further mental reflection—that is, when there is the absolute dissolution of the mind—[the state of liberation is attained]. || 1 ||
For when he had thus become tranquil and attained supreme peace,
he was like a drop of water in the ocean, merged into his own transforming state.
When [the intellect] is subject to transformation and established [as such], or there is a division [of the compound] as "non-transforming" (apariṇāminī) || 2 ||
Remaining thus motionless, that body fell into a state of withering;
having reached an inner state of saplessness, like a lotus at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
At the end of Mārgaśīrṣa, in the winter season, it is like a lotus.
Leaving their nest within the tree of his body, his vital breaths flew forth like birds released from a mechanical trap and entered the hollow of his heart.

He speaks of the withdrawal of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), which pervade the entire body, into the heart: "Of that [person]... It should not be explained that his vital breaths depart from the nest of the heart located within the tree of the body and go outside; rather, "his vital breaths do not depart; they are merged right here, and he becomes Brahman itself."

This is because it would contradict such scriptural passages as "He attains Brahman," and because, upon departing through the destruction of all karmic impressions (*vāsanā*), there would be no seed or purpose for that departure. "Acting like birds" (*vihagāyantaḥ*) means behaving like birds; the suffix *kyac* is applied here according to the rule beginning with *lohita-*.
They are like stones released from machines. || 4 ||
All beings are entirely established in the elements alone;
yet his body, a machine of flesh and bone, dwelt upon the surface of the forest and the earth.

Thus, as the scripture states— "At the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'"— beginning with "just as a weaver takes a measure of cloth," and according to the principle stated by Bādarāyaṇa: "He goes enveloped, because of the subsequent attainment [of a new body] and because of the questions and their explanations."

He describes the entry of those elemental constituents (*bhūtamātrā*) into their causes, based on the understanding that the *ap*— denoted by the word *ap* and consisting of soma, clarified butter, milk, and so forth— which were produced by the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra* in previous births, enter into the earth through the sequence beginning with ether, and subsequently attain the form of a person by entering into rice, barley, man, and woman.
"—in the elements alone. This means together with all sixteen digits (kalās), beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *nāman*.
As for that grosser portion born from the impurities of the father and mother, he states that it resides in those very [elements]—beginning with "flesh" (verse 5).
The elements of consciousness are established in the ocean of consciousness, and these elements abide within the [gross] elements;
when the sage has attained tranquility, everything abides in its own true nature.

The individual consciousness (jīvacit), reflected in the *liṅga* which serves as its own mirror, is as if entered into the ocean of consciousness (*cidarṇava*). The constituents are skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen; [these] reside within their own constituent substrates (*dhātuṣu svopādāneṣu*).
This rest of Vītahavya, rich with hundreds of reflections, has been told to you, O Rāma; discern it through your wisdom.
He summarizes: "This," etc. (7).
Having thus perceived the reality through this beautiful and kindled self-investigation, perceive its essence and abide in it; arise, O Rāghava! (8)
“With the lovely” (cārvyā) means with the charming one; the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *voto guṇavacanāt*. || 8 ||
O Rāma, all this that has been described by me to you,
as well as what I am describing today, or what I shall describe in the future— [all this is for your benefit].

Now, the Blessed Vasiṣṭha, out of his great compassion, having repeatedly examined through worldliness, scripture, and the Vedas— both by positive and negative concomitance— the investigations made in every way and many times by long-lived and all-seeing sages such as ourselves, regarding this work which has been spoken, is being spoken, and will be spoken, [proceeds as follows].
And regarding the vision [of Brahman], it has been determined that by relying on the realization of the unity of the Self, the attainment of the firm foundation of knowledge itself is the fruit;
there is nothing further to be accomplished by persons beyond this. To strengthen this conviction, he says:
"That which is this... and so forth. (9)
"By me, who perceives the three times, who lives eternally and for a long duration, all that has been personally investigated and seen. (10)
Therefore, O Mahāmati, relying upon this stainless vision, attain supreme knowledge; for through knowledge, liberation is indeed obtained. (11)
Through knowledge one attains freedom from suffering; through knowledge comes the destruction of ignorance.
O Rāma, supreme perfection arises from knowledge alone, and not from anything else in reality.
Having completely cut away all desires on every side by means of knowledge,
the lord of sages Vītahavya has shattered the entire mountain of his mind.

The remainder of the sentence is: he became one by whom the mountain of the mind was cut down, shattered, and left without any residue—not even a trace remaining in the form of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*). || 13 ||
That consciousness, whose nature is Vītahavya, is the world born of volition;
it has experienced this very visible world as that world itself.

But surely it has been stated that Vītahavya experienced the world as consisting of mental constructs (*saṃkalpamaya*) within his own heart, and that its quality (*guṇatva*) was likewise experienced there; how then, having entered the sun situated within that world, did he effect the extraction of his own body—which is established upon this earth—from within that world by means of the Tryaṃbaka-Piṅgala gate? For this is not possible.

Observing Rāma’s suspicion that the digging for a treasure while awake was seen through dream-shovels, [the author] says "Vītahavya" etc., indicating that this consciousness in the form of Vītahavya— [according to another reading, *saṃtānasaṃvit*]— is [established] in Brahman, which is characterized by one's own heart.
The meaning is that she experienced this visible world as being common to herself and others like us—a world born of her own volition—and not as something unprecedented. || 14 ||
Vītahavya [realized] that the mind alone is everything, just as the sense-possessor [realizes] "I am the mind";
this entire world is the mind—then who could perceive difference or non-difference? || 15 ||
To show that this very world is nothing other than this [mind], he says: "Vītahavya. Vītahavya, who was visible to the senses of Indra and others—such as our own eyes and so forth—is merely our mind.
For it is our own mind alone that appears as "I" and as "you. This entire universe is indeed the mind; therein, what room is there for difference or non-difference?
The meaning is that sons do not differ according to the difference among barren women; indeed, they do not differ at all. || 15 ||
Having realized the ultimate truth, with faults such as passion extinguished,
free from all impurities, transformations, limiting adjuncts, and attachments,
the discerning one has long followed his own inner nature.
Having attained the pure and infinite state, his sorrow has been stilled. || 16 ||
Having thus consoled Rāma, he speaks of the subject at hand with the words "adhigata" (attained):

that discriminating person who is free from all impurities such as ignorance, desire, and karma; from the modifications of the senses caused by them; from the limiting adjuncts of the three bodies caused by them; and from the attachment to pleasant things and so forth caused by them.
Vītahavya, for a long time, through the practice of means for purifying the mind—
namely, the stages of hearing, reflection, meditative absorption, direct realization, and samādhi—
and by following that which was experienced within his own heart, brought [the Truth] face to face.
The meaning is that he attained the state of liberation, which is his own innate nature, stainless and infinite. || 16 ||

Thus ends the eighty-eighth canto, titled "The Resting of Vītahavya," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Chapter on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Resting of Vītahavya," in the *Upaśamaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having brought oneself to the state of one who has known what is to be known, like Vītahavya—
O Raghava, remain forever free from passion, fear, and agitation.

In this context, it is proclaimed that for those who are free from desire, tranquility, and delusion, there is the attainment of powers such as moving through the sky, as well as invulnerability to wild beasts and other dangers for their respective bodies.
"Ātmānam" means oneself. According to the statement of Kātyāyana, "In the case of the roots *nī*, *vah*, and *hṛ*, there is a double object," it possesses two objects. || 1 ||
Vītahavya dwelt at his ease for thirty thousand years, free from sorrow; in that same manner, O Rāghava, do you dwell.
And other sages of great intelligence who have known that which is to be known, O King, dwell in their own kingdoms; even so, O high-minded one, do you dwell.
The self is never grasped through the sequences of pleasure and pain;
though it is omnipresent, O mighty-armed one, why do you grieve in vain? (4)
Many who have realized the self dwell here upon this earth;
none fall under the power of suffering, my dear, as you have done.
"O dear one" (aṅga) is a term of address. || 5 ||
Be established in yourself, noble one; be equanimous and be happy.
You are all-pervading and you are the Self itself; for you, there is no further rebirth.
Noble within, he is of the nature of total renunciation. || 6 ||
Those like you, who are liberated while living, do not fall under the sway of the transformations of joy and resentment,
just as lions do not come under the control of peacocks.
Of the crested ones, that is, the peacocks. || 7 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"In this very context, this doubt has arisen within me;
like the autumn season [clearing] a cloud, may you dispel it for me."
O best among the knowers of the Self, why are powers such as traveling through the sky not seen here in the bodies of those liberated while living? (9)

The intention [of the author] is that, as stated by the phrase "of bodies," when *prārabdha* karma remains—as in the case of Vītahavya’s enjoyment of the status of a *vidyādhara* and so forth—mental perfections (*mānasī siddhi*) certainly do occur. || 9 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O scion of Raghu, these powers such as traveling through the sky and so forth are indeed the innate capacities of things that have been established by authoritative means.

Established by means of valid cognition and perceived through such measures, these [powers] are inherent to the divine classes of beings, just as the upward flaming of fire is its very nature. || 10 ||
O Rāma, that manifold web of actions which is seen and again experienced is merely the nature of objective things; it is not the view of those who know the Self.
The "network of activities," such as moving through the sky, is the inherent nature of things; that is, it is the very nature of the bodies born from various wombs.
The point is that even mosquitoes and other such creatures are observed to possess the power of moving through the air. This is the desired position. || 11 ||

O Rāghava, even one who knows the Self and is liberated may attain such powers as traveling through the sky and so forth, by virtue of the potency of substances, rituals, actions, time, and mantras— [it is understood from the commentary that the reading "mantrakriyā" is appropriate]. 12.
In that case, one might ask how humans attain the ability to travel through the sky and so forth through the perfection of yoga; to this he replies:

"one who does not know the Self. Through the power of substances such as gems and herbs, the power of mantras, the power of actions such as the practice of yoga, and the power of the time of their maturation, one attains it only occasionally.

Alternatively, the mention of "time" is for the sake of providing an illustration: just as an ant, through the power of the time at the end of summer, attains the ability to fly through the sky by growing wings, so it is in this case. || 12 ||
This is not the domain of one who knows the Self; for the knower of the Self is himself possessed of the Self.
Satisfied by the Self within the Self, he does not pursue ignorance.
This [attainment of] movement through the sky and so forth is not an object fit for desire because of its insignificance. "Possessing a self" means one who has realized the Self.
Ignorance (avidyā) and that which arises from ignorance (āvidyaka) are of insignificant fruit. || 13 ||
Whatever worldly phenomena there may be, they know them to consist of ignorance;
how indeed could one who knows the Self and has abandoned ignorance immerse himself in them? (14)

Those who, by means of reasoning, establish even ignorance as being of the nature of happiness, are indeed composed of ignorance; they are not knowers of the Self, nor do they follow that [true] sequence. (15)
Through reasoning and thousands of labors such as the practice of yoga, there are likewise successions of that same kind. 15.
Whether one knows the truth or does not know the truth, for him who exerts effort in due order through time, substance, and action, the attainment of upward movement and other states is accomplished.
In that case, does those who know reality lack the power to accomplish it? No; he says: "The knower of reality.

For one who exerts effort over time through long-term practice by means of substances and rituals according to the sequence prescribed in the scriptures, for him the attainment of *ūrdhvatva*—the upward movement into the sky—and other such *siddhis* are achieved. || 16 ||
One who possesses the Self here has transcended everything and is free from desire;
for being content in the Self alone, he neither acts nor strives.
He has no interest in traveling through the sky, nor in supernatural powers, nor in enjoyments;
neither in majesty, nor in honors, nor in hope, death, or life. (18)
By power—meaning by the capacity for sovereignty, restraint, and favor—and by conceits, which are the pride of proclaiming one's own excellence. || 18 ||
Ever-contented, with a tranquil self, free from passion and devoid of latent impressions, the knower of That, whose form is like space, abides in the Self. (19)
Free from attachment, he is satisfied by both suffering and happiness that arrive unexpectedly,
and likewise by life and death.
It is satisfied; it does not abandon its natural satisfaction through the life-force of living. 20.
Like the ocean with the rivers that enter it, he remains— honoring his own self— whether by means of even or uneven things, as they arrive in due course.

With that which is even and favorable, as well as uneven and adverse—that is, with the objects of experience obtained through the sequence of *prārabdha* karma; in the case of the ocean, with objects such as floods, grass, and wood—he worships, adoring [the Lord] with the flowers of mental states (*vṛtti*) in their unbroken form. || 21 ||
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any at all through inaction;
nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object of interest.
Dependence on the meaning is subsistence upon the purpose. || 22 ||
But he who, even though his self is unrefined, desires the networks of supernatural powers, accomplishes them in due order by means of the substances used for attaining those powers. (23)
One whose self is uncultivated, even though devoid of even a trace of knowledge of the Self. || 23 ||
"This is established by reasoning alone; such is the sequence of necessity, which cannot be rendered futile even by the foremost of gods, such as the Three-eyed One. (24)

It is the established order of necessity (niyati) well-known from various scriptures that the power of traveling through the sky and so forth is accomplished precisely through the application of gems, mantras, and other means; this sequence cannot be rendered void even by the Three-Eyed Lord (Tryakṣa) and others who act as the agents of that necessity.
This is the inherent nature (svabhāva) of things, for their self-established reality arises from itself and not from anything else.
He does not abandon his fixed nature, just as the moon does not abandon its coolness. || 25 ||

As for the spontaneous attainment of powers such as moving through the air (*khecaratva*) by gods and others, this is the very nature of things; therefore, he says "it does not indeed leave [them]" to indicate that it persists from birth until the end of life. || 25 ||
Neither the Omniscient One, nor the All-Knowing One, nor Mādhava, nor even Hara— indeed, no one at all is able to act otherwise than according to destiny.
O Rāma, these powers—such as traveling through the sky and so forth—are born from the inherent nature of substances, time, ritual actions, and the application of mantras. (27)
Just as poisons kill, honey intoxicates, and fermented liquids and *madana* fruits cause vomiting; || 28 ||

Just like the potency of substances such as anti-venomous herbs, the potency of gems, mantras, and so forth is also capable of its respective effects; he states this with the word "yathā" (just as). Just as the potencies of anti-venomous substances, gems, mantras, and so forth destroy poisons; just as honey intoxicates; and just as fermented acids [act].
Honey, honey-wax, or madana fruits, when consumed, cause vomiting and induce emesis.

(28) Likewise, substances, time, and the sequence of actions, when applied according to reason and combined with proper methods, necessarily and swiftly accomplish the intended application by the power of their inherent nature. (29)
[The reading according to the commentary. || 29 ||
They are called "practices" (prayoga) because they are employed; they invariably and necessarily accomplish the various attainments (siddhi).
They are "applied" (prayukta), meaning they have been set in motion by persons skilled in yoga and other such arts. || 29 ||
O Rāghava, for one who has transcended this [world] and abandoned ignorance, there is neither agency nor non-agency regarding self-knowledge, O sinless one. (30)

The meaning is this: for one who has transcended the sphere of ignorance—characterized by substance, time, action, and sequence—and who has thus abandoned ignorance and sublated nescience through self-knowledge, there exists here, within the web of supernatural powers such as traveling through the sky, neither agency nor causality, nor non-agency nor contradiction. || 30 ||
The logical applications of substance, place, action, and time do not contribute in any way toward the attainment of the state of the supreme self for those who possess right knowledge. (31)

Just as self-knowledge is of no use for the fruit of ritual action, so too substances, place, action, and so forth are of no use for the fruit of knowledge; thus he says: "Substance," etc. [This refers to] the true knowledge of reality arising from the consciousness of the virtuous. || 31 ||
He who possesses some desire is fully capable of accomplishing success;
however, for the self-knowing one who is complete, no desire arises anywhere.
O sinless one, since the attainment of the Self arises only when the entire web of desires has been stilled, how and why could a desire, which is its opposite, ever arise?
To the question "Why is it not possible there?", he says: "All," etc. (verse 33).
In whatever way a person's desire arises, he strives accordingly;
and at the proper time, he attains that result, whether he be wise or even a fool.
With the intention that even one who knows reality may attain the supernatural powers (siddhis) if he exerts himself out of curiosity despite being free from desire, he says: "Just as... (verse 34).
Vītahavya strove for nothing at all out of a desire for knowledge;
however, one who desires knowledge strives quickly, just as that [fire] was raised up in the forest.

To the question, "In that case, why did the perfections (*siddhis*) not arise for Vītahavya?", he says: "By Vītahavya... [the answer is] "no effort was made out of a desire for perfections. To the question, "Why was that? he says: "Because of a desire for knowledge (*jñānecchayā*). The meaning is that the desire for knowledge obstructs other desires. Indeed, he did make an effort precisely through the desire for knowledge, just as he did in the forest.
The meaning is that it has already been described above how he has arisen for the practice of knowledge and is thus intent upon it. || 35 ||

Thus, the various accomplishments (siddhis), born of time, ritual action, substances, application, and intrinsic nature, are achieved according to one's desire, having been acquired through the gradual stages.
O Rāma, those successions of fruits called "accomplishments" (siddhi) which have been attained by someone, they have been acquired by him from the tree of his own exertion.

In the section on the conduct of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu-vyavahāra-prakaraṇa*), it has been explained in detail that for one whose effort does not cease regarding the domain of accomplishments (*siddhi*) or the domain of knowledge (*jñāna*), there is necessarily a fruitfulness [of that effort]. Thus he says: "Those which...
The word *yat* (which) should be understood as repeated [to form *yāḥ... yāḥ*]. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "they are seen to have been attained. (37)
For the great ones who are eternally contented, who possess that knowledge, whose selves are purified,
and who have set out upon their true quest, supernatural powers do not provide any further assistance.
"Secked" (īhitam) means everything desired, that is to say, one's own happiness which is the object of supreme love. || 38 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahmin, I have this doubt: why was that body of Vītahavya not devoured by carnivorous beasts, and why did it not decay upon the surface of the earth? (39)
"Moistened" means not shattered due to the soaking of mud and the like; such is the meaning. || 39 ||
O Lord, tell me exactly how it was that Vītahavya, having gone to the forest at that very time, quickly attained the state of liberation while in the body (videhamukti). (40)
"At that very time, when entering the earth"—thus, speak correctly the answer to these two questions. 40.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O virtuous one, that consciousness which is entwined by the foul thread of latent desires becomes here a partaker in the burning of the states of pleasure and pain. (41)
Therein, he establishes the introductory context to state the answer to the first question, beginning with the word "yā":

she who is tightly wound—that is, firmly enveloped—by the thread consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the ignorant consciousness (*ajña-saṃvit*) and the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*), which is defiled by the impurities of passion (*rāga*) and so forth; she alone...
The meaning is that she experiences the state of burning characterized by the conditions of pleasure and pain resulting from the cutting and piercing of her body. || 41 ||
But that body, consisting of pure consciousness alone and freed from latent impressions (vāsanā), remains;
for there are none here capable of cutting it asunder.
That body of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), because it is sublated, remains as consisting solely of the pure consciousness that is the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna).

No carnivorous being or anyone else is capable of cutting that pure consciousness, for such is the meaning of the Lord’s statement: "This is not to be cut, not to be burned, not to be moistened, and indeed not to be dried up. || 42 ||
Listen, O mighty-armed one, by what reasoning a yogi is not overcome even by the delusions of bodily destruction and the like, despite many hundreds of years. (43)
He promises to speak of another birth, saying: "Listen. (43)
Whenever and upon whichever object the mind falls, it immediately becomes absorbed in that very thing at that very moment. (44)
For the mind undergoes transformation upon seeing an enemy;
likewise, it is experienced by oneself that it attains a state of friendliness upon seeing a friend. (45)

The word "tathā hi" (for instance) provides the logical connection. A mind by which an enemy has been seen undergoes a transformation such as hatred and the like, as if it were a reflection of that enemy's hatred. On the other hand, a mind by which a friend has been seen attains a state of being truly heart-pleasing, as if it were a reflection of that person's affection.
This is the meaning: that this matter is directly perceived by everyone for themselves; such is the sense. || 45 ||
But when one encounters a traveler, a tree, or a mountain that are devoid of passion and hatred, it is experienced by oneself that one becomes likewise free from passion and hatred. (46)
For this very reason, he says "rāga... [and so forth], meaning that when one person is free from passion and hatred, these are not seen in another either;

the mind becomes free from attachment and aversion toward objects such as a traveler, a neutral person, a tree, or a mountain. It takes up greed for what is delicious and becomes indifferent toward what is unpalatable.
It is experienced firsthand that [the tongue] itself becomes averse to what is pungent. || 47 ||

With the intention that, in this way, even in insentient things such as food and the like, pleasure, displeasure, and indifference are well-known in the mind only through the reflection of qualities, defects, and the absence of both residing in them, he says: "In the delicious... [and so on]. Regarding "durbhojye" (in bad food): it means "nīrase" (in the tasteless), and "niḥspṛham" (indifferent) means the absence of desire.
In an *avyayībhāva* compound, there is shortening even when the object (*artha*) is absent; this is also an indication that it applies to the absence of enmity (*vaira*) as well. || 47 ||
Whenever and wherever the predatory mind falls upon the body of an ascetic, which is enriched by the play of equanimous consciousness, it immediately attains a state of equality.

Let it be so; what follows from this in the present context? To that he says: "sama... When the mind of carnivorous, flesh-eating creatures falls upon the body of a yogi—which is most fully endowed with the play of consciousness (*saṃvidvilāsa*) that is equanimous, being devoid of the inequality of attachment and aversion—then, at that very moment, immediately.

It attains a state of equality, as if through the reflection of the yogin’s consciousness in its state of equality; therefore, there is no possibility of injury caused by it—this is the meaning. And thus, having introduced the foundation of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), Patañjali stated:
"In his presence, hostility is abandoned. (Yoga Sūtra 2.35) || 48 ||

Because he is liberated from all attachments, he does not engage in cutting [trees] and such activities, just as a traveler on the road does not engage in the work of villagers in a village for no purpose. (49)

Even a person of violent nature, through association with an ascetic who is equanimous and possesses equal vision—being liberated from hatred and other such passions—does not engage in the cutting or harming of anyone. Just as a traveler does not engage in village activities, such as cutting the creepers in the forest near a village, so it is in this case. || 49 ||
Having gone near the body of the yogin, it indeed attains a predatory nature;
whatever occurs there quickly, it assumes that very form—of this there is no doubt. (50)

Having gone elsewhere away from the vicinity of the yogi’s body, whatever class of living being exists there—endowed with its respective defects and so forth—it attains a corresponding state of ferocity. || 50 ||
Thus, by predatory beasts— tigers, lions, insects, and reptiles—
the body of Vītahavya, which rested upon the surface of the earth, was not torn apart.
Thus, for these two reasons. || 51 ||
Consciousness exists everywhere, even in wood, clods of earth, stones, and so forth; it abides in the form of the universal property of existence (sattāsāmānya), like that of a mute or a child.
He provides the answer to the question, "How is it that [the body] is not moist on the ground? with the words beginning "everywhere" (sarvatra), etc. || 52 ||
Only the flickering, trembling [consciousness] is perceived, as if reflected in the waters of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), like reflections in water. 53.
If that is so, how is it perceived within the *puryaṣṭakas* (the eightfold subtle body)? To this he replies:

"As if floating" (*poplūyamānā*). It is seen as if floating, flickering, astonishing through thousands of transformations, and appearing both subtle and limited—this being understood to refer to those whose minds are not concentrated (*asamāhitacittaiḥ*). || 53 ||
By that uniform perception of earth, water, air, and fire,
O Rāghava, the body of Vītahavya was brought to a state free from transformation.

By that subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) of Vītahavya—brought to a state of non-differentiation through the realization of reality and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which possess an equal nature—his physical form was led to the state of Brahman, which is changeless and devoid of all modification; therefore, the meaning is that it did not undergo any transformation. || 54 ||
Listen further to me, O Rāma: vibration is the cause of destruction;
and that modification, whether arising from the mind or born of wind, exists for the maintenance of the world.

Listen to yet another argument. He states that very point with the words beginning "spanda" (vibration), etc.; the meaning is that [this vibration] is well-known in the maintenance of the world, that is, in worldly transaction. || 55 ||
The vitalizing force of the vital breaths is their vibration; when that ceases, they become like stones.
Since he remained fixed through meditative concentration (dhāraṇā), his body was not destroyed.
For that reason, those vital breaths remain in the body as firm as stones, having become solidified. || 56 ||
For one in whom neither mental nor physical vibration exists, whether external or internal, both Prakṛti and its destruction remain far away.

The external [body] consists of the hands, feet, and so forth; the internal [body] consists of the vital breaths and so forth; and within that body, there is nature (prakṛti), which includes growth and the like, as well as decay, which includes wasting away and the like. || 57 ||
O best among the knowers of reality, when the vibration has become stilled both internally and externally,
the elements never abandon their established state within the body.
The elements (dhātu) are the skin and so forth; "establishment" (saṃsthiti) refers to the prior state. 58.
When the movement of the body, which consists of the wind of the mind, has thus become completely stilled, the bodily constituents,
their nature being now firmly stabilized, attain the immovability of Mount Meru.
*Mairavam* means pertaining to Meru; that is to say, equal to Meru. || 59 ||
And so it is observed in the world that when vibration ceases, there is a firm stability, like the immovability of the limbs of corpses among the steadfast. (60)

"Spanda" means that which vibrates, namely the vital breath (prāṇa); [the term refers to] its cessation. Furthermore, "acopatā" means the state of being motionless or unshakable in the limbs of a corpse.
The root *cup* signifies slow movement; the suffix *ghañ* is used here to denote the abstract state (*bhāve*). || 60 ||
Thus, for thousands of years, the bodies of yogins in this world neither decay nor disintegrate, like clouds submerged in water.
Thus, by this reasoning: "They do not become moist like clouds, nor are they split apart like stones submerged in the earth"—this is the construction [of the verse] in reverse order. || 61 ||
At that very moment, listen, did not Vītahavya—knowing the reality, the best among those who have known what is to be known—attain peace by casting off his body? (62)

Having restated the final question, he provides the answer with the words beginning "tadaiva" (at that very time): for those who possess the means by which the Brahman to be known has been known, or for those who have fully realized the Self. || 62 ||
For those who have understood what is to be known, who are free from passion, and possess great intelligence—all of them, having severed the knots, remain independent while abiding in the body. (63)
They are independent, not subject to others; for the scripture says: "Neither the gods nor the power of non-existence have mastery over him, for he becomes their very Self. (63)
Neither destiny, nor past and present actions,
nor even latent impressions (vāsanā) are at all capable of restraining their mind.

He establishes this very independence [of the mind] with the words "daivam" (fate). In the doctrine that emphasizes the primacy of karma, "fate" refers to the Lord who is intent on bestowing the fruits of past actions; and regarding such karma, they cannot restrain the mind—which has been set in motion for the sake of experiencing the remainder of its *prārabdha*—nor can they cause it to function otherwise. || 64 ||
Therefore, O dear one, for those who know reality, the mind— acting like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit—
quickly and fully accomplishes whatever it contemplates.
Whatever life or death occurs by chance, like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence, brought about by the force of past karma (*prārabdha*). || 65 ||
By a chance occurrence, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, Vītahavya’s consciousness was awakened to life;
that very life has now been swiftly made firm.
But when his intuitive flash of insight (pratibhā) attained the state of being liberated from the body,
then he became one liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamukta), established in absolute sovereignty.
But when, upon the completion of what had been commenced, the intuition became established within consciousness, [she] realized it as such. || 67 ||
The mind, freed from latent impressions and swiftly attained to liberation, having arisen as the self,
becomes in an instant whatever it desires.
For Maheśvara is indeed composed of all powers. || 68 ||

He summarizes what has already been said in brief with the verse beginning "vigata": the mind, having attained a state free from bonds (*vipāśatā*), and thus arisen as the true nature of the Self (*vāstavātmasvabhāva*), is the individual soul (*jīva*) characterized by that [mind]. For (*hi*), the meaning is that Maheśvara, who consists of all powers, is Śiva himself who has become manifest. As they have said: "The grain of rice is bound by its husk."
But in the absence of husks, there is rice; likewise, the individual soul (jīva) is always bound by fetters, while Sadāśiva is forever liberated from fetters.
Thus [ends the verse]. 68.

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Yoga for the Contemplation of the Play of Reality," in the Section on Tranquility within the Means of Liberation, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Seers.

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating the Play of Reality," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Ninetieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When, through inquiry, the mind has indeed become as if it has set;
For at that time, the virtues of friendliness and the rest arose within Vītahavya. || 1 ||
Endowed with virtues such as loving-kindness and having likewise attained a state of partlessness, the two-fold dissolution of the mind is here described in detail. (1)
It is as if set, like a parched seed devoid of the power to sprout; yet, though it has set, in appearance it has not actually set—this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Sage, O Lord, you have stated that when the nature of the mind has vanished through the dawning of inquiry, qualities such as friendliness (maitrī) arise. How is this so?"
Thus, what was intended by each of the things you have said? || 2 ||
O best among speakers, tell me: when the mind has dissolved into Brahman, for whom do qualities such as loving-kindness exist, or where do they manifest?

When [the object] has set and been sublated, whose [qualities] are sublated? Is it the substratum, or do certain qualities flash forth in the appearance of something, or in the consciousness of the archetype (*bimba-citi*)? For indeed, qualities such as coolness, sweetness, and purity cannot possibly exist in a mirage-river that has been sublated, nor can they exist in the desert itself.
The meaning is that there exists something which illuminates that [object]. || 3 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The dissolution of the mind is of two kinds—having form (sarūpa) and indeed being formless (arūpa).
That which has form belongs to one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), while the formless arises from liberation from the body.
Being of similar form, it appears together with that form—like the illusion of another person in one's own reflection within a crystal wall—and yet it is also devoid of it. || 4 ||
In this world, the existence of the mind leads to suffering, while the destruction of the mind leads to happiness;
therefore, having brought the existence of the mind to an end, one should bring the mind itself to its cessation.
Know that the mind, which exists as the cause of birth and is pervaded by the web of tamasic latent impressions, leads only to suffering.

If so, what is the nature of the existence of the mind? He explains it with the words "by those consisting of darkness" (tāmasaiḥ): by those [modifications] arising from uncontradicted ignorance. || 6 ||
That mind which, ignorant of reality, highly esteems its own former accumulation of qualities as "mine," is called the suffering *jīva*.

Through the superimposition of association with the Self, one identifies as "mine" the entire collection of qualities belonging to the body, senses, objects, and so forth—a mass of attributes established by beginningless, prior superimposition. || 7 ||
As long as the mind exists, how can there be the destruction of suffering?
When the mind has set for a living being, saṃsāra has come to its end.
Know that the mind, which is firmly rooted in this very [body] and remains unmoving, exists as the sprout of the forest of the tree of suffering. (9)

Know that in this very ignorant being, the mind—which is firmly established and enveloped by the spreading network of latent impressions—is the root of the tree of suffering; it is such that from it arise the sprouts and shoots of the forest of the tree of misery. (9)
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, whose mind is lost, or what kind of thing would be lost?
What would its destruction be like, and what is the nature of that destruction's existence?
What kind of existence—what characteristic—is there for destruction, which has reached the state of non-existence, such that it would be capable of conventional usage? || 10 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O best of those who know how to inquire, O scion of Raghu’s lineage, I have now described the existence of the mind; listen now to its dissolution.
This has been stated by the passage beginning with "described by the tamasic nets of latent impressions" (vāsanājālaiḥ), and so forth. || 11 ||
They know his mind to be dead, whose state of pleasure and pain does not displace him from equanimity, just as gusts of wind do not move the lord of mountains. 12.

The wise know that the mind of one whom neither external nor internal states of pleasure can draw forth nor disturb— due to his establishment in his own self, which is the singular essence of the bliss of the full nature of equanimity— is dead and lost. || 12 ||
The thought "this is I" and "this is not I" does not diminish the Supreme among Men;
those who know him understand that his mind is never lost.

"This body, measuring seven spans, is that which is well-known as 'I'; everything beyond this is not 'I'. Such reflection and meditation do not diminish it; that is to say, they do not delimit it. || 13 ||
Calamity, wretchedness, enthusiasm, intoxication, lethargy, and great festivals—
those who do not lead him into deformity, know that his mind is lost.
Deformity is the discoloration of the face. || 14 ||
O virtuous one, this is the dissolution of the mind; here, the mind becomes destroyed.
This state of the dissolution of the *citta* belongs to the one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). (15)
He concludes the statement regarding the definition with the words: "This... (verse 15).
O sinless one, know that state of mind to be delusion; when that perishes, then the quality of goodness (sattva), which is designated as the destruction of the mind, arises fully.

"Mind-stuff" (manas) refers to the state of being fit for the perception of the visible world through the delusion of ultimate reality; "existence" (sattva) refers to the nature of pure being. || 16 ||
O Raghava, for that one who is the playfulness of being and whose mind has perished—the one whose nature is liberated while living—some have applied the designation "mind. (17)
By some who perceive that appearance of conventional usage. || 17 ||

O sinless one, the mind endowed with qualities such as loving-kindness possesses the highest latent impression; it is liberated from further birth and is the mind of one who is liberated while living. (18)
That very being becomes endowed with qualities such as mental friendliness and the like, which characterize one liberated while living. || 18 ||
O Rāma, that state in which further birth is pervaded by a liberated latent impression (vāsanā),
and wherein the mind exists as one liberated while living— that is called sattva.
By means of the latent impression (vāsanā) of the form of Brahman, it is designated by the name "sentient being" (sattva). || 19 ||

Because it has been experienced just now and is attained as a reality, this dissolution of the mind (manonāśa), which is subtle and conjoined with the body, exists for one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and possesses its own form.
Now, at the time of emergence (*vyutthāna*): because it has been experienced as a manifestation, it is "with form" (*sarūpa*), as if possessing an aspect (*sākāra*).

Through the attainment and acquisition of the nature of pure existence (*sanmātra-svabhāva*) of the sentient being (*sattva*), it is "slightly joined" (*tanu-saṃyuta*), meaning that it does not touch the limitations of the body and so forth. Furthermore, because there is an absence of anything to be contemplated, it is "the destruction of the mind" (*manonāśa*); this is the meaning. By this—
The portion of the question regarding the nature of the destruction of existence has been resolved. || 20 ||

Then, like the rays of the moon, the qualities beginning with loving-kindness (maitrī) and culminating in sympathetic joy (muditā) abide at all times and in every way within the dissolution of the mind of one liberated while living.

For this very reason, he says "maitryādayaḥ" (friendliness and so forth), meaning that qualities such as friendliness also appear there as having arisen [in them]. "Muditāḥ" means they are joyful and serene. || 21 ||
In the Himalaya known as Sattva—the dissolution of the mind of one liberated while living—the riches of virtue blossom like flower-clusters in spring. (22)
In the abode of the coolness of contentment, which is like that of snow. || 22 ||
But that formless dissolution of the mind which I have described, O scion of Raghu—
he is indeed the one liberated while in the body (videhamukta), existing as the partless Self.
He shows the second [type of] dissolution of the mind (manonāśa) with the words: "But the formless," etc. (23).
Even a being endowed with all the foremost virtues dissolves into the stainless,
supremely purifying state of disembodied liberation.
The sattva is the mental faculty (manas) which is of the nature of appearance. || 24 ||
In that state of disembodied liberation (videhamukti),
which consists of the dissolution of the sattva and the destruction of the mind known as Virūpa, nothing whatsoever exists.

Not even the slightest thing is visible; the meaning is that this is according to the Vedic scripture which states: "That wherein one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman). || 25 ||
Therein there are neither virtues nor vices, neither prosperity nor adversity, nor restlessness;
there is neither rising nor setting, nor the perceptions of joy or resentment.
He elaborates on what has already been stated with the words "not the qualities," and so forth. || 26 ||
There is neither light nor darkness, nor anything at all; there is no twilight, day, or night;
there are no directions, nor space, nor below, nor the nature of misfortune.
There is no latent impression, no construction, neither effort nor lack of effort, no attachment; there is neither being nor non-being, for that state is indeed not something to be accomplished.
Existence is being; non-existence is non-being. || 28 ||
It was like the sky when it is devoid of darkness by means of its splendor, with the moon, sun, and wind spread abroad;
it was equal to that autumnal sky, clear, free from twilight, and radiant without dust.
Deprived of dust, radiance, and the light of the sun. || 29 ||
For those who have reached the further shore of awakening and of the wandering in saṃsāra (or, according to another reading, of the ostentation of saṃsāra),
their vast abode is like the sky for the winds.
The abode is the foundation. || 30 ||
With suffering completely stilled, consisting of a non-inert self, sleeping in blissful languor, and free from the qualities of rajas and tamas—
those great ones, whose bodies are the expanse of space, are bodiless.
In that state, those whose fragments of mind have dissolved dwell. || 31 ||

Being non-inert in nature, it is as if asleep, devoid of activities such as opening the eyes; the "bodiless" (atanu) are those liberated while living (videhamukta). Those in whom even a fragment of the illusory mind has dissolved into that state remain in that state;
the meaning is that they become firmly established there, never to return. || 31 ||

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating the Teaching on Consciousness," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Rishis.

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating the Teaching on the Mind," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The ninety-first canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
[I salute him] who is like a mountain from the treasury of the supreme ether, upon which grows the tree of the various worlds.
Variegated with stars as its flowers, it has the gods and demons for its birds. || 1 ||
The body is the seed of the creeper of saṃsāra; its mental aspect, the movement of the vital breath, and latent impressions (vāsanā) are described as being within that seed. (1)

Desiring to ask about the means for cutting the root of the creeper of the soul’s transmigration—which has spread throughout the world, which is superimposed upon Brahman and takes the form of the fourteen worlds—Rāma first describes the world as a forest, beginning with the words "parama... [and so on]: "of the sheath of the supreme ether..."
Because the undifferentiated Brahman acts as a barrier like a mountain, there are "mountains" in which the unmanifested (avyākṛta) is rooted;

these are the various worlds, the distinctions of the multicolored cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), which are themselves the "trees. Thus, the qualifiers such as "variegated with the flowers of stars" also serve to establish the metaphor of the forest. || 1 ||
With its edges garlanded by lightning and its foliage of dark blue clouds,
it is beautiful in all seasons, jagged with the delightful clusters of the moon and sun.

In this [tree], the tips of the branches that are the directions have produced clusters of blossoms garlanded with lightning; its sprouts are the clouds colored blue and so forth, and its leaves are copper-green and other such hues;
it is made beautiful by the lovely, radiant blossoms characterized by the moon, sun, and the host of planets.
It stood as if smiling, jagged with flowers like protruding teeth. || 2 ||
It is encircled by seven oceans and lakes, enchanting with hundreds of rivers,
and it is the sustenance for the infinite multitude of beings born of the fourteen kinds of existence.
It is sustained by fourteen types of worlds, each inhabited by infinite varieties of living beings. || 3 ||
O Brahman, for the grape-vine of worldly existence— which has assumed an expansive form and, having invaded the forest of the world, remains there with its net already cast— [this is the fruit].

Having invaded this forest-like world and completely enveloped it on all sides with the spreading vines of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) so as to form a net, there exists the vine of *mṛdvīkā*— that is, the grapevine— characterized by *saṃsṛti*, which is the transmigratory wandering of the living being (*jīva*). || 4 ||

Of this creeper whose joints are old age and death, which bears a row of fruits consisting of pleasure and pain, and which has its roots firmly established through the handfuls of water poured by the sprinkling of delusion; (5)
Old age and death are its very joints and the knots of its sections; the word *parvan* is sometimes seen ending in the vowel *a*. Delusions are its handfuls of sprinkling water. (5)
What is the seed, and what is said to be the seed of that seed?
Furthermore, what is the seed of that [seed], and what would be the seed of that as well? (6)
The inquiry concerning the fourfold succession of seeds. || 6 ||
O best among speakers, please explain all this again in brief for the further increase of my understanding and for the attainment of the essence of knowledge.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, know that the body is the seed of the creeper of worldly existence, containing within it the great sprouts of good and evil that have begun to grow densely.

In which [body] the great sprouts are the very auspicious and inauspicious karmas—latent within the internal subtle body (liṅgadeha), hidden, dense in their inception, and initiators of various endless effects. || 8 ||
Dense with the spreading of its branches and abounding in fruits and shoots,
this earth has become flourishing through him, like the earth in the autumn season.
By means of such a body, this creeper of worldly existence becomes full and flourishes;
the remainder of the sense is that the earth [becomes] an abundance of crops. || 9 ||
The mind, which follows the dictates of desire, is the seed of this body; it is a treasury of states of existence and non-existence, and a casket for the jewels of suffering. (10)

To answer the second question—"What is its seed?"—he says: "Bhāva... etc. *Bhāva* is the increase of prosperity; *abhāva* is its decrease. [The mind] is under the sway of hope, ever following it like a servant. || 10 ||
From the mind alone this entire web of limbs, both existent and non-existent, arises intensely;
likewise, this is experienced by oneself within the delusions of dreams. (11)
The present is real, while the past and the future are unreal; this refers to the collection of limbs, that is, the body.
He establishes the experience of dreams as a proof for the arising of the body from the mind, stating: "And so it is. || 11 ||
Just as a city arises from the conceptualization of a gandharva, so too does a body— resplendent in form and complete with windows— originate from the mind.
Just as for the Gandharvas, a city arises from the mind itself through the formation of an intention to manifest [it] at the moment of death, so too does the body arise; this is the meaning. || 12 ||

Whatever is perceived as the objective world, appearing as something that can be grasped, is but the expansion of the mind’s form, just as the state of being a jar or other objects is the expansion of clay. (13)

Furthermore, it is not reasonable to entertain doubt here, because it is well-known from all the Śrutis and Purāṇas that the entire world is merely a modification of the mind belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha; thus he says:
"That which is this... (13).
There are two seeds for the tree of the mind, which bears the creepers of its activities:
one is the vibration of the vital breath, and the second is firm conceptualization. (14)
Now, he provides the answer to the third question—"What is the seed for that [ignorance]?"—by saying "two. Firm mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is latent impression (*vāsanā*). || 14 ||
When the vital breath vibrates, intent upon contact with the channels, then the mind, consisting of pure sensation, is swiftly produced. || 15 ||
He establishes the first [point] with the words "yadā" (when). It consists of consciousness (*saṃvedana*), being primarily a modification of the intellect (*cit*). || 15 ||
When the vital breath does not vibrate within the hollows of the channels of the head,
due to the power of non-perception, the mind is no longer produced within.
The "channels of the veins" (*śirāsaraṇayaḥ*) are the seventy-two thousand pathways of the *nāḍīs*; "in their cavity" means in their opening.
"Lack of awareness" (*asaṃvittiḥ*) is the non-awakening of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of external perception; it is by virtue of that [lack of awareness]. (16)

This very vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is perceived through the gateway of the mind; it has come to be called the "world" in the void, appearing in such a manner like the blueness and other qualities [of the sky]. (17)

He states that even the manifestation of the world in the form of the Hiranyagarbha-consciousness is indeed impelled by the vibration of the collective vital breath (*prāṇa*), and this is indicated by the analogy of the vibration of one's own mind—beginning with the word "prāṇa. It is "seen," meaning it is perceived. || 17 ||
The cessation of the vibration of the vital breath is called peace;
when consciousness ceases to vibrate with the vital breath, it moves like a ball that has been struck.

Thus, when [the mind] is asleep and has ceased its activity regarding the vibration of the collective vital breath (*samaṣṭiprāṇa*), that peace of consciousness—which is indeed its state of actionlessness—is called the dissolution of the world or liberation; this is the meaning. A *vīṭā* is a ball. When struck by the hands, it vibrates intensely within bodies, awakened by the pulsation of the vital breath.
Like a ball struck by the hands, she whirled about in circles in the courtyards.
The existent, all-pervading consciousness is awakened by the vibration of the vital breath,
taking a form subtler than the subtle, like a trace of fragrance carried by the wind.
Know, O Rāghava, that the supreme good lies in the restraint of consciousness;
where there is no further progression toward causal factors, there no agitation exists.

The restraint of consciousness is non-distraction; the highest good is liberation, which is the conquest and destruction of the vibration of the vital breath—the cause of agitation—through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 21 ||
Consciousness itself, having quickly arisen, eagerly moves toward the object of perception;
from that perception, endless sufferings arise for the mind. (22)
For what purpose is there a restraint [of the mind]? When consciousness arises in the form of the mind, what is the fault therein?
To this he says: "Consciousness" (saṃvit). Because of attachment to the object of perception—the external world—one undergoes passion and so forth.
And from that, due to the experience of enjoying those objects, there arise endless sufferings; such is the meaning. || 22 ||
When consciousness abides for the sake of awakening within deep sleep,
then that stainless state— the goal to be attained— has been attained.
The meaning is: when she, being as if fast asleep regarding external objects, remains intent upon awakening the internal Self—that is, when she becomes prepared for that purpose. || 23 ||
Therefore, if you do not cause consciousness to swell through the vibrations of the vital breaths and the impelling of latent impressions, then you are unborn.

If you do not act as the deluded do— by making consciousness swollen through the impulses of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) that have been attained, through the incitements of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and through the intensification of passion— or, alternatively, if "pari" here signifies exclusion, [if you do not act] by the movements of the vital breaths or by the exclusion of such movements, [then you are truly wise]. Regarding the latent impressions:

If, by means of exhortations and dispellings, you render consciousness free from swelling—that is, devoid of the state of mind characterized by swelling—then you are indeed unborn (aja), devoid of all transformations such as birth and so forth, and thus liberated; this is the meaning. || 24 ||
Know that the mind is the swelling of consciousness;
by it this web of misfortune is spread out, which cuts asunder and destroys the life-force of living beings.
By whom the livelihoods of people have been uprooted, shattered, ruined, and worn out. || 25 ||

Yogins perform the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa) for the sake of calming the mind, by means of breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāmas), meditations, and applications devised through skillful methods. || 26 ||

By means of the practice and application of those methods for that [attainment], which are declared in the Yoga scriptures and established through the techniques of the lineage of true gurus and so forth. || 26 ||
The wise know that the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa) bestows the fruit of the tranquility of the mind, is the supreme cause of equanimity, and brings about auspicious health of consciousness.
He praises the very restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa) by way of its identity with the fruit—namely, the state of the mind—thus: "The mind... (verse 27).
O Raghava, hear now about that other origin of the mind, which is revealed and experienced by the wise, and which has latent impressions as its very life.

He undertakes to describe another seed of the mind with the words "by those who possess knowledge. [This seed] is manifested, correctly taught, and personally experienced; it is sustained by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) throughout one's life. || 28 ||
The grasping of an object with firm mental cultivation, having abandoned prior and subsequent deliberation—that is proclaimed as *vāsanā*. (29)

In that regard, he first states the nature of latent impression (*vāsanā*) with the word "firm" (*dṛḍha*). When there is an appropriation of objects such as the body through a firm prior mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the form of impressions consisting of "I" and "mine," and when this occurs without having abandoned prior and subsequent inquiry, then that [cultivation] causes the Self to be permeated by the state of being the body and so forth.

The meaning is that by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that which perfumes" (*bhāvayati*), it is proclaimed as *vāsanā* (latent impression). Thus, for those who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and possess investigation into the prior and subsequent [states], the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the body and so forth do not constitute *vāsanā*; for the reason is that, being overwhelmed by investigation which opposes *vāsanā*, it is impossible for them to be perfumed by the state of the body and so forth. This is the intended sense. || 29 ||
O mighty-armed one, through intense spiritual urgency, he quickly becomes that very thing which has been cultivated by himself, his memory of other things having vanished. (30)

However, because there is no contradiction for one who does not know the Self, he is indeed able to instill [the conviction] regarding the existence of the body and so forth through the firmness of intense and forceful contemplation (note: the word *vega* is not read in some versions). With this intention, he says:
"contemplated" (*bhāvita*). || 30 ||
Such is that person, rendered helpless by latent impressions (vāsanā), that he becomes utterly deluded, thinking: "Whatever I perceive, that is the real entity. || 31 ||
It says "tādṛk" (such) because it shows existence even in external objects, just as it shows selfhood in the body and so forth.

The meaning is that the etymological derivation of *vāsanā*—as that which "dwells" (*vasati*) is a "thing" (*vastu*), and it "causes [objects] to dwell" (*vāsayati*) by means of its own existence—is applicable there as well. || 31 ||
Due to the helplessness caused by the force of latent impressions (vāsanā), that [consciousness] abandons its own true nature;
one with faulty vision perceives everything as deluded, just as if under the influence of intoxication. (32)
All that has the form of the world is presented by those latent impressions (vāsanā). || 32 ||
One who possesses incorrect knowledge alone becomes overwhelmed by mental anguish, being subdued by the latent impression residing within, as if by poison. (33)
He states the counter-example for the phrase "having abandoned prior and subsequent deliberation" with the words beginning "incorrectly" (asamyak) and so forth. || 33 ||
Since false vision is the cultivation of the notion of a self in that which is not the self, know that, O Rāghava, it is the mind that perceives substantiality in what is unsubstantial. (34)

With the intention that this very consciousness (cit), impelled by latent impressions (vāsanā), arises in the form of the mind (citta)—a reading "of consciousness" (citaḥ) not found in the printed edition—he says: "incorrectly" (asamyak). || 34 ||
Due to the singular latent impression (*vāsanā*) of objects resulting from firm habitual practice, the extremely restless mind arises as the cause of birth, old age, and death. (35)
When nothing whatsoever— whether of the nature of what is to be abandoned or what is to be accepted—
is cultivated, and one remains having relinquished everything, then the mind is not born.

For this very reason, he says "when" (yadā) to show that liberation, characterized by the mind's restoration to its natural state, results from the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā): [the mind] is not perfumed (na vāsyate), meaning it does not attain [new] existence. || 36 ||
When the mind, being perpetually free from latent impressions, does not think,
then the state of no-mind arises, which bestows supreme tranquility.
When nothing whatsoever flashes within consciousness, like a cloudless sky, then the mind is not produced within, like a lotus in the sky. (38)
Like a lotus in the sky, the mind is not born within consciousness. || 38 ||
When no entity is cultivated toward any object whatsoever in the world, then how can the mind arise within the empty sky of the heart? (39)
O Rāghava, I consider the nature of the mind to be merely this much: that it is the internal contemplation of an object as a real entity and with aesthetic relish. (40)
By means of flavor, by means of passion. || 40 ||

Therefore, for one who meditates on the visible world as being nothing whatsoever fit for conceptualization, how could the arising of the mind occur for that which is as pure as the expanse of space? (41)
It is unfit to be supported by logical arguments through conceptual construction. || 41 ||
That which consists in relying on the non-cultivation [of objects], the cultivation of their non-existence, and seeing things as they truly are—that is called "non-mind" (acittatva). || 42 ||

Now he defines "mindlessness" (acittatā) with the word "that which": *yad iti*. The meaning is this: it is that which brings about non-existence—characterized by the wiping away of all that is visible—by resorting to the yoga of cessation (*nirodhayoga*), which is the non-contemplation (*abhāvana*) or non-recollection of external objects, and whose true nature is manifested through the vision of the Supreme Self. || 42 ||
That mind which, having completely renounced everything within, abides in a cool disposition—even while remaining in active life—is declared to be of the nature of the unreal. (43)

In that case, one might ask: since those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) possess a mind accompanied by mental modifications (savṛttika-citta), how can they be said to be "mindless" (acittatva)? To this he replies with the word "all" (sarvam).
The sense is that it is impossible to say that something possesses cloth merely because there is the appearance of a burnt cloth. || 43 ||
For one in whom passion no longer exists due to the absorption in the flavor of latent impressions (vāsanā), his mind has attained the state of non-mind; that is called pure being (sattva).

The passion (*rāga*), which consists of attachment to the objects of sense (*viṣaya-rasa*) induced by meditative reflection (*ādhyāna*), is the coloring agent; the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that remains like the cloth after the ash has been removed is called *sattva*. This is the meaning. || 44 ||
He whose latent impressions (vāsanā) no longer produce rebirth is liberated while living; established in pure being (sattva), he remains like the whirling of a potter’s wheel.

If it is asked, "In that case, how does one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) maintain worldly activity?", he says: "Like the spinning of a potter's wheel whose work is finished" (verse 45). This is expressed in the verse beginning with "ghana... [45].
Those whose latent impressions (vāsanās) are like parched seeds—devoid of the capacity for rebirth and stripped of their flavor—are indeed established as liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 46 ||
Having attained minds whose nature is pure being (*sattva*), they have reached the further shore of gnosis;
they are said to be "mindless," for at the end of the body they take the form of space.

"At the end of the body" means when the *prārabdha* karma is exhausted; the sense is that this follows from the Śruti: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released from the body, then he shall be merged [in Brahman]. (47)
O Rāma, there are two seeds of the mind: the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) and latent impressions (vāsanā).
When one of these two is exhausted, both quickly perish. (48)
One might ask: "Even when the seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are destroyed, why should the mind not arise again from another seed? To this he replies: "The two" (verse 48).
For these two are mutual causes for the birth of the mind, O Rāma, just as a water-reservoir and a jar are in the act of taking up water. (49)

The meaning is that these two, when combined, are the cause for the birth of the mind, and not each one individually; just as, for example, when a jar accepts water, both the reservoir and the jar together are the cause, and not either one alone. || 49 ||
He for whom there is no dense latent impression (vāsanā) that causes rebirth—these two [the seed and the sprout] exist like sesame and its oil. (50)

The meaning is that a single dense latent impression (*vāsanā*) does not forcibly cause rebirth for the soul. Regarding the answer to the fourth question—"What would be the seed for that [rebirth]?"—the author speaks of "like the seed and the sprout" (*bījāṅkuravat*), thereby avoiding the fallacy of infinite regress. These two—the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspandana*) and the latent impression—are contained within one another, like oil in sesame seeds.

By the logic of the seed and the sprout, they are causes for one another in a sequence that requires time; this is the connection with the subsequent [verse]. (50) Thus, in a sequence requiring time, these two, which are eternally inseparable, produce everything; he is the one whose essence is consciousness and who possesses the mind. (51)
Thus, he says "all" [in verse 51], meaning that for the mind as well, there is no cause with respect to those two, nor with respect to sensory pleasure, pain, and so forth.
When both bliss and breath, together with the vital energy (prāṇa) and the mind, arise along with their latent impressions (vāsanā), that is the state of bliss. 52.
The meaning is that, in due order, first there is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), then the senses, and then the bliss produced by them—

this constitutes "everything. Thus, he states that even the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of previously experienced sensory bliss, of the momentary life-force characterized as the movement of the wind, possesses the power to generate the mind.

Regarding the phrase "the bliss and the wind": when both bliss and wind have become fully present as latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then they join together and become the generators of the mind; such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). || 52 ||

Just as fragrance resides in a flower and oil in sesame seeds, so too do latent impressions (vāsanā) reside [in the mind]; from the force of these impressions comes the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa), and from that, the impressions arise once more. (53)

Therefore, with the intention that mutual dependence and mutual causality between these two are thus established—and that consequently the fault of infinite regress does not follow—he states once more what has already been said, beginning with "āmoda" (fragrance) and so forth. // 53 //
By that [process], the sequence of seed and sprout arises for the seed of the mind,
due to the activity of the agitation of consciousness caused by the surging forth of speech.

The sequence of seed and sprout arises; that is to say, it is "produced. He demonstrates the manner in which both [the seed and the sprout] produce the mind with the word "vāsanā" (latent impression). || 54 ||

It awakens the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa), and by that, the mind is born. Because its nature is to vibrate, the vital breath vibrates when it has come into contact with the quality of the heart.
By whom the latent tendencies of passion and so forth, which are qualities of the heart, have been touched and dispelled. || 55 ||
Awakening consciousness by means of that, the childish mind is produced;
for thus, both latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) are its two causes.
Upon the destruction of one of these two, O Raghava, there is the destruction of both;
for the mind's vibration of pleasure and pain is the great fruit of the body.
For this very reason, he states that what was previously said—"when one of the two has perished"—is logically consistent, by saying "of those two.

This means the destruction of both [the tree and] the mind which is its effect. Describing the mind itself as a tree, he speaks of its uprooting through the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) with the words beginning with "pleasure" (*sukha*). [The mind is] the mental activity agitated by pleasure and pain.
That very mind is the "spanda" (vibration) of which; the body itself is the "śārīraka" (corporeal). || 57 ||
It has the appearance of sprouting with its effects, is entwined by the creepers of ritual actions,
is coiled around by the black serpent of craving, and is the dwelling place of the disease of passion.
The tree of the mind, whose root is ignorance, which is very firm, and in which the birds of the senses are nestled— its latent tendencies have indeed been brought to destruction in an instant.
The connection with the following verse is: "The latent impressions (vāsanās), once brought to exhaustion, cause such a tree of the mind to fall in an instant. || 59 ||
The torrent of wind strikes it down like a fruit ripened by time,
turning all directions white and shrouding every vision.

Representing that very mind as a mass of dust driven by the wind, he demonstrates its dissolution through the cessation of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as if through the cessation of the wind itself, by means of the passage beginning with "pāṇḍurīkṛta" (made pale).
The adjectives beginning with "pāṇḍurīkṛta" are to be applied to both [the mind and the dust] through devices such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia). "Āśā" refers to the directions.
They are metaphorical and possessed of craving; by whom the all-seeing, full form of consciousness—the eye of all people—is veiled and covered. || 60 ||
The body has the appearance of a flickering cloud, arisen from the pit of ignorance;
it is pervaded by the blades of grass that are cravings, and it has the form of a pillar. (61)
A heap of refuse, a mere pillar-like body, well-known as having the form of a whirlwind,
its thin frame quivering and slightly agitated toward the act of leaping up for pleasure—
it dissolves away when it no longer perceives the great light situated within.

Agitated by the gusts of the wind of mental fluctuations—trembling, extremely subtle, and very slight—it was skilled in leaping effortlessly in every direction; yet it was unable to perceive the great light abiding within, namely Brahman and the solar light, for it was incapable of seeing such a thing. Such is the dust of the wind of the mind.
The grammatical connection is that [it] dissolves in an instant due to the cessation of the movement of the vital air (pavana). || 62 ||
And by the cessation of the movement of the vital breath, O Rāma, the dust of the mind is instantly stilled;
for these two—the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa-pavana*)—are inseparable.
He states another seed as well: "the latent impression" (vāsanā). || 63 ||
The object of consciousness is said to be the seed, because from it those two—the vibration of the vital breath and latent impression—emanate;
having reached the object of consciousness within the heart, the vibration of the vital breath and the latent impression arise.
The object of sensation consists of pleasant and unpleasant things, such as sound and so forth; having reached them, one remembers them. 64.
Therefore, that which is to be experienced arises; this is declared to be the seed of these two.
Through the complete abandonment of the object of experience, [there follows] the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath and its latent impressions.
Know that consciousness, like a tree whose roots are severed, quickly perishes along with its object of perception and its very seed, if it is devoid of steadfastness.
He states that the very cultivation of the non-difference of consciousness is the abandonment of the object of cognition, saying "consciousness" (saṃvidam).

He establishes this very point with the verse beginning "the seed" (bījam) and so forth: consciousness itself, having abandoned its own steadfastness and become as if an object of cognition, is the seed of the mind (cittabīja). || 66 ||
An object of consciousness cannot exist, just as a sesame seed devoid of oil;
nothing whatsoever exists as a separate object of consciousness, neither externally nor internally.
For without consciousness, the object of consciousness cannot exist; that is to say, it cannot be established. || 67 ||
Consciousness, vibrating through its own volition, perceives an object of perception by itself, just as in a dream one perceives one's own death or residence in another land. (68)

The word "tathā" (likewise) is used in the sense of "as. Just as in a dream, one's own death and residence in another land occur solely through the power of consciousness's own creative wonder (*svacamatkāra*), so too is it with that which is perceived in the waking state; this is the connection with what follows. || 68 ||
Through the union with its own wonder, the object of perception likewise belongs to consciousness;
where the self-perception of consciousness exists by virtue of its own volition. (69)

In whatever state of discernment the knowledge of one's own true nature exists, even that self-awareness is produced by one's own mental constructs and is just like a dream; for neither self-awareness nor discernment, investigation, and so forth, can exist in reality within the non-dual [reality]. || 69 ||

Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, this web of the world appears just as a ghost might appear to a child arising from its own mental construction (or, according to another reading, arising from its own volition). || 70 ||
[This arises] from the delusion produced by one's own conceptual construction.
Just as the state of being a person is perceivable by a post, so too is it by consciousness;
just as the stick-like form and the dust-like nature of the rays of the moon and sun are perceived, so too is this.
Just as the rays of the moon and sun, having entered through a window, appear in the form of a staff and take on the appearance of motes of dust moving within them, so it is in this case. || 71 ||
