Just as the movement of stationary objects on a boat is perceived by consciousness, so too is [the perception of objects] by consciousness;
for this is false and difficult to discern, yet it dissolves through right knowledge.
False cognition is erroneous knowledge; it dissolves, that is, it is sublated. || 72 ||

Just as the state of being a snake is [superimposed] upon a rope, or the appearance of two moons due to a visual defect, pure consciousness alone is the three worlds; there is nothing else whatsoever to be perceived. 73.
As if from seeing the faultless after having seen the faulty, [one attains] right knowledge; he then states what that is: "Pure indeed... (verse 73).
The wise know that when such an internal certainty has taken root, it is right knowledge (samyag-jñāna), regardless of whether what appears to it was previously seen or unseen. (74)
By this, he shows that which is to be swept away—namely, "the former" (pūrva). || 74 ||
Therefore, one who possesses discernment should strive with effort to cleanse consciousness;
for it is merely the failure to cleanse it that constitutes attachment to the great cycle of worldly existence.
There is a connection and association of the self with the great cycle of existence (saṃsāra). || 75 ||
The mere cleansing of that [impurity] is experienced as liberation;
whereas consciousness leads to infinite suffering, which consists of rebirth. (76)
Perception is the observation of the object of experience. It leads to suffering, which consists of birth and so forth, for one whose nature is that of being born. || 76 ||
Be one who is non-cognition yet not insentient, because it does not produce the nature of pleasure;
be one who is non-insentient yet with bliss dissolved, having abandoned all perception.
O scion of Raghu, you are that very Self which is awakened and beyond the reach of perception.

Non-perception is the non-seeing of an object of knowledge; yet, while established in a nature whose sole essence is consciousness (*cit*), it arises from that which is unborn by nature—the eternal self-form. Therefore, the meaning is: you too, having abandoned [objective] perception, being non-inert (*ajaḍa*), having dissolved and become of one essence, become full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*). He who, though himself unperceivable, is awakened by his own nature.
That very Self is you; it is none other. || 77 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord, what is one like who is non-inert yet devoid of consciousness?
And how is it that inertness ceases when there is an absence of consciousness? (78)

The question is: since the abandonment of insentience necessarily results in the remainder of consciousness, or the abandonment of consciousness necessarily results in the remainder of insentience, how can one thing possess these two contradictory natures—being non-insentient and being non-consciousness? He clarifies this very contradiction by stating: "In the case of non-consciousness... (verse 78).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He who is established in non-abiding everywhere and finds rest nowhere at all— such a living being perceives nothing, for he is indeed consciousness itself, not insentient matter.

According to the etymology that "consciousness" (*saṃvit*) is the perception of external objects as real, even though the living being liberated while alive (*jīvanmukta*) displays a semblance of worldly activity through appearances of objects that are sublated,
he remains without fixed attachment toward all present objects, and likewise toward objects past and future.

Because they have not found rest through the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanā), they do not perceive any object of knowledge; thus, in that respect, it is said to be "unconscious," like a piece of wood or a clod of earth. However, by its own nature, because it is full of the single essence of self-luminous consciousness, it is non-inert—this is the meaning. || 79 ||
He for whom no objective support consisting of the perception of objects exists here is called non-conscious yet non-inert, even while performing hundreds of tasks. (80)
Demonstrating the etymology of the word *saṃvit* as previously stated, he supports what was said with the words "saṃviditi" (as consciousness).

The meaning is that, from the perspective of the object (*vastu-dṛśā*)—that is, through the notion of reality—the very taking of external objects as its support by consciousness (*cit*) is called *saṃvit*. By this, the intended meaning of the phrase "standing everywhere in non-abiding" (*sarvatrānavasthā-stha*) has been revealed. || 80 ||
The space of the heart is not tainted even slightly by that which is to be experienced;
he whose consciousness is non-inert is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 81 ||
Revealing that the statement "the mind rests nowhere" also refers to the past state, he says the following:
"When nothing whatsoever is cultivated within oneself due to the absence of latent impressions (nirvāsanatā), one remains steadfast, like the consciousness of a child or a mute. (82)
He reveals that [power] even regarding future objects with two verses beginning with "yadā" (when). || 82 ||
Then the wise man takes refuge in that pervasive, pure perception which is entirely free from dullness, because of which he is never again defiled. || 83 ||
For one who has abandoned all latent impressions through non-conceptual meditative absorption, an expansive bliss arises, like the blueness [appearing] from the sky. (84)
Having resolved this doubt and supporting the subject at hand, he says: "samasta... (verse 84).
There the yogins abide, being conscious yet devoid of [objective] consciousness;
because they have become one with that, even that [consciousness], which is without beginning or end, dissolves within.

[Objection: But surely, even in the absence of the cognition of any other form, the cognition consisting of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of Brahman is unavoidable even during *samādhi*; so how can there be "non-cognition" (*asaṃvitti*) therein? [The author] answers this with the words "because it consists of that" (*tanmayatvāt*).
That cognition, which has the form of Brahman—without beginning or end and unlimited—is itself [perceived] by the stainless light of Brahman (*brahmajyotis*).
The meaning is that being obstructed, it dissolves right there within. || 85 ||
Whether walking, standing, touching, or even smelling, he is said to be non-inert, with bliss dissolved, having abandoned all sensory perception, and happy. (86)
Relying upon this view, through arduous and diligent effort, cross to the further shore of the ocean of suffering, O ocean of boundless virtues. (87)
[This is] difficult [to achieve], being accomplished through the exertion of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other such practices. || 87 ||
Just as from a seed a great tree arises in time and pervades the sky,
so too this world, though unreal, has arisen from one's own volition and is perceived as such.
He says that the conscious self (cidātmā) itself imagines its own bondage and liberation, which are false, beginning with the words "Just as" (yathā). || 88 ||
Whenever consciousness, having repeatedly formed a mental resolve, assumes its own form,
that very consciousness becomes the seed of this web of births.

He explains when and how that [state] arises with the words "when" (yadā): "When, having formed resolve again and again—that is, having repeatedly made a mental construction—he attains his own *sāṃkalpika* body, which is his true nature (*svarūpa*), then [he becomes liberated]. (89)
Having generated itself by itself and deluding itself again and again, it leads itself to liberation within; know that, O Rāghava, to be your own consciousness.

The term *vit* refers to one who knows the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) situated within the heart; seeing it, he himself leads [others] to liberation (*mokṣa*). The particle *hi* indicates what is well-known through the experience of the wise. 90.
Whatever she contemplates, that very thing she becomes in an instant;
though released from the stage of becoming, her body does not return for a long time.
If that is so, why does consciousness not immediately and spontaneously attain its own true nature through the contemplation of its own self for all beings?

To this he replies: "No. Because it is not liberated from the planes (*bhūmikā*) of those states such as passion (*rāga*) and the like which constitute its current condition, it does not return to its own form even after a long time. (91)
He is neither a god, nor a celestial being, nor a rakṣasa, nor a yakṣa, nor a kinnara, nor a human;
it is the Self alone that now dances the drama of the world through its playful manifestation.
For this very reason, he states that the gods, gandharvas, and others are merely assumed appearances and not real—saying "the god" [in the verse].
This is by means of the first [power], the primordial perfection, the playful one, which is his own *māyā*. || 92 ||
Having bound itself and wept like a silkworm,
it eventually attains isolation after a long time through its own nature as pure consciousness.
Just as a magician or an actor displays himself as if binding and as if releasing, so it is said: "having bound," etc. (93).

The pure water of consciousness, having entered the nets of the world-oceans, manifests as this very unprecedented circle of directions, having assumed the form of mountains and other such features. (94)

Pure consciousness alone has become sufficient and complete as the water of the net of world-oceans; it alone is the unprecedented circle of directions and the entire expanse of the quarters; it alone has attained the state of mountains and other such things. (94)
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—these are said to be the waves of this vast expanse of the water of consciousness. (95)
The entire world is mere consciousness; there is no second conceptualization.
Through such right knowledge, consciousness does not become anything else. (96)
The meaning is non-difference, non-otherness, and non-duality. || 96 ||
When one perceives nothing at all, neither throbbing nor trembling,
and attains stability within one's own self, then consciousness is no longer stained.

He states when perfect knowledge of this [state] arises: "When... The distinction is that *kiṃciccalana* (slight movement) is *spanda* (vibration), whereas *samyakkampana* (complete shaking) is *vepana* (trembling). || 97 ||
Now, O Rāma, it is said that pure existence (sanmātra) is the seed of this consciousness;
from pure consciousness alone does this [universe] arise, just as luminosity arises from light. (98)

Having thus purified [the consciousness], he shows—by means of the analogy of sparks from a fire—that the remaining consciousness is indeed the consciousness of the reflection within the internal organ (*antahkaraṇa*), thereby dispelling the listeners' delusion; he demonstrates that the consciousness of Brahman, which is the seed of that [reflection] and consists of pure existence (*sanmātra*), according to the maxim of sparks from a fire, with the words "Now" (*atha*). This is the consciousness of the reflection.

It arises from Brahman, which is the prototype and whose nature is pure consciousness; just as light, visibility, and radiance arise from the splendor of the sun and other luminous bodies, so it is in this case. || 98 ||
Among those two forms, one consists of existence (*sattā*) abiding in various shapes; the second, however, is of a single form. Hear now this distinction between the two. (99)

When it is said "pure existence" (*sanmātra*), there might arise the misconception that the seed of this [existence] is merely conventional existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*), characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) and residing in things such as jars and cloths. To prevent such an error and to demonstrate that [the true existence] is distinct from that, he states the twofold nature of existence with the words "two forms," and so forth. (Verse 99)
The states of being a jar, being a cloth, and even "thou-ness" or "I-ness," which exist in various forms through the differentiation of the nature of existence (sattā), are so described. (100)

The intention is that potness, clothness, and so forth, as well as the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as existence and non-existence, are merely specific instances of conventional reality (vyāvahārikasattā) characterized by intrinsic capacity (svarūpayogyatā) with respect to the various differences in causal efficiency (arthakriyā). || 100 ||
But having abandoned its divisions, as it is extended through the single nature of existence, the form of existence is declared to be one by way of its universal character alone. (101)
In a general sense, by means of a common nature characterized as being the substratum of the entire world. || 101 ||
Having completely abandoned all particularity, that which is pure existence alone, untainted, uniform, and the great form—they know that to be the state of Being (sattā). 102.
The "foot" (pada) is the reality of the thing-in-itself (vastutattva). || 102 ||
Form, by virtue of its manifold shapes, can never exist as something that is not perceived; therefore, this [form] is without reality. (103)

He states that conventional existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*), however, is not real by saying "form" (*rūpam*). Since that form—such as "pot-ness"—is not perceived as persisting through subsequent states such as shards, powder, or dust, it cannot possibly be real; this is the meaning. || 103 ||
But that form which is of a single nature, whose essence is stainless existence, never undergoes destruction nor does it ever become subject to forgetfulness. (104)

But he says that the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*), which persists through all states, is not like that—namely, "of a single form" (*ekarūpam*). Furthermore, by the phrase "nor even forgetfulness," its state of being the essence of eternal consciousness is shown, because it is always manifest in its own nature. || 104 ||
Whether it be existence in time, existence in parts, or this existence as a discrete object— having abandoned the conceptualization of such divisions, become intent solely upon pure Being.

Some maintain that because the linguistic usage "it exists" is not observed regarding the past and future, the existence (*sattā*) of all things belongs only to the present time. Others hold that since it is merely the parts (*avayava*) themselves that manifest in the form of a whole (*avayavin*) when aggregated, the existence of the world consists only of these parts in the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Still others maintain that even within the whole there exists another universal (*jāti*), namely existence (*sattā*), which is inherent in it.
In this way, others also imagine it in various other ways according to their own respective intellects; the meaning is that they conceive of that imagined differentiation. || 105 ||
Although the existence of time and its own existence, being free from all mental constructs,
are of the nature of the supreme reality, nevertheless, they are not ultimately real.

Although even the existence of time and so forth—just like the entire world—is indeed the highest existence (*uttama-sattā*) because, upon the abandonment of the conceptualization of superimposed difference, only pure Being (*san-mātra*) remains; nevertheless, the meaning is that it is not real (*vāstavī*), because in its differentiated form it is subject to sublation. || 106 ||
Where the calculation of division bestows distinct states, how could that which is seen to be the cause of manifoldness be purifying? (107)
Cultivating the single universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*) as your entire body, remain filled with perfect supreme bliss, pervading all the quarters of space. 108.

Being of such a nature—that is, that universal form of existence (*sattāsāmānya*) by which the quarters of space (*digbhara*) are filled and saturated on all sides, as well as all objects to be contained therein—[he remains]. || 108 ||
O Lord of the Wise, that very limit which is existence as mere generality has become the seed-state of this [universe]; from that alone it proceeds. (109)
That existence (sattā) which is the limit—the ultimate boundary—of mere generality, has itself become the seed-nature of this world and of the consciousness that reflects it. (109)
That primordial state, which is devoid of all mental construction and extends to the limit of universal existence (sattāsāmānya), is without beginning or end; for it, no seed exists.
At the limit, at the ultimate boundary, of all existences belonging to the universal class of existence. || 110 ||
Wherein existence reaches its dissolution and remains immutable, there the person who has attained his footing does not return again to suffering. (111)

Where even existence (*sattā*) and the nature of reality (*saddharmatā*) dissolve due to the disappearance of the distinction between property and its substratum (*dharmadharmivibhāga*), he who has attained a footing there is alone a "man" (*puruṣa*), because of his capacity to accomplish the goals of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*); any other, however, is essentially like a woman—this is the intended meaning.
It is the cause of all causes, yet no cause for it is found; it is the essence of all essences, yet no essence is found in it. (112)
He praises that very state with the words beginning "That" (tad) in order to demonstrate its status as the supreme human goal. || 112 ||
In that vast mirror, all these perceptions of objects are reflected, just as trees on a bank are reflected in a lake. (113)
All these states of being there become savory for the ocean of the virtuous— [here the reading "svāduvāridheḥ" is preferred by the commentator, and that alone is correct]—
and they manifest like the six tastes to the tongue. (114)
In that very form of the Pratyagātman (the Inner Self), because they are superimposed upon it, they "taste" well—that is, they produce delight for the senses.
From that very ocean of sweetness, the ocean of bliss, [they derive] manifestation, existence, and appearance. || 114 ||
Therefore, that very state of the sky of consciousness, though more transparent than anything else, is the complete tasting of all varieties of flavors. 115.

Since even objects that are not inherently sweet become sweet through union with it, for that reason, the state—that is, the essential nature—of that space of consciousness (cidākāśa) is the ultimate relish among all categories of the sweet, the blissful, and the dear; the meaning is that it is of the nature of bliss and the most beloved of all. || 115 ||
O dear one, it is therein that the multitudes of worlds are born, exist, grow, are touched, remain, and finally dissolve. (116)

He demonstrates the concordance with the definition of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, as stated in the Śruti: "From bliss alone, indeed, these beings are born; by bliss, once born, they live;
into bliss they enter upon departing. This he shows with the words: "is born," and so on.

It exists, it is touched, and it undergoes transformation; they remain while facing toward decay. The intention is that the mention of the triad beginning with birth in the scripture is an illustration for all six modifications of being (bhāvavikāra). || 116 ||
He is the most venerable among those who are venerable, the lightest among those who are light,
the grossest among those who are gross, and the most minute among those who are minute.
With the intention that this very [consciousness] is also the sustainer of the various diversities such as heavy and light, he says "tattad" (that-that).
The second occurrences of the word "tat" refer to what is well-known. || 117 ||
For those who are farthest away, it is the most distant; for those nearby, it is close at hand.
For the youngest, it is the youngest; and for the eldest, it is likewise the eldest. (118)
From the words *dūra* (far) and so forth, the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* form *davīyas* (farther) and *daviṣṭha* (farthest);

by the rule *sthūladūra-*, there is elision of the subsequent *yaṇ*-class vowels and so on, as well as guṇa substitution for the preceding vowel. Similarly, from *yuvan* (young) and *alpa* (small), the suffix *kan* is applied; and from *praśasya* (praiseworthy) and *vṛddha* (old), the substitute *jya* is applied. || 118 ||
She is the radiance even among radiances, the darkness even among darknesses; she is the reality even among realities, and, O dear one, the supreme direction even among directions.
Therefore, that which is both nothing and something exists as it is and does not exist;
it is both visible and invisible, and I am both that and not that.
Nothing at all is renowned in the world. Even that which is slightly renowned is only that [Self].
It exists indeed as the nature of being; it does not exist as the nature of non-being. I exist as the inner self (*pratyaktayā*); I do not exist as the ego-sense (*ahaṃtayā*).
The second *ca* (and) has the sense of an unspoken conjunction, implying "not mine" (*na mama*) in addition to "I am not" (*na cāsmi*). || 120 ||
O sinless Rāma, by every possible effort, act in such a way that you may attain a firm standing in that most purifying state.
Just as you have approached; the present tense is used for the immediate future. Act accordingly. 121.
That is the stainless, ageless reality of the Self;
upon the realization of that, the mind attains peace.
Having realized the nature of that vast oneness, [one becomes liberated].
You have long since attained the state that is liberated from the fear of existence. || 122 ||

The reality of the self is its ultimate form; that alone is it. When there is the comprehension of that—when there is direct experience—one attains peace from it. Therefore, when you become one who has comprehended that vast, singular nature, at that very moment, for all eternity and without returning, you shall be of the nature of the supreme state, liberated from the fear of worldly existence.
The meaning is "it was thus. || 122 ||

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating the Seed of Saṃsāra," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 91.

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Investigating the Seed of Saṃsāra," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The ninety-second canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O giver of honor, these very seeds have been described by you."
By the application of which [practice] is that state swiftly attained? (1)

Regarding the differences in the states described here, the effort, its heaviness or lightness, the destruction of latent impressions and so forth, knowledge, and concurrent practice are now set forth. (1)

The meaning is this: these aforementioned seeds of the tree of transmigratory existence, such as the body and so forth, which were spoken of by you—by the application of which among those means (*upāya*) and through their cessation is the supreme state attained? Alternatively, "these" refers to those [seeds] present here, such as those mentioned in the passage beginning, "O Rāma, pure being (*sanmātra*) is said to be the seed of this consciousness."

The seeds of liberation, which take the form of distinctions between the stages (*bhūmikā*), have been taught by you; among those, by the application of which, or by resorting to which [seed], [is liberation attained]? (1)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Whatever answer has been stated by me for each of these seeds of suffering,
by the application of that very [remedy], the supreme state is swiftly attained.
Regarding that, he states the answer in accordance with the first explanation: "Of these," etc. (Verse 2).
If, by means of human effort, one forcibly abandons latent impressions at that very moment upon reaching the state situated at the pinnacle of universal existence; || 3 ||

In accordance with the second [verse], he also says, beginning with "existence" (*sattā*): "Existence" (*sattā*) is the universal (*sāmānya*), which is the purified referent of the word *tat*; its "limit" (*koṭi*) is its supreme pinnacle.

Abiding in that—meaning the state of the non-dual, partless, single essence through the identity of the purified referent of the word *tvam*, whose nature is consciousness—one attains the steadiness, the immobility, of the mind.
"If you bind," is to be connected with what follows. || 3 ||
O knower of reality, you establish a state that is imperishable even for a moment;
at this very moment, you shall fully attain that excellent state.
Is it by means of meditation alone? No; he says "by one who knows reality" (*tattvajña*). That is to say, by having directly realized [reality] in its true nature (*tattvataḥ*). || 4 ||
Or if you, my friend, establish your abiding in the form of universal existence (sattāsāmānya),
then you shall attain that state here with only a slight additional effort.
Regarding the case where one lacks such capacity, he says "existence" (*sattā*). This means: when the reality that is the cause of the world has been purified. "Something" (*kiñcit*):
the sense is that effort is required for the realization of undivided unity. || 5 ||
O sinless one, if you remain with your meditation fixed upon the principle of pure consciousness (saṃvittattva), then through even greater effort, you shall attain that supreme state.
In the reality of consciousness (saṃvittattva), which is the purified meaning of the term *tvaṃ*, it is the same as the previous [explanation]. || 6 ||
O Rāghava, meditation on the solitary object of perception is not possible,
because this consciousness is always present everywhere.

If it is asked, "In that case, since the aspect of consciousness (*saṃvid-aṃśa*) is lost through purification, why could even meditation (*dhyāna*) not be a means for the aspect of the object of consciousness (*saṃvedya-aṃśa*) alone?", [the author] replies "because it is impossible," stating: "in the object of consciousness" (*saṃvedye*). This is because it is impossible to cover over consciousness which shines forth prior to the objects of consciousness; therefore, in the covering of that [consciousness]...
The meaning is that because there is an absolute absence of the manifestation of anything to be experienced, meditation upon it is impossible. || 7 ||
Whatever you think, whatever you go toward, whatever you stand upon, and whatever you do—in each and every instance, consciousness is present; that very thing is indeed consciousness itself.
He demonstrates that the establishment of the thinker, the object of thought, and so forth, is dependent upon consciousness (saṃvit), stating "that which... and so on.
That which you think is consciousness alone; that which is thinking is also consciousness alone. The meaning is that everything has consciousness as its sole essence. || 8 ||
And if you make an effort toward the complete abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā),
then all mental and physical afflictions will instantly fall away from you.
He states another means: "vāsanā" (latent impression). By the word "ca" (and), it is meant that [this applies] also to the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*). That, then, is the case. || 9 ||
Indeed, this abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā) is considered more difficult than the previously mentioned efforts; it is harder to accomplish even than uprooting Mount Sumeru. (10)
Is this easier to understand than those previously mentioned? He says "no": "than those previously mentioned. || 10 ||
As long as the mind has not dissolved, so long there is no destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā);
as long as the latent impressions have not been destroyed, so long the mind does not become tranquil. || 11 ||
In order to demonstrate the difficulty [of this task], he states their mutual dependence with the words "as long as" (yāvat). || 11 ||
As long as there is no realization of reality, how can there be tranquility of mind? As long as there is no pacification of the mind, there is no knowledge of reality. || 12 ||
Thus, he states that there is likewise a mutual dependence between these two even with regard to the knowledge of reality, beginning with the words "as long as" (yāvat). || 12 ||

As long as there is no destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), how can there be the realization of reality (tattva)? As long as there is no attainment of reality, there is no exhaustion of latent impressions. || 13 ||
Knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the destruction of latent impressions—having become mutual causes for one another, these remain difficult to accomplish. (14)
Therefore, O Rāghava, with effort and discerning manliness, having abandoned the desire for enjoyment from afar, one should take refuge in these three. (15)
If it is asked, "What then is the means for its accomplishment?", he says: "Therefore," [verse 15], meaning that the practice of the three together, preceded by dispassion (vairāgya), is the means.
In every respect, as long as all these [as stated in the reading "sarva ete"] have not been repeatedly practiced equally,
the attainment of the state does not occur even in hundreds of aeons.
"Simultaneously" means at the same time; "with hundreds of equal years" means with hundreds of years. || 16 ||

O Mahāmati, O Sage, the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), the exhaustion [of the seeds], the dissolution of consciousness (vijñāna), and the cessation of the mind (manas) become fruit-bearing at the same time when practiced for a long duration. (17)
Even if these are practiced individually for a long time,
they do not bestow accomplishment, being like mantras that have been bound by a spell.
They are fettered, being obstructed by the defects mentioned in the mantra scriptures, such as fainting, death, and so forth. || 18 ||

Even though these have been cultivated over a long period of time and even by one who is wise, they are not able to be mastered individually, just like soldiers [who cannot be controlled one by one]. 19.

"Uparacitāḥ" means those who have been won over through service and the like, and then incited to perform their own tasks; "param" refers to the Supreme Enemy, the Supreme Self (Paramātman); "abhimukhatayā etum" means to go toward Him; and "sainikāḥ" means like soldiers of an army. || 19 ||
For when these have been brought to equal exertion by the wise one, they cut through the ocean of saṃsāra just as waters erode the slopes of a mountain. 20.
The waters have merged together in their primordial essence. || 20 ||

The destruction of latent impressions (vāsanākṣaya), the dissolution of consciousness (vijñāna), and the dissolution of the mind (manonāśa) must be cultivated with effort simultaneously for a long time; by that means, O dear one, you shall not be stained.
You are not stained, O unstained one; you shall abide in the intrinsic nature. || 21 ||
When these three are practiced for a long time, the firm knots of the heart are severed without remainder, like fibers from the cutting of a lotus stalk.
The knots of the heart—the superimpositions consisting of the identification with and the false attribution of the relationship between the internal organ and its attributes—are severed;
they are cut away like threads. 22.
O Rāma, this state of worldly existence has been practiced for hundreds of previous births;
it is never extinguished without the yoga of long-term cultivation. (23)

Now, one might ask: for what purpose is there long-term practice even for these three? To this he says: "In another birth... The word "hundred" (śata) signifies infinity. The continuity of saṃsāra is the latent impression (vāsanā) of duality. || 23 ||
Whether walking, hearing, touching, smelling, standing, waking, or likewise sleeping,
remain devoted to the practice of these three for the sake of your supreme welfare.
Those who know the reality understand that the restraint of the vital breath is equal to the complete abandonment of latent impressions; therefore, one should practice it in this very manner.
He states that the fourth breath-control (prāṇāyāma) should also be practiced along with the three [others], beginning with the words "vāsanā": "One should withdraw; one should practice. (25)
Through the complete relinquishing of latent impressions, the mind attains the state of non-mind;
and through the cessation of the movement of the vital breath—do as you wish.

Through long practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), by means of the method imparted by the Guru, and through the application of postures and diet, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is restrained. || 27 ||

The meaning is: by means of the method taught by a guru skilled in the practice of yoga, through mastery of postures such as the *svastika*, by means of wholesome, moderate, and pure food, and by means of yoga consisting of the restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth. || 27 ||
Because one sees things as they truly are, latent predispositions do not arise;
for that which remains non-contradictory throughout the beginning and end of all things is established as such. (28)

The meaning is that because he perceives that very reality which exists as the mere nature of existence—consistent and non-deceptive in the beginning, end, and (by the inclusion of "ca") the middle of all things—he is one who sees the object as it truly is. || 28 ||

Form, the perception thereof, and the knowledge [of it] are exhausted by that; thus, through non-attached conduct and the abandonment of worldly ideation, latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are eliminated. (29)

It is unattached, being free from association with those who look outward, and free from conceptual construction (*niḥsaṃkalpa*) because its conduct accords with whatever is encountered; it is devoid of worldly preoccupations (*bhavabhāvanā*), that is, the abandonment of all mundane desires.
Because one perceives the destruction of the body, latent impressions do not arise;
when the manifestation of latent impressions is destroyed, the mind no longer functions.
When wealth, characterized by latent impressions (vāsanā) and consisting of accumulated riches, has perished, it does not manifest again as if out of shame. || 30 ||
Just as dust in the sky settles when the movement of the wind has ceased,
so too is the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) indeed the very movement of the mind (citta).
The meaning is that, like dust, the mind also possesses a vibration dependent upon the wind. || 31 ||

Therefore, just as dust arises from refuse and the like in this world, so do [defilements] arise; hence, the wise person should exert themselves with great intensity to conquer the vibration of the vital breath. (32)
Like [a gem] from a heap of refuse, from a mound of dust. || 32 ||
Sitting down again and again with a one-pointed mind, or else, having abandoned this sequence, if there is merely the act of seizing the mind; // 33 //
He states that when one is unable to practice Haṭhayoga, Rājayoga should be practiced, beginning with the words "Or else" (athavā). || 33 ||
Whatever one desires, one attains that state after a long time;
yet it is not possible to conquer the mind without blameless means.

"By much [effort]"—the sense is that it is impossible to bring the difficult-to-tame mind under control through practice for only a short time. "Without method"—that is, without the two-fold yoga previously shown, which includes the science of the inner self (adhyātmavidyā) and association with the virtuous. || 34 ||
Just as a wild and wicked elephant cannot be controlled without a goad, so too [cannot be subdued] the attainment of inner knowledge and association with the virtuous. (35)
He states that very point: "Internally," etc. (35).
The complete abandonment of latent impressions and the cessation of the movement of the vital breath—these indeed are the mature methods for the conquest of the mind. (36)
Those who, despite these existing methods by which [the mind] is quickly conquered—just as dust on the ground is subdued by showers of rain—seek to restrain it through force, [act in vain]. (37)
Although the restraint of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃrodhana*) is indeed *haṭha* because it is a means for subduing the unsubdued, nevertheless,
[there are other practices] devoid of the path taught by true scriptures and gurus,
such as sitting, lying down, withering the body, and reckless acts like mantras, yantras, and rituals at cremation grounds.
It should be understood that here [those who act] by force are being excluded. || 37 ||
Abandoning the lamp of the mind, those deluded ones who strive to achieve mastery over the mind by force seek to destroy darkness with collyrium. (38)
They bind the intoxicated lord of serpents with lotus fibers; or rather, they bind their own body, which is not far removed from the mind, to that very mind. (39)

The meaning is that the traditionalists consider those persons to be practitioners of *haṭha*— futilely exerting themselves— who, having abandoned the fourfold reasoning (*yukti*) characterized as previously described, endeavor to stabilize the mind and the body situated within the mind by means of some other method. || 39 ||
Those who seek to accomplish [their goals] by abandoning reason are known as "forceful" (haṭhas);
they go from fear to fear and pass from affliction to affliction.

Furthermore, because they have strayed from the path of the true scriptures, nothing but a succession of misfortunes results for them, rather than the conquest of the mind and so forth; thus he says: "Out of fear... (40).
Like wretched beings, they find no relief;
subsisting on fruits and shoots, they wander among the mountain peaks. (41)
Nirdhṛti means the perfect repose of fortitude; [they were like] unfortunate, sinful beings. || 41 ||
With minds utterly bewildered, those wretched ones were like frightened deer;
their delicate bodies were shattered and their limbs mangled. (42)
Their minds, agitated by waves, place no trust whatsoever, like a doe that has entered a village, or like water in a vessel made of a harmful substance.
In a situation that causes fear; or rather, the word division is *ahite* [and *bhayasthāne*]. || 43 ||

Like a blade of grass cast far away by falling into mountain rivers, one is carried off by the delusions of time spent in sacrifices, austerities, charity, pilgrimages, and the worship of deities. (44)

It is carried away—forcibly led far off by passion and the like; it possesses a nature that follows after objects of attachment. This refers even to the performance of sacrifices, gifts, and other such acts, which have many afflictions as their result, yield little fruit, and possess a doubtful outcome regarding liberation, rather than the practice of the samādhi called the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*), which has the certain attainment of liberation as its fruit.

He says "merely afflictions" (*kleśamātram*) for the purpose of praising the subject at hand, beginning with the words "time" (*kālam*). The syntactical connection is: "they spend a long time. || 44 ||
Those who have long been possessed by mental afflictions exhaust themselves like deer;
only some rare individuals, by the power of destiny, come to know the reality of the self. (45)
Burning with hundreds of the defects of suffering, they— whether conscious or unconscious—
come and go, impermanent among those in hell, heaven, and the human realm.
Because they are scorched by hundreds of sufferings and defects such as passion (*rāga*), they either do not perceive or they perceive [the truth].

They are impermanent and unstable in one place. Having assumed various bodily forms that cause falling and rising through the instrumental causes of diverse enjoyments in hell, heaven, and the human realm, they waste away and are tormented by death and other such miseries. (46)
Taking forms like falling and rising, they perish like balls;
from here they go to hell, from there to heaven, and right here as well. (47)
Right here they turn back and revolve through births as gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like. || 47 ||
They return again and again like ripples upon a lake;
therefore, O descendant of Raghu, abandon this false view.
This [state] characterized by the previously described haṭha and so forth. || 48 ||
Relying upon pure consciousness, become firm and free from passion.
Only the man of knowledge possesses happiness; only the man of knowledge truly lives;
only the man of knowledge is powerful. Therefore, be composed of knowledge.
Having relied upon [it] and having known [it]. || 49 ||
O Great-souled One, perceiving the supreme, primordial, and unique state of pure consciousness— which is devoid of all objects of perception and free from conceptualization—
abide within your very heart, free from mental construction, while performing your activity.
While acting, he attains the state of a non-doer, his glory arising from tranquility.

Free from conceptualization, free from mental constructs, free from latent impressions, and free from modification— remaining devoid of "kalanā," which is the mind's outward orientation, and being established in the habit of its cessation, abide in the Heart, in Brahman alone. Even while performing appropriate actions at the time of worldly emergence, you shall possess the glory arisen from the peace of non-attachment.

The meaning is: being thus endowed with the aforementioned perfection of qualities of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), he should remain having attained the state of non-agency (akartṛpada). || 50 ||

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of the Sequence for Dispelling Transmigration," in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation, in the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, a work of the Seers.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of the Sequence for Dispelling Saṃsāra," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Even with a slight degree of inquiry, there is restraint of one's own mind.
By whomsoever even a slight [act] has been performed, by him the fruit of birth has been attained.

In this [chapter], the state of equanimity is described, because of its invulnerability to sense objects when one is established in awakening through the virtues of mature discernment and dispassion. (1)

In this regard, he says "even slightly" (*manāk*) to show that even a very small amount of inquiry and restraint of the mind, by way of generating interest and setting one in motion, culminates gradually in liberation. By the phrase "the fruit of birth," it is implied that for one devoid of inquiry, birth itself is fruitless. || 1 ||
This subtle spark of reflection that flickers within the heart,
through the practice of yoga, spreads forth into a hundred branches.
He establishes its utility for the fruitfulness of that [inquiry] with the verse beginning "vicāra" and so forth: it is the pericarp, the sprout, of the wish-fulfilling tree of inquiry. || 2 ||
But when a man possesses even a slight degree of mature discernment preceded by dispassion,
the [pure] qualities enter him, just as birds enter a pure, full lake.
The qualities are those previously mentioned, such as tranquility (śama), self-restraint (dama), and so forth. "Egg-born" refers to birds and fish. (3)
Even vast manifestations of ignorance do not greatly affect the wise person who investigates correctly and perceives things as they truly are.
It is his nature to perceive the reality of the self as it truly is and according to its actual state. Even vast powers—
renowned for their excellence in both magnitude and intensity, extending even to the station of Hiraṇyagarbha, yet being the products of ignorance— neither reach him nor entice him.
What can sense-objects, as well as mental fluctuations, afflictions, or even physical diseases, do here to one whose mind is firmly established in right vision? (5)
What do they do, or what transformation do they produce? The sense is that this is because he has become the Self which is devoid of all modification. || 5 ||
Where, alas, have the Puṣkarāvarta clouds— filled with swirling winds and rosy with masses of lightning— been grasped by the fists of children? (6)
He confirms his inability to entice him with other verses, beginning with "Where" (kva):
"Where were the clouds of dissolution known as Puṣkarāvarta ever grasped by the fists of children? (6)
Where, by a charming woman, has the moon situated in the midst of the sky been bound with lovely caskets of gems, out of the delusion of mistaking them for beautiful blue lotuses?
Fearing that their own beauty might be eclipsed by the lovely blossoming blue lotuses, have the deluded bees bound the moon—
the cause of those flowers' blooming— within jewel caskets situated in the midst of the sky? || 7 ||
Where are those elephants, whose heads were adorned with lotuses from which swarms of bees emerged from their temples, now being tormented by gadflies as sweet as the sighs of charming women? (8)

From their temples and cheeks, swarms of bees emerge; such are the elephants, whose crests are adorned with lotuses due to the resemblance of those bees to lotuses, and who, being driven away even by the breaths of charming women, are [themselves] sweetened by those very breaths.

"By gentle ones" means by those lacking power; "by gnats" means where were they crushed or slain? [They were not even by] charming women, for it was through their breath that they were urged toward the killing of elephants—or rather, by those who are sweet and pleasing in their enthusiasm. (8)
Lions, their rows of excellent claws gleaming with the luster of pearls from elephant tusks, were violently crushed by deer while they were still intent on the fury of battle.
Whose rows of claws were radiant with the splendors—meaning the lusters—of pearls belonging to the elephants they themselves had torn apart. || 9 ||
Where are those hungry pythons, who, having scorched the towering forest trees with the essence of their spreading poison, have now been swallowed by agitated young frogs? 10.

The forest trees were scorched by drops of poison— consisting primarily of resin— emerging from those [beings] through which there was an outburst and accumulation of poison; or rather, they were such that their resin consisted of the very outbursts of half-dried poison repeatedly flowing from the corners of their mouths onto their own bodies, owing to their dark color and their towering height.

The regions are mostly filled with date palms whose branches have been scorched. In certain areas, there are creatures resembling trees that stand upright like trees and chirp like humans; these are a species of black python known for suddenly devouring humans and others who approach them under the mistaken impression that they are trees, by turning around and opening their gaping mouths.
By young frogs—that is, small frogs. || 10 ||

How can a wise man who has attained his livelihood, who knows what is to be known, and who possesses discernment, be overcome—alas!—by the bandits of the sense-objects, even though he is valiant? (11)
One who has attained the fourth, fifth, and subsequent stages is "valiant," being intent upon the conquest of the higher stages. || 11 ||
The enemies that are the sense-objects carry away the immature intellect, just as a fierce wind sweeps away a tender creeper whose stem has been severed. 12.

He says "vicāra... because obstacles may befall those whose minds are occasionally distracted even during the preceding stages, but not in the higher ones. Evil desires are unable to shatter even a small fragment of mature discernment, which is like a creeper whose stalk has been cut and its spreading tendrils severed. (12)
Like gentle breezes [shaking] a mountain that is immensely steadfast against the turbulence of an aeon. || 13 ||
The corrupt dispositions—the fluctuations of passion and the like—are not able to break or destroy it;
just as gentle breezes are unable to break the great and steadfast mountain Meru and others during the disturbances of an intermediate kalpa, so it is here. || 13 ||

The whirlwind of anxiety shakes the tree of the flower of deliberation only when it has not taken hold of the great seat [the reading *mahīpīṭha* is to be considered doubtful]; it does not shake that which is firmly established in a stable state.
He has not grasped that great seat which is the root-binding; his occasional reflections are merely like seasonal flowers, and have not yet borne fruit like such a tree.
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping, he whose mind is not composed of inquiry is said to be dead. (15)
For this very reason, with the intention that at the time of the interruption of inquiry, one is swallowed by the death of passion and other afflictions due to negligence, he says:
"When [the mind] goes... This is to be construed as: "Whenever [this occurs], for whomever [it happens], that person is dead.
Accordingly, it is said in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: "That is a loss; that is a great flaw; that is blindness and that is muteness."
"At whatever moment or for whatever brief duration one does not contemplate Śiva alone. (15)
"What might this world be? What might the body be?"—reflect thus constantly and gradually, either by yourself through the vision of the inner self or together with virtuous people. (16)
Either alone in a secluded place, or together with virtuous people such as teachers and fellow students. || 16 ||
By means of discernment, which swiftly dispels darkness, the supreme state—
the stainless reality— is perceived, just as by a radiant lamp.
He states the necessity of the fruit of reflection with the words "andhakāra... [etc.]: by that which removes the darkness of negligence.
Through knowledge, the destruction of all sufferings arises, just as darkness is dispelled by the sun through the play of its light. (18)
He states the two fruits of knowledge with the two verses beginning with "by knowledge" (jñānena). || 18 ||
When knowledge has become manifest, the object of knowledge arises clearly;
it is like the stainless light appearing upon the earth when the sun has risen. (19)
That illumination by which the reality of Brahman is awakened through scriptural inquiry is said to exist as if non-different from the object of knowledge. (20)
He states the definition of knowledge with the words "by which":
because it has the form of the knowable Brahman and because it consists in the sublation of difference, it exists as if non-different, being firmly established. || 20 ||
O dear one, the wise know that the self-knowledge arising from investigation is true knowledge; its object of knowledge exists within itself, just as sweetness exists within milk. (21)
A person who possesses the light of right knowledge becomes himself composed of the object of knowledge,
just as one who has drunk liquor remains perpetually intoxicated.
He is eternally composed of the knowable, abounding in the bliss of Brahman as it is being experienced. || 22 ||
The wise know that the supreme Brahman is the pure, equal essential nature;
by the mere attainment of knowledge, it becomes manifest of its own accord.
It becomes completely serene, with the mire of ignorance and its effects cast away. || 23 ||
Possessing knowledge and risen bliss, he does not sink anywhere;
liberated while living and free from attachment, he remains like a sovereign emperor who is himself the Self. || 24 ||
The sovereign emperor, his desires fulfilled as if they were his own self, [was thus]. || 24 ||
The wise man remains indifferent toward pleasant sounds such as those of the lute and the flute,
as well as the charming songs of a beloved woman, even when they are stained by the context of sensual enjoyment.

He elaborates upon his non-attachment toward those objects of existence that are desirable to people possessed by passion, beginning with the words "possessed of knowledge" (jñānavān) and so forth. The connection of all the locative case forms [in the following verses] with the distant phrase "he does not bind his attachment" (ratiṃ na nibadhnāti) is to be understood. || 25 ||
And amidst the humming of bees intoxicated by the spring's passion, and amidst the thundering of clouds over the flowers blooming at the onset of the rainy season; (26)
In flowers brought forth by the onset of the rainy season. || 26 ||
Amidst peacocks with their crests tossed in wild dance and uttering soft cries, and amidst fragments of thundering clouds and the warbling of cranes; (27)

In the sounds of the *kartarī* and other instruments ending with the *karānta*, in deep-sounding drums, and in the resonances of various stringed (*tata*), percussion (*anaddha*), and wind (*suṣira*) instruments; || 28 ||
Regarding the various types of musical instruments: those played by the hand include the *kartarī* (scissors), *sūcī* (needle), *śalākā* (pin), *sūtraka* (string), and *kaṇṭaka* (thorn);

those that are stretched with strings (*tantra*) include the *vīṇā* and similar lutes; those covered with skin (*carman*) include the *muraja* drum and similar drums; those that are hollow (*suṣira*) with internal cavities include the *vaṃśa* flute and similar wind instruments; and finally, the remaining type, which is solid (*ghana*), includes the *kāṃsya* gong, cymbals (*tāla*), and so forth—in the sounds of all these musical instruments.
O Rāma, he does not bind his attachment to certain things— neither to harsh nor to sweet sounds— just as the moon does not cling to lotuses.

The wise one [was skilled] in the rows of young plantain shoots, [or "in the streaks" according to another reading], and in the joyful sports of the vine-like limbs of the daughters of the gods and gandharvas. (30)

In that place, where there were rows of sprouts on young plantain trunks— [a grove] possessing such creepers as if they were the limbs and members of the daughters of the gods and Gandharvas— in the sports and pastimes [of those women],
or in the sports within the Nandana grove by means of those creeper-limbs. 30.
O Rāma, the wise one whose intellect is unattached does not form bonds even toward things within his own power; he finds no delight in touch, just as a swan finds none on desert lands.
The delight in touch and the desire for enjoyments. || 31 ||
One who possesses knowledge [discerns] among dates, wild dates, kadamba fruits, jackfruits, and so forth; among grapes, cucumbers, walnuts, bimba fruits, citrons, and jasmine flowers. (32)
Dates and so forth are varieties of fruit species. || 32 ||
In the realms of wine, honey, maireya, mādhvīka, and asava; and in curd, milk, ghee, inspissated milk, fresh butter, boiled rice, and so forth. || 33 ||
Madirā and the others are varieties of intoxicating liquor. Āmikṣā is the substance that has become solidified by pouring curd into heated milk. 33.
Among the six flavors, various kinds of foods to be licked and drunk, other fruits, roots, vegetables, and even meats; (34)
Regarding material things, namely meats. || 34 ||
With a form of contentment and an unattached intellect, the wise man does not become bound by any of these,
taking no pleasure in their enjoyment, just as one takes no pleasure in a mere fragment of his own body.
As if toward fragments of their own bodies, like pieces of their own flesh. || 35 ||
Possessing wisdom, he dwelt in the abodes of Yama, Varuṇa, Indra, Rudra, and the Sun,
as well as on the peaks of Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Sahya, and Dardura.
From the recitation of the sequence of the guardians of the directions, Rudra is Īśāna. || 36 ||
Upon nets of silk-like leaves, within the digits of the moon’s orb, and in groves of wish-fulfilling trees that delight with the splendor of their forms; (37)

The preceding phrase is an adjective for the ridges (*sānu*), describing them as having clusters of sprouts (*pallava-samūha*) with networks of leaves (*dala-jāla*) that are soft and glossy like silk (*kauśeya*). [They are] upon those ridges which are characterized by a playful splendor through the beauty of their bodies—that is, the perfection of their divine forms.
[These ridges are] upon walls of gems and gold, and consisting of pearls and jewels.
And [he was not captivated] by Tilottamā, Urvaśī, Rambhā, Menakā, or Aṅgalatā. || 38 ||
By the word "wall," its composite whole, namely the house, is indicated. || 38 ||
The illustrious one, whose intellect is unattached, does not desire to see anyone;
he is full in mind, dignified, silent, and immovable even toward his enemies. (39)
Immovable: unshakable by hatred and other such afflictions. || 39 ||
The wise man [should offer flowers] such as the kunda, mandāra, kahlāra, and kamala;
as well as the kumuda, utpala, punnāga, ketakī, aguru, and jāti.
Among the varieties of flowers such as the *kunda* and others. || 40 ||

In the *kadamba*, *cūta*, *jambū*, *āmra*, *kiṃśuka*, and *aśoka* trees; that is, among the species of trees such as the *kadamba*; and in the species of shrubs and creepers such as the *japā*. || 41 ||
And in sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, lac, and musk; and in saffron, water-rose, cloves, cardamom, kaṅkola, tagara, and so forth. || 42 ||
In the case of various body-unguents such as sandalwood and the like; *lākṣā* is the juice of lac. || 42 ||

With a single-pointed mind and equanimity, undisturbed even by the fragrance of wine, he does not fix his delight on the scent of any particular thing, just as a twice-born man [is indifferent] to the smell of liquor.

A twice-born one, possessing an even mind toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, does not fix his attachment upon them— just as he would have no delight in the intoxicating odors of liquor— and remains undisturbed by what is disagreeable.
He is not agitated even in the slightest by the gurgling roar of the ocean, the echoing resonance of a mountain, or the roar of lions, the kings of beasts.

Thus, he says "in the ocean," etc., to show that fear does not arise in him from sounds that are causes of fear: [he hears them] as echoes, i.e., as reverberations, which are sounds in the sky produced in space. || 44 ||
He does not fear even slightly the roar of the enemy's kettledrums, the rattling of war-drums, or the sound of the harshly drawn bow.
The *paṭaha* is a specific type of musical instrument known as the *āḍambara*. || 45 ||
He does not tremble even slightly at the trumpeting of rutting elephants, at the cries of Vetālas, or at the shrieks of Piśācas and Rākṣasas.
In the trumpeting roars of rutting elephants— the suffix *ap* being applied to the root *bṛṃh* according to the rule *gurośca halaḥ*—
in the clamorous cries of vetālas, in the shrieks of piśācas and rākṣasas, amidst lion-roars,
with the thundering sound of lightning, and with the crashing noise of mountains splitting asunder.
One who is perfectly absorbed in meditation is not shaken by the roar of Airāvaṇa. || 47 ||
By the roar of that Airāvaṇa, the elephant Airāvata. || 47 ||
Though subjected to the friction of the whirling saw, the slicing of the white sword,
and the falling of arrows and thunderbolts, it does not tremble from its own nature.
By the scraping and friction of the moving saw, he does not tremble—that is, he does not waver—from his own nature, which is characterized by abiding in his true form. || 48 ||
He finds neither joy in the groves nor does he fall into weariness;
he experiences neither distress in the deserts nor does he attain delight.
Even in arid wastes where the sands were like heaps of glowing embers,
there were patches of soft, verdant ground covered with scattered blossoms.

In those desert regions (dhanva), namely arid lands where the sands are level with the glowing embers produced by the removal of the purified ashes, and which are thus unbearable and like burning sand; [in such places]. || 50 ||
Upon sharp razor-edges and beds of fresh lotuses, on the heights of lofty mountains and within the depths of wells; (51)
In the depths, that is, in the lower regions within the belly of the well—that is, the interior of the well. || 51 ||
Upon sun-scorched rocks and upon tender women;
in prosperity and in fierce calamities; and during dalliances and in festivals. (52)
In the heat of the sun's rays, which are harsh, scorching, and hard, during amorous dalliances and sports. || 52 ||
Even while dwelling [in the world], he is neither agitated nor does he attain worldly joy;
with a mind eternally liberated, he remains as if constantly performing his duties. || 53 ||

The meaning is that a person who has become weary from performing tasks such as carrying a burden, like one who has laid down the burden, remains not inactive while experiencing the bliss of rest with a mind turned inward. || 53 ||
In the forest lands of hell where limbs are contracted by iron,
amidst endless showers of spears and javelins hurled at one another.
In the forest lands of hell brought about by the remnants of their past karma, their limbs were contracted by iron machines, just as in the case of Māṇḍavya. || 54 ||
He does not fear, nor does he succumb to helplessness, nor does he fall into dejection;
equanimous, with a composed mind, silent and steadfast, he stands like a mountain. (55)
Helplessness means agitation. || 55 ||
Having consumed even that which is impure, unwholesome, smeared with poison, or full of filth,
as well as that which is moist or decomposed, one digests it quickly as if it were delicious food.

"Filth and so forth" includes cow dung and the like. "Moist" means having become wet; "spoiled" means having lost its essence; and "refined" refers to prepared food, which is similar [to the former cases]. || 56 ||
One who knows reality possesses an unattached intellect and remains equanimous toward the tasting of images, reflections, medicinal extracts, milk, sugarcane juice, water, and food.

The meaning is that he becomes one whose mind is equal toward the tasting of the bimba fruit—which is renowned for instantly robbing away the intellect—as well as toward counter-poisons, poison-like decoctions, all kinds of astringent substances, milk, sugarcane juice, water, food, and boiled rice; that is, his mind remains the same regarding all sense objects. || 57 ||
With fermented liquors, wines, milk, blood, fat, and meat-broths, and with dry bones, grass, and the ends of hair, he neither rejoices nor becomes angry. (58)
Since those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) may also exist among Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and others, he speaks of them in their commonality, saying "by means of the Maireya [liquor]," etc. || 58 ||
He gazes with an equal look, one graced by serenity and sweetness, upon both the taker of his life and the giver of it. (59)
He speaks of his impartiality toward both enemy and friend with the words "of life" (jīvitasya). The phrase "the giver of life" is also to be connected [to the preceding]. || 59 ||
Regarding stable and unstable bodies, and objects both beautiful and unattractive,
he neither rejoices nor desponds, being always kindled by equanimity.

With a steady, long-enduring, and radiant equanimity toward stable bodies such as those of gods and unstable bodies such as those of mortals, and toward both pleasant and unpleasant objects of enjoyment. || 60 ||
Because the world's stability is devoid of any fixed foundation and its nature is unreliable, and because he has certainly known all that is to be known and his own mind is free from passion; (61)

Because the mind is free from passion (*nīrāgatva*) and because it has realized that which is to be known (*viditavedyatva*), it never grants its expansion toward the objects of the senses during the maintenance of the world. This is due to its established state of liberation, and because objects, being false, are unfit for attachment. It never grants [expansion] to anyone at all—the connection between these two [reasons] is thus. 61.
A virtuous person, with a mind free from the influence of the senses, never at any time allows any sense organ to have its way when it is directed toward its object.
Swallowing quickly the senses— those which do not know reality, which find no rest, which have not attained their true self, and which are unstable— just as lions devour a sprout. (63)
What then? He says that the senses devour him by means of two verses, beginning with "one who does not know reality. (63)
Being carried away in the ocean of existence, tossed by the waves of latent impressions,
and crying out in great distress, he is swallowed by the crocodiles of the senses.
The floods of conceptual constructions do not carry away one who reflects upon the state of the worthy, whose mind finds rest in the Self, just as torrents of water cannot sweep away a mountain.
He states that even conceptual constructions such as greed do not disturb one who knows the Self, beginning with the words "the investigator" (vicāriṇam) and so forth. || 65 ||
For those who have come to rest in the supreme state at the limit of all conceptual constructions,
and who have attained their true nature, even Mount Meru is regarded as no more than a blade of grass.
To those whose minds are expanded, the entire world is like a withered blade of grass, poison is indeed nectar, and a single moment is equal to a thousand kalpas.
Of those whose minds are expanded, whose consciousness is fully pervaded by the form of the Self. || 67 ||
Realizing that the world is nothing but pure consciousness, those of joyful intellect dwell with their minds filled with bliss,
for they perceive the entire universe existing within themselves as being composed of consciousness alone.
Because they perceive the entire world as being nothing other than the inward-facing innermost Self, they have the world contained within themselves. 68.
In this cage of worldly objects, which is but the vibration of pure consciousness, what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted? This is the view of those who know reality. (69)
O sinless one, abandon this other delusion that "all this is consciousness alone.
What could that vast body of consciousness ever abandon, and what could it desire? (70)
"Ihate" means he desires; that is to say, he grasps. || 70 ||
That future sprout and shoot which arises from the earth manifests as consciousness itself; likewise, it exists as the sprout of reality.

Because no longing for the past is seen, that collection of objects— which arises from the earth as mere sprouts and shoots, and which is desirable to the ignorant deer— whether present or yet to come,
all of it exists like a sprout of the principles (tattvas) such as space, manifesting exactly as consciousness itself through the vision of one who knows reality.
The meaning is that there are also other objects, such as sound, touch, and so forth. || 71 ||
That which exists neither at the beginning nor at the end does not exist even in the present;
that appearance of existence for consciousness, seen for a mere fraction of time, is an illusion. (72)

He states the reasoning for establishing the point already mentioned: "In the beginning," etc. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "but. The meaning is that when one perceives even a small fraction of time within the present state of consciousness, it is merely an illusion. || 72 ||
Thinking thus, abandon the intellect that pursues existence and non-existence;
having reached the end of all becoming, become one whose nature is the light of unattached consciousness. 73.

Having thus reflected upon the meaning that has been stated and having made it firm through contemplation, one should abandon the intellect that follows after the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence. || 73 ||
Whether performing action with the body, mind, intellect, or even with the senses alone, one who is free from attachment is not tainted, whether acting or not acting.
By means of [the senses] alone, which are free from the defect of attachment—whether acting at the time of emergence from meditation or not acting at the time of meditative absorption. || 74 ||
Even while acting with a mind free from attachment,
O mighty-armed one, he is not tainted by pleasures and pains, as if they were merely states of a mental wish.
Just as one is not stained by pleasure or pain whether the splendors of a kingdom of the mind and the states of one's desires have perished or not, so it is [in this case]. || 75 ||
Maintaining a mind free from attachment even while moving his slender limbs,
he is not stained by pleasures or pains, just as one is not affected during the states of mere mental longing.

By means of the vision of the Self as neither agent nor enjoyer, he makes his mind free from attachment; thus, even while acting and engaging in worldly affairs by means of the "limbs" of the body and other such instruments, [he remains unattached]. 76.
One whose mind is free from attachment does not see even while looking with his eyes;
this is experienced even by a child because his mind is fixed elsewhere.

The phrase "because the mind is fixed elsewhere" means that because the mind is distracted by something else, one does not see even while looking; this is experienced even by a child—and by the word "even," by all others as well. The intention is that the Vedic scripture also corroborates this point: "My mind was elsewhere, I did not see; my mind was elsewhere, I did not hear."
A living being whose mind is possessed by attachment does not see even while seeing;
he does not hear even while hearing, nor does he touch even while touching. (78)
Even while smelling, he does not smell; even while opening or closing his eyes, he does not do so;
and though he falls upon an object, he does not fall there by force.

Even while opening his eyes, he does not open them; even while closing them, he does not close them. In this way, although the group of organs of action falls upon their respective objects by the force of latent impressions (saṃskāra), he does not fall. || 79 ||
This is clearly experienced even by those of immature intellect and fools, though their minds are situated in their own homes while they themselves reside in another land. (80)

The meaning is that there is no dispute here, because this [Self] is properly and fully experienced— even by those who do not see it while looking at it— by fools, commoners, and those of immature intellect, as well as by children, animals, and the like, whose minds are elsewhere or who are situated in other places, even while they themselves remain in their own homes. || 80 ||
Attachment is the cause of worldly objects; attachment is the cause of saṃsāra.
Attachment is the cause of desires; attachment is the cause of calamities. (81)

And thus, with the intention that it is precisely the perception of objects preceded by attachment that is the cause of bondage, and not for one whose mind is unattached, he says: "Attachment... (verse 81).
They know that liberation is the renunciation of attachment; from the renunciation of attachment comes freedom from rebirth.
O sinless one, renounce attachment to all things and become liberated while living.

Liberation (*mokṣa*) is the cessation of the connection with the present body and so forth; non-birth (*ajanmatā*) is the prevention of bondage to future bodies and so forth—this is the distinction. || 82 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, you who are like an autumnal wind that dispels the mist of all doubts, tell me, O Lord, briefly: what is attachment (saṅga) called? 83.
Why is it neuter in the general sense? The question is clear. || 83 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That impure latent impression (vāsanā) which, through the presence or absence of objects, produces the modifications of joy and resentment, is called attachment (saṅga). || 84 ||

The meaning is that attachment (*saṅga*) is said to be the very latent impression of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which causes the modifications of joy and resentment when desirable or undesirable objects exist or do not exist, and when they are joined or separated. || 84 ||
For those whose bodies are liberated while living, their latent impression (vāsanā) becomes pure, free from joy and sorrow, and brings about the state of no further rebirth.
Know that the state called attachment to darkness persists as long as the body exists;
yet, whatever action is performed [with detachment], it truly does not lead to bondage again.
"As long as the body lasts," meaning until the exhaustion of the remainder of what has been commenced. || 86 ||

For those who are not liberated while living, who are wretched and dull-witted, there exists a binding latent impression (vāsanā) consisting of joy and dejection—[according to another reading: "consisting of both joy and dejection, as well as attachment and aversion"]. || 87 ||
That very [attachment] is called by the word "saṅga" (attachment), and it causes rebirth;
whatever action is performed by means of it leads solely to bondage. (88)
Thus, having abandoned attachment to form which causes the transformation of one's own self,
if you remain undisturbed, you are not tainted even while acting.
Undisturbed and established in his own nature. || 89 ||
If you do not undergo any change of state through joy, indignation, or despondency,
then, O Rāghava, you are free from passion, fear, and anger, and thus unattached.

Because there is an intention to express a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) within an internal distributive copulative compound (*itaretara-yoga-dvandva*), the dual number is used in the phrase "by joy and dejection" (*harṣāmarṣaviṣādābhyām*). "Otherness" (*anyatā*) means dissimilarity (*vairūpya*). || 90 ||
If you do not succumb to dejection through sufferings, nor rejoice in pleasures,
having cast off the helplessness of hope, then you are unattached, O Rāghava.
Helplessness due to one's own disposition means being under the control of another. || 91 ||
While dwelling amidst worldly affairs and in states of pleasure and pain, you do not abandon your perfect equanimity; therefore, O Raghava, you are unattached.
"If you do not abandon the equality with the existent—that is, the state of being one with Brahman"—this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*). || 92 ||
If the self were indeed perceivable, it would be perceived as equal within all that is perceived;
and since you follow whatever occurs as it happens, you are unattached, O Rāghava. (93)
The self has the nature of the mind. || 93 ||
O sinless one, having attained a firm state of liberation while living— characterized by non-attachment and effortless ease— you have become equanimous, self-abiding, and free from passion.
The noble one, whose mind is liberated while living, who is silent and has restrained the grasp of the senses,
remains free from feverish distress, devoid of pride, intoxication, and envy.
By whom the snares, characterized by the senses, which seize and bind, have been restrained. || 95 ||
For even amidst the entire multitude of objects, he whose inner being is undepressed maintains an equanimous disposition;
through mere activity, arising spontaneously and following its natural sequence—
He performs nothing else whatsoever. || 96 ||
Even though the entire multitude of objects— which serve as causes for the distraction of enjoyments— is always present in great abundance, his disposition remains equanimous;
whether internally or externally, he is undaunted, free from the wretchedness of longing or begging,
and performs nothing other than the mere activity inherent to his own caste and stage of life according to its natural order.
Whatever belongs to him, however it may have been begun, and whatever is his own duty according to the sequence,
that very thing he should perform with a mind entirely free from attachment and worldly ties.
Performing [this], he delights within his intellect without weariness. || 97 ||
Free from association, attachment to action, connection, and desire for results, he rejoices within himself by means of a mind devoid of those very things. || 97 ||
Furthermore, whether encountering adversity or great prosperity,
a person of great intelligence does not abandon their own innate nature, even when shaken by a gentle breeze.
Just as whiteness [is inherent in] the ocean consisting of milk. || 98 ||

It does not abandon its own inherent nature, which is established from before and consists of tranquility, self-restraint, serenity, equanimity, and so forth; just as the ocean of milk, though churned and stirred by Mount Mandara, does not lose its innate whiteness, so it is here. || 98 ||
Having attained either sovereignty or calamity, or the state of a crawling reptile or the lordship of the gods,
he remains without the arising of weariness and with joy extinguished.
He remains uniform in nature amidst both decline and rise, like the moon. || 99 ||

"Calamity" refers to poverty and the like; "the state of a reptile" refers to birth in the womb of a *ḍuṇḍubha* snake or similar creatures. "Arising of distress" and "cessation of joy" are adjectives modifying the action of remaining [in that state]. "During the waning and waxing of the digits" refers to the times of increase and decrease of the lunar phases, or the times of their rising and setting. || 99 ||

With undaunted courage, investigate the self as one whose agitation has been cast out, whose sense of duality has been discarded, and whose various beautiful appearances resulting from diverse fruits have been stilled.
Just as Bhava is intent upon the fulfillment of the highest purpose. || 100 ||

Since the means for attaining the bliss of *jīvanmukti* characterized as described above is self-inquiry alone, accompanied by the practice of exhausting the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion, hatred, and duality, he concludes by instructing Rāma on that very point: "With [all] dispelled," etc.
*Saṃrambha* means anger. All three are adverbs. By which inquiry—namely, by what [inquiry]—...
The meaning is: "The supreme task must necessarily be accomplished; you are devoted to that which is the final human goal—reflect in such a manner. || 100 ||
With an intellect kindled by the purity of the play of the expansion described therein,
one should take refuge in the stainless state free from fever; thus, through this awakened mind, one is no longer bound here by the fetters of rebirth.
You are bound by the perception of a self that you have acquired. || 101 ||

By that intellect— which is kindled by its capacity to burn away ignorance and its effects, and which is likewise characterized by having attained the true nature of the Self through the purification resulting from the destruction of all latent impressions (vāsanās) via the play of Samādhi whose expansion has been awakened by such inquiry— one becomes free from the fever [of worldly existence]. This is achieved by means of that intellect which perceives the visible world as a reality that must necessarily be seen.

Take hold of and dwell upon that supreme state, whose nature is freedom from suffering and unsurpassed bliss. To ward off the suspicion that this might be a mere recurrence of past experience, he says: "once again here.
Therefore, because all evils—including ignorance and its effects—are pacified solely through the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), it is eternal and unsurpassed.
Thus it is established that [the Self] is grounded in the essential nature of Nanda. || 101 ||

Thus ends the ninety-third canto, titled "The Vision of Equality," in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* (Section on Quiescence) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, spoken by the Divine Messenger, and consisting of thirty-two thousand verses. || 93 ||
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Vision of Equality," in the section on Quiescence within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.

Thus ends the Chapter on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*, composed by the venerable monk named Śrīmad Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī, the preeminent teacher among the wandering mendicants of the supreme order (*paramahaṃsaparivrājakācāryavarya*), the illustrious Sarvajñasarasvatī.
Complete.
Thus ends this chapter on tranquility.
